subject.title: System design interview questions, beginner to advanced
subject.description: System design from the ground up, through the questions interviews actually ask. It starts with how networks, storage and caches work, builds up through scaling, consistency, messaging and reliability, and then answers the classic design questions (a URL shortener, a pastebin, a chat service, a social feed, a video service, a ride-hailing service, a web crawler) step by step: requirements, estimates, data model, interfaces, components and bottlenecks. Every fact comes from Wikipedia, the IETF's RFCs, original research papers or the openly licensed guides credited on each page.

How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP
How the big distributed data systems work
Event-driven architecture, event sourcing and CQRS

openers.what-system-design-is-and-how-interviews: System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements. This chapter introduces the field, the interview built around it, and the vocabulary of requirements and architecture that the rest of the course leans on. A functional requirement says what a system is supposed to accomplish, a non-functional one says how it should operate, and software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about both. The interview that tests all of this has no single expected answer.
openers.found: Before anyone draws a box on a whiteboard, a design needs requirements to satisfy. This part gives you the language to work from them: what system design is, how an interview tests it, and the standard components, six broad categories of them, that designs are assembled from. It separates the behavior a system is supposed to accomplish from the overall properties, such as availability or performance, by which its operation is judged. Along the way come eight problems that recur in large-scale production systems, each with a standard remedy, and the practices that keep an architecture honest as it evolves.
openers.latency-throughput-and-back-of-the-envel: Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response. Its companions are bandwidth, the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path, and throughput, the rate at which messages are successfully delivered. Rough latencies of common operations, from cache reads taking nanoseconds to a transatlantic packet taking 100 ms, let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow. Tail latency is measured at a high percentile, such as the 95th, 99th or 99.9th, rather than as an average. This chapter also gives you the units for sizing data and the nine metrics used to judge a website's performance.
openers.how-computers-talk-ip-tcp-and-udp: A client asks and a server answers, but between them the data passes down a stack of layers, and this chapter takes that stack apart. The OSI model splits network communication into seven abstract layers, and the TCP/IP model organizes the Internet's protocols into four. As data is sent, each layer nests it inside a packet with a header, a step called encapsulation. The transport layer carries it from an application on one host to an application on another: TCP offers reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes after a three-way handshake, while UDP just sends messages as datagrams to other hosts on an IP network. Underneath both, IP gives each device a numerical address so it can be found, and it relays datagrams across network boundaries.
openers.the-domain-name-system: Computers find each other by number, but people use names, and the Domain Name System translates one into the other. It replaced HOSTS.TXT, a single central file that grew slow and unwieldy with ARPANET, and is now a hierarchical, distributed tree of labels. This chapter covers what a domain publishes in its resource records, from addresses and aliases to mail servers, and who hands out the right to use a name. It also follows the queries themselves, sent over UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports. Time to live limits how long answers are kept, and anycast lets servers in many locations share one address.
openers.http-https-and-tls: A browser asks and a server answers, and that exchange is the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. HTTP is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol, so each request can be understood on its own. This chapter follows it from the shape of a message, through its methods and status codes, to the cookies that give it a memory. It then turns to the encryption that lets the same conversation stay private: public keys, shared secret keys and the certificates that say who owns a key.
openers.blocks: Every large system is assembled from smaller parts that each do one job well. This part gathers those building blocks, and it begins with the smallest: algorithms and data structures. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, a hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share one, and a Bloom filter tests whether an element is in a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives. Trees such as the quadtree, k-d tree and trie, and curves such as the Z-order and Hilbert curves, organize space and strings so they can be searched. Later chapters build on them with load balancing, proxies, caching and storage.
openers.algorithms-behind-the-systems: Behind the big boxes in a system diagram sit small ideas from computer science. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, and a hash collision is what happens when two distinct pieces of data share one. Base64 lets binary data travel over channels that carry only text, and MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit value. The chapter then turns to space and strings: the quadtree, the k-d tree and the trie, curves such as the Z-order and the Hilbert curve, and geohash, which encodes latitude and longitude as a short string. Along the way it meets the Bloom filter, which tests set membership with false positives but never false negatives, and similarity hashing, which shows when data is similar but not identical.
openers.load-balancing: Once one server cannot carry the traffic, you add more servers, and then something has to decide who gets each request. Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online. This chapter looks at where that decision can be made, in the DNS, in the client or in a dedicated balancer, and at the rules for making it, from taking turns to picking the least busy server. It also covers keeping a user's session together, whether a balancer reads addresses or whole requests, and what happens when a server, or the balancer itself, fails.
openers.proxies-and-api-gateways: A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it. It can face two ways: a forward proxy sits in front of a group of client machines and speaks to the Internet for them, while a reverse proxy appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests on. Add a single entry point that enforces security and throttling policies before passing requests to backend services, and you have an API gateway. This chapter also meets caching and transparent proxies, the Backend For Frontend pattern, and two widely used tools, HAProxy and nginx.
openers.caching: The fastest way to answer a request is to have answered it already, and that single trick runs through nearly every fast system. A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data so that future requests for it can be served faster. This chapter starts inside the processor and the operating system, then moves out to the caches between a web service and its data. It asks how often an item is found, what to discard when the cache is full and when a write reaches the data behind it.
openers.content-delivery-networks: A content delivery network is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them. The origin server holds the original content, and the many edge servers spread around the world cache it and serve users nearby. A request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it. This chapter follows that idea through the ways content reaches an edge, how requests find the right server and the variants built by content owners and telecommunications providers.
openers.choosing-a-database: Sooner or later every design in this course has to say where its data lives. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to it. This chapter starts with the relational database, which stores data in tables of rows and columns, and with NoSQL, which stores and retrieves it differently, as key-value pairs, documents or graphs. It also meets the transaction, a unit of work that the four ACID properties are meant to protect against errors, power failures and other mishaps. By the end you will be able to match a kind of database to the workload it suits.
openers.indexes-normalization-and-storage-engine: A database is only as fast as the structure it uses to find a row, and only as trustworthy as the way its tables are laid out. This chapter covers both. Normalization structures a relational database to reduce redundancy and improve integrity, and the anomalies it prevents are the side effects of getting that wrong. An index is a data structure that finds rows quickly at the cost of extra writes and storage, and it comes in many shapes: hash tables, B-trees, inverted indexes and R-trees. Underneath sits the storage engine, the part of the database responsible for putting data into permanent storage, with a write-ahead log recording changes before they reach the data.
openers.storage-systems: Every system you design eventually answers two questions: where does the data live, and what happens when the power goes out? The answer starts with a split in memory itself, because volatile memory needs power to keep its contents while non-volatile memory retains them after power is removed. The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage. Two kinds of drive hold data for the long term: hard disk drives, which store it magnetically on rapidly rotating platters, and solid-state drives, which use integrated circuits, typically NAND flash. This chapter follows both, shows how they fail and connect, and sees how a database builds the ACID guarantee of {{ref:sysd-blocks-210}} on them before it moves up to block storage and the layers built on it.
openers.scale: The more people use a system, the more work it has to do. Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work, and this part of the course begins with it. Beside it stands high availability, which aims to keep a system performing at an agreed level, usually uptime, for longer than normal. The tools range from adding nodes, or adding resources to a single node, to duplicating critical components as redundancy, to letting servers come and go automatically with the load. Each tool has limits, because a formula such as Amdahl's law caps how far a task can speed up as resources are added.
openers.scalability-and-availability: Two questions run through this chapter: how does a system grow, and how does it stay up? The answers start with two definitions. Scalability is the capacity to handle a growing amount of work, and high availability aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance for a higher than normal period. From there the chapter covers the strategies for scaling, the limits that Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law place on them, and the redundancy that keeps a system running when parts fail. It also shows how to measure reliability, starting with the mean time between failures, the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation.
openers.replication: Anything that exists only once can stop the whole system when it breaks. Replication answers that by maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. When one copy fails, failover lets a standby or replica take over so the system keeps operating. The hard part is writes: in single-leader replication one instance handles them all, while in multi-master replication any member can update, so conflicting changes must be prevented or resolved. Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, asynchronous replication does not, and a quorum is the minimum number of votes needed before an operation may proceed.
openers.sharding-and-partitioning: Which piece of the data lives where? That one question drives this chapter. A partition is a division of a logical database into distinct, independent parts, and a shard is a horizontal partition that may sit on its own database server. The rules for assigning data range from key ranges, like the volumes of an encyclopedia, to hash functions that turn skewed data into a uniform distribution, with refinements such as consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing. Sharding also has a price: skew and hot spots, and more complexity in the infrastructure and the application code.
openers.the-cap-theorem-and-consistency: A consistency model is a contract between the programmer and a system: follow the rules for operations, and reads, writes and updates behave predictably. This chapter asks how strong that contract can be when the network divides into relatively independent subnets, which is what a network partition is. The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, says a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance. From there the chapter covers eventual consistency, PACELC, which adds latency to the choice, the CP, AP and CA labels for databases, and why the theorem is so often misunderstood. It ends with the replication protocols, primary-backup, active and quorum-based, that put these choices into practice.
openers.consensus-ordering-and-distributed-trans: A single database can promise that a transaction is all-or-nothing. Once the data lives on several machines, that promise has to be rebuilt from messages between them, and the machines can fail or disagree about the time. This chapter starts with the distributed transaction and the voting protocol that completes one. It then turns to how machines order events without a shared clock, how they notice that a peer has died, and how a group of them can agree on a single value even when some fail. That agreement problem is the foundation for distributed locks, leader election and replicated state machines.
openers.how-the-big-distributed-data-systems-wor: Google built a distributed file system for large clusters of commodity hardware, a storage system for structured data across thousands of commodity servers, and a SQL database that is synchronously replicated around the world. Amazon built a highly available key-value store to keep persistent state reliable while components fail all the time, and AWS now sells a managed NoSQL service. Open-source projects followed: Cassandra, which handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers with no single point of failure, and Hadoop and HBase, built around HDFS or modeled after Google's storage system. This chapter opens each of them up. Each one is an answer to the same question: how do you keep working when machines fail?
openers.msg: Ask a web server for a page and you wait for the reply. That is synchronous communication, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. This part begins with the second kind. A queue holds messages until the receiver takes them, and an intermediary program translates, stores, routes and delivers them between systems. With such a buffer between producers and consumers, a system can scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures.
openers.message-queues-and-brokers: A queue is a widely used data structure: it takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other. Turn it into a software component between programs and it becomes a place where messages wait until the receiver is ready. This chapter follows that idea from the common variants of the queue to the intermediary programs, open protocols and open-source software built around it. One question keeps returning along the way: how many times does a message reach its consumer, at most once, at least once, or exactly once?
openers.event-streaming-and-kafka: Some messaging systems keep every message instead of discarding it after delivery. Apache Kafka does this: it stores messages in a durable log, so many consumers can read them. This chapter starts with jobs that run in an automated and unattended way, then moves to treating streams of events as the central input and output of computation. Along the way it looks at how Kafka organizes its data and how it can still lose messages, at engines that process streams, and at ways of copying database changes into other systems.
openers.event-driven-architecture-event-sourcing: Instead of one part of a system calling another and waiting for an answer, parts can announce that something happened and let others react. That is event-driven architecture: components communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously. This chapter follows the idea outward. It covers storing the full series of actions as the source of truth, and splitting commands that change state from queries that only read it. It also looks at how to wire such a system with or without one orchestrator, what an event carries, and how consumers and events fail.
openers.monoliths-microservices-and-service-disc: An application can be one self-contained unit that performs every step of a business function, or a collection of small, loosely coupled services that can be deployed and scaled independently. This chapter walks that range, from the monolith and the layers of an N-tier design to microservices and the older service-oriented architecture. Splitting an application creates new problems. Clients must find service instances whose locations change, a proxy paired with each service can handle their communication, and a distributed trace can track one request through all the services that fulfil it. The chapter also covers how services collaborate, through shared rules for exchanging messages or through a central coordinator.
openers.apis-rest-graphql-and-grpc: An API is the doorway through which one piece of software offers a service to another. REST draws its constraints from the architecture of the Web, GraphQL gives clients exactly the data they request and no more, and gRPC lets a program call a procedure on another computer as if it were local. Under all three lies serialization, which turns a data structure into a format that can be stored or sent and rebuilt later. The chapter also covers SOAP and the craft of documenting, versioning and changing an API without breaking the clients that depend on it.
openers.real-time-communication: A client that wants fresh information has several options. Polling means repeatedly checking a service for its status, and long polling has the server hold the request open until new information is available or a timeout is reached. Push technology turns the exchange around, so the server rather than the client starts it, as in push notifications and in web push, which delivers real-time events such as incoming calls or messages over HTTP/2. Or the browser and server can cooperate over WebSocket, a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection that begins with an HTTP Upgrade request and a 101 response, then exchanges frames and closes with its own handshake. A notification system adds the machinery to validate, schedule and deliver messages through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.
openers.reliab: The largest incidents are usually caused by something very small. A minor error starts a snowball effect that keeps building, and suddenly everything is down. This part of the course is about the designs that stop the snowball. It starts with the failure that grows on its own, where the loss of one or a few parts overloads the rest and feeds itself through positive feedback. Then come the defenses: spare components that keep a service running while some parts are faulty, limits on how much traffic a server accepts, and the algorithms that count it.
openers.resilience-circuit-breakers-rate-limitin: Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit, and it is the first of the defenses in this chapter. Around it sit the ways a system keeps operating while some components are faulty, and the ways one failure turns into many. Next come the controls that stop the spread: a server that drops some traffic as it approaches overload, a deadline that tells the caller when to give up, and a client that slows itself before the backend must refuse it. The chapter then turns to the bucket algorithms that count traffic and to retries, and it ends with two protections around them: {{ref:sysd-reliab-067}} and {{ref:sysd-reliab-071}}.
openers.service-levels-and-disaster-recovery: To a user, lost data, corrupted data and a service that stays unavailable for too long all look the same. This chapter is about preventing that and about recovering when it happens. It begins with the promises a provider makes, measured by indicators, set as objectives and written into agreements. It then turns to disaster recovery, the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other disruption, and to the copies of data that make recovery possible. Along the way come the layers that protect data and the real-time numbers that say when a system is in trouble.
openers.containers-orchestration-and-deployment: A container packages an application with its dependencies so that it runs the same in any environment, and much of this chapter grows from that idea. First come the Linux kernel features that isolate containers, from chroot to namespaces and cgroups, which control what a process can see and how much of the system it can use. Next come Docker, with its images and registries, and Kubernetes, which orchestrates containers so that one that goes down is replaced by another without downtime. Along the way you will meet nodes, Pods and the probes the kubelet runs to learn whether a container is healthy.
openers.q: The rest of the course is a set of design questions, the kind an interviewer asks and a good answer takes apart piece by piece. The first is a URL shortener, which must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original, and stay available with minimal latency. A pastebin stores plain text such as source code snippets or error logs and shares it by link, which makes it a close cousin. After that comes instant messaging, which sends messages in real time between two or more parties, and which can be built so that only the sender and the intended recipients can read them. Each question gathers the ideas it needs before it walks through a full answer.
openers.authentication-and-security: Every request that reaches a system raises two questions: who is asking, and what may they do. This chapter takes both in turn. It starts with authentication, the act of proving an assertion such as a user's identity, and the three kinds of evidence behind it: something the user knows, has or is. It then turns to authorization, which specifies rights to access resources, and to OAuth 2.0, which lets a user grant an application consented access to another site without sharing credentials. Along the way come the attacks that shape the defenses, such as cross-site scripting, and the details that matter, such as the random data called a salt that goes into password hashing.
openers.design-a-url-shortener: A short link does one job: it makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, through a redirect. That convenience has costs, because short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot (links that stop working) and privacy risks. This chapter looks at how a shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key built from letters and digits, and at Base62, which writes numbers with 62 symbols. It also covers why some providers let links expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses. It ends with a full design that must create unique aliases, redirect visitors and stay highly available with minimal latency.
openers.design-pastebin: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link. In the design question, a user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL. Pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration, and the service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available. A reader who has just met the URL shortener will find the problem familiar.
openers.design-a-chat-service-like-whatsapp: A chat message looks simple: you type, someone else reads. Underneath, the service must deliver it in real time, hold it when the recipient cannot be reached, and keep it private from everyone except the two ends. This chapter starts with instant messaging itself, then covers store and forward, end-to-end encryption and the Signal Protocol, and the argument over who should be able to read messages. It ends with two designs: a worked answer to the WhatsApp interview question, and a look at how WhatsApp itself delivers messages.
openers.design-a-social-feed-like-twitter: A social feed has one job: out of everything posted, show each reader the posts worth reading, and show them fast. That takes two decisions. The first is how a new post reaches its followers' feeds, by push, by pull or by a mix of both, and the second is how the posts in a feed are scored so the most relevant appear first. The chapter begins with two building blocks, the Apache Lucene search library and the fan-out pattern, then covers feed models, ranking, EdgeRank and trending topics. It closes with the worked Twitter design, Twitter's technology stack and a pipeline that narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set.
openers.design-a-video-streaming-service-like-ne: A video service sends a stream of packets that plays as it arrives, to viewers on very different devices and connections. This chapter follows a video from upload to screen. It starts with streaming itself and the codecs that compress video, then covers transcoding, adaptive bitrate streaming and its two main protocols, HTTP Live Streaming and MPEG-DASH. It also looks at the ways a stream reaches many viewers, from unicast copies to CDN servers, and adds recommendations and geo-blocking. It closes with a worked Netflix design and three case studies: Netflix's technology stack, YouTube's dedicated transcoding chip and Netflix Open Connect.
openers.design-a-ride-hailing-service-like-uber: Open a ride-hailing app and the screen shows nearby cabs, an ETA and a price. This chapter takes that screen apart. It starts with nearest neighbor search, the problem of finding the point closest to a query point, and the proximity service that applies it to places within a radius. It adds dynamic pricing, then ends with the worked Uber design and a look at Uber's technology stack.
openers.design-a-web-crawler: A web crawler visits the Web page by page, following links from a list of starting addresses, so that a search engine has something to index. The web is too large to fetch in full, so a crawler needs rules for what to download, when to return and how to avoid overloading the sites it visits. This chapter covers those rules, the robots.txt standard that sites use to set limits, and what happens to the pages afterward: indexing, ranking with PageRank and measuring how similar two pages are. It closes with a worked design for a crawler and the search engine behind it.
openers.design-a-personal-finance-app-like-mint: A personal finance app has four jobs: connect a financial account, extract its transactions, categorize them, and analyze monthly spending by category. Users can override a category by hand, but nothing is re-categorized automatically. Two building blocks come first in this chapter. A heap is a tree in which the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root, and open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through APIs. Then the worked design builds the whole service.
openers.design-a-cache-for-the-most-recent-searc: What happens when a search request finds its answer already in the cache, and what happens when it does not? The service in this chapter must handle both, and it must stay highly available. The chapter first introduces a data structure, the doubly linked list, whose nodes each hold a data field plus links to the previous and the next node. Then it puts that structure to work in the design of a cache for recent search queries.
openers.design-a-sales-rank-by-category: Which products sold best this past week, in each category? This service calculates the answer and lets users view it, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope. The chapter is a single worked design.
openers.design-the-data-structures-for-a-social: A social network is a graph, and the interview question is how to search it. A social graph represents social relations between entities, and it can be stored as an adjacency matrix, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent, or as an adjacency list that stores an unordered list of neighbors for each vertex. Breadth-first search explores it level by level, the shortest path problem asks for the path with the smallest total edge weight, and bidirectional search runs one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal. The folk idea of six degrees of separation says a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people. The worked design lets a user search for someone and see the shortest path to that person.
openers.scale-a-system-to-millions-of-users-on-a: A website that starts on one server has to grow without falling over. This chapter follows a simplified e-commerce site as it evolves from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture. Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. The chapter also introduces the virtual private cloud, an on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others. AWS-specific details are not required, since the principles apply outside AWS too.
openers.design-gmail: Sending an email looks like one act, but it is a relay race between programs. SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail, and a message passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role. The message itself is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, and MIME extends the format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments. This chapter follows mail through the SMTP transaction, queues and retries, bounce messages and the MX record that names a domain's mail server. It ends with retrieval by POP and with spam, the unsolicited bulk mail that every mail design must handle.
openers.design-google-maps: As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world. A simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation. Navigation leans on shortest-path algorithms, from Dijkstra's algorithm and the A* search to contraction hierarchies, which precompute shortcuts so a query can skip unimportant vertices. Rendering rests on map tiles, a world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small blocks, in Web Mercator, the standard projection for web mapping. Geocoding, which turns an address into a latitude and longitude pair, connects the two.
openers.design-a-stock-exchange: A stock exchange records the interest of buyers and sellers in an order book, and a matching engine uses that book to decide which orders can be executed. Traders place orders of standard types such as market, limit and stop. The aim is microsecond latency, reached by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. This chapter covers the parts, from FIX, the electronic protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions, and market data to processor affinity and non-blocking algorithms. Then it assembles them in one design.
openers.design-google-docs: Two people can edit the same document at once, on different devices, and the system must merge their edits automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. This chapter starts with collaborative real-time editing and the concurrency control that groupware needs. Then it turns to operational transformation, a technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits. The worked design puts these ideas into one service.
openers.design-a-payment-system: Double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems a payment system can have, so it must execute each payment order exactly once. This chapter builds toward that demand from the ground up. It starts with the bookkeeping method that keeps the books balanced and with the systems that settle financial transactions by transferring monetary value. It then follows a card payment through the third-party companies, the payment service provider and the gateway, that let businesses accept electronic payments. It ends with the process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match, and with a full design that ties it all together.
openers.design-a-notification-system: A notification system has to reach people on very different kinds of devices and networks. Firebase Cloud Messaging, or FCM, is a cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps. Apple's push notification service lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices, and the Short Message Service carries short text messages over cellular networks. At the center of the design sits a notification service that consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka, and forwards each request to FCM or Apple's service according to the device platform.
openers.design-a-permission-system: A permission system answers one question: may this subject perform this operation on this resource? Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done, and it is itself a security mechanism that must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides. The models in this chapter answer the question in different ways: a list of permissions attached to a resource, roles and privileges, the discretion of an object's owner, the evaluation of attributes, relationships between subjects and resources, or a policy set centrally. Around them sit the points that retrieve, evaluate and enforce a policy, the standards that describe them, and the requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations.

reviews.what-system-design-is-and-how-interviews: System design defines a system's architecture, interfaces and data so that it satisfies its requirements, and the interview that tests it has no single expected answer. Functional requirements say what the system is supposed to accomplish, non-functional ones say how it is supposed to be, and requirements engineering is the work of finding and managing both before architecture answers with a how. Architecture is the set of structures a team reasons with, and decision records, four core activities and watchfulness about erosion keep it honest as the system evolves. In the interview these ideas become a sequence, from clarifying requirements and estimating capacity to addressing scale and reliability, with trade-offs presented humbly along the way.
reviews.latency-throughput-and-back-of-the-envel: Latency and throughput answer different questions: latency is how long one operation takes, throughput is how many complete per unit of time, and bandwidth is the ceiling that throughput never reaches. Network latency adds propagation, queuing and processing delays, which is why round-trip time and the rough latency numbers matter, and why tail latency at a high percentile shows what an average hides. Those numbers, together with the units for data sizes, feed back-of-the-envelope estimates, and Little's law links arrival rate, time in the system and the number inside. Every technique for reducing latency, from indexes to compression, is a trade-off, as every design is.
reviews.how-computers-talk-ip-tcp-and-udp: Data is wrapped in headers layer by layer, and IP, with its addresses and subnets, relays the resulting packets across network boundaries with only best-effort delivery. Reliability is left to the hosts at the ends, and TCP supplies it with sequence numbers, acknowledgments, windows, timers and handshakes that open and close each connection. UDP keeps the datagram and drops those guarantees, so choosing between them comes down to whether late data is worse than lost data. QUIC rebuilds reliability on top of UDP, so one lost packet no longer stalls every stream. Around them, DHCP hands out addresses, ARP finds hardware addresses and ICMP reports errors.
reviews.the-domain-name-system: DNS trades instant consistency for availability and speed. The tree of names is cut into zones, each delegated to authoritative servers that secondaries keep in step by zone transfer. Every answer carries a TTL, and caches keep most lookups from having to start at a root server. The openness that lets this scale, with unsigned and unencrypted answers, is also its weakness, and DNSSEC answers part of it with a chain of trust and managed keys. Round-robin DNS, anycast and split-horizon answers show how the same system is bent to spread load and to serve different clients differently.
reviews.http-https-and-tls: HTTP keeps no memory of its own, which is why cookies and sessions are built on top of it. Its methods, status codes and cache rules mean the same in every version, while the plumbing changed from one connection per resource to multiplexed streams in {{ref:sysd-found-040}} and QUIC over UDP in HTTP/3. Security arrived as a layer underneath: {{ref:sysd-found-049}} uses public-key cryptography and certificates to agree on a symmetric session key, and that turns HTTP into HTTPS. Its weak points are the ones the chapter kept returning to: a compromised certificate authority, a first visit before HSTS, and any intermediary that sits on the path.
reviews.algorithms-behind-the-systems: Hash functions turn up almost everywhere in this chapter. They index data, they sit inside Bloom filters, Merkle trees, count-min sketches and HyperLogLog, and they build name-based UUIDs. Because collisions are certain, the structures built on them either tolerate collisions, as the Bloom filter does with false positives, or maximize them on purpose, as similarity hashing does. The second thread is space: quadtrees, k-d trees, the Z-order and Hilbert curves, and geohash all turn locations into something that can be searched, and the limits show up near borders for geohash and in many dimensions for the k-d tree. The third thread is naming, from UUID versions to Snowflake IDs, which trade sortability, size and coordination against one another.
reviews.load-balancing: Every balancer answers one question, which server gets this request, and the answers differ in where they run and what they know. Round robin is static, ignoring the system's state, while dynamic methods such as least connections and master-worker take each node's current load into account. Layer 4 balancers route on addresses and ports, layer 7 balancers on content, and either can be hardware, software or a cloud service. Health checks, spare capacity and balancers in pairs keep a failure from taking the service down. Session state kept in a shared store or in the client frees the balancer to send a user to any server.
reviews.proxies-and-api-gateways: This chapter is about things that stand between a client and a server. A forward proxy stands in for clients, a reverse proxy for servers, and a transparent proxy does it without the client choosing. A reverse proxy can balance load, terminate TLS and cache, and an API gateway adds identity checks, rate limits and routing to the right service. HAProxy and nginx are two real tools that do much of this, while the Backend For Frontend pattern gives each interface its own backend. The price of the single door is a single risk, so the choice among a reverse proxy, an API gateway and a load balancer depends on the job at hand.
reviews.caching: Every idea in this chapter grows out of one bet, that recently used data will be used again, and locality of reference is why it usually pays. The hit ratio measures how often the bet wins, and eviction policies such as LRU and LFU decide what a full cache forgets. Write policies, time to live and invalidation decide how a cache and the data behind it stay in step. Distributed caches such as Redis and Memcached carry the idea across machines, and stampedes and penetration show what happens when the bet fails at scale. The weather case shows how much one well-chosen cache key can save.
reviews.content-delivery-networks: A CDN moves content close to users by keeping copies on many edge servers while the origin server keeps the original. A request is answered from the edge's cache, or the edge fetches from the origin, and push and pull designs differ in who fills that cache. Request routing, from DNS to anycast and end-user mapping, picks which server answers, and a provider can combine several CDNs to avoid relying on one. Private, telco, virtual, image and peer-to-peer CDNs are variations on the same idea, built by different owners for different goals. Edge computing carries it from content to computation, and the same reach brings DDoS protection along with script-injection and privacy risks that Subresource Integrity helps to answer.
reviews.choosing-a-database: A database is an organized collection of data, and the relational kind keeps it in tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, queried with SQL and protected by ACID transactions. NoSQL databases, in key-value, document, wide-column and graph form, give up some of that for horizontal scaling and looser BASE guarantees. Around the transaction grew a ladder of isolation levels, with locking and multiversion methods to enforce them and write skew to show what a level can still miss. Workloads then pull the choices apart again, from OLTP systems feeding warehouses to specialized stores for text, vectors, locations and time series. Singh's advice runs through all of it: weigh the requirements, because SQL against NoSQL and ACID against BASE are trade-offs, not contests.
reviews.indexes-normalization-and-storage-engine: Two questions run through this chapter: where each fact lives, and how fast it can be found. Normalization stores each fact once and removes the anomalies that repeated data causes, while denormalization gives some of that back on purpose to make reads faster. Indexes buy fast reads with slower writes and extra storage, and the structure sets the terms: B-trees and their variants keep disk reads few, while LSM trees absorb writes in memory and merge them later. Hash tables and skip lists serve in-memory lookups, and inverted indexes, bitmap indexes and R-trees fit text, repeated values and space. Beneath all of them the storage engine does the writing, and a write-ahead log means a crash does not lose a committed change.
reviews.storage-systems: Storage is a trade between speed, cost and staying power: volatile memory is fast but forgets, non-volatile memory remembers, and the storage hierarchy gets slower and cheaper at each step down. Hard disk drives cost much less per bit but are limited by mechanics, while solid-state drives have no moving parts and spread their wear across the flash with wear leveling. On top of the devices come three ways to present data: block storage gives a server raw blocks, file storage adds paths and directories, and object storage drops the directory tree for flat, cheap scale, as in {{ref:sysd-blocks-208}}. Every device eventually fails, so RAID spreads data and parity across drives, and erasure coding spreads chunks across servers at a lower storage overhead than full copies. RAID guards against drive failure only, and a durable database adds a write-ahead log and offline copies on top.
reviews.scalability-and-availability: Scalability asks how a system grows, and high availability asks how it stays up. Growth comes from adding nodes or adding resources to a node, using strategies such as caching and sharding, and it meets limits that Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law describe. Staying up rests on redundancy, whose benefit grows when components sit in parallel and shrinks when they sit in sequence. Availability is quoted in nines and judged by what users see, and it depends on how long parts last between failures and how fast they are repaired. Clusters, load balancers and capacity planning are the working tools that turn these ideas into designs.
reviews.replication: Replication keeps several copies of data so that no single part can stop the system, and failover lets a standby or replica take over when a copy fails. Single-leader designs send every write to one node, which makes consistency easier to achieve, while multi-master and leaderless designs accept writes anywhere and must resolve conflicts, sometimes with CRDTs. Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy and loses nothing, while asynchronous replication runs faster but can lose recent data and serve stale reads. Quorums and leader election keep copies in agreement, and split-brain shows what happens when they fail. Replicas can be fed by logs, rows, blocks or files, so the right solution depends on the workload.
reviews.sharding-and-partitioning: Every scheme in this chapter answers the same question, which piece of the data lives where, with a rule applied to a partitioning key. Range partitioning keeps neighbors together, hash partitioning spreads load evenly, and each pays for it in skew or in range queries. Sharding puts the pieces on separate servers in a shared-nothing design, at the cost of harder queries, harder joins and rebalancing. Consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing and virtual nodes keep the data that moves small when servers come and go, and distributed hash tables such as Chord use the same idea with no central coordination. Because of those costs, sharding is recommended only when other optimizations have proven insufficient.
reviews.the-cap-theorem-and-consistency: A consistency model is a contract between programmer and system, and models sit on a continuum, from strict consistency, which is only a thought experiment, to eventual consistency, which promises only that reads eventually agree. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, which no distributed system is safe from, a store must choose between consistency and availability, and PACELC adds the choice between latency and consistency the rest of the time. Databases are labeled CP or AP by that choice, but choosing a database on CAP alone is not enough. Primary-backup, active and quorum-based replication show how stores pay for stronger guarantees, by waiting for acknowledgements, ordering every update or collecting votes. Between the extremes sit sequential consistency, linearizability, causal consistency and the session guarantees.
reviews.consensus-ordering-and-distributed-trans: Every thread in this chapter starts from the same fact: machines fail and messages arrive late, so nobody can be sure what the others know. Two-phase commit and three-phase commit make several databases agree on a commit, while the saga pattern gives up the single commit and relies on local transactions and compensating transactions. Lamport timestamps and vector clocks order events without a shared clock, and heartbeats tell a cluster which members are still alive. Consensus lets a group agree on a value, or a series of them, through Paxos and Raft, and it underlies replicated state machines, distributed locks and ZooKeeper. Even consensus has limits: the FLP result, the Two Generals' Problem and Byzantine failures mark what no protocol can promise, and the size and placement of the group decide how well it works in practice.
reviews.how-the-big-distributed-data-systems-wor: These systems rest on a few shared ideas applied to different jobs. Spanner stays strongly consistent through synchronous replication, DynamoDB lets a read trade consistency for availability, and Cassandra favors availability with tunable consistency. The Google File System, Bigtable, HDFS and HBase split data into chunks, tablets or blocks spread across commodity machines, with a master or NameNode holding metadata and heartbeats exposing dead nodes. Cassandra's write path, Bigtable's data model and MapReduce's shuffle show how each design pays for its strengths with a limit elsewhere. Discord's move from MongoDB to Cassandra and then to ScyllaDB shows what happens when a design meets a real workload.
reviews.message-queues-and-brokers: A message queue lets sender and receiver work at different moments, and a broker adds translation, storage and routing between them. What a consumer can rely on depends on the delivery semantics, on features such as dead letter queues, and on the protocol, which is why choosing a queue means comparing all of them. Publish–subscribe changes the shape: every subscriber of a topic gets each message, which gains decoupling but makes delivery harder to guarantee. Event streaming platforms trade delivery tracking, fault-tolerance features and routing for scale.
reviews.event-streaming-and-kafka: Kafka keeps messages in a durable log split into partitions, so many consumers can read them, yet it can still lose a message at the producer, the broker or the consumer unless acknowledgments, replicas and offset commits are set with care. Sequential disk writes and zero copy explain much of its speed. Batch processing waits for all the data, stream processing handles it as it arrives, and engines such as Spark and Flink differ in whether they work in micro-batches or event by event. Complex event processing infers bigger events from small ones, and change data capture carries database changes into other systems by reading transaction logs, using triggers or comparing columns.
reviews.event-driven-architecture-event-sourcing: The chapter's pieces fit around one habit: announce what happened and let others react. An event has a header and a payload, passes through producer, channel, processing engine and downstream activity, and is processed in simple, stream or complex ways. Event sourcing keeps those events as the source of truth, and CQRS splits commands from queries, often with read models built from the events. A broker topology gives performance and scalability, a mediator gives control, and either must cope with failing consumers, lost events, timeouts and changing schemas. McDonald's platform shows many of these pieces at work together: a registry for schemas, SDKs for errors, a gateway, and clusters split by domain.
reviews.monoliths-microservices-and-service-disc: This chapter traces one choice: how tightly to bind the parts of an application. A monolith keeps everything in one unit, N-tier design divides it into layers, and microservices and service-oriented architecture split it into loosely coupled services. Splitting creates new jobs: a registry and a discovery pattern to find instances, a service mesh to handle their communication, and distributed tracing to follow one request across them. Whether to start with a monolith or with microservices depends on team size, business maturity and latency needs, and pitfalls such as the distributed monolith show what happens when the split is done badly. Patterns like the strangler fig and incremental migration describe how to move from one to the other step by step.
reviews.apis-rest-graphql-and-grpc: An API is a contract, and the styles in this chapter are three ways of writing it. REST builds it from resources and uniform constraints, GraphQL from a schema that lets clients choose their fields, and gRPC from protocol buffers that make a remote call compact and fast. Each sends its data in a serialized form, from binary to text, so the choice of format shapes the size and readability of every message. None of the three is better in every case, and the best choice depends on the requirements and the team. Around the contract sits the daily craft of documentation, versioning, pagination and performance.
reviews.real-time-communication: Polling has the client keep asking, long polling holds each request open, and push technology lets the server start the exchange, whether through server-sent events, webhooks or push notifications. WebSocket gives the strongest form of this, a persistent channel open in both directions, and its handshakes, frames, masking, ping and pong, subprotocols and extensions are small rules that keep it working and safe. Around it sit practical concerns: proxies and load balancers that must hold connections open, reconnecting with backoff, origin checks and TLS, and a notification architecture that routes messages through queues. Presence and XMPP show the same machinery serving chat. The C10k problem explains why holding so many connections was once hard, and it is now solved.
reviews.resilience-circuit-breakers-rate-limitin: The largest incidents begin small, and a cascading failure grows by positive feedback as overloaded parts push their work onto the rest. Fault tolerance keeps a service running through faults, and rate limiting, load shedding, deadlines and quotas keep any one server from being asked for too much. The token bucket, the leaky bucket and the window algorithms count the traffic behind those limits. Retries repair transient errors only when backoff, jitter and budgets bound them, and a circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service altogether. Idempotency, with its keys and idempotent consumers, makes a repeated request safe, and that is what lets a client retry aggressively.
reviews.service-levels-and-disaster-recovery: The measures in this chapter all answer one question: how much failure can a service afford? Indicators measure the service, objectives set the target and agreements put it in a contract, while an error budget turns the gap into room for risk. Recovery has its own pair of limits, the recovery point and recovery time objectives, and backups, standby sites and tiers are chosen to meet them. Protection works in layers, because replication is not backup, soft deletion catches developer error, and recovery that is never tested may be broken when it is needed. Monitoring, alerting and incident management tell people when the layers fail, and the Gmail and Google Music recoveries show those layers holding.
reviews.containers-orchestration-and-deployment: This chapter followed an application from isolation to release. Chroot, namespaces and cgroups let the kernel give a container its own view and its own budget, and Docker packages the result into images pulled from registries. Kubernetes then runs those containers as pods on nodes, with services, labels and Ingress routing traffic to them, probes judging their health, and a control plane of controllers steering the cluster toward the declared state. Around that sit the practices that deliver change safely: continuous delivery, release pipelines, rolling updates, blue-green and canary releases, each trading speed against risk. Virtual machines show the older way of sharing a server, which containers lighten by sharing the kernel.
reviews.authentication-and-security: Authentication proves who is asking, through something the user knows, has or is. Several factors together are harder to fake than one, though even multi-factor schemes can be phished or bypassed. Passwords are kept as salted hashes, made deliberately slow by functions such as bcrypt and Argon2, so a stolen database is hard to crack. Once identity is settled, authorization decides what that user may do, guided by least privilege and, under zero trust, checked on every request. Tokens carry that decision across the web, from OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect to signed JSON Web Tokens, while single sign-on trades one convenient login for a bigger target.
reviews.design-a-url-shortener: A shortener is a redirect plus a key. The key is built from letters and digits, often in Base62, and the design has to produce it without collisions at the scale the estimates set. Short links bring their own costs, from added latency and linkrot to hidden destinations, which is one reason expiration is worth designing in. In the full design, a Key Generation Service hands out keys, a cache and a sharded database serve the redirects, and replicas remove single points of failure.
reviews.design-pastebin: Pastebin takes the shortener's idea and changes what sits behind the key: the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL. The design pairs a database that maps each generated url to the contents with an object store that holds them, and it deletes expired pastes by scanning for old timestamps. The average load is modest, 4 writes and 40 reads per second, so a memory cache and read replicas carry it. Throughout, the answer treats scaling as iterative: benchmark, find the bottleneck, weigh alternatives, and repeat.
reviews.design-a-chat-service-like-whatsapp: Every design in this chapter bends around one promise: a message sent is a message delivered, and read by no one but the recipient. Store and forward keeps the delivery half, holding a message on a server until the phone can take it, and WhatsApp deletes it once acknowledged or after 30 days. End-to-end encryption, which WhatsApp builds on the Signal Protocol, keeps the privacy half, while metadata and the argument over provider access show where the promise stops. The worked example joins both to WebSockets, queues, presence and push notifications, and the case study shows the scale WhatsApp reached: ten billion messages a day by August 2012.
reviews.design-a-social-feed-like-twitter: A feed is built twice: once when tweets are delivered and again when they are ordered. Fan-out decides delivery, with push, pull or a hybrid for celebrities, and the 60 thousand tweets delivered per second in the primer's design are why a fast-write store is needed. Ranking decides order, from EdgeRank's three parts to models that take more than 100,000 factors into account, and Twitter's pipeline cuts 500 million tweets to 1500 before it scores them. Search built on Lucene and trending topics served from a refreshed cache sit beside the feed, and the stack case study names the tools underneath.
reviews.design-a-video-streaming-service-like-ne: Every video a viewer plays has passed through a chain this chapter followed link by link. Codecs such as H.264, HEVC and AV1 compress it, transcoding makes a version for each device, and adaptive bitrate streaming, as HLS or MPEG-DASH, lets the player move between those versions as bandwidth changes. A CDN then carries the segments close to viewers, which is why Netflix's Open Connect delivers around 95% of its traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations. Recommendation and geo-blocking sit on top, deciding what each viewer is offered and where. YouTube's VCU shows what happens when transcoding at scale, 500+ hours of uploads every minute, outgrows software.
reviews.design-a-ride-hailing-service-like-uber: Two ideas carry this chapter's design: find the nearest cabs quickly, and price the ride by demand. Nearest neighbor search names the problem, a proximity service solves it for places within a radius, and geohash and quadtree are the structures that avoid measuring the distance to every driver. Dynamic pricing answers peaks in demand, with guardrails such as Uber's cap in emergencies since 2015. The worked design adds WebSockets for live location, a mutex around ride matching and sharding by region, and Uber's own stack shows the tools behind it, from gRPC and QUIC to DocStore and Kafka.
reviews.design-a-web-crawler: A crawler is a set of rules wrapped around a loop. Selection decides what to download, re-visit decides when to come back, and politeness and robots.txt decide how fast, while sitemaps, deep web crawling and focused crawlers widen or narrow what it can reach, and spider traps and duplicate URLs waste its effort. What it collects becomes an index that PageRank helps rank, and cosine similarity, the Jaccard index and W-shingling compare the pages inside it. The worked design puts the pieces together: a ranked list of links, a page signature to stop cycles, and a reverse index to answer 40,000 search requests per second.
reviews.design-a-personal-finance-app-like-mint: Open banking explains where the transactions come from: banks expose APIs that authorized third parties may use, with the customer's consent. The heap turns up inside the Category Service, where it gives the top seller override in O(1). The worked design then surrounds these pieces with a queue for slow extraction, a cache for the few reads, and SQL and object storage for the data. The sizing starts from one number, 5 billion transactions a month.
reviews.design-a-cache-for-the-most-recent-searc: The doubly linked list is what makes eviction cheap: a node already links to its predecessor, so removing it needs no traversal. The worked design pairs the list with a hash table, so lookups are fast and the least recently used entries sit at the tail. A time to live keeps entries fresh, and sharding by a hash of the query, ideally with consistent hashing, spreads the cache over many machines.
reviews.design-a-sales-rank-by-category: The sales rank is a batch job with a read-heavy front. Raw Sales API logs go to an object store, a multi-step MapReduce turns them into (category, product_id) sums, and the sorted result lands in an indexed sales_rank table. Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, so a memory cache answers most views while SQL scaling patterns cover the 400 writes per second. Older data moves to a warehouse or an object store.
reviews.design-the-data-structures-for-a-social: The chapter moves from model to method to design. The social graph is the model, and the adjacency matrix and adjacency list are two ways to store it: the matrix tests adjacency in constant time, while the list lists neighbors cheaply and saves space on sparse graphs. Breadth-first search finds the path with the fewest edges, the shortest path problem says when other algorithms are needed, and bidirectional search runs two searches that meet. Six degrees of separation adds the expectation that paths are short, with measured averages of 6 on Messenger and 4.67 on Twitter. The worked design shards 100 million users across Person Servers and runs the search from both ends.
reviews.scale-a-system-to-millions-of-users-on-a: The chapter tells the same story twice. The staged account moves from one server to separate servers, a load-balanced cluster, read replicas, and then partitioned databases, a cache and separate services. The worked example repeats the loop with numbers, 10 million users and 40,000 reads per second at a 100:1 read to write ratio, and names AWS pieces for each step. A virtual private cloud keeps those pieces private, with a public subnet for the web server and a private subnet for the rest.
reviews.design-gmail: The chapter follows one message end to end. SMTP carries it from the sender's client through submission and transfer servers, found with MX records, to the recipient's mailbox, and the envelope, not the header, decides where it goes. Queues, retries and bounce messages cover the cases where delivery fails, and security and spam filtering guard the path. POP and IMAP then let the recipient's client fetch the mail, with IMAP keeping state on the server through unique identifiers. The worked design joins these pieces: servers push mail with SMTP, and clients pull it with IMAP or POP.
reviews.design-google-maps: The chapter splits a map into a picture and a route. For the picture, Web Mercator flattens the world, map tiles cut it into blocks, and a CDN serves them from nearby. For the route, Dijkstra's algorithm gives shortest paths, A* adds a heuristic estimate, and contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts so queries answer in microseconds. Geocoding sits between them, turning an address into the coordinates that the route needs. The worked design adds a location service, whose updates help detect new and closed roads and feed live traffic data, and arranges everything in three components.
reviews.design-a-stock-exchange: Every part of the chapter serves the critical path. Order types say what traders ask for, FIX carries those orders in, and the order book holds them until the matching engine pairs buyers and sellers. Market data and reporting stay off the critical path. To keep the path fast, the matching engine runs single-threaded and pinned to a CPU, using processor affinity and non-blocking techniques rather than locks. The worked design puts it all on one server with shared memory as an event bus.
reviews.design-google-docs: The chapter starts from a problem: latency means edits land on different versions of the document. Groupware concurrency control answers with an algorithm that lets users work on the data without locks. Operational transformation makes that practical by adjusting each operation's parameters against concurrent ones, so every copy converges. The worked design sends operations through a WebSocket server and a message queue to a file operation server, and it names CRDTs and differential synchronization as alternatives.
reviews.design-a-payment-system: Every payment is recorded twice, as a debit and a credit, so the books balance. Settlement systems differ in speed, from batches through real-time gross settlement to instant transfers, and a card payment is approved in 2–3 seconds but funded 2-3 days later. The payment service provider and the gateway sit between merchant and bank, with the gateway never touching the money flow. Because many places can go wrong, even a system with exactly-once semantics needs reconciliation as a safety net, and the full design uses an idempotency key so that a retry cannot charge twice.
reviews.design-a-notification-system: The chapter's three channels each carry their own limits. SMS reaches phones over cellular networks, but delivery is not guaranteed and about 1% to 5% of messages are lost even in normal operation. FCM queues messages when a device is offline and finds each app instance through a registration token, while Apple's service accepts payloads up to 4 kilobytes. The full design puts a notification service behind a message queue, forwards each request by device platform, prunes stale tokens, and uses time to live, topics and delivery receipts to control what a device receives.
reviews.design-a-permission-system: The models differ in who holds the power. An ACL lists permissions on each resource, DAC lets the owner pass them on, MAC takes that power away with a central policy, RBAC groups permissions into roles, ABAC evaluates attributes and ReBAC follows relationships. Beneath them, the enforcement, decision and information points split the check, XACML supplies a policy language for it, and the AAA framework chains agreements between organizations. Separation of duties keeps any one person from authorizing a critical operation alone, and the worked design shows these pieces combining, at a cost in performance that grows with granularity.

entries.title: System design: choices that are hard to undo

definition.text: System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements.

facts.text: System design meets the needs of a business or organization through coherent and efficient systems, and it takes a systematic approach to building and engineering them.
A good system design requires thinking about everything, from the infrastructure all the way down to the data and how it is stored.
The study of system design is the understanding of a system's component parts and how they interact with one another.
Designing the overall structure of a system aims at a scalable, reliable and efficient system.

Architecture design covers functional and non-functional requirements, relational or NoSQL databases, vertical and horizontal scaling, sharding, message queues, publish-subscribe, monitoring and logging, and build, test and deploy automation.
System design helps define a solution that meets the business requirements and is one of the earliest decisions made when building a system.
High-level design decisions are very difficult to correct later, so it is essential to think from a high level early on.
A clear design also makes it easier to reason about and manage architectural changes as the system evolves.

entries.title: System design interview: no single right answer

definition.text: A system design interview evaluates a candidate's ability to produce technical solutions to abstract problems, so it has no single expected answer.

facts.text: System design is a very extensive topic, and interviews on it are not designed for one specific answer.
The interview is unusual because it is two-way between the candidate and the interviewer.

Expectations differ at each engineering level, because an experienced engineer approaches the problem differently from someone new, so it is hard to give one strategy that keeps every candidate organized.
System design interview questions are vague or abstract by nature.

A discussion checklist for interviews touches on load balancing, API gateway, communication protocols, CDN, message queue, unique ID generation, scalability, availability, performance, and fault tolerance and resilience.
Singh advises reading the engineering blog of the company you are interviewing with, to learn its technology stack and which problems matter to it.

entries.title: System design building blocks: six categories

definition.text: The building blocks of system design are the standard components, grouped into six broad categories, that designs are assembled from.

facts.text: The building blocks fall into six broad categories: distributed computing, scalability and performance, service management, networking and communication, data storage and management, and observability and resiliency.

Distributed computing blocks are message queues, which allow async communication and decouple services; distributed caching, which keeps frequently accessed data in memory; and a task scheduler that coordinates running tasks.

Scalability and performance blocks are scaling services that adjust capacity to demand, CDNs that serve content from geographically closer locations, and consistent hashing that minimizes key remapping when nodes join or leave.
Service discovery lets services find and talk to each other without hard-coded network locations.

Networking blocks are DNS, which maps domain names to IP addresses; the load balancer, which spreads incoming traffic across servers; and the API gateway, a single entry point for a group of microservices.

Data storage blocks are databases for structured data, object storage for images, videos and documents, sharding to partition data across nodes, and replication to scale the database by copying data to multiple nodes.
Observability and resiliency means gaining insight into the system's internal state through metrics, logging and tracing.

It also covers sharding, which partitions data across nodes, and copying data to multiple nodes, which scales the store. entries.title: Functional requirements: what the system must do

definition.text: A functional requirement defines a function of a system or component as behavior between inputs and outputs, a statement of what the system is supposed to accomplish.

facts.text: Functional requirements may involve calculations, technical details, data manipulation and processing and other specific functionality, and are usually written 'system shall do <requirement>' for one individual action or part of the system.

Functional requirements drive the application architecture of a system, while non-functional requirements drive its technical architecture; functional requirements are planned in the system design, non-functional ones in the system architecture.

Behavioral requirements describe the cases where the system uses the functional requirements and are captured in use cases; an analyst may derive functional requirements from a set of use cases, or write the use cases after gathering the requirements.
A specification has a unique name and number, a brief summary, a rationale, the required behavior and references to related use cases; the crux is a clear, readable description of the behavior.

entries.title: Non-functional requirements: how the system must be

definition.text: A non-functional requirement specifies criteria for judging how a system operates, an overall property such as availability or performance, rather than a specific behavior.

facts.text: Broadly, functional requirements define what a system is supposed to do and non-functional requirements define how it is supposed to be: they take the form 'system shall be <requirement>', an overall property rather than a specific function.

It is important to specify non-functional requirements in a specific and measurable way, because a system's overall properties commonly mark the difference between a development project succeeding or failing.

They are also called quality attributes, qualities, quality goals, quality of service requirements or constraints, informally the 'ilities', and in software architecture 'architectural characteristics'; some call them cross-functional requirements.

Qualities fall into two categories: execution qualities such as safety, security and usability are observable at run time, while evolution qualities such as testability, maintainability, extensibility and scalability are embodied in the static structure of the system.

Typical examples are availability, performance (speed, throughput, response time), reliability (mean time between failures), maintainability (mean time to repair), fault tolerance and resource constraints such as memory, disk space and network bandwidth.

A system may have to display the number of records in a database: how current that number must be is a non-functional requirement, and real-time updating obliges architects to keep the display within an acceptably short interval of the change.

In an interview, non-functional requirements sound like 'each request should be processed with the minimum latency' and 'the system should be highly available', next to portability, maintainability, reliability, scalability and security.

Non-functional requirements are usually architecturally significant, so their plan is detailed in the system architecture, which is tied more closely to quality attributes than to functionality; the architect must match these characteristics with business requirements.

entries.title: Software architecture: the blueprint behind a system

definition.text: Software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system, and the discipline of creating them.

facts.text: Each architectural structure comprises software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both the elements and the relations.
The architecture works as the blueprints for the system and the development project, and it is about fundamental structural choices that are costly to change once implemented.

Application design covers the processes and data behind the required functionality, while architecture design shapes the infrastructure in which that functionality runs so that the system's non-functional requirements are met.
Architecture is design but not all design is architectural; in practice the architect draws the line between architectural design and detailed design, and no rule fits all cases.
Two fundamental laws of software architecture are that everything is a trade-off and that why is more important than how.
Software architectures fall into two main types, monolith and distributed architecture, and tend to become more complex over time.

As an intellectually graspable abstraction, architecture lets teams analyse a system's behavior before it is built, saving cost and risk, and lets stakeholders discuss design decisions while they are still relatively easy to adapt.
Conway's observation is that organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures; Fred Brooks popularized it as Conway's Law.

entries.title: Common scaling problems and their standard fixes

definition.text: Eight problems recur in large-scale production systems, and each has a standard remedy: caching, async workers, redundancy, load balancing, CDNs, object storage, central logging and database indexing or sharding.

facts.text: A read-heavy system is helped by caching to make reads faster.
High write traffic is handled with async workers that process the writes, or with databases powered by LSM-trees.
A single point of failure is removed by redundancy and failover mechanisms for critical components such as databases.
For high availability, use load balancing so that requests go to healthy server instances, and database replication to improve durability and availability.
High latency is reduced with a content delivery network.
Large files and complex data are handled with block storage and object storage.
Monitoring and alerting use a centralized logging system, for example the ELK stack.
Slower database queries are fixed with proper indexes and by sharding to scale the database horizontally.
