entries.title: The DHCP handshake: discover, offer, request, acknowledge

definition.text: A DHCP client obtains an IP address through four exchanges (discovery, offer, request and acknowledgement) and then holds it as a lease that it must renew.

facts.text: The client starts with a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast to 255.255.255.255 or the subnet broadcast address, and may ask for a particular address that the server can take into account.
A server that gets the discover reserves an address and replies with DHCPOFFER, which carries the offered IP address, subnet mask, lease duration and the server's own address.
The client may receive several offers but accepts only one, broadcasting a DHCPREQUEST that names the chosen server; the other servers withdraw their offers and return those addresses to their pools.
The server completes the exchange with a DHCPACK that carries the lease duration and any other configuration the client asked for, ending the IP configuration process.
Before claiming an address, the client should probe it, for example with ARP, to see whether another host already uses it; a server may likewise ping an address before reusing it.

Clients start renewing once half the lease interval has passed, unicasting DHCPREQUEST to the granting server; if it stays unreachable the client rebinds by broadcasting the request so any server can renew the lease.
When a lease expires the client must stop using the address and restart with a DHCPDISCOVER; since its address then changes, any ongoing connections break.
A client may send DHCP Release to give up its address, but the protocol does not require it because devices are often unplugged without warning.

entries.title: Subnets and CIDR: where the network part ends

definition.text: A subnet is a part of an IP network; an address is split into a network prefix and a host part, and CIDR notation states where the split falls.

facts.text: IP networks may be divided into subnetworks in both IPv4 and IPv6, by designating network prefixes within the address space.
An IP address has two parts: the network prefix in the high-order bits and the remaining bits, called the host identifier (the interface identifier in IPv6), used for host numbering within a network.
The subnet mask or CIDR notation determines how the address divides into network and host parts; the term subnet mask is used only within IPv4, but both versions use CIDR.

In CIDR notation the address is followed by a slash and the number of bits of the network part; 192.0.2.1 with mask 255.255.255.0 is written 192.0.2.1/24 because the first 24 bits indicate the network.

entries.title: The retransmission timeout: how long TCP waits before resending
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.1. Retransmission Timeout

definition.text: The retransmission timeout (RTO) is how long a TCP sender waits for an acknowledgment before resending a segment, and it must be determined dynamically.

facts.text: Segments may be lost to errors or congestion, so TCP retransmits to ensure delivery of every segment, and duplicate segments may arrive because of network or TCP retransmission.
Because networks vary so much, the RTO must be determined dynamically, computed by the RFC 6298 algorithm including Karn's algorithm for taking RTT samples.
Successive RTO values for the same segment back off exponentially, and the backed-off value is kept until a segment with new data has been sent and acknowledged without retransmission.

An endpoint MUST implement slow start, congestion avoidance and exponential backoff of RTO to avoid congestion collapse; other algorithms are allowed if they conform to the IETF Standards Track specifications.

Excessive retransmission of one segment signals a remote host or path failure: at threshold R1 TCP gives negative advice to IP to trigger dead-gateway diagnosis, and at a larger R2 it closes the connection.
R1 SHOULD correspond to at least 3 retransmissions at the current RTO and R2 to at least 100 seconds, and TCP SHOULD tell the application of the delivery problem once R1 is reached.
An application MUST be able to set R2 per connection; an interactive application might set it to infinity so the user decides when to disconnect.
Opening a connection can fail through excessive SYN retransmissions, a RST or an ICMP Port Unreachable, and R2 for a SYN MUST allow retransmission for at least 3 minutes.

entries.title: TCP segments and the maximum segment size

definition.text: Segmentation is how TCP cuts an application's byte stream into segments, and the Maximum Segment Size option tells the peer the largest segment it will accept.

facts.text: Segment boundaries need not match the application's send calls: TCP guarantees no correlation between the boundaries of segments and those of the application's read or write buffers.
Larger segments mean fewer packets in flight, fewer interrupts and layer crossings, and less header overhead, though the benefit shrinks as segments grow.

Smaller segments avoid a datagram larger than the smallest MTU on the path, which means loss or fragmentation, and avoid delaying the data stream; some firewalls and middleboxes drop fragmented packets or the ICMP messages about them.
Endpoints MUST implement sending and receiving the MSS option, and SHOULD send it in every SYN when their receive MSS differs from the default.
Without an MSS option the default send MSS is 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6.
The effective send MSS must be the smaller of the peer's advertised MSS, which reflects its reassembly buffer, and the largest size the IP layer permits, less the TCP header and any IP options.
The MSS to advertise should be the effective MTU minus the fixed IP and TCP headers; when options are present, the sender must shrink the data in each packet by the option bytes.

entries.title: Nagle's algorithm: waiting to fill a packet
entries.article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Forcing data delivery

definition.text: Nagle's algorithm makes TCP wait for a full packet of data before sending, grouping small messages into a single packet.

facts.text: TCP normally waits 200 ms for a full packet to send, which creates small but potentially serious delays when repeated constantly during a file transfer.
In Telnet each keystroke is echoed back by the server before the user sees it, so the wait would be very annoying.
Setting the TCP_NODELAY socket option overrides the default 200 ms send delay, and applications use it to force output after writing a character or a line.

entries.title: TCP sequence numbers: numbering every byte

definition.text: TCP gives every octet of data on a connection a sequence number, which lets the receiver acknowledge, order and de-duplicate what it receives.

facts.text: Every octet is sequenced and so can be acknowledged; acknowledgments are cumulative, so an acknowledgment of X means all octets up to but not including X have arrived, which makes duplicate detection straightforward.
The sequence number space is finite, from 0 to 2^32 - 1, so all sequence number arithmetic is done modulo 2^32.
SYN and FIN are the only controls that occupy sequence space, so they can be retransmitted and acknowledged without confusion; a SYN counts as before the first data octet and a FIN as after the last.

A connection can be reused, and each new instance is an incarnation; TCP must not mistake duplicate segments from an earlier incarnation for new ones, which TIME-WAIT and initial sequence number selection together prevent.
A new connection takes a 32-bit initial sequence number from a clock that typically ticks about every 4 microseconds and cycles in roughly 4.55 hours, much longer than the Maximum Segment Lifetime.

Implementations SHOULD set the initial sequence number to a timer value plus a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key; it must not be computable from outside, or an attacker could guess sequence numbers.
Using up 2^32 octets of sequence space takes 4.5 hours at 2 megabits/sec, 5.4 minutes at 100 megabits/sec, 34 seconds at 1 Gbps, 3 seconds at 10 Gbps and around a third of a second at 100 Gbps.
At high data rates the sequence space can wrap within the segment lifetime, so TCP Timestamp Options and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) are needed to detect and discard old duplicates.

A new connection takes a 32-bit initial sequence number from a clock that typically ticks about every 4 microseconds and cycles in roughly 4.55 hours. Implementations should add a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key, because an attacker who could compute the number could guess sequence numbers. At high data rates the sequence space can wrap within the segment lifetime. TCP Timestamp Options and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) then detect and discard old duplicates.

entries.title: Selective acknowledgment: resend only what is missing
entries.article: Transmission Control Protocol#Protocol operation > Selective acknowledgments

definition.text: Selective acknowledgment (SACK) is a TCP option that lets the receiver acknowledge discontinuous blocks of correctly received data, so the sender resends only what is missing.

facts.text: With only cumulative acknowledgments, if the second of ten equal segments (sequence numbers 2,000 to 2,999) is lost, the receiver can only acknowledge 2,000 and the sender may have to resend everything from 2,000.
With SACK the receiver sends a cumulative ACK of 2,000 plus a SACK option with sequence numbers 3,000 and 11,000, so the sender retransmits only the second segment.
SACK is optional, works only if both parties support it, is negotiated when the connection is established, and all popular TCP stacks support it.
SACK helps throughput by more often avoiding slow start after a loss, but TCP can selectively acknowledge a maximum of three blocks of sequence numbers.

entries.title: Why TCP needs three messages to open a connection
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.5. Establishing a Connection

definition.text: The three-way handshake is the procedure TCP uses to establish a connection, in which the two peers exchange and acknowledge each other's initial sequence numbers.

facts.text: Each side sends a SYN carrying its own initial sequence number and needs it acknowledged; the acknowledgment of the first SYN and the second side's own SYN travel in one segment, which makes three messages.
The handshake is needed because sequence numbers are not tied to a global clock; the receiver of a first SYN cannot know whether it is an old one, so it asks the sender to verify it.
The principal reason for the three-way handshake is to prevent old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion.
In the basic exchange the first SYN uses sequence number 100, so the reply acknowledges 101; a bare ACK takes no sequence space, because otherwise acknowledgments would themselves need acknowledging.

If an old duplicate SYN reaches the passive peer, it replies normally; the first peer sees the wrong acknowledgment, sends a RST, the passive peer returns to LISTEN, and the genuine SYN then completes the handshake.
The handshake also works when both peers open at once: each receives a SYN without an acknowledgment after sending its own, and an implementation MUST support this simultaneous open.
Handshake segments may carry data, but the receiver must buffer it and not deliver it to the application until the connection reaches ESTABLISHED.

entries.title: The states a TCP connection moves through
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.3. TCP Terminology Overview > 3.3.2. State Machine Overview

definition.text: A TCP connection moves through a fixed set of states during its life, changing state in response to user calls, incoming segments and timeouts.

facts.text: The states are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and the fictional CLOSED, which means no connection record exists.
State changes are caused by the user calls OPEN, SEND, RECEIVE, CLOSE, ABORT and STATUS, by incoming segments carrying SYN, ACK, RST or FIN, and by timeouts.
A passive OPEN means the process wants to accept incoming connection requests; an active OPEN attempts to initiate a connection.
Opening: LISTEN waits for a request from any remote peer, SYN-SENT has sent a request and awaits a matching one, and SYN-RECEIVED has both received and sent one and awaits the acknowledgment.
ESTABLISHED is an open connection and the normal state for the data transfer phase, in which received data can be delivered to the user.

Closing: FIN-WAIT-1 and FIN-WAIT-2 wait for the peer's termination request, CLOSE-WAIT waits for the local user to close, and CLOSING and LAST-ACK wait for acknowledgment of a termination request already sent.
TIME-WAIT waits long enough to be sure the peer received the acknowledgment of its termination request and to keep delayed segments from earlier connections from affecting new ones.
A RST can be sent from any state and leads to TIME-WAIT, while receiving a RST from any state leads to LISTEN or CLOSED; the state diagram is only a summary, not the full specification.

entries.title: SYN floods and TCP hijacking

definition.text: TCP can be attacked in several ways, including denial of service by SYN flood and connection hijacking.

facts.text: In a SYN flood, an attacker uses a spoofed IP address and repeatedly sends crafted SYN packets, so the server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections.
Proposed defenses are SYN cookies and cryptographic puzzles, though SYN cookies come with their own vulnerabilities.
An attacker who can eavesdrop on a session and redirect packets can hijack it by learning the sequence number and forging a segment that looks like the next one in the stream.
The initial sequence number should be unpredictable to defend against TCP sequence prediction attacks.

The server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections. SYN cookies and cryptographic puzzles have been proposed as defenses, though SYN cookies come with their own vulnerabilities. A connection can also be hijacked. An attacker who can eavesdrop on a session and redirect packets can learn the sequence number. The attacker then forges a segment that looks like the next one in the stream. That is why the initial sequence number should be unpredictable.

entries.title: The network layer: getting packets across networks
entries.article: OSI model#Layer architecture > Layer 3: Network layer

definition.text: The network layer transfers packets from one node to another across different networks, finding a route through intermediate nodes where needed.

facts.text: In a network every node has an address, and a sender only supplies the message content and the destination address while the network finds the way, possibly routing through intermediate nodes.
If a message is too large for the data link layer between two nodes, the network may split it into fragments, send them independently and reassemble them at another node.
Network-layer delivery is not necessarily reliable: a protocol may, but need not, report delivery errors or provide reliable delivery.
If the two communicating devices are on the same network, the network layer is unnecessary.

entries.title: ICMP: how the network reports its own errors

definition.text: The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is a supporting protocol that routers and other network devices use to send error messages and operational information about IP communication.

facts.text: ICMP reports problems such as an unavailable service or an unreachable host or router; errors are directed to the source IP address of the packet that caused them.
Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP does not normally carry data between systems or serve end-user applications, apart from diagnostic tools such as ping and traceroute, and an ICMP packet has no port number.
ICMP is a network-layer protocol and an integral part of IP: its messages travel inside IPv4 packets under protocol number 1, and IPv6 uses a separate ICMPv6.

Every ICMP packet has an eight-byte header whose type and code identify the message; error messages include the offending IP header plus at least eight bytes of its data so the host can match the error to a process.
Each forwarding router decrements the IP time to live; at 0 the packet is discarded and an ICMP time exceeded message goes to the source.

Ping uses ICMP echo request and echo reply, while traceroute sends datagrams with increasing TTL values and reads the time exceeded and destination unreachable messages to find each router on the path.

Destination unreachable is sent when the host cannot be reached, the protocol or port is not active, or a packet must be fragmented but has the don't-fragment flag set, which Path MTU Discovery relies on.
ICMP Redirect lets a router tell a host that a better route to a destination goes through another router on the host's own subnet, so the host should send those packets directly there.

entries.title: Choosing TCP or UDP: completeness or speed

definition.text: Use TCP when data must arrive complete and in order, and use UDP when the lowest latency matters more than losing some data.

facts.text: TCP has built-in error checking and guarantees data is delivered in the order it was sent, which makes it suited to still images, data files and web pages.
TCP's feedback mechanisms make it reliable but add overhead, using more of the available network bandwidth.
UDP has no overhead for opening, maintaining or terminating a connection, and data is sent continuously whether or not the recipient receives it.
UDP is faster, simpler and more efficient than TCP, but retransmission of lost packets is only possible with TCP.
Use UDP over TCP when you need the lowest latency and late data is worse than the loss of data; it is largely preferred for real-time communication such as broadcast or multicast transmission.
Typical TCP uses are HTTPS, HTTP, SMTP, POP and FTP, while typical UDP uses are video streaming, DNS and VoIP.

entries.title: NAT traversal: reaching a peer behind another NAT
entries.article: Network address translation#Type of NAT and NAT traversal, role of port preservation for TCP

definition.text: NAT traversal is the set of techniques, such as port forwarding and TCP hole punching, that let peers behind different NATs communicate with each other.

facts.text: NAT traversal problems arise when peers behind different NATs try to communicate; port forwarding or traversal techniques solve them, and VoIP, videoconferencing and other peer-to-peer applications must use them to work.

A client may need to find its external address and the type of mapping its NAT uses; STUN was specified for this, and its original split into full-cone, restricted-cone, port-restricted and symmetric NAT has been deprecated.
RFC 4787 separates NAT mapping from NAT filtering: security is determined by the filtering behavior, and a NAT MUST have endpoint-independent mapping.

TCP hole punching, the most popular TCP traversal technique, needs the NAT to preserve ports for outgoing TCP connections; UDP needs no port preservation because many UDP communications can share one source port.

entries.title: Delayed ACKs: acknowledging less often
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.3. Delayed Acknowledgments -- When to Send an ACK Segment

definition.text: A delayed ACK means a receiver sends fewer than one acknowledgment per data segment received, which saves effort in both the network and the hosts.

facts.text: A TCP endpoint SHOULD delay ACKs but never excessively: the delay MUST be less than 0.5 seconds.
An ACK SHOULD be generated for at least every second full-sized segment, or 2*RMSS bytes of new data, where RMSS is the MSS specified by the endpoint receiving the segments.

Excessive ACK delays disturb round-trip timing and packet clocking, so out-of-order segments, segments above a gap and segments that fill a gap should be acknowledged immediately to speed loss recovery.

Nagle's algorithm combined with delayed ACKs, both on by default in common operating systems, can badly hurt request-response applications, and many applications simply disable Nagle with a socket option.

entries.title: Silly window syndrome: the tiny-window trap
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.2. Silly Window Syndrome Avoidance

definition.text: Silly window syndrome is a stable pattern of small incremental window movements that leaves TCP performing extremely poorly.

facts.text: A TCP implementation MUST include SWS avoidance in both sender and receiver; Nagle's algorithm curbs tiny segments from small data increments, while SWS avoidance curbs small segments from the window edge advancing in small steps.

The receiver avoids advancing its right window edge in small increments: it keeps the edge fixed until the freed space reaches the smaller of a fraction (recommended 1/2) of its buffer and the effective send MSS.
The sender transmits only if a maximum-sized segment fits, or pushed data can all be sent, or at least a fraction (recommended 1/2) of the largest window seen fits, or an override timeout fires.
The sender cannot see the receiver's buffer, so it estimates it as the maximum send window seen; an override timeout of 0.1 - 1.0 seconds forces data out so a wrong estimate cannot deadlock.

entries.title: Half-close: stop sending but keep listening
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.6. Closing a Connection > 3.6.1. Half-Closed Connections

definition.text: Because TCP closes the two directions of a connection independently, an endpoint can stop sending while it keeps receiving.

facts.text: CLOSE means 'I have no more data to send'; TCP treats it as simplex, so the closing user can keep receiving until the remote peer has closed too.
An endpoint that receives a FIN acknowledges it but does not send its own FIN until its user also closes; all data sent before the CLOSE is delivered reliably, in both directions.

A half-closed connection is closed in one direction only and the host may keep sending in the other; a host MAY instead implement a half-duplex close in which the application cannot keep reading after CLOSE.
A host using the half-duplex close SHOULD send a RST if data is still pending when CLOSE is called or arrives afterwards, to show that data was lost.

entries.title: TCP keep-alive: checking an idle peer is still there
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.4. TCP Keep-Alives

definition.text: A TCP keep-alive sends a probe on an idle connection to check that the peer is still there.

facts.text: TCP does not inherently detect whether a peer is alive; keep-alives are optional, not universally accepted, and where offered they send a probe segment designed to elicit a response from the peer.

A connection is idle when no segments have arrived for a long time and nothing new or unacknowledged is waiting to be sent; the probe usually has sequence number SND.NXT-1 and may carry one garbage octet.

Keep-alives MUST default to off with a per-connection switch, and are sent only when nothing is outstanding and nothing has arrived within a configurable interval that MUST default to no less than two hours.
Because ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted, a keep-alive MUST NOT treat the failure to answer one probe as proof that the connection is dead.

A probe goes out only after a configurable interval of silence, which must default to no less than two hours. One unanswered probe is not proof that the connection is dead, because ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted.

entries.title: TCP reset: telling a peer the connection does not exist
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.5. Establishing a Connection > 3.5.2. Reset Generation

definition.text: A reset (RST) segment tells a TCP peer that a segment does not belong to a live connection, so the receiver ignores it or aborts the connection.

facts.text: A RST is sent whenever a segment arrives that apparently is not meant for the current connection, such as a SYN that matches no existing connection, and it must not be sent if that is unclear.
A RST is valid if its sequence number is in the receive window, or in SYN-SENT if its ACK acknowledges the SYN; the receiver validates it first and only then changes state.
A receiver in LISTEN ignores a RST; in SYN-RECEIVED it returns to LISTEN if it arrived by a passive open, else aborts; in any other state it aborts the connection and tells the user.

A half-open connection exists when one peer closed, aborted or lost its state without the other knowing; it is reset automatically when either side tries to send data, as the peer with no connection answers with a reset.

entries.title: What a TCP header carries

definition.text: A TCP header follows the IP header and carries the fields TCP needs: ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window and checksum.

facts.text: The header holds 16-bit source and destination ports, a 32-bit sequence number (the initial sequence number when SYN is set) and a 32-bit acknowledgment number that is always sent once a connection is established.

The control bits, also called flags, are CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN; the Data Offset counts the 32-bit words in the header, so the header, even with options, is a multiple of 32 bits long.
The 16-bit window field says how many data octets, beginning at the one in the acknowledgment field, the sender of the segment will accept; the value is shifted when window scaling is used.
The checksum is never optional: the sender MUST generate it and the receiver MUST check it, and it covers a pseudo-header of IP information, which protects the connection against misrouted segments.

entries.title: TIME-WAIT: why a closed connection lingers
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.6. Closing a Connection

definition.text: TIME-WAIT is the state in which the endpoint that closed a TCP connection first lingers, so that late segments from the old connection cannot disturb a new one.

facts.text: A connection closed actively MUST linger in TIME-WAIT for 2xMSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), and this specification takes the MSL to be 2 minutes.
TIME-WAIT limits the rate of connection reuse, so that segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection are not confused with the new one.

A host in TIME-WAIT MAY accept a new SYN from the remote endpoint to reopen the connection directly, and a Timestamp-based algorithm that shortens TIME-WAIT supports higher connection establishment rates on busy servers.
The side that issues a reset should also enter TIME-WAIT, since this generally helps to reduce the load on busy servers.

entries.chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP
entries.text: The endpoint that closes a TCP connection first cannot walk away at once. It must linger in TIME-WAIT for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), which the specification takes to be 2 minutes. This limits the rate of connection reuse. Segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection, an earlier use of the same connection, must not be confused with the new one. A host in TIME-WAIT may accept a new SYN from the remote endpoint to reopen the connection directly. A timestamp-based algorithm that shortens TIME-WAIT supports higher connection establishment rates on busy servers.

entries.title: Zero-window probing: knocking on a closed window
entries.article: rfc>9293#3. Functional Specification > 3.8. Data Communication > 3.8.6. Managing the Window > 3.8.6.1. Zero-Window Probing

definition.text: Zero-window probing is how a TCP sender keeps testing a receiver whose window is zero, so that the reopening of the window is reliably reported.

facts.text: Even when the send window is zero, the sender must regularly transmit at least one octet of new data, or retransmit, to probe the window; this guarantees that the window reopening is reported reliably.
The first probe SHOULD be sent once a zero window has lasted the retransmission timeout, and the interval between successive probes SHOULD increase exponentially.
A receiver MAY keep its window closed indefinitely, and the sender MUST keep the connection open as long as the receiver keeps acknowledging probes, as in the 'printer ran out of paper' case.
A receiver SHOULD NOT shrink the window by moving its right edge left, but a sender MUST be robust against it, and a window that shrinks to zero MUST be probed.

entries.chapter: How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP
entries.text: A receiver's window can stay at zero, and the sender must keep checking. Zero-window probing is how it does that, so the reopening of the window is reliably reported. Even at zero, the sender must regularly transmit at least one octet of new data, or retransmit, to probe the window. The first probe should be sent once a zero window has lasted the retransmission timeout. The interval between probes should increase exponentially. A receiver may keep its window closed indefinitely, as in the 'printer ran out of paper' case. The sender must then keep the connection open while the receiver keeps acknowledging probes.

entries.title: Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest hop
entries.article: Maximum transmission unit#Internet protocol > Path MTU Discovery

definition.text: Path MTU Discovery is a technique for finding the smallest MTU along the route between two IP hosts, so packets can be sized to avoid fragmentation.

facts.text: The path MTU is the smallest MTU of any hop between source and destination, that is, the largest packet that crosses the path without fragmentation; Path MTU Discovery finds it and is defined for both IPv4 and IPv6.

The sender sets the DF (don't fragment) bit; a device with a smaller MTU drops the packet and returns an ICMP Datagram Too Big message giving its MTU, and the sender lowers its estimate and repeats until packets fit.

Networks that drop ICMP traffic, for example to resist denial-of-service attacks, break discovery; Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is more robust to ICMP filtering, and a changing route can change the path MTU mid-transfer.
A failed discovery lets a connection work for small data but stall once a host sends a large block; one workaround is to change the maximum segment size in the TCP setup packet at one's firewall.

entries.title: Reno, CUBIC and BBR: different ways to react to congestion

definition.text: TCP congestion control algorithms are variants of the window-adjustment rules, such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR, that differ in how they detect and react to congestion.

facts.text: Tahoe and Reno both treat a retransmission timeout and three duplicate ACKs as loss; on duplicate ACKs Tahoe drops the window to 1 MSS and restarts slow start, while Reno halves it and enters fast recovery.
CUBIC, a less aggressive derivative of BIC, makes the window a cubic function of time since the last congestion event; it is the default in Linux since kernel 2.6.19, and on Android and macOS.

Unlike loss-based algorithms, BBR (Google, 2016) builds a network model from the maximum bandwidth and round-trip time delivered; BBRv1's fairness is disputed, as it can take the link from a coexisting CUBIC flow.

Algorithms can be grouped by network awareness: black box ones use only binary congestion feedback, grey box ones use time measurements such as RTT variation and arrival rate, and green box ones use explicit feedback from the network.

entries.contested_note: The fairness of BBR version 1 toward other flows is disputed: Google's presentation shows it coexisting with CUBIC, while researchers found it unfair.

entries.title: DNS: the phone book of the Internet

definition.text: A hierarchical, distributed naming service that translates human-readable domain names into the numeric IP addresses that computers use to find each other.

facts.text: DNS works like the phone book of the Internet: it translates human-friendly hostnames into IP addresses, so www.example.com translates to 93.184.216.34 (IPv4) and 2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946 (IPv6).

Responsibility for each domain goes to its authoritative name servers, and administrators can delegate subdomains to other name servers, which gives a distributed, fault-tolerant service designed to avoid one large central database.
Records can be updated quickly and transparently, so a service can change its network location while users keep using the same hostname.
The distributed nature of DNS lets it work efficiently while serving billions of hosts on the worldwide Internet.
A DNS name server stores the records for a domain and answers queries against its database, which is conventionally kept in a structured text file called a zone file.
DNS runs on port 53 over UDP and TCP; it originally used UDP, and reliability, security and privacy concerns later brought TCP and other transports.
DNS stores more than addresses: it has been extended to hold records such as DNSSEC records and, as a general-purpose database, spam blocklists.
The DNS mirrors administrative responsibility on the Internet: each subdomain is a zone of administrative autonomy delegated to a manager.

entries.text:
Computers find each other by number, but people remember names. The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates the names people use into the numeric IP addresses that computers use. It works like the phone book of the Internet: www.example.com translates to 93.184.216.34 in IPv4 and to a much longer address in IPv6.

No single store holds all of this. Responsibility for each domain goes to its own authoritative servers, and administrators can hand pieces of a name to other servers. The result is a distributed, fault-tolerant service designed to avoid one large central store, and it can serve billions of hosts efficiently. It also mirrors how the Internet is run: each piece of a name is a zone of administrative autonomy, delegated to a manager.

It has been extended to hold signing records, which {{ref:sysd-found-195}} explains, and, as a general-purpose store, spam blocklists.

entries.title: Anycast: one address, many servers

definition.text: Anycast is an addressing and routing method in which one IP address is shared by servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one.

facts.text: Routers send packets for an anycast address to the location nearest the sender using their normal decision-making, typically the lowest number of BGP network hops.
In IPv4, hosts in different places share one IP address and each announces it by BGP; routers treat these as alternative routes and often pick the path with fewer hops, though some use other metrics.
IPv6 supports anycast explicitly in its addressing architecture, and the IPv4 method of advertising multiple routes for one address in BGP still works there, with the same use cases and limitations.

All Internet root name servers use anycast; many commercial DNS providers switched to it to increase query performance and redundancy and to balance load, and CDNs use it for DNS or HTTP connections to their distribution centers.

Early objections held that a long-lived TCP connection could be rerouted to another instance mid-connection; in practice this was not observed, measured failures from instance switches were below 0.017%, and CDN requests are short-lived and stateless.

Anycast gives automatic failover, usually with external heartbeat monitoring that withdraws a failed server's route announcement; if the announcement continues, the dead server becomes a black hole for nearby clients, the most serious failure mode.
The failure above hurts only clients closer to that server than to any other, not everyone; but the automation that withdraws routes can itself become a point of failure.

Anycast spreads DDoS traffic across the nearest nodes, but this depends on keeping the unicast addresses of nodes secret; and anyone whose route announcements are accepted can hijack anycast traffic, so announcements must be filtered.

entries.text:
Anycast gives one IP address to servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one. Each server announces the shared address by BGP, the protocol routers use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. Routers treat the announcements as alternative routes and often pick the path with fewer hops.

All Internet root name servers use anycast. Many commercial DNS providers switched to it for faster queries, resilience and spread-out load. An early worry was that a long-lived TCP connection could be rerouted to another server midway. In practice this was not observed, and measured failures from instance switches were below 0.017%.

The sharp edge is failure. If a dead server keeps announcing its route, it becomes a black hole for the nearby clients, the most serious failure mode. The automation that withdraws routes can itself fail. And anyone whose announcements are accepted can hijack anycast traffic, so announcements must be filtered.

entries.title: How DNS queries travel: UDP, TCP and encrypted transports

definition.text: DNS queries travel over classic UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports such as DNS over TLS, DNS over HTTPS, DNS over QUIC and DNSCrypt.

facts.text: Classic DNS sends a clear-text request in a single UDP packet to port 53 and gets a clear-text reply in a single UDP packet; with EDNS support, answers longer than 512 bytes may use larger UDP packets.

UDP is limited by its lack of transport-layer encryption, authentication, reliable delivery and message length; RFC 1123 (1989) added optional TCP, which allows longer responses, reliable delivery and reuse of long-lived connections.
UDP suits simple query-response protocols such as DNS, and TCP's complexity can be a problem for servers answering simple requests from huge numbers of clients.
DNS over TLS (2016) protects the entire connection with TLS on TCP port 853; RFC 7858 supports opportunistic and authenticated encryption but did not make server or client authentication mandatory.
DNS over HTTPS (2018) tunnels queries over HTTPS on TCP port 443, so it looks like web traffic, though the two are easily told apart without proper padding.
DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, 2022) has privacy properties similar to DoT and latency characteristics similar to classic DNS over UDP; it is not the same as DNS over HTTP/3.
DNSCrypt (2011), developed outside the IETF, has clients encrypt query payloads with servers' public keys published in the DNS, and uses TCP or UDP port 443.

entries.text:
Classic DNS is startlingly plain. A client sends a clear-text request in a single UDP packet to port 53 and gets a clear-text reply in a single UDP packet. With EDNS support, answers longer than 512 bytes may use larger UDP packets. UDP suits a simple query-response protocol, and TCP's complexity can burden a server that answers simple requests from huge numbers of clients.

Still, UDP is limited by its lack of transport-layer encryption, a way to verify who is talking and reliable delivery, and by message length. RFC 1123, in 1989, added optional TCP, which allows longer responses, reliable delivery and reuse of long-lived connections.

Encrypted transports came later. DNS over TLS, or DoT (2016), protects the entire connection with TLS on TCP port 853. Its standard, RFC 7858, supports opportunistic and authenticated encryption but did not make it mandatory for server or client to authenticate. DoH (2018) is DNS carried over {{ref:sysd-found-048}}. It tunnels queries over TCP port 443, so it looks like web traffic, though the two are easily told apart without proper padding.

DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, 2022) has privacy properties similar to DoT and latency similar to classic DNS over UDP. DNSCrypt (2011), developed outside the IETF, has clients encrypt query payloads with servers' public keys published in the DNS, and uses TCP or UDP port 443.

entries.title: Reading a domain name as a tree
entries.article: Domain Name System#Structure > Domain name space

definition.text: The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each have a label, and a full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots.

facts.text: The domain name space is a tree; each node or leaf has a label and zero or more resource records holding information about that domain name.
A domain name is its label joined by a dot to the name of its parent node on the right, and the rightmost label is the top-level domain: www.example.com belongs to the TLD com.
The hierarchy descends from right to left, each label naming a subdivision of the domain to its right, so www is a subdomain of example.com; the tree may have up to 127 levels.
The tree divides into zones beginning at the root zone, and a zone may contain as many domains and subdomains as its manager chooses.
TLDs come in several types, for example generic TLDs (.com, .org), country code TLDs (.us) and a test TLD (.test).
A label may contain zero to 63 characters and the null label is reserved for the root; a full name may not exceed 253 characters in its textual form.
Hostname labels follow the LDH rule (letters, digits, hyphen), cannot start or end with a hyphen, and are interpreted case-independently.
Applications such as web browsers use IDNA to map Unicode strings into the valid DNS character set with Punycode, which lets names appear in native alphabets.

entries.text:
Read a domain name from right to left and you are walking down a tree. The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each carry a label and zero or more records of information about that name. A full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots, so www.example.com is www joined to example.com. The rightmost label, here com, is the TLD, introduced in {{ref:sysd-found-202}}.

Each label names a subdivision of the domain to its right, and the tree may have up to 127 levels. A label may hold up to 63 characters, and a whole name may not exceed 253 characters in text form. Hostname labels use only letters, digits and hyphens, cannot start or end with a hyphen, and ignore case. To show other alphabets, browsers use IDNA, which maps Unicode strings into that character set with Punycode.

The tree divides into zones beginning at the root zone, and a zone may contain as many domains as its manager chooses.

entries.title: Top-level domains: the last label of every name

definition.text: A top-level domain is the highest level of the DNS hierarchy below the root, the last label of any domain name, such as .com in www.example.com.

facts.text: TLD names are installed in the root zone; ICANN delegates management of most of them to specific organizations and operates IANA, which maintains the DNS root zone.

IANA distinguishes infrastructure (.arpa), generic (gTLD, three or more characters), generic restricted, sponsored (private sponsors set eligibility rules), country-code (ccTLD) and internationalized country-code TLDs.

ccTLDs are two letters and, with some historical exceptions, match the territory's two-letter ISO 3166 code; internationalized ones display in native script but use a Punycode-translated ASCII name in DNS.

.arpa was the first TLD, meant temporarily to ease the move from ARPANET host names, but after being used for reverse DNS it was found impractical to retire; now it serves infrastructure uses such as in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa.

The IETF reserves special-use names such as .example, .invalid, .localhost and .test (RFC 6761), .local for multicast DNS and .onion for Tor; they should not be used in production networks on the global DNS.

Made-up internal names can collide with new TLDs: ICANN rejected .home and .corp over conflicts with networks using them, and local domains such as test.dev collided with the .dev gTLD created in 2019.
A TLD is a DNS node with records of its own; dotless domains put A, AAAA or MX records on a TLD itself, a practice ICANN and the IAB have spoken out against as a security risk.

entries.title: Time to live: giving data an expiry

definition.text: Time to live (TTL), or hop limit, is a mechanism that limits the lifespan of data in a computer or network.

facts.text: A TTL may be a counter or timestamp attached to the data; once the count or time elapses the data is discarded or revalidated, which stops packets circulating forever in networks and manages caching in applications.
In IP, TTL is an 8-bit header field with a maximum of 255, set by the sender and reduced by every router; at zero the datagram is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded error goes back to the sender.
The IP field keeps an undeliverable datagram from circulating until the system is swamped; IPv4 defines it in seconds but in practice it falls by one per hop, so IPv6 renamed it hop limit.

In DNS, the authoritative server sets a TTL per record that tells caching resolvers how long to keep it; HTTP expresses lifetime as an expiry date through Expires, Cache-Control max-age and cookie expires.

entries.title: Resource records: the entries DNS stores

definition.text: Resource records are the information elements of the DNS database, each with a type, a time to live, a class and type-specific data.

facts.text: On the wire every record has NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA fields; the TTL counts the seconds the record stays valid, up to a maximum of 2^31 minus 1, about 68 years.

TYPE gives the data's format and use, RDATA holds the type-specific data such as an address or an MX priority and hostname, and CLASS is IN for ordinary Internet records, each class being an independent name space.
Records of the same type form a resource record set (RRset) with no special ordering; resolvers return the whole set, though servers may use round-robin ordering to balance load.
Wildcard records have names starting with the asterisk label and generate records within a single zone by substituting whole labels with matching components of the query name.

entries.title: Who hands out domain names: registrars and registries

definition.text: The right to use a domain name is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the database of names for each TLD.

facts.text: A registrant is the person or organization that asked for the registration; registrants are customers of the registrar, in some cases through additional subcontracting of resellers.
A registry operates the database of names within its authoritative zone, receives registration information from accredited registrars and publishes it using the WHOIS protocol.
In the registry-registrar model used by COM, NET and ORG, the registry manages only the domain name database and its relationship with the many registrars.
Most gTLD registries have used a thick registry approach since about 2001, keeping WHOIS data centrally; COM and NET use a thin model in which the registry holds only basic WHOIS data.

That right is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the master records of names for each TLD. The registry takes registration information from registrars and publishes it using the WHOIS protocol. entries.title: Before DNS: one file called HOSTS.TXT

definition.text: DNS replaced the single centrally maintained HOSTS.TXT file of ARPANET host names, which became slow and unwieldy as the network grew.

facts.text: Before DNS, one file, HOSTS.TXT, maintained by the Network Information Center, mapped host names to the numerical addresses of ARPANET computers, and all hosts FTPed it.
The bandwidth consumed distributing each new version was proportional to the square of the number of hosts, and the outgoing FTP load on the NIC host was considerable.
Local organizations administered their own names and addresses but had to wait for the NIC to change HOSTS.TXT before changes became visible, and they also wanted local structure in the name space.

By the early 1980s a single centralized host table had become slow and unwieldy; Paul Mockapetris created DNS in 1983, and RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 superseded the original specifications in November 1987.

entries.title: DNS record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS and friends

definition.text: The record types of DNS name the kinds of information a domain publishes, such as addresses (A, AAAA), aliases (CNAME), mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), reverse pointers (PTR), services (SRV) and text (TXT).

facts.text: An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record does the same for an IPv6 address; both are essential for turning domain names into IP addresses.

A CNAME record aliases one domain name to another, often pointing subdomains at the main domain while keeping the actual domain name hidden; it forwards to the other name and does not itself provide an IP address.
An MX record directs email traffic to the correct mail server, which also adds a layer of fault tolerance and load distribution for mail delivery.
An NS record specifies the authoritative DNS servers for a domain and directs queries to the correct servers for further lookups.
A PTR record provides reverse DNS lookup by mapping an IP address back to a domain name, and is commonly used to verify the authenticity of a server.
An SRV record specifies a host and port for services such as VoIP and is used together with A records.
A TXT record lets the administrator attach human-readable text to a domain, for example verification records such as SPF for email security.
The SOA (start of authority) record stores administrative information about a domain and is among the most common types in the DNS database, alongside A, AAAA, MX, NS, PTR and CNAME.

entries.title: Reverse DNS lookup: from address back to name

definition.text: A reverse DNS lookup queries the DNS for the domain names tied to an IP address that is already known.

facts.text: Addresses are stored as PTR records under the infrastructure TLD arpa, in-addr.arpa for IPv4 and ip6.arpa for IPv6, with the address written in reverse order: 208.80.152.2 becomes 2.152.80.208.in-addr.arpa.

The client converts the address into that name and queries for a PTR record, following the delegation chain as for any DNS query; with no PTR record the lookup cannot resolve, and several names may share one IP address.
Email servers commonly use reverse lookups to check that a message came from a valid server, and many reject messages from servers that do not support reverse lookups.

Reverse lookups are not universally adopted because they are not critical to the normal function of the Internet; RFC 1034 says inverse queries are not an acceptable way to map addresses to host names and IN-ADDR.ARPA should be used.

entries.title: CNAME records: one name standing in for another
entries.article: rfc>1034#3. DOMAIN NAME SPACE and RESOURCE RECORDS > 3.6. Resource Records > 3.6.2. Aliases and canonical names

definition.text: A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and names the canonical (primary) name that holds the real data.

facts.text: A resource often has several names: one canonical (primary) name and aliases. A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and gives the canonical name, but provides no IP address itself.
If a node has a CNAME record it should hold no other data, so an alias and its canonical name cannot differ and a cached CNAME can be used without asking an authoritative server about other types.

A server that finds a CNAME instead of the wanted record includes it in the response and restarts the query at the canonical name, except for CNAME-type queries; the resolver does a whole new lookup for that name.
Records that point at another name should use the primary name, not an alias, to avoid extra indirection; software should follow CNAME chains and signal CNAME loops as an error.

entries.title: The rarer DNS records: DNAME, SVCB, CAA, TLSA and more

definition.text: Beyond A, AAAA, MX and NS, DNS defines many more record types for aliases, service discovery, certificates, DNSSEC and zone transfers.

facts.text: A DNAME record aliases a name and all its subnames, unlike CNAME, which aliases only the exact name; non-standard ALIAS or ANAME records synthesize A and AAAA records from a target so the bare domain can be aliased.

TXT began as human-readable text but since the early 1990s mostly carries machine-readable data such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC; SRV gives generalized service location for newer protocols instead of protocol-specific records like MX.

SVCB records give clients connection metadata such as supported protocols and alternative endpoints; the HTTPS record is a specialised SVCB that supplies HTTPS connection details up front, enabling Encrypted Client Hello and lower first-connection latency.
CAA constrains which certificate authorities may issue for a domain, TLSA associates a TLS server certificate or key with a name for DANE, and SSHFP publishes SSH host key fingerprints.
DNSSEC adds RRSIG for signatures, DNSKEY for the zone key, DS to identify a delegated zone's signing key, NSEC to prove a name does not exist, and NSEC3 to prove it without permitting zone walking.

Some types are used in the protocol itself: AXFR transfers a whole zone from primary to secondary, IXFR only the differences since a serial number, ANY returns all cached records, and OPT is the pseudo-record that supports EDNS.
Many early types are obsolete: MX replaced MD and MF, the WKS record is declared not to be relied upon, and HINFO is now repurposed for minimal answers to ANY queries.

entries.title: The three parts of DNS
entries.article: rfc>1034#2. INTRODUCTION > 2.4. Elements of the DNS

definition.text: DNS has three major components: the domain name space with its resource records, name servers that hold the data, and resolvers that extract it for clients.

facts.text: A name server has complete information about a subset of the space, for which it is the authority, plus pointers to other servers; authoritative information is organized into zones distributed to redundant servers.

Resolvers extract information from name servers for client requests, answering directly or following referrals; a resolver is typically a system routine, so no protocol is needed between it and the user program.
To the user DNS is a call to a local resolver over one tree; to the resolver, an unknown number of name servers; to a name server, zones it must refresh from master copies while answering queries.
Implementations may couple these functions for performance: a resolver on the same machine as a name server might share one database of the server's zones and the resolver's cache.

entries.title: What DNS was designed to do

definition.text: DNS was designed to give one consistent name space that is distributed and cached, useful for many applications, and independent of any one network, protocol or host type.

facts.text: The primary goal is a consistent name space, with names that need not contain network identifiers, addresses or routes; the database must be distributed, with local caching, rather than collected as one consistent copy.

Creating and deleting names should be distributed too, and where there are trade-offs between the cost of acquiring data, update speed and cache accuracy, the data's source should control the trade-off.
The facility should serve many applications, so all data is tagged with a type and a class, letting queries target one type and the same name space carry different protocol families' address formats.

Name server transactions should not depend on the transport, whether datagrams for queries or virtual circuits where reliability matters, and the system should suit both personal computers and large timeshared hosts.

entries.title: What a domain registrar does

definition.text: A domain name registrar is a company or office, accredited by a registry, that manages the reservation of Internet domain names for registrants.

facts.text: Registries contract with registrars to serve the public, and only a domain's designated registrar may modify or delete its information in the central registry database.

Registering a domain creates name server records in the parent zone pointing to the domain's authoritative servers, usually at least two; it does not imply DNS hosting, which most registrars offer as an optional service.
For DNSSEC, the registrar processes the owner's public key data and creates DS records for the parent zone; all new gTLD registries and registrars must support DNSSEC.

Changing registrar is a domain transfer under ICANN's transfer policy: the owner unlocks the domain and gets an authentication code from the old registrar, and the new registrar must obtain express authorization from the holder.

entries.title: Subdomains: splitting a site into sections

definition.text: A subdomain is an extra part added to a main domain name, commonly used to split a website into logical sections.

facts.text: Multiple subdomains or child domains can be created on a main domain, and they are commonly used to logically separate a website into sections.
In blog.example.com, blog is the subdomain, example is the primary domain and .com is the top-level domain; support.example.com and careers.example.com are similar examples.
Each subdomain can be delegated to its own manager as a zone of administrative autonomy.

entries.title: How a DNS lookup works, step by step
entries.article: Domain Name System#Operation > Address resolution mechanism

definition.text: To resolve a name, a resolver asks a root server, then a top-level domain server, then the domain's authoritative server, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer.

facts.text: Resolvers find the responsible servers through queries that begin with the rightmost (top-level) label, and each host is configured with hints, an initial cache of the known addresses of the root name servers.
With no cached records, resolution starts at a root server; roots usually do not answer directly but refer the resolver onward, so a query for www.wikipedia.org is referred to the org servers.
The resolver queries the servers it was referred to and repeats this iteratively until it receives an authoritative answer.

The three levels of DNS servers are the root name servers, which hold the addresses of TLD name servers; the TLD servers, which hold the addresses of authoritative servers; and the authoritative servers, which give the actual answer.
For google.com, the browser hands the name to the DNS resolver, which asks a root server for the .com TLD server, asks that server for the domain's authoritative name server, and queries it.
The authoritative name server returns the IP address for google.com to the resolver, which passes it back to the web browser.
There are 13 logical root name servers, and thirteen groups of root servers exist with additional copies distributed worldwide by anycast addressing.

Starting every lookup at the root would put a large burden on the root servers, so caching in DNS servers off-loads them and roots handle only a small fraction of all requests; lookups average 20-120 milliseconds, according to YSlow.

Roots usually do not answer directly but refer the resolver onward, so a query for www.wikipedia.org is referred to the org servers. The resolver repeats this, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer. Each host is configured with hints, an initial cache of the known addresses of the root name servers.

Starting every lookup at the root would put a large burden on the roots. There are 13 logical root name servers, with additional copies spread worldwide by anycast addressing. Caches in DNS servers keep the roots to a small fraction of all requests.

entries.title: The resolver: DNS's client side

definition.text: The client side of DNS, which initiates and sequences the queries that end in a full resolution, such as turning a domain name into an IP address.

facts.text: A resolver is a program that sits between user programs and name servers, on the same machine as the program it serves; because it may consult several servers or its cache, it can take from milliseconds to several seconds.

Applications ask the resolver in the local operating system, which answers from its cache of recent lookups if it can and otherwise queries designated DNS servers, usually the ISP's, set up manually or through DHCP.
The resolver caches the result for future use and hands it back to the software that asked.

A recursive resolver is the first stop in a DNS query and a middleman between client and name servers: it answers from cache or asks a root, then a TLD, then an authoritative name server, and replies to the client.

Caching DNS servers store results for the record's time-to-live and usually also implement recursion from the root down; ISPs typically provide such servers, and many home routers implement DNS caches and recursion.
With only authoritative servers operating, every query would have to start with recursive queries at the root zone and each user system would need resolver software capable of recursion.

entries.title: DNS caches and the TTL: why changes take time

definition.text: DNS reduces query load by caching resolution results locally or on intermediary resolvers, each result carrying a time to live (TTL) that says how long it stays valid.

facts.text: A key goal of the resolver is to remove network delay and name server load from most requests by answering from its cache, and caches shared by many processes, users or machines are more efficient than unshared ones.

The authoritative server's administrator sets the TTL, from a few seconds to several days or weeks; RFC 1912 gives 1 to 5 days as typical and 1 to 2 weeks for rarely changing records; some resolvers override TTLs.
A cached record keeps its TTL, which the server counts down every second; at zero the record is purged and the next query for it must start the resolution process again.

Because caching is distributed, record changes do not propagate immediately but only after all caches expire and refresh after the TTL; TTLs can be lowered before a change, at the cost of more network traffic.
RFC 1034 makes negative caching an optional service: a name error can be distributed with a TTL, and the SOA record's MINIMUM field limits how long the negative result may be cached.
Wikipedia describes the negative-answer TTL as set from the SOA's minimum field together with the SOA's own TTL, which reflects later practice than RFC 1034's MINIMUM-only rule.
Caching in DNS servers keeps the root name servers involved in only a small fraction of all requests.
Web browsers often keep an internal DNS cache, typically for around one minute, which obscures the history of the data and makes DNS issues harder to debug; some large ISPs even disobey TTLs.

entries.title: Spreading load with DNS

definition.text: DNS can spread traffic and add fault tolerance because hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one: one name can resolve to many addresses and different users can get different answers.

facts.text: A single hostname can resolve to many IP addresses to give fault tolerance and load distribution across server instances in an enterprise or across the Internet.

Distributed services such as cloud services and CDNs translate a domain name to the IP address of a server near the user, because different users can receive different answers for the same name at the same time.
Assigning nearby servers through DNS is key to faster and more reliable Internet responses and is widely used by most major Internet services.
Servers may use round-robin ordering of a record set to balance load, and an MX record can provide an extra layer of fault tolerance and load distribution for mail.
Multiple hostnames can map to a single IP address for virtual hosting; the HTTP Host header then tells the server which name was requested, allowing name-based virtual hosting.

entries.text:
Ask DNS for the same name from two places and you may get two different answers. That is deliberate. Hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one, so a single hostname can resolve to many addresses. That gives resilience to failures and spreads load across server instances in an enterprise or across the Internet.

Cloud services and CDNs go further. They translate a name into the address of a server near the user, because different users can receive different answers for the same name at the same time. Assigning nearby servers through DNS is key to faster and more reliable responses, and most major Internet services use it.

Servers may also rotate the order of a record set to balance load, and records of type MX can do the same for mail. The reverse works too. Many hostnames can map to one IP address for virtual hosting, and the Host header of a web request then tells the server which name was asked for.

entries.title: How DNS can be attacked

definition.text: DNS was designed without strong security, so responses can be forged or abused, and extensions such as DNSSEC and TSIG were added to authenticate them.

facts.text: In DNS cache poisoning, data is fed to caching resolvers as though from an authoritative server, polluting the cache with false information and long TTLs, so legitimate requests may be redirected to malicious hosts.

DNS responses traditionally carry no cryptographic signature; DNSSEC adds signed responses, while TSIG adds authentication between trusted peers and is commonly used to authorize zone transfers and dynamic updates.
Because DNS is often seen as innocuous and passes firewalls, it can leak from private connections or carry malware commands in TXT records, as in DNSMessenger, and be used to exfiltrate data.
Lookalike names such as paypal.com and paypa1.com can be indistinguishable in some fonts, an IDN homograph attack that is occasionally exploited in phishing.

entries.title: Recursive, iterative and non-recursive queries

definition.text: Resolvers are classified by query method: in a recursive query a server resolves the name fully on the client's behalf, in an iterative query the client follows referrals, and a non-recursive query needs no further rounds.

facts.text: Resolvers are classified by query method as recursive, non-recursive or iterative, and a single resolution may combine them.

In a recursive query the client asks one server, which answers completely by querying other name servers as needed, or returns an error; a stub resolver on a home router typically does this against the ISP's server.

In an iterative query the resolver asks a chain of servers, each referring it to the next until one can fully resolve the request: for www.example.com, a root server, then a com server, then an example.com server.
In a non-recursive query the server already has the answer, from its cache or as an authoritative server, or returns a partial result, so no further rounds of queries are needed.

Typically a client sends a recursive query to a caching recursive server, which issues non-recursive queries and returns a single answer; use of recursion is negotiated with bits in the query headers.

RFC 1034 requires name servers to implement the iterative approach, which suits datagram access, and allows the recursive approach as an option, so DNS servers are not required to support recursive queries.

entries.title: DNSSEC: signing DNS answers

definition.text: DNSSEC is a suite of IETF extensions that secures DNS data by adding digital signatures, so resolvers can detect forged or altered answers.

facts.text: The original DNS design had no security features; DNSSEC adds them while keeping backward compatibility, to stop applications accepting forged or manipulated DNS data such as that created by DNS cache poisoning.
DNSSEC gives cryptographic authentication of data, authenticated denial of existence and data integrity, but not availability or confidentiality: responses are authenticated but not encrypted.

All answers from a DNSSEC-protected zone are signed, so a resolver can check that the data is unmodified and complete as published by the zone owner; any DNS data can be protected, such as TXT and MX records.
DNSSEC signs record sets with public-key cryptography: each answer carries an RRSIG record, a signature checked with the public key found in a DNSKEY record.
A DS record placed in the parent zone refers to a DNSKEY record in the delegated zone, and NSEC or NSEC3 records give cryptographic evidence that a record does not exist.

A security-aware resolver sets the DO flag in its query; the flag lives in the EDNS extended flags, so all DNSSEC transactions must support EDNS, which also allows the much larger packets DNSSEC needs.
DNSSEC does not protect directly against DoS attacks and cannot protect against false assumptions about names; other standards secure bulk transfers between servers such as zone transfers.

Deployment has been hampered by the need for a backward-compatible standard that scales, preventing zone enumeration, rolling out across many servers and resolvers, disagreement over root key ownership, and perceived complexity.

entries.title: Round-robin DNS: simple load spreading

definition.text: Round-robin DNS spreads load across several servers by answering a name lookup with a list of IP addresses whose order is rotated on each response.

facts.text: The DNS holds several A records for one name, one per server hosting identical content; each response permutes the address list and clients normally try the first address, so successive users reach different servers.
Some resolvers reorder the list to favor numerically closer networks, which was standardized in RFC 3484 for IPv6; a Windows Vista bug on IPv4 once defeated the balancing.
Record caching in the DNS hierarchy and client-side address caching make round-robin DNS hard to manage, even though it is easy to implement.

It should not be relied on alone for availability: if a service at one listed address fails, DNS keeps handing out that address, though some desktop clients try alternates after a timeout of up to 30 seconds.

It only alternates the order of records and ignores transaction time, server load and congestion, so it suits many uniformly distributed connections to equal servers; otherwise it just distributes load.
Modified DNS servers can poll mirrored servers for availability and load and temporarily remove a server from the DNS pool until it reports being within specs again.

entries.title: DNS cache poisoning: teaching a resolver a lie

definition.text: DNS cache poisoning, also called DNS spoofing, introduces corrupt data into a resolver's cache so that it returns a wrong answer, such as an attacker's IP address.

facts.text: When a DNS server caches a false translation it is poisoned and supplies the false data to clients, diverting their traffic to a computer the attacker chooses until the cache entry expires.
Poisoning a single DNS server affects the users it serves directly and those served by its downstream servers; the attacker exploits flaws in the DNS software.
A poisoned server can send users to a fake site for phishing or malware, and opens them to further risks such as denial of service and website hijacking.

In one variant a vulnerable server caches the extra A record for the target domain's name server from an answer about the attacker's own domain, letting the attacker resolve queries for the whole target domain.
Many attacks are prevented by being less trusting of other servers and ignoring any returned records not directly relevant to the query.

Source port randomization with cryptographically secure random numbers for the port and the 16-bit nonce greatly reduces the chance of a successful race attack, but NAT devices may rewrite source ports and remove the randomness.

DNSSEC counters cache poisoning with digital signatures that authenticate the data; where it is missing, end-to-end validation such as TLS certificate checks over HTTPS mitigates the attack at the transport or application layer.

entries.title: Who can read your DNS queries?
entries.article: Domain Name System#Privacy and tracking issues

definition.text: Because DNS has no confidentiality controls, queries are exposed, and the ways of protecting them are themselves argued over.

facts.text: Designed as a public, heavily cached database, DNS has no confidentiality controls: unencrypted queries and responses allow sniffing, hijacking, cache poisoning and man-in-the-middle attacks.

Defenses include VPNs, which move resolution to the VPN operator, Tor, and proxies or public DNS servers, which move resolution to a trusted third party; some public servers support DoH, DoT and DNSCrypt.
Solutions that stop the local network operator inspecting DNS are criticized for thwarting corporate security policies and Internet censorship.
Public DNS servers are criticized for centralizing control of resolution in the few large companies that can afford to run public resolvers.

entries.title: Root servers and TLD servers

definition.text: Root name servers direct resolvers to the right top-level domain servers, and TLD name servers hold the information for every domain under one extension such as .com.

facts.text: A root server answers requests for records in the root zone and otherwise directs the resolver to the TLD name servers for the domain's extension, such as .com, .net or .org.
The root zone file, about 2 MB, lists the authoritative servers for all TLDs; a root server answers with a referral to the right TLD servers or says that no such TLD exists.
Only thirteen root server addresses exist because the original DNS limits UDP packets to 512 bytes; IPv6 addresses need more, which the EDNS0 extension allows.

The root system is far more than 13 machines: each operator runs redundant equipment in many locations using anycast addressing, so there are about 1954 instances for better performance and fault tolerance.

A resolver bootstraps from hints, a small root.hints file of root server addresses, which breaks the circular need to know a root server's address before resolving anything; caching keeps root lookups infrequent.
A TLD name server maintains information for all domain names sharing an extension, the part after the last dot, and answers with the address of the domain's authoritative name server.
TLD servers fall into two main groups: generic TLDs such as .com, .org, .net, .edu and .gov, and country code TLDs such as .uk, .us, .ru and .jp.
Each TLD is maintained and serviced technically by an administrative organization that operates a registry.

entries.title: The stub resolver: DNS work done elsewhere
entries.article: rfc>1034#5. RESOLVERS > 5.3. Resolver internals > 5.3.1. Stub resolvers

definition.text: A stub resolver moves the resolution work off the local machine and into a name server that supports recursive queries, keeping only a list of such servers.

facts.text: Moving resolution into a recursive name server gives a PC that lacks the resources to resolve names an easy way to use DNS, and can centralize the cache for a whole local network or organization.
The stub needs only a configured list of name server addresses that will perform recursive requests, and a name server is free to refuse recursive service to any or all clients.
A simple stub resolver on a home router typically makes a recursive query to the DNS server run by the user's ISP.

The drawbacks are that recursive requests take arbitrary time, so the stub struggles to tune retransmissions for lost UDP packets and dead servers, and the server can be overloaded if it treats retransmissions as new requests.

entries.title: The authoritative name server: the source of truth
entries.article: Domain Name System#Structure > Name servers > Authoritative name server

definition.text: A name server that answers DNS queries only from data configured by an original source, such as the domain administrator, rather than from a cache of another server's answers.

facts.text: Each domain has at least one authoritative server that publishes information about the domain and about the name servers of any domains subordinate to it.
An authoritative server is either primary, holding the original copies of all zone records, or secondary, which keeps an identical copy through an automatic updating mechanism in the DNS protocol.
A zone's set of authoritative name servers is stored in the parent zone as NS records; RFC 1034 requires every zone to be available on at least two servers so it survives host or link failure.
An authoritative server marks its answers as definitive by setting the Authoritative Answer (AA) bit; a server named as authoritative for a domain it has no data for causes a lame delegation.
The authoritative name server is usually the resolver's last stop: it holds information specific to its domain, such as the A record, and returns NXDOMAIN if it cannot find the domain.
Dynamic DNS updates use the UPDATE opcode to add or remove records in the zone database on an authoritative server, for example to register network clients when they boot.
The authoritative name server provides the actual answer to a DNS query, and you register authoritative name servers with a domain name registrar.

entries.title: Delegation: handing a piece of the namespace to someone else

definition.text: Delegation is the mechanism that assigns responsibility for different parts of the DNS namespace to different name servers.

facts.text: Responsibility for a zone can be divided by creating additional zones; authority over the new zone is delegated to a designated name server and the parent zone stops being authoritative for it.
Each public domain under the TLDs is delegated through an NS record in the parent domain that points to the DNS names of the name servers of the child domain.
Name servers in a delegation are identified by name rather than address, so a resolver must issue another DNS request to find the address of the server it was referred to.
If the delegated name server is a subdomain of the domain it serves, there is a circular dependency, and the delegating server must supply the server's IP addresses as glue.
A glue record combines a name server and an IP address; the delegating server returns glue in the additional section of its response and the delegation in the authority section.

For example, resolving www.example.org needs ns1.example.org, which needs example.org first; the org TLD name server breaks the loop by including address records for ns1.example.org along with the delegation.
