entries.title: Shared and private HTTP caches: whose copy is it

definition.text: A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and sits usually in an intermediary, while a private cache is dedicated to one user, often inside a user agent.

facts.text: The private response directive stops a shared cache from storing a response meant for one user, but a private cache may store it.
A shared cache needs extra permission to reuse a response to an Authorization request, and s-maxage applies only to shared caches.
Private caches are limited to one user, so they can be used to reconstruct that user's activity and users should be able to remove stored responses.

entries.title: HTTP cache security risks: poisoning, timing and leaks

definition.text: Caches add an attack surface, because their contents persist after a request ends and an attack on a cache can reveal or alter information long afterwards.

facts.text: In cache poisoning an attacker inserts a malicious response into a cache, which is especially effective when a shared cache distributes it to many clients; one vector is differences in message parsing between proxies and user agents.
Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited; adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it.
Deployment flaws can cache sensitive information, such as authentication credentials, and a cacheable response with Set-Cookie can be reused for later requests.

entries.title: Transport Layer Security: three jobs in one protocol

definition.text: TLS is a cryptographic protocol that provides secured communications over a computer network, giving applications privacy, integrity and authenticity.

facts.text: TLS does three things: encryption hides the data from third parties, authentication ensures the parties are who they claim to be, and integrity verifies the data has not been forged or tampered with.
TLS is used in email, instant messaging and voice over IP, but securing HTTPS is its most visible use; a primary use is encrypting communication between web applications and servers.
TLS evolved from SSL and is an IETF standard first defined in 1999; the current version is TLS 1.3, defined in August 2018.
TLS is made of two layers, the record protocol and the handshake protocol, and runs on top of a reliable transport such as TCP.

Because applications can run with or without TLS, the client must ask the server for a TLS connection, either with a separate port (443 for HTTPS rather than 80 for HTTP) or with a protocol-specific STARTTLS request.
The handshake uses an asymmetric cipher to set the cipher parameters and a session-specific shared key, and further communication is encrypted with a symmetric cipher.

A TLS connection is private because a symmetric key, unique to each connection and negotiated at the start, encrypts the data; it is authenticated with public-key cryptography, required for the server and optional for the client.
Each message carries a message authentication code, so lost or altered data is detected.

entries.title: HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel

definition.text: HTTPS is HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so web traffic is private, authenticated and protected from tampering in transit.

facts.text: The main motivations for HTTPS are authentication of the accessed website and protection of the privacy and integrity of exchanged data in transit.
HTTPS is not a separate protocol but ordinary HTTP over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection; its URLs begin with https:// and use port 443 by default, while HTTP uses port 80.

Plain HTTP is not encrypted, so it is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle and eavesdropping attacks that expose accounts and sensitive information or inject malware and advertisements into pages; HTTPS is designed to withstand them.
Because HTTP runs entirely on top of TLS, the URL, query parameters, headers, cookies and message data can all be encrypted.
Usually only the server is authenticated, by the client examining its certificate, which a trusted third party must sign; TLS still protects the channel when only one side is authenticated.
TLS typically uses long-term public and private keys to generate a short-term session key that encrypts the data flow between client and server; a hijacker of the traffic gets only binary data.
For HTTPS to be effective a whole site must be served over it: loading scripts or images over HTTP, or only a login page over HTTPS, leaves users open to attacks and surveillance.
Deploying HTTPS also allows HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, which are designed to reduce page load times, size and latency.

entries.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything

definition.text: A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, or on-path attack, is one where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly.

facts.text: In active eavesdropping the attacker makes independent connections with both victims and relays messages, controlling the whole conversation; this needs intercepting all relevant messages and injecting new ones, which is easy near an unencrypted Wi-Fi access point.
The attack succeeds only if the attacker impersonates each endpoint well enough to satisfy it, since it aims to circumvent mutual authentication.

Mallory replaces Bob's public key with her own, so Alice encrypts to Mallory, who decrypts, reads or alters the message and re-encrypts it with Bob's key; the parties need a way to know they hold real keys.

Variants include HTTPS spoofing with a fake certificate, SSL/TLS stripping that downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, ARP spoofing, DNS spoofing, session hijacking, evil-twin Wi-Fi and certificates signed by a fraudulent CA.

Defenses are authentication and tamper detection; most cryptographic protocols authenticate endpoints, for example TLS authenticating one or both parties through a mutually trusted certificate authority, and DNSSEC signs DNS records against redirects to malicious IPs.
Mutual authentication, where server and client validate each other, covers both ends, but most connections authenticate only the server, so MITM attacks can still occur.
Tamper detection can notice an attack through abnormal response times, because an interceptor adds latency to a transaction.

The attacker does not break the encryption: after decrypting a message, the snoop re-encrypts it with a key shared with the real recipient, or their public key in asymmetric systems, and sends it on to avoid detection.

entries.title: Securing cookies against theft, scripts and forgery
entries.article: HTTP cookie#Cookie theft and session hijacking

definition.text: Securing cookies means protecting the session identifiers that cookies carry from theft and misuse, using encryption, cookie attributes and input filtering.

facts.text: Most sites use cookies as the only identifier of a user session, so an attacker who steals a victim's full set of cookies is treated by the server as the victim's session.

Cookies sent over unencrypted HTTP can be read by anyone on the network, such as on open Wi-Fi; TLS fixes this, and the Secure attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over an encrypted channel.
A Secure cookie set from a non-secure connection can still be intercepted by a man-in-the-middle attack, so Secure cookies should only be set over a secure connection.

Cross-site scripting steals cookies by getting attacker JavaScript to send document.cookie to the attacker; an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by client-side scripts, which mitigates this, though developers must still filter malicious code.

Cross-site request forgery abuses automatic cookie sending: browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie.

SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates CSRF; Lax also allows safe requests such as GET; None allows cross-site cookies, and most browsers require Secure with it.

entries.text: Steal a user's cookies and, to most servers, you are that user. Most sites use cookies as the only identifier of a user session. An attacker who steals a victim's full set of cookies is therefore treated by the server as the victim's session. Securing cookies means protecting those identifiers from theft and misuse. Cookies sent over unencrypted HTTP can be read by anyone on the network, such as on open Wi-Fi. TLS fixes this, and the Secure attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over an encrypted channel. Attackers can also steal cookies with {{ref:sysd-reliab-127}}, by getting their JavaScript to send document.cookie to them. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by client-side scripts, which mitigates this. A second danger is {{ref:sysd-reliab-129}}, which abuses automatic cookie sending. Browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie. SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates it.

entries.title: Datagram TLS: security for UDP applications
entries.article: Transport Layer Security#Description > Datagram Transport Layer Security

definition.text: Datagram TLS (DTLS) is a protocol based on TLS that secures datagram-based applications against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery.

facts.text: DTLS is intended to give security guarantees similar to TLS but works with datagram protocols such as UDP, not only stream protocols.

Because it preserves the semantics of the underlying transport, an application avoids the delays of stream protocols but must handle packet reordering, datagram loss and data larger than one datagram.
Using UDP or SCTP rather than TCP avoids the TCP meltdown problem when creating a VPN tunnel.
All modern web browsers support DTLS-SRTP for WebRTC.

entries.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security: never again without HTTPS

definition.text: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) lets a website tell browsers to use only HTTPS connections to it, protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking.

facts.text: A server sets the policy with the Strict-Transport-Security response header, which is honored only over an HTTPS connection; max-age is in seconds, so max-age=31536000 keeps the policy for one non-leap year.

While a policy is in effect the browser rewrites insecure links to https before contacting the server, and must end the connection, without letting the user continue, if it cannot be secured, such as when the certificate is untrusted.
HSTS fixes SSL stripping, where an attacker silently turns an HTTPS connection into plain HTTP with no warning; without it the user cannot know whether the connection should have been secure.

Protection relies on trust on first use: the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected, and an attacker can strip the header on a first visit; sites should set a period of days or months.
Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS; domains can be added at no cost, but such a list cannot scale to cover every website.
Best practice is for an HSTS host to answer with the header at its top-level domain too, with the includeSubDomains directive, which helps avoid threats such as cookie injection attacks.

HSTS cannot stop attacks on TLS itself or on a compromised server, is ineffective against look-alike or spoofed domains, and, being time limited, can be defeated by shifting the victim's clock with false NTP packets.
Because browsers must persistently cache the policy and RFC 6797 makes deleting it deliberately hard, HSTS state can tag a visiting browser with identifying data that survives clearing cookies.

entries.title: HTTP origins: why the browser checks the certificate matches
entries.article: rfc>9110#4. Identifiers in HTTP > 4.3. Authoritative Access > 4.3.4. https Certificate Verification

definition.text: An origin is the scheme, host and port of a URI, and for https URIs a client must verify that the server's certificate matches that origin before trusting the connection.

facts.text: The origin of a URI is the triple of scheme, host and port after normalization.

For http, authority belongs to whoever controls the server listening on the port; for https, it rests on the server's ability to use the private key matching a certificate the client trusts for that origin.

A client must verify that the service's identity matches the URI's origin server, to prevent impersonation by an on-path attacker or one controlling name resolution; this requires configured trust anchors.

If the certificate is not valid for the origin, the user agent must get user confirmation or end the connection with a bad certificate error, since ignoring the server's identity leaves the connection open to active attack.

entries.title: SSL: the old name that will not go away

definition.text: SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, is a protocol for encrypting and securing communications on the internet, now deprecated in favor of TLS.

facts.text: SSL was first developed in 1995 and has since been deprecated in favor of TLS, yet most major certificate providers still call certificates SSL certificates.
Web data was originally sent in plaintext that anyone who intercepted it could read, and SSL was created to fix this and protect user privacy.
By encrypting data between the user and a web server, SSL also stops certain attacks by preventing tampering with data in transit.

entries.title: Forward secrecy: keeping old conversations safe from future theft

definition.text: Forward secrecy is a property of a cryptographic system that keeps a session key safe even if one of the private keys is compromised in the future.

facts.text: Without forward secrecy, a compromised server private key exposes all future sessions that use its certificate and also any past sessions that were intercepted and stored.
TLS can provide it by requiring ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish session keys; only the DHE and ECDHE exchanges provide forward secrecy.
Having one of the long-term asymmetric keys used to establish an HTTPS session should not make it easier to derive the short-term session key and decrypt the conversation later.
TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy by using ephemeral keys in the key agreement and drops support for ciphers and key exchanges without it, such as static RSA.
Many clients and servers are not configured to require it, so without Diffie-Hellman a third party that obtains the server's private key can decrypt all recorded traffic.
Session tickets and weak Diffie-Hellman parameters can weaken the forward secrecy a server tries to provide.

entries.title: TLS versions: from 1.0 to 1.3

definition.text: TLS has gone through versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, each defined in an RFC and each revised to address security threats.

facts.text: TLS 1.1 was defined in RFC 4346 in April 2006, TLS 1.2 in RFC 5246 in August 2008, and TLS 1.3 in RFC 8446 in August 2018.
TLS 1.3 supports 1-RTT handshakes with initial 0-RTT support and mandates perfect forward secrecy through ephemeral keys in the (EC)DH key agreement.
TLS 1.3 drops insecure or obsolete features, including compression, renegotiation, non-AEAD ciphers and static RSA and static DH key exchanges, and it prohibits SSL or RC4 negotiation.
TLS 1.3 encrypts all handshake messages after the ServerHello, including the server certificate.

entries.title: The TLS handshake: from hello to a shared secret
entries.article: Transport Layer Security#Protocol details > TLS handshake

definition.text: In the TLS handshake the client and server agree on cipher parameters, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive a shared session key for the secured connection.

facts.text: The client sends a ClientHello with the highest TLS version it supports, a random number, and its suggested cipher suites and compression methods; the server answers with a ServerHello choosing from them, ideally the highest version both support.

The server usually sends a digital certificate holding its name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and its public key; the client confirms the certificate is valid before proceeding.
In older TLS and SSL the client encrypts a random PreMasterSecret with the server's public key and the server decrypts it with its private key; both then derive the session key from it.

Alternatively Diffie-Hellman key exchange, or its elliptic-curve variant, generates the session key with forward secrecy; TLS 1.3 eliminated the PreMasterSecret approach when it mandated forward secrecy.
Both sides compute a master secret from the random numbers and key material, and all other key data for the connection, such as the encryption key and MAC key, is derived from it.

Each side then sends a Finished message, authenticated and encrypted, containing a hash and MAC over the previous handshake messages, and the other side verifies it; if any verification fails, the handshake fails and no connection is created.
Once the handshake completes, both sides hold the same session key and data flows over a secure bi-directional channel, encrypted and decrypted with that key until the connection closes.
The TLS 1.3 handshake takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need, because the client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello.

entries.title: Server Name Indication: which site does the client want
entries.article: Transport Layer Security#Support for name-based virtual servers

definition.text: Server Name Indication is a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so a server hosting several sites can send the right certificate.

facts.text: The TLS handshake happens before the application protocol starts, so the server must choose a certificate right after the ClientHello and co-hosted name-based virtual servers would share one certificate.
This forces a hosting provider to share one certificate among customers or give each customer its own IP address.

Two X.509 workarounds exist: a wildcard certificate when all virtual servers share a domain, or listing every virtual host name in the subjectAltName extension, which needs reissuing whenever a server is added.
SNI sends the host name before the connection is encrypted, although older browsers do not support it.

entries.title: TLS cipher suites and key exchange methods
entries.article: Transport Layer Security#Algorithms > Key exchange or key agreement

definition.text: Before sending protected data, a TLS client and server must agree on an encryption key and a cipher, choosing among several key exchange, cipher and integrity methods.

facts.text: The client presents the cipher suites (ciphers and hash functions) it supports and the server picks one it also supports and tells the client.
Key exchange or agreement methods include RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, their elliptic-curve variants, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, pre-shared key and Secure Remote Password.

Anonymous Diffie-Hellman does not authenticate the server or user and is rarely used because it is open to man-in-the-middle attacks, and only the ephemeral DHE and ECDHE methods provide forward secrecy.
A message authentication code protects data integrity: HMAC is used for CBC mode block ciphers, while authenticated encryption such as GCM and CCM has an integrated MAC.

entries.title: TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things

definition.text: TLS 1.3 is the current version of Transport Layer Security, designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery between client and server applications.

facts.text: TLS gives a secure channel over any reliable, in-order stream: the server is always authenticated and the client optionally, data is visible only to the endpoints, and tampering is detected even if an attacker controls the network.

TLS has two components: a handshake protocol that authenticates the parties, negotiates parameters and establishes keys, and is designed to resist tampering, and a record protocol that protects traffic in independently protected records.

TLS 1.3 pruned legacy features: only AEAD ciphers remain, static RSA and Diffie-Hellman suites are gone so all public-key key exchange gives forward secrecy, and compression and custom DHE groups were removed.
The handshake has three phases, key exchange, server parameters and authentication, and every handshake message after the ServerHello is now encrypted.

The ClientHello carries a random nonce, offered versions, cipher and hash pairs, and Diffie-Hellman key shares, PSK labels or both; the server's ServerHello selects the parameters, and the two messages together determine the shared keys.

Authentication uses a Certificate, a CertificateVerify that signs the entire handshake with the certificate's private key, and a Finished MAC over the handshake that confirms the keys; the client sends them too when asked.

If the client's key_share is unacceptable, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one; if no common parameters can be negotiated, the server MUST abort the handshake.

TLS supports three basic key exchange modes, including (EC)DHE and PSK with (EC)DHE, and key derivation was redesigned around HKDF, which cryptographers can analyze more easily thanks to better key separation.

entries.title: TLS interception: reading traffic that was encrypted

definition.text: TLS interception is decrypting, reading and re-encrypting an encrypted data stream in transit, usually through a transparent proxy.

facts.text: The interception software terminates the incoming TLS connection, inspects the HTTP plaintext, and opens a new TLS connection to the destination.
Network operators use it to scan for malware that encryption would otherwise hide.

It creates risks of its own: traffic is unencrypted at the interception point, which attracts attackers, and the operator or anyone who gains access to the system can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on users.

entries.title: What HTTPS does not protect

definition.text: HTTPS protects content in transit but leaves some information visible and depends on correct implementation and on clients actually using it.

facts.text: Website addresses and port numbers are part of the underlying TCP/IP protocols, so an eavesdropper can still see the server's IP address and port, sometimes the domain name, and the amount and duration of traffic.
Traffic analysis can infer properties of encrypted traffic because TLS changes the contents but has minimal impact on the size and timing of traffic.
SSL stripping turns an https link into an http link so the attacker talks in clear with the client; HTTP Strict Transport Security is the countermeasure and is recommended alongside HTTPS.
The level of protection depends on correct implementation of the software and the cryptographic algorithms in use.

entries.title: Starting an HTTP/2 connection: ALPN, h2 and the preface

definition.text: An HTTP/2 connection starts with TLS and the ALPN extension for https URIs, or with prior knowledge for cleartext http, and each side then sends a connection preface.

facts.text: An http or https URI does not say which HTTP versions the server supports; for https the client uses TLS with the ALPN extension and the identifier h2, and both sides MUST then send a connection preface.

Support over cleartext http can only be known out of band; a client with that prior knowledge opens a TCP connection and sends the preface, and the h2c Upgrade mechanism was never widely deployed and is deprecated.

The client preface is the 24-octet string PRI * HTTP/2.0 followed by SETTINGS, the server's first frame is a SETTINGS frame, and clients may send more frames at once without waiting for the server's preface.
HTTP/2 over TLS MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher with the SNI extension, and over TLS 1.2 deployments MUST disable TLS compression and renegotiation.

entries.title: Mutual TLS: when the client proves itself too

definition.text: Mutual TLS, or mTLS, is a method of mutual authentication in which both ends of a connection verify that the other holds the correct private key.

facts.text: TLS can run in a simple mode, where only the server authenticates, or a mutual mode, which requires the user to install a personal client certificate in the browser.
In a client-authenticated handshake the server requests a certificate, and the client sends its certificate plus a signature made with its private key, which proves it owns the certificate.
mTLS keeps traffic secure and trusted in both directions between client and server, adding a layer of security for users logging in to an organization's network or applications.
Microservices and distributed systems commonly use mTLS to verify each other in a zero trust security model.

entries.title: Types of TLS certificate: server, client, SAN and wildcard

definition.text: TLS certificates come in several types by what they identify: servers, clients, several names at once, or whole families of subdomains.

facts.text: A server certificate proves the server is the intended destination; a client certificate authenticates the client for access control, usually names a person, and is issued by the service provider, though username and password is more common.

A Subject Alternative Name (SAN) certificate lists several values, such as DNS names and IP addresses, in its subjectAltName field; SANs are the preferred place for DNS names, and Chrome 58 stopped checking commonName at all.

A wildcard certificate uses an asterisk so one certificate secures many subdomains, but only one level: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, not example.com or deeper names; an Extended Validation certificate cannot be a wildcard.

Other certificates include S/MIME email certificates, code-signing certificates that show binaries were not tampered with, qualified certificates identifying an individual for electronic signatures, and EMV payment-card issuer certificates.

entries.title: Why HTTPS switches to symmetric keys for the data
entries.article: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/how-does-https-work.md#Why does HTTPS switch to symmetric encryption during data transmission?

definition.text: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption only to set up a session key and then switches to symmetric encryption for the data.

facts.text: Once client and server hold the same session key, the encrypted data travels over a secure bi-directional channel using symmetric encryption.
Asymmetric encryption works only one way, so data the server encrypted for the client could be decrypted by anyone holding the public key.
Asymmetric encryption adds a lot of mathematical overhead for the server, so it is not suitable for data transmission in long sessions.

entries.title: TLS session resumption: skipping the expensive part
entries.article: rfc>8446#2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Resumption and Pre-Shared Key (PSK)

definition.text: A resumed TLS session reuses the results of an earlier handshake, through a session ID, a session ticket or, in TLS 1.3, a pre-shared key, so the handshake can skip expensive public-key operations.

facts.text: Public key operations such as RSA are relatively expensive in computational power, and resumed sessions give a secure shortcut around them.

With session IDs the server maps the ID to the previously negotiated master secret and the client sends the ID on reconnecting; both sides must hold the same master secret or the resumed handshake fails.
With session tickets the server stores its session state in an encrypted and authenticated ticket that the client keeps and presents later, so the server stores no per-session state.
Session tickets can undermine forward secrecy, because long-lived ticket keys defeat the protection of forward secrecy cipher suites.

TLS 1.3 replaces session IDs and tickets with one PSK exchange: the server sends a ticket after the handshake, the client offers it in a later ClientHello, and if accepted its key bootstraps the new connection without a full handshake.

A PSK combined with (EC)DHE keeps forward secrecy, while a PSK alone loses it for application data; the client SHOULD also send a key_share so the server can decline and fall back to a full handshake.

A ticket is an opaque label, either a database lookup key or a self-encrypted, self-authenticated value; servers MUST NOT set a lifetime above 604800 seconds (7 days), and clients MUST NOT cache a ticket longer than 7 days.

Servers may send several tickets on one connection, useful for opening multiple parallel HTTP connections; a resumed handshake omits Certificate and CertificateVerify because the server authenticates with the PSK.

entries.title: TLS 0-RTT: sending data in the first message

definition.text: TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) lets a client that shares a pre-shared key with the server send application data in its first flight, saving a round trip at the cost of weaker security.

facts.text: When both sides share a PSK, from an earlier handshake or out of band, the client encrypts early data under it in the first flight, added to the 1-RTT PSK handshake whose other messages are unchanged.
0-RTT data is weaker than other TLS data: it is not forward secret, being encrypted only under keys derived from the PSK, and nothing guarantees it is not replayed between connections.
Within one connection 0-RTT data cannot be duplicated, and an attacker cannot make it look like 1-RTT data because different keys protect it.

There are two threats: a network attacker duplicating a flight of 0-RTT data, and one exploiting client retries; the second cannot be prevented in TLS, and any application whose clients retry already needs its own anti-replay defense.

Clients cannot know what protection a server has, so they MUST send as early data only what is safe to replay; servers SHOULD ensure 0-RTT data is accepted at most once, by sharing state or equivalent means.

Single-use tickets allow each ticket once, for example by deleting it from a ticket database on use and doing a full handshake for unknown tickets; sharing that database across distributed servers makes high 0-RTT success rates hard.

ClientHello recording stores a unique value from each ClientHello within a time window and rejects duplicates; it is easier to distribute but weaker, and with several zones the best defense makes one zone authoritative per ticket.

Freshness checks accept 0-RTT only for a ClientHello that arrives about when expected, from the ticket's creation time plus an estimated round-trip time and the client's ticket age; otherwise the server falls back to 1-RTT.

entries.title: HTTP conditional requests: act only if nothing has changed

definition.text: A conditional request carries header fields that set a precondition to be tested before the method is applied to the target resource.

facts.text: Conditional GET is the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates, and conditionals on state-changing methods such as PUT and DELETE prevent the lost update problem, where one client overwrites another's work.
Each precondition compares validators from earlier representations with the current validators, so it tests whether the resource changed since a state the client knows.
HTTP/1.0 added headers for conditional GET: the server returns the full content only if the client does not know the last modified time or it changed since the last full response.

If-None-Match is mainly used in conditional GET to update caches cheaply; if a listed tag matches, the server answers 304 (Not Modified) for GET and HEAD and 412 (Precondition Failed) for other methods.
If-Modified-Since makes a GET or HEAD conditional on a newer modification date, and it is ignored when If-None-Match is present; caches build it from the cached Last-Modified value.
If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, using strong comparison; it is mostly used with POST, PUT and DELETE to prevent lost updates, and a failure gets 412.
If-None-Match with * stops an unsafe method such as PUT from overwriting a representation when the client believes none exists, a variant of the lost update problem.
When several preconditions are present they are evaluated in order: If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, then If-Range.

entries.title: HTTP range requests: asking for part of a file

definition.text: A range request asks for only part of a representation, such as the remainder of an interrupted download, by sending a Range header on a GET.

facts.text: Range requests help when transfers are interrupted by canceled requests or dropped connections, and when devices with limited storage want only a subset, such as one page of a large document.
A server fulfilling a range request sends 206 (Partial Content); a single part needs a Content-Range header, and several parts are sent as multipart/byteranges.
A server answers 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) when no requested range is satisfiable or the client asks for an excessive number of small or overlapping ranges, a potential denial of service attack.
Accept-Ranges: bytes advertises support and Accept-Ranges: none says it is unsupported; a client may try ranges regardless and must not assume a later range request will return a partial response.

entries.title: Validators and entity tags: how HTTP spots a changed resource
entries.article: rfc>9110#8. Representation Data and Metadata > 8.8. Validator Fields

definition.text: A validator is resource metadata that can be used in a precondition to make a conditional request; HTTP defines modification dates and opaque entity tags.

facts.text: An ETag is an opaque quoted string that identifies one representation of a resource, whether the versions differ over time or through content negotiation.
An entity tag can be more reliable than a modification date when storing dates is inconvenient, one-second resolution is not enough, or dates are not consistently maintained.

A strong validator changes whenever the observable representation data changes and is unique across all versions of a resource's representations over time; weak validators, marked W/, are easy to generate but less useful for comparison.
In a successful response to a state-changing request, a validator such as the ETag in a 201 describes the new representation, so later conditional requests can prevent lost updates.

entries.title: HTTP cache validation: asking the origin whether a copy is still good
entries.article: rfc>9111#4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.3. Validation

definition.text: Validation, or revalidation, is a cache using a conditional request to ask the next server whether a stored response is still valid instead of fetching it in full.

facts.text: A cache validates when it holds responses for a URI but cannot serve them, for example because they are stale; the forwarded request carries preconditions built from the stored response's validators.

The validators are the Last-Modified timestamp, sent in If-Modified-Since, and the ETag entity tags, sent in If-None-Match; a cache must send stored entity tags and should send the Last-Modified value as well.
A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated and reused, so no content is transferred.
A full response means no stored response was suitable, so the cache uses it for the request and may store it.
If validation returns a 5xx, the cache may forward it, or act as if the server did not respond and send a stored response where allowed, or retry.
On a 304 the cache updates the stored responses it identifies by strong validator, or by weak validator, using the headers in the 304.
A cache can also send a HEAD request to update or invalidate stored GET responses when validators are missing or transferring content is not wanted.
Each client in a request chain may have its own cache, so an intermediary cache often receives conditional requests from other caches; If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.

entries.title: Cache-Control response directives: the origin's instructions
entries.article: rfc>9111#5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.2. Response Directives

definition.text: Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused.

facts.text: max-age says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds, and s-maxage overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale.
no-cache means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation, while no-store means a cache must not store any part of the request or response.
no-store is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.
private means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may; it controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content.
public explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with an Authorization header, though it is unnecessary on a response that is already cacheable.
must-revalidate means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it, even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout).
Servers should use must-revalidate only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction.
proxy-revalidate is like must-revalidate but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

entries.text:
Origin servers give caches their orders in a handful of directives. Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused. The max-age directive says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds. The s-maxage directive overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale. The no-cache directive means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. The no-store directive means a cache must not store any part of the request or response. It is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.

The private directive means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may. It controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content. The public directive explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with credentials. The must-revalidate directive means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it. This holds even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout). Servers should use it only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction. The proxy-revalidate directive is like it but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused. The max-age directive says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds. The s-maxage directive overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale. The no-cache directive means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. The no-store directive means a cache must not store any part of the request or response. It is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.

The private directive means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may. It controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content. The public directive explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with credentials. The must-revalidate directive means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it. This holds even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout). Servers should use it only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction. The proxy-revalidate directive is like it but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

entries.title: HTTP cache invalidation: forgetting what a write made stale
entries.article: rfc>9111#4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.4. Invalidating Stored Responses

definition.text: Invalidation is a cache removing or marking invalid its stored responses for a URI, so a mandatory validation is needed before any is used again.

facts.text: Unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE can change state on the origin, so intervening caches are required to invalidate stored responses to keep their contents current.
A cache must invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error response, with a 2xx or 3xx status, to an unsafe method, including methods whose safety is unknown.
A cache may also invalidate other URIs, such as those in Location and Content-Location, but never when their origin differs from the target URI's, which prevents denial-of-service attacks.
Invalidation is not global: a state-changing request invalidates responses only in the caches it travels through.

entries.title: Storing and reusing HTTP cached responses: the two rule sets

definition.text: A cache may store a response only if it passes storage checks and may reuse a stored response only if the new request matches it and the response is fresh, allowed stale or validated.

facts.text: A cache must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the status code is final, and the response has no no-store directive; a shared cache also needs no restricting private directive.
A cache may reuse a stored response only if the target URIs match, the stored method allows it, and the request headers nominated by Vary match.
Even then the response must not carry no-cache unless successfully validated, and it must be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated.
A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with an Authorization header unless a response directive (must-revalidate, public or s-maxage) allows it.

entries.text: A cache follows one set of rules for what it may store and another for what it may reuse. It must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the status code is final, and the response has no no-store directive. A stored response may be reused only if the target URIs match, the stored method allows it, and the request headers nominated by Vary match. It must also be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated. A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with credentials unless must-revalidate, public or s-maxage allows it.

entries.title: Hash function: any input, one fixed-size value

definition.text: A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, called hash values, hash codes, digests or hashes, which are usually used to index a hash table.

facts.text: A hash function and its hash table give access to data in small, nearly constant time per retrieval, with storage only fractionally greater than the data itself and far less than storing every possible key.
A hash function does three jobs: it folds variable-length keys into fixed-length values, scrambles the bits so values spread uniformly, and maps the values into the size of the table.
A good hash function is fast and spreads expected inputs evenly over its output range, because the cost of hashing methods rises sharply as collisions increase. Uniform is not the same as random.
A hash function must be deterministic: the same input must always give the same hash value, which rules out functions that depend on a pseudo-random number generator or the time of day.
Average-case behavior can be nearly optimal, but a poorly designed function, pathological keys or a high load factor can push access time toward linear in the number of items.

For a table size n that can change, compute a fixed wide-range hash and take the remainder after dividing by n. Resizing should move as few records as possible, which matters most in distributed hash tables.

Hash functions also build caches for large data sets on slow media, where a collision is resolved by discarding or writing back the older item, and they are an essential ingredient of the Bloom filter.
Hash tables may use non-cryptographic hash functions, while cryptographic ones secure sensitive data in integrity checking, message authentication codes, password storage and signatures.

entries.title: Base64: carrying binary data as plain text

definition.text: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding that represents each 6-bit segment of the data with one of 64 printable characters, so binary data can travel over channels that carry only text.

facts.text: Each 6-bit group maps to one character of the alphabet, so Base64 produces four characters for every three input bytes; the encoded data is 33% larger, plus about 3% more if line breaks are inserted.
When the input is not a multiple of three bytes, the last group is padded with = characters: one = after two leftover bytes and two after one, and the decoder discards the padded zero bits.
Padding is not essential for decoding, because the length of the encoded text reveals the number of missing bytes, but when Base64 strings are concatenated, padding is required to avoid ambiguity.

The alphabet typically uses A-Z, a-z and 0-9 for the first 62 values and, in many variants, + and / for the last two; RFC 4648 describes the most common alphabet, and most variants differ only in the last two.

RFC 4648 also defines a URL and filename safe alphabet for compact identifying information, such as a 128-bit UUID in an HTTP parameter; Base64url, as used in JWTs, differs by its non-alphanumeric characters and omits padding.

Base64 embeds binary data such as images in HTML, CSS and XML, and carries e-mail attachments, because SMTP was originally designed to transport only 7-bit ASCII; MIME sets a maximum line length of 76 characters.
Some systems use other alphabets or orderings; bcrypt and Unix crypt put . and / before the alphanumeric characters, so their encoding is not compatible with RFC 4648 Base64.

entries.title: Hash collision: when two inputs share one value

definition.text: A hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share the same hash value.

facts.text: Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values, so collisions are inevitable by the pigeonhole principle: with more objects than hash values, a collision is guaranteed.

The birthday paradox makes collisions likely long before the output range is exhausted, and a birthday attack uses it: it is easier to find any two inputs that collide than one matching a specific value.

Cryptographic hash functions are designed so that finding a collision is computationally infeasible (collision resistance); non-cryptographic ones, used in Bloom filters, hash tables and count sketches, need only uniform distribution and the avalanche property.
Simple non-cryptographic hashes such as CRC have essentially no collision resistance, so they cannot be used on input an attacker can manipulate, for example against hash flooding attacks.
Hash tables handle collisions with a collision-resolution strategy; the two most common are open addressing and separate chaining.
In open addressing, cells are occupied, empty or deleted; on a collision the table is probed for an alternate empty cell, using linear probing, double hashing or quadratic probing.
In separate chaining, records that hash to the same cell go into a linked list in that cell. Keeping track of many lists can make the table slow.
The effect of collisions depends on the application: checksums minimize collisions between similar inputs, while hashes made to find similar data maximize them, using locality-sensitive hashing.

Whether collisions hurt depends on the job: checksums try to avoid them between similar inputs, while hashes built to find similar data want them.

entries.title: Bloom filter: a set that answers maybe or never

definition.text: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives.

facts.text: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits, all 0 at first, plus k hash functions; adding an element sets to 1 the k array positions its hashes select.
To test an element, check its k positions: any 0 means it is definitely not in the set, while all 1s mean it is in the set or other elements set those bits by chance, a false positive.
False positives are possible but false negatives are not, and the false positive rate climbs as items are added, until every bit is 1 and every query answers positive.
A simple filter cannot remove an element, because clearing one of its bits could erase other elements and create false negatives; the counting variant replaces each bit with a counter.

With an optimal number of hash functions, a 1% false positive rate takes only about 9.6 bits per element whatever the element size, because the filter stores no items; the data itself needs separate storage.

Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra, ScyllaDB and PostgreSQL use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for missing rows, LSM trees keep one per on-disk component, and a cache can check one so missing keys never hit the database.

Bloom's 1970 paper analyzes the trade-off between hash area size, the time to identify a message as a non-member (reject time) and an allowable error frequency, for testing messages one by one for set membership.

Its key claim is that allowing a few non-members to be falsely identified as members permits a much smaller hash area without increasing reject time, with a secondary, possibly slow test to catch those errors when necessary.

entries.title: Quadtree: cutting space into four, again and again

definition.text: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children, used to partition two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants.

facts.text: Each internal node of a quadtree has exactly four children, and the structure partitions a two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions; each child or leaf stores spatial information.
Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees, which partition three-dimensional space.

Finding how close points are with latitude, longitude and Euclidean distance does not scale on large data sets because it is CPU-intensive, whereas a quadtree searches points within a two-dimensional range efficiently.
Subdividing a node only after a size threshold saves computation, and a mapping such as the Hilbert curve can improve range query performance further.
Quadtrees are used for spatial indexing and range queries, location-based services such as Google Maps and Uber, image processing and compression, mesh generation and sparse data storage.
A quadtree leaf cell represents a unit of interesting spatial information, and the subdivided regions may be square, rectangular or of arbitrary shape.

Quadtrees are also used for efficient two-dimensional collision detection, for solving multidimensional fields such as fluid dynamics and electromagnetism, and for image processing, where union and intersection of images are simple and fast.

entries.title: MD5: a famous hash that collisions broke

definition.text: MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit hash value, typically written as 32 hexadecimal digits.

facts.text: MD5 turns a message of any length into a 128-bit output by padding it and processing it in 512-bit blocks; a small change in the message gives a mostly different hash because of the avalanche effect.

MD5 is not collision-resistant, which was shown in 2004, so it is unsuitable for SSL certificates or digital signatures; collisions can be found within seconds, and the CMU Software Engineering Institute calls it cryptographically broken.

MD5 checksums still reveal a corrupt or incomplete download, but because collisions are easy to make they cannot protect against deliberate tampering, nor can a checksum fetched over the same channel as the file be trusted.
MD5 was historically used to store one-way password hashes, but NIST does not list it among the recommended hashes for password storage.

entries.title: K-d tree: splitting space one axis at a time

definition.text: A k-d tree is a space-partitioning data structure, a binary tree whose nodes are points, for organizing points in a k-dimensional space.

facts.text: Each non-leaf node implicitly defines a splitting hyperplane perpendicular to one of the k axes: points on one side of it go to the left subtree and points on the other side to the right subtree.
In the canonical construction the splitting axis cycles as you go down the tree and each node takes the median point on that axis, which yields a balanced tree with leaves at about the same depth.
Inserting a point and removing one each take O(log n) in a balanced tree. Repeated insertion can unbalance the tree, and rotations cannot rebalance it because it is sorted in several dimensions.
Nearest-neighbor search descends as if inserting the query point, saves the point at the leaf as the current best, then unwinds the recursion, updating the best at each node.

At each node it checks whether a hypersphere around the query, with the current best distance as radius, crosses the splitting plane. If it does, the other branch is searched; if not, that whole branch is eliminated.
The search can return the k nearest neighbors by keeping k current bests, or become approximate by capping the number of points examined, which helps in real-time uses such as robotics.
Range searches, such as members aged 20 to 50 with incomes from 50,000 to 80,000, suit k-d trees because each level divides the range of a domain in half.

In low dimensions the nearest point is found in O(log n) on average, but the curse of dimensionality makes high-dimensional search evaluate most points, no better than exhaustive search, so approximate nearest-neighbour methods are advised.

entries.title: Trie: a tree that spells out its keys

definition.text: A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a search tree for storing and retrieving strings from a dictionary or set.

facts.text: Nodes do not store their keys: a node's position determines its key, edges stand for single characters, every child shares a common prefix with its parent, and the root represents the empty string.
Searching follows the key's characters from the root, and a null link means the key does not exist; the search takes O(m) time, where m is the length of the key.
Insertion follows the characters and creates new nodes wherever it meets a null link, storing the value in the last node. Deletion clears that value and removes nodes left with no children.

Compared with a hash table, a trie looks up a key in O(m) with no hash function and no collisions, and sorts keys lexicographically; it is less efficient on secondary storage with high random access time.

Each node has as many links as the alphabet has characters, 128 for ASCII, and most are null, so a pointer-vector trie is enormous; linked lists, bitmaps or alphabet reduction save memory at the cost of speed.
A radix tree, or compressed trie, merges any node that has only one child into its parent for better space and time; it works best when the trie is static and its keys are sparse.

Tries suit autocomplete and predictive text, spell checking and longest-prefix matching in IP routing, because lookups follow prefixes. Web search engines keep a compressed trie of searchable words, each leading to a list of URLs.

entries.title: Z-order curve: flattening many dimensions into one

definition.text: The Z-order, or Morton, curve maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order.

facts.text: The z-value of a point comes from interleaving the bits of its binary coordinates; two-dimensional z-values are also called quadkey values, and connecting them in numerical order draws a recursively Z-shaped curve.
Once the data are sorted by bit interleaving, any one-dimensional structure can hold them: arrays, binary search trees, B-trees, skip lists, or hash tables with the low bits truncated.

The order equals a depth-first traversal of a quadtree or octree, so sorting points by z-order builds a compressed quadtree efficiently, since the points in any quadtree square form a contiguous interval.

A multidimensional range query cannot simply use binary search. From the z-value reached, the search computes the next z-value inside the range (BIGMIN, or LITMAX when searching downward) and skips the stretch between.

The method does not depend on the one-dimensional structure, so balanced trees handle dynamic data with O(log n) insertion and deletion, and it fits existing databases more easily than R-trees, which need special handling.
Z-order is one of the few multidimensional access methods that has found its way into commercial database systems.
The Hilbert curve has been suggested as an alternative with better order-preserving behaviour and is used in the S2 geometry index; Geohash is based on the Z-order curve.
Some GPUs store texture maps in Z-order so that cache lines represent rectangular tiles, raising the chance that nearby accesses hit the cache.

entries.text: How do you put points from a map into one list so that neighbors stay neighbors? The Z-order, or Morton, curve is one answer. It maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order. The z-value of a point comes from interleaving the bits of its binary coordinates. Connecting the values in numerical order draws a recursively Z-shaped curve. Once the data are sorted this way, any one-dimensional structure can hold them, and a balanced tree handles dynamic data with O(log n) insertion and deletion. The order equals a depth-first traversal of a quadtree, so the points in any quadtree square form a contiguous interval. A range query cannot simply use binary search. From the z-value reached, the search computes the next z-value inside the range and skips the stretch between. Z-order is one of the few multidimensional access methods in commercial data stores. A rival with better order-preserving behavior is {{ref:sysd-reliab-115}}, while {{ref:sysd-reliab-005}} is based on Z-order.

entries.title: Geohash: a place as a short string

definition.text: A geocoding method that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

facts.text: A geohash is a hierarchical spatial index in a Base-32 alphabet: its first character identifies one of 32 cells, and that cell in turn contains 32 cells.
The world is recursively divided into smaller cells with each additional bit until the desired precision is reached, so a longer string means a more precise location and a smaller cell.
Points whose geohashes share a longer prefix are spatially closer; 9q8yy9mf and 9q8yy9vx are close because they share the prefix 9q8yy9.
Because a geohash is a plain string, a location is easy to store in a database column, and nearest neighbors can be found with simple string comparisons and efficient index searches.
Depending on its length, a geohash tells only that a user is somewhere within an area, which gives a degree of anonymity.

A geohash is a hierarchical spatial data structure that subdivides space into grid-shaped buckets, an application of the Z-order curve; removing characters from the end gradually reduces both the code size and the precision.
Data indexed by geohash keeps all points of a rectangular area in contiguous slices, which helps databases where queries on a single index are easier or faster than multiple-index queries.
The index also supports a quick-and-dirty proximity search, because the closest points are often among the closest geohashes.

entries.title: Hilbert curve: a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors near

definition.text: The Hilbert curve is a continuous space-filling fractal curve, first described by David Hilbert in 1891, that maps between one and two dimensions while preserving locality fairly well.

facts.text: Mapping between 1D and 2D along the Hilbert curve keeps points that are close in one dimension close after folding, and this locality property is why the curve is widely used in computer science.
The locality property has been used to index geospatial location data; Singh's Uber design applies mapping algorithms such as the Hilbert curve to run range queries that find nearby drivers.
For multidimensional databases the Hilbert order has been proposed instead of Z order because it preserves locality better; Hilbert curves have been used to compress and accelerate R-tree indexes.

The distance of a point along the curve can be converted to coordinates in n dimensions and back by standard techniques such as Skilling's method, and the curve works even when the data space is not a square.

entries.title: Similarity hashing: when similar data should collide
entries.article: Hash function#Hashing variable-length data > Fuzzy hash

definition.text: Similarity hashing, or fuzzy hashing, produces hashes that show when data is similar but not identical.

facts.text: Fuzzy hashing detects data that is similar but not exactly the same, unlike cryptographic hash functions, which are designed to give very different hashes for even minor differences.
A perceptual hash fingerprints multimedia and is a type of locality-sensitive hash, so similar features give similar hashes; it is used to find online copyright infringement and in digital forensics.
Hashes meant to find similar data, such as homologous DNA sequences or similar audio files, are designed to maximize collisions between similar items, using locality-sensitive hashing.
Fuzzy hashing has been used to identify malware and could support data loss prevention and detecting multiple versions of code.

entries.title: String hashing: folding text into a number

definition.text: String hashing folds the characters of a variable-length string into a fixed-size hash code.

facts.text: Strings have very uneven distributions, so a common fold multiplies a running total by a sizable prime constant, adds the next character and ignores overflow, then reduces the result with a modulo or mask to fit the table.

Information can cluster in the upper or lower bits of the bytes, for example because ASCII codes have a top bit of 0; the clustering survives into the hash and causes more collisions than a proper randomizing hash.
Hashing only the first and last characters or the middle of a string saves iterating over it, but such functions can readily become linear because of redundancies and clustering in the key set.
A rolling hash computes the hash of every k-character window of a text with effort proportional to mk + n rather than k·n, as in the Rabin-Karp substring search algorithm.

entries.title: Distributed unique ID generation: many machines, no clashes

definition.text: A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines.

facts.text: IDs used in social media should be roughly sorted by time, numerical values only, and highly scalable with low latency; each generator has its own pros and cons.
A UUID has 128 bits and is simple to generate without calling another service, but it is not sequential and is inefficient for database indexing, and ID conflicts, though unlikely, are possible.
A Snowflake ID is built from a timestamp, a machine ID and a serial number, with the first bit unused so IDs stay positive; it needs no network call to an ID service, so it is fast and scalable.
Snowflake implementations vary; for example, a data center ID can be added to the machine ID component to guarantee global uniqueness.
A database auto-increment column uses the database's transaction management to handle concurrent requests and guarantees uniqueness within one table.
Auto-increment IDs need network communication and may expose sensitive business data; as user IDs they give competitors a rough idea of the total number of registered users.
In the database segment approach, ID servers fetch IDs from the database in batches and cache them, each server handling a segment of IDs, which greatly saves I/O pressure on the database.
Redis can also generate unique IDs from a key-value pair, and because it stores data in memory this performs better than the database.

entries.title: Universally unique identifier: 128 bits, no registry

definition.text: A 128-bit number used to identify information in computer systems, generated without any central authority.

facts.text: A UUID is a 128-bit number, also called a GUID in software typically created by Microsoft; it is usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 hyphenated format.

UUID uniqueness depends on no central registration authority or coordination between generators, so independent parties can label information that coexists in the same databases with negligible probability of duplication.
The probability that a UUID is duplicated is not zero but close enough to zero to be negligible; for properly generated version-4 UUIDs it is one in a billion within 103 trillion of them.
Collisions in time- and MAC-based UUIDs come only from deliberate construction or error such as skewed clocks or bugs, and random UUIDs need a high-entropy source of randomness.
The meaning of the bits is set by the variant, of which variant 1 is the most common; variants 1 and 2 have versions that further define the interpretation of the UUID.

UUIDs are commonly used as unique database keys, but the random nature of versions 3, 4 and 5 and the field ordering of versions 1 and 2 can hurt database locality and performance when they are primary keys.
Reordering time-based UUIDs so the timestamp comes first averts the insertion performance loss, which is the rationale for versions 6 and 7.
A UUID is 16 octets (128 bits); the variant field in the top bits of octet 8 determines the layout of every other bit, and the version number sits in the most significant 4 bits of octet 6.

entries.title: Snowflake ID: a timestamp, a machine and a counter in one number

definition.text: A form of unique identifier used in distributed computing that packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number.

facts.text: The Snowflake format was created by Twitter, which uses it for tweet IDs; the format has since been adopted by other companies such as Discord and Instagram.

A snowflake has 41 bits of timestamp in milliseconds since a chosen epoch, 10 bits of machine ID to prevent clashes, and 12 bits of per-machine sequence number, so several IDs can be made in one millisecond.
Only 63 bits vary, so the value is a non-negative number that fits in a 64-bit signed integer; the first bit is unused to keep IDs positive.
Snowflakes sort by creation time, and the creation time can be calculated from the ID, so objects created before or after a given date can be selected by ID.
A generator needs no network call to an ID service, so Snowflake IDs are fast and scalable.

Implementations vary: the original Twitter library splits the 10-bit machine ID into a 5-bit data center ID and a 5-bit worker ID, while Instagram uses 41 timestamp bits, 13 shard ID bits and 10 sequence bits.

entries.title: UUID versions: time, name, random and custom layouts

definition.text: The UUID versions are the ways of filling a UUID's bits: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, or custom.

facts.text: Version 1 is time-based: a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 UTC, a 48-bit node ID, usually a MAC address, and a clock sequence that avoids duplicates when the clock moves backwards.

Versions 3 and 5 are name-based: they hash a namespace identifier, itself a UUID, with a name, using MD5 for version 3 and SHA-1 for version 5, so systems derive the same UUID from a name without a registry.
Version 4 is made from random or pseudorandom numbers: six bits are fixed for variant and version, leaving 122 random bits, which gives 5.3×10^36 possible version-4, variant-1 UUIDs.

Version 6 is field-compatible with version 1 but stores the timestamp from most to least significant byte for better database locality; systems without legacy version-1 UUIDs should use version 7 instead.

Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits and fills the other 74 non-version, non-variant bits with random bits, optionally a sub-millisecond fraction or counter; implementations should use it instead of versions 1 and 6.

Version 7 UUIDs are monotonically ascending, creation-time-ordered, lexically sortable keys, so new records land at the end of the key sequence, unlike random version 4, whose keys scatter across it and hurt performance.

Version 8 is for experimental or vendor-specific use: only the version and variant bits are fixed, leaving 122 bits for custom content, and its uniqueness is implementation-specific and must not be assumed.
Versions 1, 2, 6 and 7 expose the time of generation, so UUIDs can reveal when a system went live, or its growth over time; the RFC calls the embedded timestamp a very small attack surface.

entries.title: UUID best practices: storing, sorting and trusting them

definition.text: RFC 9562 advises how to generate, store, sort and protect UUIDs so that they stay unique, sortable and safe to use in databases and distributed systems.

facts.text: Where feasible, store UUIDs in a database as the 128-bit binary value: text needs 288 bits for the same value, while binary takes less space and may be faster, and text is simpler when the text form is needed.
Time-ordered monotonic UUIDs sort as opaque raw bytes and give database-index locality because new values sit near each other; the gap from random inserts can be one order of magnitude or more.

Schema designers are cautioned against name-based UUIDs as primary keys, because the name input, such as a postal code or license number, can later change; time-based surrogate keys are the general advice.

Time-based UUIDs are normally monotonic through the embedded timestamp, but batches created within one tick need a counter: dedicated counter bits after the timestamp, a randomly seeded counter, or extra clock precision in up to 12 bits.

As more nodes generate UUIDs independently, collisions become likelier. An embedded pseudorandom node ID, using version 8, adds collision resistance; a central registry that checks uniqueness can become a bottleneck and is not recommended.

Random bits should come from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator, which gives both unguessable and unique values, and its state must be reseeded after changes such as process forks.

Implementations must not assume UUIDs are hard to guess or use them as security capabilities, identifiers whose mere possession grants access; if UUIDs are needed in a security operation, version 4 should be used.

Weigh the consequences of a collision: a duplicate log entry is low impact, but where failure is unacceptable an application must use as much collision resistance as its context allows. Treat UUIDs as opaque and avoid parsing them.

entries.title: Count-min sketch: counting events in a tiny table

definition.text: A count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure that serves as a frequency table of events in a stream of data.

facts.text: It uses hash functions to map events to frequencies but, unlike a hash table, takes only sub-linear space, at the expense of overcounting some events because of collisions.

The sketch is a two-dimensional array of w columns and d rows, with a separate pairwise-independent hash function for each row; w and d are fixed at creation and set the space, time and error probability.
To record an event of type i, each row j applies its hash function to get a column index and increments the cell at that row and column by one.
A point query returns the least value among the cells for i. It never underestimates the true count, and with probability 1 − δ it exceeds it by at most εN, where N is the total number of items seen.
Choosing w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln 1/δ⌉ keeps the error in answering a query within an additive factor of ε with probability 1 − δ.
The sketch is linear: summing the sketches of two streams gives the same result as sketching the concatenated streams, so it is mergeable and suitable for distributed as well as streaming settings.
The minimum estimator is biased, as it may overestimate but never underestimate; it works well on highly skewed distributions, and conservative updating, which changes only the update, reduces error.

A count-min sketch is used differently from a counting Bloom filter: it has a sublinear number of cells set by the desired approximation quality, while a counting Bloom filter is sized to the number of elements in the set.

It uses hash functions to map events to frequencies but, unlike an ordinary hash-keyed table, takes only sub-linear space. The price is that collisions make it overcount some events. A point query returns the least value among the event's cells. Because the sketch is linear, summing the sketches of two streams gives the same result as sketching the concatenated streams, so it is mergeable and suits distributed settings.

entries.title: Merkle tree: checking big data with one root hash

definition.text: A Merkle tree, or hash tree, is a tree in which each leaf is labelled with the cryptographic hash of a data block and each inner node with the hash of its children's labels.

facts.text: A hash tree verifies a large data structure efficiently and securely: proving a leaf belongs to a binary hash tree takes hashes proportional to the logarithm of the leaf count, where a hash list needs the leaf count itself.
The root hash is obtained from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer; a tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, and another source is tried.
One branch can be downloaded and checked at a time, even before the whole tree is available, so a file split into small blocks needs only the damaged blocks downloaded again.

Most hash trees are binary, though a node can have many more children; they usually use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-2, while non-cryptographic checksums such as CRCs suffice against unintentional damage only.

Hash trees help peer-to-peer networks check that blocks arrive unaltered, and are used in ZFS, Git, Bitcoin and Ethereum, Certificate Transparency, and NoSQL systems such as Apache Cassandra, Riak and Dynamo.
The root hash does not show the tree depth, which allows a second-preimage attack with a forged document; one fix prepends a 0x00 byte when hashing leaves and 0x01 when hashing internal nodes.

entries.title: HyperLogLog: counting distinct items in tiny memory

definition.text: An algorithm for the count-distinct problem that approximates the number of distinct elements in a multiset using very little memory.

facts.text: Counting distinct elements exactly needs memory proportional to their number, which is impractical for very large data sets; HyperLogLog makes a single pass over the data using an auxiliary memory of m units and returns an estimate.
Its relative accuracy, the standard error, is typically about 1.04/√m for m units of memory.
It estimates cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% using only 1.5 kilobytes, and matches the accuracy of its predecessor LogLog with only 64% of LogLog's memory.
It hashes each element into a uniformly distributed random number and uses the maximum number of leading zeros in the binary forms of those numbers to estimate the cardinality.
A single estimate has a large variance, so the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum leading zeros is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the estimates.

The state is an array of m registers set to 0; add hashes the element, uses its first b bits to pick a register, and keeps the larger of the register's value and the leftmost-1 position of the remaining bits.

Count combines the registers with a harmonic mean, and merge takes the maximum of each pair of registers to get the union of two sets; add is O(1), count and merge O(m), and the algorithm parallelizes optimally.

HyperLogLog is biased for small cardinalities, where Linear Counting is used; HyperLogLog++ adds a 64-bit hash, an empirical bias correction and a sparse register representation to cut memory for small cardinalities.

entries.title: Cache filtering with a Bloom filter: skipping one-hit wonders
entries.article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Cache filtering

definition.text: Using a Bloom filter to remember which URLs were requested so a web cache stores an object only when it is requested a second time.

facts.text: Nearly three-quarters of the URLs accessed from a typical web cache are one-hit-wonders, requested once and never again, so storing them wastes disk resources.
A Bloom filter keeps track of all URLs users access, and a web object is cached only when it has been accessed before, that is, on its second request.
Most one-hit-wonders are never written to disk, so the disk write workload drops, cache space is saved, and cache hit rates rise.
Akamai's servers use this to keep one-hit-wonders out of their disk caches, which significantly reduces disk workload and raises disk cache hit rates.

entries.title: Counting Bloom filter: a Bloom filter that can delete
entries.article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Counting Bloom filters

definition.text: A Bloom filter variant whose array positions are counters instead of single bits, which lets it delete elements.

facts.text: A counting filter supports delete by widening each array position from one bit to a multibit counter; a regular Bloom filter is a counting filter with one-bit buckets.
Insert increments the counters its hashes select, lookup checks that each is non-zero, and delete decrements each one.
Counters are usually 3 or 4 bits, so a counting filter uses 3 to 4 times more space than a static Bloom filter, and counters must be large enough that overflow stays rare.
The table cannot be expanded, so the maximum number of keys must be known in advance, and the false positive rate grows rapidly once the designed capacity is exceeded.

entries.text: A plain Bloom filter cannot forget; a counting Bloom filter can.
