entries.title: Bloom filter alternatives: cuckoo, quotient and xor filters

definition.text: Set-membership filters such as cuckoo, quotient and xor filters that store short fingerprints of keys and can beat the classic Bloom filter on space, speed or deletion.

facts.text: Classic Bloom filters use 1.44log2(1/ε) bits per inserted key, but any structure in the same role strictly needs only log2(1/ε), so Bloom filters use 44% more space than an optimal one.

A cuckoo filter keeps short fingerprints of keys in a cuckoo hash table; a matching fingerprint means the key is probably in the set. It supports deletions and has better locality of reference than a Bloom filter.
Compared with the Bloom filter, a quotient filter has better locality of reference and supports deletions.

An xor filter stores fingerprints in a perfect hash table and is more memory efficient (1.23log2(1/ε) bits per key) and faster than Bloom or cuckoo filters, but it is harder to create and the set cannot be modified afterwards.

entries.title: Quadtree types: regions, points, lines and curves

definition.text: Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves, and by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added.

facts.text: A region quadtree decomposes a region into four equal quadrants and so on; each node has exactly four children or none, and tree height depends on the spatial distribution of interesting areas.

A point quadtree adapts a binary tree to two-dimensional points, with four pointers per node and every subdivision centered on a point; it usually runs in O(log n) time, though k-d trees have surpassed it.
A point-region (PR) quadtree stores a list of the points in each leaf cell instead of a uniform value, and, like the point quadtree, can grow to linear height on a bad set of points.
Edge quadtrees store lines and PM quadtrees store collections of polygons, while compressed quadtrees keep only subtrees with interesting data to avoid storing many empty nodes.

entries.title: Limits of geohash proximity search: where neighbors look far apart
entries.article: Geohash#Limitations when used for deciding proximity > Edge cases

definition.text: Using shared geohash prefixes to find nearby points works for most points but fails near cell borders, the poles and the 180 degree meridian.

facts.text: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close together, but the reverse is not guaranteed: two nearby points can have a short or no shared prefix.

Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian get very different geohashes, because they lie in different halves of the world.

A bounding-box search between the southwest and northeast corner geohashes retrieves every point along the z-order curve between them, which can be far too many, and it breaks down at the 180 meridians and the poles.

Distance between two geohashes reflects distance in latitude/longitude coordinates, not actual distance; despite this, geohashing has been used for proximity search in Elasticsearch, MongoDB, HBase, Redis and Accumulo.

entries.title: Nearby search with a quadtree: walking down to the origin

definition.text: A way to find nearby businesses by building an in-memory quadtree of all locations and walking it down to the leaf that holds the search origin.

facts.text: The quadtree is an in-memory data structure, not a database; it runs on each location-based-service server and is built when the server starts.
The root node represents the whole world map and is recursively divided into 4 quadrants until no node has more than 100 businesses.

To find nearby businesses, traverse from the root to the leaf node containing the search origin; if it holds 100 businesses return it, otherwise add businesses from its neighbors until enough are returned.

Building a quadtree for 200 million businesses may take a few minutes, during which the server cannot serve traffic, so new releases roll out to a small subset of servers at a time to avoid a brownout.

entries.title: Load balancing: spreading requests across many servers

definition.text: Load balancing distributes a set of tasks or incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online, so the overall work is processed more efficiently.

facts.text: Load balancing can improve response time and avoids overloading some nodes while others are left idle.
Busy websites must serve hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of concurrent requests, and the cost-effective way to meet that volume is to add more servers.
A load balancer sits in front of the servers and routes each request to one that can fulfil it, in a way that maximizes speed and capacity use, so no single server is overworked.
If a server goes down, the balancer redirects traffic to the remaining online servers; when a new server joins the group, requests start flowing to it automatically.
It enables horizontal scaling: additional servers are added to the pool and the balancer distributes traffic across all of them.
Beyond parallel computing, load balancing is widely used for HTTP requests on high-traffic sites, most commonly to provide one Internet service from many servers, sometimes known as a server farm.
A balancer's main jobs are traffic distribution, high availability, SSL termination, session persistence, scalability and health monitoring.
Which algorithm fits depends on the nature of the tasks, their complexity, the hardware and the error tolerance required, so a compromise must be found for each application.

entries.title: DNS load balancing: spreading traffic by name lookup
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Round-robin DNS

definition.text: DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to it are spread across a group of servers.

facts.text: Round-robin DNS associates several IP addresses with one domain name and hands them to clients in rotation, needing no dedicated software or hardware node.
Addresses are given a short expiration so the client is more likely to use a different IP next time; resolvers return the whole set, and servers may round-robin its order.
DNS load balancing has inherent limits: DNS does not check for server and network outages, and it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable.
In DNS delegation, a sub-domain such as www is delegated to a zone served by the website's own servers, each answering with its own address, so a down server simply does not respond.
With delegation the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the closest server, giving geo-sensitive balancing, and it works well for geographically spread servers.
A short TTL on the A-record diverts traffic quickly when a server fails, but individual clients may switch between servers in mid-session.

Returning multiple A or AAAA records and letting the client choose gives little control: records are picked randomly and each attracts roughly equal traffic, and SRV weights and priorities are not adopted for HTTP.

The authoritative server sees the recursive resolver's address, not the user's, so replies can be optimized only for the resolver; EDNS0 passes the client subnet, and anycast nameservers or network location maps steer to the closest datacenter.

entries.title: Load balancing algorithms: rules for picking a server
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Scheduling algorithms

definition.text: Scheduling algorithms, also called load-balancing methods, are the rules a load balancer uses to decide which back-end server receives each request.

facts.text: Simple algorithms include random choice, round robin and least connections.

More sophisticated balancers may also weigh a server's reported load, response times, up/down status from a monitoring poll, active connections, geographic location, capabilities or recently assigned traffic.
Round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin and hash are static algorithms; least connections and least response time are dynamic ones.
Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest current connections to clients, factoring in each server's relative computing capacity; the method can also be weighted.

Least response time sends requests to the server selected by a formula combining the fastest response time and fewest active connections, and least bandwidth picks the server carrying the least traffic in Mbps.
Hashing applies a hash function to a key the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL, and routes by the result.
Random assignment of tasks to servers works quite well, and a random permutation computed in advance avoids per-assignment communication and the need for a distribution master.
Power of two choices picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

conflicts.text: Least connections is listed among the static load distribution methods.

entries.text:
How does a balancer choose? The rules it follows are called scheduling algorithms or load-balancing methods, and they decide which back-end server receives each request. The simple ones are random choice, round robin and least connections. Round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin and hash are static algorithms. Least connections and least response time are dynamic ones.

Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest current connections to clients, factoring in each server's relative computing capacity, and it can be weighted. Least response time uses a formula that combines the fastest response time and fewest active connections. Least bandwidth picks the server carrying the least traffic in Mbps. Hashing applies a hash function to a key the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL, and routes by the result. Random assignment works quite well, and a random permutation computed in advance avoids per-assignment communication and the need for a distribution master. Power of two choices picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

More sophisticated balancers may also weigh a server's reported load, response times, up or down status from regular checks, active connections, geographic location, capabilities or recently assigned traffic. One source lists least connections among the static methods, so the labels are not universal.

entries.title: Session persistence: keeping a user on one server
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Persistence

definition.text: Session persistence, also called stickiness, sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

facts.text: Information kept across a user's session, if stored on one backend server, cannot be found when later requests go to other backends; for recomputable cached data this is only a performance issue.
Ideally the servers behind the balancer are not session-aware, usually by keeping sessions in a shared database or an in-memory store such as Memcached.
Sticky sessions send a user or device to the same resource to keep session state there; in sticky round robin, once a user's first request goes to service A, later ones do too.
The significant downside is no automatic failover: if the backend goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and sessions depending on it are lost.
Assignment can be based on username, client IP address or random choice; IP-based assignment may be unreliable because of DHCP, network address translation and web proxies.
Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, costing storage and possibly lost if it fails, and the client must keep state, which fails if a browser has disabled cookies.
Sophisticated balancers use multiple persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one method.

entries.text:
The next request from a user may land on a server that knows nothing about the last one. Information kept across a session, if stored on one backend server, cannot be found when later requests go to other backends. Session persistence, also called stickiness, is the fix. It sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

Assignment can be based on username, client IP address or random choice. IP-based assignment may be unreliable because of DHCP, network address translation and web proxies. Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, which costs storage and may be lost if it fails. The client must also keep state, which fails if a browser has disabled cookies.

The significant downside is no automatic recovery. If the backend goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and the sessions that depend on it are lost. Sophisticated balancers use several persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one.

entries.title: Static and dynamic load balancing: ignoring load or watching it
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Problem overview > Static and dynamic algorithms

definition.text: A load-balancing algorithm is static when it ignores the current state of the system and dynamic when it takes each node's current load into account.

facts.text: A static algorithm ignores system state such as processor load and relies on assumptions made beforehand about arrival times, resource needs and processor speeds.

Static algorithms are easy to set up and efficient for fairly regular tasks such as processing HTTP requests from a website, but statistical variance in assignment can still overload some computing units.
Dynamic algorithms use the current load of each node and can move tasks from an overloaded node to an underloaded one for faster processing.
Dynamic algorithms are much more complicated to design but can improve performance, particularly when execution time varies greatly from one task to another.
Dynamic algorithms need nodes to exchange information, and one that needs too much communication to reach its decisions risks slowing down the overall solution.
A dynamic architecture can be more modular because no specific node has to be dedicated to distributing the work.
The more is known about the tasks when deciding, the better the optimization; knowing the exact execution time of every task is an idealized and extremely rare situation.

entries.title: Client-side load balancing: let the client pick
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Client-side random load balancing

definition.text: In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection.

facts.text: The client is given a list of server IPs, delivered as a DNS list without round-robin or hardcoded, and randomly selects one on each connection.
It relies on all clients generating similar loads and on the law of large numbers to give a reasonably flat distribution across servers.
It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS caching servers skew round-robin DNS while random client selection is unaffected by caching.
A smart client that detects a down server and connects randomly again also provides fault tolerance.

entries.text: Sometimes the balancer is the client itself. In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection. The list is delivered as a DNS list without round-robin, or hardcoded. It relies on all clients generating similar loads and on the law of large numbers to give a reasonably flat distribution across servers. It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS servers that remember answers skew round-robin DNS, while random client selection is unaffected. A smart client that detects a down server and connects randomly again can also ride out failures.

entries.title: Master-worker load balancing: workers ask for tasks

definition.text: In a master-worker scheme, a master hands out tasks to workers that ask for them, making it one of the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms.

facts.text: All workers start idle and report to the master, which answers their requests with tasks and tells them to stop asking when no tasks remain.
The scheme can distribute work evenly when the assignment overhead is low.
It scales badly to many processors because of the high amount of communication, and the master acts as a bottleneck.
Replacing the master with a task list shared by the processors improves it and scalability, though it is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

But the scheme scales badly to many processors, because of the high amount of communication, and the master is a bottleneck. A task list shared by the processors improves it, though that is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

entries.title: Round robin load balancing: taking turns
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Approaches > Static load distribution without prior knowledge > Round-robin scheduling

definition.text: Round robin sends each new request to the next server in sequence and starts again at the first server after the last.

facts.text: The first request goes to the first server, the next to the second, and so on down to the last, then the cycle restarts; the services are usually required to be stateless.
Weighted round robin lets the administrator give each server a weight, so more powerful servers handle more requests, to account for differing compute and traffic-handling capacity.
Sticky round robin improves on round robin: if a user's first request goes to service A, the following requests go to service A as well.
Lower-powered units may receive requests needing less computation or, when request sizes are homogeneous or unknown, simply fewer requests than larger units.

entries.title: Session state storage: where a session can live instead
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Persistence

definition.text: Session state can be kept in a database, in the client's browser, or in a distributed hash table, so that the balancer is free to pick any backend server.

facts.text: Keeping per-session data in a database can reduce performance because it adds load to a database best used for less transient data; the database is often replicated and balanced to avoid a single point of failure.
When the client is a web browser, the data can live in the browser itself, through a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or through URL rewriting.

Client-side storage is generally preferred because the balancer can then pick any backend, but it may not suit complex business logic with large session state, and URL rewriting has major security issues.
Another option is to name each block of data and use a distributed hash table to assign that name pseudo-randomly to one of the available servers, which stores the block.

entries.text: If session data does not live on one server, the balancer is free to pick any backend. Session state can be kept in a data store, in the client's browser, or in a table spread over many servers. A data store adds load to a system best used for less transient data. In a web browser, the data can live in a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or in rewritten URLs. Client-side storage is generally preferred, though it may not suit large session state, and URL rewriting has major security issues. Spreading named blocks of data over servers by hash is the idea behind {{ref:sysd-scale-139}}.

entries.title: Work stealing: idle processors take work from busy ones
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Approaches > Non-hierarchical architecture, without knowledge of the system: work stealing

definition.text: Work stealing gives each processor some tasks, then lets idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones.

facts.text: It overcomes scalability problems when task completion time is unknown: tasks are assigned randomly or in a predefined way, then inactive processors steal work from active or overloaded ones.
An idle processor requests work at random from others; if the target can subdivide its task it sends part of it, otherwise it returns an empty task.
It can be particularly effective but is difficult to implement, since communication must not become the processors' primary occupation instead of solving the problem.
Its efficiency is close to the optimal prefix-sum distribution when the cost of splitting jobs and communicating is not too high compared with the work.

entries.text: Work stealing flips the usual question: instead of a balancer pushing tasks out, idle processors pull work in. Each processor is given some tasks, and then idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones. This overcomes scaling problems when task completion time is unknown. An idle processor asks others at random. If the target can subdivide its task it sends part of it, otherwise it returns an empty task. The method can be particularly effective but is difficult to implement, since communication must not become the processors' main occupation.

entries.title: Layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing: addresses or content

definition.text: A layer 4 load balancer routes on transport-level information such as IP addresses and ports, while a layer 7 load balancer reads whole requests and routes on their content.

facts.text: A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports, so it cannot perform content-based routing.
Layer 4 balancers are often dedicated hardware devices that can operate at high speed.
A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer, reads requests in their entirety and performs content-based routing, allowing load to be managed from a full understanding of the traffic.
Application-layer balancing comes in variations: host-based uses the requested hostname, path-based uses the entire URL, and content-based inspects the message, for example the value of a parameter.
Routing by URL needs plain HTTP, or HTTPS that is terminated (decrypted) at the balancer.
Platform-specific routing can send requests from different device types, such as mobiles and desktops, to specialized backend systems.

entries.title: Hardware, software and cloud load balancers

definition.text: Load balancers come as physical hardware devices, as software on standard machines, or as managed cloud services.

facts.text: A hardware balancer is physical on-premises equipment that handles a large volume of traffic but often costs a lot, is fairly inflexible and runs proprietary firmware that needs maintenance and patches.
Software balancers are usually easier to deploy than hardware, cost-effective and flexible, and can be configured to the environment, at the cost of more set-up work.

Software balancers come as installable solutions needing configuration and management, or as a managed cloud service; cloud load balancers such as AWS Elastic Load Balancer are built into the provider's infrastructure.

entries.title: Global server load balancing: balancing across the world

definition.text: Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve redundancy and performance at a global scale.

facts.text: It spreads traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve redundancy and performance on a global scale.
Cross-zone load balancing distributes incoming traffic across geographic or network zones, increasing the system's resilience and capacity for large volumes of requests.
Server-load balancing for content delivery uses service-based (global load balancing) or hardware-based techniques, such as layer 4-7 switches, to share traffic among several servers or web caches.
DNS-based delegation gives geo-sensitive balancing, since the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the network's closest server.

entries.title: Health checks: noticing which servers are down

definition.text: A health check lets the load balancer tell whether a server is down or performing poorly so it can remove that server from the pool.

facts.text: The balancer polls servers for application-layer health and removes failed servers from the pool.
Components are monitored continually, for example web servers by fetching known pages; when one becomes unresponsive the balancer stops sending it traffic, and resumes when it is back online.
Continuous evaluation of instances directs requests only to those that are fully operational, which maintains performance and keeps service uninterrupted.

entries.title: Load balancer failover: staying up when a server fails

definition.text: Load balancing is often used to implement failover, the continuation of service after the failure of one or more components.

facts.text: The balancer is informed when a component fails and stops sending it traffic, then reroutes traffic to it when it returns.
For this to work there must be at least one component in excess of the service's capacity (N+1 redundancy).
This is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a backup that takes over on failure (dual modular redundancy).
Failover can raise fault tolerance by allowing quick substitution of the most complicated, failure-prone parts, but it can make the load balancer itself a single point of failure.
To avoid that, a second or N load balancers can run in cluster mode, and if the active one fails, a passive one takes over, making the system more fault-tolerant.
Balancers are usually implemented in high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it.
Some balancers do something special when all backend servers are unavailable, such as forwarding to a backup balancer or displaying a message about the outage.

entries.text:
When a server dies, the balancer is the one that notices. Load balancing is often used to keep service going after the failure of one or more components. The balancer is informed when a component fails, stops sending it traffic, and reroutes traffic to it when it returns. For this to work there must be at least one component in excess of the service's capacity, an arrangement called N+1. That is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a standby that takes over on failure.

The catch is that the balancer itself can become the one part whose failure stops everything. To avoid that, a second or N load balancers can run in cluster mode, and if the active one fails, a passive one takes over. Balancers are usually implemented in high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it. Some balancers do something special when all backend servers are unavailable, such as forwarding to a spare balancer or displaying a message about the outage.

entries.title: TLS termination: decrypting at the balancer

definition.text: A load balancer or reverse proxy can terminate TLS connections itself, decrypting traffic and passing plain requests to the backend servers so they are spared the encryption work.

facts.text: TLS encryption and authentication can become a major part of a web server's CPU demand; a balancer can terminate TLS and pass HTTPS requests to the web servers as HTTP.
Terminating TLS at the balancer lets it balance or switch content based on data inside the HTTPS request.
The downside is that all TLS processing is concentrated on one device, the balancer, which can become a new bottleneck; adding a few web servers may be cheaper than upgrading it.

The proxy must then decrypt and re-encrypt traffic it filters, caches or compresses, so it needs the TLS certificate and private key, widening access to unencrypted data and making it a more valuable attack target.

entries.title: Load balancer features: beyond handing out requests
entries.article: Load balancing (computing)#Use cases > Internet-based services > Server-side load balancers > Load balancer features

definition.text: Beyond distributing requests, load balancers offer a range of extra features, most of them vendor specific, such as compression, caching, security and connection handling.

facts.text: The fundamental feature is distributing incoming requests over the backend servers in the cluster according to a scheduling algorithm; most other features are vendor specific.

Asymmetric load assigns a manual ratio so some backends get a bigger share, a simple way to reflect capacity differences, and priority activation brings standby servers online when too few servers remain or load is too high.
Balancers can mitigate SYN flood attacks with features such as SYN cookies and delayed binding, where backends do not see the client until it completes its TCP handshake.
HTTP compression cuts transferred data and helps more for larger responses and distant clients, but adds CPU demand on the balancer and could be done by the web servers instead.

Connection multiplexing consolidates multiple HTTP requests from multiple clients into a single TCP socket to the backends, and TCP buffering spoon-feeds responses to slow clients so web server threads are freed sooner.
An application-layer balancer may cache static content to answer some requests without contacting the servers.
HTTP security features include hiding error pages, removing server identification headers and encrypting cookies so end users cannot manipulate them.
Logging request and response metadata gives an audit trail or analytics data, and request tracing gives each request a unique id for logging, monitoring and troubleshooting.

entries.title: Proxy server: the intermediary in the middle

definition.text: A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it: the client sends the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions.

facts.text: Instead of connecting directly to a server that can fulfil a request, the client directs the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions.
The indirection controls complexity or adds benefits such as load balancing, privacy or security; proxies were devised to add structure and encapsulation to distributed systems.
A proxy may sit on the user's own computer or at any point between the user's computer and the destination servers.
Proxies typically filter requests, log requests, or transform them by adding or removing headers, encrypting or decrypting, or compressing.
A proxy that passes requests and responses on unmodified is usually called a gateway or sometimes a tunneling proxy.
A web proxy receives an ordinary HTTP request except that the full URL, not just the path, is passed; it makes the request and returns the response.

Proxies may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For, or the standardised Forwarded field, to pass on client information, but these should not be trusted blindly: they may be absent, modified or added by several proxies.
A proxy works at layer 7 of the OSI model; network address translation is similar but works at layer 3, so it is less resource-intensive and less flexible.

entries.title: Forward proxy: a middleman for clients

definition.text: A forward proxy is a server that sits in front of a group of client machines and communicates with Internet servers on their behalf.

facts.text: When the clients request sites and services on the Internet, the forward proxy intercepts the requests and communicates with the web servers on their behalf, like a middleman.
A forward proxy sits in front of the client so that no origin server ever communicates directly with that client.
It can regulate traffic by preset policies, convert and mask client IP addresses, enforce security protocols and block unknown traffic, strengthening policy enforcement inside an internal network.
Common uses are blocking access to certain content, reaching geo-restricted content, providing anonymity and avoiding other browsing restrictions.
A content-filtering proxy gives administrative control over content relayed through it, is used by organizations to enforce acceptable use policy, and often supports user authentication and logging.
An open proxy is a forwarding proxy accessible by any Internet user; an anonymous proxy reveals that it is a proxy but does not disclose the client's originating IP address.
Web filtering proxies cannot see inside HTTPS unless managed clients are configured to trust a root certificate whose private key the proxy knows.
Proxies bring anonymity but can still track personal information, and setting up and maintaining one can be costly and requires configuration.

entries.title: Reverse proxy: a front door for servers

definition.text: A reverse proxy, or surrogate server, is a proxy server that appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests to one or more ordinary web servers.

facts.text: The reverse proxy returns the original server's response as if it came from the proxy itself, so the client never learns of the original server.

It sits in front of the origin servers so no client communicates with them directly; the web servers can be hidden behind a firewall on the internal network with only the reverse proxy exposed to the Internet.
A forward proxy serves clients restricted to a private network that need public Internet resources, whereas a reverse proxy is used to protect the servers.

By inspecting HTTP headers it can present a single IP address to the Internet while relaying requests to different internal servers by URL, rewriting URLs where needed, and can balance load across servers.

It often terminates TLS connections from clients, which centralises certificate management, access control, logging and routing and reduces TLS work on backend servers; it can also compress content to speed up loading.
It can cache static and dynamic content (web acceleration), satisfying a considerable number of requests and greatly reducing the load on origin servers.
In spoon-feeding, a dynamically generated page is served to the proxy in full and fed to the slow client as the connection allows, so the generating program need not stay open.

Application firewall features can protect against DoS and DDoS attacks, and it can add authentication to a server that has none, but it gives no protection against attacks on the web application itself.

entries.title: HAProxy: an open source balancer and proxy

definition.text: HAProxy is free, open source software that provides a high-availability load balancer and proxy for TCP and HTTP-based applications, spreading requests across multiple servers.

facts.text: It balances at Layer 4 (TCP) and Layer 7 (HTTP), with scriptable multi-layer health checking, multi-factor stickiness and layer 4/7 retries.
Other features include SSL/TLS termination, URL rewriting, rate limiting, simplified circuit breaking, HTTP/2 on both sides, WebSocket and gRPC support, and hitless reloads.
Written in C with an event-driven multithreaded architecture, it has a reputation for speed and efficiency; distributed stick-tables support statistics collection and DoS mitigation.

Servers with 6 to 8 cores generally reach 200,000 to 500,000 requests per second and can saturate a 25 Gbit/s connection under Linux; 64-core ARM servers reached 2 million requests per second and 100 Gbit/s.

entries.title: API gateway: one entry point to many services

definition.text: An API gateway is an API management tool that sits between clients and a set of backend services as their single entry point, enforcing security and throttling policies before passing requests on.

facts.text: It is a single entry point into a system that encapsulates the internal architecture and provides an API tailored to each client.
It receives API requests, enforces throttling and security policies, passes requests to the back-end service and returns the result to the client.
Microservices typically expose fine-grained APIs unlike what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to multiple services; a gateway gives all clients a single entry point.
Core functions are routing requests to the appropriate backend service, load balancing, and API composition, which combines several backend API requests into one frontend request.
Security and traffic control features include authentication and authorization, data encryption, rate limiting and throttling, and IP whitelisting or blacklisting.
Resilience and visibility features include retry and circuit breaking, caching, and monitoring, logging, tracing and analytics.
Advantages: it encapsulates the internal structure of the API, gives a centralized view of the API and simplifies client code.
Disadvantages: a possible single point of failure, a possible performance impact, a bottleneck if not scaled properly, and challenging configuration.

entries.title: Caching proxy: answering from saved copies

definition.text: A caching proxy speeds up requests by returning content saved from an earlier request by the same or another client.

facts.text: Caching proxies were the first kind of proxy server, and web proxies are commonly used to cache web pages from a web server.

Keeping local copies of frequently requested resources lets large organizations significantly cut upstream bandwidth use and costs while significantly increasing performance; most ISPs and large businesses have one.
Poorly implemented caching proxies can cause problems, such as an inability to use user authentication.
A Performance Enhancing Proxy mitigates link problems, for example improving TCP performance under high round-trip times or packet loss, by merging TCP ACKs or compressing application-layer data.

entries.title: Nginx: a web server that also proxies and balances

definition.text: nginx is a web server that can also be used as a reverse proxy, load balancer, mail proxy and HTTP cache.

facts.text: It can serve static content or act as a proxy server, serve dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, WSGI servers or Phusion Passenger, and work as a software load balancer.

nginx handles requests with an asynchronous event-driven approach rather than threads, giving predictable performance under high load, and can hold more than 10,000 simultaneous connections with about 2.5 MB per 10k inactive keep-alive connections.
It offers load balancing with in-band health checks, TLS with SNI and OCSP stapling through OpenSSL, name- and IP-based virtual servers, and automatic certificate issuance and renewal with ACME.
Protocol support includes gRPC, WebSockets (reverse proxying and load balancing them), HTTP/2, including as an upstream protocol, and experimental HTTP/3.

nginx was written to be faster than Apache, which has offered similar performance since version 2.4; its speed came at the cost of flexibility, such as no per-file access overrides like Apache's .htaccess.
It can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections; the paid NGINX Plus adds advanced load balancing and an expanded suite of monitoring metrics.

entries.title: Transparent proxy: a proxy clients do not choose
entries.article: Proxy server#Implementations of proxies > Transparent proxy

definition.text: A transparent or intercepting proxy redirects or filters client traffic without being explicitly selected by the client.

facts.text: It is often deployed without browser or application proxy settings, so clients may be unaware that their traffic passes through a proxy.
It sits in the network path and commonly redirects outgoing TCP port 80 traffic; older HTTP terminology used 'transparent proxy' for a proxy that did not modify requests or responses.

Businesses use intercepting proxies to enforce acceptable use policies without configuring client browsers, and ISPs in some countries use them to save upstream bandwidth and improve response times by caching.
Interception raises problems: the original destination IP and port must reach the proxy, HTTP authentication such as NTLM breaks, and some requests and responses become uncacheable by a shared cache.

entries.title: Reverse proxy trade-offs: a single door is a single risk

definition.text: Putting a reverse proxy in front of servers adds complexity and creates a single point of failure and a high-value security target.

facts.text: A reverse proxy is a single point of failure for the back ends it fronts: misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable, and adding failover proxies increases complexity further.

To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic the proxy must decrypt and re-encrypt it, which needs the TLS certificate and private key, extends the number of systems with access to unencrypted data and makes it a more valuable attack target.
Giving a third party's reverse proxy access to private keys places confidentiality, integrity and availability in that party's hands.

It can track request IP addresses and read or modify unencrypted traffic, so anyone who compromises it can do the same; exposing internal applications not hardened to public standards through it may increase the attack surface.

entries.title: API gateway request flow: stage by stage

definition.text: An API gateway handles each request in stages: it validates the request, checks identity and rate limits, routes it to a service and deals with errors.

facts.text: The client sends an HTTP request to the gateway, which parses and validates the request's attributes and performs allow-list and deny-list checks.
The gateway talks to an identity provider for authentication and authorization, then applies rate limiting rules and rejects the request if it is over the limit.
Once the request has passed the basic checks, the gateway finds the relevant service by path matching, transforms the request into the appropriate protocol and sends it to the backend microservices.
The gateway can handle errors and use circuit breaking for faults that take longer to recover, can use the ELK stack for logging and monitoring, and sometimes caches data.

entries.text: A request to an API gateway has several hurdles to clear before any service sees it. The gateway parses and validates the request's attributes and runs allow-list and deny-list checks. It then consults an outside service that knows who the caller is, the idea behind {{ref:sysd-reliab-026}}. Next it applies rate-limit rules and rejects the request if it is over the limit. Once the basic checks pass, the gateway finds the relevant service by path matching, transforms the request into the appropriate protocol and sends it to the backend services. It can handle errors, and use circuit breaking for faults that take longer to recover.

entries.title: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer

definition.text: A reverse proxy, an API gateway and a load balancer are three components that sit in front of servers, each suited to a different job (hiding and protecting servers, routing to services, spreading traffic), and a system can use all three together.

facts.text: A reverse proxy keeps servers hidden from clients and shields sensitive websites from cyber-attacks.
An API gateway delivers requests to the right services and suits busy applications with many intercommunicating services.
A load balancer directs traffic evenly across servers to prevent bottlenecks and is essential for popular websites with heavy traffic.
A load balancer is useful when multiple servers serve the same function; a reverse proxy is useful even with one server, and can also act as a load balancer, but not the other way around.

entries.title: Backend for frontend pattern: one backend per interface

definition.text: The Backend For Frontend pattern creates a separate backend service for each specific frontend application or interface.

facts.text: It avoids customizing a single backend for multiple interfaces.
Microservice output is often not in the exact format or filtering a front end needs; BFF moves that reformatting logic from the frontend into an intermediate layer.
Its primary function is to get the required data from the appropriate service, format it and send it to the frontend; GraphQL performs really well as a BFF.

Consider it when a shared general-purpose backend carries significant development overhead, when the backend should be optimized for one client, or when customizations accommodate multiple interfaces.

entries.title: API management: publishing, controlling and measuring an API

definition.text: API management is the process of publishing web APIs, enforcing their usage policies, controlling access, supporting their users, and collecting and analyzing usage statistics and performance.

facts.text: Typical API management products combine a gateway, publishing tools, a developer portal or API store, reporting and analytics, and monetization, to support developer and subscriber communities.

The gateway is an API front end that receives requests, enforces throttling and security policies, passes requests to the back end and returns the response; it can also transform messages, cache, collect analytics and handle authentication.

Publishing tools define APIs with OpenAPI or RAML, document, test and deploy them under access and usage policies; the developer portal gathers documentation, sample code, a sandbox and subscription-key management.

Reporting monitors API usage and load, can alert in real time and analyze historical logs for trends, which helps optimize the API and define service-level agreements; monetization adds usage-based pricing and invoicing.

Reporting analyzes usage and load, which helps optimize the API and set the service levels it promises.

entries.title: Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source

definition.text: A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data, either a copy of data kept elsewhere or the result of an earlier computation, so that future requests for it can be served faster.

facts.text: A cache hit occurs when the requested data is found in the cache, and a cache miss occurs when it is not.
Serving a hit by reading the cache is faster than recomputing the result or reading a slower data store, so the more requests the cache serves, the faster the system performs.
A cache is a pool of entries. Each entry holds data that is a copy of data in a backing store, plus a tag that says which backing-store data it copies.

A client checks the cache first and uses an entry whose tag matches the data it wants. On a miss it must make a more expensive access to the backing store, and the data is typically copied into the cache.
To be cost-effective caches must be relatively small, yet they work well in many areas of computing because typical applications access data with a high degree of locality of reference.

Memory design trades capacity against speed, because larger capacity means greater physical distances for signals and so propagation delays. Fast technologies such as SRAM also cost more than commodity DRAM, flash or hard disks.
The buffering a cache provides benefits latency, throughput or both; it can raise throughput by assembling many fine-grained transfers into larger, more efficient requests.
CPUs, solid-state drives and hard disk drives often include hardware-based caches, while web browsers and web servers commonly rely on software caching.

entries.title: Locality of reference: why caches usually win

definition.text: Locality of reference is the tendency of a processor or application to access the same set of memory locations, or nearby ones, repeatedly over a short period.

facts.text: There are two basic types: temporal locality, the reuse of specific data within a relatively small time, and spatial locality, the use of data elements within relatively close storage locations. Sequential locality is a special case of spatial.
With temporal locality a referenced location is likely to be referenced again soon, so a copy of the data is kept in faster memory to cut the latency of later references.

Systems with strong locality are good candidates for caching and prefetching. Because later reads tend to land near earlier ones, a cache reads large chunks in the hope that later reads are served from nearby locations.
Caches work well in many areas of computing because typical applications show a high degree of locality; they rely on recently requested data being likely to be requested again.
Data enters a cache one cache line at a time, so spatial locality matters: when one element is referenced, a few neighboring elements are brought into the cache as well.

Poor locality causes cache thrashing and cache pollution. Row-by-row matrix traversal matches C's row-major storage and uses the cache well; as matrices grow, non-sequential traversals cause far more cache misses and RAM accesses.

entries.title: The CPU cache: tiny, costly memory beside the core

definition.text: A CPU cache is a hardware cache used by the processor to reduce the average time or energy needed to access data from main memory.

facts.text: A CPU cache is a smaller, faster memory close to a processor core that holds copies of frequently used main-memory data; main memory may be tens to hundreds of times slower. It is typically costly SRAM.

Data moves between memory and cache in fixed-size cache lines, stored as entries with a tag naming the memory location. A hit is served from the cache; on a miss the data is copied in from main memory.

Larger caches have better hit rates but longer latency, so processors use levels: L1, the smallest and fastest, is checked first, then L2, and often a larger L3 shared among cores, before main memory.

Placement can be fully associative (any slot), direct-mapped (one slot) or N-way set associative. More associativity means fewer conflict misses but more power, area and search time; doubling it up to four-way helps about as much as doubling the cache.

entries.text: Main memory can be tens to hundreds of times slower than a small memory sitting next to the processor core. Larger caches hit more often but answer more slowly, so processors use levels. L1, the smallest and fastest, is checked first, then L2, and often a larger L3 shared among cores, before main memory.

entries.title: Cache hit ratio: the number that judges a cache

definition.text: The hit ratio of a cache is how often a searched-for item is found in it, expressed as the percentage of accesses that are cache hits.

facts.text: A cache has two primary figures of merit: hit ratio, and latency, which is how long after a request the cache can return an item when there is a hit.
The miss ratio is 1 minus the hit ratio.
Hit-rate measurements are typically made on benchmark applications, and the hit ratio varies by application.
Video and audio streaming often has a hit ratio near zero, because each bit of the stream is read once (a compulsory miss), used, and never read or written again.
Many cache algorithms, LRU in particular, let streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again, which is called cache pollution.

Faster replacement strategies track less usage information to cut update time, while more efficient ones track more to raise the hit rate for a given cache size, so each is a compromise between hit rate and latency.

The ratio is not a property of the cache alone, because it varies by application. Video and audio streaming often has a hit ratio near zero, since each bit of the stream is read once, used and never read or written again. That first read is called a compulsory miss. Worse, many cache algorithms, LRU in particular, let streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again. This is called cache pollution. LRU is covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-007}}. Even the replacement strategy is a compromise between hit rate and latency. Faster strategies track less usage information, and more efficient ones track more.

entries.title: Eviction policies: what a full cache forgets

definition.text: Cache replacement policies, also called eviction policies, are algorithms that decide which items a full cache discards to make room for new data.

facts.text: Caching improves performance by keeping recent or often-used items in memory that is faster or cheaper to access than the normal store; when the cache is full, the algorithm must choose which items to discard.
On a miss, some existing entry is typically removed to make room for the new data, and the heuristic that picks the entry to replace is the replacement policy.
Least recently used (LRU) replaces the entry accessed less recently than any other entry, and more sophisticated algorithms also take into account how often entries are used.
Replacement strategies trade hit rate against latency: tracking more usage information improves the hit rate for a given cache size, while tracking less makes the policy faster.
Besides recency and frequency, a policy may weigh other factors such as item size, the time needed to obtain the item, and expiration.
Depending on cache size, no algorithm to discard items may be needed at all.

More sophisticated algorithms also take into account how often entries are used. LRU is covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-007}}. Every choice trades hit rate against latency: tracking more usage information improves the hit rate for a given cache size, while tracking less makes the policy faster. A policy may also weigh other factors, such as item size, the time needed to obtain the item and expiration. And if the cache is large enough, no discarding algorithm may be needed at all.

entries.title: Cache write policies: when the backing store finds out

definition.text: A cache's write policy governs when a write made to the cache is propagated to the backing store, and a write-miss policy governs whether data is loaded into the cache on a write miss.

facts.text: Write-through performs every write synchronously to both the cache and the backing store.
Write-back first writes only to the cache and postpones the write to the backing store until the modified content is about to be replaced by another cache block.
A write-back cache is more complex: it must track which locations were written over and mark them dirty, and writes them back only on eviction, a process called a lazy write.
A read miss in a write-back cache may need two accesses to the backing store: one to write back the dirty data and one to fetch the requested data.

On a write miss, write allocate (fetch on write) loads the missed location into the cache and then writes; no-write allocate (write around) writes directly to the backing store and loads data only on read misses.

A write-back cache typically uses write allocate, expecting later reads or writes of the same location to hit, while a write-through cache uses no-write allocate because later writes must still go to the backing store.
Write-through is common over unreliable networks, because the coherency protocol needed between several write-back caches is enormously complex when communication is unreliable.
Other entities may change the data in the backing store, or other caches may update their copies, in which case a cached copy becomes out-of-date, or stale.

The cache must track which locations were written over and mark them dirty, then write them back only on eviction, a process called a lazy write. A read miss in a write-back cache may need two trips to the backing store: one to write back dirty data, one to fetch the requested data.

On a write miss, write allocate, also called fetch on write, loads the missed location into the cache and then writes. No-write allocate, or write around, writes directly to the backing store and loads data only on read misses. The usual pairings follow the logic. A write-through cache uses no-write allocate, because later writes must still go to the backing store.

Write-through is common over unreliable networks, where the coherency protocol needed between several write-back caches is enormously complex. Whatever the policy, a cached copy can become stale, or out-of-date, when other entities change the backing store or other caches update their copies.

entries.title: Least frequently used: when popularity outlives its use

definition.text: Least frequently used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and discards the items used less often first.

facts.text: LFU is like LRU except that it stores how many times a block was accessed instead of how recently, and it removes the block used the fewest times.
An object that was accessed often in the past and then becomes unpopular stays in an LFU cache for a long time, blocking newer or less-popular objects from replacing it.
LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA) adds a cache-age factor to the reference count so such objects become eligible for replacement, and it reduces the cache pollution LFU causes when a cache is small.
Least frequent recently used (LFRU) combines the benefits of LFU and LRU by splitting the cache into a protected privileged partition for popular content and an unprivileged partition.

entries.title: Least recently used: the default eviction rule

definition.text: Least recently used (LRU) is an eviction policy that discards the least recently used items first.

facts.text: LRU must track what was used and when, which is cumbersome; it keeps age bits for cache lines and finds the least recently used line from those bits.
Whenever a cache line is used, the age of the other cache lines changes.
LRU is a family of caching algorithms that includes 2Q and LRU/K.

LRU's cost grows with hardware: for CPU caches with large associativity (generally more than four ways) it becomes prohibitive, so designers often use pseudo-LRU, which needs only one bit per cache item.
LRU cannot be implemented in the critical path of systems such as operating systems because of its high overhead, so Clock, an approximation of LRU, is commonly used instead.
Singh's case studies for a URL shortener, WhatsApp, Twitter, Netflix and Uber each pick LRU as a good eviction policy for their cache.

entries.text:
When Singh's case studies choose an eviction policy for a URL shortener, WhatsApp, Twitter, Netflix or Uber, they choose the same one each time: LRU. Least recently used (LRU) discards the least recently used items first. The idea is easy; the bookkeeping is not. LRU must track what was used and when, so it keeps age bits for cache lines and finds the least recently used line from those bits. Whenever a line is used, the age of the other lines changes.

The cost grows with the hardware. When a CPU cache lets a line sit in any of many slots, generally more than four ways, the cost becomes prohibitive. Designers then often use pseudo-LRU, which needs only one bit per cache item. Operating systems cannot afford LRU in the critical path because of its high overhead, so they commonly use Clock, an approximation of it. LRU is also a family of algorithms that includes 2Q and LRU/K.

entries.title: Cache coherence: keeping copies in agreement

definition.text: Cache coherence is the uniformity of shared resource data that is stored in multiple local caches.

facts.text: In a cache coherent system every cached copy of a shared memory region is the same; without coherence, one client's change may go unseen by others and errors result from mismatched data.

Coherence requires that changes to data in any cache reach the copies in peer caches, and that writes to the same location are sequenced, so a processor never reads a location's newer value and then its older one.

Snooping broadcasts every request to all processors: faster with enough bandwidth but not scalable. Directory-based protocols use point-to-point messages through a common directory: longer latency, much less bandwidth, used by larger systems (more than 64 processors).
A write-invalidate protocol makes other caches discard their copies when one copy is written; a write-update protocol instead updates every other copy with the new value.

entries.text: When several caches hold copies of the same data, one copy can change while the others never find out. entries.title: The page cache: free memory put to work

definition.text: A page cache, or disk cache, is a transparent cache in main memory for pages that originate from a secondary storage device such as a hard disk or SSD.

facts.text: The operating system keeps the page cache in otherwise unused main memory, mostly transparent to applications. Memory not allocated to programs is used for it and is easily reclaimed, so there is generally no performance penalty.
Disk reads and writes are slow and random accesses need expensive seeks, so more main memory means more data cached and better performance.

A write goes to the cached page, which is marked dirty and must be flushed to disk before it is freed. A clean page has an identical copy on disk, so reusing it is cheaper than paging out application memory.
Executables and libraries are also read through the page cache and mapped into process spaces, so binaries are shared between processes and unused parts are eventually flushed from memory.

entries.title: Buffer versus cache: similar parts, different jobs

definition.text: A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly, while a buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes.

facts.text: Buffering amortizes the overhead of several small transfers over fewer, larger transfers, and an intermediary buffer serves processes that cannot transfer directly to each other.
Buffering can improve transfer performance or reduce the jitter of latency even if data is written once and read once, whereas caching aims to reduce latency.
A cache must follow a possibly distributed cache coherency protocol to stay consistent with where the data resides, which strict buffering does not require.
Caching almost always involves some form of buffering, while strict buffering does not necessarily involve caching.

entries.text: A buffer and a cache both hold data on its way somewhere, so they are easy to confuse. A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly. A buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes. It spreads the overhead of several small transfers over fewer, larger ones. It can reduce the jitter of latency even when data is written once and read once. A cache also needs a possibly distributed coherency protocol to stay consistent with where the data resides, which strict buffering does not. Caching almost always involves some buffering, but strict buffering does not necessarily involve caching.

entries.title: Prefetching: fetch it before anyone asks

definition.text: Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two of data will soon be required.

facts.text: On a read miss, a cache with a demand paging policy reads only the minimum from the backing store, for example one page of virtual memory (often 4 KB) from disk into the disk cache in RAM.
Anticipatory paging reads the requested data and also prefetches the next chunk or two before they are asked for.
Anticipatory paging helps most when the backing store has a long latency to read the first chunk and much shorter times to read the next few chunks sequentially, such as disk storage and DRAM.
Prediction or explicit prefetching can guess where future reads will come from and make requests ahead of time; if done optimally, the latency is bypassed altogether.

entries.text: Why wait for a request that is probably coming? Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two will soon be required. The plain alternative, demand paging, reads only the minimum on a read miss. That might be one page of virtual memory, often 4 KB, from disk into the disk cache in RAM. Anticipatory paging also prefetches the next chunk or two. It helps most when the first chunk is slow to read but the next few arrive in much shorter times, as with disk storage and DRAM. Done optimally, prediction can bypass the latency altogether.

entries.title: Caching strategies: keeping a cache and its data in sync

definition.text: Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping a cache and its database in sync: cache-aside and read-through for reads, and write-around, write-back and write-through for writes.

facts.text: The strategies are often used in combination; for example, write-around is often used together with cache-aside to make sure the cache is up to date.

A write-through cache writes data to the cache and the database simultaneously, giving fast retrieval and complete consistency between cache and storage, at the cost of higher latency for write operations.

Write-around sends writes straight to the database or permanent storage, bypassing the cache; this may reduce latency but increases cache misses, because the cache must read from the database on a miss.
Write-around can therefore mean higher read latency for applications that write and quickly re-read data, since those reads come from slower back-end storage.
A write-back cache writes only to the caching layer and confirms the write as soon as it completes there; the cache then syncs the write to the database asynchronously.

Write-back reduces latency and gives high throughput for write-intensive applications, but risks data loss if the caching layer crashes; having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.
A read-through cache loads data from the database itself when a read misses in the cache.
The primer lists cache-aside, write-through, write-behind (write-back) and refresh-ahead as the caching strategies to discuss.

A cache and the data store behind it can drift apart. Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping them in sync, and they split by direction. For reads there are two. In the first, the application loads data into the cache itself, a pattern covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-023}}. In read-through, the cache itself loads data from the store when a read misses. For writes there are three: write-through, write-around and write-back. They are often combined. For example, write-around is often used together with that first read pattern to make sure the cache is up to date.

A write-through cache writes data to the cache and the store simultaneously. That gives fast retrieval and complete consistency between them, at the cost of higher latency for write operations. Write-around sends writes straight to permanent storage, bypassing the cache. That may reduce latency but increases cache misses, because the cache must read from the store on a miss. Applications that write and quickly re-read data pay with slower reads from back-end storage.

A write-back cache, also called write-behind, writes only to the caching layer and confirms the write as soon as it completes there. The cache then syncs the write to the store asynchronously. This reduces latency and gives high throughput for write-intensive applications, but it risks data loss if the caching layer crashes. Having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.

entries.title: Distributed cache: memory pooled across machines

definition.text: A distributed cache pools the RAM of multiple networked computers into a single in-memory data store used as a data cache to provide fast access to data.

facts.text: While most caches sit in one physical server or hardware component, a distributed cache can grow beyond the memory limits of a single computer by linking many computers together.
A distributed cache uses networked hosts to provide scalability, reliability and performance to the application, and the hosts can be co-located or spread over different geographical regions.
A global cache is a single shared cache that all application nodes use; when data is missing, the cache itself is responsible for finding it in the underlying data store.
Redis is a common distributed cache, holding key-value pairs across services with faster reads and writes than traditional databases.
A distributed cache may span multiple servers so it can grow in size and transactional capacity; it is mainly used to store application data residing in a database and web session data.
Each cache key is assigned to a specific shard, also called a partition; consistent hashing spreads keys evenly across shards even if some shards crash or become unavailable.

Distributed caching became feasible because main memory became cheap and network cards fast, with 1 Gbit standard and 10 Gbit gaining traction; it also runs well on the lower-cost machines typical of web servers.

entries.title: Redis: a cache that is also a data store

definition.text: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory key-value database used as a distributed cache and message broker, with optional durability.

facts.text: Redis is multi-modal with sub-millisecond latency, and its core idea is that a cache can also act as a full-fledged database; it stores data in key-value format.
Redis serves reads and writes from main memory but also persists data to disk with snapshots (RDB) and AOF, so it supports fully durable storage.
Redis supports data structures such as strings, bitmaps, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes and JSON.

Redis is fast for three reasons: it is RAM-based, and RAM access is at least 1000 times faster than random disk access; it uses IO multiplexing with a single-threaded execution loop; and it uses efficient lower-level data structures.

Its data structures suit counting clicks and comments per post (hash), sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set), caching user behavior history, and storing boolean flags for huge data in little space.
Top use cases are distributed caching, session storage, message queue, rate limiting and a high-speed database; Redis also supports publish-subscribe messaging.

Redis uses a data model unlike a relational database: commands specify operations on abstract data types rather than queries, data sits in structures designed for direct retrieval, and it does not rely on secondary indexes or aggregations.
Redis operates as a single process, single-threaded or double-threaded while rewriting the AOF, so a single instance cannot run tasks such as stored procedures in parallel.

entries.title: Memcached: servers that never talk to each other

definition.text: Memcached is a general-purpose distributed memory-caching system, often used to speed up dynamic database-driven websites by caching data and objects in RAM so an external data source is read less often.

facts.text: Memcached's APIs provide one large hash table distributed across multiple machines; when the table is full, later inserts purge older data in least recently used (LRU) order.
Memcached uses a client-server architecture: servers keep a key-value associative array that clients populate and query by key, with keys up to 250 bytes and values at most 1 megabyte.
Each client knows all the servers and the servers never talk to each other; the client library hashes the key to pick a server, a simple form of sharding and a scalable shared-nothing architecture.
Servers keep values in RAM and discard the oldest values when memory runs out, so clients must treat Memcached as a transitory cache and cannot assume stored data is still there.
Memcached is valuable where the number of requests for content is high, or where the cost of generating a particular piece of content is high.
In the usual read pattern the client first checks for a value under a unique key such as userrow plus the user id, and if it is absent selects from the database and adds the result to Memcached.

After a database update the cached view goes out of date unless the code also sets the new value with the Memcached set call or invalidates the entry with delete; deleted records need the same treatment.
Memcached treats all operations equally, so any client with access sees every entry; most deployments sit in trusted networks, with optional SASL authentication for untrusted ones.

entries.title: Redis replication and clustering: copies for reads, clusters for scale

definition.text: Redis scales reads and protects data through master-replica replication, and scales further through a clustering mode.

facts.text: Data from any Redis server can replicate to any number of replicas, and a replica may itself be master to another replica, giving a single-rooted replication tree.
Replication is useful for read, but not write, scalability or for data redundancy; replicas can be configured to accept writes, which permits inconsistency between instances.
A Redis cluster can scale up to 1,000 nodes, achieve acceptable write safety and continue operating when some nodes fail.
In a cluster all single-key commands are available, but multi-key operations are restricted to keys that belong to the same node.

entries.title: Memoization: remembering what a function already computed

definition.text: Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up programs by storing the results of expensive function calls and returning them when the same inputs occur again.

facts.text: Memoization is a type of caching, normally implemented with a hash table. A memoized function stores its inputs together with the computed result the first time and returns the remembered result on later calls with those inputs.
The set of remembered results may be a fixed-size set controlled by a replacement algorithm, or a fixed set, depending on the function and its use.

A function can be memoized only if it is referentially transparent, so that calling it has exactly the same effect as replacing the call with its return value. Unlike a lookup table, the results are filled in on the fly.
Memoization is a typical space-time tradeoff: runtime falls as memory use rises. It is related to dynamic programming, which can also be thought of as a means of caching.

entries.title: Belady's clairvoyant algorithm: the perfect eviction rule

definition.text: Bélády's optimal algorithm, also called the optimal replacement policy or the clairvoyant algorithm, discards the information that will not be needed for the longest time.

facts.text: It is the optimal cache replacement policy, but it needs knowledge of the future to evict the lines that will be reused farthest in the future.
Because it is generally impossible to predict how far ahead information will be needed, it is unfeasible in practice; a general-purpose operating system cannot implement it.
Its practical minimum can be calculated after experimentation, so it gives a yardstick for comparing the effectiveness of a chosen cache algorithm.
Some policies predict future reuse from past access patterns to approximate it, and some of the best-performing cache replacement policies attempt to imitate it.

entries.title: FIFO and random eviction: choosing without a memory
entries.article: Cache replacement policies#First in first out (FIFO)

definition.text: Simple eviction policies choose the victim without tracking recency or frequency: FIFO evicts the oldest entry, LIFO the newest, and random replacement an arbitrary one.

facts.text: With FIFO the cache behaves like a queue and evicts blocks in the order they were added, regardless of how often or how many times they were accessed before.
With LIFO the cache behaves like a stack and evicts the block added most recently first, regardless of how often it was accessed.
Random replacement picks an item and discards it to make space when necessary, and needs no access history.
Random replacement has been used in ARM processors because of its simplicity, and it allows efficient stochastic simulation.

entries.text: The simplest eviction rules do not track recency or frequency at all. FIFO evicts the oldest entry, LIFO the newest, and random replacement an arbitrary one. With FIFO the cache behaves like a queue and evicts blocks in the order they were added, however often they were accessed before. With LIFO it behaves like a stack and evicts the block added most recently, again regardless of how often it was accessed. Random replacement picks an item and discards it to make space when necessary, and it needs no access history. It has been used in ARM processors because of its simplicity, and it allows efficient stochastic simulation.

entries.title: Most recently used: evicting what you just touched

definition.text: Most recently used (MRU) is the reverse of LRU: it discards the most recently used items first.

facts.text: Chou and DeWitt said that when a file is repeatedly scanned in a looping sequential reference pattern, MRU is the best replacement algorithm.
For random access patterns and repeated scans over large datasets, called cyclic access patterns, MRU gets more hits than LRU because it tends to retain older data.

entries.title: SIEVE and S3-FIFO: evicting the one-hit wonders

definition.text: SIEVE is a simple eviction algorithm designed specifically for web caches such as key-value caches and content delivery networks.

facts.text: SIEVE uses lazy promotion and quick demotion: it does not update the global data structure on a hit, and it quickly evicts newly inserted objects because cache workloads show high one-hit-wonder ratios.
SIEVE keeps a single FIFO queue, with one metadata bit per object saying whether it was requested after admission, and a moving hand that selects objects to evict.
S3-FIFO, designed in 2023, uses three FIFO queues: a small queue taking 10% of cache space, a main queue taking 90%, and a ghost queue that stores only object metadata.
In S3-FIFO the small queue filters out one-hit-wonders, the main queue keeps popular objects through reinsertion, and the ghost queue catches potentially popular objects evicted from the small queue.

entries.title: Segmented LRU: making an item earn its place

definition.text: A segmented LRU (SLRU) cache is divided into a probationary segment and a protected segment.

facts.text: Data from a miss enters at the most-recently-accessed end of the probationary segment; a hit moves the line to the most-recently-accessed end of the protected segment, so protected lines have been accessed at least twice.
The protected segment is finite: promoting a line can push the protected segment's LRU line back to the probationary segment, giving it another chance to be accessed before replacement.
When data must be discarded, lines are taken from the LRU end of the probationary segment.
Adaptive replacement cache (ARC) balances between LRU and LFU, improving SLRU by using recently evicted items to resize the protected and probationary segments.
