entries.title: Adaptive replacement cache: learning from what it evicted

definition.text: The adaptive replacement cache (ARC) is a page replacement algorithm that outperforms LRU by tracking both frequently used and recently used pages plus a recent eviction history for both.

facts.text: Basic LRU keeps one list ordered by most recent access. ARC splits the directory into T1, entries seen once recently, and T2, frequent entries referenced at least twice; an entry in T1 referenced again moves to T2.
Each list gets a ghost list, B1 or B2, holding only the keys of entries recently evicted from it, never their data. Ghost hits let ARC adapt to changing usage.
A hit in B1 grows the target size of T1 and a hit in B2 shrinks it, which also decides whether T1 or T2 gives up an entry when the cache is full.
ARC runs in IBM's DS6000/DS8000 storage controllers, and ZFS uses a variant instead of the page cache; OpenZFS also runs the same algorithm on an SSD as a second-level read cache called L2ARC.

entries.title: Caching layers: caches from browser to storage

definition.text: Data is cached at many layers of a system, from the client-facing side to backend systems.

facts.text: Browsers cache HTTP responses guided by directives in response headers; CDNs cache static content such as images and JavaScript closer to users; some load balancers cache frequently requested data to answer without engaging backend servers.

Services often check an in-memory cache before querying a database and may use disk caching for larger datasets, while distributed caches such as Redis hold key-value pairs across services with faster reads and writes than traditional databases.

A full-text search index, as in Elasticsearch, is effectively a form of cache optimized for quick text retrieval, and message brokers such as Kafka keep messages on disk per a retention policy for consumers to pull.
Databases cache too: a bufferpool holds copies of data pages in memory so reads and writes avoid disk, and materialized views store the results of expensive queries so they need not be recalculated.

entries.title: Time to live: giving every cache entry an expiry date

definition.text: Time to live (TTL) gives each cache item a specific lifespan after which it is dropped or refreshed.

facts.text: TTL is not strictly an eviction algorithm; each cache item is simply given a specific lifespan.
The most straightforward way to keep cached entries fresh is a maximum time an entry may stay in the cache before it is updated, usually called time to live.
Time-aware LRU (TLRU) is an LRU variant for caches whose contents have a valid lifetime, using a time-to-use timestamp on each item set from its locality and publisher.
Avoid giving keys the same expiry time by adding a random number to the TTL, and give keys that do not exist only a short TTL.

entries.title: Cache invalidation: the famously hard problem

definition.text: Cache invalidation is the process by which a computer system declares cache entries out of date and replaces or removes them.

facts.text: Cached data goes stale when something other than the cache changes the backing store, or when a client updates data in one cache while copies of it sit in other caches.

If data is modified it should be invalidated in the cache, or the application can behave inconsistently; this is famously hard, and Phil Karlton counted cache invalidation among the two hard things in computer science.
Explicit invalidation changes the application data, which marks what the client received as out of date; once the cache is invalidated, a client that asks for the data is given the new version.

The simplest rule is a TTL, the longest an entry may stay cached before refresh; very low TTLs, validating on every request, or not caching volatile content also keep data fresh but raise load on the application.

Explicit invalidation is hard when many objects must be invalidated, invalidating several representations adds complexity to the application, and the requests go through a caching proxy, whose performance they can hurt.
Write-through, write-around and write-back caches differ in when a write reaches the cache and the database, and so in how they keep the two consistent.

Communication protocols between cache managers that keep their data consistent are called cache coherence protocols; invalidation can be one of their steps, with a processor invalidating cached copies of a location it changed.
In the query-cache design, entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or the page rank changes.

entries.title: Cache-aside: the application does the fetching

definition.text: In cache-aside the application reads from the cache first and, on a miss, reads the data from the database and then updates the cache.

facts.text: On a read the service checks the cache and returns the cached contents if present; otherwise it fetches the contents from the database and updates the cache. The primer calls this approach cache-aside.

To keep cached entries from staying stale, the simplest rule is a maximum time an entry may stay in the cache before it is updated, usually called time to live (TTL); the query-cache design describes this as cache-aside.
Write-around is often used together with cache-aside to make sure the cache is up to date.
Because a cache has limited capacity, the query-cache design uses a least recently used approach to expire older entries.

entries.title: Cache stampede: when expiry sends everyone at once

definition.text: A cache stampede, also called dog-piling, is a cascading failure in which very heavy load makes many parallel processes recompute the same expired cached value at once.

facts.text: While a page stays cached, a heavily loaded system remains responsive because requests are served from the cached copy, which keeps the expensive rendering operation to a minimum.
Under very heavy load, when the cached page expires, many threads across the server farm may all try to render it at the same time, and none of them knows the others are doing so.

That concurrent load can itself exhaust shared resources and cause congestion collapse, so every attempt to re-render the page times out, the cache hit rate drops to zero and the collapse lasts as long as the load stays heavy.
For example, if a page takes 3 seconds to render and traffic is 10 requests per second, then when the cached page expires 30 processes are recomputing it at once.

In the usual pattern a process reads the key and, on a miss, recomputes the value and writes it back with a TTL; if the recomputation is slow and the key is accessed often, many processes recompute at expiry.
Recomputing usually queries a database or other service, so at a high request rate that shared resource is overloaded, which may in turn cause a system collapse.

entries.title: Stopping a stampede: locks, early expiry and other fixes

definition.text: Cache stampede mitigation, also called dogpile prevention, covers techniques that stop many processes from recomputing one expired cache value at the same moment.

facts.text: The approaches fall roughly into three groups: locking, external recomputation and probabilistic early expiration.
With locking, a process that misses on a key tries to acquire the lock for that key and recomputes the value only if it gets the lock.
A process that fails to get the lock can return not-found for the client to handle, or serve a stale item kept in the cache while the new value is recomputed.
Locking can prevent stampedes altogether but doubles the writes, and it is hard to implement correctly: the lock holder may fail, the lock needs its own time-to-live, and race conditions arise.
External recomputation moves the work to a separate process, triggered when the cached value approaches expiration or when a process hits a miss.
External recomputation adds a moving part to maintain and monitor, needs unnatural code separation or duplication, and suits mostly static cache keys, not keys generated from an id.
With probabilistic early expiration, each process independently decides whether to recompute before expiry, with a probability that rises as expiry nears, so fewer processes expire at the same time.

An exponential-distribution implementation was shown to be optimal and works well with beta set to 1; it is simple and favors early recomputation as traffic rises, but needs extra cache memory to store the recompute time.

entries.title: Cache penetration: requests for data that does not exist

definition.text: Cache penetration happens when the requested key exists in neither the cache nor the database, so every such request ends up at the database.

facts.text: Because the database has nothing to return, the application cannot populate the cache, which puts heavy pressure on both the cache and the database; a malicious user sending many such queries can easily overload the database.
One fix is to cache a null value for keys that do not exist, giving those null entries a short TTL.
Another fix is a Bloom filter, a data structure that rapidly tells whether an element is in a set; a query for a key it says does not exist never reaches the cache or the database.

entries.title: Cache failure modes: four ways a cache goes wrong

definition.text: Caches typically go wrong in four ways: many keys expiring together, requests for keys that do not exist, a hot key expiring, and the cache crashing.

facts.text: When many keys expire at the same time, queries hit the database directly and overload it; avoid identical expiry times by adding a random number, or let only core business data reach the database until the cache is back.
A key that exists in neither cache nor database stresses both; cache a null value for it, or check a Bloom filter first to avoid hitting the database.
When a hot key expires, a large number of requests hit the database; since hot keys take up 80% of the queries, they are given no expiration time.
When the cache is down, all requests go to the database; a circuit breaker can stop services from reaching the cache or database meanwhile, and a cache cluster improves cache availability.

entries.title: Multi-level caching: falling through the levels

definition.text: Multi-level caching keeps data in a hierarchy of cache levels, labeled L1, L2, L3 and so on, with each level searched in turn.

facts.text: A lookup searches the tags in level one first; if the data is not there it searches L2, then L3 and lower until it is found and read.
Most CPUs since the 1980s have used one or more caches, sometimes in cascaded levels.
In two-tiered caching, an in-memory cache is the first layer and a distributed cache is the second layer.

Multi-level caching keeps data in a hierarchy of cache levels, labeled L1, L2, L3 and so on, with each level searched in turn. A lookup searches the tags in level one first. If the data is not there, it searches L2, then L3 and lower, until it is found and read. Most CPUs since the 1980s have used one or more caches, sometimes in cascaded levels. The same idea works in software: in two-tiered caching, an in-memory cache is the first layer and a distributed cache is the second.

entries.title: When to use a cache, and when not to

definition.text: A cache pays off when data is read repeatedly, and it should be treated as transient storage rather than a permanent store.

facts.text: Caching improves performance, reduces load on the database, reduces network cost and increases read throughput.

Caching is not helpful when accessing the cache takes as long as accessing the primary data store, or when requests have low repetition, because caching performance comes from repeated access patterns.
Caching is not helpful when data changes frequently, because the cached version gets out of sync and the primary data store must be accessed every time.
A cache should not be used as permanent data storage; caches are almost always built on volatile memory because it is faster, so they are transient.

entries.title: Redis persistence: snapshots and the append-only file

definition.text: Redis persists its in-memory dataset to disk either by snapshotting at intervals or by journaling every change to an append-only file.

facts.text: Redis typically holds the whole dataset in memory; snapshotting asynchronously dumps the dataset to disk at regular intervals as a binary dump, while journaling adds a record of each modifying operation to an append-only file (AOF) in the background.
Redis can rewrite the AOF in the background to stop the journal growing indefinitely, and journaling is generally considered the safer approach.
By default Redis writes data to a file system at least every two seconds, so a complete system failure on default settings loses only a few seconds of data.
Redis forks the process that holds the data, so the parent keeps serving clients while the child persists the in-memory data to disk.

entries.title: Memcached or Redis: the interview question and its answer

definition.text: Redis and Memcached are both used as caches, and the choice between them is a popular interview question that turns on the data structures, persistence and scaling each offers.

facts.text: Redis data structures make it a good choice for counting clicks and comments per post (hash), sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set), caching user behavior history, and storing boolean flags such as login or membership status in small space.
Memcached offers a distributed hash table of keys up to 250 bytes and values up to 1 megabyte, while Redis supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, JSON and more.
Memcached discards its oldest values when memory runs out and must be treated as transitory, while Redis can persist data with snapshots or an append-only file.
Memcached scales by clients hashing keys across servers that do not talk to each other, while Redis offers master-replica replication and a cluster mode that scales up to 1,000 nodes.

entries.title: Purge, refresh and ban: telling a caching proxy to forget

definition.text: Purge, refresh and ban are three methods of explicitly invalidating content held in a caching proxy.

facts.text: Purge removes content, including all its variants, from the caching proxy immediately; the next client request fetches the data from the application and stores it in the proxy again.
Refresh fetches the requested content from the application even when a cached copy exists and replaces the stored copy with the new version; it affects only one variant of the cached content.
Ban adds a reference to the cached content to a ban list that requests are checked against; on a match, new content is fetched, returned and cached. Unlike purge, it removes nothing at once.

entries.title: The thundering herd: many wake, one wins

definition.text: The thundering herd problem occurs when many processes or threads are awakened at once but only one can use the resource, so the rest fail and go back to sleep.

facts.text: The needless awakenings consume CPU and other system resources, potentially reducing overall performance and slowing the one process that succeeds.
When the problem occurs while accessing a cache, it is often called a cache stampede.

Operating systems mitigate it by waking one waiter: the Linux kernel serializes responses for one file descriptor, epoll's EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag wakes only one epoll set, and Windows I/O completion ports can be configured to wake one thread.
Clients that retry failed calls with a backoff wait between retries; adding jitter, randomness in the wait intervals, breaks the synchronization across clients and so avoids collisions.

entries.title: Caching weather forecasts: one answer for a whole neighborhood

definition.text: Edge servers truncated GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places so that nearby weather requests could share one cached result.

facts.text: In 2011 smartphone weather features overloaded AccuWeather servers, because two requests from the same area generated separate requests.
Edge servers truncated the GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places, so the cached results of a nearby query would be used.
The number of lookups reaching the server per day dropped by half.

entries.text:
In 2011, smartphone weather features overloaded AccuWeather servers. Two requests from the same area generated separate requests, so the servers did the same work twice for what was, to the user, the same forecast.

The fix lived at the edge. Edge servers truncated the GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places. Many slightly different positions then became one position, and the cached result of a nearby query could be used for the next. Locality of reference was doing the work here: requests from the same area are alike, so one stored answer can serve many.

The result showed in the numbers. Every request answered at the edge was one the server never saw, and the number of lookups reaching the server per day dropped by half. The lesson is about the label a cache files an answer under. A cache can reuse an answer only when a new request looks identical to an old one. Loosening what counts as identical turned near misses into hits and raised the hit ratio.

entries.title: Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby

definition.text: A geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them.

facts.text: CDNs provide high availability and performance by placing content geographically closer to end users, and arose in the late 1990s to relieve the Internet's performance bottlenecks.
CDNs now serve a large portion of Internet content: web text, graphics and scripts, downloadable files, applications, live and on-demand streaming media, and social media services.
Static files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript, photos and videos are generally the content served from a CDN, though a CDN can also deliver dynamic content.
Users fetch content from a nearby CDN node instead of the origin server, so the origin's servers do not have to handle the requests the CDN fulfills.
A visitor in the UK to a site hosted in the USA is served from a close edge location such as London, which is much quicker than a full request to the origin.
Benefits include reduced bandwidth costs, faster page loads, higher global availability and redundancy, and better security, notably protection against DDoS attacks.
Content owners pay CDN operators to deliver their content, and the CDN in turn pays ISPs, carriers and network operators for hosting its servers in their data centers.
Drawbacks: a CDN can be expensive for high-traffic services, some organizations and countries block popular CDN domains or IPs, and an audience far from any CDN server may see data travel farther.

entries.title: Peer-to-peer: when every participant is also a server

definition.text: Peer-to-peer (P2P) is a distributed architecture in which participants share part of their own resources, such as processing power, storage or network capacity, directly with other peers.

facts.text: Each peer is both resource provider and requester, with no intermediary; the client-server model instead gives the roles to different participants, with centralized servers providing and clients requesting.
Peers talk directly at the application layer over logical overlay links on top of TCP/IP; overlays handle indexing and peer discovery, and networks are classed as unstructured, structured or hybrid.
Unstructured networks form by random connections, so they are easy to build, allow local optimizations and cope well with churn, peers frequently joining and leaving. Gnutella and Kazaa are examples.

Structured networks impose a topology so any node can efficiently find even a rare resource. The most common type is a distributed hash table, where a variant of consistent hashing assigns each key to a peer.
Hybrid models mix peer-to-peer and client-server, commonly with a central server that helps peers find each other, trading centralized functionality against node equality.

Decentralization removes the single point of failure of client-server systems, and capacity grows as nodes arrive. For content delivery, serving capacity can rise as more users fetch the content, keeping the distributor's cost low.

Peers act as servers as well as clients, so they can be more exposed to remote exploits, and malicious nodes can mount routing attacks such as incorrect lookup routing or corrupting neighbors' routing tables.
P2P systems reach full potential only when many nodes contribute, but many users take without sharing, the freeloader problem, which can in some cases make the community collapse.

entries.title: DDoS: a flood from many sources at once

definition.text: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack makes a machine or network resource unavailable by flooding it with traffic that comes from many different sources.

facts.text: Denial of service is typically done by flooding the target with superfluous requests to overload it and block legitimate ones; the two general forms are attacks that crash services and attacks that flood them.
In a DDoS the flood comes from many sources, often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking a single source is not enough and more sophisticated mitigation is needed.

Common DDoS attacks are UDP flooding, SYN flooding and DNS amplification. A SYN flood leaves half-open connections that exhaust the server's available connections, because the forged sender address never replies.
In a reflected attack, forged requests with the victim's spoofed source address go to many computers whose replies flood the victim; amplification magnifies the bandwidth sent to the victim.

An application-layer (layer 7) DDoS over-exercises specific functions, such as search or database access. It needs fewer resources than network-layer attacks, often accompanies them and can look like legitimate traffic.
A yo-yo attack targets cloud applications that autoscale, alternating bursts of traffic that cause a scale-up with pauses that cause a scale-down.

Defense combines attack detection, traffic classification and response tools. Upstream filtering diverts traffic through a scrubbing center that passes only legitimate traffic, since DDoS can overwhelm any hardware firewall.
A sudden spike in popularity, such as a link on a major site, can deny service with the same effect as a DDoS attack, without any attacker.

entries.title: Origin and edge servers: where a CDN's content lives

definition.text: The origin server holds the original content, and edge servers are the many caching servers spread around the world that serve users nearby.

facts.text: The origin server is the primary source of content and holds its original versions, while the edge servers that cache and serve it are numerous and distributed across the world.
A CDN caches content in many geographic locations called edge locations, and each edge location holds several caching servers that deliver content to visitors in its proximity.
Providers serve a defined set of points of presence (PoPs) chosen for the coverage wanted, such as the United States, Asia-Pacific or global; these are also called edges, edge nodes or edge networks.
A CDN's footprint is the geographic area where its edge servers can effectively serve clients' requests.
CDN size varies: some have thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of servers on many remote PoPs, while others build a global network with only a small number of geographical PoPs.
CDN entry points are the servers that fetch content from the origin, and an origin shield is a CDN service that protects the origin server during heavy traffic.
DNS resolves the domain name to the IP address of the nearest edge server, and a control plane configures and manages the edge servers.

entries.title: Image CDN: one picture, many versions
entries.article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Image Optimization and Delivery (Image CDNs)

definition.text: An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image over HTTP depending on the properties of the requesting browser.

facts.text: An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image through HTTP, depending on the properties of the requesting browser as determined by the browser or by server-side logic.
An Image CDN generally combines three components: a CDN for fast serving of images, image manipulation and optimization, and device detection.
Image manipulation and optimization can happen on the fly through URL directives, in batch mode through manual upload of images, or fully automatically.
Device detection determines the properties of the requesting browser or device from the User-Agent string, HTTP Accept headers, Client-Hints or JavaScript.

entries.title: Peer-to-peer CDN: delivery that improves with demand
entries.article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Peer-to-peer CDNs

definition.text: A peer-to-peer CDN is one in which clients provide resources as well as use them.

facts.text: In a peer-to-peer CDN clients provide resources as well as use them; CDN offloading is the mechanism that lets clients help deliver content to each other in addition to edge server delivery.
Unlike client-server systems, a peer-to-peer content network can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share.
This property makes the setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor.
Web3 and blockchain technologies can incentivize peers to participate: nodes that take part receive crypto tokens in exchange for their involvement.

entries.article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Private CDNs

definition.text: A private CDN is a content delivery network built by a content owner, made of PoPs that serve content only for that owner.

facts.text: Content owners unsatisfied with the options or costs of a commercial CDN can build a private CDN, made of PoPs that only serve content for their owner.
The PoPs of a private CDN can be caching servers, reverse proxies or application delivery controllers, and it can be as simple as two caching servers or large enough to serve petabytes of content.
A private CDN deployed within a company network is also called an enterprise CDN or eCDN.
Large CDNs may build their own private network to distribute copies of content across cache locations, and use public networks as backup when its capacity is insufficient or reduced by a failure.

They fall back on public networks when that network's capacity is insufficient or reduced by a failure.

entries.title: Telco CDN: the network provider becomes the CDN
entries.article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Telco CDN advantages

definition.text: A telco CDN is a content delivery network launched by a telecommunications service provider on the network it owns.

facts.text: Rapid growth of streaming video traffic led telecommunications providers to launch their own CDNs, to lessen demands on the network backbone and reduce infrastructure investment.
Telco CDNs own the last mile and can cache content deep in their networks, minimizing the distance video travels over the general Internet and delivering it more quickly and reliably.
They have a built-in cost advantage, because traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs.

Operating their own delivery infrastructure gives operators control over resource utilization and better quality of service, whereas traditional CDNs manage content with little or no knowledge of the operator's network.

entries.text: Streaming video grew so fast that telecommunications providers began launching CDNs of their own. A telco CDN runs on the network the provider owns, to lessen demands on the network backbone and reduce infrastructure investment. entries.title: Virtual CDN: caches that appear where needed
entries.article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Virtual CDN (vCDN)

definition.text: A virtual CDN, also called a software-defined CDN, uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically.

facts.text: Virtual CDNs (vCDN), also called software-defined CDNs (sd-CDN), use virtualization to reduce content provider costs while increasing elasticity and decreasing service delay.

Virtual caches are deployed dynamically as virtual machines or containers on physical servers across the provider's coverage, avoiding traditional CDN limits on performance, reliability and availability.
Virtual cache placement depends on both the content type and the server or end-user location, so vCDNs significantly affect service delivery and network congestion.

entries.text: A virtual CDN can create a cache wherever one is needed. A virtual CDN (vCDN), also called a software-defined CDN (sd-CDN), uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically. The aim is to reduce content provider costs while increasing elasticity and decreasing service delay. The virtual caches are deployed on physical servers across the provider's coverage. The two technologies they run on are covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-065}} and {{ref:sysd-reliab-063}}. That avoids traditional CDN limits on performance, reliability and availability. Where a cache is placed depends on both the content type and the server or end-user location, so vCDNs significantly affect service delivery and network congestion.

entries.title: CDN request flow: edge first, origin second

definition.text: A user's request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it.

facts.text: After DNS resolution, the user's device sends its content request to the CDN edge server.
The edge server checks its local cache for the content and, if it finds it, serves it to the user.
If the content is not in the cache, the edge server forwards the request to the origin server.
After receiving the content from the origin, the edge server stores a copy in its cache and delivers it to the user.
Once static assets are cached at a location, later requests there are served from its edge servers instead of the origin, reducing origin load and improving scalability.
For streaming media, the CDN receives the stream at its origin server and replicates it to many or all of its edge cache servers, so HTTP streaming costs about the same as HTTP web caching.

entries.title: Push and pull CDNs: who fills the cache

definition.text: CDNs are divided into push CDNs, which are sent new content whenever it changes, and pull CDNs, which fetch content from the origin when a user first requests it.

facts.text: A push CDN receives new content whenever it changes on the server; the site owner uploads content directly to the CDN and rewrites URLs to point to it.
With a push CDN the owner configures when content expires and when it is updated.
Push CDNs upload content only when it is new or changed, which minimizes traffic but maximizes storage, and content is placed once instead of re-pulled at regular intervals.
Push CDNs suit sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.
In a pull CDN the cache is updated on request: if the CDN lacks an asset, it fetches it from the origin, populates its cache and sends the asset to the user.
Pull CDNs need less maintenance than push CDNs, because cache updates on CDN nodes happen in response to client requests.
Pull CDNs suit heavy-traffic sites, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN.
In general, web caches are populated from user requests (pull caching) or from preloaded content disseminated by content servers (push caching).

entries.title: CDN request routing: choosing which server answers

definition.text: Request routing directs each client request to the content source best able to serve it, such as the closest node or the one with the most capacity.

facts.text: Request routing directs a client request to the content source best able to serve it, such as the service node closest to the client or the one with the most capacity.
Routing algorithms include global server load balancing, DNS-based request routing, dynamic metafile generation, HTML rewriting and anycasting.
Global server load balancing (GSLB) routes requests by factors such as geographic proximity, server load and network conditions.
Anycast DNS lets multiple servers share the same IP address and helps route incoming traffic to the nearest data center.
Proximity, meaning the closest service node, is estimated by reactive probing, proactive probing and connection monitoring.
Choosing for performance picks the fewest hops, shortest time to the client or highest server performance; choosing for cost picks the cheapest locations. Edge servers near users tend to win on both.
CDN providers establish a presence at major Internet Exchange Points so they can exchange traffic directly with ISPs and other networks.

entries.title: Content networking techniques: intelligence at the edge

definition.text: A CDN is an intelligent overlay on the Internet's simple core network that combines web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services.

facts.text: The Internet follows the end-to-end principle: intelligence sits at the hosts and clients, so the core network is simplified to only forward data packets.
CDNs extend the transport network with intelligent applications, forming a tightly integrated overlay that uses web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services.
Web caches store popular content on servers close to the greatest demand, reducing bandwidth requirements and server load and improving client response times.
Server-load balancing shares traffic among servers or web caches, for example with a layer 4-7 switch holding one virtual IP address, adding capacity, scalability, reliability and health checks.

entries.title: Edge content services: ICAP, OPES and Edge Side Includes
entries.article: Content delivery network#Content networking techniques > Content service protocols

definition.text: Content service protocols give access to content services, such as content adaptation and dynamic page assembly, distributed through a content network.

facts.text: ICAP, developed in the late 1990s, is an open standard for connecting application servers; several protocol suites give access to content services distributed throughout a content network.
The more recent and robust OPES architecture lets service applications run on the OPES processor itself or remotely on a Callout Server.
Edge Side Includes (ESI) is a small markup language for assembling dynamic web content at the edge.
Generated content, from changing catalogs and forums or from personalization, creates a problem for caching systems, and a group of companies created ESI to overcome it.

entries.title: End-user mapping: finding the client behind the resolver
entries.article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Improving CDN performance using Extension Mechanisms for DNS

definition.text: End-user mapping lets a CDN use the client's subnet, passed in the edns-client-subnet DNS option, to pick a nearby edge server.

facts.text: CDNs traditionally located a client by the IP of its recursive DNS resolver, which gives poor performance when the client uses a non-local resolver that is far away.
A CDN may route a client in India to its edge server in Singapore because that client uses a public DNS resolver in Singapore.

With the edns-client-subnet EDNS0 option, CDNs use the IP address of the requesting client's subnet when resolving DNS requests; this end-user mapping drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers.
EDNS0 has drawbacks: it reduces the effectiveness of caching resolutions at recursive resolvers, increases total DNS resolution traffic, and raises a privacy concern by exposing the client's subnet.

entries.title: Multi-CDN: not trusting one network with a live event
entries.article: Content delivery network#CDN trends > Multi CDN and CDN selection

definition.text: Multi-CDN means a content provider combines several CDN services instead of relying on a single one.

facts.text: Combining several CDN services lets a content provider avoid relying on a single CDN, especially to handle high peak audiences during live events.
Traffic can be allocated among the CDNs on the client side, on the server side at the content provider's origin, or on the cloud side between the origin and the audience.
CDN selection criteria can be performance, availability and cost; a CDN selector is the decision-making service that chooses among multiple CDNs.
The IETF standardized a framework and request-routing interface for interconnecting CDNs so a request can be redirected between them; Open Caching APIs let a provider use several CDNs consistently.

entries.title: Edge computing: running the code near the user

definition.text: Edge computing is a distributed computing model that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, and so to users.

facts.text: Edge computing is any design that pushes computation physically closer to a user, to cut latency compared with running the application in a centralized data center.

It generalizes the CDN idea: CDN nodes at the network edge prefetch and cache content and can customize it, and edge computing extends this by leveraging cloud infrastructure. Early edge services hosted shopping carts, dealer lookup and ad placement.
Data from devices at the edge pushes network bandwidth to the limit when stored and used in cloud data centers, which cannot guarantee acceptable transfer rates and response times.

Placing analytical resources near users increases responsiveness and throughput. Processing locally avoids long transfers: recognizing speech at the edge lets a system send text to the cloud instead of audio, cutting bandwidth.
Failover management is crucial: if a node goes down users should still reach the service. A voice assistant at the edge can keep serving local users during cloud or internet outages.

Distributing logic across nodes introduces new problems: data traveling between nodes needs its own encryption and edge nodes may be resource-constrained, yet keeping data at the edge can improve privacy by sending less sensitive data to the cloud.
Offloading every task to the edge can slow things down because of transfer times between device and node, so the best configuration depends on the workload.

entries.title: Subresource Integrity: checking what a CDN delivers

definition.text: Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C recommendation that protects website delivery by validating assets served by a third party, such as a CDN, so they have not been compromised.

facts.text: The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location; the browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match.

An integrity value may hold several space-separated expressions, each a hash algorithm name plus a Base64 digest; when several recognized algorithms are given, the browser validates with the strongest.
SRI works with JavaScript files and linked stylesheets.

A resource from a different origin needs CORS for integrity checking: the server must allow access with the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, and the crossorigin attribute makes the browser request it in CORS mode.

entries.title: CDN security and privacy: protection and its price

definition.text: A CDN can add protection against attacks such as DDoS, but it also brings script-injection and privacy risks.

facts.text: A CDN can improve website security, especially against DDoS attacks, and vendors may extend into DDoS protection, web application firewalls and WAN optimization.
CDNs serving JavaScript have been targeted to inject malicious content into pages; Subresource Integrity ensures a page loads only a script whose content matches a hash the site author references.

Providers can profit from analytics and tracking data collected as their scripts load in the customer's browser origin, so CDNs are pointed out as potential privacy intrusions for behavioral targeting.
A website using a CDN may violate the EU's GDPR; in 2021 a German court ruled that sending a visitor's IP address to a CDN violated it.

entries.title: Database: an organized collection of data

definition.text: An organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it.

facts.text: A database, the DBMS that manages it and the applications around it together form a database system, though people often use the word database loosely for any of the three.
Databases support the internal operations of organizations and underpin online interactions with customers and suppliers.
Examples include library systems, flight reservation systems, parts inventory systems and many content management systems that store websites as collections of webpages in a database.
Databases can be classified by the type of their contents, by their application area, or by a technical aspect such as the database structure or interface type.
An in-memory database lives primarily in main memory with non-volatile backup; it is faster than a disk database and used where response time is critical.
A distributed database is one in which both the data and the DBMS span multiple computers.

Storage redundancy improves performance and availability: materialized views store frequently needed query results, and replication keeps copies of database objects for simultaneous access and resilience to partial failure.
A backup, taken occasionally or continuously, keeps each desired database state in backup files so the database can be restored after corruption or erroneous updates.

entries.text: A flight reservation system, a parts inventory and a website built from webpages all keep their data in a database. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it. Organizations rely on databases for their internal operations and for their online interactions with customers and suppliers. Strictly, the database, the software that manages it and the applications around it together form a database system. People often use the word loosely for any of the three. Databases can be classified by their contents, their application area, or a technical aspect such as structure. Some live primarily in main memory, which is faster than disk and used where response time is critical. Others spread both the data and the software over several computers. Copies protect it. Replicas of database objects give simultaneous access and resilience to partial failure. Saved copies, taken occasionally or continuously, let the database be restored after corruption or erroneous updates.

entries.title: Relational database: data in tables

definition.text: A database based on the relational model, which stores data in tables of rows and columns.

facts.text: A relational model organizes data into tables of columns and rows with a unique key identifying each row, and many relational systems let users query and update with SQL.
Each table generally represents one entity type, such as customer or product; its rows are instances of that type and its columns hold values attributed to each instance, such as address or price.

The model supports data integrity and avoids redundancy through keys and normalization, handles many-to-many relationships, supports complex queries and transactions, and is queried with the simple language SQL.
To operate efficiently and accurately, a relational DBMS must use ACID transactions.
No commercial implementation conforms to all of Codd's 12 rules, so the term relational has come to describe a broader class of database systems.

The relational database became the predominant type, replacing hierarchical and network databases because it was easier to implement and administer; NoSQL databases are now a popular alternative thanks to horizontal scaling of computer clusters.
Singh lists relational databases' advantages as simple and accurate, accessible, consistent and flexible.
Singh lists their disadvantages as expense to maintain, difficult schema evolution, performance hits from joins and denormalization, and difficult scaling because of poor horizontal scalability.

entries.title: NoSQL: data without the table

definition.text: A type of database design, named for "not only SQL" or "non-relational", that stores and retrieves data differently from the table-based structure of relational databases.

facts.text: Rather than rows and columns, a NoSQL database holds information in a single data structure such as key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs or documents; without a fixed schema it scales easily to large, often unstructured datasets.

NoSQL systems are sometimes called "Not only SQL" because they can support SQL-like query languages or work alongside SQL databases in polyglot-persistent setups, where multiple database types are combined.

NoSQL databases are popular in big data and real-time web applications for their simple design, horizontal scaling across clusters of machines and precise control over data availability; cheap commodity hardware can host them.

Many NoSQL systems follow the BASE model, prioritizing speed and availability over strict consistency (per the CAP theorem) through eventual consistency: updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale.
Most NoSQL systems lack full ACID transaction support, sacrificing it for performance and scalability, though some, like MongoDB, include it as a key feature.
Barriers to adoption include low-level query languages instead of SQL, no ad hoc joins across tables, no standardized interfaces and large existing investments in relational databases.

NoSQL databases are classified by data model, mainly key-value, document, wide-column and graph, plus time-series databases for time-stamped data and multi-model databases that combine several models in one backend.
NewSQL is a class of modern relational databases that aims to give NoSQL-like scalable performance for read-write online transaction processing while still using SQL and keeping ACID guarantees.

entries.title: Graph database: relationships as stored links

definition.text: A database that uses graph structures to represent and store data, with nodes for entities, edges for the relationships between them, and properties.

facts.text: Relationships are first-class: edges can be labeled, directed and given properties, and linking data items directly means they can often be retrieved with one operation.

Most use index-free adjacency, with nodes holding direct references to neighbors instead of a global index; adjacent lookups are typically O(1) versus O(log n) for an index, so query time tracks the part of the graph touched.

In the labeled-property graph model, nodes and relationships are named, carry key-value properties, and edges are directed; in RDF, each added piece of information is a separate statement of subject node, predicate arc and object node.
They handle graph-like queries naturally, such as shortest path, diameter and community detection, and new data can be added to an existing graph without planning every future use case.

Relational databases need many joins over several tables for complex relationships; a graph database follows stored links and avoids costly joins, and its advantage grows with query depth and complexity.

Relational systems suit flat data with relationships one or two levels deep and are typically faster at one operation over many elements; the graph model alone should not justify replacing a relational database without evidence of gains.

Suited to social relations, transport links, road maps and network topologies; Singh lists fraud detection, recommendation engines, social networks and network mapping, and a social network's friends relationship is essentially unbounded.
As of 2021 no graph query language had been universally adopted as SQL was; multi-vendor options include Gremlin, SPARQL and Cypher, and ISO's GQL is meant to be a declarative standard like SQL.

entries.title: Document database: one object, one document

definition.text: A database designed to store, retrieve and manage documents, or semi-structured information, and one of the main categories of NoSQL databases.

facts.text: A document is a self-contained unit encoding data in a standard format such as XML, YAML, JSON or binary BSON, and corresponds to an object in programming; the store is made for documents rather than tables.
Documents need no fixed schema: documents in one collection may have different fields, unlike rows of a table, so new information can be added to some documents without affecting others.
Each document is addressed by a unique identifier, often a string, URI or path, and most stores index that key to speed retrieval.

Beyond key access, an API or query language retrieves documents by content or metadata, such as all documents whose field matches a value; features vary by product, and an update can replace a whole document or single fields.

Key-value stores treat values as opaque, while document stores exploit internal structure: a query can find phone numbers containing 555 without matching postal code 55555; for simple needs the difference can be minimal.

Relational databases split one object across tables joined by foreign keys; a document database keeps everything about an object in one document fetched by key without multi-table lookups, which also avoids object-relational mapping.

Singh lists intuitive and flexible, easy horizontal scaling and schemaless as advantages, schemaless and non-relational as disadvantages, and calls document databases general-purpose for transactional and analytical applications.

entries.title: Elasticsearch: search over large volumes of data

definition.text: A distributed, open search and analytics engine, built on Apache Lucene, for storing, searching and analyzing large volumes of data quickly.

facts.text: Traditional databases are sometimes not fast enough to store, search and analyze huge volumes of data in near real time with results in milliseconds; Elasticsearch addresses this.
Elasticsearch is a distributed search engine for textual, numerical, geospatial, structured and unstructured data, built on Apache Lucene, with an HTTP web interface and schema-free JSON documents.
Documents are stored in indices divided into primary shards, each with zero or more replicas distributed across cluster nodes; routing and rebalancing are handled automatically.
Once an index has been created, the number of primary shards cannot be changed.
It supports full-text search, faceted search, real-time search, multitenancy and percolation, in which stored queries are matched against incoming documents rather than the reverse.
Real-time GET requests make it usable as a NoSQL datastore, though it does not support distributed transactions.
Geo data is supported by geo_point fields for lat/lon pairs and geo_shape fields for points, lines, circles and polygons.

In the primer's design the Lucene search cluster is scatter-gathered: every server is asked for matches, then results are merged, ranked, sorted and returned, with tweets kept in memory to keep latency low.

entries.title: Key-value store: lookup by key

definition.text: A data store for storing, retrieving and managing associative arrays (dictionaries), in which each record is stored and found through a unique key.

facts.text: The associative array (map or dictionary) is its data model: a collection of key-value pairs in which each key appears at most once; it is one of the simplest non-trivial models, and richer ones often extend it.

The value is opaque to the database, which typically supports only storing, retrieving, updating and deleting a value by its key; a document store can interpret record structure, a key-value store returns a value whole.

This suits low-latency, high-throughput workloads of direct key lookups, and Singh lists simple, performant, highly scalable, optimized lookups and session management as strengths; it is less suited to complex queries or relationships.

Limits: basic CRUD, values that cannot be filtered, no indexing or scanning, no optimization for complex queries; lack of standardization and limited transaction support long confined many systems to specialized uses.

Variants add structure: keys can be kept in lexicographic order so key ranges are retrieved efficiently, keys can be composite with major and minor parts, and some stores support complex values such as Redis lists.
Consistency ranges from eventual to serializable and is sometimes configurable against latency and availability; data may live in memory, on solid-state drives or on rotating disks.
In-memory examples include Memcached and Redis; persistent ones include Berkeley DB, Riak and Voldemort, and RocksDB is a persistent key-value storage engine developed at Facebook.

entries.title: Database management system: the software in the middle

definition.text: Software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database.

facts.text: The DBMS is the software between the database and its users or programs: it lets them capture, retrieve, update and analyze data, and it provides the facilities to administer the database, such as performance monitoring, tuning, and backup and recovery.
MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database and Microsoft Access are examples of DBMSs.
The core functionality of a DBMS is the storage, retrieval and update of data, but what a DBMS provides beyond that varies enormously.
Codd proposed that a general-purpose DBMS provide storage, retrieval and update, a metadata catalog, transactions and concurrency, recovery, authorization, remote access, and constraint enforcement.
The database engine is the core part of the DBMS that sits between the database and the application interface.
A general-purpose DBMS provides public APIs and optionally a processor for a database language such as SQL; a special-purpose DBMS may use a private API tied to a single application.
The acronym can name the database model: RDBMS for relational, OODBMS for object-oriented, ORDBMS for object-relational, and DDBMS for a distributed DBMS.

Client-server architecture put the application on a client and the database on a server so processing could be distributed; multitier architectures later added application and web servers, with the database connected only to the adjacent tier.

entries.title: Database transaction: a unit of work, all or nothing

definition.text: A unit of work performed in a database management system that is treated in a coherent and reliable way, independent of other transactions.

facts.text: Transactions serve two purposes: reliable units of work that allow correct recovery from failures and keep the database consistent, and isolation between programs accessing the database concurrently.
Without isolation between concurrent programs, their outcomes are possibly erroneous.
A bank transfer is one transaction: it requires subtracting the amount from one account and adding the same amount to the other.

A transaction must be atomic (complete or no effect), consistent (conform to existing constraints), isolated (not affect other transactions) and durable (written to persistent storage); these properties are abbreviated ACID.
A transactional database is a DBMS that provides the ACID properties for a bracketed set of operations (begin-commit), keeping the database consistent even under concurrent updates and failures.
The programmer sets a transaction's boundaries with special transaction commands, which define which code executions it includes.
A distributed transaction enforces the ACID properties over data on multiple nodes, and typically an entity coordinates the process so all parts are applied to all relevant systems.

Not every database supports ACID transactions, usually because it prioritizes optimizations that are hard or theoretically impossible to combine with them; relational databases usually support them and non-relational ones usually do not.

entries.title: ACID: four guarantees for every transaction

definition.text: A set of four properties of database transactions, atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps.

facts.text: Relational databases follow the ACID properties to maintain data integrity before and after a transaction.
Atomicity means all or nothing: the writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back.

Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from consistency in the CAP theorem, where every read receives the most recent write or an error.

Isolation keeps concurrent transactions from contending; the database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running.
Durability means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk, even through a system failure; in a distributed system this means the data is replicated to other nodes.

Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash, or shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy activated on commit.

Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder because a network connection or another node may fail; the two-phase commit protocol provides atomicity by having a coordinator ask participants if they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.

entries.text:
A power failure in the middle of a bank transfer should leave no trace. ACID names four properties of database transactions that are intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps. Relational databases follow it to keep data correct before and after a transaction.

Atomicity means all or nothing. The writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back. Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from the consistency meant in {{ref:sysd-scale-107}}, where every read receives the most recent write or an error. The third property, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-040}}, keeps concurrent transactions from contending. The database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running. The fourth, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-210}}, means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk even through a system failure. In a distributed system it is replicated to other nodes.

Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash. The alternative is shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy that is activated on commit. Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder, because a network connection or another node may fail. Atomicity there comes from a protocol covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}, in which a coordinator asks participants whether they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.
entries.text_plain:
A power failure in the middle of a bank transfer should leave no trace. ACID names four properties of database transactions that are intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps. Relational databases follow it to keep data correct before and after a transaction.

Atomicity means all or nothing. The writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back. Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from the consistency meant in The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything, where every read receives the most recent write or an error. The third property, covered in Isolation: how much transactions see of each other, keeps concurrent transactions from contending. The database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running. The fourth, covered in Durability: a commit that survives the crash, means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk even through a system failure. In a distributed system it is replicated to other nodes.

Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash. The alternative is shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy that is activated on commit. Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder, because a network connection or another node may fail. Atomicity there comes from a protocol covered in Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing, in which a coordinator asks participants whether they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.

entries.title: Database models: how data is organized logically

definition.text: A database model is a type of data model that determines the logical structure of a database and how its data can be stored, organized and manipulated.

facts.text: The most popular database model is the relational model, or its SQL approximation, which uses a table-based format.

Common logical data models include navigational, hierarchical, network, graph, relational, entity-relationship, object, document, entity-attribute-value and star schema models; an object-relational database combines the object and relational structures.
Other models include the inverted index (a physical data model) and the multidimensional, array and multivalue models.
Specialized models are optimized for particular types of data: XML, semantic, content store, event store and time series databases.
The flat model puts data in a single table, one record per row and one attribute per column; it is as simple as a spreadsheet but cannot efficiently handle complex relationships between entities.

The hierarchical model is a tree in which each record has one parent but can have many children; it suits clear parent-child relationships but struggles with many-to-many ones and can become complex and rigid.
The network model lets each record have multiple parents and children, forming a graph; it overcomes the hierarchical model's limits by handling many-to-many relationships efficiently.

entries.title: Isolation: how much transactions see of each other

definition.text: The ACID property that determines how a transaction's changes are visible to other users and systems.

facts.text: A lower isolation level lets more users access the same data at once but increases concurrency effects such as dirty reads or lost updates.
A higher isolation level reduces the concurrency effects users may meet, but needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another.
Of the four ACID properties, isolation is the one most often relaxed.
To keep the highest isolation, a DBMS usually acquires locks on data, which can cost concurrency, or implements multiversion concurrency control.

Most transactions can be built to avoid high isolation levels such as SERIALIZABLE, which cuts locking overhead, but the programmer must analyze access code carefully because relaxed isolation can cause bugs that are hard to find.
Higher isolation levels make deadlock more likely, which also calls for careful analysis and programming techniques to avoid.
Isolation is typically enforced at the database level, though client-side systems such as a transaction manager can also provide global isolation and atomicity.
Full isolation lets a transaction run as if no others were running concurrently; this strictest form, serializability, is hard to implement in reality, so looser isolation levels are often adopted.

entries.title: Primary and foreign keys: identifying and linking rows

definition.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a foreign key is a column that holds the key of a row in another table to link them.

facts.text: Most implementations give every row a unique primary key; a new unique value is generated when a row is written, the system uses it primarily to access the table, and system performance is optimized for it.

A surrogate key is an artificial attribute with no intrinsic meaning that uniquely identifies an object, such as a student ID; natural attributes are sometimes good primary keys, but surrogate keys are often used instead.
Natural keys can be defined as alternate keys, but they often need several columns, called a composite key; this is one reason a single integer column is usually made the primary key.
A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table; when a primary key migrates to another table it becomes a foreign key there, and foreign keys need not be unique.
A foreign key restricts the values of an attribute in the referencing table to values that exist in the referenced table, which is how tables are cross-referenced.

Migrating a primary key into another table represents a one-to-one or one-to-many relationship; most designs resolve many-to-many relationships with an extra table that holds the primary keys of both entity tables.

entries.title: Wide-column store: rows whose columns can vary

definition.text: A type of NoSQL database that uses tables, rows and columns but lets column names and formats vary from row to row, storing columns in column families.

facts.text: It can be read as a two-dimensional key-value store: each value is identified by two keys, a row identifier and a column identifier.

Columns are grouped into column families stored together on disk, inside a top-level keyspace; a row can span several families, a family is often likened to a relational table, and supercolumns nest a map of other columns.

The name once meant column-oriented relational databases like C-Store but came to mean Bigtable, Apache Cassandra and similar systems that keep column families together and drop the relational model; Bigtable is the prototypical example.

Compared with relational databases they are denormalized, with columns added dynamically and rows of varying columns; compared with document databases, records are split into column families the database treats as units, not whole documents.

Singh calls them highly scalable, able to handle petabytes and ideal for real-time big data applications, lists increased write time as a disadvantage, and names business analytics and attribute-based data storage as uses.

entries.title: OLTP and OLAP: serving users versus answering analysts

definition.text: OLTP systems serve transaction-oriented applications and respond to users in real time, while OLAP systems answer complex analytical queries for reporting and decision support.

facts.text: OLTP serves transaction-oriented applications such as order entry, retail sales, financial transactions and ATMs; it suits systems needing strong consistency, and operational databases process relatively high volumes of updates using transactions.
OLTP applications have high throughput, are insert- or update-intensive and serve hundreds of concurrent users; their key goals are availability, speed, concurrency and recoverability (durability).
OLTP is concerned with concurrency and atomicity: concurrency control stops two users modifying the same data at once, and atomicity makes all steps of a transaction succeed together or all fail.

OLAP answers multi-dimensional analytical queries for business intelligence or reporting; compared with OLTP, its queries are much more complex and run in smaller volumes, and it is optimized for complex queries and data analysis.
OLTP handles all query types (read, insert, update, delete), whereas OLAP is generally optimized for read-only operations.

OLTP databases hold detailed, current data in normalized entity schemas, usually third normal form; OLAP databases store aggregated, historical data in multi-dimensional schemas, usually star schemas.

Operational (loosely OLTP) databases benefit from row-oriented DBMSs, while analytics (loosely OLAP) databases benefit from column-oriented ones, because analytic access usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows.
OLTP performance is measured in transactions per second; OLAP is characterized by a low rate of transactions and complex queries with aggregations, and its performance measure is response time.

entries.title: Data warehouse: a separate copy built for analysis

definition.text: A central repository of data integrated from disparate sources and organized for reporting and analysis, used by analysts and managers to make decisions.

facts.text: Data from operational systems such as marketing or sales is uploaded, often cleansed first, through extract-transform-load (ETL) or extract-load-transform (ELT) workflows; the warehouse stores current and historical data organized for analysis and reporting.

Operational databases are normalized to protect integrity and record transactions fast, spreading one transaction over dozens to hundreds of tables, with quick inserts and updates and periodic purging of older data.

Warehouses are optimized for analytic access that selects specific fields, so they suit column-oriented storage while operational databases favor row-oriented DBMSs; operational systems keep a snapshot of the business, warehouses keep history.

Analysis on a separate copy relieves the lock contention long-running analysis queries cause in transaction processing databases, keeps history the source systems may not, and integrates many sources into one data model.
Warehouse data is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and nonvolatile: it spans a long horizon (up to 10 years) and is read-only once loaded, unless a regulatory obligation requires change.

The two main storage approaches are dimensional (Kimball), using star schemas that split data into facts and dimensions for easier understanding and faster retrieval, and normalized (Inmon), storing third-normal-form tables grouped by subject area.

A data mart is a simple warehouse for one subject area, often built by one department; bottom-up design builds marts first and integrates them, top-down design builds a normalized warehouse and derives dimensional marts.
A data lake instead keeps large volumes of data raw, in structured, semi-structured and unstructured form, processed at run time, which suits machine learning and big data processing.

entries.title: Star and snowflake schemas: shaping warehouse data

definition.text: A star schema is the simplest data warehouse schema: a central fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive attributes; a snowflake schema normalizes those dimension tables.

facts.text: The star schema is the simplest data mart schema style and the most widely used for warehouses: fact tables reference any number of dimension tables, and the shape gives the name, with the fact table at the center.

Facts hold measurable, quantitative data such as sales price, quantity, distance or weight; dimensions hold descriptive attributes such as product models, colors, sizes, locations and salesperson names.

Fact tables record metrics for specific events as numeric values plus foreign keys to dimensions, at a low uniform grain, so they accumulate many rows; types are transaction, snapshot and accumulating snapshot.
Dimension tables have relatively few records but many attributes each, commonly time, geography, product, employee and range, and carry a surrogate primary key mapped to the natural key.
Star schemas are denormalized: relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic and reporting, faster read-only queries and aggregations, fewer joins per query, and an efficient source for OLAP cubes.

A snowflake schema normalizes dimension hierarchies into multiple linked tables, reducing redundancy and improving integrity but needing more joins; it suits large or frequently updated dimensions, and Kimball advises avoiding it without clear need.

Analytic queries over a star schema usually join one large fact table with a handful of small dimensions, a pattern many DBMSs optimize with star-join; a sales example joins Fact_Sales to Dim_Date, Dim_Store and Dim_Product.
Dimensions with only a few attributes are simpler to maintain but force queries with many table joins, making the schema harder to use.

entries.title: Online analytical processing: slicing data cubes

definition.text: An approach to quickly answering multi-dimensional analytical queries, part of business intelligence, in which users analyze data organized in cubes interactively.

facts.text: Typical uses are business reporting for sales and marketing, budgeting, forecasting and financial reporting; OLAP tools let users analyze multidimensional data interactively from several perspectives.
At its core is the OLAP cube: numeric facts called measures, categorized by dimensions, placed at the intersections of a hypercube and usually manipulated through a pivot-table-like interface.
Cube metadata is typically built from a star or snowflake schema in a relational database: measures come from fact table records and dimensions from the dimension tables.

Three basic operations: roll-up aggregates along dimensions (offices up to a division), drill-down navigates into detail (sales by product within a region), and slicing and dicing takes a subset of the cube and views it along other dimensions.

Aggregations, built from the fact table by coarsening granularity along dimensions, are the main reason OLAP is fast; it has been claimed that cubes answer complex queries in around 0.1% of the time needed on OLTP relational data.

Because the number of possible aggregations is huge, usually only a predetermined number are fully calculated and the rest solved on demand; choosing which is the view selection problem, which is NP-complete.
COUNT, MAX, MIN and SUM can be computed per cell then combined in a roll-up, and AVERAGE needs a sum and a count; DISTINCT COUNT, MEDIAN and MODE need the whole set and are hard to do efficiently.

entries.title: Connection pooling: reusing database connections

definition.text: A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware.

facts.text: Pooling reduces the overhead of opening and closing connections, improving performance and scalability in database applications.

SQL databases typically use stateful binary protocols that keep session information such as transaction states and prepared statements, so pooling matters; DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use stateless HTTP-based protocols, which often reduces the need.
Pool settings should match the database's capacity and the workload; overprovisioned pools cause rejected connections, throttling, resource contention and higher latency.

Idle pooled connections can break through NAT timeouts, dropped connections or session invalidation, and expired authentication tokens can invalidate connections in the pool, forcing costly reconnection.
In serverless setups AWS Lambda opens a new database connection per invocation, which can cause connection storms under high concurrency; a proxy such as Amazon RDS Proxy pools the connections.

Containers hold database connections for their lifecycle and virtual machines scale connection demand with instance count, so without a pooler such as HikariCP or pgbouncer idle or excessive connections strain the database.
Pooling is usually done on the client side, by libraries such as ADO.NET and JDBC or by database SDKs, not by the database engine.
A web crawler service can improve performance by keeping many open connections at a time, which is called connection pooling.

Pooling is usually done on the client side, by libraries such as ADO.NET and JDBC, not by the database engine.
entries.text_plain: Serverless functions can flood a database with connections. AWS Lambda opens a new database connection per invocation, which under high concurrency can cause connection storms. A proxy such as Amazon RDS Proxy pools the connections to calm them. A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware. Pooling reduces the overhead of opening and closing connections, which improves performance. It matters for SQL databases, which typically use stateful binary protocols that keep session information such as the state of a transaction and prepared statements. DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use stateless HTTP-based protocols, which often reduces the need. entries.title: Database languages: four sublanguages

definition.text: Special-purpose languages for working with a database, each specific to a particular data model.

facts.text: Database languages are split into sublanguages: data control (DCL) for access, data definition (DDL) for tables and relationships, data manipulation (DML) for inserting, updating and deleting, and data query (DQL) for searching.
SQL combines data definition, data manipulation and query in a single language and is supported, with varying conformance, by all mainstream commercial relational DBMSs.

A database language may also configure the DBMS, compute over query results (counting, summing, averaging, sorting, grouping), enforce constraints, and offer an API version of the query language for programmers.
