entries.title: SQL: the declarative language of relational data

definition.text: A domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system.

facts.text: SQL is a set-based, declarative language, not an imperative one like C or BASIC, designed to query data in a relational database; extensions add procedural features such as control-of-flow constructs.
Its two advantages over older read-write APIs such as ISAM or VSAM were accessing many records with one single command and not having to specify how to reach a record, with or without an index.

Statements fall into sublanguages for data query (DQL), data definition (DDL), data control (DCL) and data manipulation (DML), covering querying, insert, update and delete, schema creation and modification, and access control.

SQL was among the first commercial languages to use Codd's relational model; it became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and despite departing from the model it became the most widely used database language.

Virtually no implementation adheres fully to the standard, so most SQL code needs changes to port between systems; the standard is large and complex and leaves behavior such as indices and file storage to implementations.
Date and time syntax, string concatenation, NULLs and comparison case sensitivity vary from vendor to vendor.

SQL deviates from the relational model: tables and query results are lists of rows, so a row may repeat and row order can be used in queries, which a primary key or unique constraint avoids for duplicates.
The Null marker indicates the absence of a value, distinct from 0 for an integer or an empty string for text, and it enforces three-valued logic of true, false and unknown.

entries.title: SQL vs NoSQL: a trade-off, not a contest

definition.text: The two main kinds of database, SQL (relational) and NoSQL (non-relational), differ in how they are built, what they store and how they store it.

facts.text: Relational databases are structured with predefined schemas, while non-relational ones are unstructured, distributed and have a dynamic schema; SQL stores data in tables of entities and data points, NoSQL in models such as key-value, graph or document.
In SQL each record has a fixed schema chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations; in NoSQL the schema is dynamic, fields are added on the fly and a record need not have every field.
SQL is a very powerful language for defining and manipulating data; NoSQL queries are focused on a collection of documents, and the syntax differs between databases.

SQL databases usually scale vertically, which can get very expensive, and scaling across servers is challenging; NoSQL databases scale horizontally on cheap commodity hardware, and many distribute data across servers automatically.

The vast majority of relational databases are ACID compliant, so for data reliability and safe transactions SQL is still the better bet; most NoSQL solutions sacrifice ACID compliance for performance and scalability.
Reasons to pick SQL: structured data with a strict schema, relational data, a need for complex joins, transactions, and very fast lookups by index.
Reasons to pick NoSQL: a dynamic or flexible schema, non-relational data, no need for complex joins, a very data-intensive workload, and very high throughput for IOPS.
Singh says to pick the technology that fits the requirements better, and warns that claiming NoSQL is simply better or SQL is not scalable reflects poorly in an interview.

entries.contested_note: Singh treats SQL and NoSQL as a trade-off to settle by requirements, not as a contest with a single winner.

entries.title: Spatial database: points, lines and polygons

definition.text: A spatial database is a general-purpose database, usually relational, enhanced with spatial data that represents objects in a geometric space, along with tools for querying and analyzing it.

facts.text: Most spatial databases represent points, lines and polygons, and their data types are mostly based on the OGC Simple Features specification.
A spatial extension adds spatial datatypes that store spatial data as column values; because locations need a spatial reference system, the database also tracks and transforms coordinate systems.

It also adds spatial functions to the query language, in most relational systems as functions in SQL SELECT statements; the OGC standard specifies measurement, geoprocessing, predicate, geometry-constructor and observer operations.

A spatial join of cities and countries is an SQL query such as SELECT * FROM cities, countries WHERE ST_Contains(countries.shape, cities.shape); predicates answer true or false questions such as whether two polygons overlap.
Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions, so spatial databases use a spatial index designed for multi-dimensional ordering.
The R-tree is typically the preferred spatial index: it groups objects by minimum bounding rectangle and adds each object to the rectangle whose size increases least.
Almost all current relational and object-relational DBMSs have spatial extensions, while some NoSQL systems such as MongoDB and CouchDB support only simplified or modified sets of the operations.
Web mapping applications need spatial databases whenever they handle dynamic data that changes frequently or a huge amount of geographic data.

entries.title: MOLAP, ROLAP and HOLAP: three ways to store OLAP data

definition.text: OLAP systems are traditionally grouped by storage into multidimensional (MOLAP), relational (ROLAP) and hybrid (HOLAP) types.

facts.text: MOLAP, the classic form of OLAP, stores data in an optimized multi-dimensional array rather than a relational database, and often precomputes derived data such as consolidations into a data cube.

ROLAP works directly with relational databases and needs no precomputation: base and dimension tables are relational tables, new tables hold the aggregates, and it depends on a specialized schema design.
ROLAP scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool, but it is generally slower than MOLAP and aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

MOLAP generally delivers better performance and needs less storage thanks to specialized indexing and compression, but can suffer database explosion from many dimensions, precomputed results and sparse data.

Most commercial OLAP tools now use Hybrid OLAP, letting the designer choose what sits in MOLAP and what in ROLAP: aggregations in MOLAP and detail in ROLAP, or recent data in MOLAP and older data in ROLAP.

entries.title: Querying and indexing in NoSQL databases
entries.article: NoSQL#Query optimization and indexing in NoSQL databases

definition.text: How NoSQL databases handle queries on fields that are not indexed, and what indexing features they offer to speed them up.

facts.text: Many NoSQL databases perform full-table or collection scans for queries on non-indexed fields, applying filters after retrieving the data; DynamoDB, MongoDB, Cassandra, Couchbase, HBase and Redis behave differently here.

Modern NoSQL databases add optimizations: MongoDB supports compound indexes, Cassandra offers secondary indexes and materialized views, Redis uses custom indexing, and Elasticsearch uses inverted indexes for text search but can still scan non-indexed fields.

Many NoSQL systems are designed for scalability and efficient key-based operations rather than arbitrary-field queries, so they excel at basic CRUD and key lookups, while suitability for complex queries or joins varies by database type and implementation.

entries.text: Ask a NoSQL database for a field it has not indexed and it may simply scan everything. Many run full scans for queries on non-indexed fields and apply filters after retrieving the data, though products behave differently here. Modern ones add optimizations. MongoDB supports compound indexes, Cassandra offers secondary indexes and materialized views, and Redis uses custom indexing. Elasticsearch uses {{ref:sysd-blocks-186}} for text search but can still scan non-indexed fields. These systems are designed to scale and to do key-based operations efficiently. They excel at basic CRUD and key lookups, while suitability for complex queries or joins varies.

entries.title: Database constraints: rules the data must satisfy

definition.text: Rules that restrict the data that can be stored in the relations of a database.

facts.text: Constraints are usually expressions that return true or false for whether the data satisfies them, and they can apply to a single attribute, to a tuple, or to an entire relation.
A domain is the set of possible values for an attribute and acts as a constraint on it: the string "ABC" is not in the integer domain but 123 is.
Constraints can restrict a domain further, such as limiting an integer attribute to values between 1 and 10, and they implement business rules in the database; SQL does this with check constraints.
The two principal rules of the relational model are entity integrity and referential integrity.

entries.title: Relational operations: selection, projection and join

definition.text: The operations of relational algebra, such as selection, projection and join, that express queries against a relational database.

facts.text: Queries on a relational database are expressed in relational calculus or relational algebra; in his original algebra Codd introduced eight operators in two groups of four.

Four operators come from set theory: union (SQL UNION), intersection (INTERSECT), set difference (EXCEPT or MINUS) and the cartesian product, which matches every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other (CROSS JOIN).
The other four are selection (SELECT with a WHERE clause), projection (extracting only specified attributes), join (connecting relations by their common attributes) and division.
In SQL an INNER JOIN prevents a cartesian product, so a query over N tables needs N-1 inner joins.

entries.title: Handling relational data in NoSQL without joins

definition.text: Because most NoSQL databases cannot join in queries, related data is handled by multiple queries, by storing copies of values, or by nesting data.

facts.text: Since most NoSQL databases cannot join data in queries, the schema generally needs to be designed differently; there are three main techniques for handling relational data.
Multiple queries: instead of one query, run several; NoSQL queries are often faster than SQL queries so the cost may be acceptable, but if too many are needed another approach is more appropriate.
Non-normalized data: instead of storing only foreign keys, store the actual foreign values with the data, such as a username in each blog comment, so no further lookup is needed.
Copied values must be changed in many places when they change, such as a username, so this approach works better when reads are much more common than writes.
Nesting data: in document databases like MongoDB, put more data in fewer collections, such as blog comments inside the post document, so one retrieval returns all the data a task needs.

entries.title: Stored procedure: code that lives in the database

definition.text: Executable code that is associated with, and generally stored in, the database.

facts.text: Stored procedures collect and customize common operations, such as inserting a tuple into a relation, gathering usage statistics, or encapsulating complex business logic and calculations.
Procedures can greatly reduce the information transferred within and outside a system, and access can be granted only to the stored procedures and not directly to the tables for added security.
Stored procedures are not part of the relational model, but all commercial implementations include them, often with vendor-specific procedural extensions to the declarative SQL syntax.

entries.title: Views and materialized views: computed relations

definition.text: A view is a relation computed from other relations by relational operations rather than one that stores data.

facts.text: Relations that store data are called base relations, and in implementations they are called tables.
Derived relations store no data but are computed by applying relational operations to other relations; in implementations they are called views or queries.
A materialized view is a pre-computed data set derived from a query and stored for later use, so querying it is faster than querying the base table, significantly so for frequent or complex queries.
Materialized views also enable data subsetting, which reduces network loads, and are mostly used for performance and replication.

entries.title: Vector database: finding what is similar

definition.text: A vector database stores and retrieves embeddings of data in vector space; it is also called a vector store or vector search engine.

facts.text: Embeddings are machine-learned vectors in a space of a few hundred to tens of thousands of dimensions, so that semantically similar items, whether words, documents, images or audio, get vectors close to each other.

Vector databases typically use approximate nearest neighbor algorithms to find records semantically similar to an input, unlike traditional databases that look up records by exact match; uses include semantic search and recommendation engines.

Common techniques for similarity search on high-dimensional vectors include Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs and locality-sensitive hashing, which may be combined; HNSW-based implementations have been among the best performers in recent benchmarks.

In retrieval-augmented generation, document embeddings are stored with a link to the document; the prompt's embedding queries the database for relevant documents, which are added to the language model's context window.

entries.title: Choosing a database by workload

definition.text: Pick the kind of database that matches the workload: transactional, analytical, text search, document, key-value, graph, vector or geospatial.

facts.text: OLTP databases suit transactional systems requiring strong consistency, and OLAP databases are optimized for complex queries and data analysis.
Full-text search databases give fast, flexible text search; document stores hold and query JSON-like documents; key-value stores offer high-speed, simple data models.
Graph databases manage highly connected data, embedding databases store and retrieve vector representations efficiently, and geospatial databases specialize in location-based data and queries.
Singh advises weighing both the ACID and BASE models and the application's own requirements when choosing a database.

entries.title: Polyglot persistence: several databases in one system

definition.text: Using multiple data storage technologies within a single system to meet varying data storage needs.

facts.text: The idea mirrors polyglot programming: as the right language for each job may beat one language for everything, an application can talk to several databases and use each for what it does best.
Forcing one database to satisfy every requirement can yield a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none solution, because different databases solve different problems.

Joins enforce relationships in a relational database but become problematic as data grows; a graph database may handle relationships at scale but not transactions, which relational systems serve better; a document database can hold the unstructured part.
Martin Fowler expects any decent-sized enterprise to use varied storage technologies for different kinds of data, first asking how the data will be manipulated and only then choosing the technology.
Knitting several database products together has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

entries.title: BASE consistency model: looser than ACID

definition.text: A looser alternative to ACID, built on basic availability, soft state and eventual consistency, that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience.

facts.text: BASE properties are much looser than ACID guarantees, and there is no direct one-for-one mapping between the two models.
In the NoSQL world ACID transactions are less common, because some databases loosen requirements for immediate consistency, data freshness and accuracy in order to gain scale and resilience.
Basic availability means the database appears to work most of the time; soft state means stores need not be write-consistent nor replicas mutually consistent all the time.
With eventual consistency, data may not be consistent immediately but eventually becomes consistent; reads remain possible but may give an incorrect response in the meantime.
To scale and stay highly available, the logic moves from the database to separate servers, so the database becomes more independent and focused on storing data.

entries.text: ACID promises a lot, and some databases deliberately promise less. BASE is a looser alternative that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience. It is built on three ideas: basic availability, soft state and a delayed kind of consistency. Soft state means stores need not be write-consistent, nor replicas mutually consistent, all the time. The third idea, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-097}}, is that data may not be consistent immediately but eventually becomes consistent. In the meantime reads remain possible but may give an incorrect response. To scale and stay highly available, the logic moves from the database to separate servers, so the database becomes more independent and focused on storing data.

entries.title: ACID vs BASE: choosing by requirements

definition.text: The choice between strict ACID transactions and looser BASE guarantees depends on the application's requirements.

facts.text: Singh says there is no right answer: both models were designed to satisfy different requirements, so choosing a database means weighing both models against the application's needs.
A fully ACID database is the perfect fit for use cases where data reliability and consistency are essential.
Given BASE's loose consistency, developers must be more rigorous about consistent data and must know the chosen database's BASE behavior and work within its constraints.
Planning around BASE limitations can be a major disadvantage compared with the simplicity of ACID transactions.

Databases built around traditional ACID guarantees, such as RDBMS, choose consistency over availability, while BASE systems common in NoSQL choose availability over consistency; MongoDB and Redis keep consistency and compromise availability on a network partition.

An ACID database fails the whole transaction if any step errors; a BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later. A database leans toward one or the other, though some NoSQL databases show certain ACID traits.
SQL databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL are structured over the ACID model, while NoSQL databases such as DynamoDB or ElasticSearch use the BASE architecture.

entries.contested_note: Singh presents ACID and BASE as fitting different requirements, with no single right answer.

entries.title: Time series database: built for timestamped data

definition.text: A database optimized for time series data, a sequence of data points indexed in chronological order.

facts.text: Early time series databases were data historians recording sensor measurements; today they also serve infrastructure and application monitoring, IoT telemetry, smart energy grids and financial tick data.

The data is uniform, timestamps mapped to metric values, and grows rapidly; entries rarely need cross-table relationships, so relational constraints are skipped, and workloads seldom need indefinite retention, which cuts storage and speeds queries.

They exploit sequential uniformity with specialized compression such as delta encoding or Gorilla compression, temporal indexing, and lifecycle management that downsamples or drops whole old partitions in bulk.

Built for append-only, high-velocity ingestion, they aim for write throughput, low-latency range queries, compression and multi-window aggregation; many tag points with key-value metadata or device IDs to query by time interval and source.

entries.title: Concurrency control: keeping simultaneous transactions correct

definition.text: The mechanisms in a DBMS that handle isolation and guarantee the correctness of concurrent transactions.

facts.text: Concurrency control constrains the timing of data access operations to orders that have the serializability and recoverability properties, which typically reduces performance.
Serializability is often compromised for better performance when correctness allows, but recoverability cannot be compromised because that typically violates database integrity.

Two-phase locking is the most common concurrency control method in DBMSs: a transaction must first acquire a lock on an object, and acquiring it may be blocked while another transaction holds a lock on it.

Many databases rely on locking to provide ACID: the transaction marks the data it accesses, even data only read, so others cannot modify it until it ends; non-trivial transactions need many locks, causing overhead and blocking.

entries.title: ETL and ELT: two ways to fill a warehouse

definition.text: Two workflows for loading a data warehouse: ETL transforms data before loading it, while ELT loads raw data into the warehouse and transforms it there.

facts.text: An ETL warehouse uses staging, integration and access layers: staging holds raw data extracted from each source, and the integration layer transforms it, often into an operational data store.

Integrated data then moves into the warehouse database, arranged into dimensions, facts and aggregate facts, and the access layer helps users retrieve it; ETL is inherently a batch process in most implementations.

ELT drops the separate transformation tool: data is extracted from heterogeneous sources and loaded straight into a staging area inside the warehouse, where all transformations run before landing in target tables.

entries.title: Multi-model database: several models, one backend

definition.text: A database management system designed to support multiple data models against a single, integrated backend.

facts.text: Most DBMSs are organized around one data model; a multi-model database stores, indexes and queries data in more than one, such as document, graph, relational and key-value.

It answers polyglot persistence, whose several products bring significant operational complexity and no consistency across stores, by offering the modeling advantages of many models in a single data store.

Reported advantages over single-model databases include ingesting varied formats such as CSV and JSON without extra effort, one query language such as AQL or SQL/JSON over related data, and multi-model ACID transactions in stand-alone mode.
Architectures differ: some engines support models such as documents and graphs natively, while others provide each model as a separate layer on top of an engine such as a key-value store.

entries.title: NewSQL: SQL with the scale of NoSQL

definition.text: A class of relational database systems that seek the scalability of NoSQL systems for online transaction processing while keeping the ACID guarantees of a traditional database.

facts.text: Financial and order-processing systems outgrew conventional relational databases but needed transactional guarantees NoSQL could not give; the old options were bigger computers or custom distribution middleware, both costly, and NewSQL tries to reconcile this.
The two common distinguishing features are the online scalability of NoSQL systems and the relational data model, including ACID consistency, with SQL as the primary interface.

Typical applications have heavy OLTP volumes of short-lived transactions that touch little data and use a small number of query forms; some systems also support hybrid transactional/analytical processing (HTAP).

Systems fall into three groups: shared-nothing clusters where each node manages a subset of the data, optimized storage engines behind a SQL interface, and transparent sharding across nodes using Raft or Paxos consensus.

entries.title: N+1 query problem: one query plus N more

definition.text: A performance problem where code runs one query plus N additional queries to fetch data that a single query could have returned.

facts.text: It happens when the data access layer executes N additional SQL statements to fetch the same data that could have been retrieved by the primary SQL query.
The larger the value of N, the more queries are executed and the larger the performance impact.
It is commonly seen in GraphQL and ORM tools, and is addressed by optimizing the SQL query or using a dataloader that batches consecutive requests into a single data request.

entries.title: Transaction states: from active to terminated

definition.text: The states a transaction passes through, from active to committed, or failed and aborted, until it is terminated.

facts.text: A transaction starts in the active state, where it is being executed; when it executes its final operation it is partially committed, and when all operations succeed it is committed and its effects are permanently established.

A transaction is failed if any check by the recovery system fails, and cannot proceed; the recovery manager then rolls back all its writes to restore the database to its state before the transaction, and the transaction is aborted.
After an abort the recovery module can restart or kill the transaction; with no rollback, or after a commit, the system is consistent and ready for a new transaction and the old one is terminated.

entries.title: Database schema: the shape of the data

definition.text: A definition of the shape of a data structure that specifies what kinds of data can go where.

facts.text: A schema can be strictly enforced across the entire database, loosely enforced on part of it, or not exist at all.
A table has columns like a spreadsheet, from two to a hundred or more; a column holds values of one type, such as text, numbers, enums or timestamps, with one value per row.
Data in a table is recorded in rows, and a table can hold thousands or millions of rows.
In SQL every record conforms to a fixed schema whose columns are chosen before data entry and changed later only through migrations; in NoSQL the schema is dynamic and fields can be added on the fly.

entries.title: Multiversion concurrency control: readers never wait for writers

definition.text: A non-locking concurrency control method that keeps multiple versions of each data item so readers see a consistent snapshot while writers write.

facts.text: Locks make readers wait for writers and cause contention, especially between long read transactions and update transactions; MVCC avoids this by keeping multiple copies of each data item.
An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting, so each user sees a snapshot of the database at one instant and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits.
The version a transaction sees depends on the isolation level; the most common with MVCC is snapshot isolation, where a transaction observes the data as of when it started.
Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID, so reads and writes are isolated without locks and writers do not block readers, though some MVCC databases such as Oracle still use locks.

In a timestamp scheme each version has read and write timestamps; a transaction reads the latest version preceding its timestamp, and a write by a transaction older than the object's read timestamp is aborted and restarted.

In one worked example each row has hidden transaction_id and roll_pointer columns, a write adds a new row pointing back to the old one, and a transaction's Read View fixed at its start keeps returning balance 100.

Obsolete versions need cleanup: some systems sweep and rewrite the table periodically, as PostgreSQL's VACUUM FREEZE does, while others keep the latest version plus an undo log, which can run out of space and abort transactions.
The drawback is the cost of storing multiple versions; the benefit is that reads are never blocked, which matters for read-heavy workloads.

entries.title: Two-phase locking: acquire everything, then release

definition.text: A pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any.

facts.text: The protocol uses locks that a transaction applies to data and that may block other transactions from accessing the same data during the transaction's life.

Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired; a transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one, and schedules obeying this are serializable.

The basic protocol uses shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks: reading needs a read or write lock, writing needs a write lock, and several locks on one object may coexist only if none is a write lock.
Because locks block, two-phase locking and its strict variants can deadlock when two or more transactions block each other.

Strict 2PL releases write locks only after the transaction commits or aborts, which gives strictness; strong strict 2PL also holds read locks until the end, so the transaction has only a growing phase until it completes.
In practice most commercial database systems use strong strict two-phase locking, which ensures global serializability if all participating databases use it.

Conservative 2PL takes every lock before execution so a lock holder never blocks; it shortens lock holding under heavy contention but over-locks under light contention and needs declared read and write sets, so it is rarely used.
Two-phase locking is a concurrency control protocol and should not be confused with the two-phase commit protocol.

entries.text: A transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one. That single rule is two-phase locking, a pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any. Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired, and schedules obeying this are serializable. The basic protocol uses shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks. Reading needs a read or write lock, writing needs a write lock, and several locks on one object may coexist only if none is a write lock. Because locks block, the protocol can deadlock when two or more transactions block each other. Strict 2PL releases write locks only after the transaction commits or aborts. Strong strict 2PL also holds read locks until the end, and most commercial database systems use it. Conservative 2PL takes every lock before execution, so a lock holder never blocks. It over-locks under light contention and needs declared read and write sets, so it is rarely used. Do not confuse any of this with {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}.

entries.title: PostgreSQL isolation levels: four names, three behaviors

definition.text: PostgreSQL accepts the four standard transaction isolation levels but implements three distinct ones, built on its multiversion concurrency control.

facts.text: PostgreSQL's Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, because that is the only sensible way to map the standard levels onto its multiversion concurrency control architecture.
Read Committed is the default: a SELECT sees only data committed before the query began, so two successive SELECTs in one transaction can see different data if others commit between them.

In Read Committed a would-be updater of a row another transaction is changing waits for it to commit or roll back; if it committed, the WHERE clause is re-evaluated on the updated row before proceeding.

Read Committed is fine for simple cases such as transferring $100 between accounts, but unsuitable for complex search conditions, because one command can see an inconsistent snapshot of rows touched by concurrent commands.
Repeatable Read sees only data committed before the transaction began; this is stronger than the standard requires, preventing every phenomenon except serialization anomalies, phantom reads included.

A Repeatable Read transaction that tries to modify a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction is rolled back with a serialization failure, so applications must retry the whole transaction; read-only transactions never conflict.

Repeatable Read gives a stable view, but not necessarily one consistent with a serial execution: a read-only transaction may see a control record updated but miss a detail record, so business rules need explicit locks.
Sequence changes are immediately visible to all other transactions and are not rolled back when the transaction that made them aborts.

entries.title: Snapshot isolation: a private snapshot for each transaction

definition.text: A guarantee that all reads in a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database and that the transaction commits only if its updates do not conflict with concurrent updates made since that snapshot.

facts.text: A transaction works on a personal snapshot taken when it starts and commits only if the values it updated have not been changed externally since; such a write-write conflict aborts it.

It is usually implemented within multiversion concurrency control, which keeps versions of each item; the transaction need only store its list of updates, which is scanned for conflicts before commit.

Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB, among others, adopted it because it performs better than serializability while still avoiding most, but not all, of the anomalies serializability avoids.

It is not serializable: it shows none of the anomalies the ANSI SQL-92 standard prohibited, yet permits others such as write skew, which is why it was used to criticize that standard's isolation levels.
The naming is confusing: Oracle, and PostgreSQL before 9.1, call snapshot isolation their serializable mode, so users must know the difference to avoid anomalous behavior.

The 1995 paper critiquing ANSI SQL isolation levels shows that dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms fail to characterize several popular isolation levels, introduces new phenomena, and defines Snapshot Isolation as an important multiversion isolation type.

PostgreSQL implements Repeatable Read with snapshot isolation: a query sees a snapshot as of the start of the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement, so successive SELECTs see the same data.
Some systems offer Repeatable Read and Snapshot Isolation as distinct levels with different behavior, whose permitted phenomena researchers formalized only after the SQL standard was written.

entries.title: Isolation levels: trading protection for concurrency

definition.text: Settings that control how much locking a transaction does when selecting data, trading protection from concurrency effects against concurrency.

facts.text: SERIALIZABLE guarantees the same effect as some serial execution, in which each transaction runs to completion before the next begins; lock-based systems hold read and write locks to the end and take range locks for ranged SELECTs.
Without locks, a serializable system detects write collisions among concurrent transactions and lets only one of them commit.
REPEATABLE READ keeps read and write locks until the end of the transaction but manages no range locks, so phantom reads can occur; write skew is possible in some systems.
READ COMMITTED guarantees that any data read was committed when read, but promises nothing if the read is repeated: data is free to change after it is read.
READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, so one transaction may see not-yet-committed changes made by others.
Each level is stronger than those below it, so the standard lets a DBMS run a transaction at a stronger level than requested, for example Read committed performed as Repeatable read.
The default isolation level varies quite widely between DBMSs, and most transactional databases let the user set any level.
The ANSI definitions based on three read phenomena have been criticized as ambiguous and as not reflecting the isolation many databases actually provide.

entries.title: Read phenomena: dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads

definition.text: The SQL-92 standard names three read phenomena that can occur when a transaction retrieves data another transaction might have updated.

facts.text: A dirty read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row that another transaction has updated but not yet committed; if that update is rolled back, the first transaction's view of the row is wrong.
A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row twice and another transaction commits an update to that row in between.
A phantom read occurs when a transaction retrieves a set of rows twice and another transaction commits an insert or removal in that set in between.
Dirty reads occur only at READ UNCOMMITTED, non-repeatable reads at READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, and phantom reads at every level except SERIALIZABLE.
Write skew lets two writers who each read the same columns both update them, leaving data that mixes the two transactions; it is possible at REPEATABLE READ in some systems.
Being free of all three phenomena is necessary but not sufficient for a serializable schedule.
A serialization anomaly is a fourth phenomenon: the result of committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with every possible ordering of running them one at a time.
The SQL standard only specifies which phenomena must not occur at each level, so a database may give stronger guarantees; PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, for example, allows no phantom reads.

entries.title: Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows

definition.text: An anomaly in which two concurrent transactions read an overlapping data set, make disjoint updates and both commit, neither having seen the other's update.

facts.text: Under serializability write skew is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other; snapshot isolation permits it.

Example: a bank lets either of two accounts run a deficit if their total stays at or above zero; two concurrent $200 withdrawals each check against their own snapshot, both commit, and the total ends at -$200.
The fix is to force a write-write conflict: add a conflict table both transactions update, or promote a read to a write, such as Oracle's SELECT FOR UPDATE or rewriting a value with itself.

The workarounds have costs: a table that materializes the constraint violates normal form, promotion is not always possible, and snapshot isolation leaves the user to maintain non-trivial constraints.

Serializable Snapshot Isolation detects and aborts dangerous triplets of concurrent transactions (shown by Cahill et al. in 2008), removing the workarounds at the cost of more aborts; PostgreSQL 9.1 adopted it.

entries.title: Normalization: storing each fact in one place

definition.text: Database normalization is the process of structuring a relational database according to normal forms to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.

facts.text: Normalization organizes a database's columns and tables so that their dependencies are properly enforced by integrity constraints.
It applies formal rules either by synthesis, creating a new database design, or by decomposition, improving an existing design.
Edgar F. Codd first proposed normalization as part of his relational model.
The goal is that each elementary fact is recorded in only one place, so insertions, updates and deletions automatically maintain consistency.
A fully normalized database can take new types of data with minimal changes to its structure, so applications that use it are minimally affected.
Normalization reduces data redundancy, increases data consistency, gives a better data design and enforces referential integrity.
Its costs are a more complex data design, more joins, slower performance and maintenance overhead.

entries.text:
Store every fact in exactly one place, and a whole class of inconsistencies cannot happen. That is the promise of database normalization: structuring a relational database by formal rules, to cut down repeated data and improve the integrity of what is stored. Edgar F. Codd first proposed it as part of his relational model. The rules are applied in one of two ways, by synthesis, which creates a new database design, or by decomposition, which improves an existing one. The rules themselves form a ladder (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-095}}).

Normalization organizes a database's columns and tables so that integrity constraints enforce their dependencies properly. The goal is that each elementary fact is recorded in only one place, so insertions, updates and deletions maintain consistency automatically. The benefits are concrete: less repeated data, more consistent data, a better data design and enforced referential integrity. A fully normalized database can also take new types of data with minimal changes to its structure, so the applications that use it are minimally affected.

The costs are just as concrete: a more complex data design, more joins, slower performance and maintenance overhead. Some designs therefore give up part of normalization on purpose (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-107}}).

entries.title: Database index: faster reads, slower writes

definition.text: A database index is a data structure that speeds up finding rows in a table, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

facts.text: An index lets the database locate rows quickly without examining every row of the table, and it can be built on one or more columns, giving rapid random lookups and efficient ordered access.
An index is a copy of selected columns, like a table of contents, storing the column and a key or pointer to the whole row so the complete row can be retrieved efficiently.
Without an index, finding a row by a field value tests items one by one, which takes O(N) linear time on average; indexes give sub-linear lookup.
Many index designs give logarithmic O(log(N)) lookup, and some applications can reach flat O(1) lookup.
An index trades increased storage and slower writes, since the index must be updated along with the data, for faster reads; designs balance lookup speed, index size and update cost.
Indexes also create different views of the same data, so large data sets can offer different filters or sorting schemes without extra copies of the data.
Some databases index values transformed by a function or expression, such as upper(last_name), or build a partial index only for records meeting a condition.
Many transactions access an index at once, so it needs concurrency control; specialized index methods exist and are applied together with the usual database ones for a performance gain.

A database index is the help: a data structure that speeds up finding rows, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

An index is a copy of selected columns, much like a table of contents. It stores the column's values together with a key or pointer to the whole row, so the complete row can be retrieved efficiently. It can be built on one or more columns, which gives rapid random lookups and efficient ordered access. Many designs reach logarithmic O(log(N)) lookup, and some applications can reach flat O(1) lookup. Either way, the lookup is sub-linear.

The bargain is write speed and storage in exchange for read speed. The index must be updated along with the data, so writes slow down, and designs balance lookup speed, index size and update cost. Indexes also create different views of the same data, so a large data set can offer different filters or sorting schemes without extra copies. Some databases index values transformed by a function or expression, such as upper(last_name), or build a partial index covering only records that meet a condition. Because many transactions access an index at once, it also needs concurrency control.

entries.title: Hash table: jumping straight to the value

definition.text: A hash table is a data structure that implements an associative array, mapping keys to values by using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets.

facts.text: During a lookup the key is hashed and the hash says where the value is stored; in a well-dimensioned table the average lookup time does not depend on how many elements it holds.
Search, insert and delete cost Θ(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case, with Θ(n) space; under reasonable assumptions the bounds beat self-balancing binary search trees.
Most designs use an imperfect hash function, so different keys can get the same index; these collisions must be handled, typically by separate chaining or open addressing.
A hash function should spread keys uniformly; a non-uniform distribution increases the number of collisions and the cost of resolving them.
The load factor is the ratio of stored elements to slots and performance deteriorates as it grows, so implementations keep it below a maximum and resize, or rehash, the table when it is reached.

Resizing needs a rehash because items cannot simply be copied to the same indices when the hash function depends on table size; rehashing is simple but expensive, so real-time systems may resize gradually.
Hashing is a space-time tradeoff, and on average hash tables are often more efficient than search trees or any other table lookup structure.

Hash tables implement associative arrays, in-memory tables, caches and sets, and can serve as disk-based database indexes, although B-trees are more popular there; Python dictionaries, Java HashMap and Go maps are built on them.

entries.title: B-tree: a search tree that grows wide, not tall

definition.text: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions and deletions in logarithmic time.

facts.text: A B-tree generalizes the binary search tree by letting nodes have more than two children, which lowers the tree's height and puts the data in fewer separate blocks.
Fewer blocks matter most for trees on disk, which have high latency and large blocks, so B-trees are used in databases and file systems, and they still help in memory because of CPU caches.
In Knuth's definition, a B-tree of order m has at most m children per node, non-root internal nodes have at least m/2 (rounded up), and all leaves are on the same level.
A non-leaf node with k children contains k-1 keys, and these keys act as separation values that divide its subtrees.
Search starts at the root and descends, at each level following the child whose key range contains the search value, usually with binary search inside each node.
Search, insert and delete all take O(log n) time in the worst case, and space is O(n).
Allowing a range of child counts means B-trees rebalance less often than other self-balancing search trees, but they may waste some space because nodes are not entirely full.
The meaning of a B-tree's order varies: Bayer and McCreight define it as the minimum number of keys in a non-root node, while Knuth defines it as the maximum number of children.

Fewer blocks matter most on disk, which has high latency and large blocks, so databases and file systems use B-trees.

Search starts at the root and follows, at each level, the child whose key range contains the search value. Because child counts may vary within a range, a B-tree rebalances less often than other self-balancing trees. The price is some wasted space in nodes that are not full.

entries.title: Write-ahead log: record the change before making it

definition.text: Write-ahead logging is a family of techniques that give a database atomicity and durability: changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage before they are written to the database.

facts.text: Every operation that modifies database state must be logged on disk before the affected pages are modified, which lets the page cache buffer page updates while durability is kept.

After a crash the log is checked to see whether an operation succeeded, partly succeeded or failed, then undone or completed; redo and undo information is usually logged, and a checkpoint applies the logged changes and clears the log.

WAL allows in-place updates, which reduces the need to modify indexes and block lists; shadow paging is the non-in-place alternative for atomic updates, and modern file systems use a WAL variant for metadata, called journaling.

ARIES, a transaction recovery method, applies not only to database systems but to persistent object-oriented languages, recoverable file systems and transaction-based operating systems, and has been implemented in IBM DB2 and other systems.
WAL's central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the WAL records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage.

Because of that rule, data pages need not be flushed at every commit: after a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the WAL, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO.
WAL reduces disk writes: only the sequentially written WAL file must be flushed to commit a transaction, and one fsync of it may commit many concurrent small transactions.
Archiving the WAL supports online backup and point-in-time recovery: restore a prior physical backup and replay the WAL up to the desired time, even if the backup was not an instantaneous snapshot.

entries.text:
Pull the plug in the middle of a transaction and the database still has to come back whole. Write-ahead logging is the family of techniques that makes this possible. Changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage, and only then written to the database. It gives a database atomicity and keeps committed changes safe, two of the ACID guarantees (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-055}}).

The central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. Because of that, data pages need not be flushed at every commit. After a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the log, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO. The log also cuts disk writes. Only the sequentially written log file must be flushed to commit a transaction, and one fsync of it may commit many concurrent small transactions. Archiving the log allows recovery to a chosen moment: restore an earlier physical copy, then replay the log to the desired time.

entries.title: Storage engine: where the database meets permanent storage

definition.text: The storage engine is the part of the database engine responsible for putting data into permanent storage.

facts.text: The storage engine uses low-level storage structures to serialize the data model so it can be written to the chosen medium, and techniques such as indexing may be used to improve performance.
Data sit in storage in structures that look completely different from the conceptual level, arranged to optimize reconstructing them when users and programs need them.

A DBMS usually reaches storage through the operating system and its file systems, and storage properties and settings are extremely important for efficient operation, so administrators maintain them closely.
Conventional storage is row-oriented, but column-oriented databases also exist.
B-tree is the most widely used indexing structure in almost all relational databases, while LSM-trees are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.

entries.title: Inverted index: from words to the documents that hold them

definition.text: An inverted index is a database index that maps content, such as words, to its locations in a table or in a document or set of documents.

facts.text: Its purpose is fast full-text search, at the cost of more processing when a document is added; it is the most popular data structure in document retrieval systems and a central component of search engines.
A forward index stores the list of words per document; inverting it gives the inverted index, which lists the documents per word.
Without it a query would iterate through every word of every document, which is often not technically realistic; with it, the query jumps to the word by random access.
A record-level inverted index lists the documents for each word; a word-level one also stores each word's positions, which supports phrase searches but needs more processing power and space to build.
PostgreSQL's GIN indexes are inverted indexes with a separate entry for each component value, suited to values that hold several components such as arrays.
Because it lists the documents containing each word, the engine can directly access the documents for each query word to find matches quickly, then rank them by relevance.

A basic inverted index is Boolean: it says whether a word occurs in a document but not how often or where, so it finds matches without ranking them. Frequencies help ranking, and positions support phrase search.

A positional index stores each token's exact positions in its postings list; phrase search fetches the postings of each word, checks the words occur in order, and can use binary search over the postings lists.

entries.title: R-tree: indexing places, rectangles and polygons

definition.text: R-trees are tree data structures for spatial access methods, indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons.

facts.text: The key idea is to group nearby objects and represent them by their minimum bounding rectangle one level up; a query that misses a bounding rectangle cannot hit any object inside it.
Like a B-tree, an R-tree is balanced, organizes data in pages and is designed for disk storage; each page holds at most M entries, and best performance has been seen with a minimum fill of 30%-40%.
Search compares each rectangle in a node with the query rectangle and descends only into overlapping children, so most nodes are never read; at the leaves the stored objects are tested precisely.
Real uses include finding all museums within 2 km of a location; nearest-neighbor search keeps a priority queue and expands the nearest entry first; spatial databases typically prefer R-trees.

Insertion descends into the subtree needing least enlargement of its bounding box; a full node is split by a heuristic such as Guttman's quadratic or linear split, and overflows can propagate up to the root, which then grows taller.
The difficulty is a tree that is balanced while its rectangles neither cover much empty space nor overlap much; R-trees give no worst-case guarantee but perform well on real-world data.
The R*-tree reduces overlap with a better subtree choice and splitting heuristic, and avoids some splits by reinserting entries.

Research aims at building an efficient tree from scratch (bulk-loading, for example Sort-Tile-Recursive) and at changing an existing tree; deleting from an underfull page dissolves it and reinserts its children.

entries.title: Anomalies: how an unnormalized table goes wrong

definition.text: Anomalies are the undesirable side effects that can arise when modifying a relation that has not been sufficiently normalized.

facts.text: Codd's objectives for normalization included freeing relations from undesirable insertion, update and deletion dependencies and reducing the need to restructure as new data types are introduced.
Insertion anomaly: some facts cannot be recorded, such as a newly hired faculty member with no course yet, unless the Course Code is set to null.
Update anomaly: the same information on several rows means a partly applied update, such as an address changed on some skill records only, leaves the relation inconsistent.
Deletion anomaly: deleting data for one fact forces deleting a different fact, such as losing a faculty member when their last course record is removed.
Most 3NF relations are free of insertion, update and deletion anomalies.

entries.text:
Hire a faculty member who has no course yet. A badly designed table may have no place to record them, unless the Course Code is set to null. That is an insertion anomaly, one of three undesirable side effects that can arise when a relation, the formal name for a table, has not been sufficiently normalized.

An update anomaly appears when the same information sits on several rows. Change an address on some skill records only, and the relation is left inconsistent. A deletion anomaly appears when deleting data for one fact forces deleting a different fact. Remove a faculty member's last course record, and the faculty member is lost with it.

Codd's objectives for normalization (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-093}}) included freeing relations from these insertion, update and deletion dependencies and reducing the need to restructure as new data types are introduced. Most relations in third normal form (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-095}}) are free of all three anomalies.

entries.title: B-trees and disk reads: why wide nodes win
entries.article: B-tree#B-tree usage in databases > Index performance

definition.text: A B-tree index breaks a database into fixed-size pages arranged in levels from a root page down to leaf pages, so a lookup needs only a few disk reads.

facts.text: A B-tree index splits a database into fixed-size pages in levels from a root page to leaf pages that mostly refer to table rows; with more than two children per node, it is shorter than a binary search tree.
Reading a record from disk costs far more than comparing keys because of seek time and rotational delay; at about 10 milliseconds per read, 20 reads to find one record in a million take 0.2 seconds.
An auxiliary index holding the first record of each disk block is about 1% of the size of the original database, and searching it tells which one block of the main database to read.
Indexing the auxiliary index again gives an index of only 100 entries that fits in one disk block, so 3 block reads replace 14 and the record takes 30 milliseconds instead of 150.
This blocking, with disk blocks forming a hierarchy of levels from the root block down to the leaf level, is the core idea behind the B-tree.
Search cost falls from roughly log2 N disk reads to logb N, where b is the blocking factor; with 100 entries per block, log100 1,000,000 is 3 reads.

A B-tree keeps keys sorted, minimizes disk reads with a hierarchical index, uses partially full blocks to speed insertions and deletions, and is the standard index implementation in almost all relational databases.
When an index is searched often, its upper levels may sit in a disk cache and incur no disk read.

entries.title: B+ tree and B* tree: two refinements of the B-tree

definition.text: The B+ tree and B* tree are variants of the B-tree that keep all record pointers in the leaves or keep nodes more densely packed.

facts.text: A B+ tree can be viewed as a B-tree whose nodes hold only keys, not key-value pairs, with an added bottom level of linked leaves; it consists of a root, internal nodes and leaves, all leaves at the same depth.

Internal nodes hold no record pointers, so every record pointer sits in a leaf; the resulting high fanout, typically 100 or more, makes the tree shallow and cuts the I/O operations needed to find an element.
Search goes from the root to the one leaf that may hold the key, following one branch at each level, so it takes O(log N) where N is the number of keys in the leaves.
Leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient; a B-tree cannot build such a list because not all its keys are in the leaves.
Building an index by inserting records one by one is expensive because each starts at the root; bulk-loading instead sorts the data entries by search key first and then builds the tree.
Relational systems such as Db2, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite use B+ trees for table indices, and file systems such as NTFS and XFS use them for metadata indexing.
A 1979 survey says B-trees have become a de facto standard for file organization and discusses their major variations, especially the B+ tree.
A B* tree keeps non-root nodes at least 2/3 full instead of 1/2 and postpones costly node splits by sharing keys with a neighbouring node, a spill that needs no new node.

entries.title: Clustered and non-clustered indexes: where the rows live
entries.article: Database index#Index architecture and indexing methods > Clustered

definition.text: A clustered index stores a table's rows in the order of the index key, while a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure that points to rows stored elsewhere.

facts.text: A clustered index puts the data rows on disk in the same order as the index, so a table can have only one clustered index.
Clustering helps mainly when data is read sequentially in index order or as a range, because neighbouring rows are adjacent and fewer data block reads are needed.
A non-clustered index keeps its keys in sorted order and its leaf level points to each record, so the physical row order differs from the index order.
A table can have many non-clustered indexes, usually on non-primary-key columns used in JOIN, WHERE and ORDER BY clauses.
In Microsoft SQL Server the leaf node of a clustered index is the actual data, not a pointer to data stored elsewhere as in a non-clustered index.

entries.title: Log-structured merge-tree: built for a flood of writes

definition.text: A log-structured merge-tree (LSM tree) is a data structure that suits indexed access to files with a high insert volume, such as transactional log data.

facts.text: An LSM tree maintains key-value pairs in two or more separate structures, each optimized for its storage medium, and synchronizes data between them efficiently in batches.
In a two-level LSM tree, a smaller component C0 lives entirely in memory and C1 lives on disk; new records go into C0, and when it exceeds a size threshold a contiguous segment is merged into C1.
Its speed comes from writing data sequentially instead of as separate random access requests, which cuts total seek time on hard-disk drives and latency on solid-state drives.
Most real LSM trees have several levels: level 0 sits in main memory and the on-disk data is organized into sorted runs, each sorted by the index key.
A query must search the level 0 tree and also each run, so the system must avoid having too many runs to keep query cost down.
LSM trees were designed for write-intensive workloads; when reads and writes mix, compaction invalidates cached data in buffer caches and reads can see high latency and low throughput.
Cassandra uses an LSM tree index to optimize write throughput, in contrast to the B-tree indexes most databases use.

entries.title: Denormalization: trading redundancy for read speed

definition.text: Denormalization is a strategy applied to a previously normalized database to increase performance, by adding redundant copies of data or grouping data.

facts.text: Denormalization improves read performance at the expense of some write performance, by adding redundant copies of data or by grouping data, often to cope with very large numbers of read operations.

In a normalized design a join across several relations stored as separate files can be slow, even prohibitively slow with many relations; once data is sharded or federated, joins across the network add more complexity.
Denormalization has two strategies: the DBMS stores and keeps consistent redundant copies, as with indexed or materialized views, or the designer denormalizes the logical design by hand.

Denormalizing by hand can match the query speed, but the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints, which slow writes, so under heavy write load it may perform worse than the normalized design.

A denormalized model is not the same as one that was never normalized: denormalization should come only after a satisfactory level of normalization, such as third normal form, with the needed constraints in place.
Typical techniques are storing the count of the many side of a one-to-many relationship in the one side, copying attributes from a relation it joins with, and star schemas.
Advantages are faster retrieval, easier queries and fewer tables; disadvantages are expensive inserts and updates, a more complex design, more redundancy and a greater chance of inconsistent data.
NoSQL databases avoid joins by storing denormalized data, and the extra storage that denormalization needs is a relatively small problem except in truly enormous systems.

entries.title: Hash collision resolution: chaining or probing

definition.text: Collision resolution is how a hash table copes with keys that hash to the same index; the two common methods are separate chaining and open addressing.

facts.text: Separate chaining builds a linked list of key-value pairs for each array index; the collided items are chained together and the list is traversed during a lookup.

Open addressing stores every entry in the bucket array and probes from the hashed-to slot, by linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing, until it finds an empty slot; lookups follow the same sequence.

Open addressing cannot exceed a load factor of 1 and degrades sharply near it, with a maximum of about 0.6 to 0.75; separate chaining degrades gradually, with the best maximum typically between 1 and 3.
Cuckoo hashing and dynamic perfect hashing guarantee O(1) worst-case lookup; cuckoo keeps two tables with separate hash functions and displaces the occupant of a collided slot into the other table.

entries.title: B-tree versus LSM-tree: faster reads or faster writes

definition.text: The biggest difference between the two index structures is that a B-tree enables faster reads while an LSM-tree enables fast writes.

facts.text: B-tree is the most widely used indexing data structure in almost all relational databases, and its basic unit of storage is usually called a page.
Looking up a key in a B-tree traces down the range of keys until the actual value is found.
LSM-tree is widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.
An LSM-tree keeps key-value pairs and persists them to disk in a Sorted Strings Table (SSTable) with sorted keys; level 0 segments are periodically merged into level 1 by compaction.
B-trees enable faster reads, while LSM-trees enable fast writes.

entries.title: Index data structures: no single best choice

definition.text: A database index can be built on several data structures, and the best choice depends on the workload.

facts.text: The index format that fits depends on whether data is indexed in memory or on disk, the data formats, and whether the system is write-heavy or read-heavy.
A skiplist is a common in-memory index type, a hash index is a common implementation of a map, and an SSTable is an immutable on-disk map.
An LSM tree combines a skiplist and SSTables for high write throughput, while a B-tree is a disk-based structure with consistent read and write performance.
An inverted index serves document indexing, a suffix tree serves string pattern search, and an R-tree serves multi-dimensional search such as finding the nearest neighbor.
Popular index implementations include balanced trees, B+ trees and hashes.

entries.title: PostgreSQL index types and what each is for

definition.text: PostgreSQL provides several index types, B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN plus the bloom extension, each using an algorithm suited to different indexable clauses.

facts.text: CREATE INDEX makes a B-tree by default, which fits the most common situations; other types are chosen with the USING keyword.

B-trees handle equality and range queries on sortable data, can return rows in sorted order, and serve prefix patterns such as LIKE 'foo%' but not LIKE '%bar'; Hash indexes store a 32-bit hash code and handle only equality.

GiST and SP-GiST are infrastructures for many indexing strategies: GiST covers geometric types and nearest-neighbor searches, SP-GiST supports non-balanced structures such as quadtrees, k-d trees and tries.

GIN indexes are inverted indexes for values with several components, such as arrays; BRIN indexes store minimum and maximum summaries of consecutive block ranges, so they work best when column values correlate with the physical row order.

entries.title: Skip list: a linked list with shortcuts

definition.text: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure that gives O(log n) average search and insertion in an ordered sequence of n elements.

facts.text: Fast search comes from a linked hierarchy of subsequences, each skipping fewer elements than the one above; the bottom layer is an ordinary ordered list and each element appears one layer up with a fixed probability p.

A search starts in the top list and moves right until the current element is greater than or equal to the target, then drops down a level; the expected cost is O(log n), and p trades search cost against storage.

Skip lists have no absolute worst-case guarantee because unlucky coin flips can unbalance them, but they work well in practice and their randomized balancing is argued to be easier to implement; parallel insertions need no global rebalancing.
Redis uses skip lists for ordered sets, RocksDB for its default memtable, and Java for ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet.

entries.title: LSM-tree writes and compaction: buffer, flush, merge

definition.text: An LSM tree absorbs writes in memory, flushes them to disk as immutable sorted components and later merges those components.

facts.text: A write is first buffered in an in-memory component, often a skip list or B+ tree; when the buffer is full it is flushed sequentially to disk as an immutable sorted component, avoiding costly random writes.
For durability the system may record every incoming write in a write-ahead log before adding it to the memory buffer, so no data is lost if a crash happens during a write.
As data accumulates on disk, a merge process like merge sort consolidates entries across levels; moving level 0 segments into level 1 is called compaction.
Updates are treated as new writes and deletes are marked with a tombstone entry, which is removed later during merging along with obsolete entries.

Levelling keeps one component per level and merges often, giving fewer components but more write amplification; tiering allows several components per level and merges less often, lowering write amplification but raising read costs.

entries.text:
An LSM tree does not edit data on disk. Every write lands first in an in-memory component, often a skip list or B+ tree. When that buffer is full, it is flushed sequentially to disk as an immutable sorted component, which avoids costly random writes. To keep data safe across a crash, the system may record every incoming write in a write-ahead log before adding it to the buffer.

As data accumulates on disk, a merge process, much like merge sort, consolidates entries across levels. Moving level 0 segments into level 1 is called compaction. Since components are immutable, an update is treated as a new write, and a delete is marked with a tombstone entry. Obsolete entries and tombstones are removed later, during merging.

How often to merge is a policy choice. Leveling keeps one component per level and merges often, which gives fewer components but more write amplification, meaning data is rewritten more often. Tiering allows several components per level and merges less often, which lowers write amplification but raises read costs.

entries.title: B-tree insertion and deletion: split and merge

definition.text: Insertion into a B-tree starts at a leaf and splits full nodes, while deletion removes a key and then rebalances nodes that fall below the minimum size.

facts.text: To insert, search for the leaf node; if it has fewer than the maximum elements, insert the key in order, otherwise split the node into two around a median key.
The median moves up to the parent as a separation value, which may split in turn; a split that reaches the root creates a new root and increases the tree's height.
Deletion has two popular strategies: delete the item and then restructure the tree, or restructure on the way down so the key can be deleted without further restructuring.
A node left below the minimum takes an element from a sibling that can spare one, called a rotation, or else merges with a sibling; merging can continue up to the root.

entries.text: A B-tree grows from the top: when a split reaches the root, the tree gets taller. Inserting starts with a search for the right leaf. If the leaf has fewer than the maximum number of elements, the key goes in, in order. Otherwise the node splits into two around a median key, and the median moves up to the parent as a separation value. The parent may split in turn. In deletion, a node left below the minimum takes an element from a sibling that can spare one, which is called a rotation. Otherwise it merges with a sibling, and merging can continue up to the root.

entries.title: Bitmap index: bit arrays for values that repeat
entries.article: Database index#Types of indexes > Bitmap index

definition.text: A bitmap index stores most of its data as bit arrays and answers queries by performing bitwise logical operations on them.

facts.text: Common indexes such as B+ trees work best when the indexed values do not repeat, or repeat only a few times.
A bitmap index is designed for values that repeat very frequently, such as a field with at most three distinct values.
For such variables a bitmap index can have a significant performance advantage over the commonly used trees.

entries.title: Covering index: answering from the index alone

definition.text: A covering index is an index that itself contains all the fields a query needs, so the query is answered without reading the table record.

facts.text: Usually an index only locates the data records and the required data is read from the table; a covering index holds the needed fields itself and can answer the query.
To find the Name for ID 13, an index on (ID) still requires reading the record, but an index on (ID, Name) removes that lookup.
A covering index can speed retrieval dramatically but may be large because of the extra keys, which slow down inserts and updates.
Some systems let non-key fields be included only at the leaf level, giving a covering index with less overall size, for example with an INCLUDE clause.

entries.title: Dense and sparse indexes: every row or some rows
entries.article: Database index#Types of indexes > Dense index

definition.text: A dense index has an entry for every record of the table, while a sparse index has entries for only some of the records.

facts.text: A dense index has an index record for every row, each holding the search key and a pointer to the actual record, so records are located directly.
Dense indexes need more write-time maintenance and more memory than sparse ones, but values are found with a binary search and the data need not be ordered.
A sparse index has entries for only some records, such as one per data block, so it needs less maintenance, makes inserts, updates and deletes faster, and uses less memory.
Finding data through a sparse index is slower because a scan across the page typically follows the binary search, and sparse indexes are optional when working with ordered data.

entries.title: Indexes and database constraints: rules enforced by indexes
entries.article: Database index#Usage > Policing the database constraints

definition.text: Databases use indexes to enforce constraints such as UNIQUE, EXCLUSION, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY.

facts.text: Declaring an index UNIQUE creates an implicit constraint on the underlying table.
Databases usually create an index implicitly on columns declared PRIMARY KEY, and some can reuse an existing index to enforce that constraint.
Many databases require both the referencing and referenced columns of a FOREIGN KEY to be indexed, which improves inserts, updates and deletes on the tables involved.
An EXCLUSION constraint ensures a predicate holds for no other record; it can implement UNIQUE or rules such as no overlapping time ranges.

entries.title: Types of database indexes beyond trees and hashes
entries.article: Database index#Types of indexes > Reverse index

definition.text: Beyond the main tree and hash designs, databases use dense, sparse, reverse-key, inverted, primary and secondary indexes, among others.

facts.text: A dense index holds a key-pointer pair for every record of the sorted data file, while a sparse index holds a pair only for every block of the data file.
A reverse-key index reverses the key before entering it, for example 24538 becomes 83542, which suits sequence numbers whose new values increase monotonically.

A primary index holds the table's key fields with a pointer to the non-key fields and is created automatically with the table; a secondary index covers fields that are neither ordering nor key fields.
An inverted index maps a content word to the document containing it, which allows full-text searches.

entries.title: Pessimistic and optimistic locking: assume the worst or the best

definition.text: Locks maintain data consistency and integrity in multi-user environments by preventing simultaneous modifications that could leave data inconsistent.

facts.text: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts will occur, so it locks the data before any change and blocks other users from accessing and updating it until the lock is released.
Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare, lets multiple users access data at once, checks for conflicts when changes are committed and rolls the operation back if one is detected.
Pessimistic locking is better for data integrity but can hurt performance; optimistic locking is better for efficiency and performance.
Good practice is to hold locks for the minimum time, lock at the most granular level such as rows rather than tables, and retry transactions that fail due to conflicts.

entries.title: LSM-tree lookups and range queries: checking newest first

definition.text: A read in an LSM tree checks the in-memory component first and then the disk components from newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip components.

facts.text: A point lookup searches the in-memory component first, then disk levels in order, checking newer levels first because they hold the latest updates and deletions, and stops as soon as the key is found.
A Bloom filter per on-disk component is a probabilistic structure that quickly shows a key is definitely absent, so the component can be skipped without reading it.
Point lookup costs O(L) without Bloom filters because each level must be searched, and lookups of existing keys cost O(1) with them.

A range query locates the start in each component, scans sequentially and merges the results in a priority queue to reconcile duplicates, updates and deletes; short ranges cost O(L) and long ranges are dominated by the largest level.

A Bloom filter kept for each on-disk component can show that a key is definitely absent, so the component is skipped unread.
