entries.title: Recovery time and recovery point: how long and how much

definition.text: Recovery time, or recovery time objective, is the total time needed to recover fully from an outage and is closely related to availability.

facts.text: Recovery time, also called recovery time objective (RTO) or estimated time of repair, is the time for a planned outage or for full recovery from an unplanned one; mean time to recovery (MTTR) is another metric.
Recovery time can be infinite, for example when a fire or flood destroys a data center and there is no secondary disaster recovery data center.
The Recovery Point Objective sets the acceptable data loss for various failure events, a concern separate from data availability, which is how faithfully databases record and report transactions.
Some users can tolerate service interruptions but not data loss, and a service level agreement formalizes an organization's availability objectives and requirements.

entries.title: Active-active and active-passive clusters

definition.text: The two most common high availability clustering configurations are active-active and active-passive.

facts.text: An active-active cluster has at least two nodes all running the same kind of service simultaneously; its main purpose is load balancing, with a load balancer spreading work so no node is overloaded.
Because more nodes are available to serve, an active-active cluster improves throughput and response times.
An active-passive cluster also has at least two nodes, but not all are active: with two nodes, if the first is active the second must be passive or on standby.

entries.title: Sequence versus parallel: how availability adds up

definition.text: Components in sequence multiply their availabilities and so lower the total, while components in parallel raise the total.

facts.text: A service made of failure-prone components has an overall availability that depends on whether the components are in sequence or in parallel.
In sequence, total availability is the product of the components' availabilities, so it decreases: two components at 99.9% each give 99.8%.
In parallel, total availability is 1 minus the product of the components' unavailabilities, so it increases: two components at 99.9% each give 99.9999%.

entries.title: Forms of redundancy: hardware, information, time and software

definition.text: Computing uses hardware, information, time and software redundancy, plus dissimilar and geographic variants, to keep a system running when parts fail.

facts.text: Computing has four major forms of redundancy: hardware (dual or triple modular), information (error detection and correction), time (repeating an operation or sending several copies of data) and software (N-version programming).

Dissimilar redundancy uses different things instead of copies of the same thing, because different things are unlikely to share identical flaws; it is common for software, since identical software contains identical flaws.
Geographic redundancy separates backup devices so that power outages, floods, fires or storms are less likely to disable most or all of the system.

Cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform and Azure use it for high availability and fault tolerance; separation ranges from over 621 miles (999 km) down to buildings over 300 feet (91 m) apart on one campus.

entries.title: Capacity planning: matching resources to demand

definition.text: Capacity planning is the process of determining the capacity needed to meet changing demand; in IT it estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources required over a future period.

facts.text: IT capacity planning estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources needed over a future period, so a system can handle more users or interactions.
A mismatch between capacity and demand leaves resources under-utilized or demand unmet; the goal of capacity planning is to minimize this gap.

Capacity strategies are lead (add capacity as demand grows), lag (add only when running at full capacity), match (add small amounts as demand changes) and adjustment; lead is risky when demand is unpredictable, lag can lose users.

The SRE book advises pairing capacity planning with performance testing to find the load at which the service fails; planning lowers the chance of cascading failure but cannot prevent it after large infrastructure losses.

entries.title: Three bottlenecks that stop a system from growing

definition.text: A scalability bottleneck is a part of the design, such as a centralized, slow or tightly coupled component, that stops a system from growing.

facts.text: A centralized component is one of three main bottlenecks to scalability and can become a single point of failure.
High-latency components, which perform time-consuming operations, are a second main bottleneck to scalability.
Tight coupling is the third main bottleneck because it makes components difficult to scale.
To build a scalable system, follow the principles of statelessness, loose coupling and asynchronous processing.

entries.title: Clustering versus load balancing: servers that know each other

definition.text: Clustering links servers that work together toward a common purpose, while load balancing spreads requests across servers that are unaware of each other.

facts.text: Load balancing shares traits with clustering but is a different process; clustering provides redundancy and boosts capacity and availability.
Servers in a cluster are aware of each other, whereas servers behind a load balancer are not and simply react to the requests it sends them.
Load balancing can be used together with clustering, and also with independent servers that share a purpose such as running a website, business application or web service.

entries.title: Replication: keeping several copies in step

definition.text: Replication in computing means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent.

facts.text: Replication is a fundamental technique across databases, file systems and distributed systems that improves availability, fault tolerance, accessibility and performance.
With replication, systems keep operating when components fail (failover), serve requests from geographically distributed locations, and balance load across machines.
The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and network partition tolerance, constraints known as the CAP theorem.
Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices; computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices (in space) or repeatedly on one device (in time).
Replication should be transparent to an external user: access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one, and a failover of replicas should be hidden as much as possible.
A backup differs from replication: a backup copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.
Replication shares information to keep redundant resources, such as multiple databases, consistent in order to improve reliability, fault tolerance or accessibility.
Database replication improves durability and availability, and copying data across multiple nodes scales read operations while improving redundancy.

Replication means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. And they balance load across machines. Copying data across multiple nodes also scales read operations while improving redundancy. Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices. Computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices, in space, or repeatedly on one device, in time.

Ideally users never notice. Access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one. The switch to a replica after a failure should be hidden as much as possible. The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and partition tolerance, constraints known as the {{ref:sysd-scale-107}}. Do not confuse replication with {{ref:sysd-reliab-189}}. That copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

Replication means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. It is a fundamental technique across databases, file systems and distributed systems. It improves availability, accessibility and performance, and in databases it improves durability too.

Replication does three jobs. Systems keep operating when components fail, through Failover: when a standby takes over. They serve requests from geographically distributed locations. And they balance load across machines. Copying data across multiple nodes also scales read operations while improving redundancy. Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices. Computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices, in space, or repeatedly on one device, in time.

Ideally users never notice. Access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one. The switch to a replica after a failure should be hidden as much as possible. The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and partition tolerance, constraints known as the The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything. Do not confuse replication with Backup: a copy kept somewhere else. That copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

entries.title: Single point of failure: the part with no spare

definition.text: A single point of failure is a part of a system that would stop the entire system from working if it failed.

facts.text: The term implies there is no backup or redundant option that would let the system keep functioning without that part.
A single point of failure is undesirable in any system aiming at high availability or reliability, because its interruption is substantially more disruptive than an error elsewhere in the system.
Systems are made robust by adding redundancy at all potential single points of failure, which are found by identifying the critical components whose malfunction would cause total failure.
In computing, fault tolerance can be achieved at the internal component level, at the system level with multiple machines, or at the site level with replication.
At the system level one normally deploys a load balancer for a server cluster, with spare servers waiting to take on the work of a failed server.
A data center can itself be a single point of failure, so at site level the whole cluster may be replicated at another location, typically as part of an IT disaster recovery program.
Scholars have argued that outsourcing that duplication to cloud providers simply moves the single point of failure and may even raise the likelihood of a failure or cyberattack.
Networks such as the Internet are designed with no single point of failure: multiple paths let packets route around damage after the failure of any one path or intermediate node.

entries.title: Failover: when a standby takes over

definition.text: Failover is when a standby or replica takes over the work of a failed component so that the system keeps operating.

facts.text: A failover of replicas should be hidden as much as possible from users with respect to quality of service.
In failover clustering, passive replica servers replicate the master's data to prepare for takeover if the master stops functioning, while the master is the only server active for client interaction.
In primary-backup replication, the backup is a standby process that takes over if the primary fails; in master-slave replication, a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned.
In master-master replication failover is simple, automatic and quick, because both masters already serve reads and writes.
At the system level, spare servers can wait to take on the work of a server that fails.
Failover is switching to a redundant or standby computer server, system, hardware component or network when the previously active one fails or terminates abnormally.
In PostgreSQL a standby leaves standby mode and becomes the primary when pg_ctl promote is run, and a warm standby is typically only moments from full availability once activated.

Automatic failover can be dangerous: if a primary cannot tell whether its secondary is healthy, one SRE design has it make itself unavailable and call a human, to avoid split-brain, which protects data but hurts availability and scales poorly.

entries.title: Gossip protocols: spreading news like an epidemic

definition.text: A gossip or epidemic protocol is a procedure of peer-to-peer communication based on the way epidemics spread.

facts.text: Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows, so a rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and the doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost.

Typical gossip traits: periodic pairwise interactions, exchanges of bounded size, reliable communication not assumed, a low interaction frequency compared with message latency, random peer selection and implicit redundancy of delivered information.

Dissemination protocols flood information through the network with bounded worst-case load; aggregation protocols compute network-wide values, such as the largest or smallest, using fixed-size pairwise exchanges over rounds logarithmic in system size.
Information reaches all nodes in time logarithmic in system size: in a 25,000-machine network a search string spreads in about 15 rounds and the best match is found after about 30 rounds in all.

Gossip is used to keep distributed databases consistent, count nodes, spread news, build overlay networks, compute aggregates and elect leaders; Dynamo uses a gossip-based membership protocol and failure detection.

Randomized update-distribution algorithms from the 1987 epidemic-algorithms paper are simple, need few guarantees from the communication system, tune cost through the randomization, and ensure every update is eventually reflected in all replicas.
The SRE book warns that ad hoc means such as heartbeats and gossip protocols will always have reliability problems for consensus-type problems like master election and group membership.

entries.title: Single-leader replication: one node takes every write

definition.text: In single-leader (primary/replica) replication, one database instance is the leader that handles all writes and propagates them to replica nodes.

facts.text: The leader logs its updates, which propagate to replica nodes, and each replica acknowledges receipt of updates.
Replicas primarily serve read requests, but they may serve stale data because of replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader.

In a primary-backup scheme the primary streams a log of updates to a standby backup that takes over if the primary fails; if part of the log is lost, the backup may differ and transactions could be lost.
A weakness of primary-backup is that only one machine is performing operations: fault tolerance is gained, but the identical backup system doubles the costs.
In master-slave replication the master serves reads and writes and replicates writes to one or more slaves, which serve only reads; slaves can replicate further slaves in a tree-like fashion.
If the master goes offline, the system keeps operating in read-only mode until a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned.

Master-slave benefits: backups of the whole database barely affect the master, applications can read from slaves without loading the master, and slaves can go offline and be synced back without downtime.
Master-slave costs: more hardware and complexity, downtime and possible data loss when the master fails, all writes still go to the master, and more read slaves mean more replication lag.

entries.title: Log shipping: a standby that replays the primary's log

definition.text: Log shipping builds a high-availability setup in which a standby server continuously replays the primary's write-ahead log and is ready to take over if the primary fails.

facts.text: Log shipping moves WAL records from one server to another: the primary runs in continuous archiving mode and each standby in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files, so the two servers are only loosely coupled.
It needs no changes to database tables, so it has low administration overhead and a relatively low performance impact on the primary compared with some other replication solutions.

File-based shipping sends WAL one 16MB segment at a time, cheaply over any distance, with bandwidth that depends on the primary's transaction rate; record-based shipping streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection.

Log shipping is asynchronous, so transactions not yet shipped are lost if the primary fails. archive_timeout can shrink that window to a few seconds at the cost of bandwidth; streaming replication allows a much smaller one.

A standby is typically moments from full availability once activated, which makes it a warm standby offering high availability; restoring from an archived base backup takes far longer and only gives disaster recovery.
A standby that also serves read-only queries is a hot standby; it applies WAL from the archive, then pg_wal, then streaming from the primary, looping until it is stopped or promoted.
Primary and standby should be as similar as possible: the hardware architecture and major PostgreSQL version must match, and the archive must stay reachable even when the primary is down.

entries.title: Leader election: choosing one organizer

definition.text: Leader election is the process of designating a single process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes.

facts.text: After a leader election algorithm runs, every node in the network recognizes the same unique node as the leader of the task.
A valid algorithm must terminate in finite time, ensure uniqueness (exactly one process considers itself leader) and agreement (all other processes know who the leader is).
The nodes must break the symmetry among them; with unique, comparable identities they can compare identities and choose the node with the highest identity as leader.

No deterministic algorithm can elect a leader in an anonymous ring, where all processes are identical and run at the same speed, because symmetry cannot be broken; randomized algorithms pick a leader with high probability.

In the Chang and Roberts ring algorithm each processor sends its ID clockwise, passing on bigger IDs and discarding smaller ones, so the highest ID wins, with O(n^2) messages worst case and O(n log n) on average.
Leader election is equivalent to distributed consensus. The SRE book recommends formally proven consensus systems wherever you see leader election, critical shared state or distributed locking.

A highly available service can replicate a simple program and use leader election so only one leader works at a time; a single leader gives coarse mutual exclusion and often coordinates a pool of workers.
In Raft a follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate and starts an election; Paxos can also select a leader, and ZooKeeper offers leader election as a use case.

entries.title: Multi-master replication: every member can write

definition.text: Multi-master replication is a method of database replication in which a group of computers stores the data and any member can update it.

facts.text: All members respond to client queries, and the system propagates each member's modifications to the rest of the group and resolves conflicts between concurrent changes made by different members.
In master-slave replication a single master per data item is the only node allowed to modify it; this makes consistency easier to achieve but is less flexible than multi-master replication.
Unlike failover clustering, where passive replicas prepare for takeover and only the master serves clients, every master in a multi-master system is active.

The primary purposes are increased availability and faster server response time: if one master fails the others keep updating, and masters can sit in several physical sites, enabling local write processing across data centers.

The drawbacks are that most systems are only loosely consistent (lazy and asynchronous), eager replication is complex and adds latency, and conflict resolution can become intractable as nodes and latency grow.

Jim Gray argued that unless data splits naturally into disjoint sub-databases, concurrency control conflicts seriously degrade performance, with slowdown possibly scaling as O(n³) in the number of replicas.
In master-master replication both masters serve reads and writes and coordinate with each other; if either goes down, the system keeps serving both reads and writes.

Master-master advantages are reading from both masters, spreading write load and simple, automatic, quick failover; drawbacks are harder setup, loose consistency or higher write latency, and conflict resolution as write nodes and latency grow.

entries.title: When two leaders disagree: resolving replication conflicts

definition.text: When concurrent modifications land on different leader nodes, a replicated database must either prevent the transactional conflict or resolve it afterwards.

facts.text: The most common challenge in multi-master replication is preventing or resolving transactional conflicts when concurrent modifications happen on different leader nodes.
Most synchronous (eager) replication solutions prevent conflicts, while asynchronous (lazy) solutions have to resolve them.

If one record changes on two nodes at once, an eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction; a lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization.
Conflict resolution methods include last-write-wins, application-specific logic and merging concurrent updates.

entries.title: CRDTs: data structures that merge themselves

definition.text: A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure replicated across computers that any replica can update independently and concurrently, with a built-in algorithm that resolves inconsistencies so replicas converge.

facts.text: Uncoordinated concurrent updates can leave replicas inconsistent in ways that may not be resolvable. Optimistic replication lets all updates through and merges later; CRDTs are the data structures for which that merge always works.
CRDTs are a common way to obtain strong eventual consistency, in two variants: state-based and operation-based.
Development was motivated by collaborative text editing and mobile computing; CRDTs have also been used in online chat, and Redis, Riak and Cosmos DB have CRDT data types.
A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to operational transformation; known ones include Treedoc, RGA, Woot, Logoot and LSEQ.
League of Legends uses the Riak CRDT implementation for in-game chat with 7.5 million concurrent users and 11,000 messages per second.

entries.title: Synchronous and asynchronous replication: wait or don't wait

definition.text: Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, while asynchronous replication completes the write once local storage acknowledges it.

facts.text: Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss with atomic write operations: a write is not complete until both local and remote storage acknowledge it.

Because most applications wait for the write to complete, synchronous replication lowers overall performance considerably, and performance drops in proportion to distance since minimum latency is set by the speed of light.
For a 10 km distance the fastest possible round trip takes 67 μs, whereas an entire local cached write completes in about 10–20 μs; latency decides how far apart sites can be.

In asynchronous replication a write is complete as soon as local storage acknowledges it and remote storage updates with a small lag, so performance is much higher but the most recent data may be lost if local storage fails.

Semi-synchronous replication counts a write as complete when local storage acknowledges and the remote server receives or logs it; the remote write itself is asynchronous, so durability is not guaranteed on local failure.

The difference between the two is how data is written to the replica: synchronous replication writes to primary storage and the replica simultaneously, so the two copies should always stay synchronized.
Asynchronous replication copies data to the replica after it is already written to primary storage; it can be near-real-time but more commonly runs on a schedule, and it is more cost-effective.

In synchronous database replication a transaction is not committed until all servers have committed it, so failover loses nothing; asynchronous replication allows delay, so transactions might be lost in a failover and replicas may return slightly stale results.

entries.text:
For a 10 km distance the fastest possible round trip takes 67 μs, whereas an entire local cached write completes in about 10–20 μs. That gap is the heart of a choice every replicated system makes: does a write wait for the remote copy?

Synchronous replication waits. A write is not complete until both local and remote storage acknowledge it, so it guarantees zero data loss with atomic write operations. In a synchronous database, a transaction is not committed until all servers have committed it, so failover loses nothing. The price is performance. Most applications wait for the write to complete, so overall performance falls considerably. It drops in proportion to distance, since minimum latency is set by the speed of light. Latency decides how far apart sites can be.

Asynchronous replication does not wait. A write is complete as soon as local storage acknowledges it, and remote storage updates with a small lag. It can be near-real-time but more commonly runs on a schedule, and it is more cost-effective. Performance is much higher. But the most recent data may be lost if local storage fails, transactions might be lost in a failover, and replicas may return slightly stale results.

Semi-synchronous replication sits between the two. A write counts as complete when local storage acknowledges it and the remote server receives or logs it. The remote write itself is asynchronous, so durability is not guaranteed on local failure.

entries.title: Quorum: how many votes are enough

definition.text: A quorum is the minimum number of votes a distributed transaction must obtain before it may perform an operation in a distributed system.

facts.text: Quorum-based techniques enforce consistent operation in a distributed system, working both as a replica control method and as a commit method that keeps transactions atomic despite network partitioning.
In replica control each copy holds a vote, and an operation needs a read quorum Vr or write quorum Vw. The rule Vr + Vw > V (V the total votes) makes every read quorum include the newest version.
A second rule ensures two write operations on the same item cannot happen concurrently; together the two rules maintain one-copy serializability.

In Gifford's weighted voting, copies get votes and r + w must exceed the file's total votes so every read quorum overlaps every write quorum; version numbers show which copies are current, and r and w tune reliability and performance.
In commit protocols a transaction runs only if a majority of sites vote for it: a commit quorum Vc is needed to commit and an abort quorum Va to abort, so it cannot commit and abort at once.
A majority quorum keeps a partitioned cluster safe: the sub-partition holding a majority of the votes stays available while the others fall into an auto-fencing mode.

entries.title: Leaderless replication: the Dynamo approach

definition.text: In leaderless replication any replica accepts writes, as in Dynamo, a set of techniques for a highly available key-value store with no distinguished node.

facts.text: Replication can be single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless. Dynamo is leaderless, while DynamoDB, built on Dynamo's principles, uses single-leader replication.

Dynamo's principles: symmetry (every node has the same responsibilities, no special node), decentralization (peer-to-peer over central control), incremental scalability (add one node at a time) and heterogeneity (work proportional to server capability).
It partitions data with consistent hashing, which gives incremental, possibly linear scalability in proportion to the number of collaborating nodes.
For highly available writes it uses vector clocks (or dotted-version-vector sets) and reconciles conflicting versions during reads.
For temporary failures it uses a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, keeping availability and durability when some replicas are unavailable.
For permanent failures it uses anti-entropy with Merkle trees, which finds differences between replica owners so divergent replicas can be synchronized proactively.
Membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol, avoiding a central registry of members and node liveness and preserving symmetry.
Cassandra, Project Voldemort and Riak were inspired by the Dynamo paper.

entries.title: The read replica pattern: writes to one, reads from many

definition.text: In the read replica pattern, all data-modifying commands go to the primary database and reads go to read replicas.

facts.text: Inserts, deletes and updates are sent to the primary DB and replicated to the read replicas, which serve reads such as viewing order details or order history.
There are two common ways to implement the pattern: embed the routing logic in the application code, or use database middleware.

Database middleware provides transparent routing between the application and the database servers, with rules customizable by user, schema, statement and so on, and acts as a proxy using the standard MySQL network protocol.
Middleware simplifies application code, since the application need not know the database topology, and any MySQL-compatible client can connect, which makes database migration easier.
Middleware adds complexity and network latency, and because all queries go through it, it usually needs a high-availability setup to avoid a single point of failure.

entries.title: Performance bottleneck: the slowest part sets the pace
entries.article: Single point of failure#Computing > Software engineering

definition.text: A bottleneck occurs when the capacity of an application or computer system is limited by a single component.

facts.text: The bottleneck is the part with the lowest throughput of all parts of the transaction path.
A common example is code that could use parallel processing but runs several independent processes sequentially instead of simultaneously.
Tracking down bottlenecks, or hot spots, is called performance analysis and is done with specialized profilers, with the objective of making those sections of code as fast as possible.
Bottlenecks, like series circuits, are design structures that create single points of failure.

entries.title: Replication lag: reading your own writes

definition.text: Replication lag is the delay in propagating changes from the leader to its replicas, which can leave replicas serving stale data.

facts.text: Under network delay or server overload, replica data might be seconds or even minutes behind the primary.
A user who checks an order right after placing it may hit a lagging replica and not see the order at all, so the setup needs read-after-write consistency.
One mitigation is to send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database.

Another is to check whether a replica has caught up with the primary, which a relational database generally supports: query the replica if it is up to date, otherwise fail the read or read from the primary.

entries.title: Active and passive replication: who does the work?

definition.text: Active replication processes the same request at every replica, while passive replication processes each request on one replica and transfers the result to the others.

facts.text: In a primary-backup or primary-replica scheme, one leader replica chosen by leader election processes all requests, a design predominant in high-availability clusters.

In a multi-primary or multi-master scheme any replica can process a request and distribute the new state, so some form of distributed concurrency control, such as a distributed lock manager, is needed.
State machine replication is sometimes mistakenly used as a synonym of active replication.

entries.text: When a request arrives, who does the work: every replica, or just one? In the active form, every replica processes the same request. entries.title: Chain replication: writes that travel down a line

definition.text: Chain replication is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency.

facts.text: Modern multi-primary replication protocols optimize for the common failure-free operation, and chain replication is a popular family of them.
Chain replication enables local reads on all replica nodes but has high latency for writes, which must traverse several nodes sequentially.
The Hermes protocol combines invalidations and logical timestamps for strong consistency with local reads and high-performance writes from all replicas, committing after one multicast round trip.

entries.text: In chain replication, a write must pass through several nodes one after another. It is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency. entries.title: Three ways to ship changes to a replica

definition.text: Databases replicate data changes between nodes by shipping SQL statements, the storage engine's write-ahead log, or row-level changes.

facts.text: Statement-based replication logs write requests such as SQL statements and sends them to replicas for execution, which is problematic with non-deterministic functions or statements with side effects.
Write-ahead log shipping replicates the storage engine's low-level log, which keeps data structures identical across nodes.
Logical (row-based) replication describes changes at the row level in a dedicated log format, giving more flexibility and independence from storage engine internals.

entries.text: A leader can describe its changes to replicas in three ways. Logical (row-based) replication describes changes at the row level in a dedicated log format, giving more flexibility and independence from storage engine internals.

entries.title: Logical replication: publishing changes row by row

definition.text: Logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, rather than copying physical blocks.

facts.text: Logical replication contrasts with physical replication, which uses exact block addresses and byte-by-byte copying; PostgreSQL supports both, and logical replication allows fine-grained control over data replication and security.
It uses a publish and subscribe model: subscribers pull data from the publications they subscribe to on a publisher node, and may re-publish it to allow cascading or more complex setups.

Replication of a table starts with a snapshot copy to the subscriber, then changes made since the copy are sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription.

Use cases include sending incremental changes of a subset of a database, consolidating several databases into one for analytics, replicating between major versions or platforms, and sharing a subset of data between databases.
A read-only subscriber causes no conflicts from a single subscription, but other writes to the same tables, by an application or other subscribers, can cause conflicts.

entries.title: Three models of replication
entries.article: Replication (computing)#Terminology > Replication models in distributed systems

definition.text: Three widely cited models for data replication are transactional replication, state machine replication and virtual synchrony.

facts.text: Transactional replication, used for replicating transactional data such as a database, follows one-copy serializability: valid outcomes on replicated data accord with ACID.

State machine replication assumes a deterministic finite automaton and atomic broadcast of every event, is based on distributed consensus, and is usually implemented as a replicated log of Paxos rounds.

In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state, and multicasts reach all members in identical order, with membership changes delivered as a new membership view.

entries.text: Three models of data replication are widely cited. The second model, {{ref:sysd-scale-020}}, assumes a deterministic finite automaton and {{ref:sysd-scale-113}} of every event. It is based on {{ref:sysd-scale-008}} and is usually implemented as a replicated log of {{ref:sysd-scale-015}} rounds. In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, and a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state. Transactional replication, used for replicating transactional data such as a database, follows one-copy serializability: valid outcomes on replicated data accord with ACID. The second model, State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands, assumes a deterministic finite automaton and Atomic broadcast: everyone sees the same messages in the same order of every event. It is based on Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures and is usually implemented as a replicated log of Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors rounds. In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, and a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state. Multicasts reach all members in identical order, with membership changes delivered as a new membership view.

entries.title: Storage replication: copying disks, not files

definition.text: Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification.

facts.text: It is implemented in hardware, in a disk array controller, or in software, in a device driver.
Disk mirroring is the most basic method and is a local, short-distance operation; replication can extend across a network so disks sit in distant locations.
The purpose is to prevent damage from failures or disasters at one location or to improve the ability to recover data.
Point-in-time replication replicates periodic snapshots of only the changed data, so it can use cheaper bandwidth links such as iSCSI or T1 instead of fiberoptic lines.

entries.text: Copy the disk and everything on it is copied too. Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification. It is implemented in a disk array controller or in a device driver. Disk mirroring is the most basic method, but replication can also cross a network to distant disks. The purpose is to prevent damage from failures or disasters at one location or to improve the ability to recover data. Point-in-time replication copies periodic snapshots of only the changed data, so it can use cheaper links such as iSCSI or T1 instead of fiberoptic lines.

entries.title: Choosing a replication solution

definition.text: Database servers can work together for high availability, by letting a second server take over if the primary fails, or for load balancing, by letting several computers serve the same data.

facts.text: Read-only servers combine easily, but read/write servers are hard: a write to any server must reach all servers so later reads stay consistent. This synchronization problem is the fundamental difficulty, and each solution minimizes it for a specific workload.

Some solutions let only one server modify data: primary servers read and write, standby servers track the primary's changes. A warm standby cannot be connected to until promoted; a hot standby accepts read-only queries.
Solutions differ in granularity: some handle only an entire database server, others allow control per table or per database.
Performance must be weighed in any choice; there is usually a trade-off between functionality and performance.

entries.title: File-based replication: copying files, not blocks

definition.text: File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level.

facts.text: It relies almost exclusively on software; a kernel filter driver can intercept file system calls such as open, write and delete and send them to another machine, which mimics them.
Like block-level replication it can be synchronous or asynchronous, but synchronous mode is less common for file replication products.
File-level replication can skip data of no business value, such as temporary files, and transmit only what an application wrote, for example 100 bytes instead of a whole 4,096-byte disk block.
Batch replication compares source and destination and makes the destination match; it is generally free or inexpensive, such as rsync, but system-intensive, so it generally runs infrequently.

entries.text: Instead of a whole 4,096-byte disk block, file-level replication can transmit just the 100 bytes an application wrote. File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level. It relies almost exclusively on software. A kernel filter driver can intercept file system calls such as open, write and delete and send them to another machine, which mimics them. It can skip data of no business value, such as temporary files. Batch replication compares source and destination and makes the destination match. It is generally free or inexpensive, such as rsync, but system-intensive, so it generally runs infrequently.

entries.title: Split-brain: two nodes that both think they are in charge

definition.text: Split-brain is a state of data or availability inconsistency caused by two separate data sets with overlapping scope, typically when servers stop communicating and synchronizing, as in a network partition.

facts.text: High-availability clusters watch node health over a private heartbeat link. If all those links fail while the nodes keep running, each node believes it is the only one running.
Each side then serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data or cause inconsistencies that need operator cleanup.
File servers that watch each other by heartbeat and shoot the other node with STONITH can both take mastership, or both go down, when the network is slow, corrupting data or making it unavailable.
The SRE book's diagnosis: the system solves a leader election problem with simple timeouts, and leader election is a form of distributed consensus that cannot be solved correctly using heartbeats.

Optimistic approaches let partitioned nodes keep working, gaining availability at the cost of correctness and reconciling afterwards; pessimistic approaches give up availability for consistency by limiting access to sub-partitions.
A typical pessimistic approach is quorum consensus: the sub-partition with a majority of the votes stays available and the rest fence themselves off; MongoDB replica sets work this way.
Modern high-availability clusters combine heartbeat connections with quorum witness storage; a two-node cluster without a witness cannot tell which member should be active when the heartbeat fails.
Two replicated file servers must never write simultaneously, because that could corrupt data, possibly unrecoverably. Each pair has a leader and a follower that monitor each other by heartbeats.

entries.title: Sending state or sending operations: two kinds of CRDT
entries.article: Conflict-free replicated data type#Types of CRDTs

definition.text: State-based CRDTs replicate by sending full state to be merged, while operation-based CRDTs replicate by sending the update operations.

facts.text: State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) send their full local state to other replicas, which merge it into theirs; the merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent so reordering and duplicated messages do no harm.
Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) have no merge function: they send update operations, such as +10 or -20, which must be commutative and associative and delivered to each replica without duplication.
State-based CRDTs are simpler to design and need only a gossip protocol from the network, but the whole state must eventually reach every replica; delta CRDTs send only recent changes.

Operation-based CRDTs send small operations, using less bandwidth when transactions are few compared with the state size, but need middleware that never drops or duplicates operations and delivers them in causal order.

entries.title: Counters and sets built as CRDTs

definition.text: Counters and sets are built as CRDTs by giving each replica its own slot or tag and merging with maximum or union operations.

facts.text: A G-Counter gives each node its own array slot that it increments; replicas merge by taking the maximum of every slot, and the value is the sum of the slots.
A PN-Counter combines two G-Counters, one counting increments and one counting decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total.
A G-Set only allows adds and merges by union. A 2P-Set adds a tombstone set so elements can be removed, but a removed element can never be added again.

An LWW-Element-Set timestamps each add and remove so the latest wins; an OR-Set tags each add uniquely and removes only the tags it has observed, so an element stays present while any add tag is unremoved.

entries.title: Database partitioning: cutting a big database into independent pieces

definition.text: A partition is a division of a logical database or its constituent elements into distinct, independent parts.

facts.text: Database partitioning means deliberately breaking a large database into smaller ones for scalability, which is distinct from a network partition, a type of network fault between nodes.
In a partitioned database each piece of data (record, row or document) belongs to exactly one partition, so each partition is effectively a small database of its own.
Partitioning is normally done for manageability, performance, availability or load balancing, spreading datasets across multiple disks and query loads across multiple processors.

A query that touches a single partition runs independently on that partition's node, so query throughput scales linearly with added nodes; more complex queries can be parallelized across nodes, with extra challenges.
Partitioning is commonly combined with replication: each record belongs to one partition but exists on several nodes, and a node can lead some partitions while following others.
Systems name partitions differently: shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud, region in HBase, tablet in Bigtable, vnode in Cassandra and Riak, vBucket in Couchbase.

entries.title: How a database decides which partition holds a row

definition.text: The rules a database uses to assign each row to a partition from its partitioning key: range, list, composite, round-robin or hash.

facts.text: Relational database systems take a partitioning key and assign a partition by a criterion: range, list, composite, round-robin or hash partitioning.
List partitioning gives each partition a list of values; a row whose key is in the list goes there, as when Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark form a partition for the Nordic countries.
Composite partitioning combines schemes, for example applying range partitioning first and then hash partitioning; consistent hashing can be seen as a composite of hash and list partitioning.

Round-robin partitioning sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n), giving uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

A sharding key is a column of the table, and the sharding algorithm uses it to decide which shard stores each row; choosing the right key and algorithm is crucial for even distribution and performance.
Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table (directory) that maps sharding keys to shard locations, and routes data by consulting it.

Consistent hashing extends hash-based sharding to move less data when shards change; virtual bucket sharding maps data to virtual buckets and buckets to physical shards, easing rebalancing without much data movement.
When shards follow a real-world segmentation, such as European versus American customers, the right shard can be inferred easily and only that shard queried.

entries.title: Range partitioning: one volume of keys per partition

definition.text: Range partitioning assigns continuous ranges of the partitioning key to partitions, like the volumes of an encyclopedia.

facts.text: Because the range boundaries are known, a request can be routed straight to the partition that holds its key.
Boundaries can be set manually or automatically so that the data is balanced across partitions.
Range partitioning makes range scans efficient, but certain access patterns, such as writing time-ordered keys, create hot spots.
A typical example is a partition for all rows whose zipcode column has a value between 70000 and 79999.
Ranges must be contiguous but not overlapping; each has a non-inclusive lower and upper bound, and key values at or above a range's upper bound go to the next partition.

Range-based sharding works on ordered columns such as integers, longs or timestamps, for example customers by alphabetical order of last name, transactions by date range, or user IDs 1 to 1000 in shard 1.

entries.title: Horizontal partitioning: same columns, fewer rows per table

definition.text: Horizontal partitioning puts different rows of a table into different tables.

facts.text: For example, customers with ZIP codes below 50000 go in CustomersEast and those at 50000 or above in CustomersWest; a view with a union over both tables gives the complete picture of all customers.
Holding fewer rows in each table reduces index size, which generally improves search performance.
It pays off when there is an obvious, robust and implicit way to tell which partition holds a row without searching the index, as a ZIP code does.

Many guides use horizontal partitioning and sharding as synonyms: a table is divided into smaller tables, each a separate data store with the same columns but fewer rows, so more machines can share the load.

entries.title: Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers

definition.text: A database shard is a horizontal partition of the data in a database or search engine, and each shard may be held on a separate database server instance.

facts.text: Each shard is the single source for its subset of data, and placing shards on separate hardware spreads a database across many machines, which can significantly improve performance.

Splitting tables over servers reduces the rows per table and the index size, which generally improves search, and the search load spreads over multiple servers rather than only over several indexes on one server.
Plain horizontal partitioning stays within one schema instance and server, while sharding partitions the table the same way across potentially multiple instances of the schema.
Sharding distributes large partitionable tables across servers while smaller tables are replicated in full on each server, and a mechanism is needed to keep the replicated tables synchronized.
Sharding relates to shared-nothing architecture, since each shard can sit in its own schema instance, server, data center or region, and it aims to minimize cross-shard access.
Every shard has the same schema and columns but holds a unique, independent subset of the data, and all shards together contain all of the data.
Sharding logic can live in the application, in a middleware layer between application and database, or in the database system itself.

Shards give logical independence, since each can be managed on its own for availability, and sensitive and non-sensitive data can be kept in different partitions for better manageability and security.

entries.title: Shared nothing: every request served by a single node

definition.text: A shared-nothing architecture is a distributed computing architecture in which each update request is satisfied by a single node (processor, memory and storage unit) in a cluster.

facts.text: Nodes do not share memory or storage, and the intent is to eliminate contention among nodes.

Shared everything satisfies requests with arbitrary combinations of nodes and so risks contention when several nodes update the same data at once; shared-disk and shared-memory architectures also contrast with shared-nothing.

It removes single points of failure, so the system keeps running despite node failures and nodes can upgrade hardware or software without a system-wide shutdown. It scales simply by adding nodes because no central resource is a bottleneck.

Data is typically partitioned among many nodes; in a database the part on one node is a shard. Commonly used but rarely modified data can be replicated across nodes so more requests resolve on a single node.
It is popular for web development and data warehousing, but requests that need data from multiple nodes can dramatically reduce throughput.

entries.title: Skew and hot spots: one partition carries the load

definition.text: Skew is uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot.

facts.text: Partitioning aims to spread data and query load evenly; with ideal distribution capacity scales linearly, so ten nodes process ten times the data and throughput of one node, while skew reduces that efficiency.
Hot spots can be countered by assigning records to nodes at random (at the cost of harder retrieval), by key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or by hash-based partitioning for even load.
With timestamp keys in a sensor network, writes concentrate in the current time period's partition; prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load.

entries.text: With ideal distribution, ten nodes process ten times the data and throughput of one node. Skew eats into that. It is the uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot. A sensor network keyed by timestamp shows how it happens: writes concentrate in the partition for the current time period. Prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load. Other remedies are assigning records to nodes at random, at the cost of harder retrieval, key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or hash-based partitioning for even load.

It is the uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot. A sensor network keyed by timestamp shows how it happens: writes concentrate in the partition for the current time period. Prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load. Other remedies are assigning records to nodes at random, at the cost of harder retrieval, key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or hash-based partitioning for even load.

entries.title: What sharding costs: harder queries and more to go wrong

definition.text: Sharding adds complexity to the database infrastructure and application code, which brings several costs: harder queries, more software that can fail, and more demanding failover, backup and schema management.

facts.text: Developers may need to write more complex SQL queries to handle the sharding logic.
The software that partitions, balances, coordinates and maintains data integrity can itself fail or introduce errors.
Corruption or failure of one shard can affect the integrity of the entire dataset, and fail-over servers must maintain copies of all shards.
Backups of the individual shards must be coordinated with each other, and adding indexes, modifying columns or altering the schema all become harder.

Joins that span several shards are often not feasible or not efficient, because the data must be retrieved from multiple servers; transactions across shards may need distributed transaction management.
When distribution is uneven or one shard is heavily loaded, shards must be rebalanced, and changing the sharding scheme after the database is sharded is complex and time-consuming.
The ORDER BY operation gets more complicated: data is usually fetched from different shards and sorted in the application's code.
Uneven distribution can leave some shards holding more data than others, which is also called a hotspot.

entries.title: Hash partitioning: trading range queries for an even load

definition.text: Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the partitioning key, turning skewed data into a uniform distribution so that load spreads evenly across partitions.

facts.text: It effectively prevents hot spots, but it sacrifices range query efficiency because adjacent keys scatter across partitions.
Common implementations use MD5, as Cassandra and MongoDB do.
Cassandra combines both approaches with compound primary keys: the first component is hashed to pick the partition, while the remaining components keep sort order within the partition.
A shard key such as a customer ID or transaction ID is hashed, which tends to spread data more evenly than range-based sharding, but a proper hash function is needed to avoid collisions.
A simple form is shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards, but dynamically adding or removing database servers then becomes expensive, which is the problem consistent hashing solves.

entries.title: Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything

definition.text: A hashing technique that lets a hash table be resized while remapping only about n/m keys on average, where n is the number of keys and m the number of slots.

facts.text: In an ordinary hash table the key-to-slot mapping is a modulo operation, so changing the number of slots (servers) remaps nearly all keys, and reassigning everything is expensive.
Consistent hashing hashes both the keys and the servers onto a circle, and assigns each key to the next server found clockwise from it.
When a server fails or is added, only the keys next to it on the circle move; adding the nth server relocates only a 1/n fraction of the keys.
It spreads cache keys evenly across shards even if some fail; DynamoDB and Cassandra use it to minimize data movement during rebalancing, and CDNs use it to spread content over edge servers.
To stay available and durable, consistent hashing replicates each data item on N nodes, where N is the replication factor; in eventually consistent systems the copies are made asynchronously.

In theory it spreads load evenly, but in practice load is often uneven and one server can become a hotspot; it also adds complexity, risks cascading failures, and makes key management costly when nodes transiently fail.
Karger et al. introduced consistent hashing as the basis of caching protocols that relieve hot spots on very large networks such as the Internet, where delays caused by hot spots can be severe.
A consistent hash function changes minimally as its range changes, so the caching protocols need no current, or even consistent, view of the whole network and scale gracefully as it grows.

entries.title: Distributed hash tables: a lookup service with no center

definition.text: A distributed hash table (DHT) is a distributed system that provides a lookup service similar to a hash table.

facts.text: Key-value pairs are stored across the participating nodes, and any node can efficiently retrieve the value for a given key.

Responsibility for the key-to-value mapping is spread over the nodes so a membership change causes minimal disruption. Nodes can be added or removed with little redistribution of keys, so a DHT scales and handles continual churn.

A DHT has three parts: an abstract keyspace such as 160-bit strings, a keyspace partitioning scheme that splits ownership among nodes, and an overlay network that lets nodes find the owner of any key.

Most DHTs map keys to nodes with consistent hashing or rendezvous hashing, so adding or removing a node changes only the keys of adjacent IDs, whereas a traditional hash table remaps nearly the whole keyspace.

Each node keeps links to a few other nodes (its routing table). Any node either owns a key or links to a node closer to it, so a lookup is forwarded greedily to the closest neighbor, called key-based routing.

A node needs to coordinate with only O(log n) of the n participants. The most common design has O(log n) neighbors and O(log n) route length, used by Chord, Kademlia, Pastry and Tapestry; shorter routes need more neighbors.
DHTs aim for autonomy and decentralization with no central coordination, fault tolerance despite nodes continuously joining, leaving and failing, and scalability to thousands or millions of nodes.

DHTs underpin services such as distributed file systems, cooperative web caching, naming and peer-to-peer file sharing, as in BitTorrent's distributed tracker and IPFS. Locality-preserving hashing eases range queries but gives up uniform load.

entries.title: Rendezvous hashing: every client picks the same server alone

definition.text: Rendezvous or highest random weight (HRW) hashing is an algorithm that lets clients reach distributed agreement on a set of k options out of a possible set of n options.

facts.text: A typical use is for clients to agree on which sites (servers or proxies) an object is assigned to; each client chooses independently, but all must end up picking the same sites, and the standard case is k = 1.
All clients share a hash function h. For object O each computes the weight h(O, S) for every site S and picks the site with the highest weight, or the k highest for k sites.

Hashing objects into a table of n sites breaks when a site fails, because the table size changes and every object is remapped. With rendezvous hashing only the failed site's objects move, to the next largest weight.
Properties include low client overhead, uniform load across sites and minimal disruption. A site with twice the capacity is listed twice, so twice as many objects map to it.
Compared with consistent hashing it is much simpler, needs no precomputed or stored tokens, and handles any k < n. A removed site's objects spread uniformly over all remaining sites.
Consistent hashing is a special case of rendezvous hashing, but not the reverse: rendezvous hashing can send a removed site's objects to an unbounded number of other sites.

Basic rendezvous hashing computes n hash values per lookup, so placement is O(n), which is fine for moderate n. A skeleton-based hierarchical variant reaches O(log n) at the cost of less uniform placement.
Designed in 1996, it is now preferred over consistent hashing in many applications, such as the GitHub load balancer, Apache Ignite, Apache Kafka and the Twitter EventBus pub/sub platform.

entries.title: Virtual nodes: giving each server many places on the ring

definition.text: A virtual node (vnode) is an existing physical node mapped multiple times across the hash ring, so that its share of the key space is made of several small ranges.

facts.text: Instead of one position, a physical node is given several smaller ranges of the hash range; the number of duplicate labels a server gets is its weight.

Without them a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load; with several positions per server, its keys are reassigned to different servers, spreading them more evenly.
Virtual nodes spread load more evenly across physical nodes, speed up rebalancing after nodes are added or removed, and lower the probability of hotspots.
Multiple labels are needed because servers are not uniformly distributed around the circle, which causes skew among nodes.

entries.title: Chord: finding the node that stores a key

definition.text: Chord is a distributed lookup protocol that lets peer-to-peer applications locate the node storing a particular data item.

facts.text: Chord supports one operation: given a key, it maps the key onto a node. Data location is built on top by storing each key and data item at the node the key maps to.
Chord uses consistent hashing: nodes are points on a circle, and the circular keyspace is split into contiguous segments whose endpoints are node identifiers.
It adapts efficiently as nodes join and leave and can answer queries even while the system is continuously changing.
Theory, simulation and experiments show Chord is scalable: both the communication cost and the state kept by each node grow logarithmically with the number of nodes.

entries.title: Vertical partitioning: splitting a table by its columns

definition.text: Vertical partitioning creates tables with fewer columns and stores the remaining columns in additional tables, so rows are split by their columns.

facts.text: It goes beyond normalization by splitting columns even when the table is already normalized; it is also called row splitting.
Infrequently used or very wide columns that take up much memory can be moved to a different machine.
A common form splits static data from dynamic data, since the static part is faster to access; a view across the two tables restores the original table at a performance penalty.
A columnar database can be regarded as a database vertically partitioned until each column is stored in its own table.

entries.title: Federation: many databases that look like one

definition.text: Federation, also called functional partitioning, splits up databases by function.

facts.text: A federation makes several distinct physical databases appear as one logical database to end users, tied together by federated schemas that express the commonality of data and specify what the components may share.
It gives a cohesive, unified view of data from multiple sources, which can include databases and other structured and unstructured data.

A federated database is transparent, so users need not know where data is stored; it copes with differing hardware, protocols and data models; and it leaves existing data sources and their interfaces unchanged.
Advantages are flexible data sharing, autonomy among components, unified access to heterogeneous data, and no tight coupling of applications with legacy databases.
Disadvantages are extra hardware and complexity, complex joins of data from two databases, dependence on autonomous data sources, and query performance and scalability limits.

entries.title: When sharding is worth it, and when it is not

definition.text: Sharding is worth using when one machine cannot hold the data or serve the requests and other optimizations are not enough, because scaling out is then cheaper than scaling up.

facts.text: Sharding is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient; sharding a table before it has been optimized locally adds needless complexity.
After a certain point it is cheaper and more feasible to scale horizontally by adding machines than to scale vertically by adding more powerful servers.
Sharding solves a single server holding too much data, serving too many requests, and rising query latency as data grows.

Singh lists reasons to shard: using existing hardware instead of high-end machines, keeping data in distinct geographic regions, scaling quickly by adding shards, lighter load per machine, and more concurrent connections.

entries.title: Consistency models: the contract between programmer and store

definition.text: A consistency model is a contract between the programmer and a system: if the programmer follows the rules for operations, reads, writes and updates behave predictably.

facts.text: Consistency models are used in distributed data stores such as filesystems, databases, optimistic replication systems and web caching.

In a store where row X is replicated on nodes M and N, the model decides whether client B, reading from N after client A wrote to M, will definitely, definitely not, or cannot count on seeing the write.
Models define rules for the apparent order and visibility of updates, and they sit on a continuum with trade-offs.
One model is stronger than another if it requires all the other's conditions and more; a model with fewer constraints is weaker.
Strict consistency is the strongest model: every write must be seen instantaneously by all processors, which makes it only a thought experiment because instantaneous message exchange is impossible.
Replicas keep a system reliable and fast, but copies can drift; synchronous replication gives tight consistency, yet applying global synchronization to keep all copies consistent is costly.
Weakening the consistency restrictions decreases the cost of global synchronization and improves performance.

entries.title: Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet

definition.text: Eventual consistency is a model used in distributed computing to achieve high availability: if no new updates are made to an item, all reads eventually return its last updated value.

facts.text: If no new updates are made to a data item, eventually all read accesses to that item return the last updated value.
Eventual consistency is also called optimistic replication, and a system that has reached it is said to have converged, or achieved replica convergence.
It is a weak guarantee, and until an update converges different queries for a record may see different values.
Eventual consistency gives only a liveness guarantee, that reads eventually return the same value, with no safety guarantee, so any intermediate value is allowed before convergence.
Eventually consistent services are often described as BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency), in contrast to traditional ACID.
Asynchronous replication helps achieve eventual consistency, but it can also leave data inconsistent.
Many NoSQL databases use eventual consistency to offer availability and partition tolerance at the price of reduced data consistency.
Critics say it adds complexity: wrong assumptions about consistency levels cause subtle bugs that only appear during network failures or high concurrency.

entries.title: Network partitions: the cluster splits but every node keeps running

definition.text: A network partition is a division of a computer network into relatively independent subnets, either by design or because network devices fail.

facts.text: With nodes A and B in one subnet and C and D in another, a partition occurs if the switch between them fails: A and B can no longer reach C and D, yet every node works as before.

Distributed software must be designed to be partition-tolerant, meaning it still works correctly after the network is partitioned; in CAP, partition tolerance is the ability to keep processing data despite communication errors between subsystems.
Partitions are inevitable because cables get cut, packets are lost or delayed by congestion, hardware breaks and network components are misconfigured.
When nodes cannot communicate, the system either stops serving some or all requests, reducing availability, or serves as usual and gives nodes inconsistent views of the data.
An apparent full partition may really be a very slow network, some but not all messages being dropped, or throttling in one direction only, which makes failures hard to reason about.
A network partition is a fault between nodes, distinct from database partitioning, which intentionally breaks a large database into smaller ones for scalability.

entries.title: The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything

definition.text: The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, says a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance.

facts.text: A distributed data store can provide at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance, the three properties commonly desired when designing distributed web services.
Consistency means every read receives the most recent write or an error, so all clients see the same data at the same time whichever node they connect to.
Availability means every request received by a non-failing node must get a response, without any guarantee that the response holds the most recent version of the data.
Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes.
No distributed system is safe from network failures, so partitions generally have to be tolerated, and during a partition one must choose between consistency and availability.

Choosing consistency, the system returns an error or times out when it cannot guarantee fresh data; choosing availability, it always answers with the most recent version it has, even if that may be stale.
In the absence of a network partition, both availability and consistency can be satisfied, and during normal operation a data store covers all three.
Gilbert and Lynch proved Brewer's conjecture in 2002 for the asynchronous network model, then discussed solutions to the dilemma in the partially synchronous model.

entries.title: Anti-entropy and reconciliation: how replicas converge

definition.text: To converge, an eventually consistent system exchanges updates between servers and reconciles concurrent updates by choosing a final state.

facts.text: Replicas converge through anti-entropy, which exchanges versions or updates of data between servers, and through reconciliation, which chooses a final state when concurrent updates have occurred.
The most appropriate way to reconcile depends on the application.
A widespread approach is last writer wins, and some use first writer wins where last writer wins is unacceptable.
Another approach is to invoke a user-specified conflict handler.
Timestamps and vector clocks are often used to detect concurrency between updates.

Reconciliation must happen before the next read: read repair fixes an inconsistency when a read finds it, write repair fixes it during a write and slows that write, and asynchronous repair runs outside reads and writes.
In an AP database, the nodes are typically re-synced to repair all inconsistencies once a partition is resolved.

entries.title: PACELC: the trade-off CAP leaves out

definition.text: PACELC extends the CAP theorem: during a network partition choose between availability and consistency, and otherwise choose between latency and consistency.

facts.text: If there is a partition (P), the trade-off is between availability (A) and consistency (C); else (E), even in normal operation, it is between latency (L) and consistency (C).
The reason for the latency trade-off is that consistent operations need a full network round trip on reads and writes, while low-latency systems relax consistency to reduce delay.
PACELC addresses a limit of CAP: ignoring the consistency-latency trade-off is a major oversight, because it is present at all times while CAP matters only during a partition.
By CAP's own wording a database counts as available if a query returns after 30 days, a latency no real application accepts.
The four configurations are PA/EL, PA/EC, PC/EL and PC/EC; PC/EC gives firm ACID-style consistency and PA/EL gives high availability and low latency with a more complex consistency model.
PA/EC and PC/EL systems give only conditional guarantees of consistency, so the developer must still write code for the cases where the guarantee is not upheld.
PC does not mean fully consistent; it means the system does not lower consistency below its baseline during a partition and reduces availability instead.

Marc Brooker argues CAP is most relevant where devices connect intermittently, such as IoT and mobile apps, while for cloud applications PACELC is more appropriate because it also covers latency versus consistency without partitions.

entries.title: Strong eventual consistency: same updates, same state

definition.text: Strong eventual consistency adds a safety guarantee to eventual consistency: any two nodes that have received the same set of updates, in any order, are in the same state.

facts.text: Plain eventual consistency is only a liveness guarantee: updates will be observed eventually, but nothing is promised about the values seen before convergence.
Strong eventual consistency adds the safety guarantee that any two nodes holding the same unordered set of updates are in the same state.
A common way to ensure it is conflict-free replicated data types.

entries.text: Deliver the same updates to two nodes in different orders, and they still end up in the same state. That is the guarantee of strong eventual consistency. Plain eventual consistency is only a liveness guarantee: updates will be observed eventually, but nothing is promised about the values seen before convergence. Strong eventual consistency adds a safety guarantee. Any two nodes that have received the same set of updates, in any order, are in the same state. A common way to ensure it is {{ref:sysd-scale-125}}.

entries.title: CP, AP and CA: sorting databases by what they sacrifice

definition.text: Because a distributed database must tolerate partitions, it is classed as CP if it keeps consistency, AP if it keeps availability, or CA if it assumes no partitions.

facts.text: The physical network cannot be guaranteed stable, so a distributed database must choose partition tolerance, which leaves a trade-off between consistency and availability.

A CA database gives consistency and availability across all nodes but cannot do so if any two nodes are partitioned, so it offers no fault tolerance; PostgreSQL and MariaDB are examples, and no NoSQL database is classed as CA.
A CP database gives consistency and partition tolerance at the expense of availability: when a partition occurs, it shuts down the non-consistent node until the partition is resolved.
MongoDB and Apache HBase are CP examples, and etcd also favors consistency over availability during a network partition.

An AP database gives availability and partition tolerance at the expense of consistency: all nodes stay available during a partition, but those on the wrong side may return an older version of the data.
Once the partition is resolved, an AP database typically re-syncs the nodes to repair inconsistencies; Cassandra, CouchDB and ScyllaDB are AP examples.
Databases built on ACID guarantees, such as relational ones, choose consistency over availability, while systems built on BASE, common in NoSQL, choose availability over consistency.
Most modern distributed databases offer configuration options for both consistency and availability.

conflicts.text: MongoDB can be classified as a PA/EC system.
