entries.title: Apache Hadoop: shipping the code to the data

definition.text: A collection of open-source software utilities for reliable, scalable, distributed computing, built around HDFS storage and MapReduce processing.

facts.text: Hadoop's core is a storage part, the Hadoop Distributed File System, and a processing part that implements the MapReduce programming model.
Hadoop splits files into large blocks spread across the cluster, then ships packaged code to the nodes so they process in parallel the data they hold, which is data locality.
This lets a dataset be processed faster and more efficiently than on a conventional supercomputer architecture that moves data over high-speed networking from a parallel file system.
The base framework has Hadoop Common, HDFS, YARN (introduced in 2012) for cluster resources and scheduling, and MapReduce; Hadoop Ozone, an object store, came in 2020.
Hadoop's MapReduce and HDFS components were inspired by Google's papers on MapReduce and the Google File System.
Hadoop could in theory serve any batch-oriented, very data-intensive workload that benefits from parallel processing; it is not for real-time work but can complement real-time systems.
Hadoop 3 allows multiple name nodes, which removes the single point of failure of Hadoop 2's one namenode, and uses erasure coding to decrease storage overhead.
Yahoo's Search Webmap, a Hadoop application on a Linux cluster of more than 10,000 cores, produced data used in every Yahoo! web search query.

entries.title: HDFS architecture: one NameNode, many DataNodes
entries.article: Apache Hadoop#Architecture > File systems > Hadoop distributed file system

definition.text: HDFS is Hadoop's distributed, scalable file system that stores large files across many machines, with one NameNode tracking metadata and many DataNodes storing blocks.

facts.text: The NameNode tracks files and holds metadata: the number of blocks, which DataNodes store them and where replicas live; it talks directly to clients, while DataNodes store the blocks.
HDFS gets reliability by replicating data across hosts, so it theoretically needs no RAID; with the default replication value 3, two copies sit on one rack and one on a different rack.
Rack-aware replication keeps data available if a rack loses power or a switch fails.
Each DataNode sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds; after 2 minutes without one, the NameNode treats the node as dead and starts replicating its blocks onto other DataNodes.
The secondary namenode is not a failover backup: it checkpoints the primary's directory information so a failed primary can restart without replaying the whole journal of file-system actions.
The single NameNode holds all metadata and can become a bottleneck with many small files; HDFS Federation allows multiple namespaces served by separate namenodes.
HDFS gives up full POSIX compliance for higher data throughput and non-POSIX operations such as Append, and it suits mostly immutable files rather than concurrent writes.

entries.title: Apache HBase: Bigtable on top of Hadoop

definition.text: HBase is an open-source non-relational distributed database modeled after Google's Bigtable and written in Java.

facts.text: It runs on top of HDFS as part of Apache Hadoop, giving Bigtable-like capabilities for Hadoop: a fault-tolerant way to store large quantities of sparse data, with fast reads and writes on large datasets at high throughput.

It is a wide-column store with compression, in-memory operation and Bloom filters per column, as in the Bigtable paper. Tables can feed MapReduce jobs and are reached through the Java API or REST, Avro or Thrift gateways.
HBase is not a direct replacement for a classic SQL database and has no SQL of its own; Apache Phoenix adds a SQL layer with a JDBC driver.
In terms of the CAP theorem HBase is a CP system, and like Bigtable it is rated PC/EC under PACELC.

entries.title: The Cassandra data model: keyspaces, tables and partition keys

definition.text: Cassandra stores data in keyspaces of tables whose rows are found by a partition key and may each have different columns.

facts.text: Data is organized as keyspace, table, then row; a keyspace is like a database and defines the replication strategy, so replication is set at the keyspace level.
Each row is identified by a primary key whose first component is the partition key; within a partition, rows are clustered by the remaining key columns.
Rows in one table can have different columns, and tables can be created, dropped or altered at run-time without blocking updates and queries.
Each column carries timestamp metadata used to resolve write conflicts by last write wins, and the data model is denormalized rather than joined.

entries.text: A Cassandra table is not as rigid as a relational one: rows in the same table can have different columns. Data is organized as keyspace, table, then row. A keyspace is like a database and sets the replication strategy. Each row is identified by a primary key whose first component is the partition key, and rows within a partition are clustered by the remaining key columns. Tables can be created, dropped or altered at run-time without blocking updates and queries. Each column carries timestamp metadata used to resolve write conflicts by last write wins, and the model is denormalized rather than joined.

entries.title: Cassandra gossip and failure handling: every node judges its peers

definition.text: Cassandra nodes spread cluster state by peer-to-peer gossip and each node detects failed peers on its own.

facts.text: Nodes routinely gossip cluster state, such as node bootstrap times and logical clock values, and use the clock values to ignore outdated state.
A few seed nodes are guaranteed gossip contact points, which removes single points of failure while keeping cluster-wide knowledge consistent.
Each node judges the availability of others with the Phi Accrual Failure Detector; a node that fails to respond is convicted and removed from writes, but can rejoin when heartbeats resume.
With hinted handoff, the coordinator stores a write meant for an offline node as a hint and forwards it when the node returns; nodes leave permanently only by explicit decommissioning or rebuilding.

entries.title: Cassandra's write and read path: commit log, Memtable, SSTable

definition.text: Cassandra writes append to a commit log and an in-memory Memtable, which later flushes to immutable SSTables.

facts.text: Cassandra uses a log-structured merge tree index to optimize write throughput, unlike the B-tree indexes most databases use.
A write goes to the commit log, a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and to the Memtable, an in-memory structure sorted by primary key.
When the Memtable reaches size or time thresholds it flushes to an SSTable, an immutable file; reads check the Memtable, then search SSTables from newest to oldest using bloom filters.
Every change adds a new entry and deletes use tombstones, which can slow delete-heavy workloads; compaction merges SSTables to cut storage, drop tombstoned rows and speed reads.

entries.title: ScyllaDB: a Cassandra-compatible rewrite in C++

definition.text: ScyllaDB is a source-available distributed NoSQL wide-column data store designed to be compatible with Apache Cassandra while reaching significantly higher throughput and lower latency.

facts.text: It speaks Cassandra's CQL protocol and reads its SSTable files, and also implements the Amazon DynamoDB API, but it is a complete rewrite in C++20 using the Seastar asynchronous library rather than threads and shared memory.
Each node is sharded per CPU core: each core handles a different subset of data, cores share nothing and communicate explicitly, which the authors say scales well with core count on NUMA machines.
The authors claim up to 2 million requests per second on one machine and a cluster matching a Cassandra cluster 10 times its size; independent tests sometimes measured only about 2x.
It is an AP database like Cassandra, uses Paxos for lightweight transactions, and uses Raft for metadata such as schema and topology changes.

entries.title: The Bigtable data model: a sorted map with timestamps

definition.text: Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map that maps a row key, a column key and a timestamp to a byte array.

facts.text: It maps two arbitrary strings, a row key and a column key, plus a timestamp, a three-dimensional mapping, to an arbitrary byte array.
It is not a relational database, is a prototypical wide-column store, and gives clients dynamic control over data layout and format.
Each cell can hold zero or more timestamped versions of its data, and timestamps allow both versioning and garbage collection of expired data.
Google's copy of the web fits one table: the row key is a domain-reversed URL, columns describe page properties, and the page column keeps versions stamped by fetch time.

entries.title: Hadoop job scheduling and YARN: from JobTracker to resource manager
entries.article: Apache Hadoop#Architecture > JobTracker and TaskTracker: the MapReduce engine

definition.text: In first-generation Hadoop a JobTracker hands MapReduce work to TaskTrackers close to the data, and YARN later replaced this engine.

facts.text: Clients submit MapReduce jobs to one JobTracker, which pushes work to available TaskTracker nodes and tries to keep work as close to the data as possible.

With a rack-aware file system, work that cannot run on the node holding the data goes to a node in the same rack, which reduces traffic on the main backbone network; a failed TaskTracker's work is rescheduled.
Hadoop schedules by FIFO with 5 priorities by default; the fair scheduler gives pools a guaranteed minimum share, and the capacity scheduler gives queues a fraction of total capacity.
YARN, the biggest change in Hadoop 2, replaced the MapReduce engine: a resource manager does job tracking and resource allocation, and an application master monitors execution of each application.

entries.title: MapReduce dataflow: from input splits to the shuffle

definition.text: A MapReduce job flows through an input reader, map, partition, shuffle, sort, reduce and output writer.

facts.text: The input reader cuts input from stable storage, typically a distributed file system, into splits of typically 64 MB to 128 MB, one per Map call; map turns each key/value pair into zero or more output pairs.
A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers; it should spread data roughly uniformly, or the job waits on slow reducers.
Between map and reduce the data is shuffled across nodes, which can take longer than the computation itself; a Combiner function can reduce the data written to disk and sent over the network.
The framework calls Reduce once per unique key in sorted order; in word count, map emits each word with a count and reduce sums them, and the output writer saves the result to stable storage.

entries.title: Discord message storage: from MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB

definition.text: Discord moved its message storage from MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB as its data grew to trillions of messages.

facts.text: Discord's first version stored messages on a single MongoDB replica.
Around Nov 2015 MongoDB held 100 million messages and RAM could no longer hold the data and index, so latency became unpredictable and storage had to move.
Cassandra was chosen: in 2017 Discord ran 12 Cassandra nodes with billions of messages, and at the start of 2022 it ran 177 nodes with trillions.
By then Cassandra latency was unpredictable and maintenance operations had become too expensive to run.
Cassandra's LSM tree makes reads more expensive than writes, and many concurrent reads on a server with hundreds of users create hotspots.
Cluster maintenance such as compacting SSTables hurts performance, and garbage collection pauses cause significant latency spikes.
ScyllaDB is a Cassandra-compatible database written in C++.
Discord redesigned its architecture around a monolithic API, a data service written in Rust, and ScyllaDB-based storage.
The p99 read latency is 15ms on ScyllaDB against 40-125ms on Cassandra; the p99 write latency is 5ms against 5-70ms.

By then Cassandra had become a burden. Its latency was unpredictable, and maintenance operations had become too expensive to run. Cassandra's LSM tree makes reads more expensive than writes, and many concurrent reads on a server with hundreds of users create hotspots. Cluster maintenance such as compacting SSTables hurts performance, and garbage collection pauses cause significant latency spikes.

entries.title: Waiting for a reply versus carrying on

definition.text: In synchronous communication the sender waits for a reply, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting.

facts.text: Many widely known communications protocols operate synchronously; HTTP is the obvious example, where a user requests a web page and then waits for the reply.
Synchronous behaviour is not always appropriate: an application may need to notify another that an event occurred without waiting for a response.
In publish/subscribe an application publishes information for any number of clients to read, and the sender should not have to wait if a recipient has crashed.
Applications need not be exclusively one or the other: an interactive application can answer part of a request at once and queue other parts, such as billing, to be done later.
A subsystem that performs message queuing, or broadcast messaging, can improve the behaviour of the overall system in these situations.
Asynchronous behaviour can be layered over a synchronous request-response protocol, which is how some queue services work over HTTP, though the underlying protocol limits what they can offer.

entries.text: Ask a web server for a page and you wait until it answers. That is synchronous communication, the way HTTP works: the sender waits for a reply. In asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. Waiting is not always the right choice. An application may only need to tell another that an event occurred, and a sender should not stall because a recipient has crashed. Most applications mix the two: an interactive one can answer part of a request at once and queue other parts, such as billing, to be done later. A subsystem that performs message queuing, or broadcast messaging, can improve the whole system's behavior in these situations, and {{ref:sysd-msg-046}} shows how. It can even be layered over a synchronous request-response protocol, as some queue services do over HTTP. The underlying protocol then limits what they can offer.

entries.title: Four kinds of queue, from plain to double-ended

definition.text: A queue is a widely used data structure that takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other; common variants are FIFO, circular, priority and double-ended queues.

facts.text: A simple queue follows FIFO: a new element is inserted at the tail and an element is removed from the head, so emails for payment responses go out in the same order.
A circular queue, also called a circular buffer or ring buffer, links its last element to its first; LMAX's low-latency ring buffer, used by trading components, runs in memory.
Elements of a priority queue have predefined priorities, and the one with the highest or lowest priority is taken first; it is implemented with a max heap or min heap.
A deque, or double-ended queue, allows insertion and deletion at both head and tail, so it supports both FIFO and LIFO and can implement a stack.

entries.title: Message queues: leave it with the queue and move on

definition.text: A message queue is a software component, typically used for communication between processes or threads, that holds messages in a queue until the receiver takes them.

facts.text: Message queues implement asynchronous communication: the sending and receiving parties do not need to interact with the queue at the same time.
Messages placed onto the queue are stored until the recipient retrieves them.
The message queue paradigm is a sibling of the publisher/subscriber pattern and is typically one part of a larger message-oriented middleware system.

An administrator configures queue-manager or broker software and defines a named queue; an application registers a routine that listens for messages, and other applications connect and put messages onto the queue.
The queue manager stores the messages until a receiving application connects, then calls the registered routine, and the application processes the message.
Queues have implicit or explicit limits on the size of a single message and on the number of messages that may remain outstanding.
Queuing systems that connect different computer systems typically provide resilience functionality so that messages do not get lost when a system fails.
Queue software can be proprietary, open source or a mix, and runs either on private servers or as an external cloud message queuing service.

entries.title: Middleware that carries messages between systems

definition.text: Message-oriented middleware is software or hardware infrastructure that supports sending and receiving messages between distributed systems.

facts.text: It insulates application developers from the details of operating systems and network interfaces, so independently developed components on different platforms can interact.
RPC- and ORB-based middleware create tightly coupled components, where a caller waits for the called procedure to return; message-oriented systems allow loose coupling.
The sender calls the provider and carries on, confident the provider keeps the message until a receiver retrieves it; queues buffer for a busy or disconnected receiver, and most systems persist them.
Sender and receiver need not be online together, and if the receiver fails, senders continue unaffected as messages accumulate in the queue until it restarts.
The provider can store, route or transform messages in transit, so one application can send in its native format and several others each receive a copy in their own format.
The main disadvantage is an extra component, the message broker, which can reduce performance and reliability and make the system harder and costlier to maintain.
Asynchronous messaging fits poorly where a sender must wait for a reply, though most systems can group request and response into one pseudo-synchronous transaction.
A sender in a loosely coupled system can keep piling work on a recipient until its resources run out and it fails, so message flow must be monitored and adjusted.

entries.title: At most once, at least once, exactly once

definition.text: Delivery semantics describe how many times a message reaches its consumer: at most once, at least once, or exactly once.

facts.text: At-most-once delivery means a message is delivered not more than once: messages may be lost but are not redelivered.
At-most-once suits use cases such as monitoring metrics, where a small amount of data loss is acceptable.
At-least-once delivery loses no message but may deliver the same message several times.
At-least-once is usually good enough when duplication is not a big issue or the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key.
Most message brokers offer at-least-once delivery, so consumers will eventually see duplicates.
Exactly-once is the most difficult semantic to implement; it is friendly to users but costs a lot in performance and complexity.
Exactly-once matters for financial use cases such as payment, trading and accounting, especially when duplication is unacceptable and the downstream service does not support idempotency.

It is friendly to users but costs a lot in performance and complexity. It matters for financial use cases such as payment, trading and accounting, especially when duplication is unacceptable and the downstream service does not support Idempotency: making a repeated request safe.

entries.title: What a buffer between producers and consumers buys

definition.text: Message queues let a system scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures by putting a buffer between producers and consumers.

facts.text: Queues are used to manage requests in large-scale distributed systems, where writes that are predictably fast in small systems can take an almost non-deterministic amount of time.
Scalability: queues make it possible to scale where needed, and at peak load multiple instances of an application can add requests to the queue without risk of collision.
Decoupling: queues remove dependencies between components and simplify the implementation of decoupled applications.
Performance: endpoints that produce and consume messages interact with the queue, not each other, so producers can add requests without waiting for them to be processed.
Reliability: queues make data persistent and reduce the errors that happen when different parts of the system go offline.

entries.title: From closed vendor protocols to open standards

definition.text: Message queuing historically used closed proprietary protocols; open standards such as AMQP, STOMP and MQTT now exist for open source implementations.

facts.text: Message queuing has historically used proprietary, closed protocols, and Sun's JMS specification gave only a Java-only abstraction of a client API.

Three standards are used in open source queues: AMQP, a feature-rich protocol approved as ISO/IEC 19464 since April 2014; STOMP, a simple text-oriented protocol; and MQTT, a lightweight protocol especially for embedded devices.
AMQP and STOMP operate at the same level as HTTP, while MQTT operates at the level of TCP/IP.
Some proprietary implementations, such as Amazon's SQS, use HTTP because asynchronous behaviour can always be layered over request-response semantics, but they are constrained by that protocol.

entries.title: The broker that sits between sender and receiver

definition.text: A message broker is an intermediary program that translates messages between the messaging protocols of sender and receiver and validates, stores, routes and delivers them.

facts.text: A broker translates a message from the sender's formal messaging protocol to the receiver's, so services written in different languages or on different platforms can talk to each other.
Brokers act as intermediaries, so senders issue messages without knowing where the receivers are, whether they are active, or how many there are, which decouples processes and services.
A broker may manage a workload queue or message queue for multiple receivers, providing reliable storage, guaranteed message delivery and perhaps transaction management.
Brokers can route messages to one or more destinations, transform messages to another representation, and provide content and topic-based routing using the publish–subscribe pattern.
Brokers offer two basic message distribution patterns: point-to-point messaging, as in message queues, and publish-subscribe messaging, where producers publish to topics that consumers subscribe to.
Message brokers are generally based on one of two architectures: hub-and-spoke, where a central server provides integration services, or a message bus acting as a communication backbone.

entries.title: AMQP, the protocol that standardizes the bytes

definition.text: AMQP is an open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware.

facts.text: AMQP is a wire-level protocol: it describes the format of the bytes sent across the network, so any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS.

Its defining features are message orientation, queuing, routing (point-to-point and publish-and-subscribe), reliability and security; it is a binary protocol that assumes a reliable transport such as TCP.
AMQP provides flow-controlled messaging with at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery guarantees, plus authentication and encryption based on SASL and TLS.
Messages travel one way over a link using transfer frames; credit-based flow control keeps a receiver from being overwhelmed and lets a subscribing link pull messages when it wants them.

Every transferred message must eventually be settled, so sender and receiver agree on the transfer's state; this settlement is how the at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once guarantees are enforced.

The bare message the application created is immutable in transit, so end-to-end signing, encryption and integrity checks stay valid; intermediaries add annotations kept separate from it, and a header carries time to live, durability and priority.

Queues and topics are distribution nodes; AMQP codifies accept and reject outcomes, competing and non-competing consumers (the move and copy distribution modes), filters, and on-demand temporary nodes.

Version 1.0 focuses on the core features needed for Internet-scale interoperability and has less explicit routing than earlier versions; broker implementations include Apache Qpid, ActiveMQ, Solace and RabbitMQ 4.0.

entries.title: RabbitMQ: an Erlang broker that learned many protocols

definition.text: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker, written in Erlang, that originally implemented AMQP and supports other protocols through plug-ins.

facts.text: RabbitMQ originally implemented the Advanced Message Queuing Protocol and has been extended through a plug-in architecture to support STOMP, MQTT and other protocols.
Written in Erlang, the server is built on the Open Telecom Platform framework for clustering and failover.
Client libraries for the broker are available for all major programming languages.

Plug-ins include Shovel, which moves or copies messages from one broker to another; Federation, which shares messages between brokers at the exchange level; and Management, which monitors and controls brokers and clusters.
RabbitMQ uses Raft to implement durable, replicated FIFO queues.
System designs place jobs on a queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ, for example for notifications, video processing and extracting transactions from accounts.

entries.title: ActiveMQ: a Java broker that speaks many protocols

definition.text: Apache ActiveMQ is an open source message broker written in Java together with a full Java Message Service client.

entries.title: Choosing a queue's semantics: durability, expiry, filtering

definition.text: Queueing systems let you choose between several semantics, such as durability, time to live, filtering and delivery guarantees, that affect reliability and efficiency.

facts.text: Durability: messages may be kept in memory, written to disk, or even committed to a database when reliability calls for a more resource-intensive solution.
Queues or messages may have a time to live, and some systems filter data so a subscriber sees only messages matching pre-specified criteria.
Delivery policies decide whether a message must be delivered at least once or no more than once; routing policies decide which servers receive a message in a system with many queue servers.
Batching policies, the criteria for when a message counts as enqueued, and receipt notification for publishers all have substantial effects on transaction semantics, reliability and efficiency.

Routing policies decide which servers receive a message when there are many queue servers. Batching policies and receipt notification for publishers also have substantial effects on transaction semantics, reliability and efficiency.

entries.title: Queues that live inside the operating system

definition.text: Operating systems and applications provide message queues that exist only for that system, such as the UNIX SYS V and POSIX queues and the event queues of graphical interfaces.

facts.text: Many message queue implementations function internally within an operating system or an application, and such queues exist for the purposes of that system only.
UNIX has two common message queue implementations, one in the SYS V API and a later, distinct but similar one in POSIX.
In SYS V a blocking receive puts the caller to sleep until a message of the requested type is posted, while a non-blocking receive returns immediately to report that it failed.
Graphical user interfaces use a message queue, also called an event queue, to pass mouse, keyboard and timer events to the application, which removes them one at a time in an event loop.

entries.title: Amazon SQS: queuing over HTTP

definition.text: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a distributed message queuing service from Amazon.

facts.text: SQS is a distributed message queuing service that supports both unlimited queues and unlimited message traffic; messages can be of any type.
SQS provides queuing over HTTP; asynchronous behaviour can always be layered over request-response semantics, but such an implementation is constrained by the underlying protocol.
SQS FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group but do not necessarily guarantee ordered delivery across retries or failures.
Message bodies are limited to 256KB; a larger message can be split into segments, or its data can be stored in Amazon S3 or DynamoDB with only a pointer sent in the SQS message.

entries.title: Dead letter queues for messages that will not go through

definition.text: A dead letter queue is a place where a messaging system stores messages that it cannot or should not deliver.

facts.text: Depending on the implementation, a message goes to the dead letter queue if its queue does not exist, its time to live expires, another queue exchange rejects it, or it was read and rejected too many times.
Setting such messages aside lets the main queue keep moving: they can be inspected later without blocking processing or spending CPU cycles on a message that may never be consumed successfully.
Routing failed messages to a dead letter queue enables analysis of common fault patterns and potential software problems.
A consumer that considers a message invalid can forward it to an Invalid Message Channel, which separates application-level faults from delivery failures.
Managing dead letter queues typically involves monitoring and alerting, and organizations may add specialized handlers for automated remediation or manual processing of the messages.

In an SQS FIFO queue, later messages in a message group wait until the preceding one is processed or moved to the dead-letter queue; once there it is no longer retried, leaving a gap, and the rest continue in order.
Many systems offer dead letter queues, including Amazon SQS and EventBridge, Apache ActiveMQ, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ and Apache Pulsar.

entries.title: Seven features most message queues offer

definition.text: Message queues commonly offer delayed delivery, delivery guarantees, dead-letter queues, ordering, poison pills, authentication and task queues.

facts.text: Many queues support setting a specific delivery time for a message, and a delay queue gives all messages a common delay.
Queues may store multiple copies for redundancy and resend messages after failures to deliver at least once, while FIFO queues filter out duplicates automatically to deliver exactly once.
A dead-letter queue receives messages other queues cannot process successfully, so they can be inspected later without blocking processing or wasting CPU on a message that may never succeed.
Most queues give best-effort ordering, so messages are generally delivered in the order sent and at least once; in a FIFO queue the oldest entry, the head, is processed first.
Poison pills are special messages that can be received but not processed; they signal a consumer to end its work, much like closing a socket in a client/server model.
Queues authenticate applications that try to access them, which allows messages to be encrypted over the network and in the queue itself.
Task queues receive tasks and their data, run them and deliver the results, can support scheduling, and can run computationally intensive jobs in the background.

entries.title: How to choose a message queue

definition.text: Choose a message queue by comparing speed, scalability, reliability, durability, ease of use, ecosystem, integration and protocol support.

facts.text: Compare speed, scalability, reliability (messages are not lost), durability (messages kept safe over time), ease of setup and management, ecosystem tools, integration with other software, and the protocols and languages supported.

Decide the pattern first: queues give one-to-one point-to-point delivery and pub/sub lets many consumers subscribe to a topic; brokers can offer both, while event streaming platforms offer only pub/sub.

Event streaming platforms scale more and are built for high volumes, but cannot guarantee delivery or track which consumers received messages, and offer fewer fault-tolerance features and less routing.

Match the delivery guarantee to the need: most brokers offer at-least-once, so consumers see duplicates, and exactly-once costs performance and complexity; MQTT orders its levels by increasing overhead.
Check the ordering guarantee: most queues give best-effort ordering, SQS FIFO orders only within a message group, and MQTT only within one client session on one topic.

Protocol matters for interoperability: JMS is an API, so JMS systems from different vendors are not interoperable, while AMQP is wire-level so compliant software interoperates; MQTT targets constrained devices.
Look for failure handling and limits: a dead-letter queue sets unprocessable messages aside, and SQS caps message bodies at 256KB, with larger payloads stored elsewhere and referenced by pointer.
Check availability beyond one node: MQTT leaves broker-to-broker communication to implementations, and ActiveMQ offers locking-based failover, ZooKeeper replication and a Network of Brokers.

Most queues give best-effort ordering, while SQS FIFO orders only within a message group. Protocol matters too. JMS is an API, so systems from different vendors are not interoperable, while AMQP is wire-level, so compliant software interoperates. Finally, look at limits and failure handling: a dead-letter queue sets unprocessable messages aside, and SQS caps message bodies at 256KB.

entries.title: The enterprise service bus, and why it fell out of favor

definition.text: An enterprise service bus is an architectural pattern in which a centralized software component performs integrations between applications.

facts.text: An ESB performs data-model transformations, handles connectivity, routes messages, converts communication protocols and may manage the composition of multiple requests, exposing these integrations as reusable service interfaces.
In theory a centralized ESB can standardize and simplify communication and integration across the enterprise, letting components scale independently and fail without affecting others.
In many organizations the ESB came to be seen as a bottleneck: a single point of failure can bring down all communications, and a change to one integration can destabilize others.
Message brokers are a lightweight alternative to ESBs that offer inter-service communication at lower cost and suit microservices architectures, as ESBs have fallen out of favor.

entries.title: Locks, waiting and non-blocking queues

definition.text: A blocking queue algorithm uses locks so a waiting thread is suspended, while a non-blocking algorithm rejects access immediately instead of making the thread wait.

facts.text: A blocking algorithm uses locks: if Thread A is suspended while holding the lock, Thread B may wait for arbitrarily long periods and can starve.
A non-blocking algorithm notifies Thread B that access is rejected rather than blocking it until the lock is released, though other threads may still starve due to rejections.
Wait-free means all threads complete their tasks within a finite number of steps, which is non-blocking plus starvation-free.
A non-blocking queue can be implemented with compare and swap (CAS), and with no thread suspension and no lock waiting, latency drops and deadlock cannot occur.

entries.title: A job's trip through a queue

definition.text: A producer puts a job on the queue and a consumer later takes it off, processes it and reports completion.

facts.text: A producer publishes a job to the queue and then notifies the user of the job status.
A consumer picks up the job from the queue, processes it, then signals that the job is complete.
Messages are stored in the queue until they are processed and deleted.
Each message is processed only once by a single consumer.

entries.title: Backpressure: stop a backlog from slowing everything

definition.text: Backpressure limits the size of a queue so that a growing backlog does not slow down the jobs already in it.

facts.text: If a queue grows beyond memory, the result is cache misses, disk reads and even slower performance.
Backpressure limits the queue size, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for jobs already in the queue.
Once the queue fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code to try again later.
Clients can retry the request at a later time, perhaps with an exponential backoff strategy.

entries.title: Push or pull: who starts the delivery

definition.text: Consumers either pull messages by repeatedly asking the queue for new ones, or have the queue push each message to them when it arrives.

facts.text: Most message queues provide both push and pull options for retrieving messages.
Pull means continuously querying the queue for new messages, and push means a consumer is notified when a message is available.
Long-polling allows pulls to wait a specified amount of time for new messages to arrive.
Pub/sub topics push notifications instantly, which eliminates the need for consumers to poll for new information.

entries.title: Six named designs for services that exchange messages

definition.text: Cloud messaging patterns are named designs for how services exchange messages, such as asynchronous request-reply, claim check, saga and competing consumers.

facts.text: Asynchronous request-reply decouples backend processing from clients for long-running tasks, with the API answering HTTP 202 (Accepted) to acknowledge the request.
Publisher-subscriber decouples senders from consumers and avoids blocking the sender to wait for a response.
Claim check handles large messages by storing the whole payload in a database and transmitting only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload.
Priority queue lets requests with a higher priority be received and processed more quickly than those with a lower priority.
Saga manages data consistency across services that each own a database, without distributed transactions, which are difficult to scale and can hurt performance.
Competing consumers lets multiple concurrent consumers process messages from the same channel without complex coordination, but cannot guarantee message ordering.

entries.title: Publish–subscribe: speak to a topic, not to a person

definition.text: Publish–subscribe is a messaging pattern in which publishers send messages to topics without knowing the receivers, and subscribers receive only the topics they asked for.

facts.text: Publishers categorize messages into classes, or topics, and send them without needing to know which components will receive them.
Subscribers express interest in one or more classes and receive only messages in those classes, without needing to know who the publishers are.
The pattern decouples the components that produce messages from those that consume them and supports asynchronous, many-to-many communication.
A message published to a topic is pushed immediately to all subscribers, which often perform different functions and can each act on the message in parallel.
Pub/sub is contrasted with queue-based and point-to-point messaging, where producers send directly to consumers; JMS, Apache Kafka and MQTT support both the pub/sub and queue-based models.
It gives greater network scalability and more dynamic topologies, but can make it harder to modify the publisher's logic or the structure of the published data.
Compared with synchronous patterns such as RPC, pub/sub gives the highest decoupling, but it can lead to semantic or format coupling that makes systems entangled or brittle over time.
Pub/sub is now distinguished from the observer pattern by its emphasis on decoupling, asynchronous messaging and broker-mediated communication across a distributed system.

entries.title: MQTT: publish-subscribe for tiny devices

definition.text: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe network protocol for machine-to-machine messaging.

facts.text: MQTT suits devices with limited resources or network bandwidth, such as Internet of things sensors; it runs over an ordered, lossless transport, typically TCP/IP, and despite its name provides publish-subscribe messaging with no queues.

Clients connect to a broker, which receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribers by topic; publishers need no knowledge of subscribers, so devices and server applications stay decoupled.
A broker discards a message with no current subscribers unless it is flagged retained; it keeps one retained message per topic and delivers it to each new subscriber immediately.
A publisher can register a default message at connect time that the broker sends to subscribers if it detects an unexpected disconnect.

Each connection chooses a quality of service in increasing order of overhead: at most once (fire and forget), at least once (acknowledged, retried) or exactly once (two-level handshake); it applies between MQTT sender and receiver, not to TCP.
With persistent sessions the broker stores each client's connection info, subscriptions and any QoS 1 or 2 messages while the device goes on and off.

The specification covers only a client talking to one broker; larger deployments use bridging, where a broker connects to another as a client, or clustering, where broker nodes share subscription and session state as one logical broker.

MQTT guarantees ordering only within one client session on one topic, so messages from independent clients can arrive out of order; mitigations are debounce windows, polling and sequence numbers, each with trade-offs.

entries.title: Why publish–subscribe scales and stays flexible

definition.text: Publish–subscribe lets publishers and subscribers work independently, avoids polling, and makes it easy to add or remove subscribers.

facts.text: Publishers are loosely coupled to subscribers and need not know they exist; with the topic as the focus, each side stays ignorant of system topology and operates independently of the other.
Many pub/sub systems also decouple publishers and subscribers in time, unlike the client-server paradigm, where neither side can post or receive while the other is not running.
Push-based delivery through topics removes the need for consumers to poll for updates, which gives faster response time and lower delivery latency.
A publisher simply posts to a topic instead of keeping a roster of peers, and subscribers can change, upgrade, multiply or disappear while the system adjusts dynamically.

Publishers and subscribers can be developed and scaled independently, and pub/sub can scale better than client-server through parallel operation, message caching and tree-based or network-based routing.
Redundant subscribers can assure delivery with minimal added complexity: an exact duplicate of a logging subscriber can be added without any impact on other equipment.

Internet-wide RSS and Atom syndication shows pub/sub scaling beyond a single data center, accepting higher latency and no delivery guarantees so a low-end web server can reach millions of subscribers.

entries.title: The observer pattern, publish–subscribe's in-process cousin

definition.text: In the observer pattern a subject keeps a list of observers and automatically notifies them of state changes, typically by calling one of their methods.

facts.text: It sets up a one-to-many dependency without tight coupling: observers register and unregister themselves with the subject, which only needs to know they implement an update operation.
Subject and observers hold direct references with no intermediary broker, and notification is typically synchronous, so the pattern suits in-process uses such as GUI toolkits.

Publish-subscribe adds a broker so publishers and subscribers are unaware of each other; it scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.
The pattern deliberately omits unsubscription, filtering, delivery guarantees and message logging, which robust message queuing systems provide.

entries.title: NATS: a plain pub/sub server that can add persistence

definition.text: NATS is an open-source messaging system under the stewardship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

facts.text: The NATS server is written in Go, with client libraries for dozens of languages; its core design principles are performance, scalability and ease of use.

Core NATS is the publish-subscribe server; JetStream is an optional built-in persistence layer adding streaming, queues, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, replay, flow control and a key/value store.
JetStream replaced the older STAN (NATS Streaming) approach and uses the Raft consensus algorithm for cluster management and data replication.

entries.title: Where publish–subscribe hurts

definition.text: The main drawbacks of publish–subscribe come from decoupling: delivery is hard to guarantee, and large systems can become unstable.

facts.text: The most serious problems are a side-effect of decoupling, and a broker that stops delivering after a specified time cannot guarantee delivery, so assured delivery needs tighter coupling such as receipt messages from subscribers.
A publisher may assume a subscriber is listening when it is not, and will not necessarily be told if a subscriber such as a logger fails.
Pub/sub scales well for small networks with low message volume, but as nodes and messages grow, instabilities such as load surges and slowdowns limit the maximum scalability.
Brokers can be overloaded tracking subscriptions or fooled into notifying the wrong client, and encryption cannot stop authorized publishers from introducing damaging messages.

entries.title: Filtering: how a subscriber gets only what it wants

definition.text: Filtering is how a pub/sub system selects the messages a subscriber receives, by topic, by content, or by both.

facts.text: In pub/sub systems subscribers typically receive only a subset of messages, and the process of selecting the relevant ones is called filtering.
Topic-based filtering publishes messages to named topics or channels, and subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it.
Content-based filtering lets subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and messages are delivered only if they match.
Hybrid systems categorize messages by topic and let subscribers apply content-based filters to the messages within those topics.

entries.title: With or without a broker in the middle

definition.text: Pub/sub systems connect publishers and subscribers either through a central broker or event bus, or directly in a brokerless arrangement.

facts.text: In most pub/sub systems publishers and subscribers communicate through a central intermediary such as a message broker or event bus.

Brokerless pub/sub systems let publishers and subscribers discover each other and exchange messages directly; the Data Distribution Service middleware uses IP multicast and metadata sharing to set up communication paths.

entries.title: Message broker or event streaming platform

definition.text: Message brokers support several messaging patterns with delivery tracking, while event streaming platforms offer pub/sub distribution of stored topic streams at higher scale.

facts.text: Message brokers can support two or more messaging patterns, including message queues and pub/sub, while event streaming platforms only offer pub/sub-style distribution.
Event streaming platforms are designed for high volumes of messages, are readily scalable, and order streams of records into topics stored for a predetermined amount of time.
Unlike message brokers, event streaming platforms cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received the messages.
Event streaming platforms offer more scalability than brokers but fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending, and more limited routing and queueing capabilities.

entries.title: One consumer or every subscriber

definition.text: A message queue gives each message to one consumer, while publish–subscribe delivers each message to every subscriber of a topic.

facts.text: In a message queue each message is processed only once by a single consumer, while in pub/sub all subscribers to the topic receive every message broadcast.
Queues hold messages until they are retrieved, whereas topics transfer messages with little or no queuing and push them out immediately to all subscribers.
With a message queue the sender often knows the destination it sends to, while in pub/sub the publisher need not know who uses its information and subscribers need not know where it comes from.
Most messaging systems support both models in their API, for example the Java Message Service.

entries.title: Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read

definition.text: Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream-processing platform that keeps messages in a durable log so many consumers can read them.

facts.text: Kafka is an open-source distributed event store and stream-processing platform, written in Java and Scala.
The project aims to provide a unified, high-throughput, low-latency platform for handling real-time data feeds.
Kafka is a distributed log-based messaging system that guarantees ordering within individual partitions rather than across the entire topic.
Unlike queue-based systems, Kafka retains messages in a durable, append-only log until they expire, so multiple consumers can read at different offsets and pull at their own pace.
Kafka can handle multiple producers and consumers while providing disk-based data retention and high scalability.
Kafka Connect moves data in and out of external systems, and the Kafka Streams libraries support stream-processing applications.
Kafka was originally built for massive log processing and is used for log analysis, data streaming such as recommendations, system monitoring and alerting, and change data capture.
Kafka Raft (KRaft) uses the Raft algorithm for metadata management.

entries.title: Batch processing: jobs that run unattended

definition.text: Batch processing is the running of a software job in an automated and unattended way.

facts.text: A user schedules a job and a processing system runs it, typically at a configured time of day, when an event occurs or when computer resources are available.
Batch processing collects data and processes it all at once, as in daily billing, while stream processing handles data in real time, as in fraud detection.

Batch applications stay critical because many business processes suit them and online systems are not optimized for high-volume repetitive tasks; they update information at day's end, generate reports and print documents by business deadlines.
If a job needs only one input at a time, flow processing lowers latency per input; if it needs totals over all records, the whole batch must finish before any result is usable.

The extract, transform, load step that fills a data warehouse is inherently batch in most implementations; an e-commerce site might refresh its recommendation model from an hourly batch of transactions to save computational resources.

A job queue holds the jobs the scheduler may run; several queues can separate jobs by priority, estimated execution time or resource needs, sharing resources, shifting work to quiet times and keeping expensive machines busy.
A batch window is a period of less-intensive online activity in which batch jobs can run without interfering with interactive systems; it shrank as demands for online uptime grew.
Batch size is the number of work units handled in one batch operation, such as lines loaded before a database commit or messages dequeued from a queue.

entries.title: Stream processing, where the data never ends

definition.text: Stream processing is a programming paradigm that treats streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation.

facts.text: Stream processing, also called event stream processing or distributed stream processing, views streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation.
It encompasses dataflow programming, reactive programming and distributed data processing.
Data is treated as an unbounded, continuous sequence of elements rather than a static dataset.
Given a stream, a series of operations called kernel functions is applied to each element, and uniform streaming, where one kernel function is applied to all elements, is typical.
The program defines a dataflow sequence and the execution environment applies the kernel automatically as new elements arrive; kernels can also do aggregation windows or stateful modifications.

The paradigm simplifies parallelism by restricting the kinds of parallel computation allowed, and it exploits data parallelism: the same function applied to all records lets many records be processed simultaneously.

It sacrifices some flexibility for easier, faster and more efficient execution, working well for data-centric workloads but less well for general-purpose processing with random data access, such as databases.
Batch processing collects data and processes it all at once, as in daily billing, while stream processing handles data in real time, as in fraud detection.

entries.title: Apache Spark: analytics without the trips to disk

definition.text: Apache Spark is an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing.

facts.text: Spark provides an interface for programming clusters with implicit data parallelism and fault tolerance, and requires a cluster manager (standalone, YARN, Mesos or Kubernetes) and a distributed storage system such as HDFS or Amazon S3.

Its foundation is the resilient distributed dataset (RDD), a read-only multiset spread over a cluster and kept fault-tolerant; RDDs are immutable, operations are lazy, and lost data is rebuilt from each RDD's lineage.

Spark was built because MapReduce forces a linear dataflow that reads from disk and writes results to disk; RDDs suit iterative algorithms and interactive analysis, cutting latency by orders of magnitude versus Hadoop MapReduce.
Spark manages the workflow as a directed acyclic graph in which nodes are RDDs and edges are the operations on them.
Spark SQL adds DataFrames for structured and semi-structured data plus SQL support; the DataFrame and Dataset APIs sit on top of the RDD, which still underlies the Dataset API.

Streaming ingests data in micro-batches, so batch code can be reused for streaming and eases a lambda architecture, at a latency penalty equal to the micro-batch duration; Storm and Flink process event by event.
Libraries on Spark Core include MLlib for distributed machine learning and GraphX for graph processing; because RDDs are immutable, GraphX is unsuitable for graphs that must be updated.

entries.title: Topics, partitions, brokers and consumer groups

definition.text: Kafka organizes messages into topics split into partitions, written by producers, read by consumer groups and stored on a cluster of brokers.

facts.text: The message is the basic unit of data in Kafka, like a record in a table consisting of headers, a key and a value.
Every message goes to a topic, which is like a folder on a computer, and topics have multiple partitions.
Producers create new messages, batch them, send them to a topic, and balance messages across the partitions.
Consumers work together as a consumer group to read messages from the broker.
A Kafka cluster consists of several brokers, and each partition is replicated across multiple brokers to ensure high availability and redundancy.
The partition-based design enables fault isolation and parallel processing: a consumer that delays committing an offset stalls only its own partition while other partitions remain unaffected.

In 2025 Kafka added share groups as an alternative to consumer groups, giving queue-like semantics with individual acknowledgment and allowing more consumers than partitions, where consumer groups assign each partition exclusively.

entries.title: How Kafka can still lose a message

definition.text: Kafka can lose messages at the producer, the broker or the consumer unless acknowledgments, replicas and offset commits are configured carefully.

facts.text: Many developers believe Kafka by design guarantees no message loss, but its architecture and configuration decide how and when it might lose messages.
producer.send() does not send directly to the broker: the application thread puts the message in a record accumulator, and a separate sender (I/O) thread sends it.
The producer needs proper acks and retries settings to make sure messages reach the broker.
A healthy broker cluster should not lose messages, but messages are usually flushed to disk asynchronously for higher I/O throughput, so an instance that goes down before the flush loses them.
Replicas must be properly configured to hold a valid copy of the data, because determinism in data synchronization is important.
Auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so if the consumer goes down mid-processing, some records may never be processed.
A good practice is to combine asynchronous commits in the processing loop for higher throughput with synchronous commits in exception handling so the last offset is always committed.
Kafka uses manual offset management, giving consumers control over retries and failure handling.

entries.title: Kafka Streams: stream processing as a Java library

definition.text: Kafka Streams is a Java library for building stateful, scalable and fault-tolerant stream-processing applications on top of Kafka.

facts.text: Kafka Streams is a stream-processing library written in Java for stateful stream-processing applications that are scalable, elastic and fully fault-tolerant.

Its main API is a domain-specific language with high-level operators such as filter, map, grouping, windowing, aggregation, joins and tables; the lower-level Processor API implements custom operators and can be mixed with it.
For stateful processing it keeps local operator state in RocksDB, which can write to disk so the state can be larger than main memory.
For fault tolerance all updates to local state stores are also written to a topic in the Kafka cluster, so state can be recreated by reading those topics back into RocksDB.

entries.title: Complex event processing: spotting the pattern in the events

definition.text: Complex event processing infers higher-level events from combinations of simpler events in streams as they arrive.

facts.text: Complex event processing is a set of techniques for processing real-time events and extracting information from event streams as they arrive, to identify meaningful events such as opportunities or threats and respond quickly.

A complex or composite event is inferred from constituent events: blowOutTire, zeroSpeed and driverLeftSeat in a short time signal an accident, though no single measurement shows it; bells, a tuxedo, a gown and rice signal a wedding.

It relies on techniques such as detecting causality, membership or timing relationships between events, and on continuous SQL queries over timestamps and windows, such as joining stock orders to trades matched within one second.
Typical uses are stock trading systems, credit-card fraud detection, business activity monitoring, security monitoring and matching patterns across dense Internet of things sensor streams.

A complex or composite event is inferred from simpler constituent events, as bells, a tuxedo, a gown and rice signal a wedding. The techniques include detecting causality, membership or timing relationships between events. They also include continuous SQL queries over timestamps and windows, such as joining stock orders to trades matched within one second. Typical uses are stock trading and credit-card fraud detection.

entries.title: Change data capture: copying database changes elsewhere

definition.text: Change data capture identifies and captures the changes made to data in a database so they can be replicated and synced to other systems.

facts.text: CDC is a set of design patterns for determining and tracking data that changed, an approach to data integration based on identifying, capturing and delivering changes made to enterprise data sources.
Constant data changes leave databases, data lakes and data warehouses out of sync, and CDC replicates and syncs data across multiple systems to overcome this.
In CDC the source is the system with data believed to have changed, and the target is the system that needs to act on the changed data.
A CDC tool monitors the database transaction logs through a source connector to capture inserts, updates and deletes.

Captured changes are transformed, published to a message queue and propagated to targets such as data warehouses, analytics platforms and distributed caches like Redis, where a sink connector consumes the log and updates the targets in real time.
A popular CDC solution uses Debezium with Kafka Connect to stream changes from source to target with Kafka as the broker, and Debezium has connectors for MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and more.
In the push model the source creates a snapshot of changes and delivers rows downstream; in the pull model the downstream target requests the data from the source.

entries.title: Three ways to detect that a row has changed

definition.text: CDC can detect changes with timestamp, version-number or status columns, with triggers that log events to a queue table, or by reading the database transaction log.

facts.text: With a timestamp column, any row stamped more recently than the last capture is considered changed.
With version numbers, changed rows are marked with a version; at capture all data with the latest version is considered changed, and the reference table then gets a new version number.
A status column can mark a row as changed, or can complement the other methods by showing that a row with a new version or later date should not yet be updated on the target.
Using time, version and status together is a particularly powerful mechanism, because the three elements are not redundant.
With triggers, events on the transactional table are logged into a queue table that can later be played back to replicate the data to a target.
Transaction-log based CDC has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed.
Reading transaction logs is hard because no standard exists for their format, most databases do not document it, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

entries.title: Three execution models for stream engines
entries.article: Stream processing#Distributed and cloud-scale execution ecosystems

definition.text: Distributed stream processing engines are grouped by execution model into native continuous engines, micro-batch engines and distributed logging fabrics.

facts.text: Native continuous engines process elements individually as they arrive, optimizing for sub-second, real-time latencies.

Apache Storm is a native low-latency real-time computation system; Apache Flink treats batch computing as a specialized subset of continuous streaming; Apache Samza is a stateful engine built over Apache Kafka.
Micro-batch engines collect incoming elements into small time windows to achieve high-throughput stream semantics; Apache Spark Streaming processes live data in small discrete chunks.
Distributed logging fabrics, such as Apache Kafka, serve as the persistent, append-only transport layer, and managed services such as AWS Kinesis and Google Cloud Dataflow run streams in the cloud.

entries.title: Apache Flink: one engine for batches and streams

definition.text: Apache Flink is an open-source, unified stream-processing and batch-processing framework.

facts.text: Flink's core is a distributed streaming dataflow engine; its pipelined runtime executes both batch and stream programs, processing events one at a time on finite and infinite datasets.
A Flink dataflow starts at sources such as a message queue or file system, applies any number of transformations, and ends at sinks; streams form a directed acyclic graph that can branch and merge.
It provides a high-throughput, low-latency engine with event-time processing and state management, running data-parallel and pipelined across a cluster.

Checkpoints are automatic asynchronous snapshots of application state and source stream position; after a failure Flink resumes from the last completed checkpoint, giving exactly-once state semantics within an application.
Checkpointing has hooks for external systems, such as opening and committing database transactions, so state changes outside Flink can take part.

Savepoints are manually triggered checkpoints: a user can stop a program and resume it from the same state and stream position, which allows updates without losing state and, since Flink 1.2, a change of parallelism.
The DataStream API handles bounded or unbounded streams, and the Table API and SQL offer relational operators on streams and batches; the DataSet API for bounded data is deprecated as of Flink 2.0.
Flink has no storage system of its own; it provides source and sink connectors to systems such as Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, HDFS, Apache Cassandra and Elasticsearch.

entries.title: Why Kafka is fast: sequential writes and zero copy

definition.text: Kafka is fast mainly because it relies on sequential disk I/O and the zero-copy principle for sending data to consumers.

facts.text: Two design decisions carry the most weight in Kafka's performance: its reliance on sequential I/O and its focus on efficiency through the zero-copy principle.
Kafka's message-set abstraction groups messages, which leads to larger network packets and larger sequential disk operations and turns a bursty stream of random message writes into linear writes.
Without zero copy, data is loaded from disk to the OS cache, copied to the Kafka application, copied to the socket buffer, then copied to the network card.
With zero copy, the OS cache copies the data directly to the network card via the sendfile() command, saving multiple copies between the application and kernel contexts.

entries.title: Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command

definition.text: A way of building a system in which parts communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously.

facts.text: An event is a data point or significant change in state, such as a car going from for sale to sold; it only announces the change and does not say what should happen next.
The publisher is unaware of who consumes an event, and the consumers are unaware of each other.
An event-driven system has three key components: producers publish events to a router, routers filter events and push them to consumers, and consumers use events to reflect changes in the system.
The style achieves loose coupling between services, which decouples producers from consumers and makes it easy to add new consumers.
Event-driven systems are highly scalable and distributed, and building on events simplifies horizontal scaling and makes systems more resilient to failure.
Challenges include guaranteed delivery, difficult error handling, and exactly-once, in-order processing of events; such systems are complex in general and inherently hard to test.
Typical uses are metadata and metrics, server and security logs, integrating heterogeneous systems, and fanout and parallel processing.
Widely used technologies for building event-driven systems include Apache Kafka, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS and Google PubSub.

The price is real. Guaranteed delivery, error handling and exactly-once, in-order processing are all hard. Such systems are complex in general and inherently hard to test.

entries.title: Domain-driven design: code that speaks the business's language

definition.text: Domain-driven design is a software design approach that models software to match a domain according to input from the domain's experts.

facts.text: Under domain-driven design the structure and language of the code, such as class and method names, should match the business domain; a loan system might have loan applications, customers, and methods like accept offer.

A ubiquitous language shared by domain experts, users and developers is used in the domain model and in describing requirements; it is a pillar of the approach alongside strategic and tactical design.

The approach rejects a single unified model and divides a large system into bounded contexts, each with its own model; context mapping patterns such as shared kernel, customer/supplier and anticorruption layer define how contexts relate.
An entity is defined by its identity, a value object is immutable with no conceptual identity, and a domain event is an event the domain experts care about.
An aggregate binds objects under a root entity: outside objects may reference only the root, which checks the consistency of changes; repositories retrieve domain objects and factories create them.

Combined with CQRS and event sourcing, aggregate roots validate and apply commands and publish events: the input is a command and the output is one or more events saved to an event store, then often published on a message broker.

Event storming is a workshop in which stakeholders, domain experts and developers map domain events, helping to discover subdomains, bounded contexts and aggregate boundaries before applying the approach.

A bounded context often maps to a microservice, ideally one to one; critics say much isolation and encapsulation is needed, and Microsoft recommends the approach only for complex domains where the model clearly helps.

entries.title: Event store: a database of nothing but events

definition.text: A database optimized for storing events, where an entity's state at any point in its history is rebuilt by replaying its events in order.

facts.text: Events and their data are the only real facts stored; every other object is derived from them and instantiated in memory by runtime code as needed.
Objects that aggregate recorded event data are not stored but built on the fly by traversing the event history, and discarded from memory when no longer needed.
Stored events are never changed, even erroneous ones; the only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values.
Backdated events, which take effect before earlier events, are easier to handle because only the new event is stored and the code redetermines the objects from the new facts, with no rollback.
The disadvantage is that code may need to re-instantiate all objects in memory from the events every time a service call arrives for a given dossier or policy.
One newspaper website keeps every article, image and byline in an event store and denormalizes the raw data into views fed to ElasticSearch nodes for website searches.
Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream-processing platform.

entries.title: Event sourcing: keep the history, derive the present

definition.text: Storing the full series of actions taken on data in an append-only event store, instead of just the current state, and treating that store as the source of truth.

facts.text: Event sourcing changes the programming paradigm from persisting states to persisting events, recorded in an append-only store.
The event store acts as the system of record and can be used to materialize the domain objects.
Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data, whereas event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries.
Event sourcing is one of several patterns for implementing an event-driven architecture, and the two are constantly confused.

Keeping the full history gives audit trails that can enable compensating actions, data can be reconstituted from the event store after a failure, and it suits real-time reporting and high-compliance audit logs.
The costs are a need for an extremely efficient network infrastructure and a reliable way to control message formats, such as a schema registry, because different events carry different payloads.
In a microservice system, a service such as the shopping cart emits events to a Kafka broker acting as the event store, and other services consume them, each determining its own domain model.
Change data capture can feed an event stream: a connector pulls data from tables and transforms it into events, which are pushed to Kafka for other sinks to consume.

entries.title: The fallacies of distributed computing

definition.text: The fallacies of distributed computing are false assumptions that programmers new to distributed applications invariably make, listed by L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems.

facts.text: The original list begins with four false assumptions: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure.
It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.
Assuming the network is reliable yields applications with little error handling that stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns.
Ignoring latency and the packet loss it causes leads developers to allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth, and ignoring bandwidth limits creates bottlenecks.
Complacency about security leaves systems blindsided by adaptive attackers; topology changes affect bandwidth and latency; multiple administrators may set conflicting policies.
The hidden costs of building and maintaining a network must be budgeted, and assuming a homogeneous network brings the same problems as the first three fallacies.

Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy, and three from Richards and Ford: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work and observability is optional.

entries.text:
Programmers new to distributed applications invariably make the same false assumptions. L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems listed them as the fallacies of distributed computing. The original list begins with four: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure. It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.

Each false belief has a price. Assume the network is reliable, and applications get little error handling. They stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns. Ignore latency and the packet loss it causes, and developers allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth. Ignore bandwidth limits, and bottlenecks appear.

Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy. Richards and Ford added three more: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work, and {{ref:sysd-reliab-098}} is optional.

Programmers new to distributed applications invariably make the same false assumptions. L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems listed them as the fallacies of distributed computing. The original list begins with four: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure. It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.

Each false belief has a price. Assume the network is reliable, and applications get little error handling. They stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns. Ignore latency and the packet loss it causes, and developers allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth. Ignore bandwidth limits, and bottlenecks appear.

Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy. Richards and Ford added three more: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work, and Observability: asking questions you did not plan for is optional.

entries.title: Broker or mediator: two ways to wire an event system

definition.text: The two main ways to wire an event-driven system: a broker topology with no central coordinator, or a mediator topology with one orchestrator that controls the workflow.

facts.text: Event-driven architecture has two primary topologies, broker and mediator, and the two can be combined in a hybrid model.
In the broker topology, components broadcast events to the entire system without any orchestrator, which gives higher performance and scalability.
In the mediator topology, a central orchestrator controls the workflow of events, which gives better control and error handling.

In the broker topology there is no orchestrator. Components broadcast events to the entire system, and the reward is higher performance and scalability. In the mediator topology a central orchestrator controls the workflow of events, and the reward is better control and error handling.

Put plainly, the choice trades the speed and scale of the first against the control and error handling of the second.
