entries.title: When consumers fail and events vanish

definition.text: Ways to cope with consumers that fail on an event and with events that get lost in transit between components.

facts.text: One way to handle consumer errors is a separate error-handler processor: a failing consumer asynchronously sends the erroneous event to it and moves on.
The error-handler processor tries to fix the event and sends it back to the original channel; if it fails, it sends the event to an administrator for inspection.
Events resubmitted through an error-handler processor are processed out of sequence.
Data loss occurs when a component crashes before processing an event and handing it to the next component, so the event is dropped and never reaches its destination.
To minimize data loss, persist in-transit events and dequeue them only after the next component acknowledges receipt, features known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.
Event-driven systems are susceptible to the fallacies of distributed computing, misconceptions that can cause significant problems in development and deployment.

entries.chapter: Event-driven architecture, event sourcing and CQRS
entries.text:
A consumer chokes on an event. What now? One answer is a separate error-handler processor. The failing consumer sends the erroneous event to it asynchronously and moves on. The processor tries to fix the event and sends it back to the original channel. If it fails, it sends the event to an administrator for inspection. The catch is that events resubmitted this way are processed out of sequence.

Data loss is the other danger. A component crashes before it has processed an event and handed it to the next component, so the event is dropped and never reaches its destination. To minimize this, persist events while they are in transit and dequeue them only after the next component acknowledges receipt. These features are known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.

Event-driven systems are also susceptible to {{ref:sysd-msg-128}}, misconceptions that can cause significant problems in development and deployment.

entries.title: Simple, stream and complex event processing

definition.text: Three general ways of processing events, simple, stream and complex, plus online event processing that works over distributed event logs.

facts.text: There are three general styles of event processing, simple, stream and complex, and a mature event-driven architecture often uses all three together.
In simple event processing, a notable event tied to a specific, measurable change of condition initiates downstream actions, driving the real-time flow of work and reducing lag time and cost.
In event stream processing, ordinary events such as orders or RFID transmissions are screened for notability and streamed to subscribers, driving real-time information flow and in-time decisions.
Complex event processing looks at patterns of simple and ordinary events to infer that a complex event has occurred, and then takes action.
The events may cross event types and span a long period, and their correlation may be causal, temporal or spatial.

Complex event processing needs sophisticated event interpreters, pattern definition and matching, and correlation techniques, and is commonly used to detect business anomalies, threats and opportunities.
Online event processing uses asynchronous distributed event logs to process complex events and manage persistent data, reliably composing related events across heterogeneous systems.
Online event processing allows very flexible distribution patterns with high scalability and strong consistency, but cannot guarantee upper bounds on processing time.

entries.title: Inside an event: header, payload and how much to carry

definition.text: An event has a header describing it and a payload carrying the details of the state change, and the payload can hold either all needed data or only keys.

facts.text: An event can be made of a header and a body, also called the payload; the header may hold the event name, a time stamp and the event type.
The payload provides the details of the detected state change and should not be confused with the logic applied in reaction to the event.
Putting all necessary attributes in the payload improves speed and scalability but can cause data consistency problems from multiple systems of record, stamp coupling and bandwidth issues at scale.
Putting only keys or IDs in the payload lets consumers fetch data from sources such as databases, which minimizes bandwidth and coupling but is less scalable and slower because of the queries.
The two payload methods are ends of a spectrum rather than binary choices, so architects must size payloads to the needs of event consumers.

entries.title: Command–query separation: asking should not change the answer

definition.text: Command–query separation is a principle that every method should be either a command that performs an action or a query that returns data, but not both.

facts.text: Devised by Bertrand Meyer, the principle says asking a question should not change the answer: a method returns a value only if it has no side effects.
Because queries never change state, any query can be called anywhere, such as in assertions, without fear of side effects; adherents say this makes state and state changes easier to understand.

CQRS generalises the principle to services, with separate query and command interfaces and usually separate data models; separate models raise the question of keeping them consistent, making eventual consistency likely.

It has limits: a combined method such as a stack's pop can be more convenient, and in multithreaded code a separate increment and value call leaves a race condition that a locked increment-and-return avoids.

entries.title: CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads

definition.text: An architectural pattern that divides a system's actions into commands that change state and queries that only read it, with separate interfaces and often separate models for each.

facts.text: A command is an instruction to perform a task that changes the system and returns only success or failure, while a query requests information without changing state or causing side effects.
CQRS extends the idea of command-query separation to the level of services, with separate interfaces to send queries and to send commands.
The core principle is separating commands from queries, which play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.
Many systems push the split into the data: read models process queries and write models process commands, usually tailored to their tasks and often held in physically separate stores.
CQRS is often combined with event sourcing: the store of events is the write model and official source of information, and the read model offers materialized, highly denormalized views.
Benefits include independent scaling of read and write workloads, easier optimization and architectural change, clear boundaries between behaviors, and no need for complex joins when querying.
Drawbacks are a more complex application design, possible message failures or duplicate messages, the challenge of eventual consistency, and more maintenance effort.

It helps when read performance must be tuned separately from write performance, when models or business rules change often, or when one subsystem's temporary failure must not affect the availability of others.

entries.title: Domain events and integration events

definition.text: Two kinds of event: domain events mark occurrences inside one business domain, and integration events carry changes across bounded contexts.

facts.text: Domain events signify important occurrences within a specific business domain, are restricted to a bounded context, and are vital for preserving business logic.
Domain events typically have lighter payloads containing only the information needed for processing.
Integration events communicate changes across different bounded contexts and are crucial for keeping data consistent across the entire system.
Integration events tend to have more complex payloads with additional attributes, because the needs of their potential listeners differ significantly.

Their payloads are typically lighter, with only the information needed for processing. Integration events communicate changes across different such areas and are crucial for keeping data consistent across the entire system. Their payloads tend to be more complex, with additional attributes, because the needs of their potential listeners differ significantly.

entries.title: The four layers an event passes through

definition.text: The four logical layers an event passes through: producer, channel, processing engine and downstream activity.

facts.text: An event-driven architecture may be built on four logical layers: the event producer, the event channel, the event processing engine and downstream event-driven activity.

The producer senses a fact and represents it as an event message, and converting data from sources as diverse as email clients, e-commerce systems and sensors to one standard form is a significant task.

An event channel carries events from the producer to the processing engine, for example over a TCP/IP connection; several can be open at once and are read asynchronously, with events queued for later processing.

The processing engine identifies an event and selects and executes the reaction, such as ordering a product and notifying personnel when stock is low, and the downstream layer shows the consequences, such as an email.

entries.title: Event granularity: how many events, how much detail

definition.text: Choosing how many event types to publish and how much each one says, so consumers neither drown in detail nor do needless work.

facts.text: Finding the right number of events is difficult: too many detailed events can overwhelm the system and make the event flow hard to analyze, a problem worse when rollbacks are required.
If events are overly consolidated, consumers do unnecessary processing and send unnecessary responses.
Mark Richards recommends considering the impact of each event and whether consumers need to read the payload to decide their actions.
In a compliance check, publishing only compliant and non-compliant events can suffice, so each event is processed only by relevant consumers and unnecessary workload falls.

entries.title: Getting a synchronous answer from an event-driven system

definition.text: A way to get a synchronous answer from an event-driven system by pairing each request event with a reply, using queues.

facts.text: Synchronous transactions in an event-driven architecture can be built on the request-response paradigm, implemented in two ways.
One way is two separate queues, one for requests and one for replies, and the event producer must wait until it receives the response.
The other way is one dedicated ephemeral queue for each request.

entries.title: The timeout antipattern: too short, too long

definition.text: The difficulty of choosing timeout values in distributed systems, where both short and long timeouts cause trouble.

facts.text: The timeout antipattern describes the challenges of setting timeout values in distributed systems.
Short timeouts may fail legitimate requests prematurely and lead to complex workarounds, while long timeouts give slow error responses and a poor user experience.
The circuit breaker pattern can address this by monitoring service health through heartbeats, synthetic transactions or real-time usage monitoring, enabling faster failure detection.

entries.title: Fixing events by adding events: the double timeline

definition.text: Giving every stored event a valid date and a transaction date so an error is fixed by adding a new event rather than editing the old one.

facts.text: Each event has two dates: the valid date when it became valid and the transaction date when it was entered into the database.
A correcting event carries the new values, keeps the event date of the event it corrects, and has a different transaction date.
This ensures reproducibility at every moment in time, even in the period before the correction took place.
It also allows situations that were based on erroneous events to be reproduced, if required.

entries.title: Apache Avro: compact binary data that carries its schema

definition.text: Avro is a row-oriented remote procedure call and data serialization framework developed within Apache's Hadoop project.

facts.text: Avro serves in Hadoop both as a serialization format for persistent data and as a wire format between Hadoop nodes and from client programs to Hadoop services.

Schemas are defined in JSON, with an optional Avro IDL syntax, and data is serialized in a compact binary format; schemas are built from primitive types and complex types such as record, enum, array, map and union.
Data can be stored with its schema, so a serialized item can be read without knowing the schema ahead of time; an object container file keeps the schema definition in its metadata.
Unlike Thrift and Protocol Buffers it needs no code-generation step when a schema changes; the binary encoding is smaller and faster, and a JSON encoding suits debugging.

entries.title: Event schema evolution: changing events without breaking consumers

definition.text: Techniques for changing the shape of events over time without breaking the services that produce and consume them.

facts.text: Event evolution is hard because schemas can become inconsistent across services and compatibility must hold during gradual system updates.
Strategies include versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility.
Adapters can translate events between old and new formats, ensuring consistent processing across components.
Event-driven systems are loosely coupled in space, time and synchronization, yet remain tightly coupled through subscriptions and patterns to the semantics of the event schema and values.

entries.title: McDonald's event platform: a registry, a gateway, regional clusters

facts.text: McDonald's standardizes events with an event registry that defines a standardized schema and custom SDKs that process events and handle errors.
An event gateway performs identity authentication and authorization, and utilities and tools fix events, keep the cluster healthy and perform administrative tasks.
To scale event processing, it uses a regional architecture on AWS that provides global availability.
Within a region, producers shard events by domain and each domain is processed by its own MSK cluster.
Each cluster auto-scales on MSK metrics such as CPU usage, using a workflow built on step-functions and re-assignment tasks.

McDonald's platform is a tour of this chapter's problems, with an answer to each.

The first problem is keeping events consistent. An event registry defines a standardized schema, and custom SDKs (software development kits) process events and handle errors. That ties together the shape of an event ({{ref:sysd-msg-028}}), the way that shape changes over time ({{ref:sysd-msg-032}}) and the failures a consumer can hit ({{ref:sysd-msg-030}}).

The second is control. An event gateway verifies who is calling and what each caller may do. Utilities and tools fix events, keep the cluster healthy and perform administrative tasks.

The third is scale. A regional architecture on AWS provides global availability. Within a region, producers shard events by domain, the sharding idea behind {{ref:sysd-scale-087}}, and each domain is processed by its own MSK cluster. Each cluster auto-scales on MSK metrics such as CPU usage, using a workflow built on step-functions and re-assignment tasks.

The thing to remember: the platform splits events by domain, with a cluster for each. A registry and its SDKs keep every producer speaking one standard schema.

entries.title: Loose coupling: changing one part without breaking the rest

definition.text: A loosely coupled system is one whose components make little or no use of knowledge of the definitions of other components, so a change in one least affects another.

facts.text: Loose coupling is the opposite of tight coupling; the subareas include the coupling of classes, interfaces, data and services.
A loosely coupled component can be replaced by another implementation of the same service, and components are less tied to one platform, language, operating system or build environment.

In code, a class that depends only on an interface can be served by any implementing class, so a new class replaces the old without changing the dependent class; a pointer to a concrete class cannot be substituted.
In distributed systems, loose coupling comes from transactions, queues in message-oriented middleware and interoperability standards; event-driven architecture also aims to promote it.

Publish-subscribe gives the highest level of decoupling compared with synchronous patterns such as RPC; RPC- and ORB-based middleware create tightly coupled components, while message-oriented middleware allows loose coupling.

Service coupling is reduced by publishing data in a standard format such as XML or JSON and by passing only key data: a letter-sending service takes a customer identifier and looks up the address itself.
Four types of autonomy promote loose coupling: reference autonomy, time autonomy, format autonomy and platform autonomy.

Loose coupling has a price: decoupling in time makes transactional integrity hard and needs extra coordination protocols, replication creates consistency issues, and an asynchronous caller can overload the recipient until it fails.

entries.title: Monolithic application: one unit that does everything

definition.text: A single, self-contained application designed as one service that performs every step needed for a business function.

facts.text: A monolith is built as a single unit and handles every step needed to satisfy a business need, rather than one particular task.
Advantages are simple development and debugging, fast and reliable communication, easy monitoring and testing, and support for ACID transactions.
Monoliths are relatively simple and low cost, but they lack elasticity, fault tolerance and scalability.
Maintenance gets harder as the codebase grows, the application is tightly coupled and hard to extend, and it commits the team to a particular technology stack.
The whole application is redeployed on each update, a single bug can bring down the entire system, and scaling or adopting new technologies is difficult.
A monolith is still a good choice for a small team and little complexity; once it becomes too complex, it can be refactored into microservices or a distributed application.
On a single machine a monolith may be performant enough for the current workload, yet it is less available, durable, changeable, fine-tuned and scalable than a well-designed distributed system.
Common architectural patterns for monoliths, each with trade-offs, are layered architecture, modular monolith and microkernel architecture.

entries.title: Microservices: small services that scale on their own

definition.text: An architecture that organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols and can be deployed and scaled independently.

facts.text: A microservice architecture organizes an application into loosely coupled, fine-grained services that communicate through lightweight protocols, which teams can develop, deploy and scale independently.
There is no universally agreed definition, but each service is generally designed around one business capability within a bounded context, with its own codebase managed by a small team.
Each service persists its own data, a database per service, unlike the traditional model where a separate data layer handles persistence.
Typical characteristics are loose coupling, small but focused scope (a matter of responsibility, not size), organization around business capabilities, resilience to failure, and high maintainability.
Services can be deployed independently, give multiple teams agility, improve fault tolerance and data isolation, and remove any long-term commitment to a particular technology stack.

Services scale independently: a monolith supporting three functions must be scaled in its entirety even if only one is constrained, whereas with microservices only that function's service is scaled out.

Costs include the complexity of a distributed system, harder testing, expensive maintenance, challenging inter-service communication, data integrity and consistency problems, and network latency and congestion.

The complexity of a monolith does not disappear when it is split into services; some becomes operational complexity, so decentralized continuous delivery and DevOps with holistic monitoring are needed.

entries.text:
A monolith that supports three functions must be scaled in its entirety, even if only one function is under strain. Microservices avoid that. The architecture organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols. Teams can develop, deploy and scale each service independently, so only the strained function's service is scaled out.

There is no universally agreed definition. Each service is generally designed around one business capability, inside the boundary of one domain model (see {{ref:sysd-msg-085}}), with its own codebase managed by a small team. Small is a matter of responsibility, not size. Each service also persists its own data, a database per service, unlike the traditional model where a separate data layer handles persistence.

The benefits follow from independence. Services deploy independently, give multiple teams agility, improve tolerance of faults and data isolation, and remove any long-term commitment to a particular technology stack. The costs are just as real. They are the complexity of a distributed system, harder testing, expensive maintenance, challenging communication between services, problems keeping data correct and consistent, and network latency and congestion.

The complexity of a monolith does not disappear when it is split into services. Some of it becomes operational complexity, so teams need decentralized delivery (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-143}}) and DevOps, with holistic watching of every service.

entries.title: Service-oriented architecture: building from services that already exist

definition.text: An architectural style built from discrete services, each a unit of functionality that can be accessed remotely and updated independently, instead of one monolithic design.

facts.text: SOA focuses on discrete services instead of a monolithic design, is intended to be independent of vendors, products and technologies, and is a good choice for system integration.

One definition gives a service four properties: it represents a repeatable business activity with a specified outcome, is self-contained, is a black box to its consumers, and may be composed of other services.

Services and consumers communicate by passing data in a well-defined, shared format or by coordinating an activity between services, and the aim is to build applications purely from existing services.
SOA promotes reuse at the macro (service) level rather than the class level, and can simplify interconnection to and use of existing legacy assets.

Treating a service as a project separate from its consumers lets it be delivered quickly and independently, and encourages good design because the service is designed without knowing who its consumers are.
SOA can be implemented with web services or microservices, commonly using web services standards such as SOAP, or with other service technologies such as REST or gRPC.

Without native or binary remote procedure call forms, applications could run more slowly and need more processing power, though SOA can be implemented with technologies that avoid RPC and XML or JSON translation.
Stateful services reduce the provider's scalability if it must keep each consumer's context and increase coupling, and testing is hard because of the lack of a uniform testing framework.

entries.title: Service discovery: finding services that keep moving

definition.text: The process of automatically detecting services on a network, so clients can find service instances whose locations change.

facts.text: Service discovery automatically detects devices and services on a network, aiming to reduce the manual configuration effort required from users and administrators.
In a monolith, services invoke one another through language-level method or procedure calls.

Microservices run in virtualized or containerized environments where the number and location of service instances change dynamically, so clients need a mechanism to reach a changing set of ephemeral instances.

A service discovery protocol is a network protocol that helps accomplish discovery, and discovery needs a common language so software agents can use one another's services without continuous user intervention.
Many protocols exist, including DNS Service Discovery, Simple Service Discovery Protocol, and DNS as used in Kubernetes.
Kubernetes provides two modes of service discovery, using environment variables or Kubernetes DNS.

Many protocols exist, including DNS Service Discovery and Simple Service Discovery Protocol. Another example is {{ref:sysd-reliab-050}}, which provides two modes of service discovery, using environment variables or its own DNS.

entries.title: Service mesh: a proxy beside every service

definition.text: A dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication using a proxy paired with each service.

facts.text: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication that gives observability into communications, secure connections, and automated retries and backoff for failed requests.
Routing service-to-service communication becomes increasingly complex as the number of services grows, and a service mesh makes it managed, observable and secure.
It consists of network proxies paired with each service, called the data plane, and a set of management processes, called the control plane.
The data plane intercepts and processes calls between services, while the control plane coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.
Each service instance is paired with a reverse proxy called a sidecar, sharing its container, with containers managed by an orchestration tool such as Kubernetes.
The sidecars can support service discovery, load balancing, authentication and authorization, and secure communications, and the mesh works with a service discovery protocol to detect services.
Istio, Cilium, Linkerd and Consul implement the architecture, and many meshes use the Envoy proxy on the data plane.

entries.title: Distributed tracing: following one request through many services

definition.text: A distributed trace is an interrelated series of discrete events, called spans, that track the progression of a single user request through the services that fulfil it.

facts.text: A cloud native application is usually made of distributed services that together fulfil one request, and a trace shows the causal and temporal relationships between those services.
Spans carry unique identifiers that let a tracing backend build parent-child relationships between them, and span information is typically passed in the HTTP headers of outbound requests.
Instrumenting an application with traces means sending span information to a tracing backend, which correlates the received spans into presentable traces.
Tracing is mainly used for anomaly detection, fault analysis, debugging and diagnosis in distributed systems such as microservices or serverless functions.
The main way to view a trace is a swimlane view, as in Jaeger, often with annotations and key-value attributes; aggregate views such as Canopy's queryable metrics help with large volumes of traces.
Tracing has overhead that depends on the framework and the features enabled, so in production there is a trade-off between how fine-grained the tracing is and its cost.
Because tracing can generate a large volume of messages, it is often necessary to be able to switch it off, either at compile time or at run time.
OpenTelemetry is a CNCF open source project with comprehensive support for distributed tracing; Jaeger is a distributed tracing system inspired by Google's Dapper paper.

entries.title: N-tier architecture: layers in the code, tiers on the machines

definition.text: An architecture that divides an application into logical layers, each with a specific responsibility, which may run on physically separate tiers.

facts.text: Layers separate responsibilities and manage dependencies: a higher layer can use services in a lower layer but not the other way around.
Tiers are physically separated and run on separate machines; a tier can call another directly or use asynchronous messaging, and several layers may share one tier.
Physically separating tiers improves scalability and resiliency but adds latency from the extra network communication.
In a closed layer architecture a layer can only call the next layer down, which limits dependencies but may create unnecessary network traffic; in an open one it can call any layer below.
The widely used 3-tier design has a presentation layer for user interactions, a business logic layer that validates data, and a data access layer that operates on the database.
In 2-tier, the presentation layer runs on the client and talks to a data store with no business logic layer; in single-tier, everything runs on one application or server.
Advantages are improved availability, firewall-like layers for security, independent scaling of tiers and easier maintenance by different people.
Disadvantages are added complexity, network latency that grows with the number of tiers, a hardware cost per tier, and harder network security.

entries.title: Orchestration versus choreography: who decides the order

definition.text: Two ways microservices collaborate: through shared rules for exchanging messages (choreography) or through a central coordinator that calls and combines the services (orchestration).

facts.text: Service choreography describes the exchange of messages and the rules by which the microservices interact, with point-to-point communication between them.
In orchestration, the orchestrator acts as a center of authority responsible for invoking and combining the services, and it describes the interactions between all participating services.
The orchestration pattern also includes transaction management among different services.

Orchestration is more reliable because it has built-in transaction management and error handling, while choreography's point-to-point communication makes fault tolerance scenarios much more complicated.
Orchestration scales more easily in one respect: adding a service means only the orchestrator changes its interaction rules, whereas in choreography all the interacting services must change.
Orchestration adds latency because all services talk through a central orchestrator, and throughput is bound to the orchestrator's capacity.
The orchestrator is a single point of failure, since if it goes down no services can talk to each other, so it must be highly available.
Netflix Conductor is a real-world microservice orchestrator.

Orchestration also scales more easily in one respect. Adding a service means only the orchestrator changes its interaction rules, whereas in choreography all the interacting services must change.

Orchestration pays for this. It adds latency, because all services talk through the central orchestrator, and throughput is bound to the orchestrator's capacity. The orchestrator is also a single point of failure: if it goes down, no services can talk to each other, so it must be highly available. Netflix Conductor is a real-world microservice orchestrator.

entries.title: Microservices versus SOA: a question of scope

definition.text: How microservices relate to service-oriented architecture: sometimes used interchangeably, but differing in scope and aim.

facts.text: Microservices and SOA are sometimes used interchangeably, but they differ, and the main distinction comes down to scope.

SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards, whereas microservices are many smallest independent service units aimed at team autonomy and decoupling.
Another view calls microservices a modern interpretation of SOA, a new implementation approach popular since 2014 that stresses continuous deployment and agile practices.

Characteristics of microservices found in the literature include fine-grained interfaces, business-driven development, polyglot programming and persistence, lightweight container deployment, decentralized continuous delivery and DevOps with holistic service monitoring.

entries.title: Service provider, broker and consumer

definition.text: The three roles in SOA: a provider publishes a service, a broker makes it findable, and a consumer finds and binds to it.

facts.text: Each SOA building block can play any of three roles: service provider, service broker (also called registry or repository), or service requester (consumer).
The provider creates a web service and provides its information to the service registry.
The broker makes information about the service available to any potential requester; public brokers are available everywhere while private brokers reach a limited public.

A consumer locates entries in the broker registry with find operations and then binds to the provider to invoke its web services, under a standardized service contract with business, functional and technical parts.

entries.title: Service-oriented design principles

definition.text: A set of published guidelines for designing services that stay loosely coupled, reusable and independent of their consumers.

facts.text: There are no industry standards for the exact composition of a service-oriented architecture, though many industry sources have published their own principles.

Services adhere to a standardized service contract and stay loosely coupled through reference autonomy, where services only know of each other's existence, and location transparency, where a service can be called from anywhere in the network.
Services act as black boxes that hide their inner logic, are autonomous over the functionality they encapsulate, and are stateless, returning a value or an exception to minimize resource use.
Services should be long lived, composable into other services, discoverable through communicative metadata, and divided to promote reuse of code.

entries.title: Service registry and registration: the address book of instances

definition.text: A highly available database of the network locations of service instances, kept current by services registering themselves or by a third party doing it for them.

facts.text: A service registry is a database containing the network locations of service instances that clients can reach, and it must be highly available and up to date.
With self-registration, a service instance registers and de-registers itself in the registry.
A self-registered instance may also send heartbeat requests to keep its registration alive.

With third-party registration, the registry tracks running instances by polling the deployment environment or subscribing to events, records newly available instances and de-registers terminated ones.

entries.title: Components of a microservice architecture

definition.text: The usual building blocks around a set of microservices: a load balancer, CDN, API gateway, identity provider, service registry, management component and domain services with their own databases.

facts.text: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend services, and a CDN, a group of geographically distributed servers holding static content, is checked first by clients before they reach the backend.
The API gateway handles incoming requests and routes them to the relevant services, talking to the identity provider and to service discovery.
The identity provider handles authentication and authorization for users.
Services register themselves in the service registry and discovery component, which the API gateway searches to find the services it needs to talk to.
A management component monitors the services.
Microservices are designed and deployed in different domains, and each domain has its own database.

entries.title: Client-side and server-side discovery

definition.text: The two main service discovery patterns: the client queries a service registry itself, or it calls a load balancer that finds an instance for it.

facts.text: In client-side discovery, one of two main patterns, the client obtains a service's location by querying a service registry that manages and stores the network locations of all services.
In server-side discovery, the client sends its request to an intermediate component such as a load balancer, which forwards it to an available service instance.
Tools used to implement service discovery include Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes Services and Apache Zookeeper.

entries.title: Microservices best practices

definition.text: A set of working rules for microservices: model them on the business domain, give each its own data, keep couplings loose and plan for failure.

facts.text: Model services around the business domain, with loose coupling and high functional cohesion, and make each microservice do one thing well.
Each service owns and manages its own data, kept private to it, so that coupling falls and services can evolve independently; shared database schemas are a cause of coupling.
Services should communicate only through well-designed APIs, avoid leaking implementation details, and keep API changes backward compatible.
Services should talk over lightweight protocols; options include REST, gRPC or message brokers.
Design for failure at infrastructure, database and service levels, using circuit breakers, bulkheads or graceful degradation, and fail fast so failures do not cascade.
Resiliency patterns such as retry policies, caching and rate limiting improve the availability of the services.
A large attack surface calls for security at every level of the communication path, and with many services centralized logging becomes critical for finding issues.
Containerization with tools like Docker and Kubernetes deploys microservices in isolation and simplifies their scaling and deployment.

entries.title: Monolith versus microservices: start simple, or split early?

definition.text: The choice between building an application as one deployable unit or as many small independent services, which depends on team, business maturity and latency needs.

facts.text: Singh's guide advises starting with a monolith when building a new system, while accepting that each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages.
Microservices are not a silver bullet; they solve an organizational problem, and adopting them is about organizational priorities and team structure as much as technology.
Questions to ask before moving to microservices include whether the team is too large for a shared codebase, whether teams are blocked on other teams, and whether they bring clear business value.
Further questions are whether the business is mature enough and whether the current architecture limits the team through communication overhead.
Not every application must be broken into microservices; they are solutions to complex concerns, and a business without such concerns does not need them.

Latency-sensitive applications such as real-time gaming, at milli-second latency, and low-latency trading, at micro-second latency, avoid microservices because network latency between separate processes is unbearable.
Microservices are usually stateless, with state kept in a database, but real-time gaming and trading keep state in memory for quick updates.
These applications also talk to the server at high frequency and must reach the same running instance, so they need web socket connections and sticky routing.

entries.title: Bounded context: where one model holds

definition.text: A natural division of business logic with an explicit boundary inside which one domain model is consistent and valid.

facts.text: A bounded context, a core idea of domain-driven design, defines an area within which a domain model is consistent and valid, ensuring clarity and separation of concerns.
A bounded context often maps to a microservice, and a one-to-one mapping is typically ideal because it keeps clear boundaries, reduces coupling and enables independent deployment and scaling.
One context may be split into several microservices for varying scalability needs, or several contexts consolidated into one microservice for simplicity or lower operational overhead.
The choice should balance domain-driven design principles with business goals, technical constraints and operational requirements.

entries.title: Cell-based architecture: limiting the blast radius

definition.text: A design that organizes resources into self-contained cells, each running a set of microservices and serving part of the requests, to limit the blast radius of failures.

facts.text: Cell-based architecture organizes computational resources into self-contained cells, each operating independently on a subset of requests while keeping scalability, fault isolation and availability.
A cell typically holds multiple microservices and acts as an autonomous unit.
Entire sets of microservices may be replicated across cells so requests can be rerouted to another operational cell on failure, limiting the impact of localized failures.
Circuit breakers within a cell mitigate cascading failures among microservices, while inter-cell circuit breakers isolate failing cells and redirect traffic to the remaining ones.

entries.title: Code sharing between microservices

definition.text: Ways to deal with the need to share code across services in an architecture that ideally shares nothing.

facts.text: Ideally microservices follow a share-nothing architecture, but in practice code must often be shared across services.

Common approaches are separate shared libraries for reusable components such as a security library, replicating stable modules with minimal changes across services, or consolidating several microservices into one.
Each approach has its own advantages and trade-offs depending on context and requirements.

entries.title: Microservice granularity: how small is small enough

definition.text: How big or small to make each service, a trade-off between independence and the cost of communication between services.

facts.text: The right granularity is found through iterative collaboration between architects and developers, weighing user requirements, service responsibilities and non-functional requirements, and is ultimately set by business drivers.

Neal Ford's integrator factors, such as shared transactions or tightly coupled processes, favor combining services, while disintegrator factors, such as fault tolerance or independent scalability, favor splitting them.
Very fine-grained services are easier to test and deploy independently but tend to have lower performance and reliability because of more interservice communication and more complex choreography.
Coarse-grained services are more robust and reliable thanks to less communication overhead and coordination complexity, but are harder to test and deploy because a change affects a wider scope.

entries.title: Reach-in reporting antipattern

definition.text: Reporting by pulling data straight out of each microservice's store, which breaks bounded contexts or delivers stale data.

facts.text: Retrieving data for a reporting service can break the bounded contexts of microservices, reduce the timeliness of the data, or both.
This holds whether data is pulled directly from databases, retrieved via HTTP, or collected in batches, and the pattern is called the reach-in reporting antipattern.
An alternative is for the databases to asynchronously push the needed data to the reporting service instead of it pulling the data.
Pushing needs a separate contract between the microservices and the reporting service and can be complex, but it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

The alternative is for the databases to push the needed data to the reporting service asynchronously. Pushing needs a separate contract between the microservices and the reporting service, and it can be complex. But it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

entries.title: Testing and observing microservices

definition.text: Practices that keep many independently deployed services testable and visible: stable interfaces, contract tests and aggregated logs, metrics and traces.

facts.text: Sam Newman suggests keeping microservice interfaces stable and making backwards-compatible changes as they evolve, so deployments need not be coordinated across services.
Newman proposes consumer-driven contract testing as a better alternative to traditional end-to-end testing for microservices.
He also suggests log aggregation, metrics aggregation and distributed tracing tools to keep systems of microservices observable.
Richards and Ford propose that each microservice have its own architectural characteristics rather than uniform ones for the whole distributed system.

entries.title: Consul: from service discovery to service networking

definition.text: Consul is a service networking platform developed by HashiCorp.

facts.text: Consul is a service networking platform that was first released as a service discovery platform.
Registered services and nodes can be queried using either a DNS interface or an HTTP interface.
It also provides a service mesh for secure service segmentation across any cloud or runtime, and distributed key-value storage for application configuration.
The Envoy proxy provides security, observability and resilience for all application traffic.
Consul can also be used to perform distributed locks.

entries.title: Distributed monolith: microservices in name only

definition.text: A system that looks like microservices but is tightly coupled internally, like a monolithic application.

facts.text: A distributed monolith resembles the microservices architecture but is tightly coupled within itself like a monolithic application.
Signs are a need for low-latency communication, services that do not scale easily, dependencies between services, shared resources such as databases, and tightly coupled systems.
Scalability is a primary reason to adopt microservices, but a distributed monolith makes most components depend on one another, which increases design complexity.

entries.title: Microservices pitfalls

definition.text: Common mistakes that make a microservices architecture fail to deliver its promised benefits.

facts.text: Service boundaries not drawn around the business domain, a lack of business alignment and a lack of clear ownership are common pitfalls.
Teams underestimate how hard it is to build a distributed system, and a lack of design for fault tolerance can cause cascading failures.
A shared database or common dependencies between services undermines their independence.
A lack of idempotency and trying to do everything ACID instead of BASE are further pitfalls.

entries.title: Modular monolith: one deployment, independent modules

definition.text: A single deployed application whose code is split into independent modules, one per feature.

facts.text: A modular monolith builds and deploys a single application but breaks the code into independent modules for each feature.
Reducing each module's dependencies lets a module be enhanced or changed without affecting other modules.
Done right, it reduces the complexity of maintaining a monolith as the system grows, which pays off in the long term.

entries.title: Strangler fig pattern: replacing old code section by section

definition.text: The strangler fig pattern wraps old code so that calls are redirected to newer code, or so that uses of the old code are logged.

facts.text: The pattern wraps old code with the intent of redirecting it to newer code, or of logging uses of the old code.
In a rewrite, the code is divided into many small sections; each is wrapped, then swapped out for new code before the next section is tackled.
Replacing code section by section is less risky and more incremental than swapping out the entire piece of software at once.
The pattern can be used on a monolithic application to migrate it to a microservices architecture.
Wrapping old code with logging shows how often it is used in production, which decides whether to delete low-usage code or rewrite high-usage code.

entries.title: Incremental migration to microservices: code first, data later

definition.text: Replacing parts of a monolith with microservices step by step, moving application code first and decoupling the data later.

facts.text: Microservices are considered a viable way to modernize an existing monolith, and modernization of legacy applications is done incrementally.
The data-driven migration antipattern is prioritizing data migration during the move from a monolith to microservices.
An iterative approach migrates application code first, with new microservices temporarily relying on the existing monolithic database.
As the system becomes better understood, data is decoupled and restructured so each microservice has its own database, which simplifies migration and reduces data migration errors.

entries.title: API: the contract between two pieces of software

definition.text: A connection between computers or programs: a software interface through which one piece of software offers a service to other pieces of software.

facts.text: API stands for Application Programming Interface: a set of definitions and protocols for building and integrating application software.
An API is sometimes called a contract between an information provider and an information user, setting out what the producer must supply and what the consumer must send.
To retrieve information or perform a function on another system, a caller uses that system's API to say what it wants, so the system can understand and complete the request.
Good API design is a crucial part of any system, and so is picking the right API technology, such as REST, GraphQL or gRPC.

An API is a type of software interface offering a service to other software; a document or standard describing it is an API specification, and a system that meets the standard is said to implement or expose the API.
Unlike a user interface, an API connects pieces of software to each other and is typically not visible to users: it is an under-the-hood part used for machine-to-machine communication.
The calls that make up an API are also known as subroutines, methods, requests or endpoints, and the API specification explains how to use or implement them.
A main purpose of an API is to hide internal details and expose only the parts a programmer finds useful, keeping them consistent even if the internal details later change.

entries.title: REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs

definition.text: A software architectural style, created to describe and guide the design of the Web's architecture, that sets constraints for how a distributed, Internet-scale hypermedia system should behave.

facts.text: A REST API, also called a RESTful API, conforms to the constraints of the REST architectural style and allows interaction with RESTful web services.
REST stands for Representational State Transfer and was first introduced by Roy Fielding in 2000.
In a REST API the fundamental unit is a resource, and HTTP request methods indicate the action to perform on a given resource.

GET requests a representation of a resource, POST submits an entity and often changes state, PUT replaces the resource with the payload, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE removes the resource.
A users resource maps /users with GET to list all users and POST to add one, and /users/{id} with GET, PATCH and DELETE to read, update or delete one user.

REST is simple, flexible, portable, cache-friendly and decoupled, but it can over-fetch data and need multiple round trips; it is used almost universally and is the default standard for designing APIs.
RESTful describes a system that follows REST's constraints, but the term now mostly means HTTP API design and verb practices, which have little to do with REST as originally formulated.

REST emphasizes uniform interfaces, independent deployment of components, scalable interactions, and a layered architecture that promotes caching to reduce user-perceived latency, enforce security and encapsulate legacy systems.

A REST API, also called a RESTful API, conforms to those constraints, which {{ref:sysd-msg-003}} lists.

PUT replaces the resource with the payload, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE removes it. A users resource shows the pattern. GET on /users lists all users, and POST on /users adds one. GET, PATCH and DELETE on /users/{id} read, update or delete a single user.

REST emphasizes uniform interfaces, independent deployment of components, scalable interactions and a layered architecture. That layering promotes caching, which reduces the latency users perceive, enforces security and encapsulates legacy systems. The style is simple, flexible, portable, cache-friendly and decoupled, but it can over-fetch data and need multiple round trips. A warning on vocabulary: RESTful properly means following the constraints. The term now mostly means HTTP API design and verb practices, which have little to do with REST as originally formulated.

entries.title: Remote procedure call: making a far-away function feel local

definition.text: An action in which a program causes a procedure to run in a different address space, commonly on another computer, written as if it were a normal local call.

facts.text: In an RPC, a program causes a procedure to execute in a different address space, commonly on another computer, written like a local call; the programmer writes essentially the same code whether the subroutine is local or remote.

An RPC is a form of server interaction, typically request-response: the client sends a request message with parameters, the server responds, and the client is blocked meanwhile unless it sends an asynchronous request.
RPC is called remote because it lets services deployed on different servers communicate under a microservice architecture; from the user's point of view it acts like a local function call.

The RPC model implies location transparency, but local and remote calls are usually not identical, and remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local calls, so distinguishing them is important.

Remote calls can fail because of unpredictable network problems, and callers generally must handle such failures without knowing whether the remote procedure was invoked; idempotent procedures are easily handled.
Standardized RPC systems mostly use an interface description language to let different platforms call the RPC, and the IDL files can generate code to interface between client and server.
Many incompatible technologies implement RPC, such as XML-RPC, JSON-RPC and SOAP, a successor of XML-RPC; in object-oriented programming RPCs are represented by remote method invocation.

Modern RPC frameworks such as gRPC and Apache Thrift add efficient binary serialization, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and built-in authentication, load balancing, streaming and error handling, suiting them to scalable microservices.

entries.title: GraphQL: asking for exactly the data you need

definition.text: A query language and server-side runtime for APIs that gives clients exactly the data they request and no more.

facts.text: GraphQL gives clients a single endpoint to query for precisely the data they need: clients name the exact fields, including nested ones, and the server returns a payload with just those fields.

A schema describes what clients can do once connected, a query is a client request made of fields and arguments, a mutation modifies server-side data, and a resolver is a query handler that generates the response.
Besides queries, GraphQL supports mutations for modifying data and subscriptions for real-time notifications.
Its advantages are no over-fetching, a strongly defined schema, code generation support and optimized payloads; maintainers can also add or deprecate fields without impacting existing queries.
Its disadvantages are that complexity shifts to the server side, caching becomes hard, versioning is ambiguous, and the N+1 problem appears.
GraphQL suits cutting app bandwidth by querying several resources in one query, rapid prototyping of complex systems, graph-like data models, and frontends whose needs change often.
A GraphQL server can process a client query using data from separate sources and present the results in a unified graph; the language is not tied to any specific database or storage engine.
GraphQL is not a full-fledged graph query language such as SPARQL: an interface reporting an individual's parents cannot return the set of all their ancestors in a single query.

conflicts.text: GraphQL shifts complexity to the client side and can allow abusive queries if not properly safeguarded.
conflicts.note: ByteByteGo says the client side; Singh says the server side. Both are curated; the Singh version fits GraphQL's server-side schema and resolvers.

entries.title: Serialization: turning data into bytes and back

definition.text: Serialization translates a data structure or object state into a format that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, possibly on another computer.

facts.text: Rereading the serialized bits according to the format creates a semantically identical clone of the original object; this is also called marshalling, and the reverse is deserialization or unmarshalling.
Serialization is used to send data over networks as messages, store data in databases and on disk, make remote procedure calls, distribute objects and detect changes in time-varying data.

The format must be architecture-independent: copying a data structure's memory layout directly cannot work reliably across architectures because of byte ordering, memory layout and per-language data representation.

Because the encoding is serial, extracting one part means reading and reconstructing the whole object from start to end; the linearity suits simple I/O, but higher performance may call for a non-linear organization.
Serialization breaks the opacity of an abstract data type by potentially exposing private implementation details, and naive implementations that serialize all data members may violate encapsulation.
Interoperability requires that applications understand each other's serialization formats, so remote method call architectures such as CORBA define their serialization formats in detail.
Some language serializers are unsafe with untrusted input: Python's pickle is not secure against erroneous or malicious data, and PHP's unserialize() is often dangerous on completely untrusted data.

entries.title: The six constraints that make an API RESTful

definition.text: The set of constraints that define the REST architectural style and that a system applies to be considered RESTful.

facts.text: REST defines six guiding constraints: uniform interface, client-server, stateless, cacheable, layered system and, optionally, code on demand.

The client-server constraint separates clients from servers by a well-defined interface, with the interaction managed through HTTP; the uniform interface constraint gives one uniform way of interacting with a given server.
Stateless means no client context is stored on the server between requests, so a client that is at rest consumes no server storage.
Cacheable means every response states whether it can be cached and for how long the client may cache it.
In a layered system the architecture is composed of multiple layers, and a client cannot ordinarily tell whether it is connected directly to the end server or to an intermediary.
Code on demand is optional: servers can temporarily extend or customize a client by sending executable logic that runs in a standard virtual machine.
Applying the constraints gives a system desirable non-functional properties: performance, scalability, simplicity, modifiability, visibility, portability and reliability.

Fielding identified embedding session information in URIs as violating REST, because it can hurt shared caching and server scalability; HTTP cookies also violate the constraints because they can fall out of sync with the browser's application state.

conflicts.text: In order for an API to be considered RESTful, it has to conform to these architectural constraints, code on demand included.
conflicts.note: Singh treats code on demand as required; the Wikipedia article marks it optional, so the optional version is stated.

entries.title: The uniform interface: one way to talk to every resource

definition.text: The REST constraint, fundamental to any RESTful system, that gives every part of the system one uniform way to interact so that each part can evolve independently.

facts.text: The uniform interface constraint is fundamental to the design of any RESTful system; it simplifies and decouples the architecture, so each part can evolve independently.

Resource identification in requests: individual resources are identified by URIs, and a resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form.
Manipulation through representations: a client holding a representation of a resource, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state.
Self-descriptive messages: each message includes enough information to describe how to process it, for example a media type that names which parser to invoke.

HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state): after the initial URI, a client uses server-provided links to discover all the resources it needs, with no hard-coded knowledge of the server's structure.
Because only the first resource's identifier needs to be known and the rest are discovered, identifiers can change without telling the client in advance, so client and server must be loosely coupled.

entries.text: In a fully RESTful system a client needs to know only one address. The uniform interface is fundamental to any RESTful system. It gives every part one uniform way to interact, which simplifies and decouples the architecture so each part can evolve independently. It has four pieces. Resources are identified by URIs. A resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form. A client holding a representation, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state. Each message is self-descriptive, carrying enough information to say how to process it, such as a media type that names which parser to invoke. The fourth piece is {{ref:sysd-msg-123}}: after the initial URI, the client follows server-provided links, with no hard-coded knowledge of the server's structure. Because only the first identifier must be known, identifiers can change without warning, so client and server must be loosely coupled.

It gives every part one uniform way to interact, which simplifies and decouples the architecture so each part can evolve independently. It has four pieces. Resources are identified by URIs. A resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form. A client holding a representation, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state. Each message is self-descriptive, carrying enough information to say how to process it, such as a media type that names which parser to invoke. entries.title: HATEOAS: letting the server say what you can do next

definition.text: Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS) is a REST constraint under which a client discovers what it can do next from hypermedia links that the server returns.

facts.text: With HATEOAS a REST client needs little to no prior knowledge of how to interact with the server beyond a generic understanding of hypermedia, unlike CORBA, where client and server share a fixed interface through documentation or an IDL.
The constraint is an essential part of REST's uniform interface; it decouples client and server and lets server functionality evolve independently.
A client enters through one entry point URL; every later request is discovered inside a response, and the client moves between application states by following links in the representation.

In the account example, a response offers links to deposit, withdraw, transfer or close; once the account is overdrawn only the deposit link remains, so the available actions vary with the resource's state.
HTML is itself hypermedia, and formats such as HAL, JSON-LD, Siren and Collection+JSON add links to JSON or XML; HAL defines links but not actions.

Fielding says the strictness of REST constraints aims at software design on the scale of decades, promoting longevity and independent evolution, and that many constraints oppose short-term efficiency.

entries.title: Serialization formats from compact binary to readable text

definition.text: Serialization formats range from compact binary encodings such as XDR to human-readable text encodings such as XML, JSON and YAML.

facts.text: Sun's External Data Representation (XDR), published in 1987, is an open binary format standardized as RFC 4506.

XML gave a human-readable text encoding useful for objects that humans read or that other systems consume regardless of language; it loses the compact byte-stream encoding, which mattered less once storage and transmission capacity grew.
JSON is a lightweight plain-text alternative to XML, commonly used for client-server communication in web applications, independent of JavaScript and standardized as RFC 8259.
YAML is a strict superset of JSON that adds data type tags, cyclic data structures, indentation-sensitive syntax and several forms of scalar quoting.
Large scientific datasets use specific binary serialization standards such as HDF, netCDF and GRIB.
Avro, from Hadoop, serves as a format for persistent data and as a wire format, with binary and JSON encodings; unlike Protocol Buffers it needs no code generation when a schema changes.

entries.title: Protocol buffers: schemas that skip the field names

definition.text: Protocol Buffers is an open-source, cross-platform data format and interface definition language for serializing structured data in a compact, forward- and backward-compatible way.

facts.text: Protocol buffers serialize structured data in a language- and platform-neutral, extensible way and were designed to be smaller and faster than XML or JSON.
Message schemas and services are described in a .proto file and compiled with protoc, which generates code, native language bindings, that a sender or recipient invokes to produce or parse the data.
A schema identifies each field by an integer, and the data carries only those numbers, not field names, which saves bandwidth and storage.

Messages are serialized into a compact binary wire format that is forward- and backward-compatible but not self-describing; the ASCII text format is self-describing but loses compatibility, so it suits only human editing and debugging.
gRPC uses protocol buffers as its interface definition language, to describe its service interface and payload messages, and to encode data.

The format suits small chunks of data, not exceeding a few megabytes, that can be loaded into memory at once, so it is not streamable; it has no built-in compression and weak support in non-object-oriented languages.

entries.title: gRPC: fast, typed calls between services

definition.text: A high-performance, open-source Remote Procedure Call framework that can run in any environment.

facts.text: gRPC efficiently connects services in and across data centers, with pluggable support for load balancing, tracing, health checking, authentication and more.
Like many RPC systems, gRPC defines a service and the methods that can be called remotely with their parameters and return types, using protocol buffers as the interface definition language.

The client encodes a call in binary and sends it over HTTP/2; the server decodes it, invokes the application and returns an encoded result. Binary encoding and network optimizations are why gRPC is said to be 5X faster than JSON.
Its advantages are being lightweight and efficient, built-in code generation and bi-directional streaming.
Its disadvantages are being relatively new compared to REST and GraphQL, limited browser support, a steeper learning curve and payloads that are not human readable.
gRPC suits real-time communication via bi-directional streaming, efficient inter-service communication in microservices, low latency and high throughput, and polyglot environments.

gRPC uses HTTP/2 for transport and Protocol Buffers as its interface description language, and provides authentication, bidirectional streaming and flow control, blocking or nonblocking bindings, and cancellation and timeouts; it generates cross-platform client and server bindings for many languages.
gRPC's use of HTTP trailers makes it impossible to implement a gRPC client in a browser, which requires a proxy instead.

entries.title: SOAP: XML envelopes for web services

definition.text: SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information in web services, usually carried over HTTP.

facts.text: SOAP uses the XML Information Set as its message format and relies on application-layer protocols for negotiation and transmission, most often HTTP, although some legacy systems use SMTP.

The protocol has three parts: an envelope that defines the message structure and how to process it, encoding rules for application-defined datatypes, and a convention for representing procedure calls and responses.
A SOAP message is an ordinary XML document with a required Envelope and Body, an optional Header, and an optional Fault element that reports processing errors.
SOAP is extensible, neutral (it can run over HTTP, SMTP, TCP or UDP) and independent (it allows any programming model).
A message travels from its originator through intermediary nodes, which process the header blocks targeted at them and forward it, to the ultimate receiver.
HTTP gained wider acceptance as transport because it works well with firewalls, a major advantage over distributed protocols such as GIOP/IIOP or DCOM, which firewalls normally filter.
XML's lengthy syntax eases error detection and avoids byte-order problems but slows processing; in financial messaging SOAP produced messages 2-4 times larger than FIX and CDR.

Being protocol-agnostic, SOAP cannot use REST's uniform interface or caching and must reimplement them; verbosity, slow XML parsing and no standard interaction model led to services using HTTP more directly, such as REST.

entries.title: API documentation: telling clients what they need to know

definition.text: A description of what services an API offers and how to use them, aiming to cover everything a client needs to know in practice.

facts.text: API documentation describes what services an API offers and how to use them, and it is crucial for developing and maintaining applications that use the API.

It may include descriptions of classes and methods, usage scenarios, code snippets, design rationales, performance discussions and contracts, but usually omits implementation details of the API services.
It also covers restrictions on use, for instance that a parameter cannot be null or that a function is not thread safe.
Because it tends to be comprehensive, writers find it hard to keep updated and users find it hard to read carefully, potentially yielding bugs.

entries.title: API release policies: private, partner and public

definition.text: The ways an API can be released: private, partner or public.

facts.text: The main policies for releasing an API are private (internal company use only), partner (only specific business partners) and public (available for use by the public).
A partner API lets a company exercise quality control by curating which apps have access to it.
Not all public APIs are accessible by everybody: access is granted either by API tokens or by customer status validations.

entries.text: Not every API is meant for the whole world. A company can release one in three ways. A private API is for internal company use only. A partner API is open only to specific business partners, which lets the company exercise quality control by curating which apps have access. A public API is available for use by the public. Public does not always mean open to everybody, though: access is granted either by API tokens or by customer status validations.

entries.title: Web API: an API reached over HTTP

definition.text: An API used in web development, defined as a set of specifications such as HTTP request messages together with the structure of the response messages.

facts.text: A web API is typically a set of specifications, such as HTTP request messages, along with a definition of the structure of response messages, usually in XML or JSON format.
The term API is often used to mean web APIs, which allow communication between computers that are joined by the internet.
Web APIs have moved from SOAP-based web services and service-oriented architecture towards REST-style web resources and resource-oriented architecture.
A shipping company's API can be added to an eCommerce site to order shipping services and include current shipping rates without the developer entering the shipper's rate table.

entries.title: API versioning and deprecation: changing without breaking clients

definition.text: Managing changes to a public API so that clients that depend on it keep working.

facts.text: When an API becomes public, its interface stability matters: changes such as adding new parameters to a function call could break compatibility with clients; parts subject to change should be documented as unstable.

A public API can declare parts deprecated, making them candidates for removal or backward-incompatible change, which lets developers transition away from them; designing the version number in advance also simplifies upgrades.
GraphQL avoids versioning: because it returns only the data explicitly requested, new types or fields can be added without a breaking change, and @deprecated marks parts of the schema being retired.
Common practice in GraphQL is to avoid breaking changes and serve a versionless API, while Singh lists its versioning as ambiguous.

entries.title: API pagination: six ways to return a big list in pieces

definition.text: Returning a large dataset from an API in pieces, which handles large datasets efficiently and improves performance.

facts.text: Offset-based pagination passes an offset and a limit, as in GET /orders?offset=0&limit=3; it is simple but inefficient for large offsets, because rows must be scanned and skipped.

Cursor-based pagination marks a position with a cursor, typically an encoded string that points to a specific record; it is efficient for large datasets because skipped records are not scanned, but slightly more complex.
Page-based pagination gives a page number and a page size, as in GET /items?page=2&size=3; it is easy to use but has the same performance issues as offsets for large page numbers.
Keyset-based pagination filters by a key, often the primary key or another indexed column, as in GET /items?after_id=102&limit=3; it is efficient but needs a unique, indexed key and can be complex.
Time-based pagination uses a timestamp or date range; it suits time-ordered data and misses no records when new ones are added, but requires a reliable and consistent timestamp.
Hybrid pagination combines techniques, such as cursor with time-based for scrolling through time-ordered records; it can offer the best performance and flexibility but needs careful design.

entries.title: API design best practices beyond the URL path

facts.text: API design is not just URL path design: it means choosing resource names, identifiers and path patterns, plus HTTP header fields and rate-limiting rules within the API gateway.
For a RESTful API, the path structure can follow the domain model, and semantic paths make APIs easier to understand so users can find the right API in the documentation.
Defining only a few basic HTTP methods simplifies API design; PATCH, for example, can often be a problem for teams.
Designing for idempotence in advance makes an API more robust: GET is idempotent, but POST has to be designed properly to be idempotent.
Limiting the HTTP status codes in use to a defined few simplifies application development.
Designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrade work.
For batch operations, use batch or bulk as a keyword and put it at the end of the path.
A set of query rules such as pagination, sorting and filtering makes an API more flexible.

entries.title: RPC call sequence: from caller to server and back
entries.article: Remote procedure call#Message passing > Sequence of events

definition.text: The steps by which a remote procedure call travels from the calling code through stubs and the network to the server procedure and back.

facts.text: The caller makes a local procedure call with parameters pushed on the stack as usual; the client stub packs the parameters into a message, called marshalling, and makes a system call to send it.
The client's operating system sends the message to the server machine, whose operating system passes the incoming packets to the server stub.
The server stub unpacks the parameters, called unmarshalling, and calls the server procedure; the reply traces the same steps in the reverse direction.

entries.text: A remote call looks like a local one, but a lot happens in between. The caller makes a local procedure call, with parameters pushed on the stack as usual. The client stub packs the parameters into a message (marshalling) and makes a system call to send it. It is the code that stands in for the remote procedure on the caller's side. The client's operating system sends the message to the server machine, whose operating system passes the incoming packets to the server stub. The server stub unpacks the parameters (unmarshalling) and calls the server procedure. The reply traces the same steps in reverse.
