entries.title: Choosing between REST, GraphQL and gRPC

definition.text: A comparison of the three main API technologies on coupling, chattiness, performance, complexity, caching, code generation, discoverability and versioning, which concludes that none is best for every case.

facts.text: The comparison criteria are tight coupling, chattiness (how many distinct API calls it takes to get the needed information), performance, integration complexity, caching, built-in tooling and code generation, discoverability, and ease of versioning.
REST rates low coupling, high chattiness, good performance, medium complexity, great caching, bad code generation, good discoverability and easy versioning.
GraphQL rates medium coupling, low chattiness, good performance, high complexity, custom caching and good code generation.
gRPC rates high coupling, medium chattiness, great performance, low complexity, custom caching, great code generation, bad discoverability and hard versioning.
REST suits applications that want simple, uniform interfaces between separate services and straightforward caching, but may need multiple round trips to assemble related data from separate endpoints.
GraphQL is good at aggregating data from multiple sources for rapidly evolving frontends, but it can allow abusive queries if not safeguarded, and its caching is more complicated than REST's.
None of the three is better: there is no silver bullet, and the best choice depends on the application's requirements and team, so focus on the domain and requirements rather than the technology.

entries.title: GraphQL schema and type system

definition.text: The schema of a GraphQL service: the types and fields that describe what data can be queried from the API.

facts.text: A GraphQL service is created by defining types with fields, which make up the schema definition, then providing functions called resolvers to retrieve and map the data for each field.
The type system describes what data can be queried, and clients use the schema to send queries that return predictable results; the root type, Query by default, holds all queryable fields.
Base types called scalars represent strings, numbers and IDs; fields are nullable by default, a trailing exclamation mark makes a field required, and square brackets make it a list.
A query is validated against the schema before the server executes it, and the result mirrors the shape of the query, typically as JSON.

entries.title: GraphQL operations: queries, mutations and subscriptions

definition.text: The three kinds of GraphQL operation: queries that read data, mutations that change it, and subscriptions that push live updates.

facts.text: GraphQL supports reading, writing (mutating) and subscribing to changes to data, with real-time updates commonly implemented using WebSockets.
A query defines the exact shape of the data the client needs, and the data is returned in the same shape.
A mutation creates, updates or deletes data; it generally takes variables that pass data from client to server and defines the shape of the data returned afterwards.
A subscription sends live updates from server to client: the client defines the shape of the data it needs, and when a mutation updates the field, data goes to all subscribed clients.

entries.title: OpenAPI Specification: writing the contract first

definition.text: The OpenAPI Specification is a machine-readable interface definition language for describing, producing, consuming and visualizing web services.

facts.text: An OpenAPI Description is a formal description of an API that tools can use to generate code, documentation, test cases and more.

Applications can generate documentation of methods, parameters and data models from it, which keeps documentation, client libraries and source code in sync; generating server code stubs from it is called scaffolding.
In contract-first development the API contract is agreed before any code is written, so downstream developers can mock the server and start testing right away, a shift-left testing practice.
The specification is language-agnostic and declarative, so clients can understand and consume a service without knowing its implementation or seeing the server code.

entries.title: API performance optimization: five cheap wins

facts.text: Result pagination optimizes large result sets by streaming them back to the client in pieces, improving service responsiveness and user experience.

Asynchronous logging sends logs to a lock-free buffer and returns immediately instead of dealing with the disk on every call; logs are flushed to disk periodically, which significantly reduces I/O overhead.
Data caching stores frequently accessed data so it is retrieved faster: callers check the cache before querying the database, and in-memory stores such as Redis are quicker.

Compressing requests and responses, for example with gzip, shortens transmission time; a connection pool reuses open database connections, avoiding the overhead of opening and closing one each time data is loaded.

entries.title: Polling: asking again and again whether anything is new

definition.text: Polling means repeatedly checking an external device or service for its status, as a synchronous activity driven by the client, to retrieve updated information.

facts.text: Polling is like constantly asking whether there is anything new, even when there may be no update, so it is resource-intensive and inefficient.
The client gets updates only when it asks, so it can miss real-time information, but developers have more control over when and how data is fetched.
With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data; polling is a solid option when an infrastructure limitation prevents the use of webhooks.

Busy-wait polling does nothing except check status until the device is ready; checking repeatedly and returning to another task wastes fewer cycles but is generally less efficient than interrupt-driven I/O.
The polling cycle is the time in which each element is monitored once; the best cycle depends on the desired speed of response and on the overhead of polling, such as processor time and bandwidth.
Polling fails to scale when there are too many devices to check: the time needed to poll them can exceed the time available to service them.
Roll call polling queries each element in a fixed sequence and needs a timeout so silent elements cannot lock it up; it is inefficient when overhead is high and few of many elements are active.

The alternative is interrupts, signals from devices that say they need attention; in many situations, such as multitasking operating systems, interrupts are more efficient because they cut processor spinning and bandwidth use.

entries.title: Push technology: the server speaks first

definition.text: Push technology, or server push, is a way of communicating in which the server, rather than the client, starts the exchange.

facts.text: In push the server initiates communication, which differs from the pull method where the client initiates it.

Clients usually state which information they want through the publish-subscribe model: a client subscribes to channels on a server, and the server pushes new content to subscribed clients automatically.
When restrictive security policies block incoming HTTP requests, push is sometimes simulated by polling, in which the client periodically checks the server for new information.
Instant messaging and synchronous conferencing are push services: chat messages are pushed to the user as soon as the messaging service receives them.
Email is partly push: SMTP is a push protocol, but the last step from mail server to desktop usually uses a pull protocol such as POP3 or IMAP, which clients poll frequently.
IMAP's IDLE command lets the server tell the client when new messages arrive.
Push-enabled web applications include software updates, stock tickers, webchat, auctions, online betting and gaming, sport results, monitoring consoles and sensor network monitoring.

entries.title: Long polling: holding the request open until there is news

definition.text: In long polling the client sends a request and the server holds it open until new information is available or a timeout is reached, then responds so the client can immediately ask again.

facts.text: If the server has nothing new when the poll arrives, it holds the request open instead of sending an empty response, and replies only when information is available or a timeout threshold is reached.

Once it has new information the server sends an HTTP response that completes the open request, and the client immediately (or after a defined interval) issues another request to re-establish a pending connection.
Long polling is not true push: it emulates server push where real push is not possible, such as sites whose security policies reject incoming HTTP requests.
Unlike normal polling, it removes the response latency between information becoming available and the client's next request.
It is easy to implement, nearly universally supported and good for small-scale projects, but usually not scalable: every response needs a new connection, which is intensive on the server.
Reliable message ordering can be an issue across multiple requests, and latency grows because the server must wait for a new request before it can send again.

entries.title: Push notification: a message from the server to your screen

definition.text: A push notification is a message pushed from a back-end server or application to a user interface such as a mobile or desktop application.

facts.text: Push notifications are either local, where the application schedules the notification with the device's OS, or remote, where a server sends them.

For a remote notification the client application registers on the server with a unique key, such as a UUID or Apple Device Token, and the server sends the message against that key over a protocol such as HTTP or XMPP.
On arrival a notification can show a short message, set a badge on the app icon, light the notification LED or play an alert sound.
Typical content is chat messages, vendor special offers, event reminders and changes to subscribed topics such as the weather.
Real-time push notifications may raise privacy issues, since they can be used to link social network pseudonyms to the real identities of smartphone owners.

entries.title: Web push: one connection for every event

definition.text: Web push is the set of web standards that deliver real-time events such as incoming calls or messages to a user, based on a simple protocol over HTTP/2.

facts.text: Radio use is a major drain on mobile devices, and separate persistent connections with their keep-alive traffic waste it, so Web push consolidates all events into one session through a single service that distributes them as they arrive.

The model has three actors: a user agent, a push service and an application server; the user agent creates a subscription and gives it to its application server, and it is the basis of all later interactions.

A subscription is two resources: a private subscription resource the user agent uses to receive messages and delete the subscription, and a public push resource shared with the application server to send messages.

The user agent POSTs to the push service to subscribe and gets 201 Created; the application server POSTs the message body to the push resource; the user agent GETs its subscription and the service answers with HTTP/2 server push.

For at-least-once delivery the user agent MUST acknowledge each message with an HTTP DELETE; an application server can ask for delivery confirmation with Prefer: respond-async, which the push service MUST support.

Web Notifications, a W3C standard, alert the user outside a web page, and the W3C Push API gives web applications the push service; Chrome, Firefox and Edge implement it fully, Safari partly (February 2023).

entries.title: Techniques for real-time updates over HTTP

definition.text: To get real-time updates from an HTTP server, either the browser does the work by polling, or the browser and server cooperate over WebSocket or server-sent events.

facts.text: An HTTP server cannot automatically initiate a connection to a browser, so the browser is the initiator.
Web applications were built around a client-server model in which the client always starts a transaction, so the server had no way to push data without first receiving a request.
One family has the browser do the heavy lifting with short polling or long polling; the other has server and browser cooperate through WebSocket or server-sent events.
With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data; with long polling the server does not return a result until new data has arrived.
With WebSocket or SSE, the server can send the latest data straight to the browser once the connection is established.
SSE is uni-directional, so the browser cannot send a new request to the server, while WebSocket is full-duplex, so the browser can keep sending new requests.

entries.title: WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways

definition.text: WebSocket is a communications protocol that gives a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection.

facts.text: The channel is a persistent connection that stays open, so client and server can each send data at any time, independently of the other.
It gives full-duplex interaction with lower overhead than half-duplex alternatives such as HTTP polling, because the server can send content without being asked first.

Before WebSocket, two-way web apps polled over several HTTP connections and sent upstream messages as separate calls, which meant multiple TCP connections per client, an HTTP header on every message and client-side tracking of replies.

RFC 6455 describes an independent TCP-based protocol: a thin layer adding an origin-based security model, naming, framing and a closing handshake; HTTP servers only see its handshake, as an Upgrade request.
TCP alone deals with streams of bytes with no inherent notion of a message; WebSocket enables streams of messages on top of TCP.
It suits games, stock tickers, multiuser applications with simultaneous editing, and user interfaces that expose server-side services in real time.
Advantages: full-duplex asynchronous messaging, a better origin-based security model, and light weight for both client and server.
Terminated connections are not automatically recovered, and older browsers lack support, though modern major browsers support the standardized protocol.

The channel is persistent, so client and server can each send data at any time, independently of the other.

That gives full-duplex interaction with lower overhead than half-duplex alternatives such as HTTP polling, because the server can send content without being asked first. RFC 6455 describes an independent TCP-based protocol: a thin layer that adds an origin-based security model, naming, framing and a closing handshake. HTTP servers see only its handshake, as an Upgrade request. TCP alone deals with streams of bytes with no inherent notion of a message. WebSocket enables streams of messages on top of it.

It suits games, stock tickers, multiuser applications with simultaneous editing, and user interfaces that expose server-side services in real time. Its advantages are full-duplex asynchronous messaging, a better origin-based security model, and light weight for both client and server. Its limits are that terminated connections are not automatically recovered and older browsers lack support, though modern major browsers support the standardized protocol.

entries.title: WebSocket opening handshake: an HTTP request that switches protocols

definition.text: The WebSocket opening handshake is an HTTP Upgrade request from the client and a 101 response from the server, after which the connection switches to the WebSocket protocol.

facts.text: The client's handshake is an HTTP GET Upgrade request (HTTP version at least 1.1), so one port can serve both HTTP clients and WebSocket clients.
The request carries Host, Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, a Sec-WebSocket-Key of 16 random bytes base64-encoded, Sec-WebSocket-Version 13, and an Origin header from browser clients.
The server must prove it received the handshake, so that it does not accept connections that are not WebSocket connections, such as crafted XMLHttpRequest or form submissions.
To prove it, the server appends a fixed GUID to the Sec-WebSocket-Key value, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes it and returns it in Sec-WebSocket-Accept.

The server replies 101 (Switching Protocols); any other status means the handshake has not completed and HTTP semantics still apply, and the client sends no frames if the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or wrong.

A server that rejects the handshake MUST return an HTTP error: for example 403 Forbidden for an unwanted origin, 426 Upgrade Required with its supported versions for a wrong version, or 404 Not Found for an unavailable service.
After the 101 response HTTP stops being used and communication switches to a binary frame-based protocol, in which both sides can send data in either direction.

A WebSocket can also be established over HTTP/2 with the extended CONNECT method of RFC 8441, which carries it in one stream so other streams keep carrying HTTP traffic; RFC 9220 adapts this for HTTP/3.

conflicts.text: Sec-WebSocket-Key and Sec-WebSocket-Accept are intended to prevent a caching proxy from re-sending a previous WebSocket conversation, and provide no authentication, privacy or integrity.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia gives a different purpose; the fact above follows RFC 6455, which says the server proves it read the handshake.

entries.title: WebSocket frames and messages

definition.text: After the opening handshake WebSocket exchanges messages made of one or more frames, which are either data frames (text or binary) or control frames (Close, Ping, Pong).

facts.text: Once the handshake is done, either side may send data messages (text or binary) and control messages (Close, Ping, Pong) at any time.

The protocol is frame-based rather than stream-based, with minimal framing; a message is one frame if unfragmented or two or more if fragmented, and intermediaries may split or coalesce frames, so endpoints must not depend on frame boundaries.
Fragmentation lets a sender start a message of unknown length without buffering it; without it the whole message must be buffered so its length can be counted before the first byte is sent.

An unfragmented message is one frame with FIN set and a non-zero opcode; a fragmented one starts with FIN clear and a non-zero opcode, continues with opcode 0 frames, and ends with an opcode 0 frame that has FIN set.

Fragments must arrive in order and must not interleave with another message's fragments unless an extension allows it; control frames may be injected between fragments, so a ping is not stuck behind a large message, but are never fragmented.
A frame header has a FIN bit, three reserved bits that must be 0 unless an extension defines them, a 4-bit opcode, a mask bit, a payload length, and a 32-bit masking key when the mask bit is 1.
Payload length uses 7 bits for 0 to 125; the value 126 means the next 16 bits hold the length and 127 means the next 64 bits do.
Opcodes are 0 continuation, 1 text, 2 binary, 8 Close, 9 Ping and 10 Pong; the protocol defines six frame types and reserves ten.

entries.title: WebSocket through proxies and load balancers

definition.text: WebSocket is unaware of proxies and firewalls, but its HTTP-compatible handshake lets it pass through HTTP infrastructure, though some proxies break it.

facts.text: The handshake is HTTP-compatible, so HTTP servers can share ports 80 and 443 with a WebSocket gateway or server; behind a configured proxy, the client sets up a persistent tunnel with HTTP CONNECT.
Some proxies are transparent and work with WebSocket, others make the connection fail; unencrypted traffic through a proxy without WebSocket support will likely fail.

Encrypted WebSocket Secure connections succeed more often: with an explicit proxy TLS ensures HTTP CONNECT is issued, and transparent proxies let encrypted traffic through; connections on port 443 are significantly more likely to succeed than on port 80.

A server may offload the connection to load balancers and reverse proxies; the RFC counts everything from the first device that terminates the TCP connection to the server that processes requests as the server.

With load balancers and multiple servers, a dedicated set of hosts for WebSocket connections, separate from the HTTP servers, is probably easier to manage, because interactive messaging traffic can induce unusual loads on some components.

Load balancers must support persistent connections so a server can keep a connection such as a WebSocket open with a client; nginx can act as reverse proxy and load balancer for WebSocket applications.

entries.title: WebSocket closing handshake: ending a connection cleanly

definition.text: The WebSocket closing handshake is an exchange of Close frames in which either peer asks to close and the other answers before the TCP connection is shut.

facts.text: Either peer can start by sending a Close control frame (opcode 8); the other replies with a Close frame if it has not already sent one, and both peers may safely start it at the same time.
After sending a Close frame a peer sends no more data frames; after receiving one it discards further data.
Once an endpoint has both sent and received Close it MUST close the TCP connection: the server immediately, the client ideally after waiting for the server to do so.
It complements the TCP closing handshake, which is not always reliable end-to-end with intercepting proxies, and avoids cases where data is lost unnecessarily.
Servers MAY close the connection whenever they want, but clients SHOULD NOT close it arbitrarily; either way closure begins with the closing handshake.
A Close frame may carry a 2-byte status code followed by a UTF-8 reason of at most 123 bytes; clients MUST NOT show the reason to end users.

Defined codes include 1000 normal closure, 1001 going away, 1002 protocol error, 1003 unsupported data, 1007 invalid payload data, 1008 policy violated, 1009 message too big and 1011 internal server error.

Codes 1005, 1006 and 1015 are reserved and MUST NOT be sent in a Close frame; 1000 to 2999 belong to the protocol, 3000 to 3999 to libraries and frameworks registered with IANA, and 4000 to 4999 to private use.

entries.title: Notification system architecture: from business service to your inbox

definition.text: A notification system takes notifications from business services, validates and schedules them, and delivers them through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.

facts.text: It covers in-app notifications, email notifications, SMS and OTP notifications, and social media pushes.
Business services send notifications to a notification gateway, which can take one notification at a time or batches of them.

The gateway forwards notifications to a distribution service that validates, formats and schedules them according to settings; a template repository pre-defines message formats and a channel preference repository pre-defines preferred delivery channels.
Notifications then go to routers, normally message queues, and channel services pass them to the internal and external delivery channels.
A tracking and analytics service captures delivery metrics so the operations team can view reports and improve the user experience.

entries.title: Webhooks: letting the other service call you

definition.text: A webhook is an endpoint in your application server that you hand to an external service as a callback, so the service calls it whenever something interesting happens.

facts.text: Instead of continuously asking for information, you create an endpoint in your application server and give it as a callback to the external service, such as a payment processor or a shipping vendor.
Every time something interesting happens, the external service calls the endpoint and provides the information.
Data is pushed to the application as soon as it is available, which makes webhooks ideal for real-time updates.
Webhooks are recommended for applications that need instant data delivery and are efficient in resource use, especially in high-throughput environments.
Network issues can cause missed notifications, so webhooks need proper retry mechanisms.
Webhooks are triggered by events such as a code push, a purchase or a blog comment, and because they use HTTP they fit into web services without new infrastructure.

The receiver should authenticate each incoming POST against spoofing and check its timestamp against replay, using an HMAC signature in a header, a shared secret, mutual TLS, basic authentication, or a sender IP list that is not sufficient alone.

Because a sender lets users set an arbitrary destination URL, OWASP names webhooks a common vector for server-side request forgery; the mitigation is to re-check the resolved IP before each delivery, not only at registration.

entries.title: WebSocket API: opening and using a socket from a browser

definition.text: The WebSocket API is the browser interface through which a web application opens a WebSocket, sends messages and reacts to events.

facts.text: The constructor new WebSocket(url [, protocols]) starts the opening handshake; the URL scheme must be ws, wss, http or https, with no fragment, and the default port is 80 for ws and http and 443 for wss and https.
send(data) takes a string, Blob, ArrayBuffer or ArrayBufferView; if the data cannot be sent because the buffer is full, the connection is closed and an error event fires.

The API raises open, message, close and error events; the close event reports a code, a reason and whether the closing handshake completed, with code 1005 when the Close frame has no payload and 1006 when none arrived.
readyState is CONNECTING (0), OPEN (1), CLOSING (2) or CLOSED (3); close(code, reason) accepts code 1000 or 3000 to 4999 and a reason of up to 123 UTF-8 bytes.

entries.title: HTTP streaming: a response that never ends

definition.text: HTTP server push, also called HTTP streaming, is a way of sending unsolicited asynchronous data from a web server to a web browser.

facts.text: The server does not close the connection after serving the response, so an event can go out immediately; otherwise it would be queued until the client's next request.
It can be built on chunked transfer encoding, or on the multipart/x-mixed-replace MIME type, which browsers treat as a document that changes whenever the server pushes a new version.
In the pushlet technique the server never ends the response and periodically sends snippets of JavaScript that update the page, so the client needs no Java applet or plug-in.
A drawback of pushlets is that the server cannot control browser timeouts, and a timeout forces a page refresh.

entries.text: The simplest way for a server to keep talking is never to finish the response. The server does not close the connection after serving the response, so an event can go out at once instead of waiting for the client's next request. It can use chunked transfer encoding or the multipart/x-mixed-replace content type from 1995. Browsers treat it as a document that changes with each push. Pushlets send snippets of JavaScript, but the server cannot control browser timeouts, and a timeout forces a page refresh.

entries.title: Server-sent events: a one-way stream over plain HTTP

definition.text: Server-sent events (SSE) is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection and the server can start sending data once the connection is established.

facts.text: The client requests a URL through the JavaScript EventSource API to receive an event stream, whose media type is text/event-stream; the API is standardized in the HTML Living Standard by the WHATWG.
The client makes a request, the connection stays open, and the server sends events whenever new data is available.
SSE is unidirectional: once the client has sent its request it can only receive responses, not send new requests over the same connection.
It is simple to implement for both client and server, supported by most browsers, and causes no trouble with firewalls.
Limits: the unidirectional nature, a cap on the number of open connections, and no support for binary data.
When sending high-frequency data the server must manage backpressure to avoid saturating clients, using client-side buffering, adaptive rate limiting that adjusts event frequency, or event batching.
Designs for real-time messaging and live location tracking can use either WebSockets or SSE.

entries.text_plain: With server-sent events, or SSE, the client makes one request and the connection stays open. The server then sends events whenever new data is available. SSE is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection. The client requests a URL through the JavaScript EventSource API to receive an event stream, whose media type is text/event-stream. The mechanism was first specified in 2004, and the W3C published it as a recommendation on February 3, 2015. SSE is simple to implement for both client and server, supported by most browsers and causes no trouble with firewalls. Its limits are that it is unidirectional, so the client can only receive once its request is sent. The number of open connections is capped, and binary data is not supported. When sending high-frequency data, the server must manage backpressure to avoid saturating clients, with client-side buffering, adaptive limits on the event rate, or event batching. Real-time messaging and live location tracking can use either WebSockets or SSE.

entries.title: Presence information: who is free, busy or away

definition.text: Presence information is a status indicator that conveys the ability and willingness of a potential communication partner to communicate.

facts.text: A client publishes a presence state to a presence service, which stores it as the user's personal availability record (the presentity) and distributes it to interested users, called watchers.
Presence is usually shown as an icon with states such as free for chat, busy, away or do not disturb; standards also allow attributes such as mood, location or free text.

Presence from several devices can be aggregated and inferred from observation, such as marking a user Away when the keyboard is idle; XMPP gives each client a resource and a priority, and messages go to the highest.
Presence is highly sensitive, so a presentity may limit what each watcher sees; a basic form is the blocking facility, which makes a user appear unavailable to selected watchers.

entries.title: XMPP: federated chat protocol with presence

definition.text: XMPP is an open, XML-based communication protocol for instant messaging, presence information and contact list maintenance, enabling near-real-time exchange of structured data between network entities.

facts.text: XMPP is extensible well beyond chat, serving as message-oriented middleware for VoIP signalling, video, file transfer and gaming, and it is defined in an open standard at the application layer.
The network is federated like email: anyone can run a server, there is no central master server, and users on any server interoperate through a Jabber ID.

A client sends a message to its own server, which delivers it instantly if the recipient is online and otherwise holds it; for a user on another server, the first server connects to that server over XMPP.

Clients reach servers over a TLS-encrypted TCP stream on port 5222 and servers talk to each other on port 5269; the core RFC 6120 uses two open-ended XML streams carrying presence, message and iq stanzas.
A Jabber ID looks like an email address, username@domain; an optional /resource suffix names one of the user's clients, such as home, work or mobile, so one user can log in from several places.
The native transport is long-lived TCP; for web clients and firewalled users there is BOSH over HTTP, which lets the server push messages as soon as they are sent, and XMPP can also use WebSockets.
Extensions called XEPs add features such as multi-user chat, Jingle for peer-to-peer VoIP sessions and OMEMO end-to-end encryption, so the server operator cannot decrypt the data it forwards.
Because XML is text, XMPP has higher network overhead than binary protocols, and in-band binary data must be base64 encoded, so large transfers such as files are best sent out-of-band.

entries.title: Push message delivery controls: TTL, urgency and topic

definition.text: Web push lets an application server control how long, how urgently and in what form a push message is held and delivered, through the TTL, Urgency and Topic headers.

facts.text: An application server MUST send a TTL header, in seconds, saying how long the push service keeps the message for intermittently connected devices; the service may keep it for less and MUST NOT deliver it once the TTL elapses.
A message with a zero TTL is delivered at once if the user agent is available and otherwise expires undelivered, so the application server cannot rely on acknowledgement receipts for it.

The Urgency header (very-low, low, normal, high; normal by default) helps battery-powered devices stay dormant: a user agent can state the lowest urgency it will accept, and the service MUST NOT deliver anything lower.
A message with a Topic header of up to 32 characters replaces any outstanding message with the same topic, so a device that was offline does not receive outdated or redundant messages.

entries.text: A web push message can be told how long to live, how urgent it is and which older message it replaces. With a zero TTL the message goes out at once if the user agent is available and otherwise expires. The Urgency header, from very-low to high, helps battery-powered devices stay dormant. A Topic header of up to 32 characters makes a message replace any outstanding one with the same topic, so an offline device receives no outdated messages.

entries.title: Reconnecting a WebSocket with backoff
entries.article: rfc>6455#7. Closing the Connection > 7.2. Abnormal Closures > 7.2.3. Recovering from Abnormal Closure

definition.text: After an abnormal closure a WebSocket client should wait a random, growing delay before reconnecting, so that many clients do not overwhelm the server.

facts.text: An abnormal closure may be transient, so reconnecting can work, or nontransient, in which case clients that all reconnect immediately and persistently amount to a denial-of-service attack that can keep the service from recovering.
Clients SHOULD use backoff when reconnecting: the first attempt SHOULD be delayed by a random time, and a value chosen randomly between 0 and 5 seconds is a reasonable initial delay.
If the first attempt fails, later attempts SHOULD wait increasingly longer, using a method such as truncated binary exponential backoff.
Terminated WebSocket connections are not automatically recovered.

entries.title: WebSocket URIs: ws and wss

definition.text: WebSocket defines two URI schemes, ws for unencrypted connections and wss for connections protected by TLS.

facts.text: The port is optional: the default is 80 for ws and 443 for wss, and a URI is called secure when its scheme is wss.
A wss URI indicates that the traffic is protected by TLS, with its usual confidentiality, integrity and endpoint authentication.
The resource name that the handshake requests is the path plus any query, or "/" when the path is empty, which lets one host and port serve several services.
Fragment identifiers are meaningless in WebSocket URIs and MUST NOT be used.

entries.title: WebSocket security: origin checks, TLS and validation

definition.text: WebSocket security rests on the browser's Origin header, TLS (wss) and server-chosen client authentication, because WebSocket requests are not covered by the same-origin policy.

facts.text: Unlike regular cross-domain HTTP requests, WebSocket requests are not restricted by the same-origin policy.

The Origin header tells the server which script origin made the request; a server meant only for certain sites SHOULD verify the origin is one it expects, and SHOULD answer an unacceptable origin with HTTP 403 Forbidden.
Without an origin check, cross-site WebSocket hijacking, similar to cross-site request forgery, is possible when the connection is authenticated with cookies or HTTP authentication.

The origin check ensures trusted browsers running malicious JavaScript cannot fake a handshake; it does not stop non-browser clients, which can send any Origin, so a server must not trust that any input is valid.
The protocol prescribes no client authentication: a server can use cookies, HTTP authentication or TLS authentication, and tokens are better when sensitive data is sent.
Confidentiality and integrity come from running over TLS (wss URIs); implementations MUST support TLS and SHOULD use it.
Incoming data MUST always be validated by both clients and servers; text messages must be valid UTF-8, and an endpoint that finds invalid UTF-8 MUST fail the connection.

A malicious endpoint can try to exhaust memory or mount denial of service with one huge frame or a long stream of small fragments, so implementations MUST protect themselves against exceeding their limits and SHOULD cap frame and message sizes.

conflicts.text: WebSocket servers must validate the Origin header against the expected origins during connection establishment.
conflicts.note: Wikipedia says must; RFC 6455 says a server that is not meant to process input from any web page SHOULD verify the Origin.

entries.title: WebSocket extensions: optional features negotiated up front

definition.text: WebSocket extensions let implementations opt in to additional protocol features, negotiated during the opening handshake.

facts.text: The base specification defines no extension; the client offers extensions in Sec-WebSocket-Extensions and the server accepts some or all by listing them in its response, never listing one the client did not request.
A client MUST NOT use an advertised extension unless the server indicates it wants to use it; the server's list is what is actually in use for the connection.
Order matters: the client's list is in order of preference, and operations are applied in the server's order, so "foo, bar" makes bar(foo(data)).
Extensions can use the three reserved RSV bits, opcodes 3 to 7 and 11 to 15, and the extension data field; permessage-deflate compresses data messages with DEFLATE and sets RSV1 on the first frame.

entries.title: WebSocket masking: stopping scripts from forging HTTP on the wire
entries.article: rfc>6455#10. Security Considerations > 10.3. Attacks On Infrastructure (Masking)

definition.text: WebSocket masking is the rule that a client XORs every frame it sends to the server with a random 32-bit key, so a script cannot control how its data looks on the wire.

facts.text: A client MUST mask all frames it sends to the server, whether or not TLS is used; a server MUST NOT mask the frames it sends, and a server MUST close the connection on receiving an unmasked frame.
Masking XORs each payload byte with the key byte at index i modulo 4 of a 32-bit masking key chosen by the client; the same algorithm masks and unmasks.
The client MUST choose a fresh masking key for every frame from a strong entropy source; unpredictability stops authors of malicious applications from selecting the bytes that appear on the wire.

The reason is an experiment in which attackers poisoned caching proxies by sending data on an upgraded connection that looked like an HTTP GET; masking client data stops a script making a message that an intermediary misreads as HTTP.

entries.title: WebSocket ping and pong: checking the other end is alive
entries.article: rfc>6455#5. Data Framing > 5.5. Control Frames > 5.5.2. Ping

definition.text: Ping and Pong are WebSocket control frames used as keepalive and heartbeat, to check that the other endpoint is still responsive.

facts.text: Either side may send a Ping at any time after the connection is established and before it is closed; it can serve as a keepalive, a latency measurement or a check that the remote endpoint is responsive.
An endpoint that receives a Ping MUST answer with a Pong, unless it already received a Close frame, as soon as practical, and the Pong must carry the same application data as the Ping.
A Pong may also be sent unsolicited as a unidirectional heartbeat, and no response to it is expected; a Pong with no prior Ping is ignored.

entries.title: WebSocket subprotocols: agreeing what the messages mean
entries.article: rfc>6455#1. Introduction > 1.9. Subprotocols Using the WebSocket Protocol

definition.text: A WebSocket subprotocol is an application-level protocol layered over WebSocket messages, which the client and server agree on in the opening handshake.

facts.text: The client lists the subprotocols it accepts in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, ordered by preference; the server selects one of those values and echoes it, and must not reply with a value the client did not offer.
Subprotocol names should be registered and should contain the ASCII domain name of the originator to avoid collisions, such as "chat.example.com".
Competing subprotocols with different names can be served at once, with the server choosing dynamically from the value the client sent.

A backward-incompatible change is versioned by renaming the subprotocol, for example to "v2.bookings.example.net", which clients treat as completely separate; a backward-compatible change reuses the same string.

entries.title: WebSocket version negotiation
entries.article: rfc>6455#4. Opening Handshake > 4.4. Supporting Multiple Versions of WebSocket Protocol

definition.text: WebSocket version negotiation lets a client request a protocol version in the handshake and the server answer with the versions it supports if it cannot accept it.

facts.text: A client states the version it prefers in Sec-WebSocket-Version, which need not be the latest it supports; if the server supports it and the handshake is otherwise valid, the server accepts that version.

If the server does not support the requested version it MUST answer with Sec-WebSocket-Version header fields listing every version it is willing to use, for example with an HTTP error such as 426 Upgrade Required.
If the client supports one of the advertised versions, it can repeat the handshake with that version value.

entries.text: What happens when a client asks for a WebSocket version the server does not speak? The refusal doubles as an offer. A client states the version it prefers in Sec-WebSocket-Version, which need not be the latest it supports. If the server supports it and the handshake is otherwise valid, the server accepts. If not, the server must answer with Sec-WebSocket-Version header fields listing every version it is willing to use. An HTTP error such as 426 Upgrade Required can carry them. A client that supports one of the advertised versions can then repeat the handshake with that version value.

entries.title: Comet: the workaround WebSocket made obsolete

definition.text: Comet is a web application model in which a long-held HTTPS request lets a web server push data to a browser without the browser explicitly requesting it.

facts.text: Comet is an umbrella term for several techniques that give the browser two-way sustained interaction with the server, all relying on default browser features such as JavaScript rather than plugins.

Implementations fall into streaming, which keeps one persistent connection for all events (a hidden iframe filled with script tags, or XMLHttpRequest), and long polling, where each response ends the request and the browser opens a new one.

No streaming transport works in every browser, so many applications use long polling, which works wherever XHR does; a held connection can block other requests under HTTP 1.1's connection advice, so a separate hostname is used (domain sharding).
The standardisation of WebSocket and Server-sent events, widely supported since 2020, has rendered the Comet model obsolete.

entries.title: The C10k problem: ten thousand connections at once

definition.text: The C10k problem was the problem of optimizing networking stacks to handle ten thousand concurrent clients at the same time.

facts.text: Handling many concurrent connections differs from handling many requests per second: the latter needs high throughput, the former needs efficient scheduling of connections to sockets or other stateful endpoints.
Supporting many clients involves operating system constraints and web server limits, a choice between multi-threading and single threading, memory management, and the strategy for I/O.
The problem is solved: by the early 2010s a commodity server held millions of connections, for example WhatsApp over 2 million with Erlang and MigratoryData 10-12 million with Java.

Nginx was originally developed to solve C10k and handles more than 10,000 simultaneous connections with a low memory footprint; very high connection counts matter for proxy servers, web servers and load balancers.

entries.title: Running a push service: connections, storage and security

definition.text: A push service must hold very many open connections and stored messages, deliver reliably, and be secured with TLS, end-to-end encryption and rate limits.

facts.text: A push service holds a very large number of open TCP connections and can redistribute load with 307 redirects or HTTP alternative services; storing messages for their TTL can also take a significant amount of storage.

Reliable delivery with receipts avoids retransmissions, polling and state resynchronization; without it a device must acknowledge directly to the application server at extra power cost, though transient messages such as an incoming call may not need reliability.

The protocol MUST use HTTP over TLS, but TLS does not hide content from the push service, so applications MUST add end-to-end confidentiality, integrity and authentication, as Message Encryption for WebPush does.

Push URIs should be hard to guess and shared only with authorized application servers; a push service SHOULD limit the message rate per user agent, can answer 429 with Retry-After, and may end subscriptions that get too many messages.

entries.text: A push service has to hold a very large number of open TCP connections, and storing messages for their TTL can take a significant amount of storage. Reliable delivery with receipts avoids retransmissions and polling. Without it, a device must acknowledge directly to the application server at extra power cost. The protocol must use HTTP over TLS, but TLS does not hide content from the push service. Applications must add end-to-end confidentiality, integrity and a way to check who sent a message. Push URIs should be hard to guess, and a push service should limit the message rate per user agent, for example by answering 429 with Retry-After.

entries.title: Rate limiting: capping how often an operation may run

definition.text: Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit.

facts.text: Large-scale systems use rate limiting to protect underlying services and resources; it is a defensive mechanism that lets shared resources stay available.
It protects APIs from unintended or malicious overuse by limiting how many requests can reach the API in a given period.
It avoids resource starvation caused by denial-of-service attacks, limits web scraping and can mitigate some other common attacks.
It controls operational costs by putting a virtual cap on auto-scaling, which unmonitored could lead to exponential bills.
It also controls data flow for APIs that process massive amounts of data, and data centers use it to share resources among tenants and applications according to their service level agreement.

A server checks the user session or IP address against a session cache, often a central in-memory key-value store such as Redis or Aerospike, and HTTP servers can answer too many requests with status 429.
Over the limit, a server or device offloads new requests without responding or queues them, but at peak times the request rate can exceed the queue capacity and requests are thrown away.
A hardware appliance limiting by IP address on layer 4 risks blocking a whole network of users behind one NAT address, so for dynamic content the limiting logic should be built into the application.

entries.title: Fault tolerance: keeping going while parts are broken

definition.text: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to contain the propagation of faults and keep operating without failure while some components are faulty.

facts.text: Faults may show up as errors, such as a bad data value or missing message, that cause incorrect system state; fault-tolerant systems mask the errors and maintain failure-free operation despite one or more faulty components.
The capability is essential for high-availability, mission-critical and life-critical systems.
Strictly, it means handling faults with no degradation or downtime and users unaware of any issue; a system that suffers some interruption or graceful degradation of performance is termed resilient.

It requires no single point of failure, fault isolation to the failing component through dedicated failure detection, fault containment so a failure does not propagate, and reversion modes that abandon recent changes.
Fault-tolerant systems are typically based on redundancy and are judged by availability expressed as a percentage; a five nines system statistically provides 99.999% availability.

Making every component fault tolerant is normally not an option because redundancy costs weight, size, power, money and design time, so choose by how critical, how likely to fail and how expensive each component is.
A system that rarely has problems is not necessarily fault tolerant: one that fails only rarely but stops operating completely when a fault occurs is fault resistant, not fault tolerant.

entries.title: Fault tolerance techniques: replicas, standbys and spare parts

definition.text: Fault tolerance techniques use spare or independent components, such as replicas, standbys, load balancing and monitoring, so that a failure does not stop the service.

facts.text: Replication runs multiple identical instances in parallel, sends requests to all of them and picks the correct result by quorum; ByteByteGo describes it more broadly as multiple copies of data or services across nodes or locations.
Redundancy provides multiple identical instances and switches to a remaining one when a failure occurs, which is failover; redundancy means additional components that can take over.
Diversity provides multiple different implementations of the same specification and uses them like replicas, to cope with errors in one specific implementation.
Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single server becomes a point of failure, and failover mechanisms automatically switch to a standby when the primary fails.

Continuous monitoring of system health and performance, with alerts for anomalies or failures, completes the six principles ByteByteGo lists: replication, redundancy, load balancing, failover, graceful degradation, monitoring.
Every RAID level except RAID 0 is a fault-tolerant storage device that uses data redundancy.
The circuit breaker design pattern is a technique to avoid catastrophic failures in distributed systems.

entries.title: Cascading failure: when one outage causes the next

definition.text: A cascading failure is a failure in a system of interconnected parts in which the failure of one or a few parts causes other parts to fail, growing progressively through positive feedback.

facts.text: When one part fails, the other parts must compensate for it; that overloads them so they fail too, prompting more nodes to fail one after another.

In computer networks it is usually caused by overloading a single crucial router or node, or by taking one down for maintenance; traffic moves to an alternative path, which becomes overloaded in turn.

Symptoms are packet loss and high latency across whole sections of a network; congested nodes stay present but pass little useful traffic, so routes still look valid. A walking failure lets sections fail and recover in turn.

In a service, overload is the most common cause: if cluster B fails and cluster A's load rises from 1,000 to 1,200 QPS, A's frontends run out of resources and successful requests fall below 1,000 QPS.

Local overload can spread to other failure domains, even globally: crashing servers push requests to other clusters and overload them, which can take only a couple of minutes because load balancers and schedulers act quickly.
Once a couple of servers crash, the rest take more load and crash too until all servers crash-loop; recovery is hard because restarted servers are bombarded with requests and fail almost immediately.
A cache stampede is one kind of cascading failure, which can occur when massively parallel systems with caches come under very high load.
Monitoring a system in real time and judiciously disconnecting parts can help stop a cascade, as can simulating possible failures to set safe operating levels below which no cascade is predicted.

entries.title: Deadline propagation: passing the remaining time down the call tree

definition.text: An RPC deadline says how long a request may wait before the caller gives up, and deadline propagation passes the remaining time down the whole call tree.

facts.text: A deadline limits how long a backend can consume a frontend's resources while the frontend waits for a reply; with no deadline or an extremely high one, long-gone problems keep consuming server resources.

Short deadlines make some expensive requests fail consistently, but deadlines orders of magnitude above mean latency are bad: at a 100-second deadline, 5% of requests hitting it would need 5,000 threads on a 1,000-thread frontend.

Servers wasting resources on requests that exceed the client's deadline is a common theme in cascading outages; a server should check the remaining deadline before each stage instead of doing work nobody will credit.

With propagation, a deadline is set high in the stack and every RPC in the tree shares the same absolute deadline: a 30-second deadline with 7 seconds spent leaves 23 seconds for the next call, then 19.

Without propagation a server keeps working on doomed requests: if B uses a hardcoded 20-second deadline after A gave it 10 seconds, C processes a request believing it has 15 seconds although the deadline has passed.

Shorten the outgoing deadline slightly for network transit and post-processing, and consider an upper bound for noncritical or usually fast backends, but know the traffic mix so large requests do not always fail.

Cancellation propagation tells servers down the call stack their work is no longer needed, as when hedged requests are cancelled after the first reply; fatal errors and timeouts sent up the stack cancel other RPCs.
Requests that cannot complete should return an error early instead of waiting the full deadline; mean latency can hide this bimodal latency, so look at the latency distribution when latency rises.

entries.title: Resource exhaustion: when a server runs out of room

definition.text: Resource exhaustion is a server running out of CPU, memory, threads or file descriptors under load, which can start a cascading failure.

facts.text: Running out of a resource raises latency and error rates or substitutes lower-quality results; it can make a server less efficient or crash it, so the load balancer shifts the problem to other servers and a cascade can follow.

With too little CPU all requests slow down, so more are in flight at once, using more memory, threads, file descriptors and backend resources, and queues saturate, which raises latency and memory use.

An overloaded server's late responses may miss client deadlines, so its work is wasted and clients retry, adding overload; thread starvation can also make health checks fail, and watchdogs may kill the server.

More in-flight requests use more RAM, and tasks can be evicted or crash; in Java, memory pressure raises garbage collection and CPU use, so less CPU slows requests further, the so-called GC death spiral.
Less RAM can shrink application-level caches, cutting hit rates and sending more RPCs to backends that may then overload.

Thread starvation causes errors or health check failures and thread overhead can use too much RAM; running out of file descriptors prevents new network connections, which in turn can make health checks fail.

Exhaustion scenarios feed one another, so an overloaded service shows secondary symptoms that look like the root cause: poor GC tuning can exhaust CPU, shrink the cache, overload the backend and fail health checks.

entries.title: Load shedding: refusing some work to finish the rest

definition.text: Load shedding drops some proportion of traffic as a server approaches overload, so the server keeps doing useful work instead of failing.

facts.text: The goal is to keep the server from running out of RAM, failing health checks or serving with extremely high latency, while still doing as much useful work as it can.

A straightforward way is per-task throttling based on CPU, memory or queue length; one effective approach returns HTTP 503 to any request when more than a given number of client requests are in flight.

Past its breaking point, a service does better to let some user-visible errors or lower-quality results through than to try to serve every request; servers should fail early and cheaply when overloaded.

Switching the queue from first-in first-out to last-in first-out, or using the CoDel algorithm, removes requests unlikely to be worth processing, such as one the user has already given up on and refreshed.
More sophisticated approaches identify clients to be more selective about what is dropped, or prioritize more important requests; such strategies are more likely to be needed for shared services.

Shedding can be indiscriminate, dropping all traffic above X requests per second, or selective, dropping low-priority work such as background synchronization while still serving interactive user sessions.

Decide which metrics trigger shedding (CPU usage, latency, queue length, threads used), whether degraded mode starts automatically, and at which layer to implement it or whether a high-level choke-point suffices.

The code path you never use often does not work: regularly run a small subset of servers near overload to exercise it, alert when many servers enter these modes, and keep a way to turn complex schemes off quickly.

entries.title: Client-side throttling: slowing down before the backend says no

definition.text: Client-side throttling lets a client that sees many of its recent requests rejected cap its own outgoing traffic, rather than leaving the backend to reject them.

facts.text: Rejecting a request still costs resources, and for cheap work such as a RAM lookup it costs almost as much as serving it, so a backend can be overloaded even when most of its CPU goes to rejecting.

When a client detects that a significant portion of its recent requests were rejected as out of quota, it self-regulates and caps its outgoing traffic; requests above the cap fail locally without reaching the network.

In adaptive throttling each client task keeps, for the last two minutes, the requests attempted by the application and the requests accepted by the backend; normally equal, accepts fall below requests as the backend rejects traffic.

Clients keep sending until requests reach K times accepts, then reject new requests locally with a probability that rises as the application's request rate grows relative to the rate the backend accepts.

A lower multiplier K makes adaptive throttling more aggressive and a higher one less aggressive: self-regulating at requests = 1.1 * accepts means the backend rejects only one request per 10 accepted.

The SRE book prefers a 2x multiplier, since letting more requests reach the backend wastes some resources but spreads backend state faster; backends then reject about one request for each they process.
The decision uses only local information, with a simple implementation and no added dependencies or latency, but it may not work well for clients that send requests only sporadically.

entries.title: Bandwidth throttling: limiting how fast data moves

definition.text: Bandwidth throttling is the limiting of the rate of data transfer to or from a network node or device such as a computer or mobile phone.

facts.text: A bandwidth-intensive device such as a server throttles the speed at which it receives or sends data so it does not overload its processing capacity or saturate network bandwidth.
Client requests peak and responses can be huge, exceeding the capacity of parts of the network and causing congestion, which leads to request failures or, in the worst case, server crashes.

Throttling can be done in a client or server program, limiting data it sends or receives, or at the network management level, typically by an ISP; limiting at the sender is more efficient because no packets are lost.

Throttling limits how much data a device receives from each client or sends per response, while capping limits total transfer capacity over a medium; unlike rate limiting, which works on client requests, it should be paired with it.

Together they can exceed the capacity of parts of the network, causing congestion, request failures and, in the worst case, server crashes. Bandwidth throttling is the limiting of the rate of data transfer to or from a network node or device, such as a computer or mobile phone. A server throttles how fast it receives or sends data so it does not overload its processing capacity or saturate network bandwidth. Limiting at the sender is more efficient, because no packets are lost. Unlike rate limiting, which works on requests, it limits data, so the two should be paired.

entries.title: Token bucket: letting bursts through at a steady average

definition.text: The token bucket is an algorithm that checks whether traffic conforms to limits on bandwidth and burstiness, using a bucket that fills with tokens at a fixed rate.

facts.text: A fixed-capacity bucket gets a token every 1/r seconds and holds at most b tokens; a token arriving at a full bucket is discarded.
A packet of n bytes conforms if at least n tokens are in the bucket, which removes n tokens and sends the packet; otherwise no tokens are removed and the packet is non-conformant.
In API rate limiting, each request must take a token, and a request is refused when no token is available, so the requester has to try again later as the bucket refreshes.
Non-conformant packets can be queued until enough tokens accumulate, or sent marked as non-conformant and possibly dropped later if the network is overloaded.
A conforming flow can have an average rate up to the token rate and a burstiness set by the depth of the bucket; over the long run the conformant output is limited by the token rate r.
It can be used for traffic shaping, where packets are delayed until they conform, or for traffic policing, where nonconforming packets are dropped or reduced in priority.
It also controls database IO flow, where the limit applies to a linear combination of IOPS and bandwidth rather than to either alone.

entries.title: Leaky bucket: a constant leak and an overflow

definition.text: The leaky bucket is an algorithm based on the analogy of a bucket with a constant leak that overflows if water is poured in faster than it leaks or all at once beyond its capacity.

facts.text: It checks whether a sequence of discrete events conforms to limits on average and peak rates, and can limit the actions tied to those events to those rates or delay them until they conform.

As a meter, a counter is incremented as each packet or event arrives and decremented at a fixed rate; the event conforms if the counter stays below a limit value, meaning the bucket does not overflow.
In the original description, the decrement rate sets the average bandwidth and the threshold sets burstiness, and the network discards a packet if the counter exceeds the threshold when incremented.
As a queue, it is a finite FIFO buffer serviced at a fixed rate: an arrival is appended if there is room and discarded otherwise, and one packet is sent per clock tick.
For API rate limiting, the queue version appends each request to the end of a queue, processes the first item at a regular interval, and discards or leaks additional requests when the queue is full.
The queue implementation is always a traffic shaping function that sends at a fixed rate, though the output has gaps if the queue becomes empty.
The queue version is a special case of the meter version.
It is used in packet-switched and telecommunications networks for traffic policing, traffic shaping and scheduling of data transmissions to defined limits on bandwidth and burstiness.

entries.title: Resilience patterns: keeping a small error small

definition.text: Resilience patterns are design patterns that limit the damage failures do, so a small error does not snowball into an outage.

facts.text: The largest incidents are usually caused by something very small: a minor error starts a snowball effect that keeps building up, and suddenly everything is down.

Patterns that reduce the damage of failures include circuit breaker, rate limiting, load shedding, back pressure and let it crash; they are usually not used alone, so know why each is needed, how it works and its limits.
A circuit breaker wraps the protected call and monitors for failures; once they reach a threshold it trips, and further calls return an error without the protected call being made.

Rate limiting is a defensive mechanism that keeps shared resources available, but it ignores overall service health, so it may not stop a failure already begun, and simple versions leave capacity unused.
Load shedding drops some proportion of traffic as a server approaches overload, so it avoids running out of RAM or failing health checks while still doing as much useful work as it can.
Back pressure limits the queue size, keeping throughput high and response times good for jobs already queued; once the queue fills, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status and try again later.
Graceful degradation takes load shedding a step further by reducing the work each request needs, for example by returning lower-quality results when the server is overloaded.
Retries must be bounded or they amplify an overload: limit retries per request, consider a server-wide retry budget and use randomized exponential backoff.

entries.title: Fail fast or fail safe: choosing how a system breaks

definition.text: A fail-fast component reports at the first point of failure, and a fail-safe design fails in a way that protects people, property or data.

facts.text: A fail-fast component is designed to report at the first point of failure rather than after downstream components fail, which allows easier diagnosis and may prevent improper operation in a broken state.
A system designed to fail safe does so in a way that protects people, property or data from injury, damage, intrusion or disclosure, whether it keeps working at a reduced level or fails completely.
A program can fail safe by exiting gracefully instead of crashing in an uncontrolled way, to prevent data corruption after an error.
Singh's guide advises microservices to fail fast by using a circuit breaker to achieve fault tolerance.

entries.title: Graceful degradation: doing less instead of stopping

definition.text: A system with graceful degradation keeps running at reduced functionality or performance after a component fails instead of failing completely.

facts.text: A system designed for graceful degradation, or to fail soft, operates at a reduced level of performance after some component fails rather than stopping.
Examples are a building that runs lighting at reduced levels after a grid failure, and a video stream that falls back to a lower-resolution version when network bandwidth is insufficient.
Progressive enhancement is another example: web pages are available in a basic functional format for limited browsers and in an enhanced version for capable ones.
In resilience, the system adapts to the error and maintains service while accepting some impact on performance.

entries.title: Recovering from a cascading failure

definition.text: Recovering from a cascading failure means identifying it, then adding capacity, reducing load, restarting wedged servers or degrading service until the system stabilizes.

facts.text: If the system runs at degraded capacity and you have idle resources, adding tasks is the most expedient recovery, though in a death spiral more resources may not be enough.

Health checking can itself make a service unhealthy, so temporarily disabling it can let the system stabilize; process health checks matter to the cluster scheduler and service health checks to the load balancer.

Restart wedged servers, for example in a GC death spiral or a deadlock, only after identifying the source of the failure, canary the change and go slowly, since a cold cache could make restarts amplify the failure.

Dropping load is a big hammer: if a service healthy at 10,000 QPS fails at 11,000, dropping to 9,000 will not stop the crashes, and with 10% of servers healthy the rate would need to fall to about 1,000 QPS.

If the whole service is crash-looping, be aggressive and let through perhaps 1% of traffic, then ramp up gradually so caches warm up; fix the root cause first or the cascade returns once traffic comes back.
Serve degraded results by doing less work or dropping unimportant traffic; this must be engineered into the service and requires knowing which traffic can be degraded.
Turn off important but not critical load such as index updates, data copies or statistics gathering, and block or eliminate queries that create heavy load or crashes, such as queries of death.

entries.title: Rate limiting algorithms: five ways to count requests

definition.text: The main rate-limiting algorithms are leaky bucket, token bucket, fixed window, sliding log and sliding window, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.

facts.text: Leaky bucket appends each request to a queue that is processed first-in, first-out at a regular interval; when the queue is full, additional requests are discarded.
Token bucket requires each request to take a token from a bucket; with no token available the request is refused and the requester must try again later, and the bucket refreshes after a time period.
Fixed window tracks a counter for a window of n seconds, increments it on each request and discards the request when the counter exceeds a threshold.
Sliding log keeps a time-stamped log for each request in a time-sorted hash set or table and discards logs whose timestamps are beyond a threshold.
For a new request, sliding log sums the logs to find the request rate and holds the request if it would exceed the threshold rate.
Sliding window is a hybrid that keeps fixed window's low processing cost and sliding log's better boundary behavior, adding a weighted value of the previous window's rate to smooth traffic bursts.

entries.title: Rate limiting across a cluster of servers

definition.text: Rate limiting across a cluster of nodes is hard because of inconsistent per-node counters and race conditions on shared counters.

facts.text: A cluster may need a global rate limit; if each node tracks its own, a consumer can exceed the global limit by sending requests to different nodes, and more nodes make that likelier.
Sticky sessions in the load balancer send each consumer to exactly one node, but cause a lack of fault tolerance and scaling problems.
A centralized data store such as Redis is another approach, but it increases latency and causes race conditions.
A naive get-then-set counter reads, increments and writes back; extra requests slip in during that cycle and store stale lower values, letting a consumer bypass the limit.
A distributed lock around the counter key prevents that race, but the lock becomes a significant bottleneck and does not scale well.
A set-then-get approach lets counters be incremented and checked quickly without atomic operations getting in the way.

entries.title: Measuring capacity beyond queries per second

definition.text: Queries per second is often a poor measure of capacity because query costs vary, so capacity is better measured directly in resources such as CPU.

facts.text: Different queries need vastly different resources, depending on arbitrary factors such as the client code issuing them or the time of day, for example home versus work users, or interactive versus batch traffic.

Modeling capacity as queries per second, or by static request features like how many keys are read, often makes a poor metric because the ratios can change, sometimes drastically after a software release.
A better solution is to measure capacity directly in available resources, for example 500 CPU cores and 1 TB of memory reserved for a service in a datacenter.

The cost of a request is a normalized measure of CPU time, and CPU consumption usually works as the provisioning signal; where over-provisioning other resources is too expensive, each resource is considered separately.

entries.title: Per-customer quotas: errors only for the misbehaving

definition.text: Per-customer quotas cap the resources each customer of a shared backend may use, so under global overload only misbehaving customers get errors.

facts.text: Global overload occurs quite frequently, especially for internal services with many clients, and when it does the service should deliver errors only to misbehaving customers while other customers remain unaffected.

Owners provision capacity from negotiated usage and set per-customer quotas, such as up to 4,000 CPU seconds per second for one client of a 10,000-CPU backend; quotas may sum above capacity since customers rarely all peak together.

Global usage is aggregated in real time from all backend tasks and effective limits are pushed to individual tasks; computing the CPU each request consumes is tricky for servers that are not thread-per-request.

entries.title: Request criticality: rejecting the least important first

definition.text: Criticality tags each request with how important it is, so an overloaded backend rejects the least critical traffic first.

facts.text: A request has one of four criticality values: CRITICAL_PLUS for the most critical, a default for production jobs, SHEDDABLE_PLUS (the batch default) where partial unavailability is expected, and a lowest tier.

A task rejects requests of one criticality only once it is rejecting all lower ones; as utilization nears configured thresholds it rejects by criticality, and adaptive throttling keeps separate stats per criticality.
Criticality is independent of latency needs: search suggestions shown while typing are highly sheddable yet have stringent latency requirements.
The RPC system propagates criticality, so requests issued while serving request A inherit it; it is set as close as possible to browsers or mobile clients, and overridden only where that makes sense.

entries.title: Cascading failure triggers: what sets off the domino effect

definition.text: Cascading failure triggers are the disturbances that start the domino effect in a service already susceptible to it, such as process death, updates, rollouts, growth and drains.

facts.text: Server tasks may die and reduce available capacity, for example from a Query of Death, an RPC whose contents trigger a failure in the process, from cluster issues or from assertion failures.

Pushing a new binary or configuration to many tasks at once can start a cascade; keep capacity overhead in the update infrastructure or push off-peak, and check recent changes and consider reverting them during one.
A cascade often has no specific change behind it: usage simply grew without an adjustment to capacity.

Planned changes, drains and turndowns can remove capacity or add latency by sending requests to a distant cluster, and shifted traffic or code changes alter the request profile and the average cost of a payload.

entries.title: Cold caches and slow starts

definition.text: A freshly started process or an empty cache serves requests more slowly than in steady state, which can overload a service that is not provisioned for it.

facts.text: Processes respond more slowly just after starting, for example while setting up connections or doing just-in-time compilation; when most requests are served from caches, an empty cache makes 100% of requests costly.
A latency cache lets a service sustain its expected load with an empty cache, while a capacity cache does not; caches added for performance can become hard dependencies.
A cache is cold when a new cluster is turned up, a cluster returns after maintenance with possibly stale contents, or a task has recently restarted and must refill it.

Mitigations are to overprovision, reject requests when overloaded, and add load to a cluster slowly so a small request rate warms the cache first; keeping all clusters at nominal load keeps caches warm.

entries.title: Load testing to failure: finding the breaking point

definition.text: Load testing to failure pushes each component until it breaks, to learn its breaking point and how it behaves beyond it before an overload hits.

facts.text: Past its limit a component should serve errors or degraded results without significantly reducing the rate of successful requests; a fragile one crashes or errors heavily, while a better one rejects a few requests and survives.

Test both gradual and impulse load because caching effects differ, and test how the component returns to nominal load: whether it leaves degraded mode without human intervention and how far load must drop after crashes.

Load test each component separately since breaking points differ, and consider failure tests in a small slice of production, which is more realistic than synthetic traffic, with extra capacity ready to fail over.

Test how large clients behave, such as whether they use randomized exponential backoff, and that a noncritical backend that blackholes requests does not make the frontend reject requests or run out of resources.
