entries.title: JWT security pitfalls

facts.text: A JWT's contents cannot be relied on in a trust decision unless they are cryptographically secured and bound to its context, and the signing key must verifiably be under the control of the party named as issuer.

Some JWT libraries validated tokens wrongly based on the alg field, most commonly by accepting alg=none; developers should never let the JWT header alone drive verification and should not depend on the alg field alone.
Even a token that validates should be rejected unless the algorithms it uses are acceptable to the application, because which algorithms may be used in a given context is an application decision.
A JWT should be sent to the client by a secure mechanism such as an HTTP-only cookie, because local or session storage can be read by client-side JavaScript, including browser extensions.

If a service must be able to invalidate a session before the token expires, it can no longer trust the token alone and must check a data store, which removes the statelessness that is the main advantage of JWTs.

A JWT may carry privacy-sensitive information. Prevent disclosure by encrypting the token and authenticating the recipient, or by sending it only over an encrypted protocol with endpoint authentication such as TLS; omitting the data is simplest.
Some have argued that JWTs are hard to use securely because the standard offers many algorithms and options, and that alternate standards should be used instead.

entries.title: Argon2: a password hash that costs memory

definition.text: Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition.

facts.text: It uses a large, fixed-size memory region to make brute-force attacks computationally expensive, and all three modes are tuned by execution time, memory required and degree of parallelism.

Argon2d maximizes resistance to GPU cracking with password-dependent memory access, which risks side-channel attacks; Argon2i accesses memory independently of the password to resist them; Argon2id is a hybrid of the two.
RFC 9106 recommends Argon2id if one does not know the difference between the types or if side-channel attacks are a viable threat, partly because published attacks target Argon2i.
RFC 9106 recommends 2 GiB of memory, 1 iteration and parallelism 4 as a default for all environments, and 64 MiB, 3 iterations and parallelism 4 for memory-constrained environments.

entries.title: bcrypt: a hash that can be made slower

definition.text: bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières.

facts.text: It incorporates a salt against rainbow table attacks and is adaptive: the iteration count can be raised over time, so it stays resistant to brute-force search as computing power grows.
Its expensive key setup uses both salt and password and repeats a configurable number of rekeying rounds, so the hashing can be made arbitrarily slow, which deters brute force.
Inputs are a password of up to 72 bytes, a cost and a 16-byte salt; the cost is log2 of the iterations, so 12 means 4,096; the output is a 24-byte hash.
Passwords are cut at 72 bytes, only 18 characters in the worst case of 4-byte UTF-8, and bcrypt is not a key derivation function: it cannot derive a 512-bit key from a password.

entries.title: How attackers get around MFA

definition.text: MFA can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws.

facts.text: Many MFA approaches remain vulnerable to phishing, man-in-the-browser and man-in-the-middle attacks, so users should not share verification codes with anyone.

SMS codes are weak: phones can be cloned, maintenance personnel can read texts, SS7 vulnerabilities let messages be redirected to attackers, and SIM swap attacks hand duplicate SIM cards to criminals.

An MFA fatigue attack floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake; number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

Implementation flaws bypass MFA too: tokens issued before MFA must not reach sensitive resources, and without rate limiting an attacker can guess codes, resetting a limit tied to a session ID with new sessions.

entries.text_plain: MFA raises the bar, but it can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws. Many approaches remain vulnerable to phishing, man-in-the-browser and man-in-the-middle attacks, so users should not share verification codes with anyone. SMS codes are weak. Phones can be cloned, and maintenance personnel can read texts. SS7 vulnerabilities let messages be redirected to attackers, and SIM swap attacks hand duplicate SIM cards to criminals. An MFA fatigue attack floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake. Number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

entries.title: Identity provider

definition.text: An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications.

facts.text: It authenticates a user either by validating a username and password or by validating an assertion about the user's identity from a separate identity provider.
It manages user identities so that service providers are freed from that responsibility; service providers rely on it to assert who a user is and typically to manage certain user attributes.
A service provider may still keep a local account for the user, holding attributes unique to its own service.
An identity broker is an intermediary connecting many service providers with different identity providers, so single sign-on works with any application regardless of the protocol it follows.

entries.title: Single sign-on: log in once, reach everything

definition.text: Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications.

facts.text: It removes the need to log in separately to each application, and true single sign-on lets the user access services without re-entering authentication factors.
Credentials and identity information are kept and managed by a central Identity Provider, a trusted system that gives access to other websites and applications.

In the flow, the user requests a resource, the application redirects them to the identity provider, the user signs in, the identity provider sends a single sign-on response to the application, and the application grants access.

Single sign-on differs from same sign-on, where every application still asks for authentication but reuses credentials from a directory server; true single sign-on passes one authentication token to the configured applications.

Because applications support different authentication mechanisms, single sign-on must store the credentials used at first sign-in and translate them for each system; the converse, single log-out, ends access to several systems with one action.

Schemes such as OpenID Connect can be configured for single sign-on if extras like user consent are disabled; federated social logons that ask for consent choices are not always single sign-on in the strictest sense.
Benefits include one set of credentials to remember, less password fatigue, enforced security and compliance, and lower IT support cost and administration time.

It is commonly used in enterprises where employees need many of the organization's applications; a simple version over IP networks uses cookies, but only if the sites share a common DNS parent domain.

entries.title: Kerberos: tickets instead of passwords on the wire

definition.text: Kerberos is a ticket-based network authentication protocol that lets nodes on a non-secure network prove their identity to one another securely.

facts.text: It targets the client-server model and gives mutual authentication, with both user and server verifying each other, and its messages are protected against eavesdropping and replay attacks.
It builds on symmetric-key cryptography and needs a trusted third party, the key distribution center (KDC), whose authentication server (AS) and ticket-granting service (TGS) issue the tickets.

At logon the client authenticates to the AS, which returns a time-stamped ticket-granting ticket (TGT) encrypted with the TGS's secret key; the password is never sent, and v5 clients prove knowledge with an encrypted timestamp.
To use a service the client sends the TGT to the TGS, which checks it and issues a service ticket and session keys; the client presents the ticket to the service server with its request.
The service decrypts the ticket with its own secret key and checks the client's authenticator; it answers with the timestamp encrypted under the session key, so the client can trust the server.
Tickets have a lifetime, so hosts' clocks must be synchronized within configured limits (five minutes apart by default in MIT's setup) or authentication fails; NTP daemons usually keep them in sync.
Because a central KDC controls all authentications, compromising it lets an attacker impersonate any user, and each network service with a different host name needs its own Kerberos keys.
Windows 2000 and later use Kerberos as the default method for domain-joined clients, and fall back to NTLM when client or server is not part of the same trusted domain environment.

entries.title: OpenID: sign in through a third-party provider

definition.text: OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider.

facts.text: A site, called the relying party, authenticates users through a third-party identity provider, so the site needs no ad hoc login system and users need no separate identity and password for each site.
The identity provider gives the user a unique identifier, an OpenID; on a supporting site the user is redirected to their identity provider, which prompts them to authenticate.

A user can use a URL they control, such as a blog, as a delegated identity, and the Attribute Exchange extension lets the identity provider pass attributes such as name and gender to the relying party.
A malicious relying party can send users to a bogus identity provider page to steal credentials, and the identity provider keeps a log of every OpenID login, which makes cross-site tracking easier.

entries.title: The risks of single sign-on

facts.text: Because one login unlocks many resources, stolen credentials do more damage and a compromised main SSO password exposes every supported application; SSO should ideally be paired with strong methods such as smart cards and one-time password tokens.
Single sign-on increases dependence on highly available authentication systems: losing them can deny access to every system unified under it, although session failover can keep operation going.
Where access must be guaranteed at all times, such as security or plant-floor systems, the risk of failure may make single sign-on undesirable.

Authentication is slower than traditional authentication because every application must ask the SSO provider to verify; some call it reduced sign-on, since different security levels may need more than one authentication server.

The SSO token cannot be protected with the HttpOnly cookie flag, so an XSS flaw on the logged-out website can let an attacker steal it and hijack the session; a stolen SSO session reaches every site using the SSO system.

Kerberos and SAML single sign-on originally gave users no choice about releasing personal information to each resource; as federated services spread and privacy rules such as the GDPR tighten, OpenID Connect has become more attractive.

entries.title: SAML: identity assertions in XML
entries.article: Single sign-on#Common configurations > Security Assertion Markup Language

definition.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider.

facts.text: SAML enables identity federation: identity providers securely pass authenticated identities and their attributes to service providers.

In SAML single sign-on, the user requests a resource at a service provider, which sends an authentication request to the identity provider through the user's browser and trusts the identity information it gets back.

SAML passes XML messages and is geared to enterprise security, but it can be complex to install and maintain, while OAuth and OIDC use JSON and RESTful communication that suit mobile and modern web applications.
SAML sets a session cookie in the browser, which suits short-lived workloads.

entries.title: Single sign-on configurations

facts.text: In Kerberos-based single sign-on, the initial sign-on gets a ticket-granting ticket, which other applications such as email clients, wikis and revision-control systems use to acquire service tickets proving the user's identity without another prompt.
In smart-card-based single sign-on, the initial sign-on prompts for the smart card, which other applications then use too, with either certificates or passwords stored on the card.

Integrated Windows Authentication is Microsoft's term for SPNEGO, Kerberos and NTLMSSP authentication, most often the automatic authentication between its web server and browser; vendors extended it to Unix and Linux.

Mobile devices can log users onto many systems, such as building-access and computer systems, using OpenID Connect or SAML with an X.509 certificate identifying the device, which counts as something you have.

entries.title: URL shortening: a short address that redirects

definition.text: URL shortening makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, by using a redirect that points to the page with the long URL.

facts.text: A short URL saves space when sharing, is less likely to be mistyped, and lets links be tracked individually across devices.
A friendly short URL helps messaging technologies that limit message length, such as SMS, reduces typing when copying from print, is easier to remember, and can serve as a permalink.
The redirect instruction sent to the browser carries an HTTP status code such as 301 (moved permanently), 302 (found), 307 (temporary redirect) or 308 (permanent redirect).
Shortening services give detailed click statistics, which can be simpler than setting up an equally powerful server-side analytics engine and need no access to the server.
Typically data: and javascript: URLs are not supported, for security reasons, to combat attacks like cross-site scripting and session hijacking.

entries.title: What short links cost

definition.text: Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks.

facts.text: Every access needs at least one more DNS lookup (possibly cached) and one more HTTP/HTTPS request, which adds latency and the risk of failure if the shortening service becomes unavailable.
Short URLs suffer linkrot: if the shortening service stops working, all URLs it issued become broken.
A short URL hides the target address, so it can redirect to unexpected or malicious sites and bypass site blocklists; some websites prevent short redirected URLs from being posted.
Browsers do not resend POST bodies when a redirect is encountered, an operational limit of shortening services.

entries.title: Short link expiration

definition.text: Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses.

facts.text: A permanent URL is not necessarily good: obsolete short URLs stay in circulation long after they stop pointing to a relevant destination, which has security implications.
A short-lived URL suits a one-off access or file download that is no longer needed within a couple of minutes.
A Microsoft Security Brief recommends creating short-lived URLs, for security reasons rather than convenience.
Providers who claim short URLs never expire may still discontinue the service at any time.

definition.text: Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9.

facts.text: A key of N Base62 characters can name 62^N different URLs, so each added character multiplies the key space by 62.
Base62 output [a-zA-Z0-9] suits URLs because no special characters need escaping, while Base 64 adds + and / characters that cause issues for URLs.
Base62 is deterministic, with no randomness: one input number or hash always gives the same encoded string.

definition.text: A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits.

facts.text: Keys are case-sensitive most of the time, so using the wrong case may lead to a different destination URL.
Keys can be written in base 36 (26 letters and 10 numbers) or, when upper and lower case differ, in base 62 (26 + 26 + 10).
A hash function can form the key, or a random number can be generated so that the key sequence is not predictable.
Users may propose their own custom keys, such as shortening a long product URL to a readable name.

entries.title: Designing a URL shortener

facts.text: The service must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original URL, and expire links after a default timespan, with high availability and minimal latency; preventing abuse and recording analytics are extended requirements.

After checking scale assumptions with the interviewer, assume a read-heavy 100:1 read/write ratio and 100 million links generated per month: about 40 URLs per second written and 4000 redirections per second.
Taking each request and each stored record as about 500 bytes, incoming bandwidth is 20 KB/second, outgoing is about 2 MB/second, and 12 billion records kept for 10 years need around 6 TB.
By the 80/20 rule, caching 20% of the 350M redirection requests per day needs around 35GB of memory per day.

Two tables suffice at first: users (name, email, createdAt) and URLs (expiration, hash, originalURL, creator's userID), with the hash column indexed. Data that is not strongly relational suits NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB.
Create URL takes an API key, the original URL and an optional expiration and returns the short URL; Get URL maps a short URL back to the original; Delete URL returns a boolean result.
The API key prevents abuse: it lets the service limit each user to a certain number of requests per second or minute, a standard practice for developer APIs.

Base62 (A-Z, a-z, 0-9) gives about 3.5 trillion 7-character keys (62^7), and MD5 hashing the URL yields 32 hex digits to make one. Both risk duplicates and collisions, and recomputing hashes adds overhead.

A counter encoded in base62 is a single point of failure, and several counters collide; ZooKeeper can hand each server a range such as 1 to 1,000,000, which guarantees non-duplicate keys, and can itself run in several instances.

A standalone Key Generation Service creates unique keys ahead of time in a separate database; used keys move to another table under locking so concurrent servers never share one, and some keys are kept in memory.

The interview question asks for a service that turns a long URL into a short alias and sends visitors back to the original. The service must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original URL, and expire links after a default timespan. It needs high availability and minimal latency. Preventing abuse and recording analytics are extended requirements.

Start by checking scale assumptions with the interviewer. Assume a read-heavy 100:1 read/write ratio and 100 million links generated per month. That is about 40 URLs per second written and 4000 redirections per second. Taking each request and each stored record as about 500 bytes, incoming bandwidth is 20 KB/second and outgoing is about 2 MB/second. Keeping 12 billion records for 10 years needs around 6 TB. By the 80/20 rule, caching 20% of the 350M redirection requests per day needs around 35GB of memory per day. This is the style of reasoning in {{ref:sysd-found-096}}.

Two tables suffice at first: users (name, email, createdAt) and URLs (expiration, hash, originalURL and the creator's userID), with the hash column indexed. Data that is not strongly relational suits NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB. The API has three calls. Create URL takes an API key, the original URL and an optional expiration, and returns the short URL. Get URL maps a short URL back to the original. Delete URL returns a boolean result. entries.title: Pastebin

definition.text: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link.

facts.text: Each stored text entry is commonly called a paste, and account holders can typically edit or delete their pastes at any time.
Accounts let users manage and organize their content, and many platforms let users set a paste as public or private.
Pastebins may add features such as commenting, rendering markup like Markdown or ReStructuredText, or version control.
Pastebins arose for chatrooms, where sending large blocks of computer data disrupts closely interleaved conversation, so users are told to paste elsewhere and share the link.
Designing a pastebin is like designing a URL shortener, except that the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL.

entries.title: Designing Pastebin

facts.text: A user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL; pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration; the service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available.
Out of scope are registering an account, verifying email, logging in, editing the document, setting visibility and letting the user choose the shortlink.

Traffic is not evenly distributed, pastes are text only and analytics need not be realtime; assume 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads per month (10:1), which is 4 writes and 40 reads per second on average.
Each paste is about 1.27 KB (1 KB of content, 7-byte shortlink, 4-byte expiration, 5-byte created_at, 255-byte paste_path), which means 12.7 GB of new content per month and ~450 GB in 3 years.

A relational database can act as a large hash table mapping the generated url to a file server and path; instead of a file server, use a managed object store such as Amazon S3 or a NoSQL document store.
A NoSQL key-value store is an alternative to the relational hash table, and the answer should discuss the trade-offs between SQL and NoSQL.
In the pastes table, a primary key on the shortlink column creates an index that enforces uniqueness, and an extra index on created_at speeds lookups to log time instead of a full table scan.

To generate the unique url, take the MD5 hash of the user's ip_address plus timestamp (or of random data), Base 62 encode it and keep the first 7 characters: 62^7 values suffice for 360 million shortlinks in 3 years.

Base 62 encodes to [a-zA-Z0-9], which suits urls without escaping special characters, and is deterministic; Base 64 is another popular encoding but its additional + and / characters cause issues for urls.

To create a paste, the Web Server, a reverse proxy, forwards the request to the Write API server, which generates a unique url, regenerates on a duplicate, saves to the SQL pastes table and Object Store, and returns the url.

To view a paste, the Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server, which checks the SQL Database for the url, fetches the contents from the Object Store if found, and otherwise returns an error message.
Clients use a public REST API, and internal communications could use Remote Procedure Calls.
Because realtime analytics are not required, MapReduce the Web Server logs to get hit counts; the Analytics Database could be a data warehouse such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery.
To delete expired pastes, scan the SQL Database for entries whose expiration timestamp is older than the current timestamp and delete them or mark them as expired.
Do not jump straight to the final design: state that scaling is iterative, benchmark and load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, and repeat.

An object store like S3 handles 12.7 GB of new content per month; a memory cache serves popular content for the 40 average reads per second and traffic spikes, and SQL read replicas handle the cache misses.

entries.title: Instant messaging

definition.text: Instant messaging is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network.

facts.text: It covers private messaging between two users and chat rooms or groups, allowing immediate receipt of acknowledgment or reply, in contrast to email, where conversations are not real-time.
Modern messaging apps go beyond text to multimedia, emojis, file transfer, voice calling and video chat, and connect known users through a contact list or chat rooms.

Modern services provide their own client, either an installed application or a browser-based one, and run as centralised networks on the operator's servers, unlike peer-to-peer protocols such as XMPP.
Most instant messaging protocols are proprietary and not interoperable, so users cannot reach people on other networks.
Messages may be kept in local device storage or in cloud-based server storage; cloud storage carries an increased risk that the provider may hold the decryption keys and view saved messages.
Encryption is the primary way messaging apps protect users' privacy and security, and privacy can be enhanced with end-to-end encryption by default.

entries.title: End-to-end encryption

definition.text: A way of building a secure communication system in which only the sender and the intended recipients can read the messages.

facts.text: The sender's device encrypts each message so that no third party, including the service provider, can decrypt it; recipients retrieve the encrypted messages and decrypt them on their own devices.
No one else, including the provider, can reach the keys needed to read or send messages, so the data can be neither read nor secretly modified except by the sender and recipients.

Encryption in transit alone is not end-to-end: in email and many chat platforms messages pass through intermediaries and are stored by the provider, which can read them even if the transport is encrypted.
Server-side disk encryption is also not end-to-end encryption, because the provider holds the keys and can simply decrypt the data.

Around 2014, when WhatsApp encrypted part of its network, the term came to also require that the provider cannot decrypt the communication and that attackers cannot decrypt it in transit; this is now the accepted meaning.
Because third parties cannot decrypt the data communicated or stored, services with end-to-end encryption protect user data better against data breaches and espionage.
It does not secure the endpoints: data may sit unencrypted on the user's device or be reached through compromised credentials, and a hacked device can leak the key or the decrypted messages.
A backdoor is a secret way of bypassing normal authentication or encryption; a company may willingly or unwillingly add one that subverts key negotiation or bypasses encryption altogether.

entries.title: Store and forward

definition.text: A technique in which data is sent to an intermediate station that keeps it in storage and sends it on later to its destination or to another intermediate station.

facts.text: The intermediate node verifies the integrity of the message before forwarding it.
The technique suits networks with intermittent connectivity or high mobility, long transmission delays, variable and high error rates, or no direct end-to-end connection.
A store-and-forward switching center accepts a message from the sender, holds it in storage, and forwards it according to the priority the sender set and the availability of an outgoing channel.
If the destination is unreachable, the center keeps the message and retries later, which raises the chance of delivery; if the destination is available, the message is sent at once.
Email over SMTP accepts, stores and forwards messages, and SMS messages wait at a Short Message service center until the recipient's phone is reachable again.
Store-and-forward networks of the delay-tolerant kind offer no real-time services.

entries.title: Signal Protocol

definition.text: A non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides end-to-end encryption for voice and instant messaging conversations.

facts.text: It combines the Double Ratchet Algorithm, prekeys (one-time ephemeral public keys uploaded in advance to a central server) and key agreement protocols: the original triple elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman handshake and the post-quantum PQXDH.

The ratchet pairs an ephemeral key exchange with a symmetric-key ratchet, and it added asynchronous communication (offline messages), better resilience to out-of-order messages and simpler conversations with several participants.
The algorithm is called self-healing because after an attacker compromises a session key it automatically blocks access to the cleartext of later messages.

It provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication, forward secrecy, post-compromise security and asynchronicity among other properties, but not anonymity, and it needs servers to relay messages and store public key material.
Group chats combine a pairwise double ratchet with multicast encryption, adding out-of-order and dropped-message resilience and membership that can expand and contract.
Users can compare public key fingerprints through an outside channel to avoid a man-in-the-middle attack, and an implementation can use trust on first use to warn when a correspondent's key changes.

WhatsApp built the protocol into its clients after a November 2014 partnership, and by April 2016 every form of communication on WhatsApp was end-to-end encrypted and users could verify each other's keys.

Other systems adopted the Double Ratchet: Matrix's Olm library uses it for room-by-room encryption and Wire has a custom implementation, while Messaging Layer Security uses asynchronous ratcheting trees to improve on its guarantees.

The protocol is a non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides {{ref:sysd-q-070}} for voice and instant messaging conversations. It combines the Double Ratchet Algorithm, prekeys and a key agreement protocol. Prekeys are one-time ephemeral public keys uploaded in advance to a central server. The ratchet pairs an ephemeral key exchange with a symmetric-key ratchet, and it added offline messages and better resilience to out-of-order messages. It is called self-healing because after an attacker compromises a session key it automatically blocks access to the cleartext of later messages. The protocol gives confidentiality, integrity, authentication, forward secrecy and post-compromise security, but not anonymity, and it needs servers to relay messages and store public key material. Group chats combine a pairwise double ratchet with multicast encryption. Users can compare public key fingerprints through an outside channel to avoid a man-in-the-middle attack.

entries.title: End-to-end encryption versus provider access

definition.text: The disagreement over whether providers, governments and employers should be able to read messages, set against the privacy that end-to-end encryption gives users.

facts.text: Without end-to-end encryption a provider can easily offer search and other features or scan for illegal content, but anyone with access to the stored data, by design or through a backdoor, can also read it.

Because end-to-end encrypted services cannot hand over decrypted messages on government request, their spread is controversial: governments, law enforcement agencies and child protection groups worry about the effect on criminal investigations.
Some governments have passed laws targeting end-to-end encryption, while bodies such as the UK's Information Commissioner's Office and the US's CISA argue for its use.

Many organizations must be able to decrypt employee communications for archival, data loss prevention, eDiscovery or malware detection, so enterprise systems may end the encryption at their own internal systems.

entries.title: Messaging metadata and sealed sender

definition.text: Encrypting message content does not hide who talks to whom and when, and sealed sender is a technique that reduces the metadata a server can see by concealing the sender's identifier.

facts.text: The Signal Protocol does not stop a provider from retaining information about when and with whom users communicate, so providers handle this metadata differently.

Signal says it keeps recipient identifiers only as long as needed to transmit each message, and that the closest thing to metadata it stores is each user's last connection time, with precision reduced to the day.

Sealed sender hides the sender from the server: the sender's identity travels inside each message, encrypted with a key the server lacks, and is used automatically for contacts or people with access to the recipient's profile.
A simultaneous wiretap of the user's device or the servers can still reveal that the device's IP address contacted a server to send or receive messages at certain times.

entries.title: Chat application on Redis pub/sub

definition.text: A simple chat application can be built on Redis publish-subscribe, with the server publishing each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up.

facts.text: A web socket connects client and server, and the pub-sub server opens several connections to Redis: one updates the data models and publishes to a topic, the others subscribe and listen for topic updates.
On connecting, the client gets the chat member list and the historical messages from Redis, and a new member is announced by publishing to the member_add topic so other participants can see them.
A new chat message is added to a Redis sorted set with zadd, sorted by arrival time, and the pub-sub server publishes it to the messages topic so the recipient's client receives it.

entries.title: Designing a chat service like WhatsApp

facts.text: Support one-on-one chat, group chats of at most 100 people and file sharing, with high availability and minimal latency; extended requirements are sent, delivered and read receipts, last seen time and push notifications.

Assume 50 million daily active users each sending at least 10 messages to 4 different people a day: 2 billion messages per day, or 24K requests per second, with 5 percent of messages being media files.
At 100 bytes per message, text needs about 200 GB a day and 100 KB media files need 10 TB a day, about 38 PB over 10 years; 10.2 TB of daily ingress needs around 120 MB per second.

Tables are users (name, phoneNumber), messages (type, content, timestamps, chatID or groupID), chats, groups and the N:M tables users_chats and users_groups; services each own a table, in PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store like Cassandra.
The API offers Get all chats or groups for a user ID, Get messages for a user ID and channel ID, Send message (user ID, channel ID, message) returning a boolean result, and Join or leave a channel.

Microservices scale horizontally and decouple, each owning its data: a user service (HTTP, authentication), chat service, notification service, presence service for last seen and media service for uploads, talking over REST or lighter gRPC.

Pulling by periodic HTTP requests or long polling is not scalable, since most responses are empty; push over WebSockets delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike one-way Server-Sent Events, and a cache of active connections shows who is online.

The sender's chat service has the sequencing service give the message a unique ID, persists it and queues it for sync; if the recipient is online it is pushed over their web socket, otherwise via the push server.

On login the client opens a web socket and the presence service updates the user's status and notifies friends; last seen uses a client heartbeat ping, with the last active timestamp kept in a Redis or Memcached cache.

If the recipient is not active, the chat service queues an event with device-platform metadata; the notification service forwards it to Firebase Cloud Messaging or Apple Push Notification Service, and queues give best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.
A client acknowledgment (ACK) shows a message was delivered and sets its deliveredAt field, and the message is marked seen, setting seenAt, once the user opens the chat.

Partition the database horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, with consistent hashing against uneven load; cache older messages with LRU eviction and paginate group history so limited-bandwidth users load old messages only on request.

Most storage is media, handled by the media service in object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or HDFS or GlusterFS, with static files served from a CDN such as CloudFront or Cloudflare.

Remove single points of failure with multiple service instances, load balancers, read replicas, a replicated cache and a standby API Gateway, the one entry point for HTTP, WebSocket and TCP/IP; use Kafka or NATS for robust notifications.

WhatsApp itself uses store and forward: its server stores a message, tries to forward it to the addressee and repeatedly requests acknowledgement of receipt, deleting it once acknowledged or, if undelivered, after 30 days.
Multimedia is sent by uploading the image, audio or video to an HTTP server, then sending a link to the content with its Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable.

entries.title: How WhatsApp delivers messages

definition.text: WhatsApp runs a customized version of the open XMPP protocol and delivers messages by store and forward.

facts.text: The protocol is a customized version of the open standard Extensible messaging and presence protocol (XMPP), named FunXMPP in a 2019 US Department of Justice document.
An account uses the phone number as username, and the app compares the address book's numbers with the central database of users to add contacts to the contact list automatically.

Store and forward: a message is stored on a server, which tries to forward it and repeatedly requests acknowledgement; once acknowledged it is deleted, and if undelivered after 30 days it is deleted too.
A multimedia message is uploaded to an HTTP server, and only a link to the content, plus a Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable, is sent in the message.
Messages are encrypted with the Signal Protocol, end-to-end encryption was completed for every form of communication in April 2016, users can verify each other's keys, and calls use SRTP.
Linked devices, up to four per account, sync with the primary phone; the phone originally had to stay online for them to work, but multi-device support removed that requirement.
WhatsApp handled ten billion messages per day in August 2012, up from two billion in April 2012.

entries.title: Apache Lucene

definition.text: A free and open-source search engine software library, originally written in Java.

facts.text: Lucene suits any application that needs full-text indexing and searching, and is recognized for building Internet search engines and local, single-site searching; it is a widely used foundation for production search.
It is only an indexing and search library with no crawling or HTML parsing, so projects such as Apache Nutch extend it with web crawling and parsing.
It offers fuzzy search based on edit distance, and its MoreLikeThis class recommends similar documents by term-vector similarity.
Search servers are built on Lucene: Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch (a fork of Elasticsearch 7), CrateDB and MongoDB Atlas Search, and Netflix's search is built on it too.

entries.title: Fan-out

definition.text: In messaging middleware, a pattern that delivers one message to one or several destinations, possibly in parallel, without waiting for a response.

facts.text: In message-oriented middleware, fan-out models an information exchange that spreads a message to one or more destinations, possibly in parallel, and does not halt the sender to wait for any response.
AMQP can be used with routing schemes such as point-to-point, fan-out, publish/subscribe and request-response, which version 1.0 of the standard leaves to the implementation or the network protocol.
A single incoming request can trigger a long transitive chain of dependent requests to several systems, potentially with high fan-out at various points.

entries.title: Feed fan-out models

definition.text: Ways to build each user's feed: push a tweet into followers' feeds when it is posted, pull it when the feed is read, or combine both.

facts.text: Generating a feed is intensive, especially for users who follow many accounts, and publishing a post to every follower's feed is heavy when a user has millions of followers.
Push (fan-out on write): a new tweet is pushed to all followers' feeds immediately, so the system need not scan a user's followers list for updates, but database writes increase.
Pull (fan-out on load): the feed is built and held in memory only when a follower reloads it, which cuts writes, but recent tweets appear only on request and server reads increase.
The hybrid model combines both: users with fewer followers use push, while users with many followers, such as celebrities, use pull.
In the primer's design, pushing a tweet places it in each follower's home timeline in a memory cache, an O(n) operation: 1,000 followers mean 1,000 lookups and inserts.
Fanning out at 60 thousand tweets delivered per second would overload a traditional relational database, so choose a store with fast writes such as a NoSQL database or memory cache.

Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes, so the primer suggests not fanning out highly followed users and merging their tweets from search into the home timeline at serve time.

entries.title: Feed ranking

definition.text: Scoring each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first.

facts.text: A feed needs a ranking algorithm that scores each tweet by its relevance to the specific user, using parameters such as relevance, time and engagement.
Facebook's EdgeRank scored each feed item as Affinity × Weight × Decay; affinity is the closeness of the user to the creator, higher when the user often likes, comments on or messages them.
Weight is a value per kind of edge, so a comment can count more than a like; decay lowers the rank of older edges.
Modern ranking uses machine learning models that can take thousands of factors into consideration.

entries.title: EdgeRank

definition.text: The name commonly given to the algorithm Facebook used to decide which posts to show in a user's News Feed.

facts.text: The simplified 2010 version scored posts on three parts: user affinity (the relationship and proximity of the user and the content), content weight (the action taken on it) and a time-based decay parameter.
Newer posts tend to hold a higher place than older ones, and some of the methods Facebook uses to adjust the parameters are proprietary.
As of 2011 Facebook stopped using EdgeRank and uses a machine learning algorithm that, as of 2013, takes more than 100,000 factors into account.
Such ranking shapes what users see out of what they follow, and can produce a filter bubble when updates confirm their opinions or alter their mood when they see mostly positive or negative updates.

entries.title: Designing a social feed like Twitter

facts.text: The system lets users post tweets (text, image or video), follow other users, read a newsfeed of tweets from the people they follow and search tweets, with high availability, minimal latency and scalability.

Extended requirements are metrics and analytics, retweets and favorites; the primer scopes out the Twitter Firehose, visibility-setting filtering, hiding @replies to people the user does not follow, and the hide-retweets setting.
Singh assumes a read-heavy system with 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 tweets per user per day, which gives 1 billion tweets per day and about 12K requests per second.
Singh assumes 100 bytes per message, about 100 GB a day, and media in 10 percent of tweets at 50 KB each, 5 TB a day: about 19 PB over 10 years and about 60 MB per second of bandwidth.

The primer instead assumes 100 million active users, 500 million tweets per day, an average fanout of 10 deliveries per tweet, 60 thousand tweets delivered on fanout per second and 100 thousand read requests per second.

Tables hold users, tweets (type, content, userID), favorites, followers (an N:M relation), feeds and feeds_tweets; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.
Post a tweet takes a user ID, content and an optional media URL; follow or unfollow takes a follower ID and a followee ID; get newsfeed takes a user ID and returns the tweets to show.

A microservices architecture scales horizontally, each service owning its data: user, newsfeed, tweet, search, media, notification and analytics services, talking over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

Building a feed retrieves the accounts a user follows, fetches their tweets, ranks them by relevance, time and engagement and returns pages; being intensive, feeds are pre-generated in the cache and refreshed periodically.

Pull builds the feed when a follower reloads (fewer writes, more reads); push writes each tweet into followers' feeds at once (more writes); the hybrid pushes for users with fewer followers and pulls for celebrities.

Posting stores the tweet in the author's SQL timeline; the fan-out service finds the followers and inserts the tweet into each home timeline in a memory cache (1,000 followers mean 1,000 inserts) and queues notifications.

Reading the home timeline, the timeline service gets tweet ids and user ids from the memory cache in O(1), then multigets tweet details and user details from the tweet info and user info services in O(n).

Search uses Elasticsearch, built on Lucene: the search service tokenizes the query, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations, then scatter-gathers the cluster and merges, ranks and sorts the results.

The fan-out service is a bottleneck: users with millions of followers can take several minutes, racing with @replies, so re-order at serve time and skip fanning out highly followed users, merging their tweets in at read time.

Keep only several hundred tweets per home timeline and only active users in the cache, rebuilding from SQL after 30 inactive days; read replicas cannot absorb cache misses, so add federation, denormalization, SQL tuning and NoSQL.
Cache the top 20% of tweets with LRU eviction and paginate; keep media in object storage behind a CDN; for resilience run multiple service instances, load balancers and read replicas.

The service must be highly available with minimal latency, and it must scale. The extended requirements are metrics and analytics, retweets and favorites. The system design primer scopes out the Twitter Firehose, filtering by visibility settings, hiding @replies to people the user does not follow, and the hide-retweets setting.

Two sets of assumptions size it. One author, Singh, assumes a read-heavy system with 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 tweets per user per day. That gives 1 billion tweets a day and about 12K requests per second. At 100 bytes per message, text is about 100 GB a day. Media is in 10 percent of tweets at 50 KB each. That adds 5 TB a day, about 19 PB over 10 years, and about 60 MB per second of bandwidth. The primer instead assumes 100 million active users and 500 million tweets per day. It assumes an average fanout of 10 deliveries per tweet, 60 thousand tweets delivered on fanout per second and 100 thousand read requests per second.

The tables hold users, tweets (type, content, userID), favorites, followers (an N:M relation), feeds and feeds_tweets. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Posting a tweet takes a user ID, content and an optional media URL. Following or unfollowing takes a follower ID and a followee ID. Getting the newsfeed takes a user ID and returns the tweets to show. A microservices architecture scales horizontally. Each service owns its data: user, newsfeed, tweet, search, media, notification and analytics. They talk over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

The heart of the design is the feed. Building one retrieves the accounts a user follows, fetches their tweets, ranks them by relevance, time and engagement, and returns pages. Because that is intensive, feeds are pre-generated in the cache and refreshed periodically. The choice is among the models of {{ref:sysd-q-021}}. Pull builds the feed when a follower reloads, with fewer writes and more reads. Push writes each tweet into followers' feeds at once, with more writes. The hybrid pushes for users with fewer followers and pulls for celebrities. In the primer's design, posting stores the tweet in the author's SQL timeline. To read the home timeline, the timeline service gets tweet ids and user ids from the memory cache in O(1). It then fetches tweet details and user details in bulk from the tweet info and user info services in O(n).

entries.title: Twitter's technology stack

definition.text: The languages, frameworks, caches and databases behind Twitter's clients and services.

facts.text: Twitter's mobile apps use Swift and Kotlin, with a PWA, and its web client uses JavaScript, React and Redux.
Services run on Mesos with Finagle.
Caching uses Pelikan Cache and Redis, and the databases are Manhattan, MySQL and PostgreSQL.

entries.text: Twitter's stack can be read layer by layer, from the phone in a user's hand down to the database. On the client side, the mobile apps use Swift and Kotlin, with a PWA, a progressive web app built to behave like an installed app. The web client uses JavaScript, React and Redux. Behind the clients, the services run on Mesos with Finagle. Below the services sit the stores. Caching, the layer that keeps frequently used data close at hand so it need not be fetched again, uses Pelikan Cache and Redis. The databases, which keep the data itself, are Manhattan, MySQL and PostgreSQL. That makes four layers: client, services, cache and database. The feed design in {{ref:sysd-q-020}} relies on the last two working together.

entries.title: Twitter's tweet recommendation pipeline

definition.text: A five-stage pipeline that narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set.

facts.text: The process has five stages: candidate sourcing, global filtering, scoring and ranking, filtering, and mixing.
Candidate sourcing starts with 500 million tweets, and global filtering cuts them down to 1500 candidates.
Scoring and ranking uses a neural network with 48M parameters.
A further filtering stage achieves author and content diversity, and the final mixing stage blends the tweets with ads recommendations and Who to Follow.

entries.text: A day's tweets are far too many to rank one by one. Twitter's recommendation pipeline narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set in five stages: candidate sourcing, global filtering, scoring and ranking, filtering, and mixing. Candidate sourcing starts with the 500 million tweets, and global filtering cuts them down to 1500 candidates. Scoring and ranking then works on those candidates with a neural network of 48M parameters. A further filtering stage achieves author and content diversity, so the timeline does not rest on one author or one kind of content. The final mixing stage blends the tweets with ads recommendations and Who to Follow. The shape is a funnel: the big cut comes first, and the relevance scoring that {{ref:sysd-q-022}} describes comes after it.

entries.title: Streaming media

definition.text: Delivering multimedia over a network as a stream of packets that is played in real time or near real time, instead of downloading the whole file first.

facts.text: Media is transferred as a stream of packets from a server to a client and rendered in real time or near real time, unlike downloading, where the user obtains the entire file before consuming it.
Live streaming is the real-time delivery of content during production, much as live television broadcasts content.

Streams are compressed with video coding formats such as H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1, assembled into a container such as MP4 or WebM, and delivered from a streaming server using a transport protocol such as RTMP or RTP.
In the 2010s HLS, Smooth Streaming, HDS and the non-proprietary MPEG-DASH emerged to provide adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP as an alternative to proprietary transport protocols.
A broadband speed of 2 Mbit/s or more is recommended for standard-definition video, 5 Mbit/s for high-definition and 25 Mbit/s for ultra-high-definition content.
Storage size in megabytes is length in seconds × bit rate in bit/s / (8 × 1024 × 1024); one hour of video encoded at 300 kbit/s needs around 128 MB.

UDP sends the stream as small packets, simple and efficient but with no delivery guarantee, so the application must recover from loss; TCP guarantees delivery but stalls the stream on loss, which client buffering softens.
Buffering delay is acceptable for video on demand, but interactive applications such as video conferencing lose fidelity if buffering delay exceeds 200 ms.

entries.title: Recommender system

definition.text: A type of information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next.

facts.text: Recommender systems generate playlists for streaming services, product suggestions for e-commerce and items on social media; they matter where users face many options, and help users discover items they might not have found by search.

Collaborative filtering builds a model from a user's past behavior and similar decisions by other users; content-based filtering uses pre-tagged characteristics of items to recommend others with similar properties.

Collaborative filtering needs a lot of data about a user, the cold start problem; content-based filtering needs very little to start but is limited in scope, recommending only items similar to the seed.
Collaborative filtering often suffers from cold start, scalability and sparsity; a commonly implemented solution to cold start is the multi-armed bandit algorithm.

Most systems are hybrids that combine collaborative, content-based and other approaches, for example by weighted scores, switching, mixed presentation, cascading or meta-level models; hybrids can be more accurate than pure approaches and ease cold start and sparsity.

Streaming services recommend from each user's view history together with all viewers' aggregated histories, extrapolating early viewers' choices to the whole user base; Netflix uses a hybrid of similar users' habits and titles resembling those a user rated highly.

Netflix's engine tracks profile information, browsing and scrolling behavior, time and date of viewing, the device used, and the number of searches and search terms, feeding a machine learning model on viewing history.

In the two-tower model for candidate retrieval, a user tower and an item tower produce embeddings in a shared vector space; relevance is a dot product or cosine similarity, and item embeddings can be pre-computed.

entries.title: Collaborative filtering

definition.text: A recommendation technique that predicts a user's interests from the preferences of many other users, assuming people who agreed before will agree again.

facts.text: It predicts a user's interests from taste information collected from many users, assuming that two people who share opinions on one issue are likelier to agree on others than a random pairing.
The prediction is specific to the user but uses information from many users, unlike the simpler approach of giving every item one average score, for example from its number of votes.

User-based filtering finds users with rating patterns like the active user's and predicts from their ratings; item-based filtering ('users who bought x also bought y') builds an item-item matrix and matches the user's data against it.
Instead of explicit ratings it can use implicit observations of behavior, such as what a user listened to or bought, together with what all users did, to predict future behavior.

Memory-based methods compute user or item similarity from ratings (Pearson correlation, cosine similarity) and predict a weighted average of neighbors' ratings; model-based methods learn a model, such as singular value decomposition latent factors, that compresses the sparse user-item matrix.

Memory-based filtering is explainable, easy to build and independent of item content, but performance drops when data is sparse and adding items means re-inserting elements in the structure; most commercial systems are hybrids of both kinds.

Key challenges are cold start (new users or items lack data), sparsity of the huge user-item matrix, and scalability, since traditional algorithms struggle with tens of millions of customers and millions of items.

Open rating systems invite shilling attacks, with positive ratings for one's own items and negative ones for competitors', so precautions are needed; and because it recommends from past ratings it favors popular products, a rich-get-richer effect.

entries.title: Video codec

definition.text: Software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, usually following a standard video coding format.

facts.text: A codec is an encoder and a decoder in one; raw video needs too much storage and bandwidth, so codecs make it feasible to record, transmit and stream it.

Video compression is typically lossy, so decompressed video has lower quality than the original; the bit rate trades off against quality, algorithm complexity, sensitivity to errors, random access and latency.

Encoding usually converts the image to YCbCr and subsamples the less perceptually important chroma, applies a transform (the 8x8 DCT is most popular), quantizes the output, then entropy-encodes the values.
Decoding inverts each stage of encoding as far as possible, but quantization is inherently non-invertible, so decoding only approximates it.
Standards specify only the decoding process; encoders are free to differ, so video quality can vary dramatically between encoders that use the same codec standard.
The trade-off between compression power, speed and fidelity, including artifacts, is usually the most important measure of a codec's technical merit.

Since H.261, DCT compression has been adopted by all major video coding standards; H.264/AVC was the most widely used format as of 2016, with HEVC as its successor and the open, free VP8, VP9 and AV1 as alternatives.

entries.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming

definition.text: A technique that encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change.

facts.text: It works by detecting the user's bandwidth, CPU capability and device type in real time and adjusting the quality of the stream, giving little buffering, faster start times and a good experience on high-end and low-end connections.
An encoder encodes one source at multiple bit rates and each stream is segmented into small multi-second parts; the client first downloads a manifest describing the segments and their bit rates.
The client starts with the lowest bit rate stream, requests a higher bit rate when throughput exceeds the downloaded segment's bit rate, and a lower one when throughput deteriorates.
The client's ABR algorithm decides which segments to download: throughput-based algorithms use recent download throughput, buffer-based ones use only the buffer level, and hybrid ones combine both.
Today's adaptive technologies are based almost exclusively on HTTP, replacing stateful single-bitrate protocols such as RTP with RTSP.
Because it is built on HTTP, packets traverse firewalls and NAT, the client drives adaptation so the server keeps no per-client session state, and existing HTTP caches and servers can be used.

Delivered over HTTP through content delivery networks it scales to millions of concurrent viewers, edge servers need only simple HTTP server software, and the CDN cost resembles that of HTTP web caching.
It needs additional encoding, adds storage and encoding costs, and is more complex to operate than traditional streaming; no single standard exists for digital rights management across the methods.

entries.title: HTTP Live Streaming

definition.text: A protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data over HTTP, in which the client downloads a playlist and the media segments it lists, adapting bit rate to network conditions.

facts.text: HLS is an HTTP-based protocol from Apple for live and on-demand video; version 7 is specified in RFC 8216, and a receiver can adapt the bit rate to current network conditions to keep playback uninterrupted.

A presentation is a URI to a UTF-8 text Playlist. A Media Playlist lists the Media Segments to play in sequence; a Master Playlist lists Variant Streams, each the same content at a particular bit rate, format and resolution.

A segmenter, also called a packager, cuts the media into segments no longer than a constant target duration, typically 10 seconds, each with its own URI, in MPEG-2 Transport Stream, fragmented MP4, packed audio or WebVTT subtitle format.
Each segment has a unique Media Sequence Number, one higher than the segment before it, and the server announces each segment's duration in the playlist, so clients can order and locate segments.

For seamless switching between Variant Streams, each must present the same content with matching timestamps and the same target duration; clients switch variants to adapt to the network and pick Renditions, such as audio languages, by user preference.

A live playlist is only appended to or trimmed from the front, with EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE incremented per removed segment and at least three target durations left; the server adds EXT-X-ENDLIST when the final segment is published.

The client downloads the playlist, then each segment in order, and reloads the playlist to find new segments: it waits at least one target duration after a changed reload and half that after an unchanged one.

Because it is plain HTTP, it works with large-scale HTTP caching infrastructure for big audiences; segments can be encrypted, with an EXT-X-KEY tag pointing to a key file whose delivery SHOULD be secured with TLS.

entries.title: Video on demand

definition.text: A media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request.

facts.text: A selected video can begin playing immediately (streaming) or be downloaded for deferred viewing; streaming has become the more popular way to provide it.
Some systems store programs on hard disks and use a memory buffer so the user can fast-forward and rewind; video servers on local networks give rapid responses.
Business models include subscription (SVOD, a regular fee for unlimited programs), transactional (TVOD, a fee per title) and advertising-based (AVOD, free to viewers).

Near video on demand broadcasts copies of a programme at staggered intervals, typically every 10-20 minutes, which is bandwidth-intensive; push VOD pre-loads popular content onto the viewer's set-top box to optimize the streaming infrastructure.

entries.title: MPEG-DASH

definition.text: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers.

facts.text: Content is split into small segments served over HTTP, each a short slice of playback time, and offered at several bit rates as alternative segments covering aligned intervals.

During playback the client's adaptation algorithm picks the highest-bit-rate segment that can be downloaded in time to avoid stalls or re-buffering, so it adapts seamlessly to changing network conditions.
The standard does not specify the adaptation logic; the reference client dash.js offers buffer-based (BOLA) and hybrid (DYNAMIC) bit rate adaptation algorithms.

A media presentation description (MPD) describes each segment's timing, URL and media characteristics such as resolution and bit rate; segments use the ISO base media file format (such as MP4) or MPEG-2 Transport Stream.

DASH reuses existing HTTP web server infrastructure and needs no special server support except for live streaming; it is not a transport protocol, running over TCP with HTTP and HTTP/2, or over QUIC with HTTP/3.

DASH was developed under MPEG and published as ISO/IEC 23009-1:2012 in April 2012; standardizing assures the market it works universally, unlike vendor-specific solutions, and it is codec-agnostic (H.265, H.264, VP9).
Netflix and YouTube support MPEG-DASH; it is not directly supported in HTML5, so JavaScript players use the Media Source Extensions, and DRM works through the Encrypted Media Extensions.

The Common Media Application Format (CMAF) container is intended to simplify delivering both HLS and MPEG-DASH; of the HTTP-based adaptive implementations, only these two are still actively developed and used in 2026.

entries.title: Video transcoding

definition.text: Converting video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices.

facts.text: Transcoding is a two-step process: the original data is decoded to an intermediate uncompressed format (YUV for video), which is then encoded into the target format.

It is used when a target device does not support the format or has limited storage; codecs adjust the bitrate, downsample images or re-encode the media into a smaller file in a format better optimized for the target.

Raw video is transcoded into different compression rates and resolutions for different devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k), so the requested quality can be fetched.
Transrating lowers the bitrate without changing the video format, while transsizing changes the picture size when the output resolution differs from the source.
The diversity of mobile devices and their capabilities makes transcoding a must in mobile content adaptation.

Transcoding to a lossy format reduces quality, and compression artifacts are cumulative, so each generation loses more (digital generation loss); it can be lossless if the output is losslessly compressed or uncompressed.
To minimize loss, treat the original recording as the master copy and transcode each desired version only from that master, since any transcoding involves some cumulative image loss.
Standalone tools such as FFmpeg or cloud services such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert can implement the transcoding step of a video pipeline.

entries.title: Live streaming

definition.text: Delivering video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.

facts.text: Live streaming differs from regular streaming because the video is sent over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.
The camera and microphone capture raw video, which goes to the server side to be compressed and encoded to a standard such as H.264, making the data much smaller.
Encoded data is divided into segments, usually seconds long, so it takes much less time to download or stream.
The streaming server must support different devices and network conditions, which means adaptive bitrate streaming and producing multiple files at different bitrates when encoding and segmenting.
Live data is pushed to CDN edge servers so millions of viewers can watch from a nearby edge server, which significantly lowers transmission latency.
Viewers' devices decode and decompress the data and play it in a player; for replay, the encoded data is also sent to a storage server that viewers can request from later.

RTMP, developed by Macromedia for Flash players and now used to stream video over the internet, HLS (needing H.264 or H.265) and DASH are standard protocols; HLS and DASH both support adaptive bitrate streaming.
Video conferencing applications such as Skype use real-time communication (RTC) protocols for lower latency.

entries.title: Streaming delivery methods

definition.text: The ways a stream reaches many viewers: separate unicast copies, a single multicast stream, peer-to-peer transfer, or CDN servers.

facts.text: Unicast sends a separate copy of the stream to each recipient; it is the norm on the Internet but does not scale when many users want the same program at once.
For a 300 kbit/s stream viewed by 1,000 people over unicast, the server needs 300 Mbit/s; with multicast it sends one common stream using only 300 kbit/s.
Multicast sends a single stream from the source to a group of recipients, cutting server and network load, but may not be feasible on every network and loses video on demand functionality.

Peer-to-peer protocols send prerecorded streams between computers so the server and its connections do not become a bottleneck, but raise technical, performance, security, quality and business issues; CDNs instead use intermediate servers to distribute the load.

entries.title: Real-Time Messaging Protocol

definition.text: A protocol for streaming audio, video and data over the Internet, originally built by Macromedia for Flash Player and running over TCP.

facts.text: RTMP runs on TCP, port 1935 by default, with persistent connections for low latency; after a handshake of three packets from each side, streams are split into fragments of dynamically negotiated size (default 64 bytes for audio, 128 for video).

Packets from several independent virtual channels, such as RPC, video, audio and control messages, are interleaved and multiplexed over a single connection so each channel meets its bandwidth and latency needs.
Variants include RTMPS (over TLS), RTMPE (Adobe's encryption), RTMPT (tunneled in HTTP on ports 80 and 443 to pass firewalls) and RTMFP (over UDP instead of TCP).

The codec selection of FLV and RTMP is limited, so the industry extended it; Enhanced RTMP adds multitrack, expanded codec support, FourCC signaling and a reconnect request while staying compatible with existing RTMP infrastructure.

entries.title: H.264

definition.text: Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10), a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard.

facts.text: H.264 is by far the most commonly used format for recording, compression and distribution of video, used by 79% of video industry developers as of December 2024, including streaming services such as Netflix, YouTube and Vimeo.
Bit rate savings of 50% or more over MPEG-2 Part 2 are reported: the same digital satellite TV quality at 1.5 Mbit/s for H.264 against around 3.5 Mbit/s for MPEG-2.

Profiles define sets of capabilities for classes of applications, High Profile being by far the most used; a level sets the maximum resolution, frame rate and bit rate, and a conforming decoder also decodes all lower levels.

H.264 is patent-restricted and commercial use requires royalties; software encoders on general-purpose CPUs are less power-efficient than hardware, but compression efficiency depends on the algorithm, so the difference is power, flexibility and cost.

entries.title: HEVC

definition.text: High Efficiency Video Coding (H.265, MPEG-H Part 2), a patent-encumbered video compression standard published in 2013 as the successor to H.264/AVC.

facts.text: HEVC achieves 25% to 50% better compression than AVC at the same quality; 4K at 30 frames per second needs about 50 Mbps and 22.5 GB per hour, against 100 Mbps and 45 GB for older H.264 profiles.

It extends AVC's idea of finding redundant areas within and between frames, using coding tree units up to 64x64 samples instead of 16x16 macroblocks; this needs much more signal processing to compress but has less impact on decompression.
HEVC supports resolutions up to 8192x4320, including 8K UHD, and improved parallel processing through tiles and wavefront parallel processing.

Combined licensing fees from the patent bodies are higher than for AVC, which is a main reason HEVC adoption on the web has been low and why large companies joined the Alliance for Open Media, which finalized the royalty-free AV1.

entries.title: AV1

definition.text: AOMedia Video 1, an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, designed for video transmission over the Internet as the successor to VP9.

facts.text: AV1 is royalty-free, unlike H.264 and H.265, so it does not hinder open-source adoption; its alliance was motivated by the high cost and uncertainty of HEVC patent licensing.
It is a block-based frequency transform format built on VP9 that gives encoders more coding options; frames are divided into superblocks of 128×128 or 64×64 pixels, and it targets lossy encoding.
Its payoff is bandwidth: Netflix's 2017 tests found AV1 about 25% more efficient than VP9, and Netflix's 2020 Android streams gave 20% improved compression efficiency over its VP9 streams.
The cost is compute: in a 2020 study AV1 encodes at 2160p took on average 590× longer than AVC (VP9 5.2×, HEVC 4.2×), and 2017 decoding ran at about half the speed of VP9.

entries.title: Geo-blocking

definition.text: Technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location.

facts.text: The user's location is found mainly from the IP address, mapped to a country or region with GeoIP databases; GPS queries, accounts and network delay measurements are also used. The result approves or denies access.

Netflix and YouTube restrict content by region: on Netflix mainly because of legal distribution laws tied to deals with producers and distributors, on YouTube because the publisher chooses when publishing.

Blocking can be network-level, filtering IP packets, or application-level, denying access after detecting the location; CDNs often integrate geo-blocking controls, and AWS offers CloudFront geographic restrictions or Route 53 geolocation routing.
IP-to-location mapping is inaccurate and its databases must be kept current, and VPN or proxy services let users evade IP-based geo-blocks by appearing in another country.

entries.title: Designing a video streaming service like Netflix

facts.text: Users stream and share videos, search by title or tag and comment, while the content team uploads new videos; the system needs high availability with minimal latency, high reliability so no uploads are lost, and scalability.
Extended requirements are geo-blocking of certain content, resuming playback from where the user left off, and recording video metrics and analytics.

The read-heavy estimate assumes 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 videos watched a day: 1 billion videos per day, 5 million uploads per day at a 200:1 read/write ratio, and 12K requests per second.
At 100 MB per video, about 500 TB of storage is needed every day and about 1,825 PB over 10 years, with a minimum ingress bandwidth of around 5.8 GB per second.
Tables hold users, videos (title, streamURL, tags, userID), tags, views and comments; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.

Upload takes a title, description, byte stream and optional tags; stream takes a video ID, codec, resolution and optional offset in seconds; search takes a query and optional next-page token; add comment takes a video ID and text.
Microservices each own their data model: user, stream, search, media (uploads and processing) and analytics services, communicating over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.
Two-hour raw 8K footage can reach 4 TB, so uploads are queued in a message queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ: processing is a long-running task and the queue decouples it from uploading.

A file chunker splits video by scene, not equal timestamps, so a requested chunk is less likely to be interrupted; a machine-learning content filter checks copyright, piracy and NSFW, sending problems to a dead-letter queue.

A transcoder decodes to an intermediate format and re-encodes with different codecs (FFmpeg or AWS Elemental MediaConvert); quality conversion yields 4K, 1440p, 1080p and 720p, stored in HDFS, GlusterFS or an object store such as Amazon S3.

A CDN stops users re-fetching content; Netflix's Open Connect partners with thousands of ISPs, delivers around 95% of traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations, and fails over to Netflix servers.
Adaptive bitrate protocols such as HLS adapt playback to network conditions; to resume playback, the offset stored in the views table retrieves the scene chunk at that timestamp.
Search runs on Elasticsearch; trending content comes from caching the most frequently searched queries of the last N seconds and refreshing them every M seconds with a batch job.

Geo-blocking, driven by legal distribution rights, finds the user's location by IP or profile region and redirects blocked users to an error page; a machine-learning model predicts what to watch next from viewing history.
Cache static media with Redis or Memcached using LRU eviction, falling back to the database on a miss; shard horizontally, using consistent hashing against uneven distribution.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of each service, place load balancers between clients, servers, databases and cache servers, use read replicas and replicate the distributed cache.

entries.title: Netflix's technology stack

definition.text: The languages, frameworks, databases and data tools behind Netflix's apps and services.

facts.text: Netflix builds native mobile apps in Swift and Kotlin and its web application in React, and uses GraphQL for frontend-server communication.
Backend services rely on ZUUL, Eureka, the Spring Boot framework and other technologies.
Databases include EVCache, Cassandra and CockroachDB; video is stored on S3 and served through Open Connect.
Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming; Flink and Spark process data, visualized with Tableau, and Redshift holds structured data warehouse information.
CI/CD relies on tools such as Jenkins, Gradle, Spinnaker and Chaos Monkey.
