entries.title: YouTube's video transcoding unit

definition.text: YouTube built a dedicated chip, the VCU, to transcode its uploads because software encoding had become slow and costly.

facts.text: YouTube handles 500+ hours of uploaded video every minute on average.
Its job is to transcode raw video into different compression rates for different viewing devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k).
Software-based encoding became slow and costly, so a processor specialized for video encoding and decoding was needed.

YouTube developed the VCU (Video transCoding Unit) for warehouse-scale video processing, as GPUs and TPUs serve graphics and machine learning: clusters of VCU servers, with accelerator trays of cards holding encoders and decoders.
The VCU cluster generates the different resolutions and stores them in cloud storage; the design gave 20-33x improvements in computing efficiency over the previous optimized system.

entries.title: Netflix Open Connect

definition.text: Netflix's purpose-built content delivery network, which places appliances at partner internet service providers.

facts.text: Open Connect is a purpose-built CDN responsible for serving Netflix's video traffic, going a step further than a traditional CDN.
Netflix partners with thousands of internet service providers (ISPs) to localize its traffic and deliver content more efficiently.
Around 95% of traffic globally is delivered via direct connections between Open Connect and the ISPs customers use to reach the internet.
Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) sit in over 1000 separate locations around the world.
If an appliance has issues it can fail over, and traffic is re-routed to Netflix servers.

entries.title: Nearest neighbor search

definition.text: The optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a given query point.

facts.text: Closeness is a dissimilarity function, most often a distance metric such as Euclidean or Manhattan distance over a d-dimensional vector space; k-nearest neighbor search returns the k closest points instead of one.
It underlies databases, recommendation systems and vector databases, where nearest-neighbor lookup over embeddings retrieves semantically similar records.

The simplest exact solution is linear search: compute the distance from the query to every point, keeping the best so far, in O(dN) time with no search structure to maintain; comparing squared distances skips the square root.

Space partitioning avoids scanning every point: a k-d tree repeatedly bisects the search space and queries walk root to leaf, with average O(log N) time for randomly distributed points; the R-tree supports inserts and deletes.

In high-dimensional Euclidean space no general-purpose exact solution has polynomial preprocessing and polylogarithmic search time, tree indexes stop helping because most nodes must be examined, and naive search can on average win.
Approximate search may return a point within c times the distance to the true nearest; it is often almost as good, and trades guaranteed answers for speed or memory savings.

Proximity graph methods such as HNSW are the current state of the art for approximate search: greedy search hops to the neighbor closest to the query until a local minimum. Locality-sensitive hashing instead puts close points in one bucket.

Compression and clustering also speed search: a compressed copy of the vectors in RAM prefilters candidates before exact distances are computed from disk, or the database is clustered and only the most promising clusters are retrieved.

entries.title: Proximity service

definition.text: A service that returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants.

facts.text: A proximity design has two key services: a business service that adds, deletes and updates place information and lets customers view details, and a location-based service that returns the places near a given location and radius.
Storing each place's latitude and longitude and computing the distance to every place makes the query very inefficient.

The geohash algorithm speeds it up: divide the planet into four quadrants along the prime meridian and equator, keep dividing each grid into four, and name a grid by alternating longitude and latitude bits.
Nearby places in a grid are then found with a prefix match on the geohash column, for example geohash LIKE '01%'.
Geohash has limits: one grid can hold very many places (downtown New York) and another none (the ocean), so more complicated algorithms optimize the process.

entries.title: Dynamic pricing

definition.text: A pricing strategy, also called surge pricing, in which flexible prices are set from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand.

facts.text: Raising prices at peak demand and lowering them at low demand encourages buying when demand is low and discourages it when demand is high; in some sectors economists see it as a more efficient allocation of limited resources.

Algorithmic pricing sets prices automatically to maximize the seller's profit, using data such as statistics on potential buyers, competitors' prices, the active buyer's personal information and the seller's own stock and sales targets.

Time-based pricing, common among online retailers, changes prices with the time of day; other methods price by cost plus a fixed profit, by competitors' prices, or by the value or elasticity of the product to buyers.

It is often criticized as price gouging, so operators add guardrails: Uber has capped how high surge pricing can go in emergencies since 2015, and drivers may hold off accepting rides until surge raises fares.

entries.title: Designing a ride-hailing service like Uber

facts.text: Customers see nearby cabs with ETA and pricing, book a cab and see the driver's location; drivers accept or deny rides, see the pickup location and mark the trip complete on reaching the destination.
The system needs high availability with minimal latency and scalability; extended requirements are trip ratings, payment processing, and metrics and analytics.

entries.title: Uber's technology stack

definition.text: The frameworks, protocols, databases and data tools behind Uber's apps and services.

facts.text: The web frontend uses Fusion.js, a React framework Uber built, and visualization.js for geospatial visualization; mobile apps use the RIB architecture with VIPER instead of MVC, in Swift for iOS and Java for Android.
Uber Gateway is a dynamic configuration on top of NGINX; client-server communication uses gRPC and QUIC, and APIs are defined with Apache Thrift.

Backend services use Spring Boot for Java, uAct for event-driven architecture and Cadence for asynchronous workflow orchestration; Flipr (later UCDP) is a unified configuration store and H3 a location-index store library.
The main OLTP store is the strongly consistent DocStore, which employs MySQL and PostgreSQL with the RocksDB engine.

Big data uses the Hadoop family with Hudi and Parquet file formats and Alluxio as cache; time-series data is in Pinot and AresDB; Hive, Spark and Marmaray process data, and Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming.
DevOps uses a monorepo with devpod environments and Spinnaker for continuous delivery, with uMetric for metrics, uMonitor for alarms and M3 as the observability database.

entries.title: Web crawler

definition.text: An Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads.

facts.text: A crawler starts from a list of seed URLs, fetches those pages, finds their hyperlinks and adds them to the list of URLs still to visit, called the crawl frontier.

Frontier URLs are visited recursively according to a set of policies: selection (which pages to download), re-visit (when to check for changes), politeness (how to avoid overloading sites) and parallelization (how to coordinate distributed crawlers).
The web is so large that a crawler can download only a limited number of pages in a given time, so it must prioritize, and fast change means pages may already be updated or deleted.

Server-side software makes duplicate content hard to avoid: a photo gallery with four sort orders, three thumbnail sizes, two file formats and an option to hide user content serves the same content under 48 different URLs.

A parallel crawler runs multiple processes at once, aiming to maximize the download rate while minimizing overhead. It needs a policy for assigning newly found URLs, because two processes can discover the same URL and download the page twice.
Crawlers typically identify themselves to a web server in the User-agent field of the HTTP request, which administrators read in server logs to see which crawlers visit and how often.

entries.title: Robots exclusion protocol

definition.text: The standard, usually called robots.txt, by which a website tells visiting web crawlers which portions of the site they may visit.

facts.text: A site owner puts a robots.txt file at the root of the site; a compliant robot fetches it before any other file, uses it to decide which links to follow, and assumes no limits if the file is missing.
The protocol is purely advisory and relies on voluntary compliance; malicious bots may ignore it or use it to find disallowed paths, and standards bodies discourage depending on secrecy for security.
Developed in 1994, it was published as a proposed standard, RFC 9309, in September 2022; crawlers must parse at least 500 kibibytes of a robots.txt file.

Disallow: /something/ blocks all files and subdirectories starting with it; a wildcard allows patterns such as /something/*/other, but not every crawler recognizes it. Some crawlers also read a Sitemap: line.

The standard sets no visit interval, the most effective way to avoid overload. The non-standard Crawl-delay is read differently: Yandex takes seconds between visits, Bing a window of 1 to 30 seconds, and Google ignores it.

Robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers act at finer grain but only after the page loads or responds, whereas robots.txt acts before the request; a page blocked by robots.txt never has its noindex tags seen.
The system design primer suggests supporting robots.txt in a crawler so webmasters control crawl frequency.

entries.title: Crawl politeness policy

definition.text: The rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits.

facts.text: Crawlers fetch data faster and deeper than human searchers, so one making many requests per second or downloading large files can cripple a site's performance.
The costs of crawlers include network bandwidth, server overload when access to one server is too frequent, and poorly written crawlers that can crash servers or routers.

The robots exclusion protocol only partly solves this: it says which parts of a server crawlers should avoid but suggests no interval between visits, though that interval is the most effective way to avoid overload.
Major search engines support an extra Crawl-delay parameter in robots.txt giving the number of seconds to wait between requests.
The first proposed interval was 60 seconds, but at that rate a site of more than 100,000 pages would take over 2 months to download; Cho uses 10 seconds, WIRE 15 seconds and Dill et al. 1 second.
The Mercator crawler is adaptive: if a download from a server took t seconds, it waits 10t seconds before fetching the next page from it.

entries.title: Crawl re-visit policy

definition.text: The rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale.

facts.text: A crawl of part of the web can take weeks or months, so creations, updates and deletions happen meanwhile, and the search engine pays a cost for holding an outdated copy.
The usual cost functions are freshness, a binary measure of whether the local copy is accurate, and age, a measure of how outdated the copy is.
A uniform policy re-visits all pages at the same frequency; a proportional policy re-visits pages that change more often more frequently, in proportion to their estimated change rate.
In average freshness the uniform policy beats the proportional one, because a proportional policy spends crawls on rapidly changing pages whose freshness lasts only briefly.

The optimal policy is closer to uniform: to keep average freshness high, ignore pages that change too often, and to keep average age low, raise access frequency sub-linearly with a page's rate of change.

entries.title: Crawl selection policy

definition.text: The rule that decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking pages by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched.

facts.text: Even large search engines cover only part of the public web; a 2009 study showed they index no more than 40-70% of the indexable web.

The downloaded fraction should hold the most relevant pages rather than a random sample, which needs an importance metric built from a page's intrinsic quality, its popularity in links or visits, and sometimes its URL.
A selection policy must work with partial information, since the complete set of web pages is not known while crawling.
A breadth-first crawl captures pages with high PageRank early, because the most important pages have many links from numerous hosts and those links are found early wherever the crawl starts.

OPIC gives each page an initial sum of cash, split equally among the pages it links to; the crawler downloads frontier pages holding the most cash first. It resembles PageRank but is faster and done in one step.
To fetch only HTML, a crawler can send an HTTP HEAD request for the MIME type before a GET, or skip URLs not ending in characters such as .html or a slash, though that may skip many HTML resources.
Some crawlers skip any URL containing a "?" to avoid spider traps that yield an infinite number of URLs from one site; this is unreliable when the site rewrites URLs.

entries.title: How search engines work

definition.text: Search engines work through three processes: crawling pages, indexing what was collected, and serving ranked results for queries.

facts.text: Crawlers start from a list of known pages (seeds) and follow links to discover and download new pages.

The collected information is analyzed and organized into a massive index, extracting keywords, content type, freshness, language and other signals to learn what each page is about and how relevant it may be to queries.
To serve a query, the engine first analyzes it for meaning and intent, identifying keywords, recognizing synonyms and interpreting context.
It then retrieves pages from the index by matching the query's keywords with indexed content, and ranks the retrieved pages by relevance and other factors.

entries.title: Search engine indexing

definition.text: The collecting, parsing and storing of data so that information can be retrieved quickly and accurately.

facts.text: Without an index the engine would scan every document in the corpus; an index of 10,000 documents can be queried within milliseconds, while a sequential scan of 10,000 large documents could take hours.
The index is paid for with extra storage and a considerably longer update time. Larger services index at a predetermined interval because of the cost, while agent-based engines index in real time.

Design factors include how data enters the index and whether several indexers can work asynchronously, how index data is stored (compressed or filtered), lookup speed, how the index is maintained over time, and fault tolerance.

Parsing breaks documents into tokens for the forward and inverted indices. With several languages, identifying each document's language comes first because later steps such as stemming depend on it, and markup must be told apart from content.

Tokenizing is hard for a multilingual indexer: Chinese or Japanese words are not delineated by whitespace, so language-specific logic finds word boundaries, which is often why a parser is built per language.
Indexing is a producer-consumer chain: the crawler fills the corpus, the forward index consumes it, and the inverted index consumes the forward index, which lets indexers work asynchronously.

Adding a document while the index keeps answering queries is a collision between competing tasks with many chances for race conditions; distributed storage and processing across machines make incoherency more likely.

A simple uncompressed index for 2 billion web pages would hold 500 billion word entries, about 2500 gigabytes at 5 bytes per word; compression shrinks it to a fraction at the cost of compression and decompression time.

entries.title: PageRank

definition.text: A link analysis algorithm, used by Google Search, that gives each page in a hyperlinked set a numerical weight measuring its relative importance.

facts.text: PageRank works by counting the number and quality of links to a page, on the assumption that more important websites receive more links from other websites.
A hyperlink counts as a vote of support; a page's rank is defined recursively from the pages that link to it, so a page linked from many high-PageRank pages gets a high rank itself.
The web is a graph with pages as nodes and hyperlinks as edges, and the output is a probability distribution: the chance that a person randomly clicking links lands on each page.
Each page passes its PageRank equally to the pages it links to, so the rank of page u is the sum, over pages v linking to u, of the rank of v divided by v's number of outbound links.
The damping factor d, generally around 0.85, is the chance the surfer keeps following links; otherwise they jump to a random page. Pages with no outbound links are treated as linking to every page.

It is computed iteratively over the whole collection until the values stop changing, using the power method; the original paper reports 322 million links converging in 52 iterations and scaling roughly linearly in log n.
Weaknesses: it favors older pages, since a new page has few links, and it can be manipulated with paid links and link farms, which Google has penalized since December 2007.

A web crawler may use PageRank as one importance metric to choose which URLs to visit; Google recalculates it each time it crawls the web and rebuilds its index, and it is only one of many ranking factors.

entries.title: Cosine similarity

definition.text: A measure of similarity between two non-zero vectors: the cosine of the angle between them, which is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths.

facts.text: It depends only on the angle between the vectors, not their magnitudes, and lies in [-1, +1]: proportional vectors score +1, orthogonal ones 0, opposite ones -1.

In text mining each word is a coordinate and a document is the vector of its word counts, so the measure shows how alike two documents are in subject matter regardless of length, between 0 and 1 for nonnegative counts.
Its cost is low, especially for sparse vectors, because only the non-zero coordinates need to be considered.
Cosine distance is not a true metric because it breaks the triangle inequality; L2-normalizing the vectors and using Euclidean distance gives the same ordering without costly trigonometry.

entries.text: Two documents of different lengths can still be about the same thing. Cosine similarity captures that. entries.title: Sitemaps

definition.text: An XML protocol that lets a webmaster tell search engines which URLs on a site are available for crawling.

facts.text: A sitemap can add each URL's last update, change frequency and relative importance; it is a URL inclusion protocol that complements robots.txt, a URL exclusion protocol.

It helps crawlers find URLs isolated from the rest of the site, and suits very large sites, sites with poorly linked pages, and rich media; it supplements crawling and guarantees neither indexing nor ranking.

The file is XML with a required loc for each URL and optional lastmod, changefreq and priority (0.0 to 1.0, default 0.5), which are only hints; it can also be a plain text list of URLs, gzip-compressed.
One sitemap holds at most 50,000 URLs or 50MiB uncompressed; larger sites split it into several and list them in a sitemap index file, which may list up to 50,000 sitemaps.

entries.title: Deep web crawling

definition.text: Reaching the large share of web pages that sit behind queries to a database and have no links pointing to them.

facts.text: A vast number of pages lie in the deep or invisible web, usually reachable only by submitting queries to a database, so regular crawlers cannot find them without links that point to them.
Google's Sitemaps protocol and mod oai are intended to let deep-web resources be discovered; deep web crawling also multiplies the number of links to crawl.
Screen scraping software can be customized to query a web form repeatedly and aggregate the results, even feeding the output of one form into another across websites.
Pages built on AJAX cause problems for crawlers, and Google has proposed a format of AJAX calls its bot can recognize and index.

entries.title: Focused crawler
entries.article: Web crawler#Crawling policy > Selection policy > Focused crawling

definition.text: A crawler that tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic, also called a topical crawler.

facts.text: A page's importance can be expressed as its similarity to a query; crawlers that fetch pages similar to each other are called focused or topical crawlers.
The main problem is predicting a page's text similarity to the query before downloading it; one predictor is the anchor text of links, and another is the full content of pages already visited.
Performance depends mostly on how rich in links the topic is, and a focused crawl usually relies on a general web search engine to supply starting points.

entries.title: URL normalization
entries.article: Web crawler#Crawling policy > Selection policy > URL normalization

definition.text: Modifying and standardizing a URL in a consistent way, also called URL canonicalization, so that one resource has one form.

facts.text: Crawlers usually normalize URLs to avoid crawling the same resource more than once.
Normalization, also called URL canonicalization, modifies and standardizes a URL in a consistent manner.
Typical normalizations convert URLs to lowercase, remove "." and ".." segments, and add trailing slashes to a non-empty path component.

entries.title: Spider trap

definition.text: A set of web pages that makes a crawler issue an infinite number of requests or crash, whether built on purpose or by accident.

facts.text: Traps are made on purpose to catch spambots or crawlers that waste bandwidth, or by accident, for example calendars whose dynamic pages keep linking to the next day or year.

Typical forms are indefinitely deep directory structures, dynamic pages that produce an unbounded number of documents, documents so full of characters that they crash the parser, and session ids that require cookies.
A trap acts like an infinite loop: it wastes the crawler's resources, lowers its productivity and can crash a poorly written crawler.

No universal algorithm detects every trap; automated methods catch some categories while new traps keep appearing. Sites with traps usually list them in robots.txt, so a polite bot that obeys it stays out.

entries.title: Jaccard index

definition.text: A statistic of how similar two sets are: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union.

facts.text: It is the intersection size over the union size, a normalized measure of overlap that runs from 0 for sets with nothing in common to 1 for equal sets; the Jaccard distance is 1 minus it.
Unlike the simple matching coefficient it ignores attributes absent from both sets, so it suits sparse data where most attributes are absent from both, such as small baskets against a large catalog.
To scale to large collections, MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing approximate it from compact fixed-size signatures built from the minimum values of a hash function.
Applied to documents, the resemblance of two documents is the Jaccard coefficient of their shingle sets, the ratio of the intersection to the union of the shinglings.

entries.title: W-shingling

definition.text: A set of unique shingles, each a run of w contiguous tokens from a document, used to measure how similar two documents are.

facts.text: A w-shingling is the set of all unique runs of w consecutive tokens (n-grams) in a document; w is the number of tokens in each shingle.
In the example 'a rose is a rose is a rose' the 4-token shingles are five runs, reduced to three unique ones because repeats collapse in the set.
The resemblance of two documents is the size of the intersection of their shinglings divided by the size of the union, from 0 to 1 with 1 meaning identical; this is the Jaccard coefficient.

entries.text: The phrase "a rose is a rose is a rose" has five runs of four words, but only three of them are different. entries.title: Designing a web crawler

facts.text: The service must crawl a list of URLs, build a reverse index of words to pages, and generate static titles and snippets; a user enters a search term and sees matching pages with those titles and snippets.

The service must be highly available and generate search results fast, and the crawler must not get stuck in an infinite loop. Search analytics and personalized results are out of scope, and only anonymous users are supported.
An infinite loop happens if the link graph contains a cycle. Search traffic is not evenly distributed: some searches are very popular, while others are executed only once.

The assumptions are 1 billion links to crawl, a refresh rate of about once per week (more often for popular sites), 4 billion links crawled each month, 500 KB average stored size per page, and 100 billion searches per month.
The estimate is 2 PB of stored page content per month (500 KB per page times 4 billion links), 72 PB in 3 years, 1,600 write requests per second and 40,000 search requests per second.

The data model is two tables: links_to_crawl, ranked initially by overall site popularity, and crawled_links, which stores processed links with their page signatures. Both could live in a key-value NoSQL database, with Redis sorted sets keeping the link ranking.
If the initial list is not reasonable, the crawler can be seeded with popular sites that link to outside content, such as Yahoo or DMOZ.
In a loop the Crawler Service takes the top ranked link and checks crawled_links for a similar page signature. If a similar page exists, it lowers the link's priority, which prevents a cycle.

Otherwise it crawls the link, queues a job for the Reverse Index Service and one for the Document Service (static title and snippet), generates the page signature, removes the link from links_to_crawl and inserts the link and signature into crawled_links.
Duplicate URLs can be removed with sort and unique for small lists. With 1 billion links to crawl, MapReduce can output only the entries that have a frequency of 1.
Detecting duplicate content is more complex: generate a signature from each page's contents and compare signatures for similarity, using an algorithm such as the Jaccard index or cosine similarity.

Each crawl result carries a timestamp of the last crawl. After a default period, say one week, all pages are refreshed, and frequently updated or popular sites are refreshed sooner. A Robots.txt file could give webmasters control of crawl frequency.

A search goes from the client to a reverse-proxy web server, then to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations.

The Query API server asks the Reverse Index Service for matching documents; it ranks them and returns the top ones, and the Document Service returns titles and snippets. The public API is REST; internal calls could use RPC.

Popular queries can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached, which cuts response times, protects the Reverse Index Service and Document Service, and absorbs uneven traffic and spikes.

The Reverse Index Service and Document Service will likely need heavy sharding and federation. The crawler itself can keep its own periodically refreshed DNS lookup, pool many open connections, and needs enough bandwidth, since crawling is bandwidth intensive.

entries.title: Heap

definition.text: A tree-based data structure in which each parent's key is at least (max heap) or at most (min heap) its children's keys, so the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root.

facts.text: A heap is only partially ordered, not sorted: the top-priority element is at the root, and there is no implied ordering between siblings or cousins.

A heap is an efficient implementation of the priority queue abstract type, which could also be built another way. It suits repeatedly removing the highest- or lowest-priority item, or interleaving insertions with removals of the root.
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array with links implied by indices: from index 0, node i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and its parent at ⌊(i−1)/2⌋. No extra memory is needed.
Insertion adds the element at the end and sifts it up until the heap property holds. Removing the root moves the last element to the root and sifts it down.

A heap gives access to the smallest or largest element in constant time. Building a binary heap from an array takes linear time with Floyd's algorithm, faster than inserting elements one by one, which is log-linear.

Heaps power heapsort (in place, no quadratic worst case), finding the k smallest elements in O(k) time, and graph algorithms such as Dijkstra's shortest-path and Prim's minimal-spanning-tree algorithms.

A heap can merge many sorted input streams into one: take the minimum, replace it with the next element of its stream, then sift down. Examples are external sorting and streaming results from a log-structured merge tree.
Java's PriorityQueue is a binary heap that is a min-heap by default; a max-heap needs a custom comparator. C++'s std::priority_queue wraps the heap algorithms but has no standard decrease-key.

entries.title: Open banking

definition.text: Open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through application programming interfaces (APIs).

facts.text: Banks traditionally kept customer data in closed systems. Open banking lets customers share it securely and electronically with other banks and authorized organizations such as payment providers, lenders and insurers.

It runs on standardised APIs that let authorised third parties read account information or initiate payments, with explicit customer consent. Banks expose dedicated interfaces separate from online banking and must manage consent lifecycles, access scopes and strong customer authentication.

Regulation drove adoption: from 2015 to 2021 several countries forced banks to open APIs to customer data. The EU adopted PSD2 in October 2015, and in 2016 the UK required its nine biggest banks to give licensed startups transaction-level access.

Opening bank APIs to third-party fintechs brings risks: hackers can target third-party apps, employees may hold excessive access privileges, phishing can trick customers, and there are privacy concerns.

entries.title: Designing a personal finance app

facts.text: The service must let a user connect a financial account, extract its transactions, categorize them (with manual category override but no automatic re-categorization), and analyze monthly spending by category.

It also recommends a budget the user may set manually, and sends notifications when spending approaches or exceeds the budget. It must be highly available; additional logging and analytics are out of scope.

Assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, adding or removing accounts is rare, budget notifications need not be instant, sellers determine a transaction's category, and the automatic daily update covers only users active in the past 30 days.

Scale: 10 million users, 30 million financial accounts, 10 budget categories per user (100 million budget items), 50,000 sellers, 5 billion transactions per month, 500 million read requests per month, and a 10:1 write to read ratio.
A transaction is about 50 bytes (user_id 8, created_at 5, seller 32, amount 5), so 5 billion a month means 250 GB of new transaction content per month and 9 TB in 3 years.
The average load is 2,000 transactions per second and 200 read requests per second. The system is write-heavy: users make transactions daily, but few visit the site daily.

To connect an account, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Accounts API server; that server writes the account to the SQL accounts table, indexed on id, user_id and created_at. The API is public REST.
Extraction runs when the user first links an account, on manual refresh, and daily for users active in the past 30 days. It takes a while, so the API server queues a job on Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ.

The Transaction Extraction Service pulls from the queue, stores raw transaction logs in an object store, calls the Category and Budget Services (the latter alerts users through a Notification Service), and updates the SQL transactions and monthly_spending tables.

The Category Service seeds a seller-to-category dictionary with popular sellers: 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each take about 12 MB of memory. Unseeded sellers are crowdsourced from user overrides, with a heap giving the top override in O(1).
Budgets start from a generic template that allocates category amounts by income tier, so the 100 million budget items need not be stored: only a user's overrides, in a budget_overrides table.

Monthly spending can come from SQL queries over transactions into monthly_spending, which has far fewer rows than 5 billion transactions. Alternatively, MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files categorize and aggregate, reducing database load.

A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached holds sessions, category stats and recent transactions. The Read API server returns hits, else reads the SQL database and updates the cache (cache-aside). Static content comes from a CDN-cached object store.

The 200 average read requests per second (higher at peak) should be served by the cache, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes; SQL read replicas handle cache misses unless bogged down replicating writes.
2,000 average writes per second might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave, so add federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and consider moving some data to NoSQL.
Keep only a month of transactions in the database and the rest in a data warehouse or object store; an object store such as Amazon S3 comfortably handles 250 GB of new content per month.

entries.title: Doubly linked list

definition.text: A linked data structure of sequentially linked nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node.

facts.text: The two links allow traversal in either direction, and the direction can change mid-way. The first and last nodes (head and tail) are directly accessible, and any node can start a new traversal.
The first and last links point to a terminator, typically null or a sentinel node. With a single sentinel the list becomes circular.

Adding or removing a node changes more links than in a singly linked list, but is simpler and often more efficient, since a node already links to its predecessor and no traversal is needed to find it.
Removal needs special handling when the node is the first or last, so the list's head and tail references are updated. Deleting the only node correctly sets both to null.

entries.title: Designing a search query cache

facts.text: The service handles a user's search request that hits the cache and one that misses it, and must be highly available.
Assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, popular queries should almost always be in the cache, serving from cache needs fast lookups, and latency between machines must be low.
Cache memory is limited yet millions of queries must be cached, so the design must decide what to keep or remove and how to expire or refresh entries.
The scale is 10 million users, 10 billion queries per month and 4,000 requests per second.
The cache stores an ordered list of key (query) and value (results); an entry is a 50-byte query, 20-byte title and 200-byte snippet, 270 bytes in total.
If all 10 billion queries were unique and all were stored, the cache data would be 2.7 TB per month (270 bytes per search times 10 billion searches per month).

A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached serves popular queries, cutting read latency and sparing the Reverse Index and Document Services. Reading 1 MB sequentially takes about 250 microseconds from memory; SSD takes 4x and disk 80x longer.

The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization, converts it to boolean operations and checks the cache.
On a cache hit, the memory cache moves the entry to the front of the LRU list and returns the cached contents.
On a miss, the Query API gets ranked matching documents from the Reverse Index Service and titles and snippets from the Document Service, then caches the entry at the front of the LRU list.
Since cache capacity is limited, a least recently used (LRU) approach expires the older entries.
The cache is a doubly-linked list, with new items added at the head and items to expire removed from the tail, plus a hash table giving fast lookup of each list node.

Entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or page rank changes. The simplest way is a maximum time an entry may stay cached, the time to live (TTL); this approach is cache-aside.

To handle the request load and memory needed, scale the cache horizontally. Giving each machine its own cache is simple but likely gives a low hit rate, and giving each a full copy is simple but wastes memory.
Sharding the cache across all machines in the cluster is more complex but likely the best option. A hash such as machine = hash(query) picks the machine, and consistent hashing is likely wanted.

entries.title: Designing a sales rank by category

facts.text: The service calculates the past week's most popular products by category and lets users view them, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope.

Assumptions: traffic is uneven; an item can be in multiple categories but cannot change category; there are no subcategories; results must be updated hourly, and more popular products might need more frequent updates.
The scale is 10 million products, 1 billion transactions per month and 100 billion read requests per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio.
A transaction is about 40 bytes: created_at 5, product_id 8, category_id 4, seller_id 8, buyer_id 8, quantity 4 and total_price 5 bytes.
That is 40 GB of new transaction content per month (40 bytes times 1 billion transactions) and 1.44 TB in 3 years, assuming most are new transactions rather than updates.
The average load is 400 transactions per second and 40,000 read requests per second.
Raw Sales API server log files go to a managed object store such as Amazon S3, rather than a self-managed distributed file system.
The Sales Rank Service runs MapReduce with the Sales API server logs as input, writing results to an aggregate table sales_rank in a SQL database.
It uses a multi-step MapReduce: first transform records to (category, product_id) with sum(quantity), then perform a distributed sort. The sorted list is inserted into the sales_rank table.
The sales_rank table is indexed on id, category_id and product_id, for log-time lookups instead of scanning the whole table and to keep the data in memory.
To view rankings, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Read API server; that server reads the SQL sales_rank table. The public API is REST, with RPC for internal calls.
The 40,000 average read requests per second (higher at peak) should be handled by a memory cache instead of the database, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes.
With such a large volume of reads, SQL read replicas might not handle the cache misses, so additional SQL scaling patterns are probably needed.

400 average writes per second (higher at peak) might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. SQL scaling patterns include federation, denormalization and SQL tuning; some data might also move to NoSQL.

The analytics database could be a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery. Keep a limited time period in the database and the rest in a warehouse or an object store, which handles 40 GB of new content per month.

The 40,000 average read requests per second, higher at peak, should be handled by a memory cache instead of the database, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. With such a large volume of reads, SQL read replicas might not handle the cache misses, so additional SQL scaling patterns are probably needed.

The 400 average writes per second, higher at peak, might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. SQL scaling patterns include federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and some data might also move to NoSQL. The analytics database could be a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery. Keep a limited time period in the database and the rest in a warehouse or an object store, which handles 40 GB of new content per month. The thing to remember is the split: the rank is computed in batch by MapReduce from raw logs, and the heavy read traffic is answered from a cache.

entries.title: Social graph

definition.text: A graph that represents social relations between entities; it is a model of a social network.

facts.text: Relations can be mutual or one-way. On Twitter the relation between users is unidirectional, unlike classical social networks such as Facebook, which makes information propagation closer to how information spreads in real life.
In 2012, Twitter's social graph held 537 million accounts connected by 23.95 billion links.

Social graphs are typically stored in graph databases that use graph query languages to query relationships efficiently. Facebook uses TAO, a custom distributed system optimized for fast reads at massive scale.

The graph personalizes the feed: instead of random posts, the app shows content based on a user's previous interactions, and likes, shares and comments reinforce links between users who enjoy the same content.

entries.title: Adjacency matrix

definition.text: A square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent.

facts.text: For a simple graph of n vertices it is an n-by-n matrix whose element Aij is 1 if an edge runs from vertex i to vertex j, else 0. The diagonal is 0, as simple graphs have no loops.
An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix, while a directed graph's matrix can be asymmetric. Edge weights can be stored directly in the elements.
Under the common convention, an undirected vertex's degree is the sum of its row or column. For a directed graph, row sums give out-degrees and column sums give in-degrees.
The matrix tests in constant time whether two vertices are adjacent, but listing a vertex's neighbours means scanning a whole row, which takes O(|V|) time.

Each entry needs one bit, so a directed graph fits in |V|²/8 bytes, and the compactness encourages locality of reference. For a large sparse graph, adjacency lists need less storage; sparse matrix representations store only non-zero entries.
Entry (i, j) of the matrix raised to the power n counts the walks of length n from vertex i to vertex j. The smallest n giving a positive entry is the distance between the two vertices.

entries.title: Adjacency list

definition.text: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbours.

facts.text: Implementations vary: a hash table from each vertex to an array of neighbours, an array indexed by vertex number pointing to linked lists, or vertex and edge objects, which use more memory but can store data per edge.
Its main operation, listing a vertex's neighbours, takes constant time per neighbour, so the total time is proportional to the vertex's degree.

Testing whether an edge exists is slower: time proportional to the smaller degree of the two vertices for unsorted neighbours, or logarithmic in the degree if neighbours form a sorted array searched by binary search.
For a sparse graph an adjacency list is far more space-efficient than an adjacency matrix: space is proportional to the vertices plus edges, against the square of the vertices for a matrix.
A naive array adjacency list of an undirected graph takes about 8|E| bytes on a 32-bit computer, against |V|²/8 bytes for a bit matrix, so it uses more space when density |E|/|V|² exceeds 1/64.

entries.title: Breadth-first search

definition.text: A graph or tree search that starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level.

facts.text: BFS keeps a queue of nodes met but not yet explored, labels each vertex explored when it is enqueued, and stores a parent link on each vertex. The parent links trace the shortest path back to the root.
BFS uses a first-in-first-out queue where depth-first search uses a last-in-first-out stack. On a tree, replacing the queue with a stack turns BFS into depth-first search.

It finds the path with the fewest edges between two nodes, an advantage over depth-first search. It is also complete: it reaches a goal if one exists, even in an infinite graph where depth-first search can get lost.
Time is O(|V|+|E|), since every vertex and edge is explored in the worst case, and space is O(|V|) when the vertex count is known and extra structures mark queued vertices.

For graphs too large to store, reaching nodes at distance d takes O(b^(d+1)) time and memory, where b is the branching factor, the average out-degree. Depth-first algorithms typically need far less extra memory.
BFS is Dijkstra's algorithm on an unweighted graph, where the priority queue degenerates into a FIFO queue. A breadth-first web crawl captures pages with high PageRank early in the crawl.

entries.title: Shortest path problem

definition.text: Finding a path between two vertices of a graph so that the sum of the weights of its edges is as small as possible.

facts.text: A road map is modeled as a graph: vertices are intersections or junctions, edges are road segments weighted by length, travel time or cost, and directed edges model one-way streets.

Algorithm choice depends on the graph: Dijkstra's for single-source with non-negative weights, Bellman–Ford if weights may be negative, A* for a single pair using heuristics, Floyd–Warshall for all pairs.
On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search solves the single-source problem in O(E + V).
On undirected graphs with positive weights, Dijkstra's original algorithm takes O(V²). A binary heap gives O((E + V) log V) and a Fibonacci heap gives O(E + V log V).
The all-pairs problem finds shortest paths between every pair of vertices. Floyd–Warshall solves it in O(V³) on directed graphs without negative cycles.
Bellman–Ford can detect a negative cycle in O(|V||E|). Adding constraints, such as keeping a second metric under a threshold, makes the problem NP-complete and harder to solve.
Real road networks are stochastic and time-dependent: travel time varies with traffic, road work, weather and accidents, and there is no accepted definition of an optimal path under uncertainty.

entries.title: Bidirectional search

definition.text: A graph search that finds a shortest path from a start vertex to a goal by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet.

facts.text: It is often faster: with branching factor b and start-to-goal distance d, each of the two searches costs O(b^(d/2)), and their sum is much less than the O(b^d) of a single search from start to goal.
The backward search must be able to find, for any node, the parent nodes that have an edge into it. Edges need not be traversable both ways, and a reverse arc uses the forward arc's cost.

The two frontiers collide when a node from one has successors in the opposing frontier. Termination needs care: Goldberg and others explained the correct conditions for bidirectional Dijkstra, and bidirectional A* needs a special stopping criterion.

Like A*, it can be guided by a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal or from the start. Front-to-front variants estimate to every node of the opposing frontier, which is computationally demanding.

Bidirectional Dijkstra often visits far fewer vertices and relaxes far fewer edges than one-directional Dijkstra on single-pair queries, since each search explores roughly half the space. Contraction hierarchies also answer queries with a bidirectional search.

entries.title: Six degrees of separation

definition.text: The idea that all people are six or fewer social connections apart, so a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people.

facts.text: The idea generalizes to an average social distance that is logarithmic in population size. With 30 contacts each, six rounds of handshakes would reach a population as large as the United States.
Watts and Strogatz showed the average path length in a random network is ln N / ln K, with N nodes and K acquaintances per node. For N = 300,000,000 and K = 30 that gives 5.7.

Measured distances are close: the average path length among 240 million Microsoft Messenger users was 6 (2007 study), and on Twitter in 2010 the average distance was 4.67, with nearly everyone five steps or less apart.

Bakhshandeh and colleagues' search technique found an average degree of separation of 3.43 between two random Twitter users with an average of only 67 requests; a near-optimal 3.88 took 13.3 requests.

entries.contested_note: Detractors argue that Milgram's small-world experiment did not demonstrate the six-degrees claim, which they call an academic urban myth.

entries.title: Designing a social network graph

facts.text: A user searches for someone and sees the shortest path to that person; the service must be highly available.
Assumptions: traffic is uneven, some searches are more popular than others, the graph data will not fit on a single machine, and graph edges are unweighted.
The scale is 100 million users with 50 friends each on average, giving 5 billion friend relationships, and 1 billion friend searches per month, or 400 search requests per second.
The exercise avoids graph-specific solutions such as GraphQL or a graph database like Neo4j; without that constraint, a graph database or graph query language could be used.
Without millions of users (vertices) and billions of friend relationships (edges), a general breadth-first search (BFS) would solve this unweighted shortest path task.
Users cannot all fit on one machine, so they are sharded across Person Servers, which are accessed through a Lookup Service.
The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Search API server, which forwards to the User Graph Service.

The User Graph Service asks the Lookup Service for the Person Server holding the current user, retrieves that user's friend_ids, and runs a BFS with the user as source and the friend_ids as adjacent nodes.
For each adjacent node it must again ask the Lookup Service which Person Server stores that id, a step with potential for optimization.
The public API is REST; internal communication could use remote procedure calls.

Person data can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached, which cuts response times and downstream traffic at 400 average read requests per second (higher at peak), especially for repeated searches and well-connected people.
Complete or partial BFS traversals can be stored in the memory cache to speed later lookups, or computed offline in batch and stored in a NoSQL database.
Reduce machine jumps by batching friend lookups hosted on the same Person Server, and shard Person Servers by location, since friends generally live closer to each other.
Run two BFS searches at once, one from the source and one from the destination, then merge the two paths.
Start the BFS from people with many friends, since they more likely shorten the degrees of separation to the target, and set a time or hop limit before asking the user whether to keep searching.

entries.title: Scaling a website in stages

facts.text: A simplified e-commerce site has an inventory service (product descriptions and inventory) and a user service (registration, login, user information) and evolves from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture.
As the user base grows, one application server cannot handle the traffic, so the application server and the database server are moved onto two separate servers.
When one application server is still not enough, a cluster of application servers is deployed, and a load balancer routes incoming requests so each server gets an even load.
If the database becomes the bottleneck, frequent read queries are sent to read replicas by separating reads from writes, which greatly increases database write throughput.

When one database cannot carry both the inventory and user tables, the options are adding CPU and RAM (which has a hard limit), partitioning horizontally across more database servers, or adding a caching layer to offload reads.
Finally the functions are modularized into separate services, making the architecture service-oriented or microservice.

entries.title: Virtual private cloud

definition.text: An on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others.

facts.text: Isolation normally comes from a private IP subnet and a virtual communication construct per user, such as a VLAN or a set of encrypted channels, so the organization works as if the cloud were not shared.
A per-VPC virtual private network function secures the organization's remote access to its VPC resources through authentication and encryption.
Amazon's VPC lets EC2 instances be connected to legacy infrastructure over an IPsec VPN.
On Google Cloud a VPC is a global resource and its subnets are regional, so users connect zones and regions without extra networking complexity.

entries.title: Scaling a system to millions of users

facts.text: Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. AWS-specific details are not required, since the principles apply outside AWS too.

A user makes a read or write request; the service processes it, stores user data and returns results. It must evolve from a few users to millions, with high availability, while discussing general scaling patterns.
Assumptions: traffic is uneven and relational data is needed. The target is 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads per month (100:1 read to write ratio), at 1 KB per write.
The estimate is 1 TB of new content per month (1 KB per write times 1 billion writes) and 36 TB in 3 years, with 400 writes per second and 40,000 reads per second on average.
With 1-2 users, start with a single box for simplicity: a web server on EC2, storage for user data and a MySQL database, scaling vertically when needed and monitoring to find bottlenecks.

Start with SQL because relational data is needed, with MySQL on the single box. Vertical scaling (a bigger box) can get very expensive and leaves no redundancy or failover; the alternative is horizontal scaling.
An Elastic IP gives a public endpoint that survives reboots and eases failover, and DNS such as Route 53 maps the domain to it. Open only needed ports: 80, 443 and 22 for SSH from whitelisted IPs.

As users grow, vertical scaling gets expensive and blocks scaling MySQL and the web server independently. So store static content in a managed object store such as S3, and move MySQL to a separate box, for example RDS.

The split adds complexity, changes to the web server and new security needs. Secure it with encryption in transit and at rest, a Virtual Private Cloud, a public subnet for the web server and a private subnet for everything else.

When one web server bottlenecks at peak hours, scale horizontally behind a load balancer such as ELB or HAProxy, terminating SSL there. Use multiple web servers and MySQL in master-slave failover across multiple availability zones.

Separate web servers (running as reverse proxy) from application servers and scale each independently, for example read-API and write-API servers. Move static and some dynamic content to a CDN such as CloudFront.

For a read-heavy (100:1) workload, move frequently accessed content and session data to a memory cache such as ElastiCache, which makes web servers stateless, and add MySQL read replicas, splitting reads and writes in the web server.
Traffic that spikes in business hours and drops after can be handled with autoscaling groups for each web and application server type across availability zones, to keep up with spikes and cut costs.

Near the full constraints, keep a limited period of data in MySQL and the rest in a warehouse such as Redshift, and scale the memory cache for 40,000 reads per second; read replicas may struggle with cache misses.
400 writes per second may strain a single SQL write master-slave: use federation, denormalization or SQL tuning, and consider moving suitable data to NoSQL such as DynamoDB.

Work that need not be real-time goes to queues and workers: in a photo service, the application server queues a job, and a worker creates the thumbnail, updates the database and stores the thumbnail in the object store.

entries.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol

definition.text: SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail.

facts.text: SMTP is a connection-oriented, text-based protocol: a sender issues command strings and a receiver replies, over a reliable ordered data stream, typically a TCP connection.
SMTP is a delivery protocol only: mail is pushed to the next-hop server as it arrives and routed by destination server, not by individual user. POP and IMAP handle retrieval.
A mail transaction is three command/reply steps: MAIL gives the return address, RCPT names one recipient (repeated per recipient), and DATA carries the header, a blank line and the body.
The server replies twice to DATA, once to say it is ready and once after the end-of-data marker to accept or reject the whole message. Replies are 2xx positive, 4xx transient or 5xx permanent.
Servers talk to each other on TCP port 25, while clients submit mail to a submission server on port 465 or 587, which requires SMTP authentication.
Fully capable servers keep queues and retry transient failures. A server that accepts a message takes responsibility for delivering it or reporting the failure.
SMTP defines message transport, the envelope, not content: RFC 5321 defines SMTP and RFC 5322 defines the message header and body.

Original SMTP could not authenticate senders, so spoofing is possible. Modern servers require client authentication and use SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

entries.title: Email message format

definition.text: An Internet email message is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies.

facts.text: A message consists of header fields, optionally followed by a body, with the header separated from the body by a blank line. RFC 5322 defines the syntax and MIME extends it.
A header field is a name, a colon and a field body. Long field bodies can be folded onto several lines by inserting a line break before whitespace and unfolded by removing it.
A conformant message uses US-ASCII characters. Each line must be at most 998 characters and should be at most 78, excluding the CRLF.
The header fields carry most of the semantic information; for RFC 5322 the body is a series of uninterpreted lines of text, and MIME defines other body structures.
Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use MIME encodings. UTF-8 in headers and addresses needs the newer internationalization extensions.
A message header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

entries.text: An email message is plain text, and one blank line splits it in two. It is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies, and a blank line separates the two. A header field is a name, a colon and a field body. A long body can be folded onto several lines by inserting a line break before whitespace. A conformant message uses US-ASCII characters, with each line at most 998 characters and ideally at most 78. The header fields carry most of the semantic information, because the RFC 5322 body is only a series of uninterpreted lines of text. Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use the encodings of {{ref:sysd-q-123}}. A header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use the encodings of MIME. A header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

entries.title: MIME
entries.article: Email#Message format > Message body > Multipart messages

definition.text: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments.

facts.text: Internet email was designed for 7-bit ASCII. MIME adds character set specifiers and two content transfer encodings: quoted printable for mostly 7-bit text and base64 for arbitrary binary data.
Base64 is widely used for attachments because SMTP in its original form transports only 7-bit ASCII; the attachment is encoded before sending and decoded on receipt.
A MIME message can hold several parts: multipart/mixed for a cover letter and documents, multipart/alternative for the same content in several formats, multipart/related for HTML with its images.
Parts can nest, and the sender can mark a part as shown inline or as an attachment.
A MIME message forms a tree whose leaves are single-part content types and whose inner nodes are multipart types, which lets IMAP fetch one part without the rest.

entries.title: Email spam

definition.text: Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email.

facts.text: Spam burdens recipients, who must manage, filter or delete it without compensation from the sender, making it a negative externality.
Sending is cheap, so spam grew to an estimated 90% of global email traffic by 2014, and about 85% of email in 2021.
Spammers need recipient addresses, so they and list merchants gather huge lists, harvesting addresses without the owners' consent.
Spammers misspell filtered words or hide the message text in an image to defeat pattern-matching and text-based filters.
Spammers use vulnerable third-party systems such as open mail relays, open proxies and networks of malware-infected PCs (zombies) to send mail.

To resist such abuse, administrators pre-emptively block dynamic IP ranges, require forward-confirmed reverse DNS and impose strict requirements on delivering servers, which can burden small domestic mail servers. Many ISPs block outgoing port 25.

entries.title: SMTP mail transaction
entries.article: rfc>5321#3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions

definition.text: An SMTP mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA.

facts.text: A session starts when the client opens a connection and the server sends a greeting; the client then normally sends EHLO to identify itself. The dialog is deliberately lock-step, one command at a time, unless pipelining is agreed.
MAIL starts a transaction and resets the receiver's state. Its reverse-path is the source mailbox used to report errors, and a 250 reply accepts it.
RCPT gives one forward-path per command and can be repeated. A recipient known to be undeliverable gets a 550 reply, and RCPT without a prior MAIL gets 503.
After DATA the server replies 354 and treats the following lines as the message until a line holding only a period. The client must not send message data unless it gets 354.
To let users send a line that is a single period, the client adds an extra leading period to any line starting with one and the server removes it.

When the server finishes storing the data it sends 250, which confirms the transaction. By returning 2yz it accepts responsibility to deliver the message, retry transient failures and notify the sender of permanent ones.
A 4yz after the end of data means the server must not deliver, and the client keeps responsibility and may requeue. A 5yz means the client should not retry to the same server without review.
The client ends the connection with QUIT, to which the receiver must send a 221 reply before closing the channel.

entries.title: SMTP envelope versus message header
entries.article: rfc>5321#2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects

definition.text: A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body.

facts.text: The envelope holds an originator address to which errors are reported, one or more recipient addresses and optional extension data. The content, sent in DATA, has a header section and a body.

Delivery follows the envelope, not the header: the To field may be unrelated to the addresses the message is delivered to, as the letter's address differs from the outer envelope, and From may not be the actual sender.
Bcc recipients are normally given only in the SMTP envelope and not listed in the message header.
Return-Path, added at final delivery, preserves the MAIL command's reverse-path, which can differ from the sender's mailbox when errors go to a special error-handling mailbox.
The content is US-ASCII text and header fields are always US-ASCII, though extensions such as 8BITMIME can relax the restriction for the body.

entries.title: Email header fields

definition.text: Email header fields fall into groups: originator, destination, identification, informational, trace and resent fields.

facts.text: From names the author, Sender names the agent that actually transmitted the message and must appear when From has several mailboxes, and Reply-To suggests where replies go. Without it, replies go to From.
To holds the primary recipients, Cc others who receive a copy, and Bcc recipients whose addresses are not revealed to the other recipients.
How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent: the Bcc line may be removed from every copy, or Bcc recipients may get a separate copy that carries it.
Every message should have a Message-ID, and replies should carry In-Reply-To and References fields.
Subject, Comments and Keywords are optional fields meant for human-readable information about the message; Subject is the most common and gives a short topic.
Each SMTP server prepends a Received trace line and must not change or delete earlier ones, and the final delivery adds Return-Path. The timestamps help find slow relays.
Servers can record authentication checks in header fields such as Authentication-Results, Received-SPF and DKIM-Signature for downstream agents.
Resent fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the transport system; they are informational and must not drive normal reply handling.

entries.text: Header fields come in six groups. Originator fields say who sent the message. From names the author, and Sender names the agent that actually transmitted it and must appear when From has several mailboxes. Reply-To suggests where replies go, or else they go to From. Destination fields name the recipients: To holds the primary recipients, Cc others who receive a copy, and Bcc recipients whose addresses are not revealed to the others. How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent. The line may be removed from every copy, or Bcc recipients may get a separate copy that carries it. Identification fields matter for conversations: every message should have a Message-ID, and replies should carry In-Reply-To and References. Informational fields are Subject, Comments and Keywords, optional and meant for humans, and Subject is the most common. Trace fields record the route. Each SMTP server prepends a Received line and must not change or delete earlier ones, and final delivery adds Return-Path, so the timestamps help find slow relays. Servers can also record authentication checks in fields such as Authentication-Results, Received-SPF and DKIM-Signature. Resent fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the transport system; they are informational and must not drive normal reply handling.

entries.title: SMTP queueing and retries
entries.article: rfc>5321#4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy

definition.text: An SMTP sender keeps mail that cannot be sent at once in a queue and retries it periodically until it succeeds or gives up.

facts.text: Mail that cannot be transmitted immediately must be queued and periodically retried, and a queue entry holds the envelope information as well as the message.
After a failed attempt the sender must delay retrying that destination. The retry interval should be at least 30 minutes, and the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4-5 days.
Failures are typically transient, which favors two connection attempts in the first hour in the queue and then backing off to one every two or three hours.
A client should keep a list of unreachable hosts with their timeouts rather than retry every queued item, because retrying many messages to a dead host wastes Internet overhead and blocks the sender.
When several recipients share a destination server only one copy should be sent: one MAIL, a RCPT for each recipient, then one DATA.
A client may run several concurrent outgoing transactions for timely delivery, with a limit to protect the host, and a server should accept more than one incoming transaction at a time.
Receiving mail from a host suggests that mail queued for it can now be sent, which can remove the need for an explicit send-queue command.
Retry parameters must be configurable and every activity must have a per-command timeout. A receiver must answer the end-of-data promptly to avoid duplicates after timeouts.

entries.title: Bounce messages
entries.article: rfc>5321#6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email

definition.text: A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it.

facts.text: A server that accepts a message with 250 after DATA accepts responsibility for delivering or relaying it, and must not lose it for frivolous reasons such as a later host crash.

If delivery fails after acceptance, the server must send a notification to the envelope return path, using a null reverse-path <> for the notice; no notification is sent when the return path is already null.
Servers must not send notifications about problems with notifications; the null reverse-path prevents error-report loops.
Some failures after acceptance cannot be avoided, for example when a soft DNS error blocks recipient validation, the target is a mailing list, or the server is a relay.
Rejecting a message during the SMTP transaction is better than bouncing it afterwards. Servers that check recipients only after receiving the text cannot tell the client which recipient failed.
Backscatter happens when a misconfigured server bounces mail whose envelope sender was forged, so the bounce lands on an innocent party; many ISPs disable non-delivery reports for this reason.
Servers should avoid sending bounces for mail judged hostile unless confident that the bounce will be usefully delivered.

entries.title: Mail agents and relays
entries.article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol#Mail processing model

definition.text: Mail passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role.

facts.text: A mail user agent submits mail to a mail submission agent, which hands it to a mail transfer agent. These two agents are often the same software started with different options.
The boundary MTA looks up the MX record for the recipient's domain and connects to the target MTA. Transfer is one connection between two MTAs or a series of hops through intermediaries.
A receiving server may be the final destination, a relay that stores and forwards, or a gateway that forwards using a protocol other than SMTP.
A relay passes on the message data without modification except for adding trace information, whereas a gateway may need to transform the message because the two transport environments differ.
Counting the Received header fields in a message is an effective way to detect mail loops; servers using it should use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 entries.
The final hop hands the message to a mail delivery agent, which saves it in the mailbox format or forwards it by SMTP or LMTP. Clients then retrieve mail with IMAP or POP.
A relay is usually the target of an MX record. It may accept or decline relaying as it would for a local user, becomes an SMTP client if it accepts, and returns 550 if policy forbids relaying.
Clients that cannot queue mail for retry, such as those paired with POP or IMAP, send everything to a single submission server; a message submission protocol is superseding such arrangements.

entries.title: MX record

definition.text: An MX record is a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of a domain.

facts.text: An MX record carries a preference value and the host name of a mail server. A domain may have one or more of them.
A sending MTA queries DNS for the MX records of each recipient's domain, gets a list of mail servers with preferences, and tries the lowest preference number first.
The preference is an unsigned 16-bit field, so valid values range from 0 to 65535.
The host named in an MX record must map to one or more address records (A or AAAA) and must not point to a CNAME record.

With no MX record, the sender treats the domain as having an implicit MX of preference 0 pointing at itself and looks up its address records. If MX records exist, other address records must not be used.
A nonexistent-domain answer must be reported as an error, while a temporary DNS error means the message must be queued and retried later.
Several MX records, typically pointing to an array of mail servers, give load balancing and redundancy, and allow high-availability clusters of mail gateways for one domain.
MX records cannot move mail service to another port and cannot weight servers of unequal priority.

entries.title: Post Office Protocol

definition.text: POP is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server.

facts.text: POP gives a client application access to a mailbox (maildrop) on a mail server and supports list, retrieve and delete operations on messages.

POP3 clients typically connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer and delete them from the server. This suited users with only temporary dial-up connections who read mail offline.
Clients may leave mail on the server and download only new messages, identified through the UIDL unique-id list command; the unique identifier is permanent for the maildrop.
Messages are retrieved and marked for deletion by message number, and mail marked for deletion is removed from the maildrop only when the client ends the session.
A POP3 server listens on TCP port 110. Encryption is requested with the STLS command, or by connecting to POP3S on port 995 using TLS.
The original POP3 allowed only an unencrypted USER/PASS login. APOP adds a challenge-response using MD5, and SASL methods are supported through the AUTH extension.
The CAPA command lists extension capabilities, but the extension RFC reaffirmed that POP3's role is simple download-and-delete mailbox handling.

entries.title: Email delivery

definition.text: Email travels from the sender's mail client through submission and transfer servers, found with DNS MX records, to the recipient's mailbox.

facts.text: The sender's mail user agent formats the message and sends it with the submission protocol, a profile of SMTP, to its local mail submission agent.
The submission agent takes the destination from the SMTP envelope, not the message header. The part before @ is the local part, the part after is a domain name it resolves in DNS.
DNS answers with the MX records listing the domain's mail exchange servers, which are MTAs, often run by the recipient's ISP.

The sending server transfers the message by SMTP. The receiving MTA may forward it to other MTAs before the mail delivery agent places it in the recipient's mailbox, from which the recipient's client collects it by POP3 or IMAP.
Domains usually have several mail exchange servers so they can keep accepting mail when the primary is unavailable.

Email favors reliability over speed to cope with unreliable links and busy servers. Overloaded servers, SMTP's many round trips and downtime slow it; mail can be queued and retried for up to five days before a permanent-failure notice.

Accepting a message obliges an MTA to deliver it or send a bounce message back. Open relays that accepted mail for anyone were exploited by spammers, so they are now rare and many MTAs refuse mail from them.
Variations exist: corporate systems use proprietary client protocols and an Internet mail gateway, and users may use webmail instead of a mail client.
