entries.title: Internet Message Access Protocol

definition.text: IMAP is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection.

facts.text: IMAP was designed for complete management of a mailbox by multiple clients, so clients generally leave messages on the server until the user deletes them. It makes remote mailboxes work like local folders.
The server holds the mailbox structure: content, folders and per-message state. Local copies are a temporary cache, and this makes IMAP need far more server resources and cost per mailbox than POP.
Clients often stay connected and download message content on demand, which can give faster response for large mailboxes. The server reports new messages and changes made by other clients.

Flags such as read, replied to or deleted are stored on the server, so different clients see each other's changes. IMAP also supports client-defined keywords and creating, renaming and deleting mailboxes.

IMAP can ask the server to search by criteria so clients need not download every message, but searching massive mailboxes can burden the server unless its storage, indexing and search are carefully built.
Clients can fetch individual MIME parts or portions of a message, such as the text without its attachments, or stream content as it is fetched.
IMAP IDLE lets the server notify connected clients of mailbox changes such as new mail, but clients must keep a TCP connection open to be notified.
An IMAP server listens on port 143, or 993 for IMAP over TLS; STARTTLS can encrypt a connection begun on port 143. RFC 9051 defines the current version.

entries.title: POP versus IMAP

definition.text: POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it.

facts.text: POP3 moves messages from the server to the client and deletes them there, though it can leave them. IMAP normally leaves all messages on the server and supports both connected and disconnected use.

POP gives a completely static view of the mailbox; the client must reconnect and re-authenticate to see changes. IMAP gives a dynamic view and reports new mail and changes made by other connected clients.
POP treats the mailbox as a single store with no folders and no server-side message state, so two POP clients cannot sync read state. IMAP keeps folders and flags on the server.
IMAP IDLE lets the server tell connected clients about new mail. POP has no such feature, so clients must reconnect periodically to check.
POP retrieves whole messages with RETR, or headers plus some body lines with TOP. IMAP can fetch individual MIME parts, such as text without attachments, and search messages on the server.
POP is a simpler protocol and easier to implement. IMAP remedies many POP shortcomings but adds complexity and keeps mailbox structure on the server, costing far more server resources per mailbox.
A POP UIDL is a string of visible ASCII characters up to 70 characters, while an IMAP UID is a number local to a folder, paired with a UIDVALIDITY value.
Both are the two most prevalent standard retrieval protocols, and webmail providers such as Gmail and Outlook.com support both.

entries.title: IMAP commands and responses
entries.article: rfc>9051#2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses

definition.text: An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result.

facts.text: IMAP assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP and listens on port 143, or 993 for implicit TLS. Everything is sent as lines ending in CRLF.
Each client command carries a tag, and the server's completion response repeats it with OK, NO or BAD (protocol error), so the tag shows which command finished when several are in progress.

Server data and non-completion status are prefixed with "*" as untagged responses, and may be sent unilaterally. A client must be ready to accept any response at any time and should cache server data.
A client may pipeline commands without waiting for completion, but if a command could affect another's results the server must execute them in the order given.
The server must send mailbox size updates automatically and should send flag updates; only EXPUNGE may reduce the message count, because EXISTS cannot.

A connection is in one of four states, not authenticated, authenticated, selected or logout; most commands are valid in only some states, and a client must select a mailbox before commands that affect messages.

entries.title: IMAP unique identifiers
entries.article: rfc>9051#2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute

definition.text: An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY.

facts.text: IMAP addresses a message by its UID or by its message sequence number, which is its relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox.
A UID is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added; UIDs need not be contiguous, unlike sequence numbers.
A UID must not change during a session and should not change between sessions. Persistent UIDs let a client resynchronize its state, for example an offline client.
UIDVALIDITY lets a client detect changed UIDs: if UIDs fail to persist, the new value must be greater than the old, and a 32-bit date-time or a global counter makes a good value.
UIDNEXT is the predicted UID of the next new message. It changes whenever messages are added, even if later expunged, so a client can tell whether mail arrived since it last checked.
The mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY and UID together must refer to a single immutable message forever, and an expunged message's UID is never reused under the same UIDVALIDITY.

entries.title: Email spoofing

definition.text: Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source.

facts.text: Spam and phishing typically use spoofing to mislead the recipient about the message's true origin.
Spoofing is possible because original SMTP could not authenticate senders, and even casual users can negotiate directly with receiving and relaying servers to build a misleading message.
A sender's own software can set From freely, but a domain owner can specify which servers may send for the domain, and servers can sign mail (SPF and DKIM), so spoofed addresses can be flagged.
These techniques do not protect against misspelled lookalike domain names.

entries.title: SMTP security
entries.article: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol#SMTP Extensions > Security extensions

definition.text: SMTP security covers authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy.

facts.text: SMTP-AUTH makes the client log in to the mail server while sending, letting legitimate users relay mail and denying relay to spammers.
SMTP-AUTH does not guarantee the authenticity of the envelope sender or the From header, so spoofing is still possible unless the server limits from-addresses to those the authenticated user may use.
STARTTLS lets a server advertise TLS and a client upgrade the connection. It is opportunistic: the server gains no security unless the client chooses to upgrade.
STARTTLS resists only passive observation, since negotiation is in plain text and an active attacker can strip the STARTTLS commands, a downgrade known as STRIPTLS.
MTA-STS lets a domain declare in a policy file and DNS TXT record that it supports secure channels; senders cache it and never use insecure channels until it expires.
DANE for SMTP lets operators publish a hash of their TLS certificate in DNS secured by DNSSEC, which reduces the chance of unencrypted delivery.
RFC 8314 declared plain text obsolete and recommends always using TLS for mail submission and access, adding ports with implicit TLS.
SMTP cannot authenticate mail or check integrity at the transport level; real mail security lies in end-to-end methods on the message body, such as digital signatures.

entries.title: Spam filtering

definition.text: Spam filtering combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail.

facts.text: Popular methods are content-based filtering, DNS-based blackhole lists (DNSBL), greylisting, spamtraps, enforcing SMTP's technical requirements, checksumming to detect bulk mail, and costs on the sender such as proof-of-work or micropayments. Each has strengths and weaknesses.
Bayesian filters rely roughly on word probabilities: a message with many words used only in spam and few never used in spam is likely spam. Machine learning more broadly can also identify spam.
Spammers adapt, for example by adding random words to weaken Bayesian filters (Bayesian poisoning), so filtering is an escalating game against new evasion techniques.
Outbound spam protection applies the same techniques to mail leaving a provider's network and blocks the message or shuts off its source.
Email authentication against forged From addresses became popular in the 2010s. Servers use SPF, DKIM and DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

Filtering has collateral damage: it uses server and network resources, rejected legitimate mail forces senders to contact recipients out of channel, and mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice.
Silently dropping mail violates the expectation that mail is delivered or returned, so it should be considered only with very high confidence that a message is seriously fraudulent.
IMAP defines $Junk and $NotJunk keywords so users or delivery agents can mark junk, and $Phishing for likely phishing mail, which should also be filed as junk.

entries.title: Designing Gmail

facts.text: The system must get a user's email into the recipient's mailbox, where the recipient's client can fetch it: Alice sends from her client, and the Gmail server stores the mail and makes it available to Bob.
SMTP's objective is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently, and email favors reliability over speed so it copes with unreliable network links and busy servers.

RFC 5321 sets minimums: message content of at least 64K octets, 100 buffered recipients, local parts up to 64 octets and domains up to 255. Providers cap attachments, typically at 25MB or less in the early 2010s.
SMTP is the protocol between client and server and between mail servers, but it only delivers; the recipient's client fetches mail from the mailbox with IMAP or POP.

A mail object is an envelope, with the error-return address and recipients, plus content of header and body. Delivery follows the envelope, so To can differ from the delivery list, and Bcc lives only in the envelope.

Every message has a globally unique Message-ID, and replies name the parent in In-Reply-To and References, which lets a client rebuild conversation threads. Headers follow RFC 5322, and non-ASCII text and attachments use MIME.

The server keeps each mailbox: messages with strictly ascending UIDs and a UIDVALIDITY value, per-message flags such as \Seen and \Deleted, and folders. This server-held state costs far more per mailbox than POP.
Alice's client submits the message by SMTP to her mail server, on port 587 or 465 with authentication, and that server hands it to its mail transfer agent.
The sending MTA asks DNS for the MX records of the recipient's domain and tries the lowest preference first, randomizing among equals. For a Gmail address the answer is Gmail's SMTP server.

The MTA connects to the receiving server on port 25 and runs MAIL, RCPT and DATA, sending one copy for all recipients there. After the final 250 the receiver owns the message and must deliver it or report failure.
A mail delivery agent saves the accepted message in the recipient's mailbox format, so the Gmail server holds the mail until Bob's client asks for it.

When Bob logs in, his client fetches new mail through the IMAP/POP server. IMAP leaves messages on the server so several clients share a mailbox, POP downloads and deletes, and IMAP IDLE pushes new-mail notices instead of polling.

IMAP lets the server search so clients need not download every message, and fetch single MIME parts such as text without attachments. Searching massive mailboxes can overload the server unless storage, indexing and search are carefully built.

About 85% of email was estimated to be spam in 2021, so incoming mail is filtered by content, DNS blocklists, greylisting, Bayesian or learned models and sender authentication. Mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice.

Attachments travel as MIME parts: original SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII, so binary files are base64-encoded into a multipart message, and the size the transport sees can differ from what the user sees.

Mail that cannot be sent is queued and retried, at least 30 minutes apart, for at least 4-5 days. Several MX servers keep a domain accepting mail if one fails, and undeliverable mail is bounced with a null return path.

entries.title: Dijkstra's algorithm

definition.text: An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network.

facts.text: It starts with distance zero at the source and infinity elsewhere, then repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the lowest distance and updates each unvisited neighbor's distance if the route through that vertex is shorter.
It computes shortest paths from the source to every other node, and can stop as soon as the shortest path to one chosen destination is known.

A min-priority queue selects the closest vertex. A binary heap gives O((V+E) log V); Fibonacci heaps have better theoretical bounds but often perform worse in real applications because of large constant factors.

Sparse networks such as road maps suit it. Modern routing systems pair it with preprocessing such as A*, landmark heuristics or contraction hierarchies; contraction hierarchies can be up to seven orders of magnitude faster.
It gives incorrect results when edges have negative weights, because its greedy strategy finalizes a vertex's distance before a cheaper path through a negative edge is seen.

Starting with a queue holding only the source and inserting vertices as they are discovered gives uniform-cost search, which can find the closest of a set of targets even on graphs too large to hold in memory.

Bidirectional Dijkstra searches forward from the source and backward from the target on the reversed graph, stopping when the two queues' minimum priorities sum to at least the best path found; it explores far fewer vertices on road-like graphs.
Shortest-path algorithms are used in network routing protocols, most notably IS-IS and OSPF.

entries.title: A* search algorithm

definition.text: A graph search algorithm that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node by extending the path with the lowest cost so far plus an estimate of the cost still to go.

facts.text: A* is an informed, best-first search on a weighted graph. It keeps a tree of paths from the start node and extends them one edge at a time until the goal is reached.
It extends the path that minimizes f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost from the start to n and h(n) is a problem-specific heuristic estimating the cheapest remaining path to the goal.
Implementations keep the frontier in a priority queue ordered by f, stop when the node removed is the goal, and store each node's predecessor to recover the path.
On a road map the heuristic can be the straight-line distance to the goal, the physically smallest possible distance; on a grid map, taxicab or Chebyshev distance fits better.
A* returns an optimal path when the heuristic is admissible. With a consistent heuristic it never processes a node more than once and equals Dijkstra's algorithm run with a reduced edge cost.
Dijkstra's algorithm is the special case where h(x) = 0 for all nodes. A* differs from greedy best-first search because it also counts the distance already travelled.

Search effort depends on the heuristic: a close estimate cuts node expansions and a poor one causes many. Relaxing admissibility trades optimality for speed, with ε-admissible variants guaranteed within (1 + ε) of optimal.

A* keeps all generated nodes in memory, its biggest practical drawback. In travel-routing systems it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph, though it is still the best solution in many cases.

entries.title: Geocoding

definition.text: Turning a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair.

facts.text: Reverse geocoding converts coordinates back to a description such as a place name or address. Geocoding relies on representations of address points, the street network, and postal and administrative boundaries.

A geocoder combines an input dataset of descriptive text, a reference dataset of feature locations in a spatial reference system, and software that matches each input to a reference feature and attaches its location.

A direct match maps an input to one whole reference feature, such as a country or ZIP code, much like a table join but with handling for approximate matches such as different capitalization or slight misspellings.

Address interpolation uses street segments tagged with address ranges. The geocoder parses the address, matches a segment whose number range includes it, and estimates the position along that segment.
Positional accuracy varies, from building centroids and interpolated street positions to postal code and administrative-division centroids.

Mismatches arise from misspelled or incomplete input and outdated reference data. Geocoders handle abbreviations such as E for East, and cleaning the input, called address scrubbing, improves accuracy.
Ambiguity such as the same street name in two towns is resolved by asking for the city and region.
On the web, geocoding powers routing and local search. A geohash is a grid-style geocode that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

entries.title: Contraction hierarchies

definition.text: A speed-up technique for shortest-path queries that precomputes shortcuts in a road graph so a query can skip unimportant vertices.

facts.text: A road network is a graph with intersections as vertices and road sections as edges weighted by travel time. Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on it because road networks have tens of millions of vertices.
The method has a preprocessing phase and a query phase. Road networks change rarely, so seconds to hours can be spent once, and queries are then answered in microseconds.

Road networks are highly hierarchical: highway junctions rank above a junction into a dead end. A shortcut joins two non-adjacent vertices with the weight of their shortest path, so queries skip the full path between important junctions.
Preprocessing contracts vertices one by one: it removes a vertex and adds a shortcut between two neighbors only if their shortest path goes through it, which a witness search checks.

The contraction order should add few shortcuts, but optimal ordering is NP-complete, so heuristics are used. Bottom-up heuristics are cheaper and greedy; top-down heuristics give better results but need more preprocessing time.
A query runs a bidirectional search from the start and target over the graph plus shortcuts. Both searches only follow edges to more important vertices, which keeps the search space small.
A query yields the travel time or distance, not the route. Shortcuts must be unpacked into road edges, and storing each shortcut's middle vertex makes the recursive unpacking linear-time.

If edge weights change more often than the road topology, a customization phase between preprocessing and query can switch between distance and time, include current traffic, or honor user preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

entries.title: Map tiles

definition.text: A world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small image blocks that the client joins seamlessly, each requested separately.

facts.text: The world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into small blocks called tiles, which the client joins seamlessly into the visible map.
When the user pans, most tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched. Tiles can be pre-computed in parallel, and serving rendered images is cheaper than rendering in the browser.

Common conventions: zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile, each zoom level doubles both dimensions so one tile becomes 4, about 22 levels suffice, and Web Mercator is used with latitude limits near 85 degrees.
The OpenStreetMap XYZ convention serves tiles at URLs like .../Z/X/Y.png, with Z the zoom level and X and Y identifying the tile. Tile Map Service numbers Y northwards, OpenStreetMap southwards.
Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage such as S3 serves them efficiently, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.

To support zooming and panning, the map blocks are pre-calculated at different zoom levels and the images are loaded when needed. A single file holding all tiles, as PMTiles does, is an alternative with good performance.
Most tiles are raster images such as PNG or JPEG. Vector tiles are rendered by the client, which can style them and keep text readable when rotating; Google and Apple have moved to vector tiles.
A web mapping framework such as the Google Maps API, OpenLayers or Leaflet retrieves, displays and caches the tiles and handles user navigation.

entries.title: Web Mercator projection

definition.text: A variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates and is the standard for web mapping.

facts.text: Virtually all major online map providers use it, including Google Maps, Mapbox, Bing Maps and OpenStreetMap; its identifier is EPSG:3857.
It uses spherical formulas at all scales on WGS 84 coordinates, which makes it slightly non-conformal, but the spherical form needs only a fraction of the computing resources of the ellipsoidal one.
World coordinates are scaled so the upper left corner is (0, 0) and the lower right is (2^zoom - 1, 2^zoom - 1) before pixel positions are computed at a zoom level.
Mercator projects the poles at infinity, so Web Mercator cannot show them; Google Maps cuts off coverage at 85.051129° north and south, the latitude at which the full map becomes a square.

entries.title: Designing Google Maps

facts.text: As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world; a simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation.
The location service records user location updates, which clients send every few seconds.
Location data is used to detect new and recently closed roads, to improve the map's accuracy over time, and as an input for live traffic data.
The road network is modelled as a graph: intersections are vertices, road sections are edges, and edge weights are the travel time along that section.
Map data can live in a spatial database, which is needed for dynamic data or a huge amount of geographic data and supports spatial queries and geometry manipulation.
For rendering, the world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into tiles. Tiled web maps use Web Mercator, and Google Maps cuts coverage at 85.051129° north and south.
Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile and each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4; about 22 zoom levels are sufficient for most practical purposes.
Clients request tiles by URL such as .../Z/X/Y.png. On a pan most displayed tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched, which beats fetching one image for the whole viewport.
Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage like S3 serves them, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.
To support zooming and panning, pre-calculate the map blocks at different zoom levels and load the images when needed; pre-computing individual tiles is easy to parallelize.
The navigation service finds a reasonably fast route from point A to point B, calling a Geocoding Service to resolve an address to a latitude/longitude pair and a Route Planner Service.
Geocoding matches an address to a street segment whose address range includes the house number and interpolates the position within that range.

The Route Planner calculates the top-K shortest paths between A and B, estimates the time of each path from current traffic and historical data, then ranks the paths by predicted time and user filtering.

Plain Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on networks with tens of millions of vertices. A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic helps, but is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph.

Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts, spending seconds to hours once because roads change rarely, then answer queries in microseconds with a bidirectional search that only climbs toward more important vertices.

When live traffic changes edge weights more often than the road topology, a customization phase re-applies the stored contractions with new weights and can honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

entries.title: Non-blocking algorithm

definition.text: An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread.

facts.text: A non-blocking algorithm is lock-free if there is guaranteed system-wide progress and wait-free if there is also guaranteed per-thread progress; obstruction-freedom is the weakest guarantee, and every lock-free algorithm is obstruction-free.

Locks block threads that cannot accomplish anything while waiting, can cause deadlock, livelock and priority inversion, and force a trade-off between coarse-grained locking, which limits parallelism, and error-prone fine-grained locking.

A lock-free data structure spends more time in parallel rather than serial execution, improving performance on a multi-core processor because access to shared data need not be serialized; it is also safe in interrupt handlers.
Non-blocking algorithms use atomic read-modify-write primitives provided by the hardware, most notably compare-and-swap, in a carefully designed order of reads, read-modify-writes and writes.
Compilers and many CPUs reorder operations unless told not to, so memory barriers are needed; C++11 std::atomic and C11 stdatomic.h supply types that stop the compiler reordering and insert barriers.
A single-reader single-writer ring buffer FIFO can be implemented safely with only a memory barrier, since some non-blocking structures are weak enough to need no special atomic primitives.

It is difficult to write lock-free code that is correct; wait-free designs from universal constructions perform below blocking designs, and without hard deadlines wait-free algorithms may not be worth their extra complexity.

entries.title: Order types

definition.text: The standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules.

facts.text: A market order executes immediately at the best available price and is filled as long as willing counterparties exist; it gives certainty of execution but no control over the price received.
In fast-moving markets a market order's fill price can differ widely from the last quote, and the order may be split across several counterparties at different prices.
A buy limit order executes only at the limit price or lower and a sell limit order only at the limit price or higher; the trader controls the price but the order may never be filled.
A limit order that the book can satisfy on arrival is marketable; it may be filled in part from the book, with the rest added to the book.

Fill-or-kill orders are filled completely on the first attempt or cancelled, all-or-none orders must be filled in full or not at all, and immediate-or-cancel orders execute at once but allow partial fills.
A day order lasts until the end of the day's trading session; a good-til-cancelled order persists until a cancelling order, although brokers may set limits such as 90 days.
A conditional order executes only when a condition is met: a stop order becomes active when the price reaches the stop price, and a stop-limit order then becomes a limit order.

entries.title: FIX protocol

definition.text: An electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets.

facts.text: FIX is the standard electronic protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, used by the buy side and sell side, including mutual funds, investment banks, brokers, stock exchanges and ECNs.
Classic FIX tagvalue messages are ASCII text: each field is a numeric tag plus a value separated by the SOH character, so messages are self-describing; a message has a header, a body and a trailer.
Body length counts characters from tag 35 up to tag 10, and the checksum is the last field, tag 10: the sum of the ASCII values of all other characters modulo 256, written as three characters.
The FIXT session layer is a point-to-point protocol usually run over TCP, and it guarantees message delivery in both directions.

Messages in each direction carry a sequence number; after a communication fault a peer may request retransmission of missed messages, and delivery survives disconnection and a later reestablished session.

Simple Binary Encoding uses native binary types in fixed positions, giving much lower latency and more deterministic performance than character-based tagvalue, whose variable-length fields were judged no longer fit for high performance trading.

The FIXP session layer for high performance trading lets peers negotiate delivery guarantees: recoverable (exactly-once, with retransmission), idempotent (at-most-once) or unsequenced; delays from retransmission are often undesirable in fast markets.
FAST is a binary protocol used mostly for sending multicast market data over UDP connections.

entries.title: Order book

definition.text: The list of orders that a trading venue, in particular a stock exchange, uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument.

facts.text: A securities order book holds a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders.
Each entry keeps the number of securities, the price the buyer or seller bids or asks, and some means of identifying the party, even if that identity is obscured as in a dark pool.
Orders at the same price sit on one price level; a bid arriving at that price could potentially be filled by any of the sell orders on that level.
A matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed; a bid equal to or higher than the lowest ask is filled at once and never joins the open book.
If such crossing orders stay unmatched because of an error or a market condition, the book is said to be crossed.
The highest bid and the lowest ask are the top of the book; they signal the prevailing market, and the difference between them is the bid-ask spread.
Book depth is the number of price levels in the book; a book can be kept to a fixed depth, with orders beyond it ignored or rejected, or hold unlimited levels.

entries.title: Market data

definition.text: Price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange.

facts.text: A market data record carries the instrument identifier (ticker symbol and exchange code), the latest bid and ask price and the time of the last trade, and may add volume traded and bid and offer sizes.
Quote data (bid, ask and their sizes) and trade data (last sale, last size, volume) are often generated over different data feeds.
Delivering prices from exchanges to users is highly time-sensitive, so specialized ticker plants collect and push massive data streams fast enough to feed trading systems before markets change.

Distribution platforms compress or represent data with specially designed protocols to raise throughput or reduce latency; UDP multicast delivers it efficiently to many recipients at once, and the FAST binary protocol exists for multicast market data.

In a feed handler, sources connect to a server that redistributes data: it forwards a client's subscription to the sources if it has no cached data, then sends every update for an instrument to all subscribed clients.
A feed handler server applies two permission levels: login permission to connect, and information permission to view an instrument.

Market data is either real-time or delayed price quotations; static reference data, such as identifier codes and security terms, does not change in real time and usually originates from the issuer, while prices originate from the exchanges.

definition.text: The component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed.

entries.title: Processor affinity

definition.text: Also called CPU pinning, it binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors.

facts.text: A thread that resumes on the CPU it ran on before may find data still in that CPU's cache and take fewer cache misses, but pinning forces it to wait for that CPU to become free.
Pinning suits CPU-intensive processes with few interrupts; an ordinary program, which is interrupted more often and ends up waiting more, might instead be slowed down.
On NUMA systems the latency comes from L3 misses and cross-node memory access, so constraining all threads of a program to one NUMA node lets them share an L3 cache.
Affinity statically divides processing resources, which leaves cores unused when no other program runs; on Linux it is set with the taskset program or the sched_setaffinity system call.

entries.title: Low-latency critical path design

definition.text: Getting very low latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

facts.text: A modern stock exchange reaches microsecond latency with the principle of doing less on the critical path.

Tasks that are not critical should be removed from the critical path; for example the market data flow and the reporting flow are off the exchange's critical path and have different latency requirements.
Key components on the critical path can be single-threaded, each pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks, and run one task after another in a single loop.
Components can talk through shared memory used as an event bus instead of a hard disk, and be deployed together on one giant server without containers.

entries.title: Designing a stock exchange

facts.text: The aim is microsecond latency, reached by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

The trading flow is the critical path with strict latency requirements: an order enters the order manager, passes mandatory risk checks, is matched, and the execution leaves through the order manager.
The market data flow and the reporting flow are not on the critical path and have different latency requirements, so non-critical tasks are removed from the trading flow.

Clients send orders, instructions to buy or sell, to a broker or directly to the exchange; FIX, the standard protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, carries them as numeric tag and value fields.

FIX sessions use sequence numbers and retransmission on request, so delivery survives a disconnection; high-performance sessions can instead pick idempotent or unsequenced delivery, since retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets.
Binary encodings such as Simple Binary Encoding cut latency, because no translation is needed to put data into a format computers can use, and fixed-length fields make performance more deterministic.
A market order executes at once at the best available price, giving certainty of execution but no price control; a limit order executes only at its limit price or better and may never fill.

Time-in-force and conditional instructions add rules: day orders expire at the session close, good-til-cancelled orders persist, immediate-or-cancel allows partial fills, and a stop order activates at its stop price.

The order book is the data model: a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders, each entry holding the party, the number of securities and the price, with orders at one price grouped into a price level.
The top of the book is the highest bid and lowest ask; their gap is the bid-ask spread, and book depth is the number of price levels kept.
The matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed; a bid at or above the lowest ask fills at once, and a partly filled limit order rests on the book.
Matching priority favors market orders, then limit orders first-come-first-served, with conditional orders ranked by when their condition is met and iceberg or dark-pool orders lower.

Market data, the latest bid, ask and last trade, is published off the critical path; delivery is highly time-sensitive, ticker plants handle the streams, and UDP multicast serves many recipients at once.
All components run on a single giant server with no containers, and shared memory serves as the event bus with no hard disk; other components listen on the bus and react.
The order manager and matching engine are single-threaded on the critical path and each is pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks; the loop runs tasks one by one in sequence.

Locks block threads and risk deadlock and priority inversion, so a design avoids them in shared structures: lock-free data structures raise parallel performance, and a single-reader single-writer ring buffer needs only a memory barrier.

entries.title: Collaborative real-time editing

definition.text: Letting several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly.

facts.text: Real-time editing synchronizes the edits of all online users automatically and periodically, often nearly instantly, which avoids or minimizes edit conflicts.
Asynchronous editing (delayed or offline) makes each user submit, update and merge manually, so several users can edit the same line and cause conflicts needing manual merging or overwriting.
The difficulty is communication latency. Users need their own edits incorporated instantly, yet instant incorporation means edits land in different versions of the document.
If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made on versions that never existed locally; the task is applying such remote edits that may conflict with local ones.
The most sophisticated solutions need no server, use no locking, so all users edit all parts at once, and support any number of users, limited only by their computers.

A basic client-server design makes one editor the collaboration server, which receives timestamped change notifications and broadcasts its changes; it is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources.
Workspace approaches that lock the document or reconcile conflicting changes are generally found unsatisfactory by users.
A sequence CRDT can serve as an alternative to operational transformation; Microsoft's Fluid Framework instead relies on total order broadcast, as opposed to OT or CRDT.

entries.title: Groupware concurrency control

definition.text: Concurrency control for groupware, computer systems that support two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment.

facts.text: Groupware systems often require fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. The paper separates real-time groupware from other multi-user systems and sets out their concurrency control requirements.
It presents a concurrency control algorithm for real-time groupware whose advantages are simplicity of use and responsiveness: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.
The algorithm must know some semantics of the operations, but its overall structure is independent of that information, so it can be adapted to many situations.
It is applied to group text editing, with a proof sketch, and the paper notes that the behavior wanted in many such systems is non-serializable.

entries.title: Operational transformation

definition.text: A technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed.

facts.text: OT was invented for consistency maintenance and concurrency control in collaborative editing of plain text, and was pioneered in 1989 by Ellis and Gibbs. It was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs.

Each client holds its own copy and edits it without locking or blocking; changes are propagated and each receiver transforms them before executing, so all sites keep their consistency invariants and the client stays responsive despite latency.
With the text abc, O1 = insert x at 0 and O2 = delete c at 2: after O1, O2 must become delete at 3. Untransformed, it would delete b instead of c.

Collaborative editing needs causality preservation (operations run in cause-effect order) and convergence (all copies identical once all operations have run); the CCI model adds intention preservation.

An OT system separates the high-level control algorithm, which decides which operations are transformed against which, from the low-level transformation functions, which transform a pair of operations by type and position.
The first OT system used a single linear address space with character-wise insert and delete; the model was later extended with an update operation and hierarchies of addressing domains.

Property TP1 requires that applying op1 then the transformed op2 equals applying op2 then the transformed op1 for concurrent operations on the same state; TP2 extends this to three concurrent operations.

OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, implementing it is painful per a former Google Wave engineer, and every edit must be captured. Differential synchronization and sequence CRDTs are alternatives.

entries.title: Designing Google Docs

facts.text: The system must merge edits from different users on different devices automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times.
The groupware concurrency algorithm of Ellis and colleagues is simple and responsive: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.
Clients send document editing operations to the WebSocket server, which handles the real-time communication.
Document operations are persisted in a message queue, and the file operation server consumes them and generates transformed operations using collaboration algorithms.
Three types of data are stored: file metadata, file content and operations.

One of the biggest challenges is real-time conflict resolution. Users need their own edits shown instantly, but because of network latency those edits are applied to different versions of the document.
If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made against versions that never existed locally, so remote edits must be applied despite conflicts with local ones.
Common conflict-resolution algorithms are operational transformation (OT), differential synchronization (DS) and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDT).
With OT each client holds its own replica, edits it without locks, and transforms changes received from others before executing them, which suits high-latency environments such as the web.

OT adjusts an operation's parameters for concurrent operations already executed. After inserting x at position 0 of abc, deleting position 2 must become position 3; untransformed, it deletes b instead of c.
OT must keep causality (operations execute in their cause-effect order) and convergence (all copies identical once every operation has run), and intention preservation is a further goal.
OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful, and every change to the data must be captured.
A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to OT; differential synchronization is another alternative.
The guide says Google Docs uses OT per its Wikipedia page, and OT was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs; CRDT remains an active research area.

A basic alternative is a client-server model where one editor acts as the collaboration server; changes may not show on a client until the server answers. It is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources.

entries.title: Double-entry bookkeeping: every debit has a credit

definition.text: A bookkeeping method in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries, debits and credits, so the books balance.

facts.text: Its purpose is to keep financial records accurate and allow errors or fraud to be detected.
It rests on the accounting equation, and every recorded transaction keeps that equation in balance.
Each transaction is entered in at least two ledger accounts so that total debits equal total credits, which is a partial check that every transaction was recorded correctly.
A debit entry is a transfer of value to an account and a credit entry a transfer from it; each transaction is a debit in one account and a credit in a second.
Each account type has a normal balance set by whether a debit or a credit increases it: a debit increases an asset, while a credit increases a liability.
Daybooks or journals serve as preliminary records and are totalled before posting to the nominal ledger, which limits ledger entries and ensures the integrity of the resulting financial information.
As transaction volume and complexity grow, companies use ledgers and accounting information systems to automate tracking of individual transactions.

entries.title: How money settles: batches, real time and instant

definition.text: A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value.

facts.text: Modern electronic payment systems move money between bank accounts without bank staff intervening, using cash substitutes such as debit and credit cards, electronic funds transfers, direct credits and debits and internet banking.

An automated clearing house processes transactions in batches and is a net settlement system, so settlement may be delayed, which poses settlement risk; it is typically used for low-value, non-urgent transactions.

Real-time gross settlement settles each transaction as soon as it is processed, one to one without netting, and payments are final and irrevocable; it is typically used for high-value, urgent transactions.
Instant payment systems typically run 24x7x365 and complete a transfer from debit of the payer's account to credit of the beneficiary's within 10–15 seconds.

entries.title: Payment service providers: accepting cards without a bank deal

definition.text: A third-party company that lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments.

facts.text: A PSP acts as an intermediary between consumers who pay and retailers who accept payment, and often also acts as a payment gateway or payment processor.

PSPs set up technical connections with acquiring banks and card networks, so merchants accept different payment methods without partnering with one bank, and the PSP manages processing and external network relationships.

Beyond processing, a PSP may offer risk management, transaction payment matching, digital wallets, reporting, fund remittance, currency exchange and fraud protection, and supplies software to integrate with e-commerce sites or point of sale systems.
PSP fees are typically charged as a percentage of each transaction or as a fixed cost per transaction.
The merchant remains responsible for data protection and must make sure the chosen provider observes the guidelines; compliance with PCI DSS is important.

A PSP must follow one of four PCI compliance levels set by annual transaction volume: Level 1 over 6 million, Level 2 between 1 and 6 million, Level 3 between 20,000 and 1 million, Level 4 under 20,000.

entries.title: Payment gateways: carrying payment details, never the money

definition.text: A merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores.

facts.text: A gateway passes payment information between a payment portal, such as a website, mobile phone or interactive voice response service, and the front end processor or acquiring bank.
The gateway is not directly involved in the money flow; typically it is a web server to which the merchant's website or POS system is connected.
One gateway often connects several acquiring banks and payment methods under one system.
A gateway may let transaction data go straight from the customer's browser to the gateway, bypassing the merchant's systems, using a redirect or an iframe.

Many gateways screen orders for fraud and calculate tax in real time before the authorization request goes to the processor, using geolocation, velocity pattern analysis, deny-list lookups, delivery address verification and basic AVS checks.
A bank or a specialised provider such as a PSP can supply a gateway, and white label gateways let PSPs, e-commerce platforms or acquiring banks brand the technology as their own.

entries.title: Approved in seconds, funded in days: a card payment

definition.text: The steps by which a card payment is authorized by the issuing bank, then cleared and settled so the merchant's acquiring bank is funded.

facts.text: The merchant forwards the transaction details to the gateway, which converts the message from XML to ISO 8583 or a variant and passes it to the processor used by the merchant's acquiring bank.
The processor forwards the details to the card association, such as Visa or Mastercard, which may act as the issuing bank or route the transaction to the correct card issuing bank.

The issuing bank approves or denies with a response code and a failure reason; the answer returns through the processor and gateway to the website in typically 2–3 seconds, and the issuer holds an authorization for the approved amount.
After the merchant fulfills the order, the process repeats to clear the authorization, which moves the issuing bank's auth-hold to a debit and prepares settlement with the acquiring bank.
At the end of the day the merchant submits its approved authorizations as a batch to its acquiring bank via its processor, and the acquiring bank makes a batch settlement request of the card issuer.

The issuer pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day, and the acquiring bank deposits the approved funds into the merchant's account the same or next day; authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days.

The issuing bank approves or denies with a response code and a failure reason. The answer returns through the processor and gateway to the website, typically in 2–3 seconds, and the issuer holds an authorization for the approved amount.

Then comes clearing and settlement. After the merchant fulfills the order, the process repeats to clear the authorization. That moves the issuing bank's auth-hold to a debit and prepares settlement with the acquiring bank. At the end of the day the merchant submits its approved authorizations as a batch to its acquiring bank via its processor. The acquiring bank then makes a batch settlement request of the card issuer. The issuer pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day, and the acquiring bank deposits the approved funds into the merchant's account the same or next day.

entries.title: Payment reconciliation: the safety net behind exactly-once

definition.text: The process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other.

facts.text: In double-entry bookkeeping a $200 PayPal purchase appears as a $200 order at the e-commerce site, a $200 PayPal transaction, and in the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.
Records in different systems come in different formats, such as the timestamp "2022/01/01" in one and "Jan 1, 2022" in another; a layer that transforms them into the same format solves it.
Massive data volume is handled with big data processing: a streaming platform such as Flink for near real-time reconciliation, or end-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop.
With a daily cut-off of 00:00:00, a record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy.
Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records; if a match is found the break is cleared and no more action is needed.
Even with exactly-once semantics a reconciliation system is always necessary, because there are many places that can go wrong; it is a safety net.

entries.text:
Even a payment system that charges each customer exactly once still needs a second system to check its work. That system performs reconciliation: comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other. It is always necessary, even with the exactly-once semantics of {{ref:sysd-reliab-070}}, because there are many places that can go wrong. It is a safety net.

Take a $200 PayPal purchase. Under double-entry bookkeeping it appears in three places. The e-commerce site holds a $200 order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller. Reconciliation lines these records up. Formats are the first obstacle: one system writes the timestamp "2022/01/01" and another "Jan 1, 2022", so a layer transforms them into the same format. Volume is the second, and big data processing handles it. A streaming platform such as Flink serves near real-time reconciliation, as in {{ref:sysd-msg-043}}. End-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop is the other route, as in {{ref:sysd-msg-133}}.

Timing is the third. Say the daily cut-off is 00:00:00. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy. Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records. If a match is found, the break is cleared and no more action is needed.

entries.title: Designing a payment system that charges exactly once

facts.text: A payment system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems it can have.
When a user clicks the Buy button, a payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores the payment event in the database.

One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout; the payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order.
The payment executor stores the payment order, then calls an external PSP, a third-party intermediary with connections to acquiring banks and card networks, to finish the credit card payment.
A card payment goes through the processor and card association to the issuing bank, which approves or denies with a response code; the round trip typically takes 2–3 seconds.
Once the payment succeeds, the payment service updates the wallet with how much the seller holds, then calls the ledger service, which appends the new ledger information to the database.

The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping: each transaction is recorded as equal and opposite debit and credit entries so debits equal credits, which keeps records accurate and lets errors or fraud be detected.
For a $200 watch paid through PayPal, the e-commerce site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.
Exactly-once becomes easier when split in two: at-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check.

An idempotency key, usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, goes in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key; checking and recording the key must be atomic, for example with a unique constraint or Redis SET NX.
When the PSP call fails on a network error or timeout, the client retries the payment, which may succeed at a later attempt; the idempotency key stops the retry from charging twice.
Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files holding the bank account balance and the day's transactions; for cards, authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days.

Reconciliation compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match: a layer transforms different formats into one, and big data processing handles volume, Flink for near real-time or end-of-day batch such as Hadoop.

A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off; it is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches.
A reconciliation system is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.
The PSP must follow PCI DSS at one of four compliance levels set by annual transaction volume, and gateways screen orders for fraud before authorization.

entries.text:
The question is how to design the system that takes a customer's payment for an order and moves the money correctly. One requirement comes before all others. The system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems it can have.

The flow starts when a user clicks the Buy button. A payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores it in the database. One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout. The payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order. The executor stores the order, then calls an external payment service provider, or PSP, to finish the credit card payment. A PSP is a third-party intermediary with connections to acquiring banks and card networks. The card payment goes through the processor and card association to the issuing bank, which approves or denies with a response code. The round trip typically takes 2–3 seconds.

Once the payment succeeds, the payment service updates the wallet with how much the seller holds. It then calls the ledger service, which appends the new ledger information to the database. The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping, explained in {{ref:sysd-q-077}}: each transaction is recorded as equal and opposite debit and credit entries, so debits equal credits. This keeps records accurate and lets errors or fraud be detected. Take a $200 watch paid through PayPal. The site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.

Exactly-once, the guarantee in {{ref:sysd-reliab-070}}, becomes easier when split in two. At-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check. When the PSP call fails on a network error or timeout, the client retries the payment, which may succeed at a later attempt. The idempotency key, covered in {{ref:sysd-reliab-073}}, stops the retry from charging twice. It is usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, and it goes in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key. Checking and recording the key must be atomic, so that no other request can slip in between, for example with a unique constraint or Redis SET NX.

Afterward the system checks itself. Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files holding the bank account balance and the day's transactions; for cards, authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days. Reconciliation, described in {{ref:sysd-q-008}}, compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match. A layer transforms different formats into one, and big data processing handles volume: Flink for near real-time, or end-of-day batch such as Hadoop. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off. It is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches. Reconciliation is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.

One duty sits outside the flow of money. The PSP must follow PCI DSS at one of four compliance levels set by annual transaction volume, and gateways screen orders for fraud before authorization. To remember: retry freely, charge once, record both sides of every transaction, and check again afterward.

entries.title: SMS: the text message that may never arrive

definition.text: A mostly paid text messaging service of telephone and mobile systems that lets phones exchange short text messages over cellular networks.

facts.text: Messages carry up to 160 characters. The signaling protocol limits the payload to 140 bytes, and messages can use the default GSM 7-bit alphabet, an 8-bit data alphabet or 16-bit UCS-2 or UTF-16.
SMS gateways let computers send messages over the Internet through a short message service center (SMSC), reaching computers, fixed landlines and satellite phones.
Application-to-person (A2P) SMS goes from an application to a subscriber or back, and businesses such as banks, e-gaming, logistics and e-commerce use it to message customers.
Delivery is not guaranteed, and many implementations give the sender no way to learn whether a message arrived in time.
Messages are treated as lower-priority traffic than voice, and studies show around 1% to 5% are lost entirely even in normal operation, while others arrive long after they matter.
SMS messages are not encrypted, so carriers and third parties can read them, phone-number metadata may leak, and senders can be spoofed.

entries.title: Firebase Cloud Messaging and the registration token

definition.text: A cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps.

facts.text: FCM superseded Google Cloud Messaging, adding delivery of push notifications to iOS and web devices as well as Android, behind a unified API between senders and client apps.
On first start the client app sends its credentials to FCM, which generates a registration token (the Instance ID) for that app instance; the token must be included in notifications.
The client passes the token to the app server, which caches it. Storing each token with a timestamp and pruning stale ones keeps the set manageable.
Messages are composed in the console or sent from the app server using the Firebase Admin SDK or HTTP.
FCM queues messages in storage when the device is offline, forwards them to a platform-level transport that handles platform-specific configuration, and routes them to the target devices.
In a typical design a notification service reads events from a message queue or broker such as Kafka and dispatches requests to FCM or APNs, which deliver to user devices.

entries.title: Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices

definition.text: Apple's platform notification service that lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices.

facts.text: A notification can carry badges, sounds or custom text alerts.
Apple stated at launch that push notifications conserve battery better than the background processes that pull technology needs to receive notifications.

Apple released an HTTP/2 provider API in December 2015 that replaced the legacy binary interface, shut down at the end of March 2021; its maximum payload is 4 kilobytes, up from 2 kilobytes on the binary interface.
The HTTP/2 provider uses TCP port 443, and port 2197 is allowed when firewalls block outbound access to 443.

entries.title: Designing a notification system for Android, iOS and the web

facts.text: A notification service consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka, and forwards each request to Firebase Cloud Messaging or Apple Push Notification service according to the device platform (Android, iOS, web).
A messaging solution such as FCM is cross-platform, composes, sends, queues and routes notifications reliably, and provides a unified API between app servers and client apps.
When the client app first starts it sends credentials (Sender ID, API Key, App ID) to FCM, which generates a registration token, also called the Instance ID, that must be included in notifications.
The client sends the registration token to the app server, which caches it. Tokens pile up, so the recommended practice is to store each with a timestamp and remove stale ones from time to time.

In the IETF Web Push protocol the user agent POSTs to the push service to subscribe; a 201 response returns the subscription URI and a push resource URI, which must be shared with the application server confidentially.
The application server requests delivery by POSTing the message to the push resource. A 201 response means the push service accepted it, not that it reached the device.

The push service stores messages for intermittently connected devices, which improves delivery reliability. The sender must give a TTL in seconds; once it elapses the service MUST NOT deliver, and the service may retain a message for less time.

A message can carry an urgency of very-low, low, normal or high, defaulting to normal; the device may ask to receive only messages at or above a level, which saves battery because radio use is costly.
A message with a topic of at most 32 characters replaces any outstanding message with the same topic, so a device that was offline gets only the latest update, not outdated or redundant ones.

The device acknowledges a message by an HTTP DELETE; without an acknowledgement the service SHOULD retry until the advertised expiration. Delivery receipts (202 on acceptance, then 204 once acknowledged, or 410 Gone on failure) tell the sender the outcome.

Receipts matter for critical messages: knowing a message arrived avoids retransmission, polling and state resynchronization, while transient messages such as an incoming call, or quickly superseded ones, may not need reliability.
A push service may expire a subscription at any time and MUST answer 404 Not Found to a sender using an expired one, so servers and clients must be prepared to manage changes in subscription state.
Apple's HTTP/2 provider API for APNs allows payloads up to 4 kilobytes and uses TCP port 443, or port 2197 when firewalls block outbound 443.
SMS is a further channel, carried over SMS gateways through an SMSC, with messages of up to 160 characters; businesses such as banks and e-commerce send application-to-person messages this way.
SMS delivery is not guaranteed and senders often cannot tell whether a message arrived in time; studies show about 1% to 5% of messages are lost even in normal operation.

A push service must hold very many open TCP connections and can redistribute load with 307 redirects. Stored messages take significant storage, so it may reject large bodies with 413 but MUST accept bodies of 4096 bytes or less.

entries.title: Access control lists: a permission list on every resource

definition.text: A list of permissions attached to a system resource that says which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform.

facts.text: An ACL specifies which users or system processes are granted or denied access to a resource and which operations are allowed; each entry in a typical ACL names a subject and an operation.
An ACL holding Alice: read, write and Bob: read gives Alice permission to read and write the file and Bob permission only to read it.

A filesystem ACL is a table of access-control entries giving individual users' or groups' rights to specific objects; each object carries an identifier to its ACL, and POSIX and NFSv4 ACLs are usually stored in extended attributes.
On routers, switches and servers an ACL applies rules to ports or IP addresses with the hosts or networks allowed to use them, for inbound and outbound traffic, much like a firewall.
Name-based network ACLs are a questionable idea because TCP, UDP and ICMP headers carry no domain names, so the enforcing device must resolve names itself, which adds attack surface.
ACLs are easy to understand but error-prone with a high maintenance cost; maintaining authorization data often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials.
A minimal RBAC model is equivalent to an ACL whose only entries are groups, and modern SQL-based ACLs manage groups and inheritance in a hierarchy, so they can express all that RBAC expresses.

entries.title: Role-based access control: permissions through roles

definition.text: An approach to restricting system access to authorized users, defined around roles and privileges rather than around individual users.

facts.text: Roles are created for job functions and permissions are assigned to roles; users get permissions only through their roles, so adding a user or changing a department means assigning the right roles.

RBAC has three rules: a subject can exercise a permission only with a selected or assigned role, the active role must be authorized for the subject, and the permission must be authorized for that role.

The model has subjects, roles, permissions and sessions, with many-to-many subject-to-role and permission-to-role assignment relations; a subject may have several simultaneous sessions in different roles.

Roles can form a hierarchy where higher-level roles subsume the permissions of sub-roles, and constraints can enforce separation of duties; the NIST/ANSI/INCITS standard adds these as hierarchical and constrained RBAC.

RBAC eases administration in large organizations with hundreds of users and thousands of permissions, is widely accepted as best practice within a single system, and is the mode Kubernetes offers, with each role listing allowed actions.
RBAC can implement DAC or MAC policies, and ABAC and relationship-based access control are models that build on it.

RBAC is criticized for role explosion when finer granularity is needed, becomes extremely complex across dozens of systems without hierarchical roles, and does not look at message context such as a connection's source.
An ACL grants or denies write access to a particular file without saying how it may change, whereas an RBAC permission is an operation, such as creating a credit account in a financial application.

entries.title: Discretionary access control: the owner decides

definition.text: A type of access control that restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to, where a subject with a permission can pass it on to others.

facts.text: DAC is discretionary because a subject holding a permission can pass it, perhaps indirectly, to any other subject, unless restrained by mandatory access control.

In the common owner-based implementation each object has an owner who controls its permissions and can make policy decisions; DAC is built on ACLs and the owner group's policy grants or restricts access.
The Unix file mode is a straightforward example, with read, write and execute bits for User, Group and Others; the Linux file system supports DAC.
Capability systems are a second implementation: subjects can transfer access, but not to just any subject, since the passer must already have access to the receiver, in line with least privilege.
A system can run MAC and DAC together, with DAC covering access that subjects can transfer among each other and MAC imposing constraints on it.
DAC is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the object's owner group has too much power.

entries.title: Attribute-based access control: rules over attributes

definition.text: An access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization to perform operations is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment.

facts.text: ABAC policy rules are Boolean functions of the subject's, the object's and the environment's attributes, so the only limits are the policy language and the availability of attributes.
Attributes fall into four categories: subject (age, clearance, department, role), action (read, delete, approve), object (type, department, classification, location) and contextual (time, location).

Unlike RBAC, ABAC expresses complex rule sets over many attributes and needs no explicit authorizations for individual subjects, reducing the work of managing access lists and groups; user-centric models ignore time of day or user IP.

A policy combines attributes into statements of what is allowed; it can grant or deny, be local or global, and override others, for example a user can edit a document if they own it and it is in draft mode.

The recommended architecture has a Policy Enforcement Point that protects the app and sends authorization requests, a Policy Decision Point that evaluates them against policies, and Policy Information Points that supply attributes from LDAP or databases.
XACML defines an architecture, a policy language and a request/response scheme for ABAC, as do ALFA and NIST's NGAC; attribute management is left to traditional IAM tools, databases and directories.

ABAC can protect API methods, such as allowing managers to approve transactions up to their approval limit, and databases with rules like a manager may SELECT a transaction if the user's region equals the transaction's region.

ABAC is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation hard, so the guide calls it not commonly used; more granular controls add performance overhead and affect the user experience.

entries.title: Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides
entries.article: rfc>2904#4. Relationship of Authorization and Policy > 4.4. Distributed Policy

definition.text: An authorization split into points: a policy is retrieved by a Policy Retrieval Point, evaluated at a Policy Decision Point and enforced at a Policy Enforcement Point.

facts.text: Each independent policy must be retrieved, evaluated and enforced; a PRP retrieves it from a policy repository, a PDP evaluates it and a PEP enforces it.

The PEP intercepts a user's request to a resource, asks the PDP whether access is approved or rejected, and acts on the answer; for example a NAS enforces destination address limits with filters and a router enforces QoS restrictions.
The PDP is the central, environment-independent point that evaluates requests against policies and makes the final access decision: Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate.
Policy Information Points hold the data policy conditions are evaluated against, such as resource status, session state or time of day; the PDP queries them for attribute values when needed.
Evaluation may need information not available where the policy was retrieved, so the evaluator must either query the remote administration for it or forward the policy to be evaluated there.
In an API, an interceptor asks the PDP whether a caller may perform an action; the PDP fetches the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only on Permit is the business logic called.
Any server in an authorization transaction may retrieve or evaluate a policy and any service equipment may enforce one; policy repositories may sit on those servers or elsewhere in the network.

entries.title: XACML: a policy language, not an engine

definition.text: An XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS.

facts.text: XACML defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model for evaluating access requests against policies; it can also implement role-based access control.
A Policy Enforcement Point intercepts the user's request, converts it to an XACML authorization request and sends it to the Policy Decision Point, which evaluates it against its configured policies.

The PDP gets policies through a Policy Retrieval Point managed by a Policy Administration Point, fetches attributes from Policy Information Points, and returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate for the PEP to enforce.

Rules approve (Permit) or reject (Deny) a request, or give Indeterminate if their conditions fail to evaluate; rules group into policies, policies into larger policies, and a target decides whether a policy applies.
Combining algorithms, such as deny-unless-permit and permit-unless-deny, resolve conflicts when rules or policies contradict each other by merging their decisions into one final decision.
An obligation is a directive from the PDP to the PEP on what must happen before or after approval, such as logging; if the PEP cannot comply, access may not be realized, while advice may be ignored.

XACML specifies only the policy language, not the design of a PDP, and leaves attribute management to IAM tools, databases and directories; many PDPs use it, and Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source PDP.
XACML 3.0 added delegation, which supports decentralized administration by letting an authority hand all or part of its authority to another user without modifying the root policy.

entries.text: XACML says how to write an access policy, but not how to build the engine that evaluates it. It is an XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS. It defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model for evaluating access requests, and it can also implement role-based access control. In the architecture of {{ref:sysd-q-085}}, the enforcement point converts the user's request into an XACML authorization request. The decision point evaluates it and returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. When rules contradict each other, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit and permit-unless-deny merge their decisions into one. An obligation is a directive from the decision point to the enforcement point on what must happen before or after approval, such as logging. If the enforcement point cannot comply, access may not be realized, while advice may be ignored. Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source decision point. XACML 3.0 added delegation, which lets an authority hand all or part of its authority to another user without modifying the root policy.
