container orchestration.text: Container orchestration automates deploying, scaling and managing containers so that, for example, a container that goes down is replaced by another without downtime.

kubernetes nodes.text: A Kubernetes node, also called a worker or minion, is a machine where containers are deployed.

kubernetes pods.text: A pod is the basic deployable unit in Kubernetes, made of one or more containers co-located on the same node.

container runtime.text: A container runtime is the software responsible for the lifecycle of containers, including launching, reconciling and killing them.

pod restart policy.text: The restartPolicy in a Pod spec tells Kubernetes whether to restart a container after it exits, and can be Always, OnFailure or Never.

crashloopbackoff.text: CrashLoopBackOff is the condition of a container that fails to start properly and keeps failing and restarting while Kubernetes delays each restart with an exponential backoff.

graceful pod termination.text: When a Pod is deleted, the kubelet first asks its containers to stop with a TERM signal and only sends KILL once a grace period has expired, so processes can clean up.

container persistent storage.text: Container filesystems are ephemeral by default, so data that must outlive a container needs a volume that provides persistent storage.

kubernetes services.text: A Kubernetes service is a set of pods that work together, such as one tier of a multi-tier application, giving them a stable address.

sidecar and init containers.text: A Pod can hold several tightly coupled containers, such as init containers that run first and sidecar containers that support the main application.

labels and selectors.text: Labels are keys that Kubernetes clients attach to any API object, such as pods and nodes, and label selectors are queries that resolve to the matching objects.

kubernetes service types.text: A Kubernetes Service type says how a Service is exposed: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName, with headless Services as a variant.

kubernetes ingress.text: An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, using rules defined on the Ingress resource.

ingress path and host matching.text: Ingress rules choose a backend by matching the request's host and URL path, using a path type of Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific.

docker run workflow.text: Running a container with Docker means the client asks the daemon to pull an image from a registry, create a container from it and start it.

virtual machine.text: A virtual machine is the virtualization or emulation of a computer system that provides the functionality of a physical computer.

hypervisor.text: A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, is software, firmware or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines.

docker compose.text: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications.

docker swarm.text: Docker Swarm provides native clustering for Docker containers, turning a group of Docker engines into a single virtual Docker engine.

virtualization versus containerization.text: Virtual machines virtualize hardware and each carry a guest operating system, while containers virtualize the operating system and carry only the application and its dependencies.

continuous delivery.text: Continuous delivery is a software engineering approach in which teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that it can be reliably released at any time.

virtual machine snapshots and migration.text: A snapshot is the state of a virtual machine, and generally its storage devices, at an exact point in time, which can be restored later.

physical, virtual and container deployme.text: Applications moved from physical servers to virtual machines to containers as each step gave better resource boundaries and utilization.

ci/cd pipeline.text: CI/CD combines the practices of continuous integration and continuous delivery or, less often, continuous deployment.

release engineering.text: Release engineering is the discipline of building and delivering software, defining every step from source storage and build rules to testing, packaging and deployment.

infrastructure as code.text: Infrastructure as code is managing and provisioning data center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools.

twelve-factor app.text: The twelve-factor app is a set of twelve best-practice principles for building modern applications that are reliable, scalable and manageable.

configmaps and secrets.text: ConfigMaps and Secrets are two closely related Kubernetes mechanisms for storing configuration, so that changes can be made without rebuilding the application.

hermetic builds.text: A hermetic build is insensitive to the software installed on the build machine, so the same revision always produces the same result.

release branching and cherry-picking.text: Release branching cuts a branch from the mainline at one revision and fixes it only by cherry-picking bug fixes, so the release contents stay known.

release pipeline.text: A release pipeline turns a tested source revision into a deployable package by branching, building, testing, packaging and canarying, logging each step.

horizontal pod autoscaler.text: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler automatically updates a workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet to scale capacity to match demand.

autoscaler flapping controls.text: Autoscaler flapping controls are settings that keep the replica count from swinging up and down as metrics fluctuate.

pod resource requests and limits.text: A container can declare how much CPU and memory it needs and how much it may use, which drives scheduling and enforcement.

rolling update.text: A rolling update replaces instances of the old version one by one with the new version, keeping the application available throughout.

deployments and replicasets.text: A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of replica pods running at any given time, and a Deployment is the higher-level mechanism that manages ReplicaSets.

scaling to zero.text: Scaling to zero lets an autoscaler reduce an idle workload to no replicas and bring it back when a metric shows demand.

kubernetes control plane.text: The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's workload and its worker nodes and directs communication across the system.

kubernetes controllers.text: A Kubernetes controller is a reconciliation loop that drives the actual cluster state toward the desired state by creating, updating and deleting the resources it manages.

statefulsets.text: A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes controller that enforces uniqueness and ordering among the instances of a pod so that stateful applications can run.

pod templates.text: A pod template is the specification a workload controller uses to create the Pods it manages.

kubernetes operators.text: A Kubernetes Operator is the combination of custom resources and custom controllers that automates how a particular application is run.

etcd.text: etcd is a persistent, lightweight, distributed key-value data store, originally developed as part of CoreOS.

ingress controllers and classes.text: An Ingress controller carries out the Ingress rules, and an IngressClass tells each Ingress which controller should implement it.

feature toggle.text: A feature toggle is a condition in the code that enables or disables a feature at runtime, as an alternative to maintaining multiple feature branches.

configuration distribution models.text: Configuration can reach a running service in several ways, each trading flexibility, simplicity and drift between the stored and running version.

blue-green deployment.text: A way of installing changes by keeping a live production environment and an idle staging copy, then swapping the two so the staged version goes live.

deployment strategies.text: Deployment strategies are different ways of replacing a running application version with a new one, each managing the update differently.

authentication.text: Authentication is the act of proving an assertion, such as the identity of a computer system user.

canary release.text: A canary release exposes a new version or feature to a small set of users first, so it can be tested incrementally before a wider rollout.

cross-site scripting.text: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a web-application vulnerability that lets attackers inject client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users.

risk-based rollouts.text: A risk-based rollout fits how fast and how widely a release is pushed to the risk profile of the service being updated.

oauth 2.0.text: OAuth 2.0 is an open standard for access delegation that lets a user grant an application consented access to resources on another site without sharing credentials.

authentication factors.text: Authentication factors are the three categories of evidence used to verify identity: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is.

cryptographic salt.text: A salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes a password or passphrase.

authorization.text: Authorization is the function of specifying rights to access resources, usually through an access policy, and then deciding whether a particular subject may access a particular resource.

principle of least privilege.text: The principle of least privilege requires that every module, such as a process, user or program, be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

multi-factor authentication.text: Multi-factor authentication grants a user access only after they present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to an authentication mechanism.

oauth pseudo-authentication.text: Pseudo-authentication means using OAuth on its own as a login method, even though OAuth is an authorization protocol that says nothing about who the user is.

continuous authentication.text: Continuous authentication keeps monitoring and verifying a user throughout a session, based on biometric traits, instead of only at the initial log-in.

access control models.text: Access control models are the ways an authorization policy is expressed and checked, such as access control lists, roles, attributes and relationships.

secure system design checklist.text: Designing secure systems protects sensitive information and keeps the infrastructure stable and reliable, so developers should apply security guidelines by default.

session and token authentication.text: A website manages a logged-in user's identity with sessions, tokens, JSON Web Tokens, single sign-on, OAuth 2.0 or QR-code login.

digital authentication.text: Digital authentication, also called electronic authentication, is a group of processes that establish and present confidence in user identities to an information system by electronic methods.

cross-site request forgery.text: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an exploit in which a web application receives unauthorized commands from a user that it trusts.

access token.text: An access token is a credential, usually an opaque string, representing an authorization issued to the client for accessing protected resources.

refresh token.text: A refresh token is a credential the authorization server issues to the client for obtaining new access tokens.

json web token.text: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an Internet standard for creating data, optionally signed and optionally encrypted, whose JSON payload asserts a number of claims.

openid connect.text: OpenID Connect is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds login and profile information about the person who is logged in.

jwt claims.text: The claims of a JWT are the name/value members of the JSON object, called the JWT Claims Set, that the token conveys.

creating and validating a jwt.text: Creating a JWT builds a claims set and then signs or encrypts it, and validating one reverses those steps and rejects the token if any step fails.

salted password hashing.text: A system stores each password as a hash of the password plus a unique random salt, never as plain text or a bare hash.

rainbow table.text: A rainbow table is a precomputed table of cryptographic hash outputs, usually used to recover passwords from stolen hashes.

oauth 2.0 authorization flow.text: In the OAuth 2.0 flow a client obtains an access token from the authorization server, with the resource owner's consent, and uses it to request resources from the resource server.

oauth 2.0 grant types.text: An authorization grant is a credential representing the resource owner's authorization that the client uses to obtain an access token; RFC 6749 defines four grant types and a way to add more.

authorization code grant.text: The authorization code grant is a redirection-based flow that obtains access and refresh tokens via the user-agent and is optimized for confidential clients.

proof key for code exchange.text: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is an OAuth 2.0 extension that stops an attacker who intercepts an authorization code from redeeming it, by binding the code to a one-time secret only the real client holds.

webauthn.text: WebAuthn is a W3C web standard defining an API that websites use to authenticate users with public-key credentials, commonly called passkeys.

zero trust security model.text: Zero trust is a security strategy in which users and devices are not trusted by default, even on a privileged network such as a corporate LAN or if previously verified.

signed, encrypted and nested jwts.text: A JWT is carried either as a signed JWS or an encrypted JWE, may nest one inside the other, and can also be left unsecured.

argon2.text: Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition.

bcrypt.text: bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières.

single sign-on.text: Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications.

mfa bypass attacks.text: MFA can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws.

identity provider.text: An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications.

kerberos.text: Kerberos is a ticket-based network authentication protocol that lets nodes on a non-secure network prove their identity to one another securely.

openid.text: OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider.

url shortening.text: URL shortening makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, by using a redirect that points to the page with the long URL.

saml.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider.

drawbacks of url shortening.text: Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks.

short link expiration.text: Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses.

base62 encoding.text: Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9.

short url key generation.text: A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits.

pastebin.text: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link.

instant messaging.text: Instant messaging is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network.

end-to-end encryption.text: A way of building a secure communication system in which only the sender and the intended recipients can read the messages.

store and forward.text: A technique in which data is sent to an intermediate station that keeps it in storage and sends it on later to its destination or to another intermediate station.

signal protocol.text: A non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides end-to-end encryption for voice and instant messaging conversations.

end-to-end encryption versus provider ac.text: The disagreement over whether providers, governments and employers should be able to read messages, set against the privacy that end-to-end encryption gives users.

messaging metadata and sealed sender.text: Encrypting message content does not hide who talks to whom and when, and sealed sender is a technique that reduces the metadata a server can see by concealing the sender's identifier.

chat application on redis pub/sub.text: A simple chat application can be built on Redis publish-subscribe, with the server publishing each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up.

feed fan-out models.text: Ways to build each user's feed: push a tweet into followers' feeds when it is posted, pull it when the feed is read, or combine both.

apache lucene.text: A free and open-source search engine software library, originally written in Java.

fan-out.text: In messaging middleware, a pattern that delivers one message to one or several destinations, possibly in parallel, without waiting for a response.

feed ranking.text: Scoring each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first.

edgerank.text: The name commonly given to the algorithm Facebook used to decide which posts to show in a user's News Feed.

trending topics.text: Showing the queries, hashtags and topics searched most often in a recent window.

streaming media.text: Delivering multimedia over a network as a stream of packets that is played in real time or near real time, instead of downloading the whole file first.

adaptive bitrate streaming.text: A technique that encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change.

recommender system.text: A type of information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next.

collaborative filtering.text: A recommendation technique that predicts a user's interests from the preferences of many other users, assuming people who agreed before will agree again.

video codec.text: Software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, usually following a standard video coding format.

http live streaming.text: A protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data over HTTP, in which the client downloads a playlist and the media segments it lists, adapting bit rate to network conditions.

mpeg-dash.text: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers.

video transcoding.text: Converting video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices.

video on demand.text: A media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request.

live streaming.text: Delivering video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.

streaming delivery methods.text: The ways a stream reaches many viewers: separate unicast copies, a single multicast stream, peer-to-peer transfer, or CDN servers.

real-time messaging protocol.text: A protocol for streaming audio, video and data over the Internet, originally built by Macromedia for Flash Player and running over TCP.

h.264.text: Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10), a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard.

hevc.text: High Efficiency Video Coding (H.265, MPEG-H Part 2), a patent-encumbered video compression standard published in 2013 as the successor to H.264/AVC.

av1.text: AOMedia Video 1, an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, designed for video transmission over the Internet as the successor to VP9.

geo-blocking.text: Technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location.

nearest neighbor search.text: The optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a given query point.

proximity service.text: A service that returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants.

dynamic pricing.text: A pricing strategy, also called surge pricing, in which flexible prices are set from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand.

web crawler.text: An Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads.

robots exclusion protocol.text: The standard, usually called robots.txt, by which a website tells visiting web crawlers which portions of the site they may visit.

crawl politeness policy.text: The rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits.

crawl re-visit policy.text: The rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale.

crawl selection policy.text: The rule that decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking pages by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched.

search engine indexing.text: The collecting, parsing and storing of data so that information can be retrieved quickly and accurately.

pagerank.text: A link analysis algorithm, used by Google Search, that gives each page in a hyperlinked set a numerical weight measuring its relative importance.

cosine similarity.text: A measure of similarity between two non-zero vectors: the cosine of the angle between them, which is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths.

sitemaps.text: An XML protocol that lets a webmaster tell search engines which URLs on a site are available for crawling.

deep web crawling.text: Reaching the large share of web pages that sit behind queries to a database and have no links pointing to them.

focused crawler.text: A crawler that tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic, also called a topical crawler.

url normalization.text: Modifying and standardizing a URL in a consistent way, also called URL canonicalization, so that one resource has one form.

spider trap.text: A set of web pages that makes a crawler issue an infinite number of requests or crash, whether built on purpose or by accident.

jaccard index.text: A statistic of how similar two sets are: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union.

w-shingling.text: A set of unique shingles, each a run of w contiguous tokens from a document, used to measure how similar two documents are.

heap.text: A tree-based data structure in which each parent's key is at least (max heap) or at most (min heap) its children's keys, so the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root.

open banking.text: Open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through application programming interfaces (APIs).

doubly linked list.text: A linked data structure of sequentially linked nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node.

social graph.text: A graph that represents social relations between entities; it is a model of a social network.

adjacency matrix.text: A square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent.

adjacency list.text: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbours.

breadth-first search.text: A graph or tree search that starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level.

shortest path problem.text: Finding a path between two vertices of a graph so that the sum of the weights of its edges is as small as possible.

bidirectional search.text: A graph search that finds a shortest path from a start vertex to a goal by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet.

six degrees of separation.text: The idea that all people are six or fewer social connections apart, so a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people.

simple mail transfer protocol.text: SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail.

virtual private cloud.text: An on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others.

email message format.text: An Internet email message is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies.

mime.text: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments.

email spam.text: Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email.

smtp mail transaction.text: An SMTP mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA.

smtp envelope versus message header.text: A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body.

email header fields.text: Email header fields fall into groups: originator, destination, identification, informational, trace and resent fields.

smtp queueing and retries.text: An SMTP sender keeps mail that cannot be sent at once in a queue and retries it periodically until it succeeds or gives up.

bounce messages.text: A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it.

mail agents and relays.text: Mail passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role.

mx record.text: An MX record is a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of a domain.

post office protocol.text: POP is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server.

email delivery.text: Email travels from the sender's mail client through submission and transfer servers, found with DNS MX records, to the recipient's mailbox.

internet message access protocol.text: IMAP is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection.

pop versus imap.text: POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it.

imap commands and responses.text: An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result.

imap unique identifiers.text: An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY.

email spoofing.text: Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source.

smtp security.text: SMTP security covers authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy.

spam filtering.text: Spam filtering combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail.

dijkstra's algorithm.text: An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network.

a* search algorithm.text: A graph search algorithm that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node by extending the path with the lowest cost so far plus an estimate of the cost still to go.

geocoding.text: Turning a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair.

contraction hierarchies.text: A speed-up technique for shortest-path queries that precomputes shortcuts in a road graph so a query can skip unimportant vertices.

map tiles.text: A world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small image blocks that the client joins seamlessly, each requested separately.

web mercator projection.text: A variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates and is the standard for web mapping.

non-blocking algorithm.text: An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread.

order types.text: The standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules.

fix protocol.text: An electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets.

order book.text: The list of orders that a trading venue, in particular a stock exchange, uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument.

market data.text: Price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange.

matching engine.text: The component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed.

processor affinity.text: Also called CPU pinning, it binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors.

collaborative real-time editing.text: Letting several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly.

low-latency critical path design.text: Getting very low latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

operational transformation.text: A technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed.

groupware concurrency control.text: Concurrency control for groupware, computer systems that support two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment.

double-entry bookkeeping.text: A bookkeeping method in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries, debits and credits, so the books balance.

payment service provider.text: A third-party company that lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments.

payment settlement systems.text: A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value.

payment gateway.text: A merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores.

card payment authorization and settlemen.text: The steps by which a card payment is authorized by the issuing bank, then cleared and settled so the merchant's acquiring bank is funded.

payment reconciliation.text: The process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other.

short message service.text: A mostly paid text messaging service of telephone and mobile systems that lets phones exchange short text messages over cellular networks.

firebase cloud messaging.text: A cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps.

apple push notification service.text: Apple's platform notification service that lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices.

access control list.text: A list of permissions attached to a system resource that says which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform.

role-based access control.text: An approach to restricting system access to authorized users, defined around roles and privileges rather than around individual users.

discretionary access control.text: A type of access control that restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to, where a subject with a permission can pass it on to others.

attribute-based access control.text: An access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization to perform operations is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment.

policy decision and enforcement points.text: An authorization split into points: a policy is retrieved by a Policy Retrieval Point, evaluated at a Policy Decision Point and enforced at a Policy Enforcement Point.

xacml.text: An XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS.

aaa authorization framework.text: An architectural framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services and for deriving requirements for authorization protocols.

mandatory access control.text: A type of access control in which a secured environment, such as an operating system or database, constrains a subject's ability to access or modify an object under a centrally set policy.

relationship-based access control.text: A model evolved from RBAC in which a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the relationships between subjects and resources.

separation of duties.text: A requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations, so no one individual can breach security through dual privilege.

sysd-found-130.q: Why does system design have to be thought through at a high level so early in a project?
sysd-found-130.a: It is one of the earliest decisions made when building a system, and high-level design decisions are very difficult to correct later.

sysd-found-207.q: How do functional and non-functional requirements differ, and which kind drives the technical architecture?
sysd-found-207.a: Functional requirements define what a system is supposed to do, while non-functional requirements define how it is supposed to be, an overall property rather than a specific function. Non-functional requirements drive the technical architecture.

sysd-found-137.q: Why do architects record each decision in a single Architecture Decision Record instead of leaving it in email?
sysd-found-137.a: Forgotten, undocumented or misunderstood decisions, often those communicated by email, cause repeated discussions without resolution. One record in an accessible repository such as a wiki gives a single updated source of truth.

sysd-found-143.q: Which of requirements engineering and software architecture addresses the 'what', and which the 'how'?
sysd-found-143.a: Requirements engineering addresses the problem space, the 'what', while software architecture targets the solution space, the 'how'; the two are complementary approaches.

sysd-found-140.q: What should you do first in a system design interview, and why?
sysd-found-140.a: Ask about the exact scope and clarify the functional and non-functional requirements early, because interview questions are vague. Ask about the core features and about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale.

sysd-found-135.q: Why does the technical structure of a product tend to mirror the organization that built it?
sysd-found-135.a: The authors of a product's parts must communicate to keep them compatible, so organizations that design systems produce designs that copy their own communication structures and the technical structure reflects the organization's social boundaries.

sysd-found-087.q: Why can no system with distance between cause and effect have zero latency?
sysd-found-087.a: Latency is physically a consequence of the limited speed at which any interaction can propagate, which never exceeds the speed of light, so any system with distance between cause and effect has some latency.

sysd-found-192.q: A web service averages 100 ms latency. Why can that number still hide a problem?
sysd-found-192.a: Average and median latency can mislead because a few outliers distort them, so such a service may have 1% of requests taking 5 seconds. Tail latency is therefore measured at high percentiles, not the average.

sysd-found-094.q: Why does adding more bandwidth not remove the delay of a long-distance request?
sysd-found-094.a: Propagation time depends on distance, and more bandwidth shrinks only transmission time, so the remaining delay is increasingly propagation.

sysd-found-098.q: What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
sysd-found-098.a: Bandwidth is the maximum achievable speed or capacity, while throughput is the speed actually achieved and is always less than bandwidth.

sysd-found-092.q: Why does TCP lose throughput when the bandwidth-delay product is larger than the TCP window?
sysd-found-092.a: The sender must wait for acknowledgements before sending more packets, so TCP flow control lowers throughput.

sysd-found-096.q: How does a back-of-the-envelope calculation differ from a guess and from an accurate calculation?
sysd-found-096.a: It is more than a guess but less than an accurate calculation or proof, and its defining characteristic is the use of simplified assumptions.

sysd-found-029.q: Why does the original end-to-end principle no longer hold fully in real networks?
sysd-found-029.a: The original principle kept state and intelligence at the edges and a simple network between them, but real-world firewalls, network address translators and web caches have since forced changes.

sysd-found-030.q: Why is TCP not particularly suitable for real-time applications such as voice over IP?
sysd-found-030.a: Handshaking, retransmission and error detection add reliability but lengthen latency. TCP is optimized for accurate rather than timely delivery, with delays on the order of seconds.

sysd-found-006.q: What do the three messages of TCP's opening handshake establish, and what does the handshake cost?
sysd-found-006.a: The client sends a SYN, the server replies with a SYN-ACK and the client answers with an ACK, after which both sides have received acknowledgments and full-duplex communication is established. It adds one round trip of latency before data can be sent.

sysd-found-021.q: If an application sends data over UDP but needs reliable delivery, who has to provide it?
sysd-found-021.a: The application itself, for example by adding its own handshaking such as confirmation that a message was received, because UDP does not guarantee delivery and gives the sender no feedback.

sysd-found-152.q: Why was IPv6 created, and how does dual stack ease the move to it?
sysd-found-152.a: The rapid exhaustion of IPv4 address space led the IETF to redesign the Internet Protocol, which became IPv6. Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time on the same devices, using whichever fits the destination address.

sysd-found-017.q: Why does TCP wait for three duplicate acknowledgments before retransmitting?
sysd-found-017.a: After three duplicate acknowledgments the sender retransmits the last unacknowledged packet; the threshold is three because the network may reorder segments.

sysd-found-009.q: What does a TCP sender do when the receiver advertises a window of 0, and why does it start a persist timer?
sysd-found-009.a: The sender stops and starts a persist timer, which protects against deadlock if the window update is lost. On expiry the sender sends a small packet to get a fresh window size.

sysd-found-010.q: How does TCP's congestion window differ from the receive window?
sysd-found-010.a: The congestion window limits unacknowledged data in flight to protect the network, while the receive window protects the receiver, and the sender stays within both.

sysd-found-149.q: Why does one lost packet stall several HTTP/2 streams over TCP but not over QUIC?
sysd-found-149.a: TCP treats any error as blocking, so a single lost packet stalls every stream sharing the connection, which is head-of-line blocking. QUIC flow-controls each stream separately and retransmits lost data at the QUIC level, so an error in one stream does not block the others.

sysd-found-146.q: Why does a network need DHCP relay agents on its routers?
sysd-found-146.a: A client's broadcast stays on its own subnet, so relay agents on routers forward it by unicast to configured DHCP servers, and the GIADDR field tells the server which subnet's address pool to use.

sysd-found-162.q: Why must a TCP initial sequence number not be computable from outside the connection?
sysd-found-162.a: Otherwise an attacker could guess sequence numbers. Implementations should set it to a timer value plus a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key.

sysd-found-008.q: Why does TCP need a three-way handshake rather than a simpler exchange?
sysd-found-008.a: Sequence numbers are not tied to a global clock, so the receiver of a first SYN cannot know whether it is an old one and asks the sender to verify it. The principal reason is to prevent old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion.

sysd-found-013.q: How does a SYN flood overload a server?
sysd-found-013.a: An attacker uses a spoofed IP address and repeatedly sends crafted SYN packets, so the server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections.

sysd-found-145.q: Why do many applications switch off Nagle's algorithm?
sysd-found-145.a: Nagle's algorithm combined with delayed ACKs, both on by default in common operating systems, can badly hurt request-response applications, so many applications simply disable Nagle with a socket option.

sysd-found-163.q: Why must a keep-alive not treat one unanswered probe as proof that the connection is dead?
sysd-found-163.a: ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted, so a single missing answer does not prove the connection is dead.

sysd-found-166.q: How does Path MTU Discovery find the largest packet a path can carry?
sysd-found-166.a: The sender sets the DF (don't fragment) bit. A device with a smaller MTU drops the packet and returns an ICMP Datagram Too Big message giving its MTU, and the sender lowers its estimate and repeats until packets fit.

sysd-found-201.q: What is the most serious failure mode of an anycast service, and what normally prevents it?
sysd-found-201.a: If a failed server keeps announcing its route, it becomes a black hole for nearby clients. Anycast normally gives automatic failover, usually with external heartbeat monitoring that withdraws a failed server's route announcement.

sysd-found-202.q: Why is it risky to use a made-up top-level domain for an internal network?
sysd-found-202.a: New TLDs can collide with the made-up names: ICANN rejected .home and .corp over conflicts with networks using them, and local domains such as test.dev collided with the .dev gTLD created in 2019.

sysd-found-117.q: Why did the single HOSTS.TXT file stop working as the network grew, leading to DNS?
sysd-found-117.a: The bandwidth consumed distributing each new version was proportional to the square of the number of hosts, and local organizations had to wait for the central host table to change before their changes became visible. A single centralized host table had become slow and unwieldy.

sysd-found-111.q: Why should a node with a CNAME record hold no other data?
sysd-found-111.a: Then an alias and its canonical name cannot differ, so a cached CNAME can be used without asking an authoritative server about other types.

sysd-found-121.q: What is the difference between a DNS name server and a resolver?
sysd-found-121.a: A name server has complete information about a subset of the name space, for which it is the authority, plus pointers to other servers. Resolvers extract information from name servers for client requests, answering directly or following referrals.

sysd-found-129.q: What are the three levels of DNS servers a lookup passes through, and what does each hold?
sysd-found-129.a: The root name servers hold the addresses of TLD name servers, the TLD servers hold the addresses of authoritative servers, and the authoritative servers give the actual answer.

sysd-found-108.q: Why does a changed DNS record not take effect everywhere at once?
sysd-found-108.a: Because caching is distributed, record changes do not propagate immediately but only after all caches expire and refresh after the TTL. TTLs can be lowered before a change, at the cost of more network traffic.

sysd-found-107.q: How does a recursive DNS query differ from an iterative one?
sysd-found-107.a: In a recursive query the client asks one server, which answers completely by querying other name servers as needed, or returns an error. In an iterative query the resolver asks a chain of servers, each referring it to the next until one can fully resolve the request.

sysd-found-116.q: Why are there only thirteen root server addresses, yet far more than thirteen root server machines?
sysd-found-116.a: The original DNS limits UDP packets to 512 bytes, which leaves room for only thirteen root server addresses. But each operator runs redundant equipment in many locations using anycast addressing, so there are about 1954 instances for better performance and fault tolerance.

sysd-found-103.q: Why does a delegation sometimes need glue records?
sysd-found-103.a: Name servers in a delegation are identified by name, so if the delegated name server is a subdomain of the domain it serves there is a circular dependency, and the delegating server must supply the server's IP addresses as glue.

sysd-found-120.q: How can a DNSSEC resolver prove an answer is correct, and where does the proof start?
sysd-found-120.a: An answer can be proved correct only if at least one key or DS record is known to be correct from a source other than DNS; these starting points are trust anchors. An authentication chain of linked DS and DNSKEY records then runs from a trust anchor to the domain's authoritative server.

sysd-found-205.q: Why can one DNS name lead a local client and a distant client to different addresses?
sysd-found-205.a: With split-horizon DNS, a server that has both a private LAN address and a public one resolves to either, depending on the client. Local clients then reach it directly with lower latency, while internal DNS information stays separate from access over an unsecure public network such as the Internet.

sysd-found-032.q: Why do TLS, SSH and PGP use public-key cryptography only to share a key, then switch to symmetric encryption?
sysd-found-032.a: Public-key algorithms are far more computationally intensive than symmetric ones. So a public-key exchange shares a symmetric key, which then encrypts the data at higher throughput without pre-sharing a key.

sysd-found-038.q: Which HTTP method lets the client choose the target URI, and what happens if the same request is sent twice?
sysd-found-038.a: PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state with the state in the request, and unlike POST the client chooses the target URI. Repeating the same PUT updates the same resource.

sysd-found-168.q: What can a client safely do if the connection closes after it sent a PUT but before it read the response?
sysd-found-168.a: It can reconnect and retry, because PUT is idempotent and the effect is the same. It should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request such as POST unless it knows the request is really idempotent or can detect the original was never applied.

sysd-found-035.q: Why does HTTP separate safe methods from unsafe ones?
sysd-found-035.a: It lets automated retrieval by spiders and cache prefetching work without fear of causing harm, and lets a user agent warn the user before an unsafe action.

sysd-found-174.q: How can two parties who have never met agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel?
sysd-found-174.a: Both publicly agree on a prime modulus p and base g, each picks a secret number and sends g raised to it mod p, then raises the received value to its own secret to reach the same shared value. An eavesdropper sees only the public values and must solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is hard for large groups.

sysd-found-191.a: A 401 (Unauthorized) says the request lacks valid authentication credentials and must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge. A 403 (Forbidden) says the server understood the request but refuses it, even with credentials that are insufficient.

sysd-found-062.q: Why were 307 and 308 added alongside 302 and 301?
sysd-found-062.a: For historical reasons a client may turn a POST into a GET after a 301 or 302. A 308 (Permanent Redirect) and a 307 (Temporary Redirect) avoid this, and 307 forbids changing the method on automatic redirection.

sysd-found-190.q: How does a cache work out a response's freshness lifetime?
sysd-found-190.a: It takes it from the first matching rule: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then the Expires value minus the Date value. If none applies, no explicit expiration exists.

sysd-found-054.q: Why did HTTP/1 clients open several connections to one server, and what does HTTP/2 need instead?
sysd-found-054.a: HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection and HTTP/1.1 pipelining only partly helped, so clients opened several connections. HTTP/2 needs one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8.

sysd-found-041.q: Why does QUIC fix the head-of-line blocking that HTTP/2 still has over TCP?
sysd-found-041.a: TCP cannot see HTTP/2's parallel streams, so one lost packet stalls every transaction. QUIC's native multiplexing makes a lost packet affect only the streams that lost data.

sysd-found-172.q: How does Expect: 100-continue save a client from wasting an upload?
sysd-found-172.a: A 100 (Continue) response says the initial part of a request was received and not rejected. A client waits for it before sending a large body, so a request rejected on its headers wastes no upload.

sysd-found-066.q: What does proactive content negotiation gain, and what does it cost?
sysd-found-066.a: The server picks from the client's stated preferences and can send its best guess with the first response, saving a round trip. The cost is that describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches.

sysd-found-187.q: What happens if an HTTP/2 receiver's flow-control window is smaller than the bandwidth * delay product?
sysd-found-187.a: Receive throughput is limited and performance degrades. Timely WINDOW_UPDATE frames help.

sysd-found-075.q: What does the Vary header tell a cache?
sysd-found-075.a: Its value lists the selecting header field names, such as accept-encoding and accept-language. A cache may reuse the response only for a later request with the same values in those fields, unless the origin validates it, so Vary expands the cache key.

sysd-found-084.q: What does cache timing leak, and how does double keying mitigate it?
sysd-found-084.a: Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited. Adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it.

sysd-found-048.q: How does SameSite=Strict help against cross-site request forgery?
sysd-found-048.a: CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie. SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates CSRF.

sysd-found-180.q: Why is the first visit to an HSTS site still unprotected, and what closes that gap?
sysd-found-180.a: HSTS relies on trust on first use, so the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected. Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS, though such a list cannot scale to cover every website.

sysd-found-055.q: Why does the TLS 1.3 handshake take only one round trip?
sysd-found-055.a: The client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello. That takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need.

sysd-found-056.q: What happens in TLS 1.3 if the client's key_share is unacceptable?
sysd-found-056.a: The server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one. If no common parameters can be negotiated, the server must abort the handshake.

sysd-found-186.q: Which names does a wildcard certificate for *.example.com cover?
sysd-found-186.a: It covers only one level of subdomain: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, but not example.com or deeper names.

sysd-found-051.q: How does If-Match prevent the lost update problem?
sysd-found-051.a: If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, and a failure gets 412 (Precondition Failed). Used with POST, PUT and DELETE, it stops one client from overwriting another's work.

sysd-found-069.q: How can a cache revalidate a stale response without downloading it again?
sysd-found-069.a: It forwards a request with preconditions built from the stored response's validators: the Last-Modified timestamp in If-Modified-Since and the entity tags in If-None-Match. A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated and reused, so no content is transferred.

sysd-found-083.q: How is no-cache different from no-store?
sysd-found-083.a: No-cache means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. No-store means a cache must not store any part of the request or response.

sysd-reliab-106.q: Why can't a hash function avoid collisions, and how do hash tables cope?
sysd-reliab-106.a: Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values, so by the pigeonhole principle a collision is guaranteed once there are more objects than hash values. Hash tables handle collisions with a collision-resolution strategy, most commonly open addressing or separate chaining.

sysd-reliab-001.q: Can a Bloom filter give a false negative or a false positive, and why?
sysd-reliab-001.a: It can give false positives but never false negatives. A 0 among an element's positions means it is definitely not in the set, while all 1s mean it is in the set or other elements set those bits by chance.

sysd-reliab-116.q: Why can nearest-neighbor search in a k-d tree skip an entire branch?
sysd-reliab-116.a: At each node it checks whether a hypersphere around the query, with the current best distance as radius, crosses the splitting plane. If it does not, that whole branch is eliminated.

sysd-reliab-115.q: Why would a ride-hailing design map locations along a Hilbert curve?
sysd-reliab-115.a: Mapping along the Hilbert curve keeps points that are close in one dimension close after folding, a locality property used to index geospatial location data. One Uber design applies it to run range queries that find nearby drivers.

sysd-reliab-013.q: Why prefer version 7 UUIDs over random version 4 as database keys?
sysd-reliab-013.a: Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits, so its keys are creation-time-ordered and new records land at the end of the key sequence. Random version 4 keys scatter across the sequence and hurt performance.

sysd-reliab-118.q: How can a peer verify a file from an untrusted source using a hash tree?
sysd-reliab-118.a: It gets the root hash from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer. A tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, and another source is tried.

sysd-reliab-010.q: Why does HyperLogLog split the hashed values into many subsets instead of using one maximum?
sysd-reliab-010.a: A single estimate from the maximum number of leading zeros has a large variance. So the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the estimates.

sysd-reliab-003.q: Why can two nearby points have very different geohashes?
sysd-reliab-003.a: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close, but the reverse is not guaranteed. Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian lie in different halves of the world, so their geohashes differ greatly.

sysd-blocks-112.q: Why is round-robin DNS a weak way to balance load?
sysd-blocks-112.a: DNS does not check for server and network outages, so it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable.

sysd-blocks-120.q: What happens to a user's session under sticky sessions if the pinned backend goes down?
sysd-blocks-120.a: There is no automatic failover: the backend's per-session information becomes inaccessible, and sessions depending on it are lost.

sysd-blocks-127.q: Why does the master-worker scheme scale badly to many processors?
sysd-blocks-127.a: It needs a high amount of communication, and the master acts as a bottleneck. Replacing the master with a task list shared by the processors helps, but is still insufficient for very large computing centers.

sysd-blocks-116.q: Why can a layer 4 balancer not route on content when a layer 7 balancer can?
sysd-blocks-116.a: A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer and reads requests in their entirety, so it can route on content.

sysd-blocks-123.q: Why do load balancers use N+1 redundancy for failover instead of backing up every component?
sysd-blocks-123.a: Failover needs at least one component in excess of the service's capacity (N+1 redundancy). That is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a backup that takes over on failure (dual modular redundancy).

sysd-blocks-129.q: Which proxy hides origin servers from clients, a forward or a reverse proxy?
sysd-blocks-129.a: A reverse proxy: it sits in front of the origin servers so no client communicates with them directly, and the client never learns of the original server. A forward proxy instead sits in front of the client, so no origin server communicates directly with that client.

sysd-blocks-191.q: Why do microservices call for an API gateway?
sysd-blocks-191.a: Microservices typically expose fine-grained APIs unlike what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to multiple services. A gateway gives all clients a single entry point.

sysd-blocks-190.q: Why does putting a reverse proxy in front of back ends create both an availability risk and a security risk?
sysd-blocks-190.a: It is a single point of failure: misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable. To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic it must decrypt and re-encrypt it, which needs the TLS certificate and private key and makes it a more valuable attack target.

sysd-blocks-136.q: Which is still useful with only one server, a reverse proxy or a load balancer, and which can stand in for the other?
sysd-blocks-136.a: A reverse proxy is useful even with one server and can also act as a load balancer, but not the other way around. A load balancer is useful when multiple servers serve the same function.

sysd-blocks-002.q: Why does video and audio streaming usually have a hit ratio near zero, and what does that do to an LRU cache?
sysd-blocks-002.a: Each bit of the stream is read once (a compulsory miss), used, and never read or written again. LRU in particular lets streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again, which is called cache pollution.

sysd-blocks-005.q: What happens in an LFU cache to an object that was accessed often in the past and then becomes unpopular, and how does LFUDA fix it?
sysd-blocks-005.a: It stays in an LFU cache for a long time, blocking newer or less-popular objects from replacing it. LFU with dynamic aging adds a cache-age factor to the reference count so such objects become eligible for replacement.

sysd-blocks-007.q: Why do CPU caches with large associativity often use pseudo-LRU instead of true LRU?
sysd-blocks-007.a: LRU must track what was used and when, and for caches with large associativity (generally more than four ways) that cost becomes prohibitive. Pseudo-LRU needs only one bit per cache item.

sysd-blocks-015.q: What does a write-back cache risk if the caching layer crashes, and how can that risk be reduced?
sysd-blocks-015.a: It confirms the write as soon as it completes in the caching layer and syncs it to the database asynchronously, so it risks data loss if the caching layer crashes. Having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.

sysd-blocks-029.q: How does a Memcached client decide which server holds a key, and why does that make the design scale?
sysd-blocks-029.a: Each client knows all the servers, and the client library hashes the key to pick one, a simple form of sharding. Because the servers never talk to each other, it is a scalable shared-nothing architecture.

sysd-blocks-014.q: Why can't a general-purpose operating system implement the optimal replacement policy, and what is it still good for?
sysd-blocks-014.a: It needs knowledge of the future to evict the lines that will be reused farthest ahead, and it is generally impossible to predict how far ahead information will be needed. Its practical minimum can still be calculated after experimentation, so it gives a yardstick for comparing the effectiveness of a chosen cache algorithm.

sysd-blocks-009.q: Which access pattern makes MRU beat LRU, and why?
sysd-blocks-009.a: For random access patterns and repeated scans over large datasets, called cyclic access patterns, MRU gets more hits than LRU because it tends to retain older data. It is most useful where the older an item is, the more likely it is to be accessed.

sysd-blocks-161.q: How does ARC adapt to changing usage without keeping the data of recently evicted entries?
sysd-blocks-161.a: Each of its lists gets a ghost list holding only the keys of entries recently evicted from it, never their data. A hit in B1 grows the target size of T1 and a hit in B2 shrinks it, which also decides whether T1 or T2 gives up an entry when the cache is full.

sysd-blocks-024.q: Why can the expiry of a heavily requested cached page bring a system down?
sysd-blocks-024.a: When the cached page expires under very heavy load, many threads across the server farm all try to render it at the same time, and none of them knows the others are doing so. That concurrent load can exhaust shared resources and cause congestion collapse, so every attempt to re-render times out and the cache hit rate drops to zero.

sysd-blocks-018.q: What happens if a malicious user floods the system with queries for keys that exist in neither the cache nor the database, and how can the cache help?
sysd-blocks-018.a: Because the database has nothing to return, the application cannot populate the cache, which puts heavy pressure on both the cache and the database, so the database can easily be overloaded. One fix is to cache a null value for such keys with a short TTL; another is a Bloom filter, which stops queries for keys it says do not exist from reaching the cache or the database.

sysd-blocks-026.a: It does not help when accessing the cache takes as long as accessing the primary data store, or when requests have low repetition, because caching performance comes from repeated access patterns. It also does not help when data changes frequently, because the cached version gets out of sync and the primary data store must be accessed every time.

sysd-blocks-033.q: How does banning cached content differ from purging it?
sysd-blocks-033.a: Purge removes content, including all its variants, from the caching proxy immediately. Ban adds a reference to the cached content to a ban list that requests are checked against, and on a match new content is fetched, returned and cached, so unlike purge it removes nothing at once.

sysd-blocks-069.q: Why is blocking a single source not enough to stop a distributed denial-of-service attack?
sysd-blocks-069.a: In a DDoS the flood comes from many sources, often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking one source does not stop it and more sophisticated mitigation is needed.

sysd-blocks-070.q: Why does a peer-to-peer content network keep the original distributor's setup and running costs very small?
sysd-blocks-070.a: Unlike client-server systems, it can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share. That property makes the setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor.

sysd-blocks-077.q: Why do telco CDNs have a built-in cost advantage over traditional CDNs?
sysd-blocks-077.a: Traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs, while telco CDNs own the last mile and operate their own delivery infrastructure.

sysd-blocks-072.q: Which kind of site suits a pull CDN rather than a push CDN, and why?
sysd-blocks-072.a: Heavy-traffic sites suit a pull CDN, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN. Push CDNs suit sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.

sysd-blocks-081.q: Why can locating a client by its resolver's IP route it badly, and what does the edns-client-subnet option change?
sysd-blocks-081.a: A client that uses a non-local resolver that is far away gets poor performance when the CDN locates it by the resolver's IP. With the edns-client-subnet EDNS0 option, CDNs use the IP address of the requesting client's subnet instead, which drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers.

sysd-blocks-178.q: How does Subresource Integrity keep a tampered CDN-hosted script from running in a page?
sysd-blocks-178.a: The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location, and the browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match. A page therefore loads only a script whose content matches the hash the site author references.

sysd-blocks-035.q: What do many NoSQL systems trade away to gain speed and availability?
sysd-blocks-035.a: Many follow the BASE model, prioritizing speed and availability over strict consistency through eventual consistency: updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale. Most also lack full ACID transaction support, sacrificing it for performance and scalability.

sysd-blocks-061.q: Why does a graph database pull ahead of a relational one as relationships get deeper?
sysd-blocks-061.a: Relational databases need many joins over several tables for complex relationships, while a graph database follows stored links and avoids costly joins. Its advantage grows with query depth and complexity.

sysd-blocks-060.q: Why must a bank transfer be handled as a single transaction?
sysd-blocks-060.a: It requires subtracting the amount from one account and adding the same amount to the other, and a transaction must be atomic, meaning it completes or has no effect.

sysd-blocks-055.q: What do you gain and what do you lose by choosing a higher isolation level?
sysd-blocks-055.a: A higher isolation level reduces the concurrency effects users may meet, but it needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another. A lower level lets more users access the same data at once but increases effects such as dirty reads or lost updates.

sysd-blocks-045.q: Why do analytics databases favor column-oriented storage while operational databases favor row-oriented storage?
sysd-blocks-045.a: Analytic access usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows, so analytics databases benefit from column-oriented DBMSs, while operational databases benefit from row-oriented ones.

sysd-blocks-052.q: Why do star schemas deliberately relax normalization?
sysd-blocks-052.a: Relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic and reporting, faster read-only queries and aggregations, fewer joins per query, and an efficient source for OLAP cubes.

sysd-blocks-066.q: Why is an ordinary index a poor fit for spatial queries, and what do spatial databases use instead?
sysd-blocks-066.a: Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions. Spatial databases use a spatial index designed for multi-dimensional ordering, and the R-tree is typically the preferred one.

sysd-blocks-169.q: What does ROLAP gain and what does it give up compared with MOLAP?
sysd-blocks-169.a: ROLAP scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool. It is generally slower than MOLAP, and its aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

sysd-blocks-067.q: Why does copying values such as a username into each record only suit workloads where reads are much more common than writes?
sysd-blocks-067.a: Instead of storing only foreign keys, this approach stores the actual foreign values with the data so no further lookup is needed. But copied values must be changed in many places when they change, so it works better when reads are much more common than writes.

sysd-blocks-053.q: Why can forcing one database to satisfy every requirement backfire, and what does using several databases cost?
sysd-blocks-053.a: Forcing one database to satisfy every requirement can yield a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master-of-none solution, because different databases solve different problems. Knitting several database products together has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

sysd-blocks-057.q: What happens when a step errors in an ACID database compared with a BASE database?
sysd-blocks-057.a: An ACID database fails the whole transaction if any step errors. A BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later.

sysd-blocks-171.q: Why did financial and order-processing systems turn to NewSQL?
sysd-blocks-171.a: They outgrew conventional relational databases but needed transactional guarantees that NoSQL could not give. The old options were bigger computers or custom distribution middleware, both costly, and NewSQL tries to reconcile this.

sysd-blocks-063.q: How does multiversion concurrency control keep readers from waiting for writers?
sysd-blocks-063.a: An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting, so each user sees a snapshot of the database at one instant and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits. Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID, so reads and writes are isolated without locks and writers do not block readers.

sysd-blocks-165.q: What rule must a transaction follow under two-phase locking, and what does obeying it guarantee?
sysd-blocks-165.a: Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired, so a transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one. Schedules that obey this rule are serializable.

sysd-blocks-042.q: Under snapshot isolation, how can two concurrent withdrawals each pass a balance check and still leave the accounts in deficit?
sysd-blocks-042.a: Each transaction checks the rule against its own snapshot, so with two concurrent $200 withdrawals both commit and the total ends at -$200; this is write skew, which snapshot isolation permits. Under serializability it is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other.

sysd-blocks-182.q: Why does a write-ahead log let a database avoid flushing its data pages at every commit?
sysd-blocks-182.a: The central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the WAL records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. So after a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the WAL, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO.

sysd-blocks-186.q: How does an inverted index differ from a forward index, and why does that make full-text search practical?
sysd-blocks-186.a: A forward index stores the list of words per document, and inverting it gives the inverted index, which lists the documents per word. Without it a query would iterate through every word of every document, which is often not technically realistic; with it, the query jumps to the word by random access.

sysd-blocks-105.q: Why can a B+ tree handle range queries and ordered iteration better than a B-tree?
sysd-blocks-105.a: Its leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient. A B-tree cannot build such a list because not all its keys are in the leaves.

sysd-blocks-107.q: Why might denormalizing a design by hand perform worse than the normalized design?
sysd-blocks-107.a: Denormalizing by hand can match the query speed, but the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints, which slow writes. Under heavy write load it may therefore perform worse than the normalized design.

sysd-blocks-188.q: What happens in a B-tree when a key is inserted into a leaf that is already full, and what if the split reaches the root?
sysd-blocks-188.a: The leaf is split into two around a median key, which moves up to the parent as a separation value; a split that reaches the root creates a new root and increases the tree's height.

sysd-blocks-091.q: Why does an index on (ID, Name) let a query for a record's Name skip the table lookup, and what does that cost?
sysd-blocks-091.a: A covering index holds the needed fields itself, so the index alone answers the query and the record lookup disappears; the cost is a larger index, because the extra keys slow down inserts and updates.

sysd-blocks-092.q: How do pessimistic and optimistic locking differ in handling conflicts, and which favors data integrity?
sysd-blocks-092.a: Pessimistic locking locks the data before any change and blocks other users, which is better for data integrity but can hurt performance; optimistic locking lets many users in, checks for conflicts at commit and rolls back if one is found, which is better for efficiency and performance.

sysd-blocks-086.q: Why does a search on city and first_name use only the city part of an index on (city, last_name, first_name)?
sysd-blocks-086.a: Only the first indexed column can be used on its own, so the search uses city and then checks first_name sequentially; creating the index in the order of the search columns avoids this.

sysd-blocks-096.q: Why is 6NF unsuitable for databases serving online transaction processing?
sysd-blocks-096.a: Its drawback is a proliferation of tables: a 5NF table with one key column and N attributes needs N tables, so multi-field updates, inserts and deletes touch several tables.

sysd-blocks-199.q: Why can't SRAM, though much faster than DRAM, match DRAM's storage capacity?
sysd-blocks-199.a: Each SRAM bit takes a cell of six transistors, whereas DRAM needs only one capacitor and one transistor per bit, which makes DRAM space-efficient and inexpensive.

sysd-blocks-210.q: Why must a database flush its log to non-volatile storage before acknowledging a commit?
sysd-blocks-210.a: So that the effects of committed transactions survive the loss of volatile memory: because changes are logged before they modify database state, committed transactions can be redone from the log after a crash and incomplete ones undone, recreating the state right before the failure.

sysd-blocks-200.q: Which kind of storage is fully owned by a single server, and why do databases and virtual machine engines still want it?
sysd-blocks-200.a: Block storage: it is the most flexible and versatile form, so databases and virtual machine engines manage blocks directly to squeeze out the most performance, but it is fully owned by a single server and is not a shared resource.

sysd-blocks-149.q: What does data scrubbing do in a RAID array, and why does it reduce risk during a rebuild?
sysd-blocks-149.a: The controller periodically reads and checks all blocks, including those not otherwise accessed, and uses the array's redundancy to recover a bad block and reassign it to spare blocks; this catches unrecoverable read errors early, reducing the risk of double-drive failures during a rebuild.

sysd-blocks-156.q: Why is object storage not suited to transactional data?
sysd-blocks-156.a: It lacks the locking and sharing mechanisms that keep a single, accurately updated version of a file; it deliberately trades performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost, and targets relatively cold data such as archives and backups.

sysd-blocks-147.q: How does network-attached storage differ from direct-attached storage?
sysd-blocks-147.a: Direct-attached storage is traditional mass storage that uses no network, while network-attached storage is accessed by another computer at file level over a local or wide area network or the Internet, commonly using the Network File System and Server Message Block protocols.

sysd-blocks-207.q: Why does SMB2 perform better than SMB 1.0 over high-latency links?
sysd-blocks-207.a: SMB 1.0 is chatty, block-level and limited to a 64K block size; SMB2 cuts the commands from over a hundred to nineteen, pipelines requests before earlier responses arrive, and compounds multiple actions into one request to save round trips.

sysd-blocks-198.q: Why does an SSD controller do wear leveling, and what does it cost?
sysd-blocks-198.a: Without it, specific blocks would wear out early from repeated use and shorten the life of the whole drive; the controller moves cold data off heavily used blocks so hot data can be written there, and the extra writes, called write amplification, must be balanced against performance and durability.

sysd-blocks-203.q: How do object stores differ from key-value stores?
sysd-blocks-203.a: Object stores associate a limited set of attributes (metadata) with each piece of data, are optimized for hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes and usually offer weaker consistency such as eventual consistency; key-value stores expect small values (kilobytes) and offer strong consistency.

sysd-blocks-148.q: How does 4 + 2 erasure coding compare with 3-copy replication on storage overhead and durability?
sysd-blocks-148.a: In 4 + 2 erasure coding every two chunks of data need one parity block, so the storage overhead is 50% against 200% for 3-copy replication; Backblaze's calculation, assuming a 0.81% annual node failure rate, gives 11 nines of durability against 6 nines.

sysd-blocks-153.q: A highly available design adds redundant components. Why must it also provide reliable crossover?
sysd-blocks-153.a: In redundant systems the crossover point itself tends to become a single point of failure, so reliable systems must provide for reliable crossover.

sysd-scale-073.q: What is the chance that a system survives to its MTBF, and why does it matter?
sysd-scale-073.a: About 37% (1/e), not the 50% many engineers assume, and that misreading can lead to bad design decisions.

sysd-scale-136.q: Why does speeding up one part of a system by a huge factor often barely help overall?
