sysd-scale-136.a: The overall gain is limited by the fraction of time that part is actually used: speeding up a part that takes 10% of execution time by a factor of 10,000 gives an overall speedup of only 1.11, an 11% improvement.

sysd-scale-066.q: What do contention and coherency mean in the Universal Scalability Law, and what does high contention suggest?
sysd-scale-066.a: Contention is delay from waiting or queueing for shared resources, and coherence is delay for data to become consistent; high contention indicates sequential processing that could be parallelized, while high coherency suggests excessive dependencies among processes.

sysd-scale-067.q: How can a site claim very high availability while its service goes down for maintenance?
sysd-scale-067.a: Many sites exclude scheduled downtime from their availability calculations, but for true high availability downtime is downtime whether or not it is scheduled.

sysd-scale-134.q: A system stays up all year but suffers a 9-hour network failure at peak usage. Is it 100% available?
sysd-scale-134.a: No: users see it as unavailable even though the administrator claims 100% uptime. By the true definition it is approximately 99.9% available, three nines: 8751 hours of available time out of 8760 hours.

sysd-scale-076.q: Why does chaining two 99.9%-available components lower availability, while running them in parallel raises it?
sysd-scale-076.a: In sequence, total availability is the product of the components' availabilities, so two at 99.9% each give 99.8%; in parallel it is 1 minus the product of their unavailabilities, so two at 99.9% each give 99.9999%.

sysd-scale-063.q: Why can't replication stand in for a backup?
sysd-scale-063.a: A backup copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

sysd-scale-058.q: Why does a gossip protocol keep spreading information even when some messages are lost?
sysd-scale-058.a: Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows, so a rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and that doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost.

sysd-scale-131.q: Why can no deterministic algorithm elect a leader in an anonymous ring?
sysd-scale-131.a: All the processes are identical and run at the same speed, so symmetry cannot be broken; randomized algorithms can pick a leader with high probability.

sysd-scale-046.q: What happens if one record is changed on two nodes at once under eager versus lazy multi-master replication?
sysd-scale-046.a: An eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction; a lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization.

sysd-scale-122.q: Why does requiring Vr + Vw > V guarantee that a read sees the newest version?
sysd-scale-122.a: Because the read and write quorum votes together must exceed the total votes, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum and so includes the newest version, with version numbers showing which copies are current.

sysd-scale-048.q: How can a system keep a user from missing an order they just placed when a replica lags behind the primary?
sysd-scale-048.a: Send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database; or check whether the replica has caught up with the primary and, if not, fail the read or read from the primary.

sysd-scale-132.q: How does PostgreSQL logical replication start replicating a table and keep its changes consistent?
sysd-scale-132.a: A snapshot of the table is copied to the subscriber first, then changes made since the copy are sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription.

sysd-scale-130.q: What happens if every heartbeat link between cluster nodes fails while the nodes keep running?
sysd-scale-130.a: Each node believes it is the only one running, so each serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data or cause inconsistencies that need operator cleanup.

sysd-scale-126.q: A G-Counter can only increment. How does a PN-Counter support decrements?
sysd-scale-126.a: It combines two G-Counters, one counting increments and one counting decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total.

sysd-scale-082.q: How does round-robin partitioning place rows, and what is its drawback?
sysd-scale-082.a: It sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n), giving uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

sysd-scale-087.q: Why do timestamp keys pile writes onto one partition in a sensor network, and how does a compound key help?
sysd-scale-087.a: With timestamp keys, writes concentrate in the partition of the current time period; prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load.

sysd-scale-088.q: Why does shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards make adding database servers expensive, and what fixes it?
sysd-scale-088.a: Changing the number of slots remaps nearly all keys, so adding or removing servers is expensive; consistent hashing, which hashes keys and servers onto a circle, fixes this by moving only the keys next to the changed server, a 1/n fraction when adding the nth server.

sysd-scale-139.q: Why do virtual nodes spread load more evenly after a server fails?
sysd-scale-139.a: Without them a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load; with several positions per server, its keys are reassigned to different servers, spreading them more evenly.

sysd-scale-140.q: Why should a table be optimized locally before it is sharded?
sysd-scale-140.a: Sharding is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient, and sharding a table before it has been optimized locally adds needless complexity.

sysd-scale-092.q: Why is eventual consistency only a liveness guarantee and not a safety one?
sysd-scale-092.a: It promises only that reads eventually return the same value, with no safety guarantee, so any intermediate value is allowed before convergence.

sysd-scale-107.q: What trade-off does PACELC add to CAP that applies even when there is no partition?
sysd-scale-107.a: Latency versus consistency: consistent operations need a full network round trip on reads and writes, so low-latency systems relax consistency to reduce delay. CAP matters only during a partition, but this trade-off is present at all times.

sysd-scale-099.q: What part of the design space does CAP actually rule out?
sysd-scale-099.a: Only a tiny part: perfect availability and consistency in the presence of partitions, which are rare. Designers need to sacrifice consistency or availability only when a partition is present.

sysd-scale-106.q: Why is a counter that reads its value, adds one and writes it back not linearizable, and how can it be fixed?
sysd-scale-106.a: Two processes can both read 0 and both write 1, so one increment is lost. An atomic compare-and-swap retried on failure, an atomic fetch-and-increment, or a lock around the critical section makes it linearizable.

sysd-scale-095.q: Under causal consistency, which writes must every process see in the same order, and which may be seen in different orders?
sysd-scale-095.a: Writes that are potentially causally related must be seen by all processes in the same order, while concurrent writes may be seen in a different order on different machines. Two writes are causally related when the processor doing the second write has just read the first.

sysd-scale-001.q: Why is two-phase commit called a blocking protocol?
sysd-scale-001.a: A participant that has voted Yes blocks until it receives commit or rollback, so if the coordinator fails permanently some participants never resolve their transactions.

sysd-scale-112.q: What makes one vector clock less than another, and what does that guarantee for events that happened before one another?
sysd-scale-112.a: VC(x) is less than VC(y) when every component of VC(x) is at most that of VC(y) and at least one is strictly smaller. If x happened before y, then VC(x) < VC(y).

sysd-scale-007.q: Why does the Google SRE book recommend renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite locks?
sysd-scale-007.a: Because they stop a crashed process from holding a lock forever.

sysd-scale-004.q: How does the pre-commit step of three-phase commit fix the ambiguity left by two-phase commit?
sysd-scale-004.a: The coordinator sends doCommit only after all participants have acknowledged they are prepared, so no participant can have committed before all know the decision.

sysd-scale-113.q: Why are atomic broadcast and consensus equivalent when processes can crash?
sysd-scale-113.a: Consensus reduces to atomic broadcast by proposing a value as a broadcast and deciding the first message received; the reverse runs consensus repeatedly on the next message.

sysd-scale-109.q: How many participants does it take to tolerate F Byzantine failures, compared with crash-only majority consensus?
sysd-scale-109.a: Tolerating F Byzantine failures needs at least 3F+1 participants, while majority-quorum consensus that tolerates only crashes needs just 2f+1 replicas for f failures.

sysd-scale-118.q: In Paxos, which value does the Proposer put in its Accept message once a quorum has promised?
sysd-scale-118.a: The value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported by the Acceptors, or the Proposer's own value if none was reported.

sysd-scale-119.q: In a consensus group, what does it signal when the term or view number rises fast, and what if it decreases?
sysd-scale-119.a: A fast increase signals a flapping leader, perhaps from network problems, and a decrease signals a serious bug.

sysd-scale-022.q: What happens in a leader election when a follower hears no heartbeat from the leader before its election timeout?
sysd-scale-022.a: It becomes a candidate: it increases the term counter, votes for itself and requests votes from all other servers, and a majority of votes makes it leader.

sysd-scale-026.q: What does Spanner's time API expose, and why does that matter?
sysd-scale-026.a: It exposes clock uncertainty, which is critical to external consistency, nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free snapshot transactions and atomic schema changes.

sysd-scale-028.q: How does a DynamoDB table keyed by a partition key plus a sort key differ from one keyed by a partition key alone?
sysd-scale-028.a: With a partition key alone, no two items can have the same partition key. With a sort key added, the partition key picks the physical location and the sort key orders items inside it, so items may share a partition key but not a sort key.

sysd-scale-031.q: Why does Cassandra not support multi-table JOINs, ad hoc aggregations or complex queries?
sysd-scale-031.a: Its distributed architecture optimizes for scalability and availability instead.

sysd-scale-120.q: What do the commit log and the Memtable each do when Cassandra takes a write?
sysd-scale-120.a: The commit log is a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and the Memtable is an in-memory structure sorted by primary key.

sysd-scale-121.q: How does ScyllaDB use a node's CPU cores differently from a design built on threads and shared memory?
sysd-scale-121.a: Each node is sharded per CPU core: each core handles a different subset of data, and the cores share nothing and communicate explicitly.

sysd-scale-041.q: Why should a MapReduce partition function spread keys roughly uniformly across reducers?
sysd-scale-041.a: A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers; if the data is not spread roughly uniformly, the job waits on slow reducers.

sysd-msg-056.q: What happens to senders when the receiver of a message queue fails?
sysd-msg-056.a: Senders continue unaffected, because sender and receiver need not be online together; messages accumulate in the queue until the receiver restarts.

sysd-msg-050.q: When is at-least-once delivery good enough even though it can deliver the same message several times?
sysd-msg-050.a: When duplication is not a big issue or the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key.

sysd-msg-136.q: What does it mean that AMQP is a wire-level protocol, and why does that matter?
sysd-msg-136.a: It describes the format of the bytes sent across the network, so any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS.

sysd-msg-058.q: How does a dead letter queue keep the main queue moving?
sysd-msg-058.a: It sets aside messages that cannot be processed, so they can be inspected later without blocking processing or spending CPU cycles on a message that may never be consumed successfully.

sysd-msg-059.q: What do event streaming platforms give up in return for more scalability than message brokers?
sysd-msg-059.a: They cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received messages, and they offer fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending and more limited routing and queueing.

sysd-msg-071.q: What does backpressure do for a queue, and what do clients see once the queue is full?
sysd-msg-071.a: Backpressure limits the queue size, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for jobs already in the queue. Once it fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code to try again later.

sysd-msg-054.q: How does the claim check pattern handle large messages?
sysd-msg-054.a: It stores the whole payload in a database and transmits only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload.

sysd-msg-064.q: What does publish-subscribe add to the observer pattern?
sysd-msg-064.a: A broker, so publishers and subscribers are unaware of each other; it scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.

sysd-msg-065.q: How do topic-based and content-based filtering differ in pub/sub?
sysd-msg-065.a: With topic-based filtering, subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it. With content-based filtering, subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and messages are delivered only if they match.

sysd-msg-066.q: Who receives each message in a pub/sub topic, and how does that differ from a message queue?
sysd-msg-066.a: In pub/sub all subscribers to the topic receive every message broadcast, while in a message queue each message is processed only once by a single consumer.

sysd-msg-043.q: How does Spark rebuild data that is lost?
sysd-msg-043.a: Its resilient distributed datasets are immutable and operations are lazy, so lost data is rebuilt from each RDD's lineage.

sysd-msg-038.q: What can go wrong if a Kafka consumer relies on auto-committing offsets?
sysd-msg-038.a: Auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so if the consumer goes down mid-processing, some records may never be processed.

sysd-msg-042.q: Why is transaction-log based change data capture attractive, and what makes it hard?
sysd-msg-042.a: It has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed. But no standard exists for log formats, most databases do not document them, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

sysd-msg-020.q: How is a mistaken event corrected in an event-sourced system?
sysd-msg-020.a: Stored events are never changed, even erroneous ones; the only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values.

sysd-msg-021.q: What is the difference between event sourcing and event-driven architecture?
sysd-msg-021.a: Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data, whereas event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries.

sysd-msg-030.q: How can an event-driven system avoid losing an event when a component crashes before handing it on?
sysd-msg-030.a: It persists in-transit events and dequeues them only after the next component acknowledges receipt, features known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.

sysd-msg-024.q: What does CQRS separate, and why?
sysd-msg-024.a: It separates commands, which change the system and return only success or failure, from queries, which request information without changing state. The two play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.

sysd-msg-034.q: Why do both short and long timeouts cause trouble in distributed systems, and which pattern helps?
sysd-msg-034.a: Short timeouts may fail legitimate requests prematurely, while long timeouts give slow error responses and a poor user experience. The circuit breaker pattern helps by monitoring service health, enabling faster failure detection.

sysd-msg-032.q: How can an event-driven system cope with event schemas that change across services?
sysd-msg-032.a: By versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility, and by using adapters that translate events between old and new formats.

sysd-msg-083.q: How does scaling differ between a monolith and microservices when only one function is constrained?
sysd-msg-083.a: A monolith supporting three functions must be scaled in its entirety even if only one is constrained, whereas with microservices only that function's service is scaled out.

sysd-msg-093.q: What are the data plane and the control plane of a service mesh?
sysd-msg-093.a: The data plane is the network proxies paired with each service, which intercept and process calls between services. The control plane is the set of management processes that coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.

sysd-msg-097.q: What is the main distinction between SOA and microservices?
sysd-msg-097.a: Scope: SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards, whereas microservices are many smallest independent service units aimed at team autonomy and decoupling.

sysd-msg-079.q: Why should each microservice keep its own data private instead of sharing a database schema?
sysd-msg-079.a: Private data lowers coupling, so services can evolve independently, while shared database schemas are a cause of coupling.

sysd-msg-085.q: When might one bounded context be split into several microservices, or several contexts merged into one?
sysd-msg-085.a: A context may be split for varying scalability needs, and several contexts may be consolidated into one microservice for simplicity or lower operational overhead.

sysd-msg-088.q: What is the reach-in reporting antipattern, and what is the alternative?
sysd-msg-088.a: Pulling data for a reporting service, whether directly from databases, over HTTP or in batches, can break bounded contexts or reduce the timeliness of the data. Having the databases push the data asynchronously needs a separate contract and can be complex, but it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

sysd-msg-075.q: When moving from a monolith to microservices, which should be migrated first, the code or the data?
sysd-msg-075.a: The code: new microservices temporarily rely on the existing monolithic database, and data is decoupled later so each service has its own database. Prioritizing data migration first is the data-driven migration antipattern.

sysd-msg-001.q: Why must callers treat a remote procedure call differently from a local one, even though it is written like a local call?
sysd-msg-001.a: Remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local calls, and they can fail from unpredictable network problems without the caller knowing whether the remote procedure was actually invoked.

sysd-msg-004.q: Why can a data structure not be serialized by copying its memory layout directly?
sysd-msg-004.a: The serialization format must be architecture-independent, and a raw memory layout cannot work reliably across architectures because of byte ordering, memory layout and per-language data representation.

sysd-msg-123.q: How does a Protocol Buffers message save bandwidth compared with sending field names?
sysd-msg-123.a: A schema identifies each field by an integer, and the data carries only those numbers, not the field names, which saves bandwidth and storage.

sysd-msg-122.q: Why did services move from SOAP towards using HTTP more directly, as REST does?
sysd-msg-122.a: Being protocol-agnostic, SOAP cannot use REST's uniform interface or caching and must reimplement them. Its verbosity, slow XML parsing and lack of a standard interaction model led services to use HTTP more directly.

sysd-msg-013.q: How does cursor-based pagination avoid the cost of offset-based pagination on large datasets?
sysd-msg-013.a: Offset-based pagination must scan and skip rows, which is inefficient for large offsets, while cursor-based pagination marks a position with a cursor so skipped records are not scanned. The price is slightly more complexity.

sysd-msg-019.q: Which should you pick for an API: REST, GraphQL or gRPC?
sysd-msg-019.a: None is better: there is no silver bullet, and the best choice depends on the application's requirements and team, so focus on the domain and requirements rather than the technology.

sysd-msg-016.q: What does agreeing an API contract before writing any code let downstream developers do?
sysd-msg-016.a: They can mock the server and start testing right away, which is a shift-left testing practice.

sysd-msg-101.q: Why does long polling remove the response latency of normal polling, yet usually not scale?
sysd-msg-101.a: The server holds the request open until information is available or a timeout is reached, so it can respond as soon as there is news. But it creates a new connection each time, which is intensive on the server.

sysd-msg-107.q: Which of SSE and WebSocket lets the browser keep sending new requests to the server, and why?
sysd-msg-107.a: WebSocket, because it is full-duplex, whereas SSE is uni-directional so the browser cannot send a new request to the server.

sysd-msg-110.q: What does fragmentation let a WebSocket sender avoid?
sysd-msg-110.a: Buffering a whole message: it lets the sender start a message of unknown length, whereas without fragmentation the complete length is needed before the first byte can be sent, which requires a buffer.

sysd-msg-106.q: How does a webhook differ from polling an external service?
sysd-msg-106.a: Instead of continuously asking, you give the external service an endpoint as a callback, and it calls that endpoint every time something interesting happens, so data is pushed as soon as it is available.

sysd-msg-103.q: How does a message get from a user on one XMPP server to a user on another?
sysd-msg-103.a: The client sends it to its own server, which delivers it instantly if the recipient is online and otherwise holds it. For a user on another server, the first server connects to that server over XMPP.

sysd-msg-150.q: Why should WebSocket clients wait a random, growing time before reconnecting after an abnormal closure?
sysd-msg-150.a: Clients that all reconnect immediately and persistently after a nontransient failure amount to a denial-of-service attack that can keep the service from recovering. So the first attempt is delayed by a random time, and later attempts wait increasingly longer.

sysd-msg-118.q: What attack does masking the frames a WebSocket client sends prevent?
sysd-msg-118.a: In an experiment, attackers poisoned caching proxies by sending data on an upgraded connection that looked like an HTTP GET. Masking client data stops a script from making a message that an intermediary misreads as HTTP.

sysd-msg-120.q: How does handling many concurrent connections differ from handling many requests per second?
sysd-msg-120.a: Many requests per second needs high throughput, whereas many concurrent connections needs efficient scheduling of connections to sockets or other stateful endpoints.

sysd-reliab-075.q: What happens when one part of a system fails and the other parts must compensate for it?
sysd-reliab-075.a: That overloads the other parts so they fail too, which prompts more nodes to fail one after another: a cascading failure.

sysd-reliab-176.q: Why should a deadline be propagated down the call stack?
sysd-reliab-176.a: With propagation, every RPC in the tree shares the same absolute deadline, so each call knows how much time remains. Without it, a server keeps working on doomed requests, such as one that believes it has time left after the caller's deadline has already passed.

sysd-reliab-171.q: How does adaptive throttling decide when a client should reject its own requests?
sysd-reliab-171.a: Each client task tracks, for the last two minutes, the requests its application attempted and the requests the backend accepted. It keeps sending until requests reach K times accepts, then rejects new requests locally with a probability that rises as the application's request rate grows relative to the accepted rate.

sysd-reliab-086.q: How does graceful degradation go further than load shedding?
sysd-reliab-086.a: Load shedding drops some proportion of traffic as a server approaches overload. Graceful degradation takes it a step further by reducing the work each request needs, for example by returning lower-quality results.

sysd-reliab-181.q: Why is a rate limit tracked separately on each node not enough for a cluster-wide limit?
sysd-reliab-181.a: A consumer can exceed the global limit by sending requests to different nodes, and the more nodes there are, the likelier that becomes.

sysd-reliab-172.q: When a service is globally overloaded, who should receive the errors, and how do owners arrange this?
sysd-reliab-172.a: Only the misbehaving customers should get errors, while other customers remain unaffected. Owners provision capacity from negotiated usage and set per-customer quotas.

sysd-reliab-180.q: What is the difference between a latency cache and a capacity cache?
sysd-reliab-180.a: A latency cache lets a service sustain its expected load with an empty cache, while a capacity cache does not; caches added for performance can become hard dependencies.

sysd-reliab-182.q: Why can retrying a timed-out payment request charge the customer twice?
sysd-reliab-182.a: The client cannot tell whether the server missed the request, processed it with the response lost, or is still processing it. Retrying without idempotency can therefore charge the customer twice.

sysd-reliab-079.q: How can a payment system get exactly-once execution from retries and an idempotency check?
sysd-reliab-079.a: It splits the problem in two: retry provides at-least-once delivery, since a client retries after an error or timeout, and an idempotency key lets the server discard duplicates, providing at-most-once.

sysd-reliab-068.q: What happens in a circuit breaker's half-open state?
sysd-reliab-068.a: A limited number of requests pass through; if they succeed the breaker returns to closed, and if they keep failing it goes back to open.

sysd-reliab-089.q: How does the token bucket relate to the leaky bucket used as a meter?
sysd-reliab-089.a: They are mirror images: implemented correctly with the same parameters, they see exactly the same packets as conforming and nonconforming. The leaky bucket as a queue is different, a special case of the meter version that applies only to traffic shaping and gives jitter-free output.

sysd-reliab-091.q: Why can a 99.99% uptime SLO still hide a catastrophic integrity failure?
sysd-reliab-091.a: Each service has independent uptime and integrity requirements: 99.99% uptime allows about an hour of downtime a year, but 99.99% good bytes in a 2 GB artifact means up to 200 KB garbled, which is catastrophic.

sysd-reliab-099.q: How do SLIs, SLOs and SLAs build on one another?
sysd-reliab-099.a: SLIs form the basis of service level objectives, which in turn form the basis of service level agreements. An SLI is the measured value of the metric an SLO describes, and it must always meet or exceed the SLO's value to stay in compliance with the SLA.

sysd-reliab-190.q: How does a differential backup differ from an incremental one?
sysd-reliab-190.a: An incremental copies changes since the most recent backup of any type, while a differential copies changes since the last full backup. A restore from differentials needs at most two backups, but each differential takes longer as changes accumulate.

sysd-reliab-210.q: Why is replication a flawed answer to the question of whether you have a backup?
sysd-reliab-210.a: Replication gives data locality and protection from a site-specific disaster, but it cannot protect against many sources of data loss.

sysd-reliab-224.q: How does an error budget resolve the tension between developers and SREs?
sysd-reliab-224.a: Developers are judged on velocity and SREs on reliability, so they pull in opposite directions. The error budget is an objective, agreed metric that removes politics and gives both a common incentive.

sysd-reliab-197.q: Why is a 99.99% availability target both a minimum and a maximum?
sysd-reliab-197.a: The goal is reliable enough but no more: exceeding the target by much wastes chances to add features, clean up technical debt or cut costs.

sysd-reliab-194.q: What goes wrong if you pick an SLO target simply from current performance?
sysd-reliab-194.a: Adopting values without reflection can lock you into a system that needs heroic efforts to meet its targets and cannot improve without redesign.

sysd-reliab-097.q: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
sysd-reliab-097.a: Monitoring watches predefined sets of telemetry, whereas observability is based on exploring properties and patterns that were not defined in advance.

sysd-reliab-209.q: What is a fuzzy backup, and why is it dangerous?
sysd-reliab-209.a: It comes from snapshotting a file while it changes, or across interrelated files such as a database, which yields a corrupted file. It looks successful but does not show the data at a single point in time.

sysd-reliab-096.q: Why should recovery be tested continuously rather than only after a disaster?
sysd-reliab-096.a: Components not continually exercised fail when you need them most, so regular tests make failures happen before a real catastrophe, when problems can be fixed without harm.

sysd-reliab-213.q: Why must a data validator be neither too strict nor too lax?
sysd-reliab-213.a: Too strict and engineers abandon it, too lax and corruption slips through, so it should validate only invariants whose failure devastates users, such as file contents matching folder listings.

sysd-reliab-221.q: How does packet encapsulation free a load balancer from the limits of layer 2 forwarding, and what does it cost?
sysd-reliab-221.a: It wraps the packet in a GRE-encapsulated IP packet addressed to the backend, so balancer and backend can be on separate continents, at the price of 24 bytes of overhead that may exceed the MTU; layer 2 forwarding instead needs every balancer and backend in one broadcast domain.

sysd-reliab-200.q: Why can a throughput cluster cost far less than a low-latency cluster for the same storage system?
sysd-reliab-200.a: Low-latency clusters carry substantial slack capacity for short queues and isolation, while throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy, perhaps at as little as 10-50% of the cost.

sysd-reliab-218.q: A service expects a peak of about 3,470 QPS and each task handles about 100 QPS. How many tasks does it need with N+2?
sysd-reliab-218.a: At least 35 tasks are needed for the peak, and N+2 raises this to 37, since an update plus a machine failure could otherwise leave only 35.

sysd-reliab-204.q: Why should a frequently firing alert be removed or automated instead of left to page a human?
sysd-reliab-204.a: Pages with rote responses are a red flag: when an alert becomes frequent, remove its root cause or fully automate the response, since every page distracts a human from improving the system.

sysd-reliab-185.q: Why did Gmail still need an offline tape layer despite large disk and network resources for replication?
sysd-reliab-185.a: Multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism, so large disk and network resources for replication did not remove the need for a tape layer.

sysd-reliab-146.q: Why are containers cheaper than full virtualization, and what do they give up?
sysd-reliab-146.a: Programs use the operating system's normal system call interface and need no emulation or intermediate virtual machine, so containers are lightweight; the trade-off is that a container cannot host a guest operating system different from the host's, or a different guest kernel.

sysd-reliab-145.q: What is the difference between what cgroups and namespaces control?
sysd-reliab-145.a: Cgroups dictate how much of the system a process can use, such as CPU, memory and disk I/O limits, while namespaces dictate what it may see; together they underpin Docker, Kubernetes, LXC and Podman.

sysd-reliab-161.q: What happens when a liveness probe keeps failing, compared with a failing readiness probe?
sysd-reliab-161.a: After more failures than the configured tolerance, a failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container; a failing readiness probe instead gets the Pod's IP removed from the EndpointSlices of every matching Service.

sysd-reliab-148.q: Why are Pods rarely created directly?
sysd-reliab-148.a: Pods are relatively ephemeral and disposable, so a workload resource such as a Deployment creates them, replicates them for scale, and replaces them when a node fails.

sysd-reliab-228.q: What happens to the restart delay of a container that keeps crashing, and why?
sysd-reliab-228.a: After the first crash it restarts immediately, but repeated crashes get an exponential backoff delay, which stops a faulty container from overwhelming the system with failed start attempts; the delay starts at 10s and doubles up to a default cap of 300s.

sysd-reliab-159.q: Why does a Service give frontends one stable endpoint instead of letting them track backend Pod IPs?
sysd-reliab-159.a: Pods are ephemeral and the set of healthy Pods changes from moment to moment, so frontends cannot track backend IPs; a Service decouples them by giving the group one stable endpoint.

sysd-reliab-151.q: What happens if you create an Ingress resource in a cluster that has no Ingress controller?
sysd-reliab-151.a: It has no effect, because an Ingress controller fulfils the Ingress, usually with a load balancer.

sysd-reliab-047.q: How does a hypervisor guest differ from an emulator and from OS-level virtualization?
sysd-reliab-047.a: Unlike an emulator, the guest executes most instructions on native hardware; this contrasts with OS-level virtualization, where containers must share a single kernel.

sysd-reliab-043.q: Why are containers much more lightweight than virtual machines?
sysd-reliab-043.a: Containers virtualize the operating system instead of the hardware, so each contains only the application and its dependencies; they share the OS kernel and use a fraction of the memory VMs require.

sysd-reliab-144.q: Why do frequent releases make testing and troubleshooting easier?
sysd-reliab-144.a: Frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier.

sysd-reliab-059.q: How is a bug fixed in an older release without picking up unrelated mainline changes?
sysd-reliab-059.a: The fix goes to the mainline first and is then cherry picked into the release branch, rebuilt at the same revision as the original build with the specific later changes included, so unrelated mainline changes are avoided and the exact contents of each release are known.

sysd-reliab-163.q: Why does the autoscaler use the highest desired count from a stabilization window when scaling down?
sysd-reliab-163.a: So that it does not remove Pods only to recreate them moments later; replica counts that fluctuate frequently as metrics change are called thrashing or flapping, and the default window is 300 seconds.

sysd-reliab-157.q: Why can't maxUnavailable and maxSurge both be 0 in a rolling update?
sysd-reliab-157.a: At least one of the two must allow change, so maxUnavailable cannot be 0 when maxSurge is 0, and maxSurge cannot be 0 when maxUnavailable is 0.

sysd-reliab-057.q: How does Kubernetes act on the gap between desired and current state?
sysd-reliab-057.a: Objects record the desired state in a spec field while the controller keeps a status field describing the current state; if an operator declares three instances of a pod and the Deployment controller finds only two running, it schedules the creation of another instance.

sysd-reliab-158.q: What happens to running Pods when you change a Pod template?
sysd-reliab-158.a: A change has no direct effect on existing Pods: the controller creates replacement Pods from the new template instead of patching the old ones, until all old Pods are replaced.

sysd-reliab-141.q: What is toggle debt, and why does it cost something?
sysd-reliab-141.a: It arises when a feature is toggled on permanently and dead code remains; it adds overhead, and the code must be removed carefully so other parts are not disturbed.

sysd-reliab-142.q: How does a canary release limit the damage from a bad new version?
sysd-reliab-142.a: It turns the feature on for a sampled cohort, such as 1% of users, while everyone else stays off, and if the feature's performance is not satisfactory it can be rolled back without adverse effects.

sysd-reliab-016.q: Why is reusing one salt for all passwords dangerous?
sysd-reliab-016.a: A precomputed table that accounts for the salt becomes viable, and cracking one hash also exposes others with the same password.

sysd-reliab-126.q: Why is treating a successful OAuth token request as proof of who the user is risky?
sysd-reliab-126.a: OAuth tells the application nothing about the user or whether they are present, and it was not designed for authentication, so the assumption can cause major security flaws.

sysd-reliab-019.q: How does tracking a logged-in user with a session differ from tracking with a token?
sysd-reliab-019.a: With a session the server stores the user's identity and gives the browser a session ID cookie; with a token the identity is encoded into a token the browser sends on later requests, so no server session storage is needed.

sysd-reliab-129.q: Why does a forged request from another page look genuine to the server in a CSRF attack?
sysd-reliab-129.a: Browsers automatically and invisibly include a domain's cookies, session cookies among them, in any request to that domain, so a forged request from another page looks genuine to the server.

sysd-reliab-024.q: What does OpenID Connect add to OAuth 2.0?
sysd-reliab-024.a: OAuth 2.0 only grants access to data and features from one application to another; OpenID Connect lets clients verify an end user's identity from the authorization server's authentication and fetch basic profile information.

sysd-reliab-130.q: How does the synchronizer token pattern stop a CSRF attack?
sysd-reliab-130.a: It embeds a secret, unique token in every HTML form and verifies it on the server, so the attacker cannot put a correct token in forged requests.

sysd-reliab-023.q: In OAuth 2.0's authorization code grant, what happens if a code is used more than once?
sysd-reliab-023.a: The server must deny the request and should revoke tokens previously issued from it; the code is bound to the client identifier and redirection URI.

sysd-reliab-035.q: How does PKCE stop an attacker who intercepts an authorization code from redeeming it?
sysd-reliab-035.a: The client sends only a code challenge derived from a random secret, the code verifier, and later sends the verifier with the code; the server compares the transformed verifier with the stored challenge and denies access if they differ, and the attacker never saw the verifier because it was never sent over any channel the attacker can observe.

sysd-reliab-029.q: Why is trusting users and devices inside a corporate perimeter or behind a VPN commonly not sufficient?
sysd-reliab-029.a: Networks have many zones, cloud services, remote and mobile environments and IoT devices, so zero trust instead checks the identity and integrity of users and devices regardless of location.

sysd-reliab-033.q: Why does invalidating a session before a JWT expires undo the main advantage of JWTs?
sysd-reliab-033.a: The service can no longer trust the token alone and must check a data store, which removes the statelessness that is the main advantage of JWTs.

sysd-reliab-119.q: How does an MFA fatigue attack work, and what is advised instead of push notifications?
sysd-reliab-119.a: It floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake; number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

sysd-reliab-125.q: What happens in Kerberos if the clocks of hosts drift too far apart?
sysd-reliab-125.a: Authentication fails: tickets have a lifetime, so hosts' clocks must be synchronized within configured limits (five minutes apart by default in MIT's setup).

sysd-reliab-027.q: What extra cost does every access through a short URL carry?
sysd-reliab-027.a: Every access needs at least one more DNS lookup (possibly cached) and one more HTTP/HTTPS request, which adds latency and the risk of failure if the shortening service becomes unavailable.

sysd-q-033.q: How does a standalone Key Generation Service keep concurrent servers from getting the same key?
sysd-q-033.a: It creates unique keys ahead of time in a separate database, and used keys move to another table under locking, so concurrent servers never share one.

sysd-q-063.q: How does designing a pastebin differ from designing a URL shortener?
sysd-q-063.a: It is like designing a URL shortener, except that the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL.

sysd-q-069.q: Why does a store-and-forward switching center hold a message when the destination is unreachable?
sysd-q-069.a: It keeps the message and retries later, which raises the chance of delivery; if the destination is available, the message is sent at once.

sysd-q-073.q: Why do chat designs push messages over WebSockets instead of polling?
sysd-q-073.a: Pulling by periodic HTTP requests or long polling is not scalable because most responses are empty, while push over WebSockets delivers data without delay.

sysd-q-093.q: Why does a hybrid feed use pull for users with millions of followers and push for users with fewer?
sysd-q-093.a: Publishing a post to every follower's feed is heavy when a user has millions of followers, so those users use pull, while users with fewer followers use push.

sysd-q-022.q: What does each of the three terms in Facebook's EdgeRank score capture?
sysd-q-022.a: Affinity is the closeness of the user to the creator, weight is a value per kind of edge so a comment can count more than a like, and decay lowers the rank of older edges.

sysd-q-020.q: Why does a Twitter-style design skip fanning out tweets from highly followed users?
sysd-q-020.a: Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes and races with @replies, so the design skips them and merges their tweets in at read time.

sysd-q-047.q: Why is content-based filtering easier to start than collaborative filtering?
sysd-q-047.a: Collaborative filtering needs a lot of data about a user, the cold start problem, while content-based filtering needs very little to start, though it recommends only items similar to the seed.

sysd-q-043.q: How does an adaptive streaming client avoid stalls as network conditions change?
sysd-q-043.a: Content is offered at several bit rates as short segments, and the client's adaptation algorithm picks the highest-bit-rate segment that can be downloaded in time to avoid stalls or re-buffering.

sysd-q-036.q: What happens to server bandwidth when 1,000 people watch a 300 kbit/s stream over unicast instead of multicast?
sysd-q-036.a: Unicast needs 300 Mbit/s, while multicast sends one common stream using only 300 kbit/s.

sysd-q-106.q: What does AV1 trade for its bandwidth savings over VP9?
sysd-q-106.a: It saves bandwidth, with Netflix's 2017 tests finding it about 25% more efficient than VP9, but it costs compute: 2017 decoding ran at about half the speed of VP9.

sysd-q-035.q: Why does a video platform put a message queue between upload and processing?
sysd-q-035.a: Processing is a long-running task, so the queue decouples it from uploading.

sysd-q-090.q: Why does a proximity service use geohash instead of computing the distance to every place?
sysd-q-090.a: Computing the distance to every place makes the query very inefficient, while geohash divides the planet into ever smaller grids so nearby places are found by a prefix match on the geohash column.

sysd-q-016.q: Why is the ride matching logic wrapped in a mutex?
sysd-q-016.a: Race conditions arise when many customers request rides at once, so the matching logic is wrapped in a mutex and every action is transactional.

sysd-q-054.q: Why does a proportional re-visit policy lose to a uniform one on average freshness?
sysd-q-054.a: A proportional policy spends crawls on rapidly changing pages whose freshness lasts only briefly.

sysd-q-108.q: Why does a page linked from many high-PageRank pages get a high rank itself?
sysd-q-108.a: A hyperlink counts as a vote of support, and a page's rank is defined recursively from the pages that link to it.

sysd-q-112.q: How does a sitemap differ from robots.txt in what it tells crawlers?
sysd-q-112.a: A sitemap is a URL inclusion protocol that complements robots.txt, which is a URL exclusion protocol.

sysd-q-113.q: What happens when the crawler service takes the top ranked link and finds a similar page signature already in crawled_links?
sysd-q-113.a: It lowers the link's priority, which prevents a cycle.

sysd-q-087.q: Why can a heap deliver the highest-priority item immediately even though it is not sorted?
sysd-q-087.a: The top-priority element sits at the root, and a heap gives access to the smallest or largest element in constant time; it is only partially ordered, with no implied ordering between siblings or cousins.

sysd-q-068.q: Why does the LRU search cache pair a doubly-linked list with a hash table?
sysd-q-068.a: The doubly-linked list adds new items at the head and removes items to expire from the tail, while the hash table gives fast lookup of each list node.

sysd-q-159.q: What is the trade-off between an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list for testing adjacency versus listing neighbours?
sysd-q-159.a: The matrix tests in constant time whether two vertices are adjacent, but listing a vertex's neighbours means scanning a whole row; an adjacency list lists neighbours in constant time per neighbour but tests whether an edge exists more slowly.

sysd-q-154.q: Why is a bidirectional search often faster than a single search from start to goal?
sysd-q-154.a: With branching factor b and start-to-goal distance d, each of the two searches costs O(b^(d/2)), and their sum is much less than the O(b^d) of a single search from start to goal.

sysd-q-066.q: Why does a growing service move MySQL off the web server's box and static content to an object store?
sysd-q-066.a: Vertical scaling gets expensive and blocks scaling MySQL and the web server independently, so static content goes to a managed object store and MySQL to a separate box.

sysd-q-136.q: What does a mail server take on by replying 250 after the end of the message data?
sysd-q-136.a: By returning a 2yz reply it accepts responsibility to deliver the message, retry transient failures and notify the sender of permanent ones.

sysd-q-134.q: Why can the To field of an email differ from the addresses it is actually delivered to?
sysd-q-134.a: Delivery follows the envelope, not the header, so To may be unrelated to the delivery addresses, and Bcc recipients are normally given only in the SMTP envelope.

sysd-q-133.q: Why must a notification about a failed delivery use a null reverse-path?
sysd-q-133.a: Servers must not send notifications about problems with notifications, and the null reverse-path prevents error-report loops.

sysd-q-120.q: How does IMAP differ from POP3 in where a user's messages live?
sysd-q-120.a: POP3 clients typically retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer and delete them from the server, while IMAP clients generally leave messages on the server until the user deletes them.

sysd-q-121.q: What does UIDVALIDITY let an IMAP client detect?
sysd-q-121.a: It lets a client detect changed UIDs: if UIDs fail to persist, the new value must be greater than the old.

sysd-q-118.q: Why does STARTTLS protect only against passive observation?
sysd-q-118.a: Its negotiation is in plain text, so an active attacker can strip the STARTTLS commands, a downgrade known as STRIPTLS.

sysd-q-148.q: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm give incorrect results when edges have negative weights?
sysd-q-148.a: Its greedy strategy finalizes a vertex's distance before a cheaper path through a negative edge is seen.

sysd-q-150.q: How does a contraction-hierarchy query stay fast on a huge road network?
sysd-q-150.a: It runs a bidirectional search from the start and target over the graph plus shortcuts, and both searches only follow edges to more important vertices, which keeps the search space small.

sysd-q-100.q: Why can a lock-free data structure outperform a lock-based one on a multi-core processor?
sysd-q-100.a: It spends more time in parallel rather than serial execution, because access to shared data need not be serialized.

sysd-q-097.q: Why does a low-latency exchange pin its single-threaded matching engine to a CPU?
sysd-q-097.a: The engine is single-threaded and pinned, so there is no context switch and no locks, and a thread resuming on its previous CPU may find its data still in that CPU's cache and take fewer cache misses.

sysd-q-028.q: How does a modern stock exchange reach microsecond latency?
sysd-q-028.a: By doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

sysd-q-147.q: What goes wrong if an operational transformation system skips transforming a delete after a concurrent insert at the start of the text abc?
sysd-q-147.a: After inserting x at position 0 of abc, deleting position 2 must become position 3; untransformed, it deletes b instead of c.

sysd-q-077.q: How does real-time gross settlement differ from an automated clearing house?
sysd-q-077.a: An automated clearing house processes transactions in batches and nets them, so settlement may be delayed; real-time gross settlement settles each transaction as soon as it is processed, one to one without netting, and payments are final and irrevocable.

sysd-q-079.q: Why does a payment system send an idempotency key when it retries a payment after a PSP timeout?
sysd-q-079.a: The retry may succeed at a later attempt, and the idempotency key stops it from charging the customer twice.

sysd-q-076.q: Why does a web push message carry a topic?
sysd-q-076.a: A message with a topic replaces any outstanding message with the same topic, so a device that was offline gets only the latest update, not outdated or redundant ones.

sysd-q-010.q: How does RBAC change the way users receive permissions compared with listing individual users in an ACL?
sysd-q-010.a: Roles are created for job functions and permissions are assigned to roles, so users get permissions only through their roles, and adding a user or changing a department means assigning the right roles.

sysd-q-013.q: In the recommended ABAC architecture, which component evaluates an authorization request and which one protects the app?
sysd-q-013.a: The Policy Decision Point evaluates requests against policies, while the Policy Enforcement Point protects the app and sends the authorization requests; Policy Information Points supply attributes.

sysd-q-012.q: How does mandatory access control differ from DAC in who sets the access policy?
sysd-q-012.a: In MAC the policy is centrally controlled by a policy administrator and enforced for all users, who cannot override it or grant access to files that would otherwise be restricted, unlike DAC where users set policy.

a2248a2fc855.title: Functional requirement
a2248a2fc855.sentence: In software engineering and systems engineering, a functional requirement defines a function of a system or its component, where a function is described as a summary (or specification or statement) of behavior between inputs and outputs.

3ab9d382268f.title: Functional requirement
3ab9d382268f.sentence: Functional requirements may involve calculations, technical details, data manipulation and processing, and other specific functionality that define what a system is supposed to accomplish.

22167c38c3de.title: Non-functional requirement
22167c38c3de.sentence: Functional requirements are usually in the form of "system shall do <requirement>", an individual action or part of the system, perhaps explicitly in the sense of a mathematical function, a black box description input, output, process and control functional model or IPO model.

378e64cadc3c.title: Functional requirement
378e64cadc3c.sentence: Functional requirements drive the application architecture of a system, while non-functional requirements drive the technical architecture of a system.

3a274d8476bd.title: Functional requirement
3a274d8476bd.sentence: Generally, functional requirements are expressed in the form "system must do <requirement>," while non-functional requirements take the form "system shall be <requirement>." The plan for implementing functional requirements is detailed in the system design, whereas non-functional requirements are detailed in the system architecture.

e7584ca47cc0.title: Functional requirement
e7584ca47cc0.sentence: Behavioral requirements describe all the cases where the system uses the functional requirements, these are captured in use cases.

2368c5f422ed.title: Functional requirement
2368c5f422ed.sentence: Often, though, an analyst will begin by eliciting a set of use cases, from which the analyst can derive the functional requirements that must be implemented to allow a user to perform each use case.

24644b852323.title: Functional requirement
24644b852323.sentence: In some cases, a requirements analyst generates use cases after gathering and validating a set of functional requirements.

c754b7b80b58.title: Functional requirement
c754b7b80b58.sentence: A typical specification of a functional requirement will contain a unique name and number, a brief summary, a rationale describing the reason it is needed, the requirements of behaviour or function, and references to use cases and other requirements relevant to understanding this one.

549a21540d96.title: Functional requirement
549a21540d96.sentence: The crux of the requirement is the description of the required behavior, which must be clear and readable.

b3456f97fd5e.title: Non-functional requirement
b3456f97fd5e.sentence: In systems engineering and requirements engineering, a non-functional requirement (NFR) is a requirement that specifies criteria that can be used to judge the operation of a system, rather than specific behaviours.

8ae8e4c0e14b.title: Non-functional requirement
8ae8e4c0e14b.sentence: In contrast, non-functional requirements are in the form of "system shall be <requirement>", an overall property of the system as a whole or of a particular aspect and not a specific function.

f0bb63399664.title: Non-functional requirement
f0bb63399664.sentence: Broadly, functional requirements define what a system is supposed to do and non-functional requirements define how a system is supposed to be.

aa7cdfef4513.title: Non-functional requirement
aa7cdfef4513.sentence: It is important to specify non-functional requirements in a specific and measurable way.

c3b74127efe6.title: Non-functional requirement
c3b74127efe6.sentence: The system's overall properties commonly mark the difference between whether the development project has succeeded or failed.

d828ee79b666.title: Non-functional requirement
d828ee79b666.sentence: Non-functional requirements are often called the "quality attributes" of a system.

cb150b5457e0.title: Non-functional requirement
cb150b5457e0.sentence: Other terms for non-functional requirements are "qualities", "quality goals", "quality of service requirements", "constraints", "non-behavioral requirements", or "technical requirements".

f23b16826f2a.title: Non-functional requirement
f23b16826f2a.sentence: Informally these are sometimes called the "ilities", from attributes like stability and portability.

706e08c80b9f.title: Non-functional requirement
706e08c80b9f.sentence: In software architecture, non-functional requirements are known as "architectural characteristics".

9b93070c41d7.title: Non-functional requirement
9b93070c41d7.sentence: Non-functional requirements are also known as cross-functional requirements by some.

ecd9e24970ce.title: Non-functional requirement
ecd9e24970ce.sentence: Qualities—that is non-functional requirements—can be divided into two main categories:

52ec0c10a8a7.title: Non-functional requirement
52ec0c10a8a7.sentence: - Execution qualities, such as safety, security and usability, which are observable during operation (at run time).

c20840a3c94f.title: Non-functional requirement
c20840a3c94f.sentence: - Evolution qualities, such as testability, maintainability, extensibility and scalability, which are embodied in the static structure of the system.

8e0bfd62b2f9.title: Non-functional requirement
8e0bfd62b2f9.sentence: - Performance (speed, battery life, throughput, response time (performance engineering))

d5c6a6c569b2.title: Non-functional requirement
d5c6a6c569b2.sentence: - Reliability (e.g. mean time between/to failures – MTBF/MTTF)

232563ce3049.title: Non-functional requirement
232563ce3049.sentence: - Maintainability (e.g. mean time to repair – MTTR)

c97ca6e68edb.title: Non-functional requirement
c97ca6e68edb.sentence: - Fault tolerance (e.g. operational system monitoring, measuring, and management)

970855140a67.title: Non-functional requirement
970855140a67.sentence: - Resource constraints (processor speed, memory, disk space, network bandwidth, etc.)

323e6c2cbd14.title: Non-functional requirement
323e6c2cbd14.sentence: A system may be required to present the user with a display of the number of records in a database.

fa47c733e10d.title: Non-functional requirement
fa47c733e10d.sentence: How current this number needs to be, is a non-functional requirement.

f88957e96beb.title: Non-functional requirement
f88957e96beb.sentence: If the number needs to be updated in real time, the system architects must ensure that the system is capable of displaying the record count within an acceptably short interval of the number of records changing.

dd39046c45ff.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::system-design-interviews
dd39046c45ff.sentence: For example, portability, maintainability, reliability, scalability, security, etc.

fc679c899546.sentence: - "Each request should be processed with the minimum latency"

e34f6b4e2cf6.title: Non-functional requirement
e34f6b4e2cf6.sentence: The plan for implementing non-functional requirements is detailed in the system architecture, because they are usually architecturally significant requirements.

cf01cb636d70.title: Software architecture
cf01cb636d70.sentence: Quality-driven: classic software design approaches (e.g. Jackson Structured Programming) were driven by required functionality and the flow of data through the system, but the current insight is that the architecture of a software system is more closely related to its quality attributes such as fault-tolerance, backward compatibility, extensibility, reliability, maintainability, availability, security, usability, and other such –ilities.

e349570716b2.title: Software architecture
e349570716b2.sentence: It's software architect's responsibility to match architectural characteristics (aka non-functional requirements) with business requirements.

26c29672b723.title: Software architecture
26c29672b723.sentence: Software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system and the discipline of creating such structures and systems.

9774bdfcdffe.title: Software architecture
9774bdfcdffe.sentence: Each structure comprises software elements, relations among them, and properties of both elements and relations.

02e1e00dd626.title: Software architecture
02e1e00dd626.sentence: The architecture of a software system is a metaphor, analogous to the architecture of a building.

752f4ea462ab.title: Software architecture
752f4ea462ab.sentence: It functions as the blueprints for the system and the development project, which project management can later use to extrapolate the tasks necessary to be executed by the teams and people involved.

be1ed87de74a.title: Software architecture
be1ed87de74a.sentence: Software architecture is about making fundamental structural choices that are costly to change once implemented.

aa420b19d257.title: Software architecture
aa420b19d257.sentence: Software architecture design is commonly juxtaposed with software application design.

c44545832c3a.title: Software architecture
c44545832c3a.sentence: Whilst application design focuses on the design of the processes and data supporting the required functionality (the services offered by the system), software architecture design focuses on designing the infrastructure within which application functionality can be realized and executed such that the functionality is provided in a way which meets the system's non-functional requirements.

7bf15bf1e9de.title: Software architecture
7bf15bf1e9de.sentence: Architecture is design but not all design is architectural.

9763dcb8c6da.title: Software architecture
9763dcb8c6da.sentence: In practice, the architect is the one who draws the line between software architecture (architectural design) and detailed design (non-architectural design).

75ce3040bd07.title: Software architecture
75ce3040bd07.sentence: There are no rules or guidelines that fit all cases, although there have been attempts to formalize the distinction.

8cf05b0b09c9.title: Software architecture
8cf05b0b09c9.sentence: There are two fundamental laws in software architecture:

4a42225504ef.title: Software architecture
4a42225504ef.sentence: Software architectures can be categorized into two main types: monolith and distributed architecture, each having its own subcategories.

9c657e96aa54.title: Software architecture
9c657e96aa54.sentence: Software architecture tends to become more complex over time.

6b3eba461fc9.title: Software architecture
6b3eba461fc9.sentence: Software architecture is an "intellectually graspable" abstraction of a complex system.

05260c39b996.title: Software architecture
05260c39b996.sentence: - It gives a basis for analysis of software systems' behavior before the system has been built.

c487ff7642f3.title: Software architecture
c487ff7642f3.sentence: The ability to verify that a future software system fulfills its stakeholders' needs without actually having to build it represents substantial cost-saving and risk-mitigation.

e253ee6accde.title: Software architecture
e253ee6accde.sentence: Architecture gives the ability to communicate about design decisions before the system is implemented, when they are still relatively easy to adapt.
