4fc9ca8ab339.sentence: The 413 (Content Too Large) status code indicates that the server is refusing to process a request because the request content is larger than the server is willing or able to process.

7466decdd312.title: rfc>9110
7466decdd312.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.14. 413 Content Too Large
7466decdd312.sentence: If the condition is temporary, the server SHOULD generate a Retry-After header field to indicate that it is temporary and after what time the client MAY try again.

e2d80b5585d7.title: rfc>9110
e2d80b5585d7.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.15. 414 URI Too Long
e2d80b5585d7.sentence: The 414 (URI Too Long) status code indicates that the server is refusing to service the request because the target URI is longer than the server is willing to interpret.

a9d7d3e47556.title: rfc>9110
a9d7d3e47556.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.16. 415 Unsupported Media Type
a9d7d3e47556.sentence: The 415 (Unsupported Media Type) status code indicates that the origin server is refusing to service the request because the content is in a format not supported by this method on the target resource.

dd8811b98e44.title: rfc>9110
dd8811b98e44.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.9. 408 Request Timeout
dd8811b98e44.sentence: The 408 (Request Timeout) status code indicates that the server did not receive a complete request message within the time that it was prepared to wait.

187db0a022e4.title: rfc>9110
187db0a022e4.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.9. 408 Request Timeout
187db0a022e4.sentence: If the client has an outstanding request in transit, it MAY repeat that request.

0f227655f29f.title: rfc>9110
0f227655f29f.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.5. Client Error 4xx > 15.5.9. 408 Request Timeout
0f227655f29f.sentence: If the current connection is not usable (e.g., as it would be in HTTP/1.1 because request delimitation is lost), a new connection will be used.

811db1f292e3.title: rfc>9110
811db1f292e3.sentence: HTTP enables the use of intermediaries to satisfy requests through a chain of connections.

243c0c274be3.title: rfc>9110
243c0c274be3.sentence: There are three common forms of HTTP "intermediary": proxy, gateway, and tunnel.

a723ab642f04.title: rfc>9110
a723ab642f04.sentence: The figure above shows three intermediaries (A, B, and C) between the user agent and origin server.

b747469c12a6.title: rfc>9110
b747469c12a6.sentence: A request or response message that travels the whole chain will pass through four separate connections.

b226d7bf3466.title: rfc>9110
b226d7bf3466.sentence: Some HTTP communication options might apply only to the connection with the nearest, non-tunnel neighbor, only to the endpoints of the chain, or to all connections along the chain.

b9edfe246958.title: rfc>9110
b9edfe246958.sentence: A "proxy" is a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client, usually via local configuration rules, to receive requests for some type(s) of absolute URI and attempt to satisfy those requests via translation through the HTTP interface.

f1413116e89b.title: rfc>9110
f1413116e89b.sentence: Proxies are often used to group an organization's HTTP requests through a common intermediary for the sake of security services, annotation services, or shared caching.

8c567ce96ed6.title: rfc>9110
8c567ce96ed6.sentence: "reverse proxy") is an intermediary that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection but translates received requests and forwards them inbound to another server or servers.

6c2bc89e8c8a.title: rfc>9110
6c2bc89e8c8a.sentence: Gateways are often used to encapsulate legacy or untrusted information services, to improve server performance through "accelerator" caching, and to enable partitioning or load balancing of HTTP services across multiple machines.

f07c6ad7c1f3.title: rfc>9110
f07c6ad7c1f3.sentence: A "tunnel" acts as a blind relay between two connections without changing the messages.

3d6c94dcbf3b.title: rfc>9110
3d6c94dcbf3b.sentence: Tunnels are used to extend a virtual connection through an intermediary, such as when Transport Layer Security (TLS, ) is used to establish confidential communication through a shared firewall proxy.

ee38254fde37.title: rfc>9110
ee38254fde37.sentence: A tunnel ceases to exist when both ends of the relayed connection are closed.

6e5ac17c45e6.title: rfc>9110
6e5ac17c45e6.sentence: For example, an "interception proxy" (also commonly known as a "transparent proxy" ) differs from an HTTP proxy because it is not chosen by the client.

84e6423fd9f8.title: rfc>9110
84e6423fd9f8.sentence: Instead, an interception proxy filters or redirects outgoing TCP port 80 packets (and occasionally other common port traffic).

ee37482c5d18.title: rfc>9110
ee37482c5d18.sentence: Network intermediaries are indistinguishable (at a protocol level) from an on-path attacker, often introducing security flaws or interoperability problems due to mistakenly violating HTTP semantics.

92db15d02e34.title: rfc>9110
92db15d02e34.section: 7. Routing HTTP Messages > 7.6. Message Forwarding > 7.6.3. Via
92db15d02e34.sentence: A proxy MUST send an appropriate Via header field, as described below, in each message that it forwards.

3691cd688549.title: rfc>9110
3691cd688549.section: 7. Routing HTTP Messages > 7.6. Message Forwarding > 7.6.3. Via
3691cd688549.sentence: Via can be used for tracking message forwards, avoiding request loops, and identifying the protocol capabilities of senders along the request/response chain.

4d28c0ffaa6d.title: rfc>9110
4d28c0ffaa6d.section: 7. Routing HTTP Messages > 7.6. Message Forwarding > 7.6.3. Via
4d28c0ffaa6d.sentence: Each intermediary appends its own information about how the message was received, such that the end result is ordered according to the sequence of forwarding recipients.

dbd8e095a949.title: rfc>9110
dbd8e095a949.sentence: HTTP intermediaries are inherently situated for on-path attacks.

eec1af952ace.title: rfc>9110
eec1af952ace.sentence: Intermediaries that contain a shared cache are especially vulnerable to cache poisoning attacks, as described in Section 7 of.

8e7983ec9bff.title: rfc>9110
8e7983ec9bff.sentence: The 3xx (Redirection) class of status code indicates that further action needs to be taken by the user agent in order to fulfill the request.

fc661311cd99.title: rfc>9110
fc661311cd99.sentence: - Redirects that indicate this resource might be available at a different URI, as provided by the Location header field, as in the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently), 302 (Found), 307 (Temporary Redirect), and 308 (Permanent Redirect).

c7a40b0be87b.title: rfc>9110
c7a40b0be87b.sentence: - Redirection that offers a choice among matching resources capable of representing this resource, as in the 300 (Multiple Choices) status code.

a1fdc162a3e9.title: rfc>9110
a1fdc162a3e9.sentence: - Redirection to a different resource, identified by the Location header field, that can represent an indirect response to the request, as in the 303 (See Other) status code.

2269c6af7d0b.title: rfc>9110
2269c6af7d0b.sentence: - Redirection to a previously stored result, as in the 304 (Not Modified) status code.

845bd4b87116.title: rfc>9110
845bd4b87116.sentence: The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs.

4611e3f2251b.title: rfc>9110
4611e3f2251b.sentence: The 302 (Found) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI.

21f901656efe.title: rfc>9110
21f901656efe.sentence: Since the redirection might be altered on occasion, the client ought to continue to use the target URI for future requests.

e5b84befb7c9.title: rfc>9110
e5b84befb7c9.sentence: A 301 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of ).

168bef3053cd.title: rfc>9110
168bef3053cd.sentence: | *Note:* For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the | request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request. If | this behavior is undesired, the 308 (Permanent Redirect) status | code can be used instead.

1f91a4033ccf.title: rfc>9110
1f91a4033ccf.sentence: | *Note:* For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the | request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request. If | this behavior is undesired, the 307 (Temporary Redirect) status | code can be used instead.

084363ed4c16.title: rfc>9110
084363ed4c16.sentence: The 307 (Temporary Redirect) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI and the user agent MUST NOT change the request method if it performs an automatic redirection to that URI.

c66cfb4c419d.title: rfc>9110
c66cfb4c419d.sentence: The 308 (Permanent Redirect) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs.

000ae06c3f5f.title: rfc>9110
000ae06c3f5f.sentence: The 303 (See Other) status code indicates that the server is redirecting the user agent to a different resource, as indicated by a URI in the Location header field, which is intended to provide an indirect response to the original request.

ae70883f5ee5.title: rfc>9110
ae70883f5ee5.sentence: A user agent can perform a retrieval request targeting that URI (a GET or HEAD request if using HTTP), which might also be redirected, and present the eventual result as an answer to the original request.

8dfe513bf72f.title: rfc>9110
8dfe513bf72f.sentence: It is primarily used to allow the output of a POST action to redirect the user agent to a different resource, since doing so provides the information corresponding to the POST response as a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked, and cached.

ba84fad7aef7.title: rfc>9110
ba84fad7aef7.sentence: The 304 (Not Modified) status code indicates that a conditional GET or HEAD request has been received and would have resulted in a 200 (OK) response if it were not for the fact that the condition evaluated to false.

66ab3bfacd9a.title: rfc>9110
66ab3bfacd9a.sentence: In other words, there is no need for the server to transfer a representation of the target resource because the request indicates that the client, which made the request conditional, already has a valid representation; the server is therefore redirecting the client to make use of that stored representation as if it were the content of a 200 (OK) response.

6dd1bf453ff9.title: rfc>9110
6dd1bf453ff9.sentence: A 304 response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers.

8623ff70750b.title: rfc>9110
8623ff70750b.sentence: If a Location header field (Section 10.2.2) is provided, the user agent MAY automatically redirect its request to the URI referenced by the Location field value, even if the specific status code is not understood.

9c73ff86124f.title: rfc>9110
9c73ff86124f.sentence: Automatic redirection needs to be done with care for methods not known to be safe, as defined in Section 9.2.1, since the user might not wish to redirect an unsafe request.

9cd3e4749292.title: rfc>9110
9cd3e4749292.sentence: When automatically following a redirected request, the user agent SHOULD resend the original request message with the following modifications:

317fb3223cba.title: rfc>9110
317fb3223cba.sentence: - Replace the target URI with the URI referenced by the redirection response's Location header field value after resolving it relative to the original request's target URI.

3a07cc90cc2d.title: rfc>9110
3a07cc90cc2d.sentence: - Remove header fields that were automatically generated by the implementation, replacing them with updated values as appropriate to the new request.

6c5f9094a0ca.title: rfc>9110
6c5f9094a0ca.sentence: - Consider removing header fields that were not automatically generated by the implementation (i.e., those present in the request because they were added by the calling context) where there are security implications; this includes but is not limited to Authorization and Cookie.

b5ce4bd570fc.title: rfc>9110
b5ce4bd570fc.sentence: A client SHOULD detect and intervene in cyclical redirections (i.e., "infinite" redirection loops).

acf29a7c9322.title: rfc>9110
acf29a7c9322.sentence: | *Note:* An earlier version of this specification recommended a | maximum of five redirections (, Section 10.3). | Content developers need to be aware that some clients might | implement such a fixed limitation.

df56fc61b63b.title: rfc>9110
df56fc61b63b.sentence: The 5xx (Server Error) class of status code indicates that the server is aware that it has erred or is incapable of performing the requested method.

2f961a337223.title: rfc>9110
2f961a337223.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.1. 500 Internal Server Error
2f961a337223.sentence: The 500 (Internal Server Error) status code indicates that the server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request.

78ed4068bc45.title: rfc>9110
78ed4068bc45.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.2. 501 Not Implemented
78ed4068bc45.sentence: The 501 (Not Implemented) status code indicates that the server does not support the functionality required to fulfill the request.

6939180fc14c.title: rfc>9110
6939180fc14c.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.2. 501 Not Implemented
6939180fc14c.sentence: This is the appropriate response when the server does not recognize the request method and is not capable of supporting it for any resource.

b9c53c390521.title: rfc>9110
b9c53c390521.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.3. 502 Bad Gateway
b9c53c390521.sentence: The 502 (Bad Gateway) status code indicates that the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an inbound server it accessed while attempting to fulfill the request.

f72f612acf36.title: rfc>9110
f72f612acf36.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.5. 504 Gateway Timeout
f72f612acf36.sentence: The 504 (Gateway Timeout) status code indicates that the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, did not receive a timely response from an upstream server it needed to access in order to complete the request.

caf5c29392e2.title: rfc>9110
caf5c29392e2.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.4. 503 Service Unavailable
caf5c29392e2.sentence: The 503 (Service Unavailable) status code indicates that the server is currently unable to handle the request due to a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance, which will likely be alleviated after some delay.

80259a252c40.title: rfc>9110
80259a252c40.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.4. 503 Service Unavailable
80259a252c40.sentence: The server MAY send a Retry-After header field (Section 10.2.3) to suggest an appropriate amount of time for the client to wait before retrying the request.

788b3a7092d1.title: rfc>9110
788b3a7092d1.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.4. 503 Service Unavailable
788b3a7092d1.sentence: | *Note:* The existence of the 503 status code does not imply | that a server has to use it when becoming overloaded. Some | servers might simply refuse the connection.

386583573aba.title: rfc>9110
386583573aba.section: 10. Message Context > 10.2. Response Context Fields > 10.2.3. Retry-After
386583573aba.sentence: Servers send the "Retry-After" header field to indicate how long the user agent ought to wait before making a follow-up request.

7b8b32da7091.title: rfc>9110
7b8b32da7091.section: 10. Message Context > 10.2. Response Context Fields > 10.2.3. Retry-After
7b8b32da7091.sentence: When sent with a 503 (Service Unavailable) response, Retry-After indicates how long the service is expected to be unavailable to the client.

cb3d4c3b1afe.title: rfc>9110
cb3d4c3b1afe.section: 10. Message Context > 10.2. Response Context Fields > 10.2.3. Retry-After
cb3d4c3b1afe.sentence: The Retry-After field value can be either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds to delay after receiving the response.

c4095b8b0104.title: rfc>9110
c4095b8b0104.section: 15. Status Codes > 15.6. Server Error 5xx > 15.6.6. 505 HTTP Version Not Supported
c4095b8b0104.sentence: The 505 (HTTP Version Not Supported) status code indicates that the server does not support, or refuses to support, the major version of HTTP that was used in the request message.

a89d98b05f6f.title: rfc>6585
a89d98b05f6f.sentence: This document specifies additional HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) status codes for a variety of common situations.

97dfa9d26f87.title: rfc>6585
97dfa9d26f87.sentence: This document specifies additional HTTP status codes for a variety of common situations, to improve interoperability and avoid confusion when other, less precise status codes are used.

3ffd42af7518.title: rfc>6585
3ffd42af7518.sentence: Note that these status codes are optional; servers cannot be required to support them.

d6c7c7296a2a.title: rfc>6585
d6c7c7296a2a.sentence: However, because clients will treat unknown status codes as a generic error of the same class (e.g., 499 is treated as 400 if it is not recognized), they can be safely deployed by existing servers (see Section 6.1.1 for more information).

343570444ffe.title: rfc>6585
343570444ffe.sentence: Responses with the 428 status code MUST NOT be stored by a cache.

23c227bc7868.title: rfc>6585
23c227bc7868.sentence: Responses with the 429 status code MUST NOT be stored by a cache.

7a12bf90d1c8.title: rfc>6585
7a12bf90d1c8.sentence: The 428 status code indicates that the origin server requires the request to be conditional.

60548f52ea77.title: rfc>6585
60548f52ea77.sentence: Its typical use is to avoid the "lost update" problem, where a client GETs a resource's state, modifies it, and PUTs it back to the server, when meanwhile a third party has modified the state on the server, leading to a conflict.

1cb380edc94a.title: rfc>6585
1cb380edc94a.sentence: By requiring requests to be conditional, the server can assure that clients are working with the correct copies.

a39cb0beff6a.title: rfc>6585
a39cb0beff6a.sentence: The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ("rate limiting").

0b7191725866.title: rfc>6585
0b7191725866.sentence: The response representations SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.

8c533bcfc784.title: rfc>6585
8c533bcfc784.sentence: Note that this specification does not define how the origin server identifies the user, nor how it counts requests.

520e4608b12a.title: rfc>6585
520e4608b12a.sentence: For example, an origin server that is limiting request rates can do so based upon counts of requests on a per-resource basis, across the entire server, or even among a set of servers.

c29fec28ac98.title: rfc>6585
c29fec28ac98.sentence: Likewise, it might identify the user by its authentication credentials, or a stateful cookie.

26492bac2352.title: rfc>6585
26492bac2352.sentence: The 431 status code indicates that the server is unwilling to process the request because its header fields are too large.

bc0bf5c0413a.title: rfc>6585
bc0bf5c0413a.sentence: The request MAY be resubmitted after reducing the size of the request header fields.

f2e5db958c3e.title: rfc>6585
f2e5db958c3e.sentence: It can be used both when the set of request header fields in total is too large, and when a single header field is at fault.

ce945183d217.title: rfc>6585
ce945183d217.sentence: The 511 status code indicates that the client needs to authenticate to gain network access.

a9354a4f292e.title: rfc>6585
a9354a4f292e.sentence: The 511 status SHOULD NOT be generated by origin servers; it is intended for use by intercepting proxies that are interposed as a means of controlling access to the network.

964d47091909.title: rfc>9111
964d47091909.sentence: An HTTP "cache" is a local store of response messages and the subsystem that controls storage, retrieval, and deletion of messages in it.

eab3dfab77a4.title: rfc>9111
eab3dfab77a4.sentence: The goal of HTTP caching is significantly improving performance by reusing a prior response message to satisfy a current request.

3e6dc7a3802d.title: rfc>9111
3e6dc7a3802d.sentence: A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce the response time and network bandwidth consumption on future equivalent requests.

bff97e816e32.title: rfc>9110
bff97e816e32.sentence: The effect of a cache is that the request/response chain is shortened if one of the participants along the chain has a cached response applicable to that request.

25cc8cf01938.title: rfc>9111
25cc8cf01938.sentence: A fresh response can therefore reduce both latency and network overhead each time the cache reuses it.

b390d8ba17ce.title: rfc>9111
b390d8ba17ce.sentence: Although caching is an entirely OPTIONAL feature of HTTP, it can be assumed that reusing a cached response is desirable and that such reuse is the default behavior when no requirement or local configuration prevents it.

e3cddbafe760.title: rfc>9111
e3cddbafe760.sentence: Therefore, HTTP cache requirements are focused on preventing a cache from either storing a non-reusable response or reusing a stored response inappropriately, rather than mandating that caches always store and reuse particular responses.

55ce21c6b908.title: rfc>9111
55ce21c6b908.sentence: Proper cache operation preserves the semantics of HTTP transfers while reducing the transmission of information already held in the cache.

14e57f26f75e.title: rfc>9111
14e57f26f75e.sentence: The "cache key" is the information a cache uses to choose a response and is composed from, at a minimum, the request method and target URI used to retrieve the stored response; the method determines under which circumstances that response can be used to satisfy a subsequent request.

319fe1edf86e.title: rfc>9111
319fe1edf86e.sentence: However, many HTTP caches in common use today only cache GET responses and therefore only use the URI as the cache key.

c7f6e3e528e5.title: rfc>9111
c7f6e3e528e5.sentence: Caches differentiate these responses by incorporating some of the original request's header fields into the cache key as well, using information in the Vary response header field, as per Section 4.1.

5394deccc333.title: rfc>9111
5394deccc333.sentence: Most commonly, caches store the successful result of a retrieval request: i.e., a 200 (OK) response to a GET request, which contains a representation of the target resource (Section 9.3.1 of ).

5a113004585f.title: rfc>9111
5a113004585f.sentence: However, it is also possible to store redirects, negative results (e.g., 404 (Not Found)), incomplete results (e.g., 206 (Partial Content)), and responses to methods other than GET if the method's definition allows such caching and defines something suitable for use as a cache key.

d5fe9cbf9663.title: rfc>9110
d5fe9cbf9663.sentence: These include national hierarchies of proxy caches to save bandwidth and reduce latency, content delivery networks that use gateway caching to optimize regional and global distribution of popular sites, collaborative systems that broadcast or multicast cache entries, archives of pre-fetched cache entries for use in off-line or high-latency environments, and so on.

aaf862327a1d.title: rfc>9111
aaf862327a1d.sentence: A cache can use a response that is stored or storable to satisfy multiple requests, provided that it is allowed to reuse that response for the requests in question.

cee68260ee02.title: rfc>9111
cee68260ee02.sentence: This enables a cache to "collapse requests" -- or combine multiple incoming requests into a single forward request upon a cache miss -- thereby reducing load on the origin server and network.

51c363f69212.title: rfc>9111
51c363f69212.sentence: A cache MUST write through requests with methods that are unsafe (Section 9.2.1 of ) to the origin server; i.e., a cache is not allowed to generate a reply to such a request before having forwarded the request and having received a corresponding response.

c7041b7f8aeb.title: rfc>9111
c7041b7f8aeb.sentence: Also, note that unsafe requests might invalidate already-stored responses; see Section 4.4.

8ec1f0bfd38c.title: rfc>9111
8ec1f0bfd38c.sentence: A cache is "disconnected" when it cannot contact the origin server or otherwise find a forward path for a request.

bc93dedb6570.title: rfc>9111
bc93dedb6570.sentence: A disconnected cache can serve stale responses in some circumstances (Section 4.2.4).

c52cbf6dcad2.title: rfc>9111
c52cbf6dcad2.sentence: A "fresh" response is one whose age has not yet exceeded its freshness lifetime.

3b2518ea3058.title: rfc>9111
3b2518ea3058.sentence: When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server, thereby improving efficiency.

230c9a5bc311.title: rfc>9111
230c9a5bc311.sentence: A response's "freshness lifetime" is the length of time between its generation by the origin server and its expiration time.

238062ce0673.title: rfc>9111
238062ce0673.sentence: A response's "age" is the time that has passed since it was generated by, or successfully validated with, the origin server.

d3c6e651dac0.title: rfc>9111
d3c6e651dac0.sentence: Conversely, a "stale" response is one where it has.

65368d3075ff.title: rfc>9111
65368d3075ff.sentence: The primary mechanism for determining freshness is for an origin server to provide an explicit expiration time in the future, using either the Expires header field (Section 5.3) or the max-age response directive (Section 5.2.2.1).

05c34b5141c8.title: rfc>9111
05c34b5141c8.sentence: If an origin server wishes to force a cache to validate every request, it can assign an explicit expiration time in the past to indicate that the response is already stale.

be8fb02da1f3.title: rfc>9111
be8fb02da1f3.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.1. Calculating Freshness Lifetime
be8fb02da1f3.sentence: A cache can calculate the freshness lifetime (denoted as freshness_lifetime) of a response by evaluating the following rules and using the first match:

5b040124247f.title: rfc>9111
5b040124247f.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.1. Calculating Freshness Lifetime
5b040124247f.sentence: - If the cache is shared and the s-maxage response directive (Section 5.2.2.10) is present, use its value, or

1ca12510b1e1.title: rfc>9111
1ca12510b1e1.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.1. Calculating Freshness Lifetime
1ca12510b1e1.sentence: - If the max-age response directive (Section 5.2.2.1) is present, use its value, or

6e6e2dfcec42.title: rfc>9111
6e6e2dfcec42.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.1. Calculating Freshness Lifetime
6e6e2dfcec42.sentence: - If the Expires response header field (Section 5.3) is present, use its value minus the value of the Date response header field (using the time the message was received if it is not present, as per Section 6.6.1 of ), or

2cdbc5d5c898.title: rfc>9111
2cdbc5d5c898.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.1. Calculating Freshness Lifetime
2cdbc5d5c898.sentence: - Otherwise, no explicit expiration time is present in the response.

744591850132.title: rfc>9111
744591850132.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.2. Calculating Heuristic Freshness
744591850132.sentence: Since origin servers do not always provide explicit expiration times, a cache MAY assign a heuristic expiration time when an explicit time is not specified, employing algorithms that use other field values (such as the Last-Modified time) to estimate a plausible expiration time.

9c9d90effa12.title: rfc>9111
9c9d90effa12.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.2. Calculating Heuristic Freshness
9c9d90effa12.sentence: A cache MUST NOT use heuristics to determine freshness when an explicit expiration time is present in the stored response.

8664e8802eca.title: rfc>9111
8664e8802eca.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.2. Calculating Heuristic Freshness
8664e8802eca.sentence: Because of the requirements in Section 3, heuristics can only be used on responses without explicit freshness whose status codes are defined as "heuristically cacheable" (e.g., see Section 15.1 of ) and on responses without explicit freshness that have been marked as explicitly cacheable (e.g., with a public response directive).

e9a6bf0d3ac9.title: rfc>9111
e9a6bf0d3ac9.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.2. Calculating Heuristic Freshness
e9a6bf0d3ac9.sentence: If the response has a Last-Modified header field (Section 8.8.2 of ), caches are encouraged to use a heuristic expiration value that is no more than some fraction of the interval since that time.

576e17861262.title: rfc>9111
576e17861262.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.2. Calculating Heuristic Freshness
576e17861262.sentence: A typical setting of this fraction might be 10%.

d9eed3b4a1ab.title: rfc>9111
d9eed3b4a1ab.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.3. Calculating Age
d9eed3b4a1ab.sentence: The Age field value is the cache's estimate of the number of seconds since the origin server generated or validated the response.

ad4875b23536.title: rfc>9111
ad4875b23536.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.3. Calculating Age
ad4875b23536.sentence: The Age value is therefore the sum of the time that the response has been resident in each of the caches along the path from the origin server, plus the time it has been in transit along network paths.

ce90e94c93eb.title: rfc>9111
ce90e94c93eb.sentence: The "Age" response header field conveys the sender's estimate of the time since the response was generated or successfully validated at the origin server.

1966f90ce855.title: rfc>9111
1966f90ce855.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.3. Calculating Age
1966f90ce855.sentence: The current_age of a stored response can then be calculated by adding the time (in seconds) since the stored response was last validated by the origin server to the corrected_initial_age.

e1b5b79d57fe.title: rfc>9111
e1b5b79d57fe.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.3. Calculating Age
e1b5b79d57fe.sentence: resident_time = now - response_time; current_age = corrected_initial_age + resident_time;

bd7b23d8c58b.title: rfc>9111
bd7b23d8c58b.sentence: The "Expires" response header field gives the date/time after which the response is considered stale.

f4401f8bae38.title: rfc>9111
f4401f8bae38.sentence: If a response includes a Cache-Control header field with the max-age directive (Section 5.2.2.1), a recipient MUST ignore the Expires header field.

ca641c6f9249.title: rfc>9111
ca641c6f9249.sentence: Likewise, if a response includes the s-maxage directive (Section 5.2.2.10), a shared cache recipient MUST ignore the Expires header field.

5a3e1e9fee5e.title: rfc>9111
5a3e1e9fee5e.sentence: A cache recipient MUST interpret invalid date formats, especially the value "0", as representing a time in the past (i.e., "already expired").

b5fa1b0f9314.title: rfc>9111
b5fa1b0f9314.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.4. Serving Stale Responses
b5fa1b0f9314.sentence: A cache MUST NOT generate a stale response if it is prohibited by an explicit in-protocol directive (e.g., by a no-cache response directive, a must-revalidate response directive, or an applicable s-maxage or proxy-revalidate response directive; see Section 5.2.2).

0ae07cf19c78.title: rfc>9111
0ae07cf19c78.section: 4. Constructing Responses from Caches > 4.2. Freshness > 4.2.4. Serving Stale Responses
0ae07cf19c78.sentence: A cache MUST NOT generate a stale response unless it is disconnected or doing so is explicitly permitted by the client or origin server (e.g., by the max-stale request directive in Section 5.2.1, extension directives such as those defined in, or configuration in accordance with an out-of-band contract).

c53f83a5c5fc.title: HTTPS
c53f83a5c5fc.section: Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation
c53f83a5c5fc.sentence: A certificate may be revoked before it expires, for example because the secrecy of the private key has been compromised.

e588e803ae93.title: HTTPS
e588e803ae93.section: Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation
e588e803ae93.sentence: Newer versions of popular browsers such as Firefox, Opera, and Internet Explorer on Windows Vista implement the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) to verify that this is not the case.

2819101c5c5f.title: HTTPS
2819101c5c5f.section: Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation
2819101c5c5f.sentence: The browser sends the certificate's serial number to the certificate authority or its delegate via OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) and the authority responds, telling the browser whether the certificate is still valid or not.

78b6e768bef2.title: HTTPS
78b6e768bef2.section: Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation
78b6e768bef2.sentence: The CA may also issue a CRL to tell people that these certificates are revoked.

629800b2078b.title: HTTPS
629800b2078b.section: Technical > Server setup > In case of compromised secret (private) key > Certificate revocation
629800b2078b.sentence: CRLs are no longer required by the CA/Browser forum, [needs update] nevertheless, they are still widely used by the CAs.

55c2ad09f4e8.title: Transport Layer Security
55c2ad09f4e8.sentence: - Adding support for sending multiple OCSP responses

11f3974f1d11.title: Certificate authority
11f3974f1d11.sentence: Revocation is performed by the issuing CA, which produces a cryptographically authenticated statement of revocation.

4b11139c693a.title: Certificate authority
4b11139c693a.sentence: Without revocation, an attacker would be able to exploit such a compromised or misissued certificate until expiry.

a9a2066efa99.title: Certificate authority
a9a2066efa99.sentence: Hence, revocation is an important part of a public key infrastructure.

8b6cd659a1b6.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
8b6cd659a1b6.sentence: - Bob enters a URL into the browser and hits Enter.

88da65ca563d.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
88da65ca563d.sentence: - The browser looks up the IP address for the domain with a domain name system (DNS) lookup.

c3029ca8b55e.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
c3029ca8b55e.sentence: - Now that we have the IP address of the server, the browser establishes a TCP connection with the server.

453abe373048.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
453abe373048.sentence: - The browser sends an HTTP request to the server.

a6b277cb7f19.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
a6b277cb7f19.sentence: - The browser renders the HTML content.

d3cc8ca9add1.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
d3cc8ca9add1.sentence: In this example, the URL is composed of 4 parts:

444552b33778.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
444552b33778.sentence: This tells the browser to send a connection to the server using HTTP.

57a54e40454d.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
57a54e40454d.sentence: This is the domain name of the site.

e47be29827d6.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
e47be29827d6.sentence: It is the path on the server to the requested resource: phone.

1c10a1b406ac.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
1c10a1b406ac.sentence: To make the lookup process fast, data is cached at different layers: browser cache, OS cache, local network cache, and ISP cache.

7481ae7731fa.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
7481ae7731fa.sentence: - If the IP address cannot be found at any of the caches, the browser goes to DNS servers to do a recursive DNS lookup until the IP address is found (this will be covered in another post).

42b584d98407.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
42b584d98407.sentence: The request looks like this: 𝘎𝘌𝘛 /𝘱𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘏𝘛𝘛𝘗/1.1 𝘏𝘰𝘴𝘵: 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦.𝘤𝘰𝘮

c528b04906fe.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
c528b04906fe.sentence: - The server processes the request and sends back the response.

69247790a334.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-your-browser.md
69247790a334.sentence: For a successful response (the status code is 200).

48fa4a34b8d9.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
48fa4a34b8d9.sentence: HTTP 1 started in 1996 followed by HTTP 1.1 the very next year.

f7901aaf4fa0.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
f7901aaf4fa0.sentence: In 2015, HTTP 2 came about and in 2019 we got HTTP 3.

4938181c4145.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
4938181c4145.sentence: With each iteration, the protocol has evolved in new and interesting ways.

a19e556511a1.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
a19e556511a1.sentence: - HTTP 1 (and its sub-versions) introduced features like persistent connections, pipelining, and the concept of headers.

01e3b3a49e17.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
01e3b3a49e17.sentence: The protocol was built on top of TCP and provided a reliable way of communication over the World Wide Web.

22a94f325c2b.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
22a94f325c2b.sentence: - HTTP 2 brought new features such as multiplexing, stream prioritization, server push, and HPACK compression.

f3acf064ecd3.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
f3acf064ecd3.sentence: However, it still used TCP as the underlying protocol.

098001eb6604.title: HTTP
098001eb6604.sentence: - a compressed binary representation of metadata (HTTP headers) instead of a textual one, so that headers require much less space;

9d8992d604e0.title: HTTP
9d8992d604e0.sentence: - a single TCP/IP (usually encrypted) connection per accessed server domain instead of 2 to 8 TCP/IP connections;

8c96535363a5.title: HTTP
8c96535363a5.sentence: - one or more bidirectional streams per TCP/IP connection in which HTTP requests and responses are broken down and transmitted in small packets to almost solve the problem of the HOLB (head-of-line blocking);

062566604bf7.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
062566604bf7.sentence: - HTTP 3 uses Google’s QUIC, which is built on top of UDP.

c0c7c9a583e0.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/http1-http2-http3.md
c0c7c9a583e0.sentence: In other words, HTTP 3 has moved away from TCP.

83d90a423de8.title: HTTP
83d90a423de8.sentence: HTTP/3 uses QUIC + UDP transport protocols instead of TCP.

f483cae8489e.title: HTTP
f483cae8489e.sentence: Like HTTP/2, it does not obsolete previous major versions of the protocol.

6f8d46276da6.title: rfc>9113
6f8d46276da6.sentence: This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2).

b17356b7d805.title: rfc>9113
b17356b7d805.sentence: HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network resources and a reduced latency by introducing field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection.

eabf48123c69.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
eabf48123c69.sentence: - Binary Framing Layer HTTP2 encodes the messages into binary format.

3e261eb3ae07.title: rfc>9113
3e261eb3ae07.sentence: HTTP/2 supports all of the core features of HTTP but aims to be more efficient than HTTP/1.1.

5cdfe0064788.title: rfc>9113
5cdfe0064788.sentence: HTTP/1.0 allowed only one request to be outstanding at a time on a given TCP connection.

ff914ed615fa.title: rfc>9113
ff914ed615fa.sentence: HTTP/1.1 [HTTP/1.1] added request pipelining, but this only partially addressed request concurrency and still suffers from application-layer head-of-line blocking.

375ada4c3080.title: rfc>9113
375ada4c3080.sentence: Therefore, HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 clients use multiple connections to a server to make concurrent requests.

9663e9fb30b9.title: rfc>9113
9663e9fb30b9.sentence: The resulting protocol is more friendly to the network because fewer TCP connections can be used in comparison to HTTP/1.x.

3f64f232a2bb.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
3f64f232a2bb.sentence: This allows the messages into smaller units called frames, which are then sent over the TCP connection, resulting in more efficient processing.

b293c67b8e35.title: rfc>9113
b293c67b8e35.sentence: Finally, HTTP/2 also enables more efficient processing of messages through use of binary message framing.

cf1de89b0412.title: rfc>9113
cf1de89b0412.sentence: Multiplexing of requests is achieved by having each HTTP request/ response exchange associated with its own stream (Section 5).

4f133fda17f5.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
4f133fda17f5.sentence: Clients and servers can interleave frames during transmissions and reassemble them on the other side.

557a80fba5f9.title: rfc>9113
557a80fba5f9.sentence: Furthermore, HTTP fields are often repetitive and verbose, causing unnecessary network traffic as well as causing the initial TCP congestion window to quickly fill.

3cea038fdbb9.title: rfc>9113
3cea038fdbb9.sentence: Because HTTP fields used in a connection can contain large amounts of redundant data, frames that contain them are compressed (Section 4.3).

b1a4cde48bb7.title: rfc>9113
b1a4cde48bb7.sentence: This has especially advantageous impact upon request sizes in the common case, allowing many requests to be compressed into one packet.

e23cdbe7d4bc.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
e23cdbe7d4bc.sentence: - HPACK Header Compression HTTP2 uses a special compression algorithm called HPACK to make the headers smaller for multiple requests, thereby saving bandwidth.

6c11fe662efe.title: rfc>9113
6c11fe662efe.sentence: In a multiplexed protocol like HTTP/2, prioritizing allocation of bandwidth and computation resources to streams can be critical to attaining good performance.

14e1969e3f44.title: rfc>9113
14e1969e3f44.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.3. Prioritization > 5.3.1. Background on Priority in RFC 7540
14e1969e3f44.sentence: However, this system proved to be complex, and it was not uniformly implemented.

7efe8f971c93.title: rfc>9113
7efe8f971c93.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.3. Prioritization > 5.3.1. Background on Priority in RFC 7540
7efe8f971c93.sentence: In short, the prioritization signaling in RFC 7540 was not successful.

eaced469ee9f.title: rfc>9113
eaced469ee9f.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.3. Prioritization > 5.3.2. Priority Signaling in This Document
eaced469ee9f.sentence: This update to HTTP/2 deprecates the priority signaling defined in RFC 7540.

ae7de402815e.title: rfc>9113
ae7de402815e.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.3. Prioritization > 5.3.2. Priority Signaling in This Document
ae7de402815e.sentence: Where signaling priority information is important, endpoints are encouraged to use an alternative scheme, such as the scheme described in [HTTP-PRIORITY].

f129db7b792f.title: rfc>9113
f129db7b792f.sentence: Finally, HTTP/2 adds a new, optional interaction mode whereby a server can push responses to a client (Section 8.4).

77db77602570.title: rfc>9113
77db77602570.sentence: This is intended to allow a server to speculatively send data to a client that the server anticipates the client will need, trading off some network usage against a potential latency gain.

7c064a067c5f.title: rfc>9113
7c064a067c5f.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
7c064a067c5f.sentence: In practice, server push is difficult to use effectively, because it requires the server to correctly anticipate the additional requests the client will make, taking into account factors such as caching, content negotiation, and user behavior.

7be787450135.title: HTTP
7be787450135.sentence: It is also supported by major web servers over Transport Layer Security (TLS) using an Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) extension where TLS 1.2 or newer is required.

d6b69a1611f9.title: rfc>9113
d6b69a1611f9.sentence: This identifier is used in the TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) extension field and in any place where HTTP/2 over TLS is identified.

590055e5e4ba.title: rfc>9113
590055e5e4ba.section: 9. HTTP/2 Connections > 9.2. Use of TLS Features
590055e5e4ba.sentence: Implementations of HTTP/2 MUST use TLS version 1.2 or higher for HTTP/2 over TLS.

1fbf7c540e77.title: rfc>9113
1fbf7c540e77.sentence: Note, however, that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol.

c06dc2c94add.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
c06dc2c94add.sentence: Of course, despite these features, HTTP2 can also be slow depending on the exact technical scenario.

df5e06f9db91.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/what-makes-http2-faster-than-http1.md
df5e06f9db91.sentence: Therefore, developers need to test and optimize things to maximize the benefits of HTTP2.

3490d538f0c8.title: HTTP/3
3490d538f0c8.sentence: HTTP/3 is the third major version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol used to exchange information on the World Wide Web, complementing the widely deployed HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

00b827a613bb.title: HTTP/3
00b827a613bb.sentence: Unlike previous versions which relied on the well-established TCP (published in 1974), HTTP/3 uses QUIC (officially introduced in 2021), a multiplexed transport protocol built on UDP.

c6ac570c8352.title: HTTP/3
c6ac570c8352.sentence: International standard | RFC 9114 (HTTP/3 also uses the completed QUIC protocol described in RFC 9000 and related RFCs such as RFC 9001)

d1ed2b756e95.title: HTTP/3
d1ed2b756e95.sentence: HTTP/3 uses QUIC, a transport layer network protocol which uses user space congestion control over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP).

a3c87578c3c1.title: HTTP
a3c87578c3c1.sentence: HTTP/3 uses a different transport layer called QUIC, which provides reliability on top of the unreliable User Datagram Protocol (UDP).

27e72b4cff8a.title: HTTP
27e72b4cff8a.sentence: HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead of TCP for the underlying transport protocol.

c40e8f452899.title: HTTP/3
c40e8f452899.sentence: HTTP/3 uses similar semantics compared to earlier revisions of the protocol, including the same request methods, status codes, and message fields, but encodes them and maintains session state differently.

d7c489036ed4.title: HTTP/3
d7c489036ed4.sentence: HTTP semantics are consistent across versions: the same request methods, status codes, and message fields are typically applicable to all versions.

6cf0beff3bf0.title: HTTP/3
6cf0beff3bf0.sentence: The differences are in the mapping of these semantics to underlying transports.

5afcdd930ed2.title: HTTP/3
5afcdd930ed2.sentence: The switch to QUIC aims to fix a major problem of HTTP/2 called "head-of-line blocking": because the parallel nature of HTTP/2's multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms, a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall regardless of whether that transaction was impacted by the lost packet.

58ed15b65995.title: HTTP/3
58ed15b65995.sentence: Because QUIC provides native multiplexing, lost packets only impact the streams where data has been lost.

34c5cabb334b.title: HTTP
34c5cabb334b.sentence: This slightly improves the average speed of communications and avoids the occasional problem of TCP connection congestion that can temporarily block or slow down the data flow of all its streams (another form of "head of line blocking").

ac08e8ecb706.title: HTTP/3
ac08e8ecb706.sentence: HTTP/3 uses QPACK to compress HTTP header and trailer fields, replacing the HPACK scheme used by HTTP/2.

188874c26a6d.title: HTTP/3
188874c26a6d.sentence: QPACK accommodates independently delivered QUIC streams by using separate unidirectional streams for compression-table updates, reducing compression-related head-of-line blocking.

699c3f1ab060.title: HTTP/3
699c3f1ab060.sentence: The HTTPS DNS resource record as defined in RFC 9460 allows for connecting without first receiving the Alt-Svc header via previous HTTP versions, therefore removing the 1 RTT of handshaking of TCP.

67a91857b508.title: HTTP/3
67a91857b508.sentence: However, partially due to the protocol's adoption of QUIC, HTTP/3 has lower latency and loads more quickly in real-world usage when compared with previous versions: in some cases over four times faster than with HTTP/1.1 (which, for many websites, is the only HTTP version deployed).

1de7bc5c8241.title: HTTP/3
1de7bc5c8241.sentence: As of July 2026, HTTP/3 is supported by more than 95% of major web browsers in use and 40% of the top 10 million websites.

f365fd03c3c5.title: rfc>9113
f365fd03c3c5.sentence: A "stream" is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames exchanged between the client and server within an HTTP/2 connection.

be76d98ebd24.title: rfc>9113
be76d98ebd24.sentence: - A single HTTP/2 connection can contain multiple concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from multiple streams.

6f84fccebd85.title: rfc>9113
6f84fccebd85.sentence: Streams are largely independent of each other, so a blocked or stalled request or response does not prevent progress on other streams.

50e5f9c5ba98.title: rfc>9113
50e5f9c5ba98.sentence: The basic protocol unit in HTTP/2 is a frame (Section 4.1).

a07649ce9968.title: rfc>9113
a07649ce9968.sentence: All frames begin with a fixed 9-octet header followed by a variable-length frame payload.

d6723f216862.title: rfc>9113
d6723f216862.sentence: Values greater than 2^14 (16,384) MUST NOT be sent unless the receiver has set a larger value for SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE.

e9186e464b42.title: rfc>9113
e9186e464b42.sentence: For example, HEADERS and DATA frames form the basis of HTTP requests and responses (Section 8.1); other frame types like SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, and PUSH_PROMISE are used in support of other HTTP/2 features.

d74ad7700167.title: rfc>9113
d74ad7700167.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
d74ad7700167.sentence: Streams are identified by an unsigned 31-bit integer.

84a930c5b3ed.title: rfc>9113
84a930c5b3ed.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
84a930c5b3ed.sentence: Streams initiated by a client MUST use odd-numbered stream identifiers; those initiated by the server MUST use even-numbered stream identifiers.

716c4a34ef93.title: rfc>9113
716c4a34ef93.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
716c4a34ef93.sentence: The identifier of a newly established stream MUST be numerically greater than all streams that the initiating endpoint has opened or reserved.

a65dbf77b598.title: rfc>9113
a65dbf77b598.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers

b76468c1191f.title: rfc>9113
b76468c1191f.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
b76468c1191f.sentence: Long-lived connections can result in an endpoint exhausting the available range of stream identifiers.

5a3b7ffde100.title: rfc>9113
5a3b7ffde100.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
5a3b7ffde100.sentence: A client that is unable to establish a new stream identifier can establish a new connection for new streams.

14094cb410b0.title: rfc>9113
14094cb410b0.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.1. Stream Identifiers
14094cb410b0.sentence: A server that is unable to establish a new stream identifier can send a GOAWAY frame so that the client is forced to open a new connection for new streams.

6eae5cb95c3d.title: rfc>9113
6eae5cb95c3d.sentence: idle: All streams start in the "idle" state.

390f3d7d90ae.title: rfc>9113
390f3d7d90ae.sentence: open: A stream in the "open" state may be used by both peers to send frames of any type.

341310fd937d.title: rfc>9113
341310fd937d.sentence: From this state, either endpoint can send a frame with an END_STREAM flag set, which causes the stream to transition into one of the "half-closed" states.

f61a062210ee.title: rfc>9113
f61a062210ee.sentence: A stream enters the "closed" state after an endpoint both sends and receives a frame with an END_STREAM flag set.

fc3c0fe6b5d4.title: rfc>9113
fc3c0fe6b5d4.sentence: A stream also enters the "closed" state after an endpoint either sends or receives a RST_STREAM frame.

46aba5e7eae2.title: rfc>9113
46aba5e7eae2.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.1. Stream States > 5.1.2. Stream Concurrency
46aba5e7eae2.sentence: A peer can limit the number of concurrently active streams using the SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS parameter (see Section 6.5.2) within a SETTINGS frame.

5d8d7ee73a5c.title: rfc>9113
5d8d7ee73a5c.sentence: This limit is directional: it applies to the number of streams that the sender permits the receiver to create.

5ced165a39a0.title: rfc>9113
5ced165a39a0.sentence: Initially, there is no limit to this value.

59fcd1c0ff16.title: rfc>9113
59fcd1c0ff16.sentence: It is recommended that this value be no smaller than 100, so as to not unnecessarily limit parallelism.

dc7cd497178c.title: rfc>9113
dc7cd497178c.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.4. Error Handling > 5.4.1. Connection Error Handling
dc7cd497178c.sentence: A connection error is any error that prevents further processing of the frame layer or corrupts any connection state.

590ec815e102.title: rfc>9113
590ec815e102.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.4. Error Handling > 5.4.1. Connection Error Handling
590ec815e102.sentence: An endpoint that encounters a connection error SHOULD first send a GOAWAY frame (Section 6.8) with the stream identifier of the last stream that it successfully received from its peer.

0cc11951ba74.title: rfc>9113
0cc11951ba74.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.4. Error Handling > 5.4.1. Connection Error Handling
0cc11951ba74.sentence: After sending the GOAWAY frame for an error condition, the endpoint MUST close the TCP connection.

c6e8c8b1c403.title: rfc>9113
c6e8c8b1c403.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.4. Error Handling > 5.4.2. Stream Error Handling
c6e8c8b1c403.sentence: A stream error is an error related to a specific stream that does not affect processing of other streams.

254401c56863.title: rfc>9113
254401c56863.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.4. Error Handling > 5.4.2. Stream Error Handling
254401c56863.sentence: An endpoint that detects a stream error sends a RST_STREAM frame (Section 6.4) that contains the stream identifier of the stream where the error occurred.

f4f8e2473482.title: HTTP pipelining
f4f8e2473482.sentence: HTTP pipelining is a feature of HTTP/1.1 that allows multiple HTTP requests to be sent over a single TCP connection without waiting for the corresponding responses.

96dc6163fa42.title: HTTP pipelining
96dc6163fa42.sentence: The pipelining of requests results in a dramatic improvement in the loading times of HTML pages, especially over high latency connections such as satellite Internet connections.

643ae6df5b84.title: HTTP pipelining
643ae6df5b84.sentence: The speedup is less apparent on broadband connections, as the limitation of HTTP 1.1 still applies: the server must send its responses in the same order that the requests were received—so the entire connection remains first-in-first-out and HOL blocking can occur.

74f3d5d035a7.title: HTTP pipelining
74f3d5d035a7.sentence: Read requests like GET and HEAD can always be pipelined.

9b8c0b64a18e.title: HTTP pipelining
9b8c0b64a18e.sentence: Non-idempotent requests such as POST should not be pipelined.

24f1ace7ae92.title: HTTP pipelining
24f1ace7ae92.sentence: A sequence of other idempotent requests like PUT and DELETE can be pipelined or not depending on whether requests in the sequence depend on the effect of others.

ff7754416849.title: HTTP pipelining
ff7754416849.sentence: Despite this requirement, many legacy HTTP/1.1 servers do not support pipelining correctly, forcing most HTTP clients not to use HTTP pipelining.

af86da4c77ce.title: HTTP pipelining
af86da4c77ce.sentence: Most pipelining problems happen in HTTP intermediate nodes (hop-by-hop), i.e. in proxy servers, especially in transparent proxy servers (if one of them along the HTTP chain does not handle pipelined requests properly then nothing works as it should).

dc427984ed0d.title: HTTP pipelining
dc427984ed0d.section: Implementation status > Implementation in web proxy servers
dc427984ed0d.sentence: Some HTTP proxies, including transparent HTTP proxies, may manage pipelined requests very badly (e.g. by mixing up the order of pipelined responses).

d71998ba870d.title: HTTP pipelining
d71998ba870d.section: Implementation status > Implementation in web browsers
d71998ba870d.sentence: - Google Chrome previously supported pipelining, but it has been disabled due to bugs and problems with poorly behaving servers.

03cde30a8694.title: HTTP pipelining
03cde30a8694.section: Implementation status > Implementation in web browsers
03cde30a8694.sentence: - Mozilla browsers (such as Mozilla Firefox, SeaMonkey and Camino) used to support pipelining; however, it was removed in Firefox 54.

8360a4d74e1c.title: HTTP pipelining
8360a4d74e1c.sentence: The technique was superseded by multiplexing via HTTP/2, which is supported by most modern browsers.

80885c60dbbe.title: HTTP pipelining
80885c60dbbe.sentence: In HTTP/3, multiplexing is accomplished via QUIC which replaces TCP.

cf8e13c34877.title: HTTP pipelining
cf8e13c34877.sentence: This further reduces loading time, as there is no head-of-line blocking even if some packets are lost.

881b4ee04fbd.title: Public key certificate
881b4ee04fbd.section: Website security > Validation levels > Domain validation
881b4ee04fbd.sentence: A certificate provider will issue a domain-validated (DV) certificate to a purchaser if the purchaser can demonstrate one vetting criterion: the right to administratively manage the affected DNS domain(s).

9229883baf44.title: Public key certificate
9229883baf44.section: Website security > Validation levels > Organization validation
9229883baf44.sentence: A certificate provider will issue an organization validation (OV) class certificate to a purchaser if the purchaser can meet two criteria: the right to administratively manage the domain name in question, and perhaps, the organization's actual existence as a legal entity.

cc6693b61de5.title: Public key certificate
cc6693b61de5.section: Website security > Validation levels > Extended validation
cc6693b61de5.sentence: To acquire an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, the purchaser must persuade the certificate provider of its legal identity, including manual verification checks by a human.

ef23286331c0.title: Certificate authority
ef23286331c0.sentence: The commercial CAs that issue the bulk of certificates for HTTPS servers typically use a technique called "domain validation" to authenticate the recipient of the certificate.

23bd665b78e6.title: Certificate authority
23bd665b78e6.sentence: The techniques used for domain validation vary between CAs, but in general domain validation techniques are meant to prove that the certificate applicant controls a given domain name, not any information about the applicant's identity.

3a8c5f0af5c0.title: Public key certificate
3a8c5f0af5c0.section: Website security > Validation levels > Organization validation
3a8c5f0af5c0.sentence: A certificate provider publishes its OV vetting criteria through its certificate policy.

d3046b13f264.title: Public key certificate
d3046b13f264.section: Website security > Validation levels > Extended validation
d3046b13f264.sentence: As with OV certificates, a certificate provider publishes its EV vetting criteria through its certificate policy.

c6a890793345.title: Certificate authority
c6a890793345.sentence: Domain validation suffers from certain structural security limitations.

25c6ed9abe1f.title: Certificate authority
25c6ed9abe1f.sentence: In particular, it is always vulnerable to attacks that allow an adversary to observe the domain validation probes that CAs send.

347eff3a3cf4.title: Certificate authority
347eff3a3cf4.sentence: These can include attacks against the DNS, TCP, or BGP protocols (which lack the cryptographic protections of TLS/SSL), or the compromise of routers.

843f7e8981d0.title: Certificate authority
843f7e8981d0.sentence: One of the most common domain validation techniques involves sending an email containing an authentication token or link to an email address that is likely to be administratively responsible for the domain.

1cd6ac3a7d01.title: Certificate authority
1cd6ac3a7d01.sentence: This could be the technical contact email address listed in the domain's WHOIS entry, or an administrative email like admin@, administrator@, webmaster@, hostmaster@ or postmaster@ the domain.

d4de5456b4b5.title: Certificate authority
d4de5456b4b5.sentence: One limitation of EV as a solution to the weaknesses of domain validation is that attackers could still obtain a domain validated certificate for the victim domain, and deploy it during an attack; if that occurred, the difference observable to the victim user would be the absence of a green bar with the company name.

7af723692314.title: Public key certificate
7af723692314.section: Website security > Validation levels > Extended validation
7af723692314.sentence: Until 2019, major browsers such as Chrome and Firefox generally offered users a visual indication of the legal identity when a site presented an EV certificate.

4cc48f31d67c.title: List of HTTP status codes
4cc48f31d67c.sentence: The following codes are used by various web servers but not specified by an IETF standard.

bb3d1d947862.title: List of HTTP status codes
bb3d1d947862.sentence: Other, non-standard values are used by various servers.

8ee06fc530b5.title: List of HTTP status codes
8ee06fc530b5.sentence: Standardized codes are defined by IETF as documented in Request for Comments (RFC) publications and maintained by the IANA.

7ec3f0ea2472.title: List of HTTP status codes
7ec3f0ea2472.sentence: The descriptive text after the numeric code – the reason phrase – is shown here with typical value, but in practice, can be different or omitted.

7a698ff89381.title: List of HTTP status codes
7a698ff89381.sentence: The nginx web server software expands the 4xx error space to signal issues with the client's request.

8c33cfbe5ce1.title: List of HTTP status codes
8c33cfbe5ce1.sentence: Used internally to instruct the server to return no information to the client and close the connection immediately.

a801bf86e7cf.title: List of HTTP status codes
a801bf86e7cf.sentence: An expansion of the 400 Bad Request response code, used when the client has provided an invalid client certificate.

4ce0ec0331aa.title: List of HTTP status codes
4ce0ec0331aa.sentence: An expansion of the 400 Bad Request response code, used when a client certificate is required but not provided.

8406bdd81fb5.title: List of HTTP status codes
8406bdd81fb5.sentence: An expansion of the 400 Bad Request response code, used when the client has made a HTTP request to a port listening for HTTPS requests.

251a15e924f7.title: List of HTTP status codes
251a15e924f7.sentence: Used when the client has closed the request before the server could send a response.

ccc0cee3192e.title: List of HTTP status codes
ccc0cee3192e.sentence: Cloudflare's reverse proxy service expands the 5xx series of errors space to signal issues with the origin server.

4be4f0fb7658.title: List of HTTP status codes
4be4f0fb7658.sentence: The origin server refused connections from Cloudflare.

9371d3a91c28.title: List of HTTP status codes
9371d3a91c28.sentence: Cloudflare timed out contacting the origin server.

18a1ab26ceb1.title: List of HTTP status codes
18a1ab26ceb1.sentence: Cloudflare was able to complete a TCP connection to the origin server, but the origin did not provide a timely HTTP response.

85175873adf5.title: List of HTTP status codes
85175873adf5.sentence: Cloudflare could not negotiate a SSL/TLS handshake with the origin server.

085f35aaec2b.title: List of HTTP status codes
085f35aaec2b.sentence: Cloudflare could not validate the SSL certificate on the origin web server.

b27b6b00b2c6.title: List of HTTP status codes
b27b6b00b2c6.sentence: An informal convention used by some HTTP proxies to signal a network read timeout behind the proxy to a client in front of the proxy.

425cc1de2325.title: List of HTTP status codes
425cc1de2325.sentence: An error used by some HTTP proxies to signal a network connect timeout behind the proxy to a client in front of the proxy.

1fb8872a7389.title: rfc>9110
1fb8872a7389.sentence: HTTP defines a number of generic extension points that can be used to introduce capabilities to the protocol without introducing a new version, including methods, status codes, field names, and further extensibility points within defined fields, such as authentication schemes and cache directives (see Cache-Control extensions in Section 5.2.3 of ).

bfe04e2564a4.title: rfc>9110
bfe04e2564a4.sentence: Additionally, specific versions of HTTP might have their own extensibility points, such as transfer codings in HTTP/1.1 (Section 6.1 of [HTTP/1.1]) and HTTP/2 SETTINGS or frame types ([HTTP/2]).

0f80198d05a0.title: rfc>9110
0f80198d05a0.sentence: Version-specific extensions cannot override or modify the semantics of a version-independent mechanism or extension point (like a method or header field) without explicitly being allowed by that protocol element.

2192ecbae77b.title: rfc>9110
2192ecbae77b.sentence: For example, the CONNECT method (Section 9.3.6) allows this.

d5c21c4cca16.title: rfc>9110
d5c21c4cca16.sentence: All such methods ought to be registered within the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Method Registry", as described in Section 16.1.

e17c40082ec9.title: rfc>9110
e17c40082ec9.sentence: The 1xx (Informational) class of status code indicates an interim response for communicating connection status or request progress prior to completing the requested action and sending a final response.

a60c9acb2d29.title: rfc>9110
a60c9acb2d29.sentence: A 1xx response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers.

b12530236040.title: rfc>9110
b12530236040.sentence: Since HTTP/1.0 did not define any 1xx status codes, a server MUST NOT send a 1xx response to an HTTP/1.0 client.

48dd1ed24271.title: rfc>9110
48dd1ed24271.sentence: A client MUST be able to parse one or more 1xx responses received prior to a final response, even if the client does not expect one.

dd9c0a8c7472.title: rfc>9110
dd9c0a8c7472.sentence: The 100 (Continue) status code indicates that the initial part of a request has been received and has not yet been rejected by the server.

cfe117bbd234.title: rfc>9110
cfe117bbd234.sentence: When the request contains an Expect header field that includes a 100-continue expectation, the 100 response indicates that the server wishes to receive the request content, as described in Section 10.1.1.

298f8ab3242f.title: List of HTTP status codes
298f8ab3242f.sentence: Sending a large request body to a server after a request has been rejected for inappropriate headers would be inefficient.

beeca7b6d573.title: List of HTTP status codes
beeca7b6d573.sentence: To have a server check the request's headers, a client must send Expect: 100-continue as a header in its initial request and receive a 100 Continue status code in response before sending the body.

de9fd7ab4d44.title: rfc>9110
de9fd7ab4d44.sentence: The 101 (Switching Protocols) status code indicates that the server understands and is willing to comply with the client's request, via the Upgrade header field (Section 7.8), for a change in the application protocol being used on this connection.

8c550f0a6be2.title: rfc>9110
8c550f0a6be2.sentence: The server MUST generate an Upgrade header field in the response that indicates which protocol(s) will be in effect after this response.

94bca6629e27.title: rfc>9110
94bca6629e27.sentence: For example, switching to a newer version of HTTP might be advantageous over older versions, and switching to a real-time, synchronous protocol might be advantageous when delivering resources that use such features.

4e2bbe33d460.title: WebSocket
4e2bbe33d460.sentence: The client sends an HTTP request (method GET, version ≥ 1.1) and the server returns an HTTP response with status code 101 (Switching Protocols) on success.

fadd46e364f4.title: List of HTTP status codes
fadd46e364f4.sentence: Used to return some response headers before final HTTP message.

c21f539698ee.title: List of HTTP status codes
c21f539698ee.sentence: This code indicates that the server has received and is processing the request, but no response is available yet.

6cdf9fe13eba.title: List of HTTP status codes
6cdf9fe13eba.sentence: This prevents the client from timing out and assuming the request was lost.

ea21654baf84.title: rfc>9110
ea21654baf84.sentence: The target of an HTTP request is called a "resource".

97b40f364813.title: rfc>9110
97b40f364813.sentence: A "representation" is information that is intended to reflect a past, current, or desired state of a given resource, in a format that can be readily communicated via the protocol.

bd9632959a6f.title: rfc>9110
bd9632959a6f.sentence: HTTP provides a uniform interface for interacting with a resource (Section 3.1) -- regardless of its type, nature, or implementation --by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations (Section 3.2).

9909cdaece7d.title: rfc>9110
9909cdaece7d.sentence: HTTP hides the details of how a service is implemented by presenting a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of resources provided.

5fa2e1513932.title: rfc>9110
5fa2e1513932.sentence: HTTP does not limit the nature of a resource; it merely defines an interface that might be used to interact with resources.

d852c8404792.title: rfc>9110
d852c8404792.sentence: Most resources are identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), as described in Section 4.

0ca61c730a22.title: rfc>9110
0ca61c730a22.sentence: One design goal of HTTP is to separate resource identification from request semantics, which is made possible by vesting the request semantics in the request method (Section 9) and a few request-modifying header fields.

7a7e92bc1dc2.title: rfc>9110
7a7e92bc1dc2.sentence: HTTP allows "information hiding" behind its uniform interface by defining communication with respect to a transferable representation of the resource state, rather than transferring the resource itself.

d0ff74cf8a97.title: rfc>9110
d0ff74cf8a97.sentence: This allows the resource identified by a URI to be anything, including temporal functions like "the current weather in Laguna Beach", while potentially providing information that represents that resource at the time a message is generated.

507051fe09da.title: rfc>9110
507051fe09da.sentence: A target resource might be provided with, or be capable of generating, multiple representations that are each intended to reflect the resource's current state.

829db81cb280.title: rfc>9110
829db81cb280.sentence: An algorithm, usually based on content negotiation (Section 12), would be used to select one of those representations as being most applicable to a given request.

85eddc3944b4.title: rfc>9110
85eddc3944b4.sentence: This "selected representation" provides the data and metadata for evaluating conditional requests (Section 13) and constructing the content for 200 (OK), 206 (Partial Content), and 304 (Not Modified) responses to GET (Section 9.3.1).

25bd12025fc6.title: rfc>9110
25bd12025fc6.sentence: The "Content-Type" header field indicates the media type of the associated representation: either the representation enclosed in the message content or the selected representation, as determined by the message semantics.

bb9115d4d493.title: rfc>9110
bb9115d4d493.sentence: The "Content-Encoding" header field indicates what content codings have been applied to the representation, beyond those inherent in the media type, and thus what decoding mechanisms have to be applied in order to obtain data in the media type referenced by the Content-Type header field.

a3e1a6125a0c.title: rfc>9110
a3e1a6125a0c.sentence: The "Content-Length" header field indicates the associated representation's data length as a decimal non-negative integer number of octets.

cc5c46b67b2c.title: rfc>9110
cc5c46b67b2c.sentence: The indicated media type defines both the data format and how that data is intended to be processed by a recipient, within the scope of the received message semantics, after any content codings indicated by Content-Encoding are decoded.

6e3e245e13cd.title: rfc>9110
6e3e245e13cd.sentence: A sender that generates a message containing content SHOULD generate a Content-Type header field in that message unless the intended media type of the enclosed representation is unknown to the sender.

1fa6004e542f.title: rfc>9110
1fa6004e542f.sentence: Content-Encoding is primarily used to allow a representation's data to be compressed without losing the identity of its underlying media type.

013fb3879800.title: HTTP
013fb3879800.section: Technology > Data exchange > Content retrieval optimizations
013fb3879800.sentence: - Header Content-Encoding was added to specify whether the returned content is compressed.

4678517c9209.title: rfc>9110
4678517c9209.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.3. Accept-Encoding
4678517c9209.sentence: When sent by a user agent in a request, Accept-Encoding indicates the content codings acceptable in a response.

d12195c1ff79.title: rfc>9110
d12195c1ff79.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.3. Accept-Encoding
d12195c1ff79.sentence: When selecting between multiple content codings that have the same purpose, the acceptable content coding with the highest non-zero qvalue is preferred.

5bcf990180f8.title: rfc>9110
5bcf990180f8.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.3. Accept-Encoding
5bcf990180f8.sentence: An "identity" token is used as a synonym for "no encoding" in order to communicate when no encoding is preferred.

f6e3ad3e9c97.title: HTTP
f6e3ad3e9c97.section: Technology > Data exchange > Content retrieval optimizations
f6e3ad3e9c97.sentence: - If the size of the content is not known in advance (i.e. because it is dynamically generated) then the header Content-Length would not be included.

44316023bdba.title: HTTP
44316023bdba.section: Technology > Data exchange > Content retrieval optimizations
44316023bdba.sentence: The client would assume that transfer was complete when the connection closed, but a premature close would leave the client with partial content yet the client would not know it is partial.

ce4cbdc2ad2e.title: HTTP
ce4cbdc2ad2e.section: Technology > Data exchange > Content retrieval optimizations
ce4cbdc2ad2e.sentence: - Chunked transfer encoding allows content to be streamed in chunks in order to reliably send it even when the server does not know its length in advance (i.e. because it is dynamically generated, etc.).

b704c43bbc1b.title: rfc>9110
b704c43bbc1b.sentence: When responses convey content, whether indicating a success or an error, the origin server often has different ways of representing that information; for example, in different formats, languages, or encodings.

c14dea578712.title: rfc>9110
c14dea578712.sentence: Likewise, different users or user agents might have differing capabilities, characteristics, or preferences that could influence which representation, among those available, would be best to deliver.

1aa3738ea260.title: rfc>9110
1aa3738ea260.sentence: For this reason, HTTP provides mechanisms for content negotiation.

430510e709a9.title: rfc>9110
430510e709a9.sentence: This specification defines three patterns of content negotiation that can be made visible within the protocol: "proactive" negotiation, where the server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated preferences; "reactive" negotiation, where the server provides a list of representations for the user agent to choose from; and "request content" negotiation, where the user agent selects the representation for a future request based upon the server's stated preferences in past responses.

d81fc6a9e0c9.title: rfc>9110
d81fc6a9e0c9.sentence: When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the preferred representation, it is called "proactive negotiation" (a.k.a., "server-driven negotiation").

0fd3ed15316c.title: rfc>9110
0fd3ed15316c.sentence: With "reactive negotiation" (a.k.a., "agent-driven negotiation"), selection of content (regardless of the status code) is performed by the user agent after receiving an initial response.

afd55bb1d998.title: rfc>9110
afd55bb1d998.sentence: When content negotiation preferences are sent in a server's response, the listed preferences are called "request content negotiation" because they intend to influence selection of an appropriate content for subsequent requests to that resource.

b0da68c160bf.title: rfc>9110
b0da68c160bf.sentence: The request header fields Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding, and Accept-Language are defined below for a user agent to engage in proactive negotiation of the response content.

6d395dd39d6a.title: rfc>9110
6d395dd39d6a.sentence: Selection is based on the available representations for a response (the dimensions over which it might vary, such as language, content coding, etc.) compared to various information supplied in the request, including both the explicit negotiation header fields below and implicit characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of the User-Agent field.

8b641b7e0110.title: rfc>9110
