8b641b7e0110.sentence: Proactive negotiation is advantageous when the algorithm for selecting from among the available representations is difficult to describe to a user agent, or when the server desires to send its "best guess" to the user agent along with the first response (when that "best guess" is good enough for the user, this avoids the round-trip delay of a subsequent request).

2709d1ffe9e7.title: rfc>9110
2709d1ffe9e7.sentence: - It is impossible for the server to accurately determine what might be "best" for any given user, since that would require complete knowledge of both the capabilities of the user agent and the intended use for the response (e.g., does the user want to view it on screen or print it on paper?);

b46579815575.title: rfc>9110
b46579815575.sentence: - Having the user agent describe its capabilities in every request can be both very inefficient (given that only a small percentage of responses have multiple representations) and a potential risk to the user's privacy;

92dd639e4b90.title: rfc>9110
92dd639e4b90.sentence: - It complicates the implementation of an origin server and the algorithms for generating responses to a request; and,

700d19428670.title: rfc>9110
700d19428670.sentence: - It limits the reusability of responses for shared caching.

82108c83e95d.title: rfc>9110
82108c83e95d.sentence: The mechanism for reactive negotiation might be as simple as a list of references to alternative representations.

0b82f0330d46.title: rfc>9110
0b82f0330d46.sentence: If the user agent is not satisfied by the initial response content, it can perform a GET request on one or more of the alternative resources to obtain a different representation.

de3e4ad7a448.title: rfc>9110
de3e4ad7a448.sentence: For example, the alternatives listed in responses with the 300 (Multiple Choices) and 406 (Not Acceptable) status codes include information about available representations so that the user or user agent can react by making a selection.

17a3b439a7d2.title: rfc>9110
17a3b439a7d2.sentence: Reactive negotiation is advantageous when the response would vary over commonly used dimensions (such as type, language, or encoding), when the origin server is unable to determine a user agent's capabilities from examining the request, and generally when public caches are used to distribute server load and reduce network usage.

7f8232bf8094.title: rfc>9110
7f8232bf8094.sentence: Reactive negotiation suffers from the disadvantages of transmitting a list of alternatives to the user agent, which degrades user-perceived latency if transmitted in the header section, and needing a second request to obtain an alternate representation.

99fb26afcebd.title: rfc>9110
99fb26afcebd.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.4. Content Negotiation Field Features > 12.4.2. Quality Values
99fb26afcebd.sentence: The content negotiation fields defined by this specification use a common parameter, named "q" (case-insensitive), to assign a relative "weight" to the preference for that associated kind of content.

dbe88547912f.title: rfc>9110
dbe88547912f.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.4. Content Negotiation Field Features > 12.4.2. Quality Values
dbe88547912f.sentence: The weight is normalized to a real number in the range 0 through 1, where 0.001 is the least preferred and 1 is the most preferred; a value of 0 means "not acceptable".

51e4bcce97ea.title: rfc>9110
51e4bcce97ea.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.4. Content Negotiation Field Features > 12.4.2. Quality Values
51e4bcce97ea.sentence: If no "q" parameter is present, the default weight is 1.

12aa708b24eb.title: rfc>9110
12aa708b24eb.sentence: A user agent cannot rely on proactive negotiation preferences being consistently honored, since the origin server might not implement proactive negotiation for the requested resource or might decide that sending a response that doesn't conform to the user agent's preferences is better than sending a 406 (Not Acceptable) response.

e3f4e6b6e533.title: rfc>9110
e3f4e6b6e533.sentence: A Vary header field (Section 12.5.5) is often sent in a response subject to proactive negotiation to indicate what parts of the request information were used in the selection algorithm.

a1bed5f58803.title: rfc>9110
a1bed5f58803.sentence: The 2xx (Successful) class of status code indicates that the client's request was successfully received, understood, and accepted.

cdde17080c33.title: rfc>9110
cdde17080c33.sentence: The 200 (OK) status code indicates that the request has succeeded.

0bc95bd93819.title: rfc>9110
0bc95bd93819.sentence: The content sent in a 200 response depends on the request method.

3fc902361d73.title: rfc>9110
3fc902361d73.sentence: The 201 (Created) status code indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created.

3a330b43d457.title: rfc>9110
3a330b43d457.sentence: The primary resource created by the request is identified by either a Location header field in the response or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI.

a4c30a319dd9.title: rfc>9110
a4c30a319dd9.sentence: The 202 (Accepted) status code indicates that the request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed.

602fe33e64a4.title: rfc>9110
602fe33e64a4.sentence: The request might or might not eventually be acted upon, as it might be disallowed when processing actually takes place.

670fc99a3c3d.title: rfc>9110
670fc99a3c3d.sentence: There is no facility in HTTP for re-sending a status code from an asynchronous operation.

a20affc4f246.title: rfc>9110
a20affc4f246.sentence: The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response content.

fc14bddf272b.title: rfc>9110
fc14bddf272b.sentence: The 206 (Partial Content) status code indicates that the server is successfully fulfilling a range request for the target resource by transferring one or more parts of the selected representation.

a06911b26778.title: rfc>9113
a06911b26778.sentence: Clients SHOULD NOT open more than one HTTP/2 connection to a given host and port pair, where the host is derived from a URI, a selected alternative service, or a configured proxy.

87b0158091c1.title: rfc>9113
87b0158091c1.sentence: When either endpoint chooses to close the transport-layer TCP connection, the terminating endpoint SHOULD first send a GOAWAY (Section 6.8) frame so that both endpoints can reliably determine whether previously sent frames have been processed and gracefully complete or terminate any necessary remaining tasks.

fcfbfed384c8.title: rfc>9113
fcfbfed384c8.sentence: For best performance, it is expected that clients will not close connections until it is determined that no further communication with a server is necessary (for example, when a user navigates away from a particular web page) or until the server closes the connection.

1fb98a0e863f.title: rfc>9113
1fb98a0e863f.sentence: A client can create additional connections as replacements, either to replace connections that are near to exhausting the available stream identifier space (Section 5.1.1), to refresh the keying material for a TLS connection, or to replace connections that have encountered errors (Section 5.4.1).

56c2e8e6b7ac.title: rfc>9113
56c2e8e6b7ac.section: 9. HTTP/2 Connections > 9.1. Connection Management > 9.1.1. Connection Reuse
56c2e8e6b7ac.sentence: Connections that are made to an origin server, either directly or through a tunnel created using the CONNECT method (Section 8.5), MAY be reused for requests with multiple different URI authority components.

ac53526b0e90.title: rfc>9113
ac53526b0e90.section: 9. HTTP/2 Connections > 9.1. Connection Management > 9.1.1. Connection Reuse
ac53526b0e90.sentence: A connection can be reused as long as the origin server is authoritative (Section 10.1).

be5adf962fac.title: rfc>9113
be5adf962fac.section: 9. HTTP/2 Connections > 9.1. Connection Management > 9.1.1. Connection Reuse
be5adf962fac.sentence: For "https" resources, connection reuse additionally depends on having a certificate that is valid for the host in the URI.

aa2abf9a1c72.title: rfc>9113
aa2abf9a1c72.section: 9. HTTP/2 Connections > 9.1. Connection Management > 9.1.1. Connection Reuse
aa2abf9a1c72.sentence: A server that does not wish clients to reuse connections can indicate that it is not authoritative for a request by sending a 421 (Misdirected Request) status code in response to the request (see Section 15.5.20 of ).

6d9338d2e4c0.title: rfc>9113
6d9338d2e4c0.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
6d9338d2e4c0.sentence: - The GOAWAY frame indicates the highest stream number that might have been processed.

b3d6f69c30d9.title: rfc>9113
b3d6f69c30d9.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
b3d6f69c30d9.sentence: Requests on streams with higher numbers are therefore guaranteed to be safe to retry.

3e012dab7c3e.title: rfc>9113
3e012dab7c3e.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
3e012dab7c3e.sentence: - The REFUSED_STREAM error code can be included in a RST_STREAM frame to indicate that the stream is being closed prior to any processing having occurred.

5506b4684bc2.title: rfc>9113
5506b4684bc2.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
5506b4684bc2.sentence: Any request that was sent on the reset stream can be safely retried.

1f5ab2b88088.title: rfc>9113
1f5ab2b88088.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
1f5ab2b88088.sentence: Requests that have not been processed have not failed; clients MAY automatically retry them, even those with non-idempotent methods.

30c917add423.title: rfc>9113
30c917add423.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
30c917add423.sentence: Connections that remain idle can become broken, because some middleboxes (for instance, network address translators or load balancers) silently discard connection bindings.

af88552736e0.title: rfc>9113
af88552736e0.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
af88552736e0.sentence: The PING frame allows a client to safely test whether a connection is still active without sending a request.

772e0c50d6a7.title: rfc>9113
772e0c50d6a7.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.7. Request Reliability
772e0c50d6a7.sentence: In addition to these mechanisms, the PING frame provides a way for a client to easily test a connection.

80f7b3c0993f.title: rfc>9113
80f7b3c0993f.sentence: A flow-control scheme ensures that streams on the same connection do not destructively interfere with each other.

c87769798379.title: rfc>9113
c87769798379.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles

d9011f522de7.title: rfc>9113
d9011f522de7.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
d9011f522de7.sentence: - Flow control is directional with overall control provided by the receiver.

2f3ce78cb118.title: rfc>9113
2f3ce78cb118.sentence: Using streams for multiplexing introduces contention over use of the TCP connection, resulting in blocked streams.

f11eb7ffb56b.title: rfc>9113
f11eb7ffb56b.sentence: Flow control is used for both individual streams and the connection as a whole.

e80700958b39.title: rfc>9113
e80700958b39.sentence: HTTP/2 provides for flow control through use of the WINDOW_UPDATE frame (Section 6.9).

2ff807f2cf66.title: rfc>9113
2ff807f2cf66.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
2ff807f2cf66.sentence: Receivers advertise how many octets they are prepared to receive on a stream and for the entire connection.

7f61fd39b431.title: rfc>9113
7f61fd39b431.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
7f61fd39b431.sentence: - The initial value for the flow-control window is 65,535 octets for both new streams and the overall connection.

c64127f1e6b2.title: rfc>9113
c64127f1e6b2.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
c64127f1e6b2.sentence: Of the frames specified in this document, only DATA frames are subject to flow control; all other frame types do not consume space in the advertised flow-control window.

375d48875ad5.title: rfc>9113
375d48875ad5.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
375d48875ad5.sentence: This ensures that important control frames are not blocked by flow control.

e13c683cc0d8.title: rfc>9113
e13c683cc0d8.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.1. Flow-Control Principles
e13c683cc0d8.sentence: HTTP/2 flow control operates between the endpoints of a single hop and not over the entire end-to-end path.

f1a9f01093bf.title: rfc>9113
f1a9f01093bf.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
f1a9f01093bf.sentence: Flow control is defined to protect endpoints that are operating under resource constraints.

5dba2ae15244.title: rfc>9113
5dba2ae15244.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
5dba2ae15244.sentence: For example, a proxy needs to share memory between many connections and also might have a slow upstream connection and a fast downstream one.

966e52c485da.title: rfc>9113
966e52c485da.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
966e52c485da.sentence: Deployments that do not require this capability can advertise a flow-control window of the maximum size (2^31-1) and can maintain this window by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame when any data is received.

23375f72c3bb.title: rfc>9113
23375f72c3bb.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
23375f72c3bb.sentence: This effectively disables flow control for that receiver.

8f61b2908341.title: rfc>9113
8f61b2908341.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.3. Flow-Control Performance
8f61b2908341.sentence: If an endpoint cannot ensure that its peer always has available flow-control window space that is greater than the peer's bandwidth * delay product on this connection, its receive throughput will be limited by HTTP/2 flow control.

743d1ffffc46.title: rfc>9113
743d1ffffc46.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.3. Flow-Control Performance
743d1ffffc46.sentence: This will result in degraded performance.

4bff669eb35c.title: rfc>9113
4bff669eb35c.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.3. Flow-Control Performance
4bff669eb35c.sentence: Sending timely WINDOW_UPDATE frames can improve performance.

78bd9abc20bc.title: rfc>9113
78bd9abc20bc.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
78bd9abc20bc.sentence: Endpoints MUST read and process HTTP/2 frames from the TCP receive buffer as soon as data is available.

caf4a0145e32.title: rfc>9113
caf4a0145e32.section: 5. Streams and Multiplexing > 5.2. Flow Control > 5.2.2. Appropriate Use of Flow Control
caf4a0145e32.sentence: Failure to read promptly could lead to a deadlock when critical frames, such as WINDOW_UPDATE, are not read and acted upon.

7302bb2fd78f.title: rfc>9113
7302bb2fd78f.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
7302bb2fd78f.sentence: Field section compression is the process of compressing a set of field lines (Section 5.2 of ) to form a field block.

d7a7551fd17e.title: rfc>9113
d7a7551fd17e.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
d7a7551fd17e.sentence: Details of HTTP/2 field section compression and decompression are defined in, which, for historical reasons, refers to these processes as header compression and decompression.

293635ffe880.title: rfc>9113
293635ffe880.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression > 4.3.1. Compression State

d66b7da34e3e.title: rfc>9113
d66b7da34e3e.sentence: This can result in excessive latency when multiple requests are made on a new TCP connection.

24dff58c74e0.title: rfc>9113
24dff58c74e0.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression > 4.3.1. Compression State
24dff58c74e0.sentence: Each endpoint has an HPACK encoder context and an HPACK decoder context that are used for encoding and decoding all field blocks on a connection.

d1a2367ca534.title: rfc>9113
d1a2367ca534.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression > 4.3.1. Compression State
d1a2367ca534.sentence: The dynamic table has a maximum size that is set by an HPACK decoder.

ebfa5e8a7c9e.title: rfc>9113
ebfa5e8a7c9e.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression > 4.3.1. Compression State
ebfa5e8a7c9e.sentence: An endpoint communicates the size chosen by its HPACK decoder context using the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE setting; see Section 6.5.2.

bc321dbab08b.title: rfc>9113
bc321dbab08b.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression > 4.3.1. Compression State
bc321dbab08b.sentence: When a connection is established, the dynamic table size for the HPACK decoder and encoder at both endpoints starts at 4,096 bytes, the initial value of the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE setting.

27db0dd358d5.title: rfc>9113
27db0dd358d5.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
27db0dd358d5.sentence: Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream.

321c1db57086.title: rfc>9113
321c1db57086.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
321c1db57086.sentence: Field block fragments can only be sent as the frame payload of HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE, or CONTINUATION frames because these frames carry data that can modify the compression context maintained by a receiver.

c63aa0ce6574.title: rfc>9113
c63aa0ce6574.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
c63aa0ce6574.sentence: An endpoint receiving HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE, or CONTINUATION frames needs to reassemble field blocks and perform decompression even if the frames are to be discarded.

e1cfd45b28ec.title: rfc>9113
e1cfd45b28ec.section: 4. HTTP Frames > 4.3. Field Section Compression and Decompression
e1cfd45b28ec.sentence: A decoding error in a field block MUST be treated as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type COMPRESSION_ERROR.

38740b94984c.title: rfc>9113
38740b94984c.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.2. HTTP Fields > 8.2.3. Compressing the Cookie Header Field
38740b94984c.sentence: This can significantly reduce compression efficiency, as updates to individual cookie-pairs would invalidate any field lines that are stored in the HPACK table.

61f7856a087a.title: rfc>9113
61f7856a087a.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.2. HTTP Fields > 8.2.3. Compressing the Cookie Header Field
61f7856a087a.sentence: To allow for better compression efficiency, the Cookie header field MAY be split into separate header fields, each with one or more cookie-pairs.

1664b8a5d80f.title: rfc>9113
1664b8a5d80f.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
1664b8a5d80f.sentence: HTTP/2 allows a server to preemptively send (or "push") responses (along with corresponding "promised" requests) to a client in association with a previous client-initiated request.

c5a3a4794c36.title: rfc>9113
c5a3a4794c36.sentence: The server does this by synthesizing a request, which it sends as a PUSH_PROMISE frame.

c482b073a438.title: rfc>9113
c482b073a438.sentence: The server is then able to send a response to the synthetic request on a separate stream.

7d48b279cc1c.title: rfc>9113
7d48b279cc1c.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
7d48b279cc1c.sentence: Server push was designed to allow a server to improve client-perceived performance by predicting what requests will follow those that it receives, thereby removing a round trip for them.

1f108f1c95bf.title: rfc>9113
1f108f1c95bf.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
1f108f1c95bf.sentence: For example, a request for HTML is often followed by requests for stylesheets and scripts referenced by that page.

2c6a708f9eb7.title: rfc>9113
2c6a708f9eb7.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
2c6a708f9eb7.sentence: When these requests are pushed, the client does not need to wait to receive the references to them in the HTML and issue separate requests.

a9db19f72a6e.title: rfc>9113
a9db19f72a6e.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
a9db19f72a6e.sentence: Errors in prediction can lead to performance degradation, due to the opportunity cost that the additional data on the wire represents.

daea6bf40960.title: rfc>9113
daea6bf40960.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
daea6bf40960.sentence: In particular, pushing any significant amount of data can cause contention issues with responses that are more important.

76308dc1de5f.title: rfc>9113
76308dc1de5f.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
76308dc1de5f.sentence: Promised requests MUST be safe (see Section 9.2.1 of ) and cacheable (see Section 9.2.3 of ).

3b8075477a29.title: rfc>9113
3b8075477a29.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
3b8075477a29.sentence: Promised requests cannot include any content or a trailer section.

b24b8d958efd.title: rfc>9113
b24b8d958efd.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
b24b8d958efd.sentence: A client can request that server push be disabled, though this is negotiated for each hop independently.

b9b20ccbff82.title: rfc>9113
b9b20ccbff82.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
b9b20ccbff82.sentence: The SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH setting can be set to 0 to indicate that server push is disabled.

83deed731f48.title: rfc>9113
83deed731f48.section: 8. Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/2 > 8.4. Server Push
83deed731f48.sentence: Clients that receive a promised request that is not cacheable, that is not known to be safe, or that indicates the presence of request content MUST reset the promised stream with a stream error (Section 5.4.2) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

853dd874c333.title: rfc>9110
853dd874c333.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
853dd874c333.sentence: URIs are intended to be shared, not secured, even when they identify secure resources.

c9a53e6e61b1.title: rfc>9110
c9a53e6e61b1.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
c9a53e6e61b1.sentence: It is therefore unwise to include information within a URI that is sensitive, personally identifiable, or a risk to disclose.

53a3fcbd0cd5.title: rfc>9110
53a3fcbd0cd5.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
53a3fcbd0cd5.sentence: URIs are often shown on displays, added to templates when a page is printed, and stored in a variety of unprotected bookmark lists.

d535b31362de.title: rfc>9110
d535b31362de.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
d535b31362de.sentence: Many servers, proxies, and user agents log or display the target URI in places where it might be visible to third parties.

58277357f4cb.title: rfc>9110
58277357f4cb.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
58277357f4cb.sentence: When an application uses client-side mechanisms to construct a target URI out of user-provided information, such as the query fields of a form using GET, potentially sensitive data might be provided that would not be appropriate for disclosure within a URI.

cee8d8ff4717.title: rfc>9110
cee8d8ff4717.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
cee8d8ff4717.sentence: POST is often preferred in such cases because it usually doesn't construct a URI; instead, POST of a form transmits the potentially sensitive data in the request content.

7af12bc7b32d.title: rfc>9110
7af12bc7b32d.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
7af12bc7b32d.sentence: However, this hinders caching and uses an unsafe method for what would otherwise be a safe request.

047b6e567e2b.title: rfc>9110
047b6e567e2b.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
047b6e567e2b.sentence: Alternative workarounds include transforming the user-provided data prior to constructing the URI or filtering the data to only include common values that are not sensitive.

8c7d54c74ee5.title: rfc>9110
8c7d54c74ee5.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
8c7d54c74ee5.sentence: Likewise, redirecting the result of a query to a different (server-generated) URI can remove potentially sensitive data from later links and provide a cacheable response for later reuse.

eb9d782fe0c6.title: rfc>9110
eb9d782fe0c6.section: 17. Security Considerations > 17.9. Disclosure of Sensitive Information in URIs
eb9d782fe0c6.sentence: Since the Referer header field tells a target site about the context that resulted in a request, it has the potential to reveal information about the user's immediate browsing history and any personal information that might be found in the referring resource's URI.

cc9b6672f78a.title: rfc>9110
cc9b6672f78a.sentence: The target resource in a POST request is intended to handle the enclosed representation according to the resource's own semantics, whereas the enclosed representation in a PUT request is defined as replacing the state of the target resource.

d5e60f7caab4.title: rfc>9110
d5e60f7caab4.sentence: The fundamental difference between the POST and PUT methods is highlighted by the different intent for the enclosed representation.

28c71b0c22ff.title: rfc>9110
28c71b0c22ff.sentence: Hence, the intent of PUT is idempotent and visible to intermediaries, even though the exact effect is only known by the origin server.

76531c7e69a6.title: rfc>9110
76531c7e69a6.sentence: Proper interpretation of a PUT request presumes that the user agent knows which target resource is desired.

676f31c96f5a.title: rfc>9110
676f31c96f5a.sentence: A service that selects a proper URI on behalf of the client, after receiving a state-changing request, SHOULD be implemented using the POST method rather than PUT.

7cadb5f22e03.title: rfc>9110
7cadb5f22e03.sentence: If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response.

8c5958e5cea7.title: rfc>9110
8c5958e5cea7.sentence: If the target resource does have a current representation and that representation is successfully modified in accordance with the state of the enclosed representation, then the origin server MUST send either a 200 (OK) or a 204 (No Content) response to indicate successful completion of the request.

956a78572922.title: rfc>9110
956a78572922.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
956a78572922.sentence: The "Vary" header field in a response describes what parts of a request message, aside from the method and target URI, might have influenced the origin server's process for selecting the content of this response.

0ccd42540f7a.title: rfc>9110
0ccd42540f7a.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
0ccd42540f7a.sentence: A Vary field value is either the wildcard member "*" or a list of request field names, known as the selecting header fields, that might have had a role in selecting the representation for this response.

6a52c3284836.title: rfc>9110
6a52c3284836.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary

0ba42dc91b5e.title: rfc>9110
0ba42dc91b5e.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
0ba42dc91b5e.sentence: indicates that the origin server might have used the request's Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language header fields (or lack thereof) as determining factors while choosing the content for this response.

236934670433.title: rfc>9110
236934670433.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
236934670433.sentence: - To inform cache recipients that they MUST NOT use this response to satisfy a later request unless the later request has the same values for the listed header fields as the original request (Section 4.1 of ) or reuse of the response has been validated by the origin server.

a14eeaa0549e.title: rfc>9110
a14eeaa0549e.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
a14eeaa0549e.sentence: In other words, Vary expands the cache key required to match a new request to the stored cache entry.

b215f02dca42.title: rfc>9110
b215f02dca42.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
b215f02dca42.sentence: An origin server SHOULD generate a Vary header field on a cacheable response when it wishes that response to be selectively reused for subsequent requests.

9924e62079fa.title: rfc>9110
9924e62079fa.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
9924e62079fa.sentence: Generally, that is the case when the response content has been tailored to better fit the preferences expressed by those selecting header fields, such as when an origin server has selected the response's language based on the request's Accept-Language header field.

1d38badbcc84.title: rfc>9110
1d38badbcc84.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
1d38badbcc84.sentence: Vary might be elided when an origin server considers variance in content selection to be less significant than Vary's performance impact on caching, particularly when reuse is already limited by cache response directives (Section 5.2 of ).

2949e3a19e71.title: rfc>9110
2949e3a19e71.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
2949e3a19e71.sentence: A list containing the member "*" signals that other aspects of the request might have played a role in selecting the response representation, possibly including aspects outside the message syntax (e.g., the client's network address).

6830b6f04d9f.title: rfc>9110
6830b6f04d9f.section: 12. Content Negotiation > 12.5. Content Negotiation Fields > 12.5.5. Vary
6830b6f04d9f.sentence: A recipient will not be able to determine whether this response is appropriate for a later request without forwarding the request to the origin server.

6e3107a74251.title: rfc>9111
6e3107a74251.sentence: The "Cache-Control" header field is used to list directives for caches along the request/response chain.

11f7b65cbfcf.title: rfc>9111
11f7b65cbfcf.sentence: Cache directives are unidirectional, in that the presence of a directive in a request does not imply that the same directive is present or copied in the response.

6c0fc170bc07.title: rfc>9111
6c0fc170bc07.sentence: A proxy, whether or not it implements a cache, MUST pass cache directives through in forwarded messages, regardless of their significance to that application, since the directives might apply to all recipients along the request/response chain.

24a62d876732.title: rfc>9111
24a62d876732.sentence: It is not possible to target a directive to a specific cache.

a6f5967e0c4c.title: rfc>9111
a6f5967e0c4c.sentence: They are advisory; caches MAY implement them, but are not required to.

6a4cf9bd5834.title: rfc>9111
6a4cf9bd5834.sentence: A cache MUST obey the Cache-Control directives defined in this section.

68fd309ee14d.title: rfc>9111
68fd309ee14d.sentence: In both these cases, the value in Expires is only intended for recipients that have not yet implemented the Cache-Control header field.

d0b392999550.title: rfc>9111
d0b392999550.sentence: This section defines cache request directives.

54006c037960.title: rfc>9111
54006c037960.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.1. max-age
54006c037960.sentence: The max-age request directive indicates that the client prefers a response whose age is less than or equal to the specified number of seconds.

474a8dad76d5.title: rfc>9111
474a8dad76d5.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.2. max-stale
474a8dad76d5.sentence: The max-stale request directive indicates that the client will accept a response that has exceeded its freshness lifetime.

3bbccad28e0d.title: rfc>9111
3bbccad28e0d.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.2. max-stale
3bbccad28e0d.sentence: If a value is present, then the client is willing to accept a response that has exceeded its freshness lifetime by no more than the specified number of seconds.

b55eaa963170.title: rfc>9111
b55eaa963170.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.3. min-fresh
b55eaa963170.sentence: The min-fresh request directive indicates that the client prefers a response whose freshness lifetime is no less than its current age plus the specified time in seconds.

e6593617a913.title: rfc>9111
e6593617a913.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.4. no-cache
e6593617a913.sentence: The no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server.

2d2b3b8507eb.title: rfc>9111
2d2b3b8507eb.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.5. no-store
2d2b3b8507eb.sentence: The no-store request directive indicates that a cache MUST NOT store any part of either this request or any response to it.

146209e83015.title: rfc>9111
146209e83015.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.7. only-if-cached
146209e83015.sentence: The only-if-cached request directive indicates that the client only wishes to obtain a stored response.

ca06a4c9be06.title: rfc>9111
ca06a4c9be06.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.1. Request Directives > 5.2.1.7. only-if-cached
ca06a4c9be06.sentence: Caches that honor this request directive SHOULD, upon receiving it, respond with either a stored response consistent with the other constraints of the request or a 504 (Gateway Timeout) status code.

9ec0c2807d87.title: rfc>9111
9ec0c2807d87.sentence: A "shared cache" is a cache that stores responses for reuse by more than one user; shared caches are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary.

ee9092312eee.title: rfc>9111
ee9092312eee.sentence: A "private cache", in contrast, is dedicated to a single user; often, they are deployed as a component of a user agent.

0560857d070c.title: rfc>9111
0560857d070c.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.2. Response Directives > 5.2.2.7. private
0560857d070c.sentence: The unqualified private response directive indicates that a shared cache MUST NOT store the response (i.e., the response is intended for a single user).

414075fd64ce.title: rfc>9111
414075fd64ce.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.2. Response Directives > 5.2.2.7. private
414075fd64ce.sentence: It also indicates that a private cache MAY store the response, subject to the constraints defined in Section 3, even if the response would not otherwise be heuristically cacheable by a private cache.

22a74051ef52.title: rfc>9111
22a74051ef52.section: 3. Storing Responses in Caches > 3.5. Storing Responses to Authenticated Requests
22a74051ef52.sentence: A shared cache MUST NOT use a cached response to a request with an Authorization header field (Section 11.6.2 of ) to satisfy any subsequent request unless the response contains a Cache-Control field with a response directive (Section 5.2.2) that allows it to be stored by a shared cache, and the cache conforms to the requirements of that directive for that response.

298702968178.title: rfc>9111
298702968178.section: 5. Field Definitions > 5.2. Cache-Control > 5.2.2. Response Directives > 5.2.2.10. s-maxage
298702968178.sentence: The s-maxage response directive indicates that, for a shared cache, the maximum age specified by this directive overrides the maximum age specified by either the max-age directive or the Expires header field.

7c19e7cadb40.title: rfc>9111
7c19e7cadb40.sentence: In particular, because private caches are restricted to a single user, they can be used to reconstruct a user's activity.

c43279458a22.title: rfc>9111
c43279458a22.sentence: As a result, it is important for user agents to allow end users to control them, for example, by allowing stored responses to be removed for some or all origin servers.

2f8e7c4484c6.title: rfc>9111
2f8e7c4484c6.sentence: Caches expose an additional attack surface because the contents of the cache represent an attractive target for malicious exploitation.

ff16e1290226.title: rfc>9111
ff16e1290226.sentence: Since cache contents persist after an HTTP request is complete, an attack on the cache can reveal information long after a user believes that the information has been removed from the network.

509cd795dad4.title: rfc>9111
509cd795dad4.sentence: Storing malicious content in a cache can extend the reach of an attacker to affect multiple users.

e684543030a6.title: rfc>9111
e684543030a6.sentence: Such "cache poisoning" attacks happen when an attacker uses implementation flaws, elevated privileges, or other techniques to insert a response into a cache.

b04385f8eac0.title: rfc>9111
b04385f8eac0.sentence: This is especially effective when shared caches are used to distribute malicious content to many clients.

e029f6f16a35.title: rfc>9111
e029f6f16a35.sentence: One common attack vector for cache poisoning is to exploit differences in message parsing on proxies and in user agents; see Section 6.3 of [HTTP/1.1] for the relevant requirements regarding HTTP/1.1.

31d3ef3b49b3.title: rfc>9111
31d3ef3b49b3.sentence: Because one of the primary uses of a cache is to optimize performance, its use can "leak" information about which resources have been previously requested.

64a1382a58a5.title: rfc>9111
64a1382a58a5.sentence: For example, if a user visits a site and their browser caches some of its responses and then navigates to a second site, that site can attempt to load responses it knows exist on the first site.

931f62c3818c.title: rfc>9111
931f62c3818c.sentence: If they load quickly, it can be assumed that the user has visited that site, or even a specific page on it.

fa6dbb8847e9.title: rfc>9111
fa6dbb8847e9.sentence: Such "timing attacks" can be mitigated by adding more information to the cache key, such as the identity of the referring site (to prevent the attack described above).

7744ffda849b.title: rfc>9111
7744ffda849b.section: 7. Security Considerations > 7.3. Caching of Sensitive Information
7744ffda849b.sentence: Implementation and deployment flaws (often led to by the misunderstanding of cache operation) might lead to the caching of sensitive information (e.g., authentication credentials) that is thought to be private, exposing it to unauthorized parties.

525eed0e4224.title: rfc>9111
525eed0e4224.section: 7. Security Considerations > 7.3. Caching of Sensitive Information
525eed0e4224.sentence: Note that the Set-Cookie response header field does not inhibit caching; a cacheable response with a Set-Cookie header field can be (and often is) used to satisfy subsequent requests to caches.

105b95625b39.title: Transport Layer Security
105b95625b39.sentence: Transport Layer Security (TLS) is a cryptographic protocol designed to provide secured communications over a computer network, such as the Internet.

153d17857fa2.title: Transport Layer Security
153d17857fa2.sentence: The TLS protocol aims primarily to provide security, including privacy (confidentiality), integrity, and authenticity through the use of cryptography, such as the use of certificates, between two or more communicating computer applications.

f607812fde08.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
f607812fde08.sentence: There are three main components to what the TLS protocol accomplishes:

fc98b7a7d7ab.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
fc98b7a7d7ab.sentence: - Encryption: hides the data being transferred from third parties.

9f4c72bd5c68.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
9f4c72bd5c68.sentence: - Authentication: ensures that the parties exchanging information are who they claim to be.

ef67fdd5edbc.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
ef67fdd5edbc.sentence: - Integrity: verifies that the data has not been forged or tampered with.

7c353f0caac3.title: Transport Layer Security
7c353f0caac3.sentence: The protocol is widely used in applications such as email, instant messaging, and voice over IP, but its use in securing HTTPS remains the most publicly visible.

7cc187b4f3c9.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
7cc187b4f3c9.sentence: A primary use case of TLS is encrypting the communication between web applications and servers.

d199ac0c38e9.title: Transport Layer Security
d199ac0c38e9.sentence: This use of TLS to secure HTTP traffic constitutes the HTTPS protocol.

7fa44641edb2.title: gh>karanpratapsingh/system-design/README.md::ssl-tls-mtls
7fa44641edb2.sentence: TLS evolved from a previous encryption protocol called Secure Sockets Layer (SSL).

7e28736cef36.title: Transport Layer Security
7e28736cef36.sentence: TLS is a proposed Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) standard, first defined in 1999, and the current version is TLS 1.3, defined in August 2018.

cd638508623b.title: Transport Layer Security
cd638508623b.sentence: TLS builds on the now-deprecated SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) specifications (1994, 1995, 1996) developed by Netscape Communications for adding the HTTPS protocol to their Netscape Navigator web browser.

ce862db6fa46.title: Transport Layer Security
ce862db6fa46.sentence: It runs in the presentation layer and is itself composed of two layers: the TLS record and the TLS handshake protocols.

20fc864996ee.title: Transport Layer Security
20fc864996ee.sentence: TLS runs "on top of some reliable transport protocol (e.g., TCP)", which would imply that it is above the transport layer.

76403310ce5f.title: Transport Layer Security
76403310ce5f.sentence: Since applications can communicate either with or without TLS (or SSL), it is necessary for the client to request that the server set up a TLS connection.

dc5b102667b5.title: Transport Layer Security
dc5b102667b5.sentence: One of the main ways of achieving this is to use a different port number for TLS connections.

c77524dac57c.title: Transport Layer Security
c77524dac57c.sentence: Port 80 is typically used for unencrypted HTTP traffic while port 443 is the common port used for encrypted HTTPS traffic.

fdb9a3f26f19.title: Transport Layer Security
fdb9a3f26f19.sentence: Another mechanism is to make a protocol-specific STARTTLS request to the server to switch the connection to TLS – for example, when using some mail and news protocols.

8029b7768163.title: Transport Layer Security
8029b7768163.sentence: The protocols use a handshake with an asymmetric cipher to establish not only cipher settings but also a session-specific shared key with which further communication is encrypted using a symmetric cipher.

6c5563da51d1.title: Transport Layer Security
6c5563da51d1.sentence: - The connection is private (or has confidentiality) because a symmetric-key algorithm is used to encrypt the data transmitted.

f60980a20778.title: Transport Layer Security
f60980a20778.sentence: The keys for this symmetric encryption are generated uniquely for each connection and are based on a shared secret that was negotiated at the start of the session.

ad15623a7d71.title: Transport Layer Security
ad15623a7d71.sentence: - The identity of the communicating parties can be authenticated using public-key cryptography.

16e3e8388c6a.title: Transport Layer Security
16e3e8388c6a.sentence: This authentication is required for the server and optional for the client.

fc3b732b4079.title: Transport Layer Security
fc3b732b4079.sentence: - The connection is reliable (or has integrity) because each message transmitted includes a message integrity check using a message authentication code to prevent undetected loss or alteration of the data during transmission.

af58a95db7f6.title: HTTPS
af58a95db7f6.sentence: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) is an extension of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

5c2997b604e2.title: HTTPS
5c2997b604e2.sentence: It uses encryption for secure communication over a computer network, and is widely used on the Internet.

322a610b236f.title: HTTPS
322a610b236f.sentence: In HTTPS, the communication protocol is encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS) or, formerly, Secure Sockets Layer (SSL).

cfc115101fe0.title: gh>ByteByteGoHq/system-design-101/data/guides/how-does-https-work.md
cfc115101fe0.sentence: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) is an extension of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP.) HTTPS transmits encrypted data using Transport Layer Security (TLS.) If the data is hijacked online, all the hijacker gets is binary code.

743faa8467e2.title: HTTPS
743faa8467e2.sentence: The principal motivations for HTTPS are authentication of the accessed website and protection of the privacy and integrity of the exchanged data while it is in transit.

f08e8fc558d6.title: HTTPS
f08e8fc558d6.sentence: Strictly speaking, HTTPS is not a separate protocol, but refers to the use of ordinary HTTP over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection.

0bb482a2a67b.title: HTTPS
0bb482a2a67b.sentence: HTTPS URLs begin with "https://" and use port 443 by default, whereas HTTP URLs begin with "http://" and use port 80 by default.

3b53ece3c8fe.title: HTTPS
3b53ece3c8fe.sentence: HTTP is not encrypted and thus is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle and eavesdropping attacks, which can let attackers gain access to website accounts and sensitive information, and modify webpages to inject malware or advertisements.

1bfd0cc74200.title: HTTPS
1bfd0cc74200.sentence: HTTPS is designed to withstand such attacks and is considered secure against them (with the exception of HTTPS implementations that use deprecated versions of SSL).

895aae7af67b.title: HTTPS
895aae7af67b.sentence: Because HTTPS piggybacks HTTP entirely on top of TLS, the entirety of the underlying HTTP protocol can be encrypted.

f674f29a0f03.title: HTTPS
f674f29a0f03.sentence: This includes the request's URL, query parameters, headers, and cookies (which often contain identifying information about the user).

aad099a42f22.title: HTTPS
aad099a42f22.sentence: HTTPS encrypts all message contents, including the HTTP headers and the request/response data.

2866a5b7aea2.title: HTTPS
2866a5b7aea2.sentence: SSL/TLS is especially suited for HTTP, since it can provide some protection even if only one side of the communication is authenticated.

7d6e673d57e7.title: HTTPS
7d6e673d57e7.sentence: This is the case with HTTP transactions over the Internet, where typically only the server is authenticated (by the client examining the server's certificate).

3ba27012f751.title: HTTPS
3ba27012f751.sentence: The authentication aspect of HTTPS requires a trusted third party to sign server-side digital certificates.

7d959e8f6412.title: HTTPS
7d959e8f6412.sentence: The security of HTTPS is that of the underlying TLS, which typically uses long-term public and private keys to generate a short-term session key, which is then used to encrypt the data flow between the client and the server.

7fd2b73e1ebc.title: HTTPS
7fd2b73e1ebc.sentence: For HTTPS to be effective, a site must be completely hosted over HTTPS.

ccd10640de2c.title: HTTPS
ccd10640de2c.sentence: If some of the site's contents are loaded over HTTP (scripts or images, for example), or if only a certain page that contains sensitive information, such as a log-in page, is loaded over HTTPS while the rest of the site is loaded over plain HTTP, the user will be vulnerable to attacks and surveillance.

784d122a7686.title: HTTPS
784d122a7686.sentence: Deploying HTTPS also allows the use of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (and their predecessors SPDY and QUIC), which are new HTTP versions designed to reduce page load times, size, and latency.

2c2b0e83d62f.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
2c2b0e83d62f.sentence: In information security, a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, or on-path attack, is a scenario where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters the communications between two parties who believe that they are directly communicating with each other.

0b6a8144d1f2.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
0b6a8144d1f2.sentence: One example of a MITM attack is active eavesdropping, in which the attacker makes independent connections with the victims and relays messages between them to make them believe they are talking directly to each other over a private connection, when in fact the entire conversation is controlled by the attacker.

23b0b6489d1f.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
23b0b6489d1f.sentence: In this scenario, the attacker must be able to intercept all relevant messages passing between the two victims and inject new ones.

e3eaab9558ad.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
e3eaab9558ad.sentence: This is straightforward in many circumstances; for example, an attacker within range of a Wi-Fi access point hosting a network without encryption could insert themselves as a man in the middle.

cabdae0c07bd.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
cabdae0c07bd.sentence: As it aims to circumvent mutual authentication, a MITM attack can succeed only when the attacker impersonates each endpoint sufficiently well to satisfy their expectations.

6c2ff5de84c4.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
6c2ff5de84c4.sentence: - Mallory replaces Bob's key with her own, and relays this to Alice, claiming that it is Bob's key: Alice ← [Mallory's key] Mallory Bob

5d71cc1a4c12.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
5d71cc1a4c12.sentence: - Alice encrypts a message with what she believes to be Bob's key, thinking that only Bob can read it: Alice "Meet me at the bus stop!" [encrypted with Mallory's key] → Mallory Bob

a25786c3415b.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
a25786c3415b.sentence: - However, because it was actually encrypted with Mallory's key, Mallory can decrypt it, read it, modify it (if desired), re-encrypt with Bob's key, and forward it to Bob: Alice Mallory "Meet me at the park!" [encrypted with Bob's key] → Bob

0801465198c6.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
0801465198c6.sentence: This example shows the need for Alice and Bob to have a means to ensure that they are truly each using each other's public keys, and not the public key of an attacker.

7066e70026f0.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
7066e70026f0.sentence: - HTTPS spoofing: The attacker tricks the victim into believing their connection is secure by substituting a fake SSL/TLS certificate.

97be3cefcd0a.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
97be3cefcd0a.sentence: - SSL/TLS stripping: Downgrades HTTPS traffic to HTTP, intercepting and reading unencrypted data.

1e79a2456393.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
1e79a2456393.sentence: - ARP spoofing: Sends fake ARP messages to associate the attacker's MAC address with a target IP, intercepting local network traffic.

6b5b24b89e44.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
6b5b24b89e44.sentence: - DNS spoofing or poisoning: Redirects DNS queries to malicious servers, leading victims to fake websites.

09a4ae73488d.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
09a4ae73488d.sentence: - Session hijacking: Steals session cookies or tokens to impersonate a legitimate user in an active session.

70bb69f43478.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
70bb69f43478.sentence: - Wi-Fi MITM (evil twin attack): Creates a fake Wi-Fi hotspot to intercept communications from connected devices.

f715e1254f29.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
f715e1254f29.sentence: - Fake certificate authority (CA): Uses a fraudulent CA to sign fake certificates, tricking victims into trusting malicious connections.

d420a21a1d05.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
d420a21a1d05.sentence: MITM attacks can be prevented or detected by two means: authentication and tamper detection.

19f2d45b8c11.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
19f2d45b8c11.sentence: Most cryptographic protocols include some form of endpoint authentication specifically to prevent MITM attacks.

f481107f8a12.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
f481107f8a12.sentence: For example, TLS can authenticate one or both parties using a mutually trusted certificate authority.

66dd76987ee2.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
66dd76987ee2.sentence: In such structures, clients and servers exchange certificates which are issued and verified by a trusted third party called a certificate authority (CA).

4c7f64df7b70.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
4c7f64df7b70.sentence: DNSSEC extends the DNS protocol to use signatures to authenticate DNS records, preventing simple MITM attacks from directing a client to a malicious IP address.

4bb52f7b71b6.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
4bb52f7b71b6.sentence: Use of mutual authentication, in which both the server and the client validate the other's communication, covers both ends of a MITM attack.

72c1957c3ff5.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
72c1957c3ff5.sentence: However, the default behavior of most connections is to only authenticate the server, which means mutual authentication is not always employed and MITM attacks can still occur.

e2a7b1d7f4d8.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
e2a7b1d7f4d8.sentence: To detect potential attacks, parties check for discrepancies in response times.

4356cdb73a49.title: Man-in-the-middle attack
4356cdb73a49.sentence: If one transaction, however, were to take an abnormal length of time to reach the other party, this could be indicative of a third party's presence interfering with the connection and inserting additional latency in the transaction.

2a18a2d04c2c.title: End-to-end encryption
2a18a2d04c2c.sentence: But, rather than try to break the encryption, an eavesdropper may impersonate a message recipient (during key exchange or by substituting their public key for the recipient's), so that messages are encrypted with a key known to the attacker.

56f67bd3a382.title: End-to-end encryption
56f67bd3a382.sentence: After decrypting the message, the snoop can then encrypt it with a key that they share with the actual recipient, or their public key in case of asymmetric systems, and send the message on again to avoid detection.

ed972a839d89.title: HTTP cookie
ed972a839d89.sentence: Most websites use cookies as the only identifiers for user sessions, because other methods of identifying web users have limitations and vulnerabilities.

b3883e885896.title: HTTP cookie
b3883e885896.sentence: If a website uses cookies as session identifiers, attackers can impersonate users' requests by stealing a full set of victims' cookies.

61248b8a150f.title: HTTP cookie
61248b8a150f.sentence: From the web server's point of view, a request from an attacker then has the same authentication as the victim's requests; thus the request is performed on behalf of the victim's session.

a2805d56b3b0.title: HTTP cookie
a2805d56b3b0.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Network eavesdropping
a2805d56b3b0.sentence: Traffic on a network can be intercepted and read by computers on the network other than the sender and receiver (particularly over unencrypted open Wi-Fi).

689e545be478.title: HTTP cookie
689e545be478.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Network eavesdropping
689e545be478.sentence: This traffic includes cookies sent on ordinary unencrypted HTTP sessions.

b7fcd24bc785.title: HTTP cookie
b7fcd24bc785.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Network eavesdropping
b7fcd24bc785.sentence: This issue can be resolved by securing the communication between the user's computer and the server by employing Transport Layer Security (HTTPS protocol) to encrypt the connection.

e38201ff6173.title: HTTP cookie
e38201ff6173.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Network eavesdropping
e38201ff6173.sentence: A server can specify the Secure flag while setting a cookie, which will cause the browser to send the cookie only over an encrypted channel, such as a TLS connection.

645c7ee114bb.title: HTTP cookie
645c7ee114bb.section: Implementation > Cookie attributes > Secure and HttpOnly
645c7ee114bb.sentence: The Secure attribute is meant to keep cookie communication limited to encrypted transmission, directing browsers to use cookies only via secure/encrypted connections.

05e0bbc4e362.title: HTTP cookie
05e0bbc4e362.section: Implementation > Cookie attributes > Secure and HttpOnly
05e0bbc4e362.sentence: However, if a web server sets a cookie with a secure attribute from a non-secure connection, the cookie can still be intercepted when it is sent to the user by man-in-the-middle attacks.

fd3139ffa80b.title: HTTP cookie
fd3139ffa80b.section: Implementation > Cookie attributes > Secure and HttpOnly
fd3139ffa80b.sentence: Therefore, for maximum security, cookies with the Secure attribute should only be set over a secure connection.

31f4a15ced7a.title: HTTP cookie
31f4a15ced7a.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site scripting: cookie theft
31f4a15ced7a.sentence: Cookies can also be stolen using a technique called cross-site scripting.

e110bf9c7e6d.title: HTTP cookie
e110bf9c7e6d.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site scripting: cookie theft
e110bf9c7e6d.sentence: By posting malicious HTML and JavaScript code, the attacker can cause the victim's web browser to send the victim's cookies to a website the attacker controls.

18b06febb22c.title: HTTP cookie
18b06febb22c.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site scripting: cookie theft
18b06febb22c.sentence: Such attacks can be mitigated by using HttpOnly cookies.

4d2a21b28413.title: HTTP cookie
4d2a21b28413.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site scripting: cookie theft
4d2a21b28413.sentence: These cookies will not be accessible by client-side scripting languages like JavaScript, and therefore, the attacker will not be able to gather these cookies.

bf37828335d4.title: HTTP cookie
bf37828335d4.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site scripting: cookie theft
bf37828335d4.sentence: It is the responsibility of the website developers to filter out such malicious code.

5af057aef19a.title: Cross-site request forgery
5af057aef19a.sentence: A general property of web browsers is that they will automatically and invisibly include any cookies (including session cookies and others) used by a given domain in any web request sent to that domain.

0e83b26b1f99.title: HTTP cookie
0e83b26b1f99.section: Cookie theft and session hijacking > Cross-site request forgery
0e83b26b1f99.sentence: If Bob's bank keeps his authentication information in a cookie, and if the cookie hasn't expired, then the attempt by Bob's browser to load the image will submit the withdrawal form with his cookie, thus authorizing a transaction without Bob's approval.

9c358e9e318b.title: Cross-site request forgery
9c358e9e318b.sentence: The web server will not be able to identify the forgery because the request was made by a user that was logged in, and submitted all the requisite cookies.

7ad588b79ac4.title: HTTP cookie
7ad588b79ac4.sentence: With attribute SameSite=Strict, the browsers would only send cookies to a target domain that is the same as the origin domain.

8386d37e70ea.title: HTTP cookie
8386d37e70ea.sentence: This would effectively mitigate cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks.

15cadb0235f2.title: HTTP cookie
15cadb0235f2.sentence: With SameSite=Lax, browsers would send cookies with requests to a target domain even it is different from the origin domain, but only for safe requests such as GET (POST is unsafe) and not third-party cookies (inside iframe).

ed90bfe0b562.title: HTTP cookie
ed90bfe0b562.sentence: Attribute SameSite=None would allow third-party (cross-site) cookies, however, most browsers require secure attribute on SameSite=None cookies.

607589f13f4f.title: Transport Layer Security
607589f13f4f.sentence: Datagram Transport Layer Security, abbreviated DTLS, is a related communications protocol providing security to datagram-based applications by allowing them to communicate in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, or message forgery.

b029ccb51c9b.title: Transport Layer Security
b029ccb51c9b.sentence: The DTLS protocol is based on the stream-oriented Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol and is intended to provide similar security guarantees.

03220cf4b7d4.title: Transport Layer Security
03220cf4b7d4.sentence: However, unlike TLS, it can be used with most datagram oriented protocols including User Datagram Protocol (UDP), Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP), Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) encapsulation, and Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP).

10a6c393bf75.title: Transport Layer Security
10a6c393bf75.sentence: As the DTLS protocol datagram preserves the semantics of the underlying transport, the application does not suffer from the delays associated with stream protocols.

50edcee08f93.title: Transport Layer Security
50edcee08f93.sentence: However, the application has to deal with packet reordering, loss of datagram and data larger than the size of a datagram network packet.

c335304dfbb2.title: Transport Layer Security
c335304dfbb2.sentence: Because DTLS uses UDP or SCTP rather than TCP, it avoids the TCP meltdown problem, when being used to create a VPN tunnel.

c61c37dbef5d.title: Transport Layer Security
c61c37dbef5d.sentence: In addition all modern web browsers support DTLS-SRTP for WebRTC.

9442c4af601f.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
9442c4af601f.sentence: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a policy mechanism that helps to protect websites against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrade attacks and cookie hijacking.

b64eaf53b349.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
b64eaf53b349.sentence: It allows web servers to declare that web browsers (or other complying user agents) should automatically interact with it using only HTTPS connections, which provide Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL), unlike the insecure HTTP used alone.

e09156a3c12f.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
e09156a3c12f.sentence: The HSTS Policy is communicated by the server to the user agent via an HTTP response header field named Strict-Transport-Security.

5592619cc4ac.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
5592619cc4ac.sentence: A server implements an HSTS policy by supplying a header over an HTTPS connection (HSTS headers over HTTP are ignored).

6ee8b6ab9a67.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
6ee8b6ab9a67.sentence: For example, a server could send a header such that future requests to the domain for the next year (max-age is specified in seconds; 31,536,000 is equal to one non-leap year) use only HTTPS: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000.

43d7ce9ca288.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
43d7ce9ca288.sentence: HSTS Policy specifies a period of time during which the user agent should only access the server in a secure fashion.

b6c61eb5f38b.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
b6c61eb5f38b.sentence: - Automatically turn any insecure links referencing the web application into secure links (e.g. http://example.com/some/page/ will be modified to https://example.com/some/page/ before accessing the server).

dacf9f757239.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
dacf9f757239.sentence: - If the security of the connection cannot be ensured (e.g. the server's TLS certificate is not trusted), the user agent must terminate the connection and should not allow the user to access the web application.

30901ced4a6b.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
30901ced4a6b.sentence: The way this protection works is that when a user enters or selects an HTTP (not HTTPS) URL to the site, the client, such as a Web browser, will automatically upgrade to HTTPS without making an HTTP request, thereby preventing any HTTP man-in-the-middle attack from occurring.

454ffd2162cd.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
454ffd2162cd.sentence: The SSL (and TLS) stripping attack works by transparently converting a secure HTTPS connection into a plain HTTP connection.

9e9127ce85fe.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
9e9127ce85fe.sentence: The user can see that the connection is insecure, but crucially there is no way of knowing whether the connection should be secure.

8f277b7e57ea.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
8f277b7e57ea.sentence: Additionally, no warnings are presented to the user during the downgrade process, making the attack fairly subtle to all but the most vigilant.

30b6ed4eb583.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
30b6ed4eb583.sentence: HSTS addresses this problem by informing the browser that connections to the site should always use TLS/SSL.

5a3c4c0e9185.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
5a3c4c0e9185.sentence: The most important security vulnerability that HSTS can fix is SSL-stripping man-in-the-middle attacks, first publicly introduced by Moxie Marlinspike in his 2009 BlackHat Federal talk "New Tricks For Defeating SSL In Practice".

c14345a0e7b1.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
c14345a0e7b1.sentence: The protection normally only applies after a user has visited the site at least once, relying on the principle of "trust on first use".

7eb0844b9588.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
7eb0844b9588.sentence: The initial request remains unprotected from active attacks if it uses an insecure protocol such as plain HTTP or if the URI for the initial request was obtained over an insecure channel.

9cf8f789c7c4.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
9cf8f789c7c4.sentence: The same applies to the first request after the activity period specified in the advertised HSTS Policy max-age (sites should set a period of several days or months depending on user activity and behavior).

27b68a5294f2.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
27b68a5294f2.sentence: The HSTS header can be stripped by the attacker if this is the user's first visit.

8ba772d9065d.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
8ba772d9065d.sentence: To counteract this problem, an HSTS preload list maintained by Google Chrome and used by other major web browsers is maintained.

23e42bce3ee6.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
23e42bce3ee6.sentence: If a domain is on this list, the browser skips the initial request and encrypts all communication immediately.

d5c8190542dc.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
d5c8190542dc.sentence: Additional domains can be registered at no cost.

f1e7bedc0ecd.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
f1e7bedc0ecd.sentence: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Internet Explorer/Microsoft Edge address this limitation by implementing a "HSTS preloaded list", which is a list that contains known sites supporting HSTS.

c6bd9d784736.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
c6bd9d784736.sentence: This list is distributed with the browser so that it uses HTTPS for the initial request to the listed sites as well.

1e3acef44c15.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
1e3acef44c15.sentence: Unfortunately this solution cannot scale to include all websites on the internet.

17e7779d0270.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
17e7779d0270.sentence: Depending on the actual deployment there are certain threats (e.g. cookie injection attacks) that can be avoided by following best practices.

f77cc751ac63.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
f77cc751ac63.sentence: - HSTS hosts should declare HSTS policy at their top-level domain name.

b7f49d01e81b.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
b7f49d01e81b.sentence: For example, an HSTS host at https://sub.example.com should also answer with the HSTS header at https://example.com.

53e2af3bffd3.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
53e2af3bffd3.sentence: The header should specify the includeSubDomains directive.

2fdcd514f1fd.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
2fdcd514f1fd.sentence: - In addition to HSTS deployment, a host for https://www.example.com should include a request to a resource from https://example.com to make sure that HSTS for the parent domain is set and protects the user from potential cookie injection attacks performed by a MITM that would inject a reference to the parent domain (or even http://nonexistentpeer.example.com), which the attacker then would answer.

437744ef79bf.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
437744ef79bf.sentence: Even with an HSTS preloaded list, HSTS cannot prevent advanced attacks against TLS itself, such as the BEAST or CRIME attacks introduced by Juliano Rizzo and Thai Duong.

c635ec28a277.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
c635ec28a277.sentence: Neither can it protect against attacks on the server - if someone compromises it, it will happily serve any content over TLS.

9490027e661e.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
9490027e661e.sentence: Junade Ali has noted that HSTS is ineffective against the use of false domains; by using DNS-based attacks, it is possible for a man-in-the-middle interceptor to serve traffic from an artificial domain which is not on the HSTS Preload list, this can be made possible by DNS Spoofing Attacks, or simply a domain name that misleadingly resembles the real domain name such as www.example.org instead of www.example.com.

dcd6e4b34f5b.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
dcd6e4b34f5b.sentence: Because HSTS is time limited, it is sensitive to attacks involving shifting the victim's computer time e.g. using false NTP packets.

855db06b09c8.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
855db06b09c8.sentence: HSTS can be used to tag visiting browsers with recoverable identifying data which can persist even after clearing cookies.

7ec438c9e9d5.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
7ec438c9e9d5.sentence: The difficulty of deleting the HSTS policy of visited domains is a deliberate decision defined in RFC 6797.

d9dad5166ecb.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
d9dad5166ecb.sentence: Because web browsers are required to persistently cache the HSTS policy of previously-visited domains, a webpage that makes multiple HTTP requests to selected domains whose HSTS states are coordinated at page-visit time can fingerprint visitors by observing which requests are upgraded to HTTPS on repeated visits.

f6ce32640c42.title: rfc>9110
f6ce32640c42.section: 4. Identifiers in HTTP > 4.3. Authoritative Access > 4.3.1. URI Origin
f6ce32640c42.sentence: The "origin" for a given URI is the triple of scheme, host, and port after normalizing the scheme and host to lowercase and normalizing the port to remove any leading zeros.

73f9766b2a85.title: rfc>9110
73f9766b2a85.section: 4. Identifiers in HTTP > 4.3. Authoritative Access > 4.3.4. https Certificate Verification
73f9766b2a85.sentence: To establish a secured connection to dereference a URI, a client MUST verify that the service's identity is an acceptable match for the URI's origin server.

8f7f75662179.title: rfc>8446
8f7f75662179.sentence: TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.

5de672d3b11e.title: rfc>8446
5de672d3b11e.sentence: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol.

772e328c7a81.title: rfc>8446
772e328c7a81.sentence: The primary goal of TLS is to provide a secure channel between two communicating peers; the only requirement from the underlying transport is a reliable, in-order data stream.

2d430e027656.title: rfc>8446
2d430e027656.sentence: - Authentication: The server side of the channel is always authenticated; the client side is optionally authenticated.

686f6a98c415.title: rfc>8446
686f6a98c415.sentence: - Confidentiality: Data sent over the channel after establishment is only visible to the endpoints.

cbd86348e39e.title: rfc>8446
cbd86348e39e.sentence: - Integrity: Data sent over the channel after establishment cannot be modified by attackers without detection.

4ff150af9259.title: rfc>8446
4ff150af9259.sentence: These properties should be true even in the face of an attacker who has complete control of the network, as described in.

99d879043d92.title: rfc>8446
99d879043d92.sentence: TLS consists of two primary components:

59366f384768.title: rfc>8446
59366f384768.sentence: - A handshake protocol (Section 4) that authenticates the communicating parties, negotiates cryptographic modes and parameters, and establishes shared keying material.

b9b6225e7e5e.title: rfc>8446
b9b6225e7e5e.sentence: The handshake protocol is designed to resist tampering; an active attacker should not be able to force the peers to negotiate different parameters than they would if the connection were not under attack.

6be27c9561c4.title: rfc>8446
6be27c9561c4.sentence: - A record protocol (Section 5) that uses the parameters established by the handshake protocol to protect traffic between the communicating peers.

fce2a2c19a90.title: rfc>8446
fce2a2c19a90.sentence: The record protocol divides traffic up into a series of records, each of which is independently protected using the traffic keys.

6043c868915e.title: rfc>8446
6043c868915e.sentence: - The list of supported symmetric encryption algorithms has been pruned of all algorithms that are considered legacy.

8d33684da566.title: rfc>8446
8d33684da566.sentence: Those that remain are all Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms.

d2d664ecdced.title: rfc>8446
d2d664ecdced.sentence: - Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy.

cfb61da4c850.title: rfc>8446
cfb61da4c850.sentence: - Other cryptographic improvements were made, including changing the RSA padding to use the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS), and the removal of compression, the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), and custom Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) groups.

851e297ad093.title: rfc>8446
851e297ad093.sentence: The handshake can be thought of as having three phases (indicated in the diagram above):

988993e5fc87.title: rfc>8446
988993e5fc87.sentence: - Key Exchange: Establish shared keying material and select the cryptographic parameters.

77643578d5ce.title: rfc>8446
77643578d5ce.sentence: - Server Parameters: Establish other handshake parameters (whether the client is authenticated, application-layer protocol support, etc.).

daac84d2299d.title: rfc>8446
daac84d2299d.sentence: - Authentication: Authenticate the server (and, optionally, the client) and provide key confirmation and handshake integrity.

a1982d076105.title: rfc>8446
a1982d076105.sentence: - All handshake messages after the ServerHello are now encrypted.

ac3bd7c82812.title: rfc>8446
ac3bd7c82812.sentence: In the Key Exchange phase, the client sends the ClientHello (Section 4.1.2) message, which contains a random nonce (ClientHello.random); its offered protocol versions; a list of symmetric cipher/HKDF hash pairs; either a set of Diffie-Hellman key shares (in the "key_share" (Section 4.2.8) extension), a set of pre-shared key labels (in the "pre_shared_key" (Section 4.2.11) extension), or both; and potentially additional extensions.

da49699b97fb.title: rfc>8446
da49699b97fb.sentence: The server processes the ClientHello and determines the appropriate cryptographic parameters for the connection.

59c59d3d84ec.title: rfc>8446
59c59d3d84ec.sentence: It then responds with its own ServerHello (Section 4.1.3), which indicates the negotiated connection parameters.

eada88d6af6f.title: rfc>8446
eada88d6af6f.sentence: The combination of the ClientHello and the ServerHello determines the shared keys.

3decdba1f324.title: rfc>8446
3decdba1f324.sentence: TLS uses the same set of messages every time that certificate-based authentication is needed.

69702bfc5ad9.title: rfc>8446
69702bfc5ad9.sentence: Certificate: The certificate of the endpoint and any per-certificate extensions.

1c7b7a934229.title: rfc>8446
1c7b7a934229.sentence: CertificateVerify: A signature over the entire handshake using the private key corresponding to the public key in the Certificate message.

ee4c142e125a.title: rfc>8446
ee4c142e125a.sentence: Finished: A MAC (Message Authentication Code) over the entire handshake.

b4526fcd9573.title: rfc>8446
b4526fcd9573.sentence: This message provides key confirmation, binds the endpoint's identity to the exchanged keys, and in PSK mode also authenticates the handshake.

95d29d30b87a.title: rfc>8446
95d29d30b87a.sentence: Upon receiving the server's messages, the client responds with its Authentication messages, namely Certificate and CertificateVerify (if requested), and Finished.

d656ba225661.title: rfc>8446
d656ba225661.sentence: If the client has not provided a sufficient "key_share" extension (e.g., it includes only DHE or ECDHE groups unacceptable to or unsupported by the server), the server corrects the mismatch with a HelloRetryRequest and the client needs to restart the handshake with an appropriate "key_share" extension, as shown in Figure 2.

e8ac451fdd42.title: rfc>8446
e8ac451fdd42.sentence: If no common cryptographic parameters can be negotiated, the server MUST abort the handshake with an appropriate alert.

4dff04c5672a.title: rfc>8446
4dff04c5672a.sentence: TLS supports three basic key exchange modes:

4d3a4a0841d4.title: rfc>8446
4d3a4a0841d4.sentence: - (EC)DHE (Diffie-Hellman over either finite fields or elliptic curves)

5b1df12d3837.title: rfc>8446
5b1df12d3837.sentence: - The key derivation functions have been redesigned.

5807fef4822e.title: rfc>8446
5807fef4822e.sentence: The new design allows easier analysis by cryptographers due to their improved key separation properties.

bcbe06b4ada8.title: rfc>8446

ec6b39ede3e6.sentence: The simplest form of anti-replay defense is for the server to only allow each session ticket to be used once.

dd25916680d8.title: rfc>8446
dd25916680d8.sentence: For instance, the server can maintain a database of all outstanding valid tickets, deleting each ticket from the database as it is used.

f8a9f7a14aaa.title: rfc>8446
f8a9f7a14aaa.sentence: If an unknown ticket is provided, the server would then fall back to a full handshake.

05076feb9753.title: rfc>8446
05076feb9753.sentence: Because this mechanism requires sharing the session database between server nodes in environments with multiple distributed servers, it may be hard to achieve high rates of successful PSK 0-RTT connections when compared to self-encrypted tickets.

9a6e232f2746.title: rfc>8446
9a6e232f2746.sentence: An alternative form of anti-replay is to record a unique value derived from the ClientHello (generally either the random value or the PSK binder) and reject duplicates.

4ae3ca543bf3.title: rfc>8446
4ae3ca543bf3.sentence: Recording all ClientHellos causes state to grow without bound, but a server can instead record ClientHellos within a given time window and use the "obfuscated_ticket_age" to ensure that tickets aren't reused outside that window.

618908219205.title: rfc>8446
