74907af4d057.title: Email
74907af4d057.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
74907af4d057.sentence: - Date: The local time and date the message was written.

5bd46fbc5227.title: Email
5bd46fbc5227.section: Message format > Message body > Content encoding
5bd46fbc5227.sentence: Internet email was designed for 7-bit ASCII.

e3240a00086e.title: Email
e3240a00086e.section: Message format > Message body > Multipart messages
e3240a00086e.sentence: MIME allows including several parts in an email message, such as a cover letter and the related documents (multipart/mixed), the same part as plain text, ODF and PDF (multipart/alternative) or a HTML page with related javascript, CSS and images (multipart/related).

c560df7370c3.title: Email
c560df7370c3.section: Message format > Message body > Multipart messages
c560df7370c3.sentence: The parts can themselves be multipart, such as with a cover letter and an HTML attachment containing images.

c56c63748e19.title: Email
c56c63748e19.section: Message format > Message body > Multipart messages
c56c63748e19.sentence: The sender can (if their software supports it) specify whether a part is to be shown inline by default or to be regarded as an attachment.

374d5edfd8bd.section: Advantages over POP > Access to MIME message parts and partial fetch
374d5edfd8bd.sentence: Usually all Internet e-mail is transmitted in MIME format, allowing messages to have a tree structure where the leaf nodes are any of a variety of single part content types and the non-leaf nodes are any of a variety of multipart types.

967e2a40c929.sentence: The IMAP4 protocol allows clients to retrieve any of the individual MIME parts separately and also to retrieve portions of either individual parts or the entire message.

48736891ed5d.title: Email spam
48736891ed5d.sentence: Email spam, also referred to as junk email, spam mail, or simply spam, refers to unsolicited messages sent in bulk via email.

2ab20515685e.title: Email spam
2ab20515685e.sentence: Spam is a burden for the recipient, who may be required to manage, filter, or delete these unwanted messages.

d9e2115a9951.title: Email spam
d9e2115a9951.sentence: This cost imposed on recipients, without compensation from the sender, makes spam an example of a "negative externality" (a side effect of an activity that affects others who are not involved in the decision).

f69fb0406b58.title: Email
f69fb0406b58.sentence: The low cost of sending such email meant that, by 2003, up to 30% of total email traffic was spam, and was threatening the usefulness of email as a practical tool.

f30914b779c9.title: Email spam
f30914b779c9.sentence: Since the early 1990s, spam has grown significantly, with estimates suggesting that by 2014, it comprised around 90% of all global email traffic.

e722e0630d9c.title: Email

92290fd771e6.sentence: In order to send spam, spammers need to obtain the email addresses of the intended recipients.

827b432b7609.title: Email spam

827b432b7609.sentence: To this end, both spammers themselves and list merchants gather huge lists of potential email addresses.

8da8b28ceded.title: Email spam

8da8b28ceded.sentence: Since spam is, by definition, unsolicited, this address harvesting is done without the consent (and sometimes against the expressed will) of the address owners.

87278c6120eb.title: Email spam

87278c6120eb.sentence: Many spam-filtering techniques work by searching for patterns in the headers or bodies of messages.

92b46674adf4.sentence: To defeat such filters, the spammer may intentionally misspell commonly filtered words or insert other characters, often in a style similar to leetspeak, as in the following examples: V1agra, Via'gra, Vi@graa, vi*gra, \/iagra.

f5e150c29a5a.title: Email spam
f5e150c29a5a.sentence: Image spam, or image-based spam, is an obfuscation method by which text of the message is stored as a GIF or JPEG image and displayed in the email.

592eb224ecf5.title: Email spam
592eb224ecf5.sentence: This prevents text-based spam filters from detecting and blocking spam messages.

f32de4c10822.title: Email spam
f32de4c10822.sentence: Spammers frequently seek out and make use of vulnerable third-party systems such as open mail relays and open proxy servers.

893e76359050.title: Email spam
893e76359050.sentence: Increasingly, spammers use networks of malware-infected PCs (zombies) to send their spam.

6f41021140e8.title: Email spam
6f41021140e8.sentence: To combat the problems posed by botnets, open relays, and proxy servers, many email server administrators pre-emptively block dynamic IP ranges and impose stringent requirements on other servers wishing to deliver mail.

5cc0b0dbd1a9.title: Email spam
5cc0b0dbd1a9.sentence: Forward-confirmed reverse DNS must be correctly set for the outgoing mail server and large swaths of IP addresses are blocked, sometimes pre-emptively, to prevent spam.

ab41ca3567ff.title: Email spam
ab41ca3567ff.sentence: These measures can pose problems for those wanting to run a small email server off an inexpensive domestic connection.

ea600e945897.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
ea600e945897.sentence: Many Internet service providers now block all outgoing port 25 traffic from their customers, mainly as an anti-spam measure, but also to reduce costs.

fcfe21c2a2ee.title: rfc>5321
fcfe21c2a2ee.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
fcfe21c2a2ee.sentence: There are three steps to SMTP mail transactions.

8028b993868d.title: rfc>5321
8028b993868d.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
8028b993868d.sentence: The transaction starts with a MAIL command that gives the sender identification.

5cebdf66bf89.title: rfc>5321
5cebdf66bf89.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
5cebdf66bf89.sentence: (In general, the MAIL command may be sent only when no mail transaction is in progress; see Section 4.1.4.) A series of one or more RCPT commands follows, giving the receiver information.

e96d78e6c4e3.title: rfc>5321
e96d78e6c4e3.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
e96d78e6c4e3.sentence: Then, a DATA command initiates transfer of the mail data and is terminated by the "end of mail" data indicator, which also confirms the transaction.

82d9b0b8e7f5.title: rfc>5321
82d9b0b8e7f5.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.1. Session Initiation
82d9b0b8e7f5.sentence: An SMTP session is initiated when a client opens a connection to a server and the server responds with an opening message.

25ce3ffc664d.title: rfc>5321
25ce3ffc664d.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.2. Client Initiation
25ce3ffc664d.sentence: Once the server has sent the greeting (welcoming) message and the client has received it, the client normally sends the EHLO command to the server, indicating the client's identity.

69602d712799.title: rfc>5321
69602d712799.sentence: The dialog is purposely lock-step, one-at-a-time, although this can be modified by mutually agreed upon extension requests such as command pipelining (RFC 2920 ).

d7a9ff4c71f5.title: rfc>5321
d7a9ff4c71f5.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
d7a9ff4c71f5.sentence: This command tells the SMTP-receiver that a new mail transaction is starting and to reset all its state tables and buffers, including any recipients or mail data.

267ded0bc160.title: rfc>5321
267ded0bc160.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
267ded0bc160.sentence: The <reverse-path> portion of the first or only argument contains the source mailbox (between "<" and ">" brackets), which can be used to report errors (see Section 4.2 for a discussion of error reporting).

52753358d7ca.title: rfc>5321
52753358d7ca.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
52753358d7ca.sentence: If accepted, the SMTP server returns a "250 OK" reply.

4876face943d.title: rfc>5321
4876face943d.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
4876face943d.sentence: The second step in the procedure is the RCPT command.

67b39ad027ea.title: rfc>5321
67b39ad027ea.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
67b39ad027ea.sentence: This step of the procedure can be repeated any number of times.

5bb020aad169.title: rfc>5321
5bb020aad169.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
5bb020aad169.sentence: If accepted, the SMTP server returns a "250 OK" reply and stores the forward-path.

1ec777919b7e.title: rfc>5321
1ec777919b7e.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
1ec777919b7e.sentence: recipient is known not to be a deliverable address, the SMTP server returns a 550 reply, typically with a string such as "no such user - " and the mailbox name (other circumstances and reply codes are possible).

b6483a098a97.title: rfc>5321
b6483a098a97.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
b6483a098a97.sentence: If a RCPT command appears without a previous MAIL command, the server MUST return a 503 "Bad sequence of commands" response.

43d61cfe47b0.title: rfc>5321
43d61cfe47b0.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
43d61cfe47b0.sentence: If accepted, the SMTP server returns a 354 Intermediate reply and considers all succeeding lines up to but not including the end of mail data indicator to be the message text.

04574fff34bb.title: rfc>5321
04574fff34bb.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
04574fff34bb.sentence: SMTP indicates the end of the mail data by sending a line containing only a "." (period or full stop).

cf54375e30c4.title: rfc>5321
cf54375e30c4.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
cf54375e30c4.sentence: If one of those replies (or any other 5yz reply) is received, the client MUST NOT send the message data; more generally, message data MUST NOT be sent unless a 354 reply is received.

fdc979af22ac.title: rfc>5321
fdc979af22ac.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.2. Transparency
fdc979af22ac.sentence: Without some provision for data transparency, the character sequence "<CRLF>.<CRLF>" ends the mail text and cannot be sent by the user.

46b082c550f2.title: rfc>5321
46b082c550f2.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.2. Transparency
46b082c550f2.sentence: If it is a period, one additional period is inserted at the beginning of the line.

5f7931f551a9.title: rfc>5321
5f7931f551a9.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.2. Transparency
5f7931f551a9.sentence: If the first character is a period and there are other characters on the line, the first character is deleted.

ce60eb1e47c8.title: rfc>5321
ce60eb1e47c8.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
ce60eb1e47c8.sentence: When the end of text is successfully received and stored, the SMTP-receiver sends a "250 OK" reply.

da1629c72292.title: rfc>5321
da1629c72292.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
da1629c72292.sentence: The end of mail data indicator also confirms the mail transaction and tells the SMTP server to now process the stored recipients and mail

129360edeeeb.title: rfc>5321
129360edeeeb.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
129360edeeeb.sentence: When an SMTP server returns a positive completion status (2yz code) after the DATA command is completed with <CRLF>.<CRLF>, it accepts responsibility for:

3d01440dd417.title: rfc>5321
3d01440dd417.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
3d01440dd417.sentence: - delivering the message (if the recipient mailbox exists), or

79fb7a9d1f7a.title: rfc>5321
79fb7a9d1f7a.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
79fb7a9d1f7a.sentence: - if attempts to deliver the message fail due to transient conditions, retrying delivery some reasonable number of times at intervals as specified in Section 4.5.4.

826d90a164ea.title: rfc>5321
826d90a164ea.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
826d90a164ea.sentence: - if attempts to deliver the message fail due to permanent conditions, or if repeated attempts to deliver the message fail due to transient conditions, returning appropriate notification to the sender of the original message (using the address in the SMTP MAIL command).

7e2f2e2e8ba0.title: rfc>5321
7e2f2e2e8ba0.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
7e2f2e2e8ba0.sentence: When an SMTP server returns a temporary error status (4yz) code after the DATA command is completed with <CRLF>.<CRLF>, it MUST NOT make a subsequent attempt to deliver that message.

e6ddaa5e137e.title: rfc>5321
e6ddaa5e137e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
e6ddaa5e137e.sentence: The SMTP client retains responsibility for the delivery of that message and may either return it to the user or requeue it for a subsequent attempt (see Section 4.5.4.1).

4be912283e62.title: rfc>5321
4be912283e62.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
4be912283e62.sentence: When an SMTP server returns a permanent error status (5yz) code after the DATA command is completed with <CRLF>.<CRLF>, it MUST NOT make any subsequent attempt to deliver the message.

623bf71930db.title: rfc>5321
623bf71930db.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.2. SMTP Replies > 4.2.5. Reply Codes after DATA and the Subsequent <CRLF>.<CRLF>
623bf71930db.sentence: As with temporary error status codes, the SMTP client retains responsibility for the message, but SHOULD not again attempt delivery to the same server without user review of the message and response and appropriate intervention.

4a47629424e2.title: rfc>5321
4a47629424e2.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.8. Terminating Sessions and Connections
4a47629424e2.sentence: An SMTP connection is terminated when the client sends a QUIT command.

ca7caed3756e.title: rfc>5321
ca7caed3756e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.1. SMTP Commands > 4.1.1. Command Semantics and Syntax > 4.1.1.10. QUIT (QUIT)
ca7caed3756e.sentence: This command specifies that the receiver MUST send a "221 OK" reply, and then close the transmission channel.

40135ecf2b82.title: rfc>5321
40135ecf2b82.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
40135ecf2b82.sentence: A mail object contains an envelope and content.

b2650f9c092c.title: rfc>5321
b2650f9c092c.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
b2650f9c092c.sentence: The SMTP content is sent in the SMTP DATA protocol unit and has two parts: the header section and the body.

e6bc1a733894.title: rfc>5321
e6bc1a733894.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
e6bc1a733894.sentence: It consists of an originator address (to

6c36dae9998c.title: rfc>5321
6c36dae9998c.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
6c36dae9998c.sentence: which error reports should be directed), one or more recipient addresses, and optional protocol extension material.

a8ed12942fca.title: Email
a8ed12942fca.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
a8ed12942fca.sentence: The To: field may be unrelated to the addresses to which the message is delivered.

a63f52a6053e.title: Email
a63f52a6053e.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
a63f52a6053e.sentence: The delivery list is supplied separately to the transport protocol, SMTP, which may be extracted from the header content.

d915390ecb05.title: Email
d915390ecb05.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
d915390ecb05.sentence: The "To:" field is similar to the addressing at the top of a conventional letter delivered according to the address on the outer envelope.

12ff49e21016.title: Email
12ff49e21016.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
12ff49e21016.sentence: In the same way, the "From:" field may not be the sender.

cfbee634a847.title: Email
cfbee634a847.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
cfbee634a847.sentence: - Bcc: Blind carbon copy; addresses are usually only specified during SMTP delivery, and not usually listed in the message header.

cce5170cee5d.title: rfc>5321
cce5170cee5d.sentence: When the delivery SMTP server makes the "final delivery" of a message, it inserts a return-path line at the beginning of the mail data.

eeee79b46835.title: rfc>5321
eeee79b46835.sentence: The return-path line preserves the information in the <reverse-path> from the MAIL command.

666c8229e76f.title: rfc>5321
666c8229e76f.sentence: It is possible for the mailbox in the return path to be different from the actual sender's mailbox, for example, if error responses are to be delivered to a special error handling mailbox rather than to the message sender.

77d50896841c.title: rfc>5321
77d50896841c.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
77d50896841c.sentence: The content is textual in nature, expressed using the US-ASCII repertoire.

bce2b389ffae.title: rfc>5321
bce2b389ffae.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.1. Mail Objects
bce2b389ffae.sentence: Although SMTP extensions (such as "8BITMIME", RFC 1652 ) may relax this restriction for the content body, the content header fields are always encoded using the US-ASCII repertoire.

130583817f20.title: rfc>5322
130583817f20.sentence: The header fields of a message are defined here.

72264ebf069a.title: rfc>5322
72264ebf069a.sentence: The originator fields of a message consist of the from field, the sender field (when applicable), and optionally the reply-to field.

a6ced36e8728.title: rfc>5322
a6ced36e8728.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
a6ced36e8728.sentence: The destination fields of a message consist of three possible fields, each of the same form: the field name, which is either "To", "Cc", or "Bcc", followed by a comma-separated list of one or more addresses (either mailbox or group syntax).

7cd61a78aa1d.title: rfc>5322
7cd61a78aa1d.sentence: The "From:" field specifies the author(s) of the message, that is, the mailbox(es) of the person(s) or system(s) responsible for the writing of the message.

db35f18d4ab6.title: rfc>5322
db35f18d4ab6.sentence: The "Sender:" field specifies the mailbox of the agent responsible for the actual transmission of the message.

7d6df0a2d2ce.title: rfc>5322
7d6df0a2d2ce.sentence: If the from field contains more than one mailbox specification in the mailbox-list, then the sender field, containing the field name "Sender" and a single mailbox specification, MUST appear in the message.

08e7a1c257ad.title: rfc>5322
08e7a1c257ad.sentence: When the "Reply-To:" field is present, it indicates the address(es) to which the author of the message suggests that replies be sent.

f8135dfbcc0b.title: rfc>5322
f8135dfbcc0b.sentence: In the absence of the "Reply-To:" field, replies SHOULD by default be sent to the mailbox(es) specified in the "From:" field unless otherwise specified by the person composing the reply.

4c4688f045b6.title: rfc>5322
4c4688f045b6.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
4c4688f045b6.sentence: The "To:" field contains the address(es) of the primary recipient(s) of the message.

e512cfe2e89c.title: rfc>5322
e512cfe2e89c.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
e512cfe2e89c.sentence: The "Cc:" field (where the "Cc" means "Carbon Copy" in the sense of making a copy on a typewriter using carbon paper) contains the addresses of others who are to receive the message, though the content of the message may not be directed at them.

013932833f02.title: rfc>5322
013932833f02.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
013932833f02.sentence: The "Bcc:" field (where the "Bcc" means "Blind Carbon Copy") contains addresses of recipients of the message whose addresses are not to be revealed to other recipients of the message.

6d3d45deb6ed.title: rfc>5322
6d3d45deb6ed.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
6d3d45deb6ed.sentence: In the first case, when a message containing a "Bcc:" field is prepared to be sent, the "Bcc:" line is removed even though all of the recipients (including those specified in the "Bcc:" field) are sent a copy of the message.

b4a95b610dd0.title: rfc>5322
b4a95b610dd0.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
b4a95b610dd0.sentence: In the second case, recipients specified in the "To:" and "Cc:" lines each are sent a copy of the message with the "Bcc:" line removed as above, but the recipients on the "Bcc:" line get a separate copy of the message containing a "Bcc:" line.

8d0c2293a148.title: rfc>5322
8d0c2293a148.section: 3. Syntax > 3.6. Field Definitions > 3.6.3. Destination Address Fields
8d0c2293a148.sentence: Which method to use with "Bcc:" fields is implementation dependent, but refer to the "Security Considerations" section of this document for a discussion of each.

5b8dcd3d6ef6.title: rfc>5322
5b8dcd3d6ef6.sentence: Though listed as optional in the table in section 3.6, every message SHOULD have a "Message-ID:" field.

70b99575dbf0.title: rfc>5322
70b99575dbf0.sentence: Furthermore, reply messages SHOULD have "In-Reply-To:" and "References:" fields as appropriate and as described below.

5660d87e8898.title: rfc>5322
5660d87e8898.sentence: These three fields are intended to have only human-readable content with information about the message.

9aa8526ca6f1.title: rfc>5322
9aa8526ca6f1.sentence: The "Subject:" field is the most common and contains a short string identifying the topic of the

0b9845fd60ea.title: rfc>5322
0b9845fd60ea.sentence: The trace fields are a group of header fields consisting of an optional "Return-Path:" field, and one or more "Received:" fields.

6497527c5640.title: rfc>5321
6497527c5640.sentence: SMTP servers MUST prepend Received lines to messages; they MUST NOT change the order of existing lines or insert Received lines in any other location.

1711dc03efbd.title: rfc>5321
1711dc03efbd.sentence: An Internet mail program MUST NOT change or delete a Received: line that was previously added to the message header section.

ffc5889bbf76.title: rfc>5321
ffc5889bbf76.sentence: As the Internet grows, comparability of Received header fields is important for detecting problems, especially slow relays.

fc2b2d00ce4c.title: Email
fc2b2d00ce4c.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
fc2b2d00ce4c.sentence: - Authentication-Results: after a server verifies authentication, it can save the results in this field for consumption by downstream agents.

80fd42e298ab.title: Email
80fd42e298ab.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
80fd42e298ab.sentence: - Received-SPF: stores results of SPF checks in more detail than Authentication-Results.

cdad45e0e2d1.title: Email
cdad45e0e2d1.section: Message format > Message header > Header fields
cdad45e0e2d1.sentence: - DKIM-Signature: stores results of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) decryption to verify the message was not changed after it was sent.

8c649af48107.title: rfc>5322
8c649af48107.sentence: Resent fields SHOULD be added to any message that is reintroduced by a user into the transport system.

4d612dbe1574.title: rfc>5322
4d612dbe1574.sentence: The resent fields are only informational and MUST NOT be used in the normal processing of replies.

47404a90a6b0.title: rfc>5321
47404a90a6b0.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
47404a90a6b0.sentence: In a typical system, the program that composes a message has some method for requesting immediate attention for a new piece of outgoing mail, while mail that cannot be transmitted immediately MUST be queued and periodically retried by the sender.

f9a4a66c059e.title: rfc>5321
f9a4a66c059e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
f9a4a66c059e.sentence: Retries continue until the message is transmitted or the sender gives up; the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4-5 days.

e970ff27b23d.title: rfc>5321
e970ff27b23d.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
e970ff27b23d.sentence: The general model for an SMTP client is one or more processes that periodically attempt to transmit outgoing mail.

fa1a69c0f79a.title: rfc>5321
fa1a69c0f79a.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
fa1a69c0f79a.sentence: A mail queue entry will include not only the message itself but also the envelope information.

699e22e65b61.title: rfc>5321
699e22e65b61.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
699e22e65b61.sentence: The sender MUST delay retrying a particular destination after one attempt has failed.

133e5085dcc3.title: rfc>5321
133e5085dcc3.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
133e5085dcc3.sentence: In general, the retry interval SHOULD be at least 30 minutes; however, more sophisticated and variable strategies will be beneficial when the SMTP client can determine the reason for non-delivery.

9834fac043da.title: rfc>5321
9834fac043da.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
9834fac043da.sentence: Experience suggests that failures are typically transient (the target system or its connection has crashed), favoring a policy of two connection attempts in the first hour the message is in the queue, and then backing off to one every two or three hours.

a327446c2298.title: rfc>5321
a327446c2298.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
a327446c2298.sentence: A client SHOULD keep a list of hosts it cannot reach and corresponding connection timeouts, rather than just retrying queued mail items.

ee42f2632af9.title: rfc>5321
ee42f2632af9.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
ee42f2632af9.sentence: An SMTP client may have a large queue of messages for each unavailable destination host.

179d1cd02548.title: rfc>5321
179d1cd02548.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
179d1cd02548.sentence: If all of these messages were retried in every retry cycle, there would be excessive Internet overhead and the sending system would be blocked for a long period.

63d3903c44d8.title: rfc>5321
63d3903c44d8.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
63d3903c44d8.sentence: Note that an SMTP client can generally determine that a delivery attempt has failed only after a timeout of several minutes, and even a one-minute timeout per connection will result in a very large delay if retries are repeated for dozens, or even hundreds, of queued messages to the same host.

8c9db2d8ff4e.title: rfc>5321
8c9db2d8ff4e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
8c9db2d8ff4e.sentence: When a mail message is to be delivered to multiple recipients, and the SMTP server to which a copy of the message is to be sent is the same for multiple recipients, then only one copy of the message SHOULD be transmitted.

600ee200b1a8.title: rfc>5321
600ee200b1a8.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
600ee200b1a8.sentence: That is, the SMTP client SHOULD use the command sequence: MAIL, RCPT, RCPT,..., RCPT, DATA instead of the sequence: MAIL, RCPT, DATA,..., MAIL, RCPT, DATA.

1ad42bc4aee4.title: rfc>5321
1ad42bc4aee4.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
1ad42bc4aee4.sentence: Similarly, to achieve timely delivery, the SMTP client MAY support multiple concurrent outgoing mail transactions.

c4d5c4d1a38e.title: rfc>5321
c4d5c4d1a38e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
c4d5c4d1a38e.sentence: However, some limit may be appropriate to protect the host from devoting all its resources to mail.

a9517720da9e.title: rfc>5321
a9517720da9e.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.2. Receiving Strategy
a9517720da9e.sentence: Some limit MAY be imposed, but servers that cannot handle more than one SMTP transaction at a time are not in conformance with the intent of this specification.

927e0d94a3ca.title: rfc>5321
927e0d94a3ca.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
927e0d94a3ca.sentence: The SMTP client can shorten the queuing delay in cooperation with the SMTP server.

cdb651897c89.title: rfc>5321
cdb651897c89.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
cdb651897c89.sentence: For example, if mail is received from a particular address, it is likely that mail queued for that host can now be sent.

c85669af06bf.title: rfc>5321
c85669af06bf.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
c85669af06bf.sentence: Application of this principle may, in many cases, eliminate the requirement for an explicit "send queues now" function such as ETRN, RFC 1985.

685a922cb141.title: rfc>5321
685a922cb141.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies > 4.5.4.1. Sending Strategy
685a922cb141.sentence: The parameters to the retry algorithm MUST be configurable.

fae0d57a0dc9.title: rfc>5321
fae0d57a0dc9.section: 4. The SMTP Specifications > 4.5. Additional Implementation Issues > 4.5.4. Retry Strategies
fae0d57a0dc9.sentence: Any queuing strategy MUST include timeouts on all activities on a per-command basis.

4ae9df254cbd.title: rfc>5321
4ae9df254cbd.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
4ae9df254cbd.sentence: To avoid receiving duplicate messages as the result of timeouts, a receiver-SMTP MUST seek to minimize the time required to respond to the final <CRLF>.<CRLF> end of data indicator.

4c2a2672b99b.title: rfc>5321
4c2a2672b99b.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
4c2a2672b99b.sentence: If there is a delivery failure after acceptance of a message, the receiver-SMTP MUST formulate and mail a notification message.

a651856e9825.title: rfc>5321
a651856e9825.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
a651856e9825.sentence: If an SMTP server has accepted the task of relaying the mail and later finds that the destination is incorrect or that the mail cannot be delivered for some other reason, then it MUST construct an "undeliverable mail" notification message and send it to the originator of the undeliverable mail (as indicated by the reverse-path).

3718baed5bed.title: rfc>5321
3718baed5bed.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
3718baed5bed.sentence: When the receiver-SMTP accepts a piece of mail (by sending a "250 OK" message in response to DATA), it is accepting responsibility for delivering or relaying the message.

5b9268eb9373.title: rfc>5321
5b9268eb9373.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
5b9268eb9373.sentence: It MUST NOT lose the message for frivolous reasons, such as because the host later crashes or because of a predictable resource shortage.

4db4f001cf6d.title: rfc>5321
4db4f001cf6d.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
4db4f001cf6d.sentence: This notification MUST be sent using a null ("<>") reverse-path in the envelope.

f4d24d1d26af.title: rfc>5321
f4d24d1d26af.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
f4d24d1d26af.sentence: The recipient of this notification MUST be the address from the envelope return path (or the Return-Path: line).

9d9a1d3a0554.title: rfc>5321
9d9a1d3a0554.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
9d9a1d3a0554.sentence: if this address is null ("<>"), the receiver-SMTP MUST NOT send a notification.

1e4a40581113.title: rfc>5321
1e4a40581113.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
1e4a40581113.sentence: Of course, SMTP servers MUST NOT send notification messages about problems transporting notification messages.

ba9a1534e555.title: rfc>5321
ba9a1534e555.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
ba9a1534e555.sentence: One way to prevent loops in error reporting is to specify a null reverse-path in the MAIL command of a notification message.

31001b460989.title: rfc>5321
31001b460989.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
31001b460989.sentence: Some delivery failures after the message is accepted by SMTP will be unavoidable.

ea2978d45004.title: rfc>5321
ea2978d45004.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.1. Reliable Delivery and Replies by Email
ea2978d45004.sentence: For example, it may be impossible for the receiving SMTP server to validate all the delivery addresses in RCPT command(s) due to a "soft" domain system error, because the target is a mailing list (see earlier discussion of RCPT), or because the server is acting as a relay and has no immediate access to the delivering system.

8275dde4794d.title: rfc>5321
8275dde4794d.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.2. Unwanted, Unsolicited, and "Attack" Messages
8275dde4794d.sentence: If they cannot be delivered, and cannot be rejected by the SMTP server during the SMTP transaction, they should be "bounced" (returned with non-delivery notification messages) as described above.

5661cf64f4e6.title: rfc>5321
5661cf64f4e6.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
5661cf64f4e6.sentence: However, in practice, some servers do not perform recipient verification until after the message text is received.

41342fe3896a.title: rfc>5321
41342fe3896a.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.3. Mail Transactions
41342fe3896a.sentence: Using a "550 mailbox not found" (or equivalent) reply code after the data are accepted makes it difficult or impossible for the client to determine which recipients failed.

c36b9f3c66cc.title: Email spam
c36b9f3c66cc.sentence: It happens when email servers are misconfigured to send a bogus bounce message to the envelope sender when rejecting or quarantining email (rather than simply rejecting the attempt to send the message).

7bdf4f8a6326.title: Email spam
7bdf4f8a6326.sentence: If the sender's address was forged, then the bounce may go to an innocent party.

5f73f1732686.title: Email
5f73f1732686.sentence: Many ISPs now deliberately disable non-delivery reports (NDRs) and delivery receipts due to the activities of spammers:

728ff3d1e9b8.title: Email
728ff3d1e9b8.sentence: - If the spammer uses a forged sender email address (email spoofing), then the innocent email address that was used can be flooded with NDRs from the many invalid email addresses the spammer may have attempted to mail.

590872d6b14b.title: rfc>5321
590872d6b14b.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.2. Unwanted, Unsolicited, and "Attack" Messages
590872d6b14b.sentence: Conversely, if a message is rejected because it is found to contain hostile content (a decision that is outside the scope of an SMTP server as defined in this document), rejection ("bounce") messages SHOULD NOT be sent unless the receiving site is confident that those messages will be usefully delivered.

77c6e742f591.title: rfc>5321
77c6e742f591.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.2. Unwanted, Unsolicited, and "Attack" Messages
77c6e742f591.sentence: The preference and default in these cases is to avoid sending non-delivery messages when the incoming message is determined to contain hostile content.

ee6255854fe8.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
ee6255854fe8.sentence: The MSA delivers the mail to its mail transfer agent (MTA).

54e3726a355e.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
54e3726a355e.sentence: Once the final hop accepts the incoming message, it hands it to a mail delivery agent (MDA) for local delivery.

f46f29306125.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
f46f29306125.sentence: Often, these two agents are instances of the same software launched with different options on the same machine.

f8d32e051236.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
f8d32e051236.sentence: The boundary MTA uses DNS to look up the MX (mail exchanger) record for the recipient's domain (the part of the email address on the right of @).

e9ec14d87159.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
e9ec14d87159.sentence: The MX record contains the name of the target MTA.

42efeb920c01.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
42efeb920c01.sentence: Message transfer can occur in a single connection between two MTAs, or in a series of hops through intermediary systems.

9810e439e4ef.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
9810e439e4ef.sentence: A receiving SMTP server may be the ultimate destination, an intermediate "relay" (that is, it stores and forwards the message) or a "gateway" (that is, it may forward the message using some protocol other than SMTP).

b039f1749528.title: rfc>5321
b039f1749528.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.10. Originator, Delivery, Relay, and Gateway Systems
b039f1749528.sentence: A "relay" SMTP system (usually referred to just as a "relay") receives mail from an SMTP client and transmits it, without modification to the message data other than adding trace information, to another SMTP server for further relaying or for delivery.

b8c5486edcfe.title: rfc>5321
b8c5486edcfe.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.10. Originator, Delivery, Relay, and Gateway Systems
b8c5486edcfe.sentence: A "gateway" SMTP system (usually referred to just as a "gateway") receives mail from a client system in one transport environment and transmits it to a server system in another transport environment.

a003351d3be0.title: rfc>5321
a003351d3be0.section: 2. The SMTP Model > 2.3. SMTP Terminology > 2.3.10. Originator, Delivery, Relay, and Gateway Systems
a003351d3be0.sentence: Differences in protocols or message semantics between the transport environments on either side of a gateway may require that the gateway system perform transformations to the message that are not permitted to SMTP relay systems.

7076fd1ab06e.title: rfc>5321
7076fd1ab06e.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.3. Loop Detection
7076fd1ab06e.sentence: Simple counting of the number of "Received:" header fields in a message has proven to be an effective, although rarely optimal, method of detecting loops in mail systems.

eb7c6146cfff.title: rfc>5321
eb7c6146cfff.section: 6. Problem Detection and Handling > 6.3. Loop Detection
eb7c6146cfff.sentence: SMTP servers using this technique SHOULD use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 Received entries.

b8c8effeb817.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
b8c8effeb817.sentence: An MDA saves messages in the relevant mailbox format.

a6960ce92009.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
a6960ce92009.sentence: An MDA may deliver messages directly to storage, or forward them over a network using SMTP or other protocol such as Local Mail Transfer Protocol (LMTP), a derivative of SMTP designed for this purpose.

26713d8e95ec.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
26713d8e95ec.sentence: Mail is retrieved by end-user applications, called email clients, using Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP), a protocol that both facilitates access to mail and manages stored mail, or the Post Office Protocol (POP) which typically uses the traditional mbox mail file format or a proprietary system such as Microsoft Exchange/Outlook or Lotus Notes/Domino.

0d77c50d299e.title: rfc>5321
0d77c50d299e.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.2. Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
0d77c50d299e.sentence: A relay SMTP server is usually the target of a DNS MX record that designates it, rather than the final delivery system.

623347b50fea.title: rfc>5321
623347b50fea.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.2. Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
623347b50fea.sentence: The relay server may accept or reject the task of relaying the mail in the same way it accepts or rejects mail for a local user.

cc1550db1c31.title: rfc>5321
cc1550db1c31.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.2. Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
cc1550db1c31.sentence: If it accepts the task, it then becomes an SMTP client, establishes a transmission channel to the next SMTP server specified in the DNS (according to the rules in Section 5), and sends it the mail.

bb4126d05bbf.title: rfc>5321
bb4126d05bbf.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.2. Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
bb4126d05bbf.sentence: relay mail to a particular address for policy reasons, a 550 response SHOULD be returned.

d01beb431c11.title: rfc>5321
d01beb431c11.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
d01beb431c11.sentence: Many mail-sending clients exist, especially in conjunction with facilities that receive mail via POP3 or IMAP, that have limited capability to support some of the requirements of this specification, such as the ability to queue messages for subsequent delivery attempts.

4c365ad95ee5.title: rfc>5321
4c365ad95ee5.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
4c365ad95ee5.sentence: For these clients, it is common practice to make private arrangements to send all messages to a single server for processing and subsequent distribution.

f03f84930bb8.title: rfc>5321
f03f84930bb8.section: 3. The SMTP Procedures: An Overview > 3.6. Relaying and Mail Routing > 3.6.3. Message Submission Servers as Relays
f03f84930bb8.sentence: A standardized mail submission protocol has been developed that is gradually superseding practices based on SMTP (see RFC 4409 ).

0332130868fe.title: rfc>5321
0332130868fe.sentence: SMTP clients that transfer all traffic regardless of the target domains associated with the individual messages, or that do not maintain queues for retrying message transmissions that initially cannot be completed, may otherwise conform to this specification but are not considered fully-capable.

4926d14515bb.title: MX record
4926d14515bb.sentence: A mail exchanger record (MX record) specifies the mail server responsible for accepting email messages on behalf of a domain name.

55017f970bab.title: MX record
55017f970bab.sentence: It is a resource record in the Domain Name System (DNS).

09fb59da8d97.title: MX record
09fb59da8d97.sentence: The characteristic payload information of an MX record is a preference value (above labelled "Priority"), and the domain name of a mailserver ("Host" above).

0f83b605b06b.title: MX record
0f83b605b06b.sentence: An MX record is one of these, and a domain may have one or more of these set up, as below:

78112708c84f.title: MX record
78112708c84f.sentence: When an e-mail message is sent through the Internet, the sending mail transfer agent (MTA) queries the Domain Name System for the MX records of each recipient's domain name.

ca8c227ed8df.title: MX record
ca8c227ed8df.sentence: This query returns a list of host names of mail exchange servers accepting incoming mail for that domain and their preferences.

6f88253de5c9.title: MX record
6f88253de5c9.sentence: The sending agent then attempts to establish an SMTP connection, trying the host with the lowest "Priority" value first.

f72cc816d224.title: MX record
f72cc816d224.sentence: According to RFC 5321, the lowest-numbered records are the most preferred.

4f2ce34aa23f.title: rfc>5321
4f2ce34aa23f.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
4f2ce34aa23f.sentence: Lower numbers are more preferred than higher ones.

3c85e6e38dd1.title: MX record
3c85e6e38dd1.sentence: The preference number is an unsigned 16-bit field, thus valid values range from 0 to 65535.

0a35d85092ec.title: MX record
0a35d85092ec.sentence: The host name must map directly to one or more address records (A, or AAAA) in the DNS, and must not point to any CNAME records.

9bd25d423181.title: rfc>5321
9bd25d423181.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
9bd25d423181.sentence: When a domain name associated with an MX RR is looked up and the associated data field obtained, the data field of that response MUST contain a domain name.

63b79e1ee9b5.title: rfc>5321
63b79e1ee9b5.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
63b79e1ee9b5.sentence: That domain name, when queried, MUST return at least one address record (e.g., A or AAAA RR) that gives the IP address of the SMTP server to which the message should be directed.

7779f89f38e0.title: rfc>5321
7779f89f38e0.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
7779f89f38e0.sentence: If an empty list of MXs is returned, the address is treated as if it was associated with an implicit MX RR, with a preference of 0, pointing to that host.

29733d29e5e7.title: rfc>5321
29733d29e5e7.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
29733d29e5e7.sentence: If one or more MX RRs are found for a given name, SMTP systems MUST NOT utilize any address RRs associated with that name unless they are located using the MX RRs; the "implicit MX" rule above applies only if there are no MX records present.

e06c99def9a3.title: MX record
e06c99def9a3.sentence: - If (and only if) no MX record for the domain is present, treat the domain as if it had an MX record with the given domain as the target hostname and a preference value of 0

aced9f6b9917.title: rfc>5321
aced9f6b9917.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
aced9f6b9917.sentence: If a non-existent domain error is returned, this situation MUST be reported as an error.

52c78ecbfdb9.title: rfc>5321
52c78ecbfdb9.section: 5. Address Resolution and Mail Handling > 5.1. Locating the Target Host
52c78ecbfdb9.sentence: If a temporary error is returned, the message MUST be queued and retried later (see Section 4.5.4.1).

7d48e73b86ba.title: MX record
7d48e73b86ba.sentence: It is possible to configure several MX records, typically pointing to an array of mail servers for load balancing and redundancy.

43c91af1568d.title: MX record
43c91af1568d.sentence: The system allows high-availability clusters of mail gateways to be built for one domain if necessary.

7718de2cd73b.title: MX record
7718de2cd73b.sentence: The MX mechanism does not grant the ability to provide mail service on alternative port numbers, nor does it provide the ability to distribute mail delivery across a set of unequal-priority mail servers by assigning a weighting value to each one.

1288b7897073.title: Post Office Protocol
1288b7897073.sentence: In computing, the Post Office Protocol (POP) is an application-layer Internet standard protocol used by e-mail clients to retrieve e-mail from a mail server.

5972d9054a30.title: Post Office Protocol
5972d9054a30.sentence: The Post Office Protocol provides access via an Internet Protocol (IP) network for a user client application to a mailbox (maildrop) maintained on a mail server.

08af431d46ee.title: Post Office Protocol
08af431d46ee.sentence: The protocol supports list, retrieve and delete operations for messages.

e7d59d5087c8.title: Post Office Protocol
e7d59d5087c8.sentence: POP3 clients connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer, and finally delete them from the server.

ec3ea5d2b1e7.title: Post Office Protocol
ec3ea5d2b1e7.sentence: This design of POP and its procedures was driven by the need of users having only temporary Internet connections, such as dial-up access, allowing these users to retrieve e-mail when connected, and subsequently to view and manipulate the retrieved messages when offline.

17844f618d77.title: Post Office Protocol
17844f618d77.sentence: POP3 clients also have an option to leave mail on the server after retrieval, and in this mode of operation, clients will only download new messages which are identified by using the UIDL command (unique-id list).

dded75a58950.title: Post Office Protocol
dded75a58950.sentence: Messages available to the client are determined when a POP3 session opens the maildrop, and are identified by message-number local to that session or, optionally, by a unique identifier assigned to the message by the POP server.

a0582c316475.title: Post Office Protocol
a0582c316475.sentence: This unique identifier is permanent and unique to the maildrop and allows a client to access the same message in different POP sessions.

cab035bdeec4.title: Post Office Protocol
cab035bdeec4.sentence: Mail is retrieved and marked for deletion by the message-number.

c6355f8530a8.title: Post Office Protocol
c6355f8530a8.sentence: When the client exits the session, mail marked for deletion is removed from the maildrop.

2f54a02aeddd.title: Post Office Protocol
2f54a02aeddd.sentence: A POP3 server listens on TCP well-known port number 110 for service requests.

453c2f5132af.title: Post Office Protocol
453c2f5132af.sentence: Encrypted communication for POP3 is either requested after protocol initiation, using the STLS command, if supported, or by POP3S, which connects to the server using Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) on well-known TCP port number 995.

e6d8b98be0ef.title: Post Office Protocol
e6d8b98be0ef.sentence: While the original POP3 specification supported only an unencrypted USER/PASS login mechanism or Berkeley.rhosts access control, today POP3 supports several authentication methods to provide varying levels of protection against illegitimate access to a user's e-mail.

088940e8c53e.title: Post Office Protocol
088940e8c53e.sentence: APOP is a challenge–response protocol which uses the MD5 hash function in an attempt to avoid replay attacks and disclosure of the shared secret.

99ae5efec782.title: Post Office Protocol
99ae5efec782.sentence: POP3 clients support SASL authentication methods via the AUTH extension.

a56fc3d0bf9a.title: Post Office Protocol
a56fc3d0bf9a.sentence: An extension mechanism was proposed in RFC 2449 to accommodate general extensions as well as announce in an organized manner support for optional commands, such as TOP and UIDL.

505a7b2b931e.title: Post Office Protocol
505a7b2b931e.sentence: The RFC did not intend to encourage extensions, and reaffirmed that the role of POP3 is to provide simple support for mainly download-and-delete requirements of mailbox handling.

40a2f0bf2a44.title: Post Office Protocol
40a2f0bf2a44.sentence: The extensions are termed capabilities and are listed by the CAPA command.

3d568af8ecc9.title: Email
3d568af8ecc9.sentence: The following is a typical sequence of events that takes place when sender Alice transmits a message using a mail user agent (MUA) addressed to the email address of the recipient.

f1909928983f.title: Email
f1909928983f.sentence: - The MUA formats the message in email format and uses the submission protocol, a profile of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), to send the message content to the local mail submission agent (MSA), in this case smtp.a.org.

03883d50bea2.title: Email
03883d50bea2.sentence: - The DNS server for the domain b.org (ns.b.org) responds with any MX records listing the mail exchange servers for that domain, in this case mx.b.org, a message transfer agent (MTA) server run by the recipient's ISP.

e53941d54e68.title: Email
e53941d54e68.sentence: - The MSA determines the destination address provided in the SMTP protocol (not from the message header)—in this case, bob@b.org—which is a fully qualified domain address (FQDA).

f2014b1cf469.title: Email
f2014b1cf469.sentence: The part before the @ sign is the local part of the address, often the username of the recipient, and the part after the @ sign is a domain name.

c53a098d6425.title: Email
c53a098d6425.sentence: The MSA resolves a domain name to determine the fully qualified domain name of the mail server in the Domain Name System (DNS).

4fed0b3a5df0.title: Email
4fed0b3a5df0.sentence: - smtp.a.org sends the message to mx.b.org using SMTP.

e00d142a76dc.title: Email
e00d142a76dc.sentence: This server may need to forward the message to other MTAs before the message reaches the final message delivery agent (MDA).

4cff283b1abf.title: Email
4cff283b1abf.sentence: - The MDA delivers it to the mailbox of user bob.

21f087382d34.title: Email
21f087382d34.sentence: - Bob's MUA picks up the message using either the Post Office Protocol (POP3) or the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP).

6ed6939ccbd1.title: Email
6ed6939ccbd1.sentence: - Domains usually have several mail exchange servers so that they can continue to accept mail even if the primary is not available.

176731a1b5e5.title: Email
176731a1b5e5.sentence: Email pre-dates instant messaging, and transmission favors reliability over speed, in order to be able to cope with unreliable network links and busy servers (more common in the early days of the Internet).

8c1a95118f7b.title: Email
8c1a95118f7b.sentence: - One or more mail servers are overloaded (possibly due to spam or denial-of-service attack) and queuing incoming mail or temporarily refusing incoming connections

fee83b4d3f29.title: Email
fee83b4d3f29.sentence: - SMTP requires multiple back-and-forths, which can amplify the impact of a slow network or dropped packets

498b1fac1e73.title: Email
498b1fac1e73.sentence: - Server down for maintenance or malfunction

768560416b26.title: Email
768560416b26.sentence: Mail can be queued and retried for up to five days before senders are notified of a permanent delivery failure.

46eb14d40203.title: Email
46eb14d40203.sentence: Accepting a message obliges an MTA to deliver it, and when a message cannot be delivered, that MTA must send a bounce message back to the sender, indicating the problem.

39868d6b8c89.title: Email
39868d6b8c89.sentence: Many MTAs used to accept messages for any recipient on the Internet and do their best to deliver them.

906221cc4e46.title: Email
906221cc4e46.sentence: Such MTAs are called open mail relays.

fb298a9ff5f7.title: Email
fb298a9ff5f7.sentence: However, this mechanism proved to be exploitable by originators of unsolicited bulk email and as a consequence open mail relays have become rare, and many MTAs do not accept messages from open mail relays.

25bd2dd440af.title: Email
25bd2dd440af.sentence: - Alice or Bob may use a client connected to a corporate email system, such as IBM Lotus Notes or Microsoft Exchange.

11e64a02d0d6.title: Email
11e64a02d0d6.sentence: These systems often have their own internal email format and their clients typically communicate with the email server using a vendor-specific, proprietary protocol.

8ef1217cb9aa.title: Email
8ef1217cb9aa.sentence: The server sends or receives email via the Internet through the product's Internet mail gateway which also does any necessary reformatting.

5833be147c8e.title: Email
5833be147c8e.sentence: - Alice may not have an MUA on her computer but instead may connect to a webmail service.

5556ae5de181.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
5556ae5de181.sentence: In computing, the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) is an Internet standard protocol used by email clients to retrieve email messages from a mail server over a TCP/IP connection.

033d2a4b5e5b.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
033d2a4b5e5b.sentence: The Internet Message Access Protocol is an application layer Internet protocol that allows an e-mail client to access email on a remote mail server.

18643e7e315f.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
18643e7e315f.sentence: IMAP was designed with the goal of permitting complete management of an email box by multiple email clients; therefore, clients generally leave messages on the server until the user explicitly deletes them.

1535bdd696d6.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
1535bdd696d6.sentence: This and other characteristics of IMAP operation allow multiple clients to manage the same mailbox.

73c3316c8125.title: rfc>9051
73c3316c8125.sentence: IMAP4rev2 permits manipulation of mailboxes (remote message folders) in a way that is functionally equivalent to local folders.

379956525ec6.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
379956525ec6.sentence: IMAP maintains a mailbox structure (content, folder structure, individual message state, etc.) on the mail server, whereas POP maintains it on the user's local device.

b9a61d3d1c6a.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
b9a61d3d1c6a.sentence: Clients may store local copies of the messages, but these are considered to be a temporary cache.

ffb8b5f21bf8.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
ffb8b5f21bf8.sentence: Thus, IMAP requires far more server side resources, incurring a significantly higher cost per mailbox.

91573589d444.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
91573589d444.section: Advantages over POP > Connected and disconnected modes
91573589d444.sentence: When using IMAP4, clients often stay connected as long as the user interface is active and download message content on demand.

7ed29ebec95e.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
7ed29ebec95e.section: Advantages over POP > Connected and disconnected modes
7ed29ebec95e.sentence: For users with many or large messages, this IMAP4 usage pattern can result in faster response times.

110df8e34dfc.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
110df8e34dfc.section: Advantages over POP > Reporting of external changes
110df8e34dfc.sentence: In contrast, the IMAP protocol provides a dynamic view, and requires that external changes in state, including newly arrived messages, as well as changes made to the mailbox by other concurrently connected clients, are detected and appropriate responses are sent between commands as well as during an IDLE command, as described in RFC 2177.

345d51f18886.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
345d51f18886.section: Advantages over POP > Message state information
345d51f18886.sentence: Through the use of flags defined in the IMAP4 protocol, clients can keep track of message state: for example, whether or not the message has been read, replied to, or deleted.

58f43c7ac8ea.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
58f43c7ac8ea.section: Advantages over POP > Message state information
58f43c7ac8ea.sentence: These flags are stored on the server, so different clients accessing the same mailbox at different times can detect state changes made by other clients.

14651be57cea.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
14651be57cea.section: Advantages over POP > Message state information
14651be57cea.sentence: The IMAP4 protocol supports both predefined system flags and client-defined keywords.

b13b2b9cdef2.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
b13b2b9cdef2.section: Advantages over POP > Multiple mailboxes on the server
b13b2b9cdef2.sentence: IMAP4 clients can create, rename, and delete mailboxes (usually presented to the user as folders) on the server, and copy messages between mailboxes.

d35a01809b92.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
d35a01809b92.sentence: IMAP4 provides a mechanism for a client to ask the server to search for messages meeting a variety of criteria.

7bf11fa86751.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
7bf11fa86751.sentence: This mechanism avoids requiring clients to download every message in the mailbox in order to perform these searches.

b9c53f1f2cc9.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
b9c53f1f2cc9.sentence: Clients can potentially consume large amounts of server resources when searching massive mailboxes if the server's storage, indexing, and search algorithms are not carefully implemented.

24650e9a16c3.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
24650e9a16c3.section: Advantages over POP > Access to MIME message parts and partial fetch
24650e9a16c3.sentence: These mechanisms allow clients to retrieve the text portion of a message without retrieving attached files or to stream content as it is being fetched.

9cc01386e66e.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
9cc01386e66e.section: Advantages over POP > Server push notifications
9cc01386e66e.sentence: IMAP IDLE provides a way for the mail server to notify connected clients that there were changes to a mailbox, for example because a new mail has arrived.

0611fc03e3a3.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
0611fc03e3a3.sentence: IMAP4 clients need to maintain a TCP/IP connection to the IMAP server in order to be notified of the arrival of new mail.

2ed005704ed8.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
2ed005704ed8.sentence: An IMAP server typically listens on well-known port 143, while IMAP over SSL/TLS (IMAPS) uses 993.

77b7bd9804f9.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
77b7bd9804f9.sentence: To cryptographically protect IMAP connections between the client and server, IMAPS on TCP port 993 can be used, which utilizes SSL/TLS.

ab5626170c7b.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
ab5626170c7b.sentence: Alternatively, STARTTLS can be used to encrypt the connection when connecting to port 143 after initially communicating over plaintext.

3ce96601db63.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
3ce96601db63.sentence: The current version is defined by RFC 9051.

3d806fd37fce.title: Post Office Protocol
3d806fd37fce.sentence: By contrast, the Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) was designed to normally leave all messages on the server to permit management with multiple client applications, and to support both connected (online) and disconnected (offline) modes of operation.

96130b987a34.title: Post Office Protocol
96130b987a34.sentence: In short: IMAP is designed to permit manipulation of remote mailboxes as if they were local.

ce5bb7f02cd1.title: Post Office Protocol
ce5bb7f02cd1.sentence: - POP moves the message from the email server to the local computer, although there is usually an option in email clients to leave the messages on the email server as well.

445205dc5e32.title: Post Office Protocol
445205dc5e32.sentence: IMAP defaults to leaving the message on the email server, simply downloading a local copy.

2a3070085d74.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
2a3070085d74.section: Advantages over POP > Reporting of external changes
2a3070085d74.sentence: After successful authentication, the POP protocol provides a completely static view of the current state of the mailbox, and does not provide a mechanism to show any external changes in state during the session (the POP client must reconnect and re-authenticate to get an updated view).

8a78d4966903.title: Post Office Protocol
8a78d4966903.sentence: - POP provides a completely static view of the current state of the mailbox, and does not provide a mechanism to show any external changes in state during the session (the client must reconnect and re-authenticate to get an updated view).

b115707dc25d.title: Post Office Protocol
b115707dc25d.sentence: - IMAP provides a dynamic view, and sends responses for external changes in state, including newly arrived messages, as well as changes made to the mailbox by other concurrently connected clients.

baa4e5ac63fb.title: Post Office Protocol
baa4e5ac63fb.sentence: - POP treats the mailbox as a single store, and has no concept of folders

cc3ba5b19c69.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
cc3ba5b19c69.section: Advantages over POP > Message state information
cc3ba5b19c69.sentence: POP provides no mechanism for clients to store such state information on the server so if a single user accesses a mailbox with two different POP clients (at different times), state information—such as whether a message has been accessed—cannot be synchronized between the clients.

8f9d2503b5fc.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
8f9d2503b5fc.section: Advantages over POP > Server push notifications
8f9d2503b5fc.sentence: POP provides no comparable feature, and email clients need to periodically connect to the POP server to check for new mail.

ac74c311deb0.title: Post Office Protocol
ac74c311deb0.sentence: - POP can either retrieve an entire message with the RETR command, and for servers that support it, the headers, as well as a specified number of body lines can be accessed with the TOP command.

f366ad84e48c.title: Post Office Protocol
f366ad84e48c.sentence: - IMAP allows clients to retrieve any of the individual MIME parts separately – for example, retrieving the plain text without retrieving attached files, or retrieving only one of many attached files.

cf54d1cf2702.title: Post Office Protocol
cf54d1cf2702.sentence: - POP is a simpler protocol, making implementation easier.

ad2ff3628c17.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
ad2ff3628c17.sentence: While IMAP remedies many of the shortcomings of POP, this inherently introduces additional complexity.

386fe3d1de35.title: Post Office Protocol
386fe3d1de35.sentence: - POP provides the ability to associate unique identifiers with each message for servers which support the UIDL command.

5816cb199a2c.title: Post Office Protocol
5816cb199a2c.sentence: This can be any string of standard visible (non-whitespace) 7-bit ASCII characters up to 70 characters.

ed22ad00c7c0.title: Post Office Protocol
ed22ad00c7c0.sentence: - IMAP instead provides unique numerical identifiers for each message, local to each folder, in conjunction with a folder specific UIDVALIDITY number.

8f8a11d1107a.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
8f8a11d1107a.sentence: Virtually all modern e-mail clients and servers support IMAP, which along with the earlier POP3 (Post Office Protocol) are the two most prevalent standard protocols for email retrieval.

37ca40ec231f.title: Internet Message Access Protocol
37ca40ec231f.sentence: Many webmail service providers such as Gmail and Outlook.com also support both IMAP and POP3.

23a4e6a52d99.title: rfc>9051
23a4e6a52d99.sentence: An IMAP4rev2 connection consists of the establishment of a client/ server network connection, an initial greeting from the server, and client/server interactions.

01be3051c03b.title: rfc>9051
01be3051c03b.sentence: These client/server interactions consist of a client command, server data, and a server completion result response.

e32ec36d3bef.title: rfc>9051
e32ec36d3bef.sentence: The IMAP4rev2 protocol assumes a reliable data stream such as that provided by TCP.

141ef312ad62.title: rfc>9051
141ef312ad62.sentence: When TCP is used, an IMAP4rev2 server listens on port 143 (cleartext port) or port 993 (Implicit TLS port).

9ab101725924.title: rfc>9051
9ab101725924.sentence: All interactions transmitted by client and server are in the form of lines, that is, strings that end with a CRLF.

8a24a06ddce1.title: rfc>9051
8a24a06ddce1.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.1. Client Protocol Sender and Server Protocol Receiver
8a24a06ddce1.sentence: Each client command is prefixed with an identifier (typically a short alphanumeric string, e.g., A0001, A0002, etc.) called a "tag".

764f737ac2f1.title: rfc>9051
764f737ac2f1.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
764f737ac2f1.sentence: It is tagged with the same tag as the client command that began the operation.

f6c7ddb12880.title: rfc>9051
f6c7ddb12880.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
f6c7ddb12880.sentence: Thus, if more than one command is in progress, the tag in a server completion response identifies the command to which the response applies.

8fc6e6cdf495.title: rfc>9051
8fc6e6cdf495.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
8fc6e6cdf495.sentence: There are three possible server completion responses: OK (indicating success), NO (indicating failure), or BAD (indicating a protocol error such as unrecognized command or command syntax error).

3d5cf4597087.title: rfc>9051
3d5cf4597087.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
3d5cf4597087.sentence: Data transmitted by the server to the client and status responses that do not indicate command completion are prefixed with the token "*" and are called untagged responses.

29f736a90db6.title: rfc>9051
29f736a90db6.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
29f736a90db6.sentence: Server data MAY be sent as a result of a client command or MAY be sent unilaterally by the server.

c1514aad7633.title: rfc>9051
c1514aad7633.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
c1514aad7633.sentence: A client MUST be prepared to accept any server response at all times.

a5e1dcd318e3.title: rfc>9051
a5e1dcd318e3.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.2. Commands and Responses > 2.2.2. Server Protocol Sender and Client Protocol Receiver
a5e1dcd318e3.sentence: Server data SHOULD be remembered (cached), so that the client can reference its remembered copy rather than sending a command to the server to request the data.

19a790eac375.title: rfc>9051
19a790eac375.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.5. Multiple Commands in Progress (Command Pipelining)
19a790eac375.sentence: The client MAY send another command without waiting for the completion result response of a command, subject to ambiguity rules (see below) and flow control constraints on the underlying data stream.

964d09e57951.title: rfc>9051
964d09e57951.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.5. Multiple Commands in Progress (Command Pipelining)
964d09e57951.sentence: Similarly, a server MAY begin processing another command before processing the current command to completion, subject to ambiguity rules.

b07add52bdc4.title: rfc>9051
b07add52bdc4.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.5. Multiple Commands in Progress (Command Pipelining)
b07add52bdc4.sentence: If the server detects a possible ambiguity, it MUST execute commands to completion in the order given by the client.

09c861caf942.title: rfc>9051
09c861caf942.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.2. Mailbox Size and Message Status Updates
09c861caf942.sentence: A server MUST send mailbox size updates automatically if a mailbox size change is observed during the processing of a command.

d4f68ec95df0.title: rfc>9051
d4f68ec95df0.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.2. Mailbox Size and Message Status Updates
d4f68ec95df0.sentence: A server SHOULD send message flag updates automatically, without requiring the client to request such updates explicitly.

97633a7b3e23.title: rfc>9051
97633a7b3e23.section: 5. Operational Considerations > 5.2. Mailbox Size and Message Status Updates
97633a7b3e23.sentence: In particular, it is NOT permitted to send an EXISTS response that would reduce the number of messages in the mailbox; only the EXPUNGE response can do this.

cb405f5a37bc.title: rfc>9051
cb405f5a37bc.sentence: Once the connection between client and server is established, an IMAP4rev2 connection is in one of four states.

871c0b97bbad.title: rfc>9051
871c0b97bbad.section: 3. State and Flow Diagram > 3.1. Not Authenticated State
871c0b97bbad.sentence: In the not authenticated state, the client MUST supply authentication credentials before most commands will be permitted.

452a82695ed0.title: rfc>9051
452a82695ed0.section: 3. State and Flow Diagram > 3.2. Authenticated State
452a82695ed0.sentence: In the authenticated state, the client is authenticated and MUST select a mailbox to access before commands that affect messages will be permitted.

58b20456cfa1.title: rfc>9051
58b20456cfa1.section: 3. State and Flow Diagram > 3.3. Selected State
58b20456cfa1.sentence: In a selected state, a mailbox has been selected to access.

165a4d2221f0.title: rfc>9051
165a4d2221f0.section: 3. State and Flow Diagram > 3.4. Logout State
165a4d2221f0.sentence: In the logout state, the connection is being terminated.

37fe07704015.title: rfc>9051
37fe07704015.sentence: Most commands are only valid in certain states.

1a4ab03bd201.title: rfc>9051
1a4ab03bd201.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
1a4ab03bd201.sentence: A UID is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value assigned to each message, which when used with the unique identifier validity value (see below) forms a 64-bit value that MUST NOT refer to any other message in the mailbox or any subsequent mailbox with the same name forever.

bf334b6670b0.title: rfc>9051
bf334b6670b0.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
bf334b6670b0.sentence: The unique identifier of a message MUST NOT change during the session and SHOULD NOT change between sessions.

eaf63c694b44.title: rfc>9051
eaf63c694b44.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers
eaf63c694b44.sentence: Messages in IMAP4rev2 are accessed by one of two numbers: the Unique Identifier (UID) or the message sequence number.

4bde61d4d9ce.title: rfc>9051
4bde61d4d9ce.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.2. Message Sequence Number Message Attribute
4bde61d4d9ce.sentence: A message sequence number is a relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox.

3a30ee312fbe.title: rfc>9051
3a30ee312fbe.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
3a30ee312fbe.sentence: Unique identifiers are assigned in a strictly ascending fashion in the mailbox; as each message is added to the mailbox, it is assigned a higher UID than those of all message(s) that are already in the mailbox.

69a362bacbf1.title: rfc>9051
69a362bacbf1.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
69a362bacbf1.sentence: Unlike message sequence numbers, unique identifiers are not necessarily contiguous.

8a69faf80c45.title: rfc>9051
8a69faf80c45.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
8a69faf80c45.sentence: Persistent unique identifiers are required for a client to resynchronize its state from a previous session with the server (e.g., disconnected or offline access clients [IMAP-MODEL]); this is discussed further in [IMAP-DISC].

20c6942cbfc0.title: rfc>9051
20c6942cbfc0.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
20c6942cbfc0.sentence: Any change of unique identifiers between sessions MUST be detectable using the UIDVALIDITY mechanism discussed below.

edaf546c07e4.title: rfc>9051
edaf546c07e4.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
edaf546c07e4.sentence: If unique identifiers from an earlier session fail to persist in this session, the unique identifier validity value MUST be greater than the one used in the earlier session.

2b08bb5b37cf.title: rfc>9051
2b08bb5b37cf.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
2b08bb5b37cf.sentence: A good UIDVALIDITY value to use is a 32-bit representation of the current date/time when the value is assigned: this ensures that the value is unique and always increases.

b8dff5be4628.title: rfc>9051
b8dff5be4628.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
b8dff5be4628.sentence: Another possible alternative is a global counter that gets incremented every time a mailbox is created.

c8706aa919a4.title: rfc>9051
c8706aa919a4.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
c8706aa919a4.sentence: The next unique identifier value is the predicted value that will be assigned to a new message in the mailbox.

386d55695085.title: rfc>9051
386d55695085.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
386d55695085.sentence: First, the next unique identifier value MUST NOT change unless new messages are added to the mailbox; and second, the next unique identifier value MUST change whenever new messages are added to the mailbox, even if those new messages are subsequently expunged.

1519b4395ef4.title: rfc>9051
1519b4395ef4.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
1519b4395ef4.sentence: | Note: The next unique identifier value is intended to provide a | means for a client to determine whether any messages have been | delivered to the mailbox since the previous time it checked | this value. It is not intended to provide any guarantee that | any message will have this unique identifier. A client can | only assume, at the time that it obtains the next unique | identifier value, that messages arriving after that time will | have a UID greater than or equal to that value.

1276fa1ac8db.title: rfc>9051
1276fa1ac8db.section: 2. Protocol Overview > 2.3. Message Attributes > 2.3.1. Message Numbers > 2.3.1.1. Unique Identifier (UID) Message Attribute
1276fa1ac8db.sentence: - The combination of mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY, and UID must refer to a single, immutable (or expunged) message on that server forever.

934b3499ef9b.title: rfc>9051
